_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: I think Exo One starts off strong, but cannot quite find its way in the latter half in terms of structure and progression. The player is introduced to challenges that merely hamper the flow-state and don't do much for the story. In fact, I did not connect with the game's story, at all, but I still enjoyed the game's overall atmosphere. The game is quite short, so it does not overstay its welcome in the latter half and invites players to come back for another play-through. - I did have a good time with this.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface, Exo One is what you'd get if you combined Marble Madness with the 1990's movie Contact. The game play mixes the elements of gravity and gliding while you explore alien worlds. Through exploration the player gradually uncovers clues as to the origins of the craft/probe/metal thing you are controlling through light story-telling text and flashbacks. The end result is very soothing with a few gliding challenges thrown in here and there. I was able to complete Exo One is a little over 2 hours.On a different note, I couldn't have come across this title at a better time. I recently lost my Mother last week. She died youngish at the age of 62 (also on her birthday). In my mourning her I have contemplated many things. What did she mean to me, and I to her? Does she live on in an afterlife, or is her essence imbued within inanimate objects, or Both?? Is entropy just a spiral into oblivion, or a transitioning process into something grander? What is my role on this planet, the Galaxy, the Universe, this Dimension? Playing Exo One has provided me a brief but appreciated reprieve from these thoughts. As I traversed icy mountains and soared through dense clouds towards distant beacons of light, I experienced a sense of grandness, but also smallness.All in all, Exo One was a fantastic experience for me, and I highly recommend that if you enjoy games like Abzu or Journey, add this to your playlist.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: 7 / 10A friend of mine gave this to me as an early Christmas present, so I quickly played it from start to finish. It just about met my expectations, I knew that the gameplay is going to feel limited, but the experience is pretty decent if you want to chill out for a few hours. Very fast and ethereal. The game could've been expanded more with more variety of levels and puzzle elements because you're just flying around. Also found the controls of camera quite awkward at times, especially at the level where you are bouncing between asteroids orbiting a sun. And although the graphics aren't up to standard compared to modern games, it is pretty and colourful. Not an amazing game, but good ideas and I quite enjoyed it overall today.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible! Stunning visuals, immersive sound design & music - the most basic controls yet delivers the most satisfying experience any explorer of the cosmos could want. Light story delivers just enough context to keep you interested.If you're looking for a break from No Man's Sky this will scratch that itch until the next update/expedition.Really looking forward to what this team brings next and I won't be mad if it's more of this!
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very 2001esque, and I mean Kubrick's movie, not the year. Trouble is, I adore or at the very least respect every single Kubrick's movie starting with Dr. Strangelove, but 2001 is the sole exception.Exo One certainly does some things right, maybe even outstandingly so. It's pretty, and that's an understatement; I haven't felt a genuine urge to make a bunch of screenshots in a while, so props for reigniting that. And moving around feels absolutely on point.But then we have the level design, which is problematic no matter how I think about it. The levels are pretty damn big, yet empty; I get that plenty of space is needed for the movement system to truly shine, yet I feel they could've been safely made smaller after all.There's clearly a story somewhere in there, but the way it's presented is not something I appreciate. Cutscenes of sorts between level transitions? Okay, fine, I can live with those. Flashing images at me out of the blue while I'm moving somewhere, admiring the landscape, though? Who thought this was a good idea? I think I'd easily take good old audio logs over that, as trite as they are.And speaking of audio, sound design is at least good enough, music is great, but "voice acting" is grating. It's not actual voice acting, sure, and I get that it's meant to be all jumbled, but the end result is more irritating and annoying than unsettling or whatever it was meant to be.Also, good lord, it sure can be bright and flashy (literally). Overly so. I don't have any medical conditions that make such things impossible to safely bear, and yet I still feel they were excessive.In the end, I think Exo One was awfully close to hitting the mark, and hitting it hard, but it got waylaid at some point. Or maybe (and more likely), the two of us were just travelling to different places, and this is where my path takes me elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: Here's the thing. It's a dope looking game, I can't deny that. But, upon first opening the game, I was confused about what was happening. The story is difficult to follow. All you're doing is flying around as a magic space ball that can glide. Every time you land on a new planet, it's a straight shot to a giant blue laser that takes you to the next planet. _childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: Much more boring than I thought it would be, unfortunately.  There's just not enough going on.  Most walking simulators at least have an engaging narrative to compel you to go forward and explore.  This one doesn't.  The controls/gameplay looked like it would be interesting, but it isn't.  Traversal feels surprisingly slow and it feels like I'm waiting most of the time.  The planets are very empty and probably procedurally generated.  The music is nice but if you've heard Sigur Ros, you've heard it before--and I didn't buy the game for music.  Underwhelming across the board, and arguably pretentious.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: FANTASTIC and utterly different exploration game. There's no conflict, no "combat", just an amazing and unique experience you won't find anywhere else. The environments are *gorgeous* and the feeling of being on another world is spot-on. The surrealistic visuals make the whole game look like a highly-polished work of '70s space art. An overarching story is delivered in little bits and pieces, and is heavily inspired by Contact and classic sci-fi - it's simple but adds a nice element of flavor and world-building. Soaking in the atmosphere of each world is its own reward, but if you play it through and get everything, you won't be disappointed.Short game, but it REPSECTS YOUR TIME, which is something I greatly appreciate. And you can always go back & play it again.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: If the budget for this game was increased by like, 10 more dollars it would be amazing. 50% of the time, the game looks absolutely gorgeous. The other 50%, you see water and you realize that it's just a very good asset flip.The traversal system is very fun. But, the game is 2 hours long and gets close to overstaying its welcome. The only thing here is the traversal system, and there is only one attempt to shake things up. There is a narrative, but it doesn't matter.  It's a good two hour experience, but that's about it. Since it's only two hours, its worth it if the price isn't a barrier.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: Almost every aspect of Exo One is either frustrating or not polished enough.What some call a "meditative" game, for me, was more of a mess.First of all, the main aspect of the game - the ship you fly - feels clunky.The game expects you to aim the ship into specific spots with specific timing to gain momentum, but at the same time makes this extremely difficult, by restricting your manoeuvrability, limiting your gliding time, inverting the colours, hiding the ship etc.Maybe after some time you can get used to it, but after 45 minutes it didn't get much better and the whole game is 2 hours long.(BTW Steam refund is valid up to exactly 2 hours hmmmmmm)And this isn't the problem of me just being bad. I got some achievements for high speeds that only 6% of players got.So I'm guessing that the other 94% were struggling even more than me.Long story short - the ship just doesn't feel good.So that's just the controls, but the art-direction is also bad.When you gain a specific amount of speed, the ship releases a fart cloud for some reason, which completely covers it and you don't know where you're going.During this, you can just bump into a cube coming out of the earth, losing all your speed.No idea why this is a thing.When you gain even more speed, all the colours in the game start changing. They are either inverted or go into "rainbow mode" and change every 3 seconds.During this, you can't see much and the game looks awful.Again, I have no idea why this is a thing.Is it supposed to be a reward for reaching high speeds? Cause I feel like I'm being punished.I think the developers just thought that the game would feel too simplistic without it?The sound quality ranges from pretty good to just horrible, with some sounds resembling recordings through a copper wire.If this is intended, then I have no idea why they would do it like this.Some textures and planets are great, while others look like they are from Minecraft.Lava looks like some fluorescent liquid from a glowstick, water looks unnatural and geysers/volcanoes push out square-shaped smoke.This includes volumetric fog, with clouds letting smoke behind them completely pass through. You can fly into a cloud, and the whole world is obstructed from view, except for smoke coming from meteors that are 20 kms behind the clouds.And all of this was in 4K ultra settings. Overall, this feels like a great demo for a work-in-progress game.But the game is fully released and it's been on Steam for over 2 years.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: Simultaneously unique and technically impressive, this short and sometimes weird adventure is definitely one to try. Visuals are gorgeous, and often feel so inventive, I'd almost forget how much of the areas is procedurally generated. Similarly, the sound design follows through with quite enough musical variation and strong work with the non musical ambiance. There is some kind of story, but its content remains mostly unclear (I believe intentionally), which never felt problematic as it seems to exist more to give some dark, foreign, sci-fi vibe, than to act as the centerpiece of the experience. Good news: it all works perfectly.Controls are fresh and simple enough to be understood regardless of the lack of hand-holding. On that matter, the tutorial is very basic, the controls being swiftly presented with texts and icons without a lot of explanation at the beginning of the game. The more in-depth intricacies, like how to break the sound barrier for a long time or to gain continuous speed in more difficult terrain, is left to the player to discover. Without any loss condition, this doesn't feel too big of a challenge, and the rewards come quickly as you blast through the sky, water, electrical clouds, even space. Really cool feeling. Also, considering the nature of the levels and some of the effects, the whole experience runs surprisingly well even at ultra settings across the board.There is some replayability considering the openness of the controls and the extremely gigantic levels configurations, supported mainly in the form of a timer, coupled with related achievements (beating the whole game under certain times), as well as some other achievements that manage well enough to make me want to explore the levels and mechanics a bit more. I'm surprised there aren't similar timers level by level (unless I missed something?), but that's not a problem per say.The only serious issue I can easily imagine many having with the game is its relatively short length (I finished the whole thing on my first try in under 2 hours). That being said, there's just nothing like it, and frankly, it's just such an amazing experience that I wouldn't care, even at full price. In fact, for an optimal experience, I'd strongly recommend playing the full game in one sitting, really just like a movie.All in all, I wholeheartedly recommend this game!10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: I think there's something quite curious about this game that made me really invested in it despite the short playthrough. There's a satisfaction of just rolling or gliding freely around different planets while building speed and momentum. The visuals are excellent and successfully makes the environment immersive. Some sequences are speedy and breathtaking while some have more gloomy and eerie feel to it. The water planets were really nice and reminded me of that part in interstellar.The story clearly takes a back seat to the experience but it would be nice to expand on it more rather than just leaving vague shards and flashbacks. The sound design is satisfactory but maybe the music needs more work to compliment the whole experience.Overall, it's a good game but maybe get it on discount. _childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like a walking simulator but replace walking with rolling and gliding. In Exo One you play as a shiny metal ball that can do the former. The game play is simplistic and can be summed up as getting from point A to point B and picking up a power up if you're willing to go out of your way.Thing's I'm pretty sure you'll hate about this game:- Repetitive scenery, each level is practically the same, which is a shame.- Repetitive game play, the previous bullet point kind of contributes to this.- How long and boring it'll get for you to finish a single level.- This game is short (this might be a good or bad thing), I beat it in 3 hours.- One mechanic in the game is wind gusts that messes with your rhythm as you navigate your way across the landscape.- The story, or lack thereof.Thing I'm pretty sure you'll like about this game:- It's a physics game that's done right.- Rolling and gliding yourself across the landscape is fun, but see 1st bullet point in the "Things you'll hate ... " section.So yeah, that's Exo One for you. IMO wait for a sale on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Exo One is certainly a pretty game, and the soundtrack is very good - but what kills it is the janky, unintuitive control method for your ball, which isn't explained well enough at the start at all. There was something about pressing the mouse button to increase gravity and then releasing it to reduce it, but how and why that should increase your speed isn't clear (and doing what it suggests doesn't seem to have much effect either, and there's no speedometer to track how fast you're going anyway). Also your glide is very limited and runs out far too quickly (even when you pick up a power up that supposedly gives you indefinite glide, it runs out a few seconds later). It was OK on the first few levels where you're swooping over wide open spaces and have lots of ways to pick up speed but then when you get to the jungle planet things are more constricted, and then the Coronides level just kills any enjoyment as all you seem to do is orbit asteroids with no discernible way to go to the next one (maybe there is if you fully understand the movement system, but if not you're just screwed), and that's where I gave up - which is a shame really. Some kind of practice level or a decent tutorial level that actually explains things beyond the meagre explanation at the start would have saved this game for me. I got it on sale and for the first few levels the experience was fun at least, and the soundtrack is good. But I wouldn't get this for full price.

_childDocuments_.review: ✅ Stunning atmosphere and visuals✅ High replayability if you’re looking for something relaxing✅ Kubrick style space atmosphere✅ Immersive sound design❌ Most maps work well, but a few can feel rather slow. As is evident by the trailer, you play the game in control of a morphing frisbee-ball machine. Though there’s a small amount of lore explanation, much like everything in the game your imagination does most of the hard lifting, which I love. The controls are simple and yet provide so much movement and freedom. Who knew you could have so much fun using only gravity? The game teaches you these controls but doesn’t hold your hand on how to best utilize them, you can truly pioneer your own movement. Simple mechanics to achieve complex tasks are as far as I’m concerned the pinnacle of game design.Even if I wanted to spoil the story for you, it would simply be impossible, all the hints you get are through gargled messages and obfuscated images. Yet even though the story might as well be sent via dial-up internet, it provides an atmosphere I haven’t experienced in many games. You truly have no idea and are trying to piece together the world you are in by observation, not by exposition. Though it could be called lazy game design, I feel this has a far greater impact than if it were properly explainedThough from the store page the game looks good it doesn’t even nearly do it enough justice, the game simply looks stunning. It may not be photoreal but the look it has really tickles every nerve I have. The very last level in the game made me say wow out loud. I have seen great forests, tall mountains, and sparkling caves yet the visual of this level is something I regard as a profound experience. Only when moving slow does it start to look slightly less sparkling, which is why the slow levels looked a lot duller. The developer has added a new test mode allowing you to skip to any level in the game, which means you don't have to go through every time and you can relax on your favorite levels after you've completed the game.At the time of writing Exo One is 15,99 on steam, for the number of hours it offers that’s not a great deal but for the experience I will say it’s certainly worth it. Especially if the developer adds a more relaxed mode where you can play every level independently. It would add the replayability to just kick back and soar through glistening skies while listening to some smooth jazz, and that experience is priceless.Exo One while visually marvelous isn’t a very intense game since there’s not a lot of game objects, which means most computers should be able to run it, I certainly had no issue doing so on my GTX 1080, Ryzen 7 2700 and 32 Gigs of ram.Exo One is a fantastic experience which is truly and utterly unique, if the developer added more options for replayability, I’d love this game to bits. If effortlessly gliding through vast and beautiful skies sounds like something you could enjoy from time to time, this might be the game for you. It’s not terribly long so if it turns out you don’t enjoy pure bliss you can always return it halfway through, but I doubt that will be necessary.

_childDocuments_.review: If I were to encapsulate my thoughts on Exo One in two words, it'd be 'missed potential' because what starts with a game all about efficient movement and speed had the potential to expand on these mechanics in a variety of fun ways—except it doesn't, leading me to want a bit more after the credits roll. Exo One is a game that delivers at the end of the day, but only just.Exo One has a story, but it's a thin backdrop (granted, my understanding of the story is muddy even after finishing the game): There's an expedition to Jupiter that goes disastrously, resulting in the astronauts' deaths. A probe (controlled by the player) is supposedly sent out to investigate how to bring the astronauts back, going across distant planets in another galaxy and searching for a means. Snippets of the plot are told via voice-over which only adds to some of the confusion; there's some implication that the probe you control is either controlled by a person also travelling to these other galaxies, or that the probe is sentient?It isn't a criticism since the story isn't necessary for Exo One's enjoyment; just how it's presented comes across as artsy. If anything, the flashes of imagery that occasionally pop up to remind you about the lost crew and Jupiter would be comical if not for how sudden and jarring they are.The main appeal of Exo One is its gameplay, as the spherical probe has few mechanics but makes for immense satisfaction once mastered. The probe can glide, dive and double jump - Bare basics, yes, but linking these inputs together can bring incredible speed and height when traversing the alien worlds. There's no benefit to achieving incredible velocity other than letting you get around faster, yet the first planet you start on makes for an excellent case in going as swiftly as possible; when you clear the clouds for the first time and get that beautifully picturesque view? Whoof. Exo One is great if you like taking frequent screenshots, as excluding close-up textures, the visuals are something else regarding the splendour and lighting.Using downward slopes to build up momentum then launching off a ramp, using updrafts and lightning to ascend and recharge the probe to continue gliding - It's all in service to reach a teleporter to progress to the next level, though there isn't much that stops you from goofing around. While I ran into two instances of invisible walls, the maps are big, open-ended and affords you plenty of time to practice movement techniques.Each planet throws in a gimmick, like a water planet where gliding lets the probe skip across the surface or booster gates that fire the probe off like a bullet. Not all planets are fun, however, as one saps most of your abilities while the other has powerful gusts blowing against your path. This leads to my biggest issue with Exo One: it isn't interested in expanding upon the probe in its gamified aspects. There are upgrades to pick up in each level, but as far as I could tell, they only improve upon the probe's energy capacity for extended gliding, yet the improvements were nominal at best. I had hoped there would be other upgrades, like adding more jumps when in midair and a turbo dash to regain speed after coming to a stop - Ultimately, the upgrades went from something to actively gun for to simply regarding them as items for the achievement checklist.I finished Exo One in under two and a half hours, not including going for every upgrade and hunting for achievements. It's ultimately difficult to recommend Exo One, as its storytelling is flaccid and pursuing upgrades isn't terribly fulfilling. However, the replay value in getting faster, more efficient times or just mastering the controls in general to fly across levels is incredibly satisfying, so if excellent visuals and good game feel are up your alley, then these criticisms won't keep you from enjoying Exo One for a few evenings.

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid title that does exactly what it sets out to do. Exo One remembers what a lot of exploration games tend to forget - if the gameplay revolves entirely around moving from point to point, that movement needs to be satisfying and engaging. A lot of games use player movement as a means to an end, so it's very refreshing to have a game where it's actually fun in-and-of itself. It's also an absolutely gorgeous game, and the planetary vistas combine with delicious sound design to produce a really satisfying atmosphere. The game captures the beautiful desolation of space perfectly, and it does so without saying a single word. It's the sort of vibe I really adore in space games, and Exo One hits it home like no other game I've played.I think the story is a bit weak, though? I think the game doesn't know whether it's metaphoric or not, itself. It reveals too much information too early to be mysterious, but too little information to be captivating. It has interesting moments, but it ultimately feels like it was something thought of after the game was made as a justification. Seeing as it's a game about exploration, it also feels weird that most of the plot is more or less delivered straight to you after every level - you don't have to seek the story out to understand it, which is fine if you like a straight narrative, but it doesn't feel like you're uncovering a plot. It feels more like you're playing a fun non-traditional vehicle game that occasionally stops for a minute to deliver some obligatory exposition, and then you go back to the rover funtimes. It's also a shame, because the premise and general outline of the story feels really promising, and there's a ton of thematic mileage you could get out of it, it's just delivered in a way that doesn't really emotionally resonate.Overall, despite the story that I genuinely wish could've been better, I absolutely enjoyed my time with this. It's a pretty short game, but well worth it if you want to chill out for a little while breaking the sound barrier.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. Absolutely beautiful, and in my opinion, worth the relatively small price. With that being said, it is not for everyone. The replay value is probably slim for most players, but the potential for future patches and speedrunning is huge. Even so, the game as is, in my opinion was fantastic. It had a small "storyline" with a satisfying and euphoric ending, and again, the visuals and gameplay mechanics are so good from an indy developer. It's a 3GB short game that is satisfying to play, but it shows just how amazing games full size games can be with effort. I don't leave reviews often, and I am a picky gamer. I try most AAA titles and very few impress. This kickstarter success story really reinvigorated my sense of satisfaction and hope for gaming. P.S. (If even possible, a VR port would be sick)

_childDocuments_.review: 2001: Space Odyssey meets Flight of the Navigator. A true breath of fresh air in the gaming world! Have had this game on my wish list for over a year, and was excited to finally see it available. Did not disappoint one bit.A bit short as far as most games go, but that doesn't mean it's lacking. As an experience, it is top notch. Has  surreal, some time eerie, unique environments, while maintaining a very relaxed chill vibe, except for when I dove into the depths of Nautica... got slight anxiety until I came back to the surface. lolAs of writing this I would give it a 4.5 out of 5, with the reason being I see some room for a little improvement. Not much, just some polishing. Such as having a type of "Free play" mode, where you can play certain stages individually after you've unlocked them/played them once, instead of having to play all the way to the story again to play a certain level. I like how the game keeps track of the time it took to complete, and think it would be cool if there were some sort of history or record to keep track of the times you've played, and how long it took to complete. So, ideally, from my pov, there would be Story mode, which is what it is now, along with a Free Play, then a Time Trial mode that actually shows the timer where we can race against the clock, either through the whole story, or just individual levels.

_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic experience, I've been waiting for over a year for this game and I feel as if it's been completely worth it.I can forgive the shortness of it, since this has been in development for 5-6 years by a single man and a helper, for one guy there's some absolutely INSANE visuals, this meets the bar easily of what VFX should be possible in that timeframe.It's quite a short game, but the visuals & gameplay make me feel like few games have ever made me feel.I beat it in 2.4 hours, but it certainly didn't feel like the journey was cut short. You can spend a lot more time in this game, if you just soar the skies as if it were a sandbox, there's no time limit as far as I know.It's practically like a movie with the visuals, the atmosphere pulls you in so you don't get off the game until its finished.The gameplay is dynamic enough where you can progress through any path. Though the levels are linear, and if you go too far to the left or right the game will put you back on path. Though this only happens if you deliberately try to break off the path, there's still tons of leniency.The main point of replayability is shortening your times, and clearing all of the achievements for certain tasks like "Break the sound barrier and hold faster than sound speed for more than two seconds on X planet".It's certainly a game I'm expecting to pick up again when I've forgotten about it, or just want to soar through some of the nicest clouds & landscape I've ever seen.My favorite level has to be the really cool If the developer were to ever make new content in this game, (and I understand it would be a long while from now, don't underestimate developer schedules.) I'd fully recommend trying to build a sandbox level, or an endless mode with procedurally generated levels (nothing complex, just some tiles so it's not nonsense) where you'd have to collect power orbs to not game over from power loss.This is fully worth it, developer deserves the money from this masterwork.

_childDocuments_.review: Proof that a simple concept done right can be more fun than a game that has 200 times more money behind it in many cases.You are a little black marble. A marble that moves with moon gravity, regardless of the location. You can also press a button and instantly increase your gravity by 10x that of earth. And this game has physics, so have fun with that as you travel across various planets, into giant clouds, oceans of water, towards some of the most terrifying celestial phenomenon known to exist, etc. I don't know if its actually possible to "die" in this game. You can also turn into a disk, an gently weave through the clouds for a few moments, before dive bombing, breaking the sound barrier in the process, and accelerating yourself forward so fast the entire world inverts color for a bit (no seriously, this can happen).Its amazing to look at, has a great soundtrack, and its extremely fun in spite of its simplicity. _childDocuments_.review: I think you'll see a lot of "on the fence" reviews for Exo One.  Choosing thumbs up or down is really hard here.  Let me start by explaining what it is: a short physics-based walking simulator.  Except instead of walk you roll and glide, which I'll be the first to admit is a huge step up for the genre.  Still, while I don't think Exo One is bad or anything, it's just not much at all.  I gave it a shot for the visuals and I suppose I got what I expected out of it, but it has a pretty bad case of indie-game-itis.  In short, there's very little gameplay and it refuses to have a story while simultaneously pretending like it totally has a story.  Oh my, what *exactly* happened in this game?  What's the meaning behind exploding into a universe after entering a black hole?  Did we go back in time and change history?  DID WE ACTUALLY DIE!?!  So, just for the writer's sake: no one cares.  We can't care about characters we don't know, we can't get invested in a plot we don't understand.  It seems like it's here because that's just what walking simulators have to have, loose scraps of a plot that if assembled would have trouble filling a page.Now, to be fair to the game, and as other people have seemed to agree, what plot do you even give a game like this?  Still, I would've rather they tossed the narrative in the bin and tacked a few more levels onto the game since, ultimately, exploring these alien worlds and trying to "master" the controls is the highlight.  It does a decent job conveying information to the player without having to explain anything and yeah, that's a difficult thing to get right.  The game has great conveyance.  Unfortunately for that, the game ends just after it ran out of ideas.  I know more could be done with these mechanics, but this is about as much as can be done with this game.  And so, thumbs down.  While I think this is interesting to talk about, I couldn't really tell someone, "Oh, you need to play this."  You'd get the same experience watching the trailer.  I don't regret spending money or time on it, but unless you fancy yourself a patron of the arts, you aren't going to get much out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: First heard of this game from a small video essay youtuber called The Cursed Judge. The topic was about games with balls (featuring games like super monkey ball. I have no idea how this could be interpreted differently) and this was the last game mentioned in that video. I found it strange that while you do control a 'ball' in this game like the others, it felt weird to feature this game along the other games showcased. One day I saw this game for sale on steam for a reasonable price and figured I'd try the game for myself.Generally this game consists of shifting the gravity of the ball to travel to the magnet beam and be launched to the next planet. Not sure if I explained that correctly but it's quite fun to master the mechanics. Each planet features a different environment in which you will learn and apply different mechanics. Sometimes worlds have lots of updraft for flying, some feature lots of water, some are cramped in space, and some give you all the space you want. The game's story was quite lost on me, but since the game is around 2 hours to beat I was able to enjoy it for the gameplay.Overall if you like games like Journey, Flower, and Abzu, this game gives a similar vibe and is comparable to those games. I'd recommend this game for those who also enjoyed the games mentioned.

_childDocuments_.review: This is like Solaris, the game. At least some of the maps look like how I pictured Solaris to be. The game is fairly simple: you pilot a spherical spacecraft and essentially have to navigate from point A to point B on a given planet. You can roll or fly. There are various ways to "slingshot" yourself so you can fly farther and faster. The game was clearly designed for speed running in mind as there are various gates that can blast your ship through the air. There is no timer or really any objectives, so you definitely don't have to speed run. The planets are immeasurably large. You can't really tell where they begin or end. I didn't spend much time veering off into the horizon so I'm not sure if there are invisible walls, or if they procedurally generate a never ending landscape. Bottom line, the game is pretty a pretty chill vibe and something you can sit down and just relax to while playing. The landscapes are often times awe inspiring. There is a basic story that actually ends up being fairly poignant, but this isn't narrative driven at all. It is pretty short at around 4 hours, but I think the overall experience makes up for it. This is definitely a game that begs for expansions, and would be truly amazing if they ever allow for community designed worlds. The possibilities are endless.

_childDocuments_.review: Whether you're looking for a chill "Space Walking Sim" or a competitive speedrun challenge - Exo One has you covered. It's a very unique and stylish game, that you can finish in less than three hours but also one that may last you for a long time after getting all achievements. However, it's not a game that I would recommend to everyone. If you're not willing to spend some time learning the controls, it will be a frustrating experience.If you expect to breeze through the levels as shown in the trailers on your first playthrough, you will be sad. It was only towards the final third of the game that I started feeling confident with the controls.When I was done with my first playthrough, I wanted to start another one immediately so I could apply what I had learned so far.For these reasons the game is very rewarding if you stick with it. Getting better at this game is a lot of fun and being able to beat it in as little time as possible is the ultimate goal.The music is utterly fantastic with warm, welcoming guitar tones right from the start and supersweet ambient tracks throughout the game. The overall sound design can only be described as fantastic.Worth the full price for me, and certainly worth taking a look at during sale.

Sure you want to go as fast as possible and watch the level scream past in a blur of crazy colours and cool sound design, because boy is it satisfying, but the visuals and scenery deserve proper appreciation as well. The game encourages, and deserves, multiple playthroughs because there are definitely some places and mechanics you might miss the first time through. Maybe it was because you hadn't mastered the controls, or that you missed an entire area of the map due to the blinding urge to go faster but I found myself enjoying the second time through more than the first. _childDocuments_.review: "Experience the essence of freedom"- me"Frisbee simulator"- moi+In all seriousness, this game is a relaxing and almost meditative experience. The art direction is very impressive and the audio design/music are a great enhancer of the overall experience. The arrival on each planet triggered my curiosity on what would happen next. Using gravity to slingshot from asteroid to asteroid was incredibly fun. I would have loved to do this in later levels too.-I would like to point out that some elements of the visual presentation are somewhat lacking in quality. But I understand that the sheer amount of work for a single person is too great to refine everything. There is one planet, I won't spoil, is quite underwhelming and feels somewhat displaced (due to narrative) in gameplay between the others.The narrative was simple and straightforward. I found myself more engaged with the visual presentation and gameplay.The time to finish the game compared to the price is barely justified, although it should never be more expensive than 16 euros. If you doubt the value, wait for a possible sale. Conclusion:Exo One is a mesmerizing game with fascinating music and sounds to immerse the player. I would recommend this to people who love to empty their heads and relax a bit. Also space lovers, you would want to play this! To the dev: create longevity by adding a roaming mode or a more fancy sandbox mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: An indie with an interesting idea, that doesn't manage to carry it's momentum.Exo One is a relaxing movement based game. The mechanics are fun to learn and try out.The problem arises when you realize, that all the core mechanics are given to you in the first level. It simply doesn't expand in any way in the following 2 hours of gameplay. The developers tried to make up for this by introducing some unique mechanics to the levels themself, but these are simply not strong enough to keep interest high.Each level is, while being very large at first sight, very linear. You see a goal in the distance and have only minimal incentive to stray from your path. THe proceduralness of the landscape doesn't help that either.There is some lore you get after completing each level, but I found it to be more confusing than anything else. If theres some deeper meaning behind it the game didn't manage to get me hooked so I could analyse it more deeply.To conclude - Exo One is very fun to expirement in the first 30mins or so, but really drags on after that. THe experience is still pretty unique so I wasn't sad about playing it, but I wouldn't buy a dlc aswell. I think the game really missed out by not introducing more mechanics over the levels.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: I need more. This sort of physics based locomotion is exactly the kind of thing that make games like Tribes, Portal and Spider-Man 2 (2004) so damn addictive. Easy to learn, but difficult to master. Unfortunately there isn't much  to Exo One. You can't crash and the levels are mostly flat. A fleshed out game, with huge canyons, caves, difficult to reach areas, pitfalls and death traps would make using the glide and roll flight mechanics exceedingly satisfying. Some actual danger and challenging paths would have made this a proper game that if done right could be as engaging and interesting as the Portal games. Despite what I wish the game was, it's still pretty fun with some really nice visuals and I enjoyed the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: The haunting visions/distortions are among the many innovative stylish gems of this game. A very exhilarating surreal game. Even though it gets a little tired out/boring throughout.. the duration of the game is very much appropriate and saves it a lot. it is still VERY enjoyable, amazing, and fresh. Completely worth it. Buy this game now.

If that's what you are into this is the game for you, but don't expect much more from it. + Nice graphics+ Satisfying mechanics+ Enjoyable soundtrack- Gets repetitive quick- Not really a very interesting storyline

_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: This game is 2001: Space Odyssey and a mobile game Last Voyage by Semidome smashed together, and I'm not complaining.If you are entranced by ideas such as cosmos, higher knowledge/power in cosmos that might be undiscovered yet, our place in infinite universe and so on, this game is for you. It is a short, 2hr. EXPERIENCE (and not a story, even though there is some) where you fly around on different planets with different environments - massive clouds, Solaris-type oceans, deserts with forgotten pyramids, active volcanoes, e.t. It's truly a visual feast - beautiful and immersive. There're two things I'd like to point out as nitpicks: 1) I wish soundtrack was more prominent and a bit more memorable. Yes, ambiance music can be memorable, but here it's just pretty background noise. 2) On some planets it was kinda obvious that they didn't have as much money as their ambitions required to cope with the beauty and scale of the environment. Clouds and oceans are Amazing but when it comes to little objects such as trees, or details on big objects, an "indie-game" feeling creeps in.Otherwise, its' a very, very high quality game. Just know what you are getting into - a 2hr visual experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A game with a pretty simple premise: get to the end of each level. However the end of the level is pretty damn far away. You are a ball, and can roll forward like a ball - but that's not all. Press the right trigger to turn gravity to max and become really heavy, release again to become really light. Sounds kind of pointless at first, until you realise that when you're rolling down an incline, turning the gravity up lets you gain momentum really quickly, momentum you retain when you release the trigger and become light again. You can use this to launch yourself off of terrain like a rocket. Then you can hold the left trigger to turn into a disc and glide aerodynamically through the air. Now we're talking - even if you can only sustain frisbee mode for a short while at a time (which you can extend by grabbing collectibles from each stage.) Add to that using level features like wind currents, clouds and boosters you can start flying around the level at Mach 100 Gorillion once you get a good roll going.The graphics are pretty basic tech-wise but are really striking anyway, especially when you're blasting through it at lightspeed. Each level has its own gimmicks and aesthetic to make each unique, plus fittingly ambient music.The game also has a story that's delivered pretty vaguely and dare I say a bit pretentiously, in my opinion, though maybe you'll enjoy it more than I did. It's also very short, though I think the length is just right for the kind of game this is. Probably has good reply value if speedrunning is your thing. Overall, I quite enjoyed Exo One, 7.5/10, would destroy the sound barrier using gravity and conveniently placed inclines again.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: A chill & relaxing atmospheric game where flying through the clouds just feels so satisfying!The controls are easy to learn, the landscapes look great, the soundtrack is very calming, and you really do get a sense of distance from each of the planets. Speaking of planets, there was only one that didn't flow as well as the others, but I enjoyed them all.Unfortunately I experienced a lot of random crashes and black screens which was extremely frustrating. Tried reinstalling the game, steam, and updating all my drivers to no avail. I couldn't even manage a normal playthrough without it crashing on me. 😒Despite the issues I had, it's a fantastic game definitely worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: I do not think Exo One is a bad game.But, it's one of those games that's hard to recommend. As in, if people asked me is it good... I'd say it depends.TIMEThis game is, first and foremost, an experience... and a very short one at that. Around 2h on my first play-through. That's very short and I got around 19/28 achievements from it.LORE/STORYThere is very little to comprehend here in the experience, as in there's meaning but more of a big picture you are trying to grasp, and determine your own interpretation at the very end.GAMEPLAYThe games mechanics, and/or physics rather, are sometimes excellent and sometimes pulled down by jarring playing field with lack of "oumphe" to make the "speed" constant and consistant, I felt. ART DIRECTIONIf some shots are very nice to take beautiful screengrabs many left me unphased as too few of them are fulfilling. You will be seeing mostly teared textures on the ground to catapult yourself from, and skip most "money shots", let's say, trying to figure out where to find a decent slope or mount than appreciate the full-on beauty experience.SOUND/MUSICA big part of the enjoyment for Exo One lies in its immersion, sounds and feeling of speed. There is a lot of satisfaction to get here from gameplay tied to the sounds; hitting the sound barrier is a very enjoyable feeling. Alas, many sounds are you falling on the ground, crawling on slopes, hitting walls you don't want to, and those sounds get really repetitive and annoying. There's a lack of variants in the sound library here, as you will quickly notice it's the same sound back used over and over everywhere. Music is, very underwhelming, it's ambience with eerie melodies, it was not my jam.REPLAYABILITYIt's "OK-ish", but if you are an achiever you are into replaying constantly levels to break sound barrier speeds or go as high as you can and finish the game under 60 minutes. Enjoy!PERFORMANCEOn a good rig here:4K 43" MonitorAMD RX6800XTAMD RYZEN 5950X128GB DDR4 3600Mhz980Pro Samsung 2tb NVME DriveHad excellent FPS (Over 240 fps on FSR 1440p upscale, 160 at 4K) but had many frame cutting probably due to shader compilings. That really marred my whole experience. Some levels were perfect, but more than half had constant lags spikes and that was very frustrating.Might not be optimised for recent AMD Cards... Beware.CONCLUSIONIt's a 3 devs project.If you are curious, i'd say give it a go, I'd recommend but only on sale and don't expect to squeeze a lot from it... sadly.As for me I did my playthrough, I'm done and I'll be uninstalling it.[EDIT] Few typos, syntax and verb corrections

_childDocuments_.review: Exo One is a breathtaking odyssey that transcends the boundaries of traditional gaming, immersing players in a mesmerizing interstellar experience that defies expectations and captivates the imagination. After embarking on a journey through time and space with Exo One, I can confidently say that this game is a true gem that deserves a spotlight in the world of indie gaming.From the moment you pilot the Exo One spacecraft and soar through alien landscapes, you are enveloped in a sense of wonder and awe that is rarely found in gaming. The game's visuals are a symphony of beauty and mystery, with otherworldly environments, dynamic weather effects, and surreal vistas that evoke a sense of cosmic grandeur and exploration.The gameplay mechanics of Exo One are a delicate balance of exhilarating flight, precise maneuvering, and gravity-defying traversal that make every moment in the Exo One spacecraft a thrilling experience. As you navigate through wormholes, glide over alien terrain, and harness the power of gravity to propel yourself through the cosmos, you are met with a sense of freedom and discovery that is truly unique.Beyond its stunning visuals and engaging gameplay, Exo One presents a narrative that is both enigmatic and thought-provoking, inviting players to contemplate the mysteries of the universe and their place within it. The game's minimalist storytelling approach leaves room for interpretation and introspection, adding a layer of depth and intrigue to the overall experience.Exo One is not just a game; it is a work of art that pushes the boundaries of interactive storytelling and visual design. Its seamless blend of exploration, flight mechanics, and atmospheric storytelling creates a harmonious and immersive experience that lingers in the mind long after the journey ends.In conclusion, Exo One is a masterpiece of indie game development that offers a transcendent and unforgettable journey through the cosmos. If you're looking for a game that challenges your perceptions, sparks your imagination, and transports you to new realms of possibility, look no further than Exo One - a stellar experience that showcases the beauty and wonder of the universe in all its glory.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: First I want to say that the art direction in this game is unique and for the developers first game it is a great start. The aestetic sense of the graphics themselves is well put together too. Here's why I stopped playing though. The controls are somewhat unintuitive and even after an hour I was having trouble with the gravity mechanic. This is coming from someone who really enjoyed Flower. I think there's potential but I feel like the controls need work. The intrusive static images that pop up mid gameplay for the story are really annoying and ruin the experience. There's an annoying overlay with crosses all over the screen all the time and makes the game feel cheap and pulls me out of the world I'm looking at. I bought the game to fly through these beautiful worlds so let me see them. The story and cutscenes are very forced and feel like they are superfluous. The game is pretty, if the game needs a story it should be more subtle or well executed. Why am I having the same image of the these astronauts shoved into my face over and over again with no context? If your story is good it will speak for itself, not force the player to engage with it. There are masterbatory references that come off like the game is more important than it is. Why is the planet named Sagan before I've even played a level or had an opportunity to understand the story? This game isn't Nier Automata, and there isn't a well written dialogue with a robot named Engles. The sound design switches between being pleasent and setting a mood in some scenes to being utterly jarring, repetitive, and ear grating. What is that awful sound playing on loop in the title screen when I'm trying to configure my settings? This game isn't Merzbow. Why are the ambient noises so repetitive in general in some sections? Why do some of the sound samples sound like they're balanced differently compared to others and why do some sound lower quality than others? This all detracts from the gamefeel significantly. The game is overpriced, it should be 5-10$ for what's on offer here. I'm sure a lot of hard work went into the physics engine and building of these massive worlds but the execution feels like an elongated tech demo with a story shoehorned in. A solid 5-6/10. I think the developers vision exceeded their grasp with this game but that doesn't mean it has to in the future and I look forward to what comes next from Exbleative.

_childDocuments_.review: My friend gifted me this game, and I immediately jumped in and played it.To be honest, the game starts out a bit slow, with some of the cooler stages being saved for later, which is an interesting choice to make as most games try to dazzle you in the first level. However, It makes finishing the game feel absolutely rewarding if you stick past the first planet or two and master the mechanics.The controls and movement mechanics takes a bit to understand. Well, no. Actually it's more that it's easy to learn but difficult to master, but there's a lot of joy to be found in figuring these things out, it really feels like *play*, that's probably the best way I can put it. There are many little subtleties in the mechanics that takes a bit of figuring out but doing so feels absolutely enjoyable. The levels are also designed in a way that very very gently guides you, but still rewards your for exploring and trying things- or even just fooling around. Not to mention, the worlds are vast. It does not fake the space and ensures you feel the scale of the different planets. There are a few bugs here and there (like your spaceship spinning like crazy, or some music issues) but none of them really ruins the experience (if anything, i thought the spaceship freewheeling like that when i make a funny jump was hilarious and adds some joy to the the overall melancholic mood just for a bit ^^)The art and sound direction is gorgeous, The clinks and clatter of your little spaceship rolling on different materials, the gentle whistle of your spaceship just gliding through the clouds. The sparse but  beautiful guitars plucking in the background at just the right times, and even the silence as you rise above stormy clouds to finally, finally, see the star it's orbiting, the art direction and sound design for this game is phenomenal and fills me with absolute awe.The story is a little sparse but effective and impactful, The story happens in small bits and pieces, in visual form, or little subtitled texts in a way that almost makes it optional for you to follow. But even if you're not following it or you don't quite understand, you'll most likely feel *something* at the end of the game even if you're not sure what it is. You can tell the game was made with a lot of heart, and I'm glad I got to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly anything after level 2 kinda sucks. The level design clashes with the mechanics, you have to constantly slow down, and there's not much of anything to explore. I don't know if it's an issue with the camera or the mechanics, but often it feels like a slope should or shouldn't speed you up, but then it does/doesn't. The water levels are absolutely boring, especially the first one. I can't imagine there is much replay value, unless you like getting a slightly faster time or the 6 or so nothing-burger collectibles. Game takes pretty much exactly 2 hours to finish, so it's like they just wanted to get the bare minimum out, I don't think $16 is worth such a small amount of content. The only cool section past level 2 is an area where your going between a bunch of asteroids, but even that feels half baked, the gravity doesn't have nice smooth transitions between bodies--just pop your now in the other gravity well. If you really want to play the game just get the prologue, its free and you get to play the only good part of the game--level 1. Though if you can snag this for like $5 it's probably worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted a game where I'd feel the exhilaration of flying a UFO at gravity-defying, breathtaking speeds.This is NOT that game.While real UFOs are anti-gravity based, this game is the polar opposite, namely that it is heavily bound and tied to gravity dragging you back down into the dirt like you already struggle with in your daily life.  The feeling of being so heavily bound like that is gut-wrenchingly awful.That's basically all you need to know: the core gameplay loop of this game feels terrible.The other thing I have to mention is the story-mechanic and/or art direction of the game. If you like edgy, un-nerving, amorphous story delivered to you in a 2001 Space Odyssey style where you have no idea what the #%$ is going on, then this is definitely the story/narrative for you.  If you dislike not knowing where you are or why as your gravity-bound marble sludges through terrain, then you either need to play far more than the 3 hours (Steam rounded my 2.9 hours down to 2 go figure) I've devoted in order to have even the slightest inkling of what's going on or you need to just give this game a pass.  Yes, I do know that somehow this awful UFO marble I'm "piloting" (I wouldn't call constantly falling into the dirt/water/lava piloting) is somehow connected to the fictitious NASA mission that I still know next-to-nothing about, but I can only tolerate the awful gameplay loop for so long before giving up on the fact that the game may never actually tell me what really happened or what this awful marble actually is and just chalk it up to something vague like "artistic license" or some other wishy-washy nonsense.I'm still going to play whenever I get the stomach for more UFO-crashing-marble-rolling just in the slightest chance that somehow at the end of the game you're rewarded for stomaching the nonsensical gameplay/art with a UFO that actually flies instead of this marble-brick they've given us.I'm not holding my breath though about the ending.  You've been warned.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game, though it's more of an experience. The movement is fantastic and the levels are some of the best you will see in a game today. It is fairly one-note, as there really aren't new mechanics introduced and the goal for each level remains largely the same. Not a huge problem since the core gameplay is so fluid, but it can leave you wanting more. The story is fairly vague and told sparingly, so it ends up being somewhat uninteresting despite having a neat premise.The biggest flaw of the game though is the length. My first playthrough, even when messing around, taking my time, and exploring, clocked in at 1 hour 40 minutes. I spent some additional time getting achievements and doing another run focused on speed, but it was still extremely short. There are no additional modes or even a level select, so replayability is entirely dependent on you finding extra things to do.It puts the game in a weird spot where it feels too highly polished and well-produced to have a lower price, but has too little play time to really justify the cost where it is. My best recommendation is to simply play the demo (Exo One: Prologue in the store) and consider if you feel it worth the price to have that same gameplay across different levels for under 2 hours. If not, just wait for a sale. If you're into games like Journey, Abzu, etc. it'll be one that you won't want to miss.

_childDocuments_.review: Been waiting for this one for a long time because its so unique and beautiful. Originally I was attracted to the movement in the game which is kind of like an inverse Tribes-- instead of jetting upwards to skate across abstract mountains and valleys you increase your mass and plummet into the curves in the landscape. it's a classic mechanic with a zen like beauty and freedom of expression spun a new way here. the levels change up the gravity and your perks so that none of them feel too samey, but dont expect game like level design here, its more of a two to three hour journey, kind of like those psychedelic pink floyd planetarium shows you might have visited before, and the accompanying music album is really nice. One thing to note is that the movement does take some time to learn and you wont be able to effortlessly fly through the maps at supersonic speed until probably after your first playthrough. it can be frustrating when you are still slow and end up hiking more than gliding but this also adds replay value and satisfaction once you learn how to maintain your speed and change form to fit the landscape. one thing i didn't expect from the game but was pleasantly surprised by was the strength of the narrative. it's told in bits and pieces as a flashback in a very oblique way such that you are left open to interpret how the events unfolded, but without spoiling you with my interpretation its heavy on tropes from Contact and 2001: A Space Odyssey and gives a great mood to the game. the narrative along with the landscapes really conjures the sublime and makes you feel a mix of awe and terror and the feeling that you're never going home again, but just onward into the unknown.i really don't want to give a wishlist of changes here since I view this more as a piece of art than a game but there were a few things I found kind of unpleasant along the way:theres one foresty map where the screenshake from the wind is very strong and kind of disorienting and it also plays very slow and clunky compared to the other maps. on its own i didnt like it but it did provide a good change of pace at least to keep things feeling fresh.one other thing is the overlaid lines on the screen which i think are meant to give the feeling that you are watching through a camera or scanner but the way they cover the screen makes them feel more like a watermark for copy protection or something which is vaguely annoying. maybe if the lines just in the center most part of the screen were removed and the others left it would feel less intrusive but its an artistic choice at the end of the day so I can't say if it would actually be better without it. you do have quite a bit of control over the video settings and control bindings so I give it an A for that. the performance might suffer on older systems. I played on pretty good recent hardware such that I was pulling 350-380 fps most of the time but for some reason moving the camera and some portions of the game felt choppier like i expected im not sure if there was some interference from the fullscreen mode or my gsync or something or maybe the screenshake and camera movement just made it feel that way but it was mostly a smooth and gorgeous experience on a recent pc with high refresh monitor. highly recommended if you enjoy shorter, artistic games you can play in one sitting with unique movement systems

_childDocuments_.review: This game immediately peaked my interest, and i don't regret a single penny spent. The landscapes are foreign, while also seeming very familiar to the planet we call home. Entire worlds covered with a never ending oceans, massive jungles, rolling hills and dunes, mountains to climb, and foreign structures to find. Gameplay never so much as skipped a frame, and felt incredibly smooth with the transitions between sphere and glide mode. It also took me just over 2 hours to complete the game one time around. But with so many achievements left to unlock, I can only imagine what wonders I must have missed, meaning that I have an excuse to play again. On top of all of that, the music was absolutely enchanting. If I'm not able to get this soundtrack on Spotify, I will be buying my first soundtrack from any game that I've ever played. Immerse yourself in the wonderful journey of Exo One for a guaranteed out of this world experience. 10/10 will absolutely play again

_childDocuments_.review: What can be said that hasn't been already said? It is awe-inspiring, exhilarating, meditative, thought-provoking and sometimes a bit tedious. I wouldn't expect or want space travel to be any other way.My favorite elements were the textures, surfaces and weather, their design and physicality. This made the sensation of flight more tactile, knowing that your fleeting acceleration was determined by your actions and the environment itself. Nothing to clip through artificially and everything impedes or increases your momentum. It was also the closest I've felt to the sensation of sailing through rough seas. I felt like I had to use a similar logic to maintain my course and speed.I'm left wanting more but that doesn't mean there isn't enough, far from it.

_childDocuments_.review: A really neat and unique experience! Finished this one on Xbox Game Pass and I liked it quite a bit. It has a very relaxing feel to it and does a good job of transporting your mind to this calming alien world when you play the game. The sound design is excellent, and while there can be some areas that look a bit rough, the prettier spots look downright gorgeous at times! I love the overall imagery on display, it sort of reminds me of 2001 A Space Odyssey at times when you complete a planet and warp to the next one. Plus I can forgive that slight inconsistency since this is an indie title developed by a solo dev. I really enjoyed the flying system/controls that were designed and implemented in this game too, once you got a hold of it, you really started to have fun flying around as this little alien ship/entity. Again, even the controls in spots could be just a tad unpolished and odd, but overall this is still a pretty great try for their first attempt. I also liked the very surreal and abstract approach to narrative tried in this game. I felt it was refreshing from the usual stuff we see in games.  I think there is a lot of potential with this idea to go even further with a potential sequel or spiritual successor honestly. And I am pretty impressed that Exo One was developed by just one person. But I do gotta say, as much as I liked Exo One, I wasn't completely blown away by it (which is fine of course). As a game, it's solid, but I feel that the potential for a truly incredible game is certainly here! And I definitely think developer Exbleative is onto something here.Anyways, I give Exo One a strong 7/10 (Good) and recommend it if you enjoy shorter more relaxed experiences. And I look forward to what this developer makes in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: Exo One is a really odd thing. Skill Up has called it a "flow state" game, and I get that, but "game" is the far-fetched bit. It's *so* aimless, and each level is really drawn out. When you're whipping along with some nice speed (which never lasts long) it feels pretty great, but then a bunch of the time you're ambling along in search of a rare ramp to zip down, and a good chunk of it has been more Super Monke Ball (and/or Marble Madness) than the 2001 A Space Odyssey Simulator it looks like it should be.The sense of speed is a really odd aspect. It feels fast from time to time but then you lose speed *so* quickly, and with all the dolly-zoom-esque modifying of the camera's focal length being done to help convey the speed sensation it's actually *really* difficult to get any idea how fast you're going. Some form of bar that fills up or something, *anything*, would be useful.The volumetric clouds are *sublime* and look so great, but then there's *terrain pop-in*, and I'm running this at max settings on a 4080, and it's pretty geometrically sparse. So odd.I saw some reviews saying it felt like someone had figured out how to do some neat gravity stuff in Unity (or whatever) and then just chucked this out the door as fast as they could - I wouldn't go *that* far, but there really isn't that much "game" here. Exo Nought Point Five, more like.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent experience. I wouldn't call it a "game" but its still very engaging.It's a hard game to recommend outright, because of it's nature.If you've played SpaceEngine, Noctis, or Journey, and enjoyed the exploration/discovery elements from those games, this might be for you.Narrative is very vague, but its enough to provide a driving force.The gameplay is very simple, with only a handful of mechanics, but the game consistently introduces new environments to switch things up.Graphics are overall very pretty. _childDocuments_.review: Great experience, but a bit flawed. The audio visual experience is honestly totally unique for any form of interactive medium I've come across, I adored how it looked and was directed and the soundtrack was really chill and fitting (Prey is another great proponent of nice clean guitar in space). The only part I have to fault the visuals on is some horrid ground textures that kinda broke the immersion, which was admittedly already gone by that point but I'll get to that. The trippy space visuals and striking colour and lighting really looked incredible whacked up to ultra and the overall sound design really did make you feel like this alien object ripping through orbit, but that's about all that did unfortunately.As soon as it becomes a game it kind of became a bit of a hassle at points. The gameplay concept is really cool and simple and it's what sold me on the game and made me love the prologue, but at a point the level design and gameplay mechanics made it feel like I was constantly fighting the game. The Jungle reeeeaaaaaaly highlights this and that level and a few other had me restarting because I had zero momentum and I figured I was approaching it all wrong. The camera really didn't help things either, I'm sure there was some reason for it not being as such, but I feel if the camera was anchored to the player it'd be immediately 10 times better and would probably make getting around the levels less of a hassle too.How the player controlled was so nearly there but fell short in a few ways for me, like some levels relentlessly dragging you up when not necessary which results in an eyefull of sky and total disorientation. I also felt getting up to speed was really hard at points and your deceleration from high speeds was pretty punishing so it felt super momentary. There was a few other slight annoyances I couldn't put into words right now but might edit in later but it didn't feel as free as I'd hoped.The story was 100% far too in your face, especially with the overdone looping reversed voices to accompany every line of "dialogue" to the extent it got funny. By the end I felt like I had played a game and had the blurb of a mostly unrelated work described to me.tl;dr I know this review comes off mostly negative but these were my only complaints holding the game back from being the best it can be and if I were to talk in detail about all I liked this would be FAR longer (and you're better off just playing it, me describing visuals I liked would suck). Overall it was a great experience, as it is right now I'd have preferred if it been something I watched when really high because it did not feel amazing to play but looked pretty mind bendingly amazing at points. It's a bit short, only an hour and a half but I will replay it, especially if the gameplay gets a slight tuning. I'll for sure be showing friends this, purely for the visual aspect and mostly inoffensive "ball game" nature of it. I wish the devs great success with this and I'd love to see it continue to flourish because there's not a lot else in this "deep space trip" genre

_childDocuments_.review: Update: I've now played through the whole game, and am on my second round.  Beautiful, immersive atmospheres and sound... the movement is mesmerising... and I particularly love that it's about discovery.The game is deceptively simple. _childDocuments_.review: I had played the demo previously for this game a few months before I purchased, and I am so glad they had a demo up to play. This is a very satisfying and unique game fit for anyone looking to relax and explore. From skipping your ship against waves larger than cities, to breaking the sound barrier to gain ridiculous speed. This was a trip. Going between these unique worlds and marveling at the beauty between all of them really sold this game to me. Soundtrack also give this game its own set of tones, that really builds the games atmosphere. It gave my imagination room to wander and was just satisfying to play. _childDocuments_.review: This was quite a unique experience.Exo One gave me a great sense of wonder, I felt curious the whole playthrough.The game is about cruising/rolling around on mostly empty planets.You can try to get to the next part as fast as you can and break the sound barrier or you can enjoy yourself and just glide across the endless plains, taking in the sights.Overall the gameplay is easy but satisfying, you can chill while playing this game and listen to music of your choice.The planets are interesting and feel huge. You can look for these energy balls to expand your energy pool so that the Exo One can hold more power and there are wind and storm mechanics to help you fly and achieve greater height and speed.There's some story here about humanity making first contact with aliens but it's nothing memorable and can get a bit confusing as the story is done via some kind of distorted flashbacks that the player has to piece together.Recommended for people that like space, exploration and for people that don't mind playing a game that's a bit short but unique. I'd also recommend playing with a controller if you can.
_childDocuments_.name: Exo One

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, disappointing.The game starts you off with this awesome feeling of wonder, you can roll and glide as fast as you can get, and it's really fun! And then it immediately kicks in the creepy atmosphere and the fun stops there. It feels like the game is confused, has no idea what it wants to be and just decides to do everything at once without consistency. -Reverse voices, after about 30 minutes, I wanted to scream, I hate them and they add nothing to the game other than making it even more annoying-some of the levels actively fight the player. You'd think in a game that's only control scheme is based on going fast and smooth movement, the game wouldn't then decide to throw entire mazes at you that force you to slow down, push you around with hard wind thats also super buggy and limits your ability to move and go fast, and at one point literally takes away your controls and says FU to the player.This has been one of the most disappointing waits for any game ever for me, and I will be refunding it immediately. Do not Buy

_childDocuments_.review: a friend of mine played the demo and then recommended it to me. I probably played the demo about 6 or so times before the game came out simply by how beautiful, fun, and relaxing it all was. the game is very straightforward; you control an alien spacecraft and fly around in a unique and charming gravity-driven control set. learning to fly and gain some real speed is such a rewarding feeling! launching yourself and simply cruising, viewing the beautiful vistas this game has to offer... it's a truly fantastic experience.the only critiques I really have for this are the lack of expansive exploration within these beautiful alien worlds and the lack of level selection. I could spend hours going around some of these levels to their full extent if it were possible. I'm hopeful that these changes may be implemented in the future, but for the time being, this game is a nice experience and change of pace from games I normally play. _childDocuments_.review: I came in with wrong expectations and was at first disappointed. However, by the time the credits rolled (after 3 hours of play) I think I got it and can now give this a reluctant "thumbs up" insofar as it delivers on its intention:  should be understood as an atmospheric (literally!) interactive art project, not a game, and not even a "walking sim" game.There is not much to do per se, rather it is a series of extraordinary planetary vistas, most of which seem extremely inhospitable for life. You glide/roll/skim through them in a fairly enjoyable way, but ultimately it's just about getting to the end of one experience and continuing to the next one. There is a very, very thin story presented like wisps of memory. Really, the whole game is more like an intense dream than an actual lived reality.My main critique is that the planets are too empty. There are structures, but they don't have any apparent story role. Thus every world became boring for me before too long, overstaying its welcome. I also think a few of the worlds are too similar to each other, such that they are superfluous. In summary,  could have been half its length and still be satisfying.My second critique has to do with "difficulty". It's easy enough to finish the game, but in later worlds the physics, weather, and terrain work against the flow of movement and can potentially put you in frustrating places from where it's hard to move on. I guess this was meant as a challenge, but it's just a very uninteresting one and gets in the way of the total experience.Which leads me to my final critique. There are a few "gamey" additions, notably collectibles, some of which are challenging to reach later in the game. They simply boost your movement ability a little and don't provide any story insight. And, unfortunately, there are a whole bunch of typical gamey achievements, which I feel are a very poor fit for this experience. Thankfully, the devs disabled achievement notifications by default so you won't be distracted during a naïve playthrough. But, really, why do they even exist? This is just not that kind of game, if it's a game at all.All in all, it's a very cool art project, which unfortunately doesn't always know if it wants to be a game or not. I suggest ignoring the game elements and just experiencing these stunning planets.

_childDocuments_.review: 5 minutes in: "Heh, what a strange intro- Wait there's a story?"15 minutes in: "Okay... this is pretty neat but surely I'll be bored soon."20 minutes in: "Dude... speedrunners would love this."2.5 hours in: "Noooo that's it!? I want to do more fun maps! However, I feel oddly emotional and the story didn't even make sense... must've been the music. I admit... that did end up being pretty sweet."Short and sweet man. It's a satisfying and fun physics game with an oddly attached story and music that makes you feel relaxed yet... emotional? If that was the goal then I guess they nailed it. It's also very pretty. It's a great sandbox for playing around in and I actually think there's a high skill floor for it that would be rewarding to masterIf it were up to me I would do 2 things: - Make another mode that is arcade-y. Perhaps time trials and speed challenges. Getting a flow going and maintaining momentum is so freaking satisfying and fun and would be totally fine without the story and music. - More levels. This adventure is really short but most parts are still quite repayable.In the end I'm happy to have given these guys my money. I do recommend the game but I admit it would be easier to recommend if it were cheaper. I don't want to suggest a price but I just feel it's a bit expensive for what it is. If they end up adding more to it I'd be really happy. However, in the end, I do not regret this purchase. I really enjoyed this and would love to see more like it.
