_childDocuments_.review: Gloomhaven is a fantastic game, and the digital version is a great way to play it., this recommendation does come with some caveats. In particular,- The UI for some effects can be quite confusing, and it's really easy to accidentally make mistakes. There are all sorts of situations where you can make a mistake with no way to undo it, whereas in the physical board game you'd just quickly correct it and move on.- The game doesn't give enough explanation or details for some things, especially in side scenarios with unusual rules. For example, in "Well of the Unfortunate", we completely lost track of who was carrying the key item. Many rules are obvious in the physical edition due to the design of the components, but are lost in translation to digital (e.g. the fact that the outcome of city/road events can depend on the composition of your party)- A major upside of the digital edition is that you don't need to run the monster AI yourselves. However, to plan a turn in a difficult scenario correctly, you still need to know how the monsters are going to behave. The game doesn't give any help with this, so someone still probably needs to learn the AI rules and execute them in their head, in order to figure out how to plan the turn.None of these are deal breakers, but I'd personally love to see another quality of life update focusing on some of these rules explanation type things. Until that happens, expect a pretty steep learning curve to get in to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty descent adaptation of the tabletop version. Has a different feel to the game when just clicking as oppose to physically handling all of the figures and tokens. I enjoy playing both versions of Gloomhaven. It can be difficult to get people together for a session playing the tabletop version, especially if you want the consistency of playing with the same people. So when I have the itch to play, I just hop on my laptop and play. Graphics and animations are okay. Having the voice acting for scenarios is nice. For those who don't want to spend over a hundred for the tabletop version, this is a nice alternative.Like:- Not having to spend so much time setting up and cleaning up- Playing with others online- Being able to stop play and pick it back up another day without having to leave everything out and worrying if the pets will knock over everything- Not having to make decisions based off of ambiguity of rules- Plays true to the table top version (except for the bugs noted below)Dislike:- Game has many bugs that can ruin game play and make it very frustrating:1. Attack modifiers are not randomized. The algorithms used to determine modifier appears to make them predetermined. There are certain tendencies when the null modifier will show up and it can be pretty predictable when it will appear. It is NOT BAD LUCK. More like bad programming.2. The same thing can be said about when you have to discard a card when you short rest. 3. I've noticed a bug with an issue regarding enemy targeting in a recent scenario I played. In the scenario I was in a situation where two characters were right next to an enemy, but the enemy targeted a character with the faster initiative. This happened more than once.4. I've also came across another targeting issue where the enemy would target a character that was actually farther away. I moved a Brute in the line of fire of a spitting drake and it still attacked the Beast Master's Bear that was behind it.5. This other issue I've come across could be a use case. I was using Cragheart ability to move an adjacent obstacle and drop it in an open space within a range of 4. The game would not let me drop it in an open spot adjacent to a spitting drake and two cultists. The damage would've taken out the drake, but not matter how I rotated the camera, I was not allowed to drop it into that open spot. So instead I use an area attack that targeted all three enemies and of course I would draw a null for the drake. Prior to that round, the Cragheart had just drawn the null card when I was trying to finish off a cave bear with low health.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome 5 star game once you learn the mechanics (I am still learning, but can beat scenarios).1. Read some guides posted on steam 2 x over before starting to play and watch youtube videos. (I really wish I found these before playing)Recommendations:Neural Net Games (all of his videos are awesome)MandatoryQuest (this guy is amazing and scientific with his approach)ChistopherOddUseful links:2. Do the in game walk through.3. Play the game on the easiest setting in the beginning. Understand the game is way over tuned in the beginning and expect to die on the first 2 scenarios quite a few times. Just power level and learn until you can beat it. The difficulty level in the beginning even on the easiest setting is ridiculous. The Dev's should not have done this as I am sure 90% of the people that gave up would really enjoy this game...4. Personal Quests matter! They decide which characters you unlock when in character creation you choose them so I don't feel this is a spoiler. I restarted after playing for weeks a ton to choose my starting party and 'ending' party better. I hope this saves others a lot of time.I quit playing several times and started over every time. You don't need to do that failing doesn't do anything permanent or long term. Just keep learning the decks when you start off and things will make sense eventually and you will be able to form strategies.Edit:This game is incredible. I'd give 6 stars if possible. I am so glad I chose to not give up. The mechanics and math are perfection. The diversity in classes and skills is vast and awesome. The definition of 'original'. Creative beacon of light to the videogame industry. I will put hundreds of hours into this one. I really hope it gets lots of expansions. I will buy every one of them.I updated the original review to include helpful videos and links I found to be absolutely necessary and incredibly useful.

_childDocuments_.review: It is only appropriate that one of the most ludicrously ambitious board games ever should get one of the most ambitious ports ever. It is far better than I'd have dared hope for - combining faithful translation of the board game, excellent UX, and decadent 3d graphics. The departures from the board game are all good choices: resolving AI ties with randomness instead of player choice, replacing a couple abilities that would have made the interface much worse, etc. In addition, it is both wonderful and kind of insane that they added an entirely new semi-random campaign mode ("Guildmaster"), that is arguably better than the original's campaign.I do have some criticism. Better "undo" support would have been fantastic. It would also have allowed removing some of the "comfirm action" buttons. I also wish they supported harder difficulties than +2 out of the box, but since they have provided modding support, it's not too big a problem.Playing Gloomhaven has never been easier. Overall, wow, great job Flaming Fowl!!

_childDocuments_.review: Gloomhaven is unique. If you've delved deep into the world of board games, so be it in actual board games or discovering them through Tabletop Sim, such as I did, you will find that there are many, many imaginative, interesting and strangely complex games out there. Of them all that I tried, Gloomhaven outdoes, outshines, outperforms in every aspect. As a tactical, turn-based RPG, it has half the industry to compete with, and yet, it manages to do everything right. From the smallest system of using cards instead of dice, to every unique scenario mechanic, Gloomhaven is never lazy nor boring with its design. It always considers what every other game is doing, and introduces its own thing that defies the norm, so be it in lore, setting and mechanic. You would think that by saying this, the game is astoundingly complex and it would have a rule book the size of a barn. No, not quite - the rules are intuitive, predictable, and easy to memorize to the point that you will never forget the basics. Not quite perfect, as there is some fiddling with some unintuitive mechanics that will require to check what manner of event happens where, or at least make you question how do you have line of sight through a solid wall. Overall, Gloomhaven is one of the best co-op, campaign-based RPGs I've played in my life, and it might be one of the few games I don't mind paying full price for. I do hope it continues to get updated, as there are still some avenues the game can be improved, in performance, content and graphics.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: This game is brilliant! I do not post reviews very often, only when a game gives me an extraordinary impression, and this game is a gem. The gameplay is pretty much exactly as the tabletop game. i still prefer the tabletop game, but this was actually a good way of learning the mechanics and gameplay of the tabletop game.A few days ago I figured i wanted to play Gloomhaven. I open steam, find Gloomhaven in my library and press play. Nothing happens. I was wondering if there was a bug, or if i missed the butten. I move the cursor over the button "pause" button, and i am a bit surprised. Then i read the news: Gloomhaven 1.0 release available now". I giggled like a liitle girl as the game was uppdating to full release. I start up the game, start a campaign for the first time, and again im extatic. _childDocuments_.review: I own Gloomhaven, the tabletop game. I am ashamed to admit it, but I prefer Gloomhaven the video game. The honest truth of the matter is that the video game automates so much of what you need to do for setup that it makes playing the game far more accessible.If you enjoy games that have deep strategy and tactics, Gloomhaven is an excellent choice. But if you're not enamoured of setting up combos and contemplating decks, you may want to pass. It's a great game, but it is one which leans more on the moment-to-moment mechanics in order to accomplish your objectives than many other board games. Poor choices can sink your attempts at a given scenario and it can be frustrating (albiet less-so with the digital game) to need to repeat quests.There's a reason this is one of the highest rated tabletop games ever made, but that doesn't mean it's for everyone! Stay away if fantasy games aren't your cup of tea, if you don't like deterministic games (this one definitely leans Euro), or if you're looking for quick/light gameplay.

It has a lot of depth to it, and the game is set up with progression for your world based on the missions your team chooses to do. _childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game. Love-hate relationship. This is a game deeply-deeply-deeply focussed on strategy that at my opinion goes too far every single damn time. Going too far means that the game's randomness can often be your downfall. Normal difficulty is a no go, but Easy is still over-the-top hard for me. I think as a board game or a cooperative multiplayer experience, it is great, as we can all suffer together or encourage each other the many times the game utterly destroys us, but as a solo game, this is not great. Too much limitations, game pace way way too slow, too many missclicks completely ruining the scenario unless you do the whole turn all over again, and again, etc. Repeating the same scenarios to beat them is not much of a fun either and break the immersion a bit. And finally, level scalling feels too intense, as leveling up to gain more chances of beating a scenario you are struggling with does not help, and sometimes even make things harder for you. Imagine failing a scenario at the last moment, leveling up, and trying it again to realize it is way harder now? Unnecessary. So, yeah, a bit too many frustrations for this game to be enjoyable appart from coop play and the classic table top.

_childDocuments_.review: Keep up the good work guys. I see where you are going with things thanks to your road map and I look forward to the improvements you  are bound to make. Early access is practically Alpha so we should all expect bugs, clunky UI, unfinished content, etc. The main thing I am concerned about is whether you have the soul of the game and I feel like it is there. Do your best to make sure we have all of the finer details that make Gloomhaven so great by the full release in 2020 and this will surely be a hit. Some minor suggestions that I know are already being worked on and some that are not: - Make the level up process cleaner. We should be able to do everything we do in the board game in this game. Perks for attack modifiers, and two new card options for each level (with the option to choose a previously lower level that was not selected in the skill tree).  - Add enhancements- Show attack modifiers clearly when an attack is made by your own characters as well as your enemies.-There is no shame in giving us practically the same game as the board game on the PC. _childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly, I can't recommend this game. The game design doesn't quite feel right. I suspect it works a lot better as a board game than it does as a video game.Retirement feels like such an awkward mechanic. If you retire quickly to unlock new mercenaries, you miss out on really getting to build up your mercenary with enhancements, high level cards, and cool items. If you don't retire your mercenaries, you don't unlock new mercenaries to try. Differing opinions on which is better, the powerful, high-level play, or the novel mercs and interactions, can cause your party to suffer from awkward disparities in power and goals. The further we got into the game, the more we felt that issue.For example, earning perk points through secret missions was lame. If you're not planning on retiring your merc, then completing your secret goal is important. More important than keeping it a secret, since there's no penalty for telling people or just letting them find out. Irl, you can just house rule that if people find out your secret mission, you don't get the points. No such option in a video game. Meanwhile, if you're planning to retire your character soon, the perk points, the gold, the items, etc. are all pretty meaningless. Also, some of the enhancements are so expensive, even playing with the rules that make them non-permanent. Who wants to invest that much into a character just to have them retire? Who wants to make a new character knowing that they'll have to stand on the same stage as the brute that's been growing in gold and power since day one?Unrelated, the enemies and summons could definitely be made smarter in a video game than they can in a board game. Completely random actions are annoying in that they're difficult to plan around. For example, the enemies may end up staying where they are and attacking the air. That could be super convenient, or it could have ruined the turn you were planning. But you won't know until after you've chosen the cards you want to play. That's made worse by the time pressure the game puts on you to complete a mission. The number of rounds you get is limited, and it's not unreasonable to fail missions because you didn't go fast enough. Dealing with output randomness from enemies just exacerbates the issue, and isn't necessary in a video game.Plus, the number of uses you get from items doesn't feel great, and the classes as a whole don't feel super balanced. I don't know. It felt like a slog and a bit of a mess at times. I wish I could recommend it, but I think there are better video games in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun turn-based strategy board game.  The best part is unlocking new characters and learning how to play them.  Its also fun figuring out synergies between abilities and equipment and executing your powerful combos.  It starts out hard and gets much easier once you become more powerful. _childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Information is WAY too front-loaded. I didn’t find it “too hard” personally - I have seen replies to similar reviews saying to “lower the difficulty” but the difficulty is not the problem. I finished the first few fights on my first attempts and I wasn’t even playing on the lowest difficulty.The problem is that it feels very tedious and unfun to make decisions without any internalized, intuitive basis for doing so. In your first encounter with your first two characters you already have access to something like 40 distinct abilities (20 different cards each representing two options). When you’re just starting you essentially have to read through all your 30-40 abilities every turn to make decisions, while also remembering all the core mechanics you just learned from the 10 or so tutorials (which take a couple hours to finish, as others have pointed out). There's no chance given to build "reflex" or "intuition" for what an ability/card does.I can see this game being fun and tactically engaging if you really knew all your possible actions and the interactions off by heart, but the game gives you no chance to gain that intuition. I don’t really have a suggestion for doing so exactly. I wish you could start with fewer cards but the burning mechanics makes that infeasible.I am someone very familiar with and fond of "information-heavy" games, and I'm writing this because I think the game is very deep and interesting tactically, but I think most people will be immediately turned off for this same reason that I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Chess, Magic The Gathering, and D&D all in one place. I thought the card interactions worked all too well in some scenarios - even when nonoptimal - so I believed that MATLAB might have been utilized to simulate outcomes. _childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the board game. The graphics are amazing and game play is everything I thought would be in a video game version. There are some small changes from the board game like items degrade over time. I haven't tried multiplayer yet but I'd bet that it is just as fun if not better than playing alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Now that multiplayer is more stable, I’m happy to say this game is totally awesome. Super fun co-op. Highly recommended.Update: This game is just the best. I can see why it's one of the top rated board games of all time--and the digital version takes all of the setup/rules/controlling monsters/etc work out of it. So you just get to enjoy playing the game. Strongly recommend playing co-op if possible. Really looking forward to the campaign.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Not a fun game for multiplayer. Turns take forever and rules are too clunky. In order to move your character you need a card. In order to pickup loot off the ground from a defeated enemy you need a card. Movement and looting share the same action point pool with attacking and skills. This can easily leave your character stationary with nothing to do if you do not plan your cards out correctly. But cards are also spent and end up discarded or destroyed. When you have no cards your character dies. When your character loses all HP they die. So this is a combination of a RPG and a card game. I'm sure that can be very strategic but it also means it is very limiting. Instead of controlling your character and fighting the enemies in the dungeon you feel like you are fighting the game mechanic itself just to keep your character alive. It's like playing poker with one hand while waving off someone physically fighting you with the other.This is probably a better single player experience but for a group of friends to play together it is more frustrating than fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Not my type of game.Certainly I have in mind some people that may enjoy it. I never played the board game, so for a very beginner I did pass the tutorial with some difficulty trying to get all the rules. I'm pretty sure if I keep playing it at some point I would enjoy it but it seems to be that at that point it takes some time. I like to enjoy games from the very beginning and knowing that over time it will become more exciting. I feel the learning curve for this game is above average, and that makes it tedious for me to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Very much a work in progress.  Pros:-Does not follow board game story line; you can play this to get your fix or try things out without spoiling a first play thru.-Looks and sounds great.-Plays like Gloomhaven.-Character selection is currently very limited; does not yet include all of the basic starting classes even. -Some card effects, notably "push", multi-target and element consuming effects don't seem to function yet.-The game balance is way off, as the scenarios are RNG created.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Instead of recreating the Gloomhaven tabletop game the developer has decided to make a separate campaign that is inferior in almost every way.  This is made all the more frustrating in that they seem to have a solid recreation of the core Gloomhaven tactical dungeon battles but have decided to go a different route for the over all experience.  it's decent for an early access but beware this is not the Gloomhaven tabletop game if that is what you are looking for.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: This is a 1to1 conversion of the tabletop version of Gloomhaven. Right now it has a very barebones "adventure mode" that lacks the magic and charm of the original's campaign. Eventually the campaign and other characters will be added later in development. For those that have never played the original, it is an incredible experience, with some of the most engaging and exciting combat of any table top dungeon crawler. This game promises to be an excellent substitute for those that don't have a few faithful friends to go through the massive campaign or a swole enough  body to lift the massive game box. Warning: As of this writing, there is no tutorial, and Gloomhaven is not exactly like much of anything else. Most of what is going on is explained in the compendium, but for those unfamiliar with how the table top version functions this is going to prove confounding until better guidance is implemented or you go read how to play the table top version. In particular, pay attention to what cards are "burned" when used vs those that are only discarded.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Installed on Linux/Ubuntu 22.04 Jammy Jellyfish. The game runs very well with Steam on Linux. I own the Gloomhaven board game and this plays almost exactly like the board game. The game looks and plays great on the PC. This game starts hard because your characters are not leveled and have few items. But leveling up and buying/finding items is very rewarding. The development team did a great job.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure why the ratings of this game are so low.  In the board-game world, this game is top tier.  This digital version is better imo.I get that the digital version has a few bugs, but the simple truth is - this is a great digital game.  I've played the board-game - once, and the simple truth about the board game is - it's a mess to administer and takes absolutely forever to play.  Do you really think a few bugs (things that are simply different than the board-game) happen more often than the tedious attempt to keep track of all of your modifiers and cards and items irl?  After playing this online, I have zero interest in the effort to play the actual board-game, unless someone else is doing all the work.The only "real" reason to rate this game anything other than top tier, is that it's a slow turn based strategy game.  That's just not for everyone.  The game is grindy and takes a ton of time, just like any other dungeon crawl.  It's the opposite of a high paced action game.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like the board game? You'll like this.  You get 2 guys and you play them.  So that is the big difference, you can time their initiatives and you know what each one is going to do.  This is NOT a replacement for the tabletop, no multiplayer (yet) and the story is weak (just feels like random dungeons so far).  That being said.. very fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: I don't want to think about how many hours I have clocked playing Gloomhaven the board game over the last few years, it is one of my favorite board game experiences.  This has faithfully recreated the original campaign and is so much more.  The boardgame is a commitment, in setup times, play times and everything, this version just takes that all away, playing a multiplayer scenario here takes way less time than the boardgame.  It makes great improvements throughout in being so accessible.  This is in turn leads to you being able to enjoy the core mechanics of the game on an even deeper level as your able to iterate and replay so easily.  It's wonderfully gorgeous, and well put together.  If you have any interest in the boardgame at all, I highly recommend you check out this digital edition.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Gloomhaven player here, decided to pick this up because I am excited to play more of this damn game whenever possible. My team has been playing once a week since early October 2018 and I've taken 3 characters to ~ level 7.Some current downsides- the pace is slow. Some of it is understandable (you have to confirm every action with an additional click since you can do tons of stuff mid turn), but some of it needs to change (the animations for attacks, movement, and casting are way, way too slow).- gold is shared across the party.... i don't like that thematically but it makes it better if you ever play with scoundrel who steals everything in classical multiplayer. - when you attack, there is no clear deck draw to show you your modifier. It is this tiny number. They need a full deck draw to make it clear.- it is hard to discern monster play order because their number is not shown.- The ui could use some improvements. There is input lag with the mouse over the buttons and some of the buttons seem harder to click than I would like. Additionally, if you had an item equipped and you sell it, the character's inventory icon will still show that you have something equipped until you open that slot again to "refresh" it. However, this game is a very good translation of the board game so far. The rules are well implemented and the challenge is really there for sure. This is such a challenging board game so it is nice to see that difficulty carry over. Additionally, the game looks very nice. Even though I mentioned that the animations are way too slow (is a slider possible?), they look great.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: I understand it's based on a board game, but does it have to be so rigidly board game like? I find the reams of cards too abstract to understand, and the combat mechanics of drawing them and picking which half to activate just seems very far removed from anything immersive. There are so many rules you need to remember just to get through the simplest of encounters that I just can't for the life of me be arsed to go any further!

_childDocuments_.review: Buggy, unpolished.  Enemies attack us through walls, but we cannot attack the same enemy back in the same place.  You can't hover over enemies to see what effects do. _childDocuments_.review: I do have to admit, I have never played the board game version of this. This is an amazing game. both with its turn based strategical elements as well as card based tactics. It is super fun with friends in regards to challenging the many unique ways you can blend a variety of combinations and characters. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: I was really glad to stumble upon this game. Prior to the release of Gloomhaven on Steam i had no idea that a tabletop version had existed. I typically like to play turn based games with a focus on tactics and planning such as: XCOM series, Shadowrun, Divinity OS:2 and Torment Tides of Numenara. This game popped up on my queue and it was also on sale. At the start of the game i didnt really know what i was doing but having played turn based games before some of this seemed familiar. What really makes this game different is that every character has a deck of cards in which they choose 2 for their turn. As you progress in the game you will level up which in turn allows you to add new cards to your characters deck, you also can equip items in each of your characters slots. As you progress through the game you will also free up more spots to take more companions with you rather than the starting of 2 characters only. The game is in EA, however, the devs of this game are excellent. They are easily reachable and always answer questions, the flow of new content has been released in a timely manner and they have a great roadmap for the game that once all complete will result in a fantastic game. So, if you enjoy turn based games with a focus on tactics, strategies and team synergies then i think this game is worth your consideration!

_childDocuments_.review: Good old times, when people were ready to play anything to have a bit of fun. You would need something to keep people gathering and playing, so prolonging sessions and adding some gimmicks would be fine for a tabletop.Take your friends out, and what's left is an extremely gridny, poorly balanced, punishing, anti-fun game.- Allows coop- Challenging at first glance- Voice acting is good.- : 50 fps dropping with freezes at RTX3070- . The camera is crazy during enemy turns, frequent Network crashes. Enemy AI like archers walking into their own traps, refusing to act. Sometimes enemies from hidden rooms will move faster than you even if their initiative is lower.- . Enemies will metagame their best to counterplay not only players abilities but even quests and dungeon challenges. The summoner is able to teleport into doors but is still trying to summon minions onto blocked tiles. Enemies are damaging themselves. Enemies sharing the same action locking them on undesirable action (1 low-HP skeleton would lock 2 other skeletons on "heal + shield" action even if they could've killed you).-  and grind are intended and encouraged. As you don't get basic rewards such as exp and gold by doing missions in this game, you need to abuse it by repeating the same missions over and over in order to keep your level, stats, cards, potions, and gear relevant.-  are pure RNG and meta - encouraged. You can try to "roleplay", but ultimately they are the same gimmicks with no logic or explanation. Just metagame it (or just Google it). Blue water = poison, yellow water = healing. Ha-ha, joke on you, yellow water = nothing happens, as events are not counted as "Rewards" in this game. There is no "carrot", only a "stick". We've played 4 missions, and in City events (which should be a reward after doing a mission), we've lost 35 coins—more than my character was even able to loot in total. After that, we'd done an Extremely Important Task For The City and we were rewarded with...20 gold coins.-  in general. All enemies drop 3-4 coins on death. An item costs from 20 to 50 coins. You can't share items with teammates. If I bought a shield for 20g and I want to give it to my teammate - so I need to sell it for 10g, then my mate would be able to buy it for 20g from the shop. Once your character retires, all of your items, enchantments, and perks are gone.- . As maps and AI are predetermined, there is no real challenge in completing the map. You just have to find the optimal solution for that map. Once you get the idea, it takes another 3-5 runs to "perfect" it, as a single mistake can cost you a run. There is no variety, so re-doing the same map over and over is not fun, plain boring. One might watch a youtube walkthrough from the start.- . Other people have already said it, but it does not seem "random". A "Cancel" card reshuffles the modifiers, that's fine. So you can reshuffle the deck and draw 3-4 "Cancels" per 5 turns - typical scenario, we've seen it a least once per two missons. Have we ever seen two x2 in a row? Nope, sorry. It is OK for this game to draw your full negative hand of modifiers, then draw zero, reshuffle the deck, and draw them all over again.-  is nonexistent, even 200$ budget indie titles had better OSTs in 2020.- : No fast-forward animations, no simple hex map view, no damage-modifiers chance preview etc.They sell you this game as a "Tactical coop RPG dungeon crawler"What they don't say is that it lacks actual content, requires tons of grinding, has no respect for player time, and that you have almost zero agency in "playing" your "role" in this game.This game is so "good", that only 20% of players actually cared to finish first 3 missions.

_childDocuments_.review: Faithful adaptation of the board game. Too faithful IMO. Playing this reminded me how many house rules we had to make the board game enjoyable and less tedious. Unfortunately with the digital version that kind of stuff has to be programmed in and outside of a few options that's not available.In particular I wish there was a way to undo more actions in case you accidentally select the wrong tile/card or got your character order mixed up. There is a restart round option but if you make some mistake towards the end of a round you get to replay the last 5-20 minutes. Or worse, if it's your last action the next round begins automatically and you have to restart the entire mission (some of which can take multiple hours). Those restarts can add up over the very lengthy campaign. Suffice it to say after just a few missions I realized there was no way I was going to enjoy putting in hundreds of hours to get through the campaign and uninstalled the game.Also of note is that some features of the board game did not make it over to this digital version, in particular the random missions which are kind of required if you want to get the most out your characters. This should've been included or the campaign mission rewards re-balanced to take it's omission into account.Not bad if you're looking for a difficult card based strategy game, but expect to replay through the same multi-hour missions due to a single error.

_childDocuments_.review: Great turn-based strategy game. Lots of content and still being updated towards its full release. The only complaint I have about the game lies in its netcode as desyncs are quite frequent and ruin my enjoyment since it is a bit tedious to re-add friends in the middle of a mission, but hopefully that will get resolved soon. _childDocuments_.review: I came to Gloomhaven after putting tens of hours into the physical board game. It was a great way for me and my friends to play and enjoy the game without having to nail down a time for us all to be in the same place. I can honestly say that I enjoy the digital version more than the physical. Pound for pound, the digital version of the game captures all the things that are great about the board game, save maybe the sheer awe that is instilled by the depth and complexity that the board game evokes upon playing. If you like the board game, you will like this game. Period. Nothing of value is truly lost, and one major negative aspect of the physical game is removed: set-up. That's right. No more 45 minutes of set-up for an hour session, segueing into another 15-20 minutes of clean up. That alone makes it worth it, because there are times with the board game that I felt I spent more time setting up than actually playing.For those that haven't played the board game, Gloomhaven is a tabletop tactics game set in a unique fantasy universe. The lore is deep enough to be interesting and the mechanics are where it really shines. Completing scenarios always feel like you're accomplishing something to progress and the variability in play style is impressive to me. There's a lot of card and inventory management and forward-thinking required. It's definitely not a mindless game, and it punishes mistakes handily and without mercy. So be prepared! You're going to lose. Quite a bit. Unless you have some virtuosic command of the game, it will deliver several defeats to your doorstep. If you don't like losing, or get easily frustrated by a couple of random sequences resulting in your total demise, then stay away. BUT. If you don't mind getting bodied here and there, and enjoy learning and growing your playstyle while unlocking cool treasures and characters, this game is tirelessly rewarding as well.I highly recommend with the caveat that its hard as hell and doesn't care who knows it.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is it tough. I recommend any newbies play this game on easy the first time through. Seriously. I'm an XCOM and Darkest Dungeon Veteran (the two games that sort of come closest to this one) and this game has kicked my ass even on easy. That said, once you get used to its unique gameplay style it gets definitely more manageable...but like I said, boy is it still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tough.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Since they have introduced more content (character classes, enemy and zone variety, items, enchantments etc.) the game has gotten significantly better. With a full tutorial, a completely revamped Guildmaster game mode which is a huge upgrade to what they started with, and now online co-op this game is shaping up very nicely. The UI changes since the launch of EA are very welcome and the game runs a lot better. Highly recommend.Very barebones at the moment, but you can tell the devs have put a lot of effort into getting the game to where it is now. _childDocuments_.review: was originally a tabletop game that has now been developed into a digital version. This is a faithful representation of the board game with a few balancing differences, quality of life improvements, and a few tweaks. Whilst this version improves on some of the critiques that the original board game had, there are some newfound problems that can’t go overlooked.• Heavily strategy focused• Diverse range of Mercenaries that have their own strengths and weaknesses• Numerous unique monsters• Multiple levels of difficulty to suit newcomers and seasoned veterans• High replay value• Over 100 hours worth of content• A big learning curve to overcome• Scenario 1 is make or break for newcomers• Playable tutorial doesn’t explain some of the more valuable rules#• UI can be very crowded• Bugs and performance issues here and there is not for the faint-hearted. Don’t come into this game expecting it to be another RPG you can haphazardly stumble through and win. Admittedly, it’s a steep learning curve to climb, one that may cause players to become frustrated and give up. There’s an intricate set of mechanics that requires a lot of strategic thinking, planning, and improvisation to triumph in . Gathering knowledge about how this game works, and figuring out some nuance mechanics is what will give you the edge, which sometimes you need. Are you still here? Great, let's talk about the game.At the start of the campaign, you’ll be greeted with six mercenaries that you can choose to form a team. Each of them has their own play styles that they specialise in, but also have downfalls that need to be considered. From a weak but powerful mage to a hard-hitting but slow Inox Warrior, there is a surprisingly diverse group to pick from. Every class has a set number of cards they pick to build their deck. The cards mostly have unique actions on them for each class, but at low levels, there isn’t much to be excited about. For such a small roster to select from, there are various different teams you can build. Part of the fun is finding new combinations and strategies between the original six and how their actions can complement each other. That being said, no Mercenary wants to be diving in dungeons forever, they want to move on with their retirement goal at some point.Once a Mercenary has achieved their retirement goal, they will leave the team. You’ll be awarded a new class for your efforts, and can recruit another Mercenary if you wish. Although it's difficult to let go of the characters that you’re used to playing, it's a core element of the game. The new classes are far more powerful than the original six. It takes some time to become accustomed to your new recruit before you realise their full potential. So, what do you say to a bit of good old-fashioned dungeon delving?Every scenario you encounter has a goal to achieve in order to win. Most of the time it’s simply ‘kill all enemies’ or kill a specific enemy, which leaves a lot to be desired. However, mowing down enemies is still satisfying nonetheless, almost feeling like a delicate puzzle that could fall apart with a few wrong moves.At the start of each round you’ll pick two cards from your deck of cards with each Mercenary you control. The actions of cards can vary widely depending on what class you play. Usually, the top action is an attack of some kind, and the bottom is movement. Once the enemy card has revealed itself and your turn rolls over depending on initiative order (number in the middle of the card, the lowest goes first). You then use the top action on one card, and the bottom action on the other. These are then placed in a discard pile and the cycle continues. Once you are unable to play a pair of cards on your turn, you’ll have to rest to get them back. However, upon resting you’ll be forced to  a card, which makes it unavailable for the rest of the scenario. The number of cards you have represents your longevity in the scenario before you become exhausted.You’ll find most cards have average damage or movement, but there are far more compelling actions that might catch your eye. Massively devastating singular attacks or huge AOE attacks that apply a status effect to all targeted enemies. Whilst these are extremely valuable, they do come at a cost. Burning them after use. This forces you into a balancing act, whereby burning powerful cards early on, though might prove useful in the short-term, will jeopardise your longevity in the scenario. Consequently, making you exhaust faster. really does push you to get the most out of every action that you play. You need to be aggressive, but also mindful of how monsters will act. Every scenario is tight to win and only gives you a small amount of leeway (depending on the difficulty). It will punish you if you attempt to play it at your own pace. Whilst the first scenario is notoriously difficult for new players, it sets you up for how the game is going to play. It’s a steep learning curve that you can’t overcome with pure luck, it requires a lot of tactical movement and strategy.For such an extensive campaign, you’ll encounter a multitude of different monsters, all with their own attack deck and unique actions. There are only about four to six cards in each deck, so it's possible to memorise each monster deck and attempt to predict what they do next. Some enemies such as cultists can summon the living dead, whilst others such as the demons have a shield value that soaks up damage before you can deplete their health.Upon completing a scenario, you’re more than likely to be rewarded with experience. As each character levels up, you’ll gain stronger cards to add to your deck, which further diversifies each class. It does feel like a chore however when you have to choose a card to burn when your deck gets more streamlined with better cards. You’ll also gain perks that modify your attack deck (a deck that you draw every time you attack that modifies your attack) by removing negative cards (-1, -2), adding positive cards (+1, +2), or including new cards altogether. This allows you to streamline each modifier deck and, once again, adds even more variety to each class as they’ll have unique perks available to them.Whilst the digital version handles a lot of the automation that you would usually control in the tabletop version, there are new problems that need to be addressed. There are still bugs and performance issues throughout, the playable tutorial leaves valuable information out. Crowded areas make it difficult to figure out who you’re attacking, occasional soft locks, and so on. These don’t necessarily break the game by any means, but become annoying to deal with. isn’t a game for everyone. It takes a while to wrap your head around, but it seems some people are bashing their heads against a wall playing this game. Whilst the digital version makes it more accessible, it doesn't do itself any favours with annoying bugs, performance issues, and an average tutorial. Overall, I’d only recommend  if you're willing to put in the time and dedication to learn the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially did not recommend Gloomhaven, because it was missing so much interaction, and so faithful to the board game that it wasn't truly enjoyable as more than a spare moment of play. The changes that have been made to date, give the user a better experience in general. The flow of the game has been improved. There is now multiplayer, and there seems to be enough that deviates from the board game, to even out the change in experience.  These developers, have truly taken our time, and feedback in a way that is respectful to us. You can wait for the campaign; however, as it is, you are able to experience the game without too much of the early access rough edges.  Below is the original review, in which I did not recomend the game:I love the tabletop version of Gloomhaven. It is an exceptional in person experience, with too many chits, rules, and exceptions to be properly tracked. And it is glorious. This is a nearly one to one digital recreation of the tabletop experience. It's good, except a video game experience and tabletop experience focus on completely different aspects for enjoyment.  Unfortunately the camaraderie, and joint experience that makes Gloomhaven (Tabletop) so good, is not present here. Instead it has become a slogging dungeon crawling experience, that is far too slow, and does not provide the peaks and enjoyment of traditional GH.  A tabletop game is half about the game, and half about the way the game makes you interact with others. This is a solo experience, to it's detriment.Hopefully the experience will be refined to accomodate the shift from Tabletop to Digital by the time it is released as a 1.0.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good game. And even in its currently incomplete form, it is absolutely worth the up front asking price. If you enjoy strategic games with a brutally fair and punishing combat and unique resource management systems, you will have an absolute blast with the digital gloomhaven.That being said, I also feel like this has to be stressed: This is not Gloomhaven the board game, and it will not be an accurate representation of that game until multiplayer and a campaign is added. This version cuts out or is missing some pieces which makes people fall in love with or despise gloomhaven and should be considered its own standalone piece.There is no setup and no forced cooperation between players, no real difficult choices to make and less of a meta progression when it comes to unlocking units and items. All of which are very integral to the original experience. However, this is not entirely without merit.The current guildmaster mode is a great way to just sit down with a fun game for a bit. Crank the difficulty up to hard or insane and don't for a moment fear that Frank the scoundrel will sacrifice the entire groups success for two gold tokens or that Adam always makes the monsters act slightly worse than they are suppsed to because he is scared to take hits. Simply revel in the fact that all the annoying bookkeeping and monster AI is completely automated and completely fair and that when you fail, you were the cause and when you win, it was because you played well. So if what you want out of this game is a good strategy video game with turn based combat which will put you in diffuclt spots, absolutely get it right this very moment. If what you want is Gloomhaven, but on the computer, your best bet is still to get tabletop simulator, a voice program and one of the gloomhaven mods.

_childDocuments_.review: After carefully monitoring Gloomhaven's early access for over 2 years I decided to purchase it during the last patch before the 1.0 release. I am an avid board game player and have bought the physical game. What's most interesting to me, is that I actually did NOT enjoy the board game for various reasons. That being said, you would probably expect me to dislike and not recommend this game for the above reason. The funny thing is, the digital implementation of Gloomhaven made things a lot of easier for me and made me realise that one of the most frustrating things about the board game is actually the setup and tear down time which spanned from 30 minutes to 1 hour (excluding the hour length games). Suffice to say the digital game has none of that issue, therefore it makes Gloomhaven a much more desirable experience!Gloomhaven is a long campaign game, dungeon crawler with minatures, card management and RPG elements amongst other things. Yeah...it's complicated. You gather your party of 2-4 merchenaries (characters), each and every one of them dinstinct from one another. Each character has their own personal deck of cards that represent their abilities in the game. They also have a personal gold stash, aditionally, they also have personal equipment that they purchase and do not share. Each character also has a personal goal; A card that you draw uppon creating your character that represents their ultimate dream, their life goal. Uppon completing that (and trust me it will take some time) your character actually retires, effectively granting you unique one time bonuses such as new unlockable chacters but also deleting themselves! Despair not though, as the game has a deep legacy system that allows you to upgrade and enhance the character class, allowing you to begin a new character of the same class with increased power and perks! It's all an organic experience that makes you "feel" that you are not a player in a game revolving around you, but rather a guest in a fully fledged world!The campaign fearures numerous scripted scenarios, each and every one of them offering a unique challenge that you must overcome as a group. It is worth noting that the scenarios are handcrafted and extensively playtested in the board game, so there is a pretty good storytelling with pretty solid difficulty curves. The digital game also features Guildmaster mode, which is essentially a freestyle adventure mode, having the same rules but randomized dungeons with no story involved.Gloomhaven is a dark fantasy adventure that resonates better at older players. It's dark theme and it's complex mechanics are a lot to take in, but in return for investing your time and brainpower at it, it unfolds a beautiful world like a rose blossoming it's petals. It's many systems have a most organic feeling, like picking a character and embarking on an adventure with your friends. It's digital implimentation is far superior to the physical board game and I can only assume that it will get even better as time goes by. If you are looking for a deep engrossing experience with dark fantasy theme and superbly handcrafted gameplay involving minatures (character models digitaly), you need not look any further. Gloomhaven has been the number 1 board game of all times for a long time and we can finaly enjoy it for about 1/4 of it's physical price, with the added perks of the digital adaptation. If you enjoy a good challenge, be sure to enter this grim world and leave your mark uppon the city of Gloomhaven!Pros:A deep, dark, fantasy world +Personal characters that feel alive +Mechanics that feel organic +Handcrafted scripted scenarios +Lot's of different enemies to best and overcome +Lot's of uniquely different characters to unlock and master +New character/enemy models that really elevate immersion +A character-unique customizable card system +A legacy system that allows you to leave your mark +Rewards progress constantly +Guildmaster mode +Various difficulties that even scale with playercount +Digital implimentation saves your precious time +Insane replay value that doesn't really ever end +Insanely good price compared to physical game +Multiplayer +Cons:User Interface could be better -Animations could be better -Requires a lot of brainpower -Can be stressful -Requires patience -Mistakes are usually unforgiving -No rewind for moves -Verdict: A dark handcrafted fantasy world that begs to be explored! 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Much easier than the board game, AND they made improvements to the original in the Guildmaster mode. Great strategy, turn-based RPG.  Each class is so unique that this game has a high level of replayability and even within each class you can vary gear, cards, and perks.  Will be playing this one a lot.Pros:-No setup like boardgame-Much lower cost than the boardgame-Although also considered a con, each class has a learning curve, but they're unique-Leveling seems balanced-Multiplayer is a great experience-Solo is awesome and enjoyable-Unlock new classes as you explore, which is awesome-Hand management is unique and mostly enjoyable-Game has insane difficulty modes I can't imagine being able to play. Best on Normal/Easy in the beginning. Happy to have the option!Cons:-Gold pickup is frustratingly difficult. If you have cards left after you clear a room, you should be able to keep looting until exhausted.-Although also considered a pro, each class has a learning curve-Actions can be frustrating when you just want to take one step and can't, or you have one card left in your hand and instead of just being able to use it, you are exhausted instead (each round requires 2 cards).-Not all classes are playable at first-Attack card modifiers can be frustrating when you get a -1, -2, or X-Most frustrating is the random encounters to your next quest - these feel like they're designed to screw you regardless of the decision made, hurting your chances for success in a 30 minute dungeon crawl.  Starting with low health, a wound, whatever... it is pretty harsh.You're going to love this game or hate it.  I think most people will love it.  Good luck and enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all - this review is meant for players who have not played the board game and were intrigued by the presentation of this game ticking all the right boxes (fantasy tactical RPG with customizable heroes and dungeon exploration, etc). I believe the impression will be completely different for someone who is a fan of board games and this one in particular, but I am not an avid board game player, and came here as a fan of turn based games. First, the positives - the art is really well done, nothing triple A, but it has its own thing going and I can appreciate, looking impressive in details in quite a few places. The music is at worst not intrusitive and at best kinda immersive.  The narration is good, and there is limited opportunity for decision making in dialogue/encounters outside of combat, which I can always appreciate as at least something when we can't have a deep, branching storyline. Now, for the negatives... they are all in the combat gameplay, and sadly, that is all the game is based about.  Not sure why it says I've played this game for 2 hours at the time of the review, certainly been more, around five at least... or maybe it just feels this way, in which case that can go into the negative part of the review. To come to the main point - if I was writing this review for a community for board games, and specifically for this one's implementation, I would vote it positively. That, however, would not be my recommendation to a general, non-niche gaming community, such as the one of Steam players. I found the gameplay to be too slow (even when sped up), and it felt too punishing (not hard, mind you, just punishing), the destruction of your own resources to "flush" your hand provides an interesting tactical challenge, but it really does not feel satisfying. Succeeding in your attacks or strategical plays simply does not seem to outweigh the demotivating feeling of the sacrifice. Additionally, there seem to be some weird internal rulings (like a Pull ability that targeting up to three hexes not working one time three hexes ahead and working another, possibly based by something weird that is more clear on the actual board game) which end up making a move you have mapped up in your head not possible to be pulled off. In fact, the whole gameplay feels very "importent" - tactical setups seem to work out a lot less often than the other way around, and there is A LOT less focus on abilities and tactical opportunities than there is of card management. Honestly, if this game was advertised as turn based card game rather than turn based strategy game it would have been more accurate. There is really very little depth in regards to positioning and choice of abilities compared to the depth involved with hand management. It all just feels very unsatisfying even when it works, and like more of a hassle than a thrill. I find myself unenthusiastic to play this game and forcing myself to start it up just because I purchased it, which to me is a sign that it is not the game for me. TL;DR: This does not fit well with other games of the turn-based tactical RPG genre and if you go in with that attitude, as I did (which the game tags and advertisements may lead you believe it is) you may be disappointed. This is a negative review, but more on the "this game is not good for as many people as may be interested in it" than "this game is not good, period", which is something I wish to distinguish. Have fun and a nice year!

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR; Crunch, the "RPG" game.Gloomhaven is in this odd situation where it is so notorious that it sells incredibly well just because of its reputation in spite of some issues. And to be sure it is a good game that is well-designed... for a specific group of people. That group of people being gamers who like very very technical and very gamey games where the rules aren't always intuitive or make sense flavour-wise (mercs cannot share gold, exhaustion mechanics, card burn, etc.). Example: Your characters cannot stop to pick up gold lying on the ground unless they end their turn on it or use a skill. All the gold which is not picked up at the end of the mission after you beat all the monsters is lost. It's gamification for the sake of crunch. It's not really an rpg, it's a board game with elements vaguely familiar to RPG gamers.Folks who'd enjoy this game may have probably have played a lot of eurogames and ameritrash board games. If you're one of those gamers you probably already know you want Gloomhaven. I do, and I intend to keep playing it.As for everyone else, you may want to reconsider. The game is just too finicky. Technical. Plain difficult. There's a huge number of finicky rules to familiarise yourself with. I cannot in good conscience recommend this game for everyone as I know most people would find it just too tedious. The gaming community may scoff at the term "accessible" and think of unskilled game journalists, but this is one example where even most seasoned Steam gamers may find it too challenging. But if you know you can handle that level of technical gameplay, you'll likely get the hang of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: At the core, I really like Gloomhaven for what it is trying to do. Even played the physical board game and enjoyed myself. But playing it for more time revealed its many flaws. It just isn't balanced for enjoyable play. It will punish you over and over again, and not even in a way that makes you want to get back up and try again (like dark souls). The easiest difficulty leaves you gouging your eyes out after attempting the same quest for the 4th time only to have the enemy draw a "Shield 5" card when you would have killed them and won. RNG can be fun. I'm an avid DnD player myself...but the odds are stacked heavily against you in this game. Way too many enemies that all have some quirk to make them as annoying as possible. TLDR; Claims to be a tactical game, but you can have the perfect plan and execution, but the heavily negativley stacked RNG will ruin your plans every time...seriously frusterating and unsatisfying. Logged off today feeling like I payed this dev to waste my time.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the board game before and while it was very hard it was possible to beat the dungeons, level up and progress. Not on this version. It's just too hard to be enjoyable. I played 6 dungeons and managed to clear just one. It seems the number of cards is never enough for just two characters to clear the dungeons no matter which characters you choose. There are too many enemies and random spawns, and the modifiers affect your attacks negatively almost always. I won't even go into the item durability thing everyone else already mentioned.Only adventure mode is available right now, which means that after clearing one dungeon and getting killed in the next one, all XP, gold, and items are lost and you have to start again. It becomes tiring very quickly. It's just not fun *yet*. The graphics are nice and it's pretty cool to have such a complex board game on the PC, and so faithfully recreated, but it needs to be better balanced. _childDocuments_.review: Modern games shouldn't be this ♥♥♥♥♥.Skeleton summoned from a ring stands on a pressure plate. Plate does not activate. Summon does not move. You cannot control it. You cannot unsummon item summons. You have broken the scenario.If you win two of the same item and bind both to the same character the game eats one. For example, two major health potions on your tank.An Earth Elemental with a move 0 attack 4 card just moved two spaces and hit my tank for 16 damageHeals are buggy healing new party members after a retirement when replacing them with the same character until you heal them with a direct heal.Summons will ignore enemies if there are destructible terrain nearby and just endlessly attack terrain/open new rooms.An ooze just warped across the map right in front of my party.I'm on a map that hasn't rendered the board or the traps or the doors. Just the enemies.I restarted a round and now I cannot target any enemies with attacks.I put my fourth team member on a pressure plate in a quest that needed 4 pressure plates activated. It did not activate at the end of their turn. At the end of the next members turn the quest activated.After an enemy took control of a merc, I was forced to pick two cards for the merc on the next turn but the merc took a long rest any discarded the two cards I picked and didn't force me to burn a card.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played the board game version of this game so I was not sure what I was getting into, and I now regret my purchase. I'm sure those who have enjoyed the board game can find enjoyment with Gloomhaven, but the game is simply not enjoyable.The game is too slow and too hard (and not in the fun way), and the RNG mechanics make it unpredictable. A single encounter can take upwards of 45 minutes, only for you to fail because you rolled poorly on damage and ran out of cards. I can't even refund the game now because I spent 2.5 hours stuck on the first dungeon.Do not recommend for anyone unless you're prepared for a slog of a game. The "Very Positive" label is misleading.

_childDocuments_.review: Great way to play Gloomhaven solo. Playing digitally allows the computer to take care of a lot of the work you need to do when playing on tabletop like pulling attack modifiers, determining monster focus and movement, etc. There are some slight differences in rules because of this but it doesn't affect much; for instance, on tabletop when a monster is moving towards your characters and there are multiple valid spaces they could go to the players can choose which space they end on, but you don't get that choice on here. Not a huge deal.The voice acting is great and for those who have no experience with the tabletop games campaign, the world-building is amazing, a very unique fantasy world with creative races and magics. For years people have said Gloomhaven is the best board game ever created. A very intense tactical strategy game with inventive combat mechanics. The difficulty scales to the # of mercenaries in your party and their individual levels. Don't be surprised if you fail the first few missions because you have a limited number of abilities you can play and making one mistake can lose you the whole mission. As you get more gear and unlock new classes it will be more forgiving.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: I guess if you like the board game you might just understand the logic behind how this game works.  But from someone who did not play the board game this game is very frustrating as many of the mechanics simply don't make sense.  For example; if I don't want one of my characters to take any actions this turn I simply don't have that option and I MUST use some of my valuable cards to then sit there and hit take no action, but the cards are still used.  Secondly, even on the Easy setting you get your butt handed to you the very first encounter.  Tried it twice and both times all my characters were almost out of action cards after the first of 3 encounters.  By the time I got into the final room, all characters were exhausted and I failed the mission.  This could possibly be because the game makes no sense to me and the mechanics of it are just goofy.In the end.....if you don't love the board game, or have never played it, AVOID this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Was excited for a cheaper and more accessible option than the physical version. Well, cheaper is exactly what I got.Multiplayer has frequent desync issues (the host's data not transferring in full or correctly) even after it takes 10 minutes for other players to load in. The solution is for the non-hosts to delete any local save data in LocalLow and the host to re-sync on Steam.There's apparently plenty of soft-locks where missions are unwinnable because the game is broken: My group got stuck on Infernal Throne (Scenario #21) and in trying to find a solution, found posts reporting the bug in 2021 but with no solution from the community and much less from the devs. With my own knowledge of Unity3D, I believe it should have been an easy fix.The graphics are so-so.The narration is top notch, but it's all one guy.Gameplay is **hard** but house rules + mods make it more casual-friendly and a tolerable challenge.The events are the same as in the physical game. I don't know how much, if any, of the narrative content here is unique.All the localizations are player-made mods, which means quality will undoubtedly vary.Whole game ends up feeling cheap and flimsy with just as much time wasted debugging it as getting clobbered in 1-2 hr long dungeons.It's a cheap way to learn the rules of Gloomhaven but it's not guaranteed to be playable. The physical version might be >$100 USD but at least it works.

_childDocuments_.review: 1.0 Release Update - I love it.  Campaign mode is as the boardgame, but with fantastic graphics.  This is an excellent adaptation (I have tried the tabletop simulator adaption which is OK but quite fiddly, and I have the physical boardgame as well).Compared to the physical boardgame - there's the obvious quality of life upgrade of NOT digging through a box of hundreds of cards, tokens and standees.  Fiddling with monster cards, difficulty dials blah blah blah.  Some people like this stuff, I don't mind it but for a drawn out campaign game where each mission can take 2+ hours depending on what's going on, removing 30 minutes of setup and teardown has to be a good thing!  My boardgame map pieces are alphabetised in an accordian folder for gods sake.As to networking issues - well I haven't encountered too much drama as I mainly play 2 player with my wife.  We've played 5 missions at this point (which IRL would have taken us weeks because we have kids).  We had one weird drop out during a road event which rolled back when I reset the game, no issues during missions (fingers crossed) and a few times where there was some delay joining the game.  I can imagine it might be difficult and frustrating with 2 more players and people dropping out.If you like the boardgame and want a very accessible way to play it.  This is great!  EARLY ACCESS PART : Does a good job of employing the game mechanics into a pc game... at this stage not exactly like the real game in terms of the campaign mode (that said campaign mode isn't yet out so we would need to wait on that).  'Guildmaster' mode lets you play coop relatively smoothly, key things to note on this is there's no Battle Goals or Personal Goals.  Unlocking perk points and classes seems more related to the 'trainer' quests, which are basic milestones like 'do X non combat damage'/'inflict status effects x number of times' etc etc.  Can't say much as to the campaign mode as its not out, but if its done well, this will be a winner.. as it is, if you like gloomhaven the boardgame, this is very promising

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played the board game, this retains a lot of the spirit and strategy of the original. If you haven't, welcome to Gloomhaven! It is a punishing but beautifully executed turn-based combat tactics game with card mechanics. You slowly build a deck of ability cards for your chosen character(s) and you use them in combat scenarios on a hex grid to progress through the story of the city of Gloomhaven and the world it occupies. There are unique races, interesting lore, and of course lots of fun combat. I played the original board game version for some time, but I'm much happier with this version.
_childDocuments_.name: Gloomhaven

_childDocuments_.review: Although Gloomhaven is a turn based RPG, it is very unique and extremely immersive and challenging.You start by picking 2 characters of which I have found Cragheart and the Scoundrel to be the best combo for me.Others might like other combos, so just play to find out.There is a very RPGish map to plan your partys moves as well as color codes indicating the difficulty of each route taken to the objectives and destinations along the way.Once inside your destination, the game becomes a dungeon crawl requiring deep thinking, strategy and tactics.At first you might lose many many times, but you will learn and once you learn this very unique and complex battle system the game becomes extremely fun.Moreover, even when your learning and dying the game becomes extremely addictive.Now I know most gamers are very intelligent, but this game will require FULL use of your brain cells.The reason is that each of your two characters have a hand of several cards.You must manage the use of these cards in a few ways:1) Before performing an action with a card, you must take notice of the little "burn" icon on the card in the lower right.That icon means once its used its GONE forever.2)The order in which you select your 2 cards each turn and the order you use them.In addition, the cards are split into an upper and lower section, i.e. each card actually equals 2 cards and depending what you pick out fo the 2 selections on each card determines whats available on the 2nd card.I think I got that right...its easier to watch a video or just play the game to see what I mean.3) If you do not manage your cards properly you will run out of cards and die.Thus, try not to use any cards with the burn icon unless its a life or death situation.I like to save mine for the last room.It is much better to use one card and skip the 2nd card in order to preserve it as a "discard".You can get the discards back a couple of ways, which adds to your thinking.4) I can not stress card management enough, you cannot play like other games where you can just play a card for the sake of playing it...nope...one mistake can cost you, two will really hurt you so you must THINK and PLAN.One of the KEY decisions you will have to make is when to take damage and when to lose a card(s) instead.This increases the intensity of the game, as it is very common at least for me to bring my characters health down to 1, in order to preserve my cards.Also, the AI is very very good and some types of enemies that are fragile in other games, these same enemies such as archers and skeletal fighters are quite tough in this game, i.e. the archers will shoot you to shreds and the skeletons heal and buff themselves,Here are the Pros and Cons:PROS:Great graphics and good sound effects.Very unique and original.Extremely addictive.Fun once you get the hang of it.Immense feeling of accomplishment after each dungeon.Very very immersive....time will fly by in the real world!CONS:The game is in Alpha, so there are a few bugs and missing features such as multiplayer.Those who played the board game by the same name have different opinions of how it compares or duplicates that experience.Very challenging to learn as there are no instructions yet, but tons of Utube videos to help you.In conclusion, if you want a hardcore turn based  RPG that requires you to THINK and consider your tactics, then this game is for you.If you want forgiveness and a feeling of being special and not having to use your brain then it is not for you.The game is so good and challenging at this point it will only get better, which is incredible, considering how much of a fun challenge ot is now.The discussion forum and community is very helpful so dont be afraid to ask them questions.Use the Alpha to become a MASTER, which will take time, but will be worth it come multiplayer later on.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good, but not flawless version of a hardcore, ultra-instinct nerd board game that you are most likely to enjoy in this format if you enjoyed it in the previous one. Me and my friends bought the OG board game couple of years ago but we struggled to finish it because it became progressively harder and harder to get 4 people together in one space and the game takes quite some time to set up plus the tedium of keeping track of xp, achievements etc. So we stopped midway, therefore this digital version was a godsent for us as we really enjoyed the core gameplay of Gloomhaven. So here's a quick rundown of the good and the bad:Pros - 1) Challenging (on all difficulties) and tactical gameplay 2) A lot of classes/characters to choose from and  almost all of them are very unique and the enemy variety is also really high 3) Animations, character/environmental design and artstyle are not amazing however they are very fitting to the game and at the same time they represent accurate renditions of the board game 4) No more time lost on setting up or restarting the game, forgetting or breaking rules. All of the comforts of a digital version 5) Game greatly rewards cooperative and thoughtful plays and on the right difficulty setting provides a tense "all odds against you" situations where it feels more like a puzzle game, if you and your mates play your hands right you will win. I loved this aspect 6) A lot of content even after finishing the campaign 7) The price which is below 20 bucks in my region, that's a huge plus right there.Cons - 1) Lacks polish in some aspects. We had frequent desyncs, quest/item marker bugs, soft locks etc. 2) Even though the system requirements are very low, this game runs horribly on low-end pcs and it also causes the game to slow down for the whole party as the game waits for the player who is experiencing issues. 3) Sometimes the A.I takes a long time to figure out its' turn. 4) Character balance. Some of them are very underpowered (but not useless) while certain others are completely broken. For example the nightshroud is insanely strong but nothing even comes close to a fully decked out level 9 berzerker with the correct item build. The berzerker can run through a whole map and kill a 50 hp boss and then clear the whole last room and survive on their first turn, it is so broken it's not even funny. 5) Missing features like party/global achievements from the board game and steam achievements too for that matter 6) Story and characters are not interesting at all 7) Mission variety... This and performance issues were the biggest ones for me. Missions get repetitive very soon but there are several unique encounters which are super fun and I wish there were more of those. 8) Rng can be a huge factor and pain in the a.. but this game still offers a much better system than just regular dice rolls so this one's mixed.Overall I mostly enjoyed this experience and I think that the pricing is on point too so it is definitely worth purchasing in my opinion. I am looking forward to the 2 expansions and maybe frosthaven because I have been convinced that the digital version is the way to go in this case.
