_childDocuments_.review: Hell yeah I'd recommend this.. but not vanilla. As great as the foundation laid out by PGI is, the base game is just too barren and missing that bit of OOMPH to really make it shine. Enter; MODDERS. Once again, another game greatly amplified and extended and improved upon by the homebrew community. These are not just outstanding mods, but I would say they are close to as essential as you can get. Each one offers massive, yet balanced, additions and changes to the game and turns it from an okay 'Mech shooter into a sprawling, in-depth, strategy-laced, supreme RPG -- taking you right the way into the Clan Invasion! It's a fantastic game, truly engrossing, the 'Mech construction and kitting out is so enjoyable, the missions varied (though with only 6 or 7 archetypes they can get more than a little stale towards the end of the 100+ hour playthrough), and the overall story is enjoyable enough to keep your attention.Sadly the performance leaves a lot to be desire, it's truly wretched more often than not, regardless of how powerful your machine is - the engine just buckles and it can't seem to handle its own weight. It's not uncommon to see framerates dropping to the low teens during heavy fights, yet CPU and GPU usage remain frustratingly low. Still, if you can put up with that (and if I can, you can!) you're in for one hell of a 'Mech stompy adventure. Just, again, don't play vanilla.. get those mods (or the likes of YAML and TTRulez AI) to truly experience what this game can offer.

_childDocuments_.review: The game at its core is absolutely worth buying. This is what AAA games ought to strive for. Right out of the box, you have decent Mech customization and the Singleplayer story is very much worthwhile. I appreciate the fact that you can get people to join your Singleplayer game by loading the file in the multiplayer menu. The music is wonderful and I'd love to get a copy of the soundtrack to listen to on occasion.The single player story is wonderful and ties in well to the lore, which I recommend delving into while playing, especially if you're not doing something story critical. YouTube channels I highly recommend for lore dives: Big Red 40 Tech (for technical delves into individual mechs, some lore, and even exposure to the TTG) and Sven van der Plank (for raw lore). The lore of this franchise is rich and certainly worthwhile.Pay attention to the news crawl on the bottom of the screen when playing or in mission selection.While the game is wonderful on its own, it's best with mods, especially the ones in the Yet Another series. YAML (Yet Another MechLab) is an absolute must as it drastically improves the customization of your Mechs. Armor Green and Colorized Heat Gauge will make it easier to track the status of Mechs (yours and your targets). Mod Options to have a tighter control over how the mods behave, MechAssault Mechs will bring in the heavy metal found in that spinoff. Finally, Yet Another Clan Invasion to add Clan Era mechs, the Clan faction and some absolutely worthwhile parts; this particular one is not only large (2GB download at time of writing), but is practically its own DLC. No Vortex required, you can mix Workshop mods and Nexus mods and it's easy to mod the game. Furthermore, the devs do a wonderful job supporting their modding community. When Rise of Rasalhauge dropped, most of the big mods (especially of the Yet Another series) had updates within 48 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: (WAFFLING, SEE-SAWING HAND GESTURE)This is a pretty good game......It is NOT, however, a very good MECHWARRIOR game.I would recommend almost any other mainline Mechwarrior game before this one. Every one of them has: better AI, better AI MANAGEMENT, WAY better mechlabs, better map layouts, better sense of scale, MORE THAN 3 FRIGGIN' LANCEMATES, ACTUALLY varied objectives, stories that ACTUALLY make sense, better selection and variety of mechs, (sigh)... I could go on.What MW5 DOES have is: it looks good, it sounds good, it runs on modern hardware, the few missions that ARE unique tend to be decent and.... Uhhh.... Well, that's about it, really.--And YES, before all the pedants come stampeding in; there lots of mods that fix lots of these issues. I even started a second playthrough just so that I could mod it up to what it should have been in the first place. BUT, MW5 itself (and PGI, more importantly) deserve ZERO credit for a bunch of mods being practically required to make their game a proper Mechwarrior game. ALSO, a lot of the mods aren't even use-able anymore, usually because they got sick of PGI breaking them all the time.I'd say this is a SOFT recommend, especially on sale. Don't bother with ANY of the DLC until you're sure you like the game though- it's all pretty lackluster anyway. It's kind of a shame though, because there's elements in here that prove it COULD have been a truly amazing MW game. SOME people obviously cared about the game and put in solid work. And then everybody ELSE had just been brainwashed by PGI and put in the bare minimum effort and pushed it out the door.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the people with rose-tinted glasses or the disgruntled MWO players fool you. This game  is a serious contender on my list for probably being one of the best MechWarrior/BattleTech universe games in the franchise I've played as a long-time fan. Yes, that includes MechWarrior 2, 3, 4, and all the expansions that came with them. (2 Mercs, 3 Pirate's Moon, 4 Black Knight, Mercs, etc.)Here's why.Let's start off with the elephant in the room:  There isn't a wide range of options for mech customization compared to other games: the mechlab is overly simplified, the storyline and mission design feel less interesting than those in the previous MechWarrior entries, the base AI is pretty bad (then again, friendly AI always seemed terrible in MW games that included them), there's no official Clan content yet as of writing this review, no Elementals, no pilotable vehicles, no championship arena, I could go on. But, with mods, I can easily say that MW5: Mercs has the most in-depth mechlab customization and amount of fun I've experienced in any MechWarrior game.I'm a real stickler for more options. Yet Another Mechlab and its associated mods deserve some special recognition here, as it gives you the same amount of options for mechlab customization as MW3's or MWO's (such as the choice of installing Ferro-Fibrous armor, Endo-Steel internal structures, XL engines, double heat sinks, Clan versions of weapons/equipment, and so on) but now with current-gen graphics and a MWO-style UI all in a singleplayer package. I could even argue that the amount of possible Mech customization rivals or exceeds what you could do in MW3 or MW4: Mercs. The customization doesn't simply extend to mechs alone. There are mods that improve the AI (both friendly & enemy) to play reasonably well and you'll find your teammates holding their own in a fight quite often, even occasionally rivaling the damage output a human player could achieve. Another mod can add repair bays to maps based on the context of the mission, like the ones you could find in MW4's campaigns. Others can change your HUD to a 3D version for more immersion, change the soundscape to make weapon reports and projectile impacts feel far more visceral, add such an insane amount of extra particle effects and smoke to make mech combat & map destruction become an incredibly cinematic spectacle at the cost of eating your GPU. It's hard to put into words just how many options are at your disposal to fine tune for an optimal MechWarrior experience.Best of all,  It's been an absolute blast playing through the base game's campaign with friends, something I always wished was possible in previous MechWarrior games.I'd like to finish off this review with admitting that I'm generally biased against most newer entries in beloved franchises. I understand that many fans of a franchise, including myself, often have valid criticisms for what they see as "downgrades" over previous entries. Sometimes, we do get blinded by nostalgia factor alone in spite of the improvements.And here I am telling you that MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries is absolutely worthy of being called a real MechWarrior game. Is MW5: Mercs objectively better than MW2-4? Probably not. But, with the right mods, it just might be.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a flawed, flawed, seriously flawed game. But... it is pretty fun. So positives and negatives, negatives first, because there's more of them:Negatives:The story is beyond terrible. So bland and uninteresting it actually brings the experience down a bit. Luckily it's something you can pretty much ignore as it is a sandbox style game.Voice Acting is pretty bad - ties in with the terrible story.Mech lab is clunky and limited. The upgrades you can do to mechs is surprisingly limited - and the way repairs and changes work is unnecessarily clunky. Battletech and MWO are far superior in pretty much all aspects here.Your AI lance hover between idiotic and MWO pubs. In fact, I have a sneaky suspicion that PGI based the AI on MWO pub matches, as they tend to act in a similar fashion - stepping directly in front of you, stomping through and destroying defensive positions, ignoring targeting orders to hide on the backline...Mission variety isn't great. Probably because of the sandbox nature preventing crafted missions, it does all blend together after a while.Positives:It's fun. Walking around in a stompy mech and shooting other stompy mechs is fun. The core gameplay loop is enjoyable, and to be honest, that covers a lot of sins.The 'gotta catch em all' is strong - building up a stable of bigger and stronger mechs and equipment is a fun driver that has had me play 20 odd hours in the last week. Conclusion:It's good. Not great, not bad, but good. Mods will probably help, future patches will probably help - but the game is decent now.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a simple answer to "should you play MW5". If you love BattleTech universe and spent your childhood piloting virtual mechs, its an absolute Yes.MechWarrior games were never examples of the best game craft, having technical issues, poor plots, changing mechanics throughout the years. But MW series were always a staple in a genre it helped create and almost single handedly promoted. There were some good games insipred by MW, the likes of Heavy Gear, StarSiege, G-Nome, but MechWarrior was always the pinnacle, and given the lack of MW-clones now, it is the only game that helps satiate the hunger for piloting a giant steel robot shining with firing guns like a christmas tree. The more precious this game is to me, as it brings a full single player campaign to the franchise that previously was available only in online format, Enter MechWarrior Online, from which MW5 takes design, art and mechanics.The solo campaign is your typical mercenary story, too similar to what we experienced in recent BattleTech game, and at times it feels as I am playing that same campaign, albeit not commanding the Mechs, but piloting one of them directly. There are your story missions, side missions chained together in small stories that revolve around Succession Wars, and one-off missions that you do if you need extra C-bills, or try to salvage a ceratin Mech before you progress the sotry. It could be better, but at least it's a serviceable package to wrap the mech piloting in. I wish, the next thing the devs do is the Clan invasion, which will hopefully bring not only the iconic Onmi Mechs (ah, Timber Wolf, i miss you so much), but also better campaign that would not require you to roam the Inner Sphere and instead take part in Invasion campaign (and i can only hope, we would be able to choose sides).Gameplay-wise, it's the same good old MechWarrior game with the physics and mechanics from MWO, which were polished during the online game's life. Mechs feel good to control, you feel the weight of the machines on the field. Combat missions are diverse, you have your typical protect the settlement, destroy the settlement, survive the assault, and raid a zone (destroy several key targets scattered on the map). Nothing too fancy, but it allows you to choose from what you want to do and forego what you dont want to.However, the one thing to spoil the fun is you team mates' AI. They are dumb. An AI pilot can wreck his 100 tons mech if they solo rush an enemy squad, and they do that a lot. They pay no attention to damaged parts, and keep on pushing the enemy even if they are one shot way from death. One thing I found that somehow counteracts the AI behaviour is not giving them close range weapons (SRM first and foremost), as the AI seemingly chooses the weapon with highest DPS and prioritizes its usage over anything else (so if an enemy is not in range, they simply rush them).The enemies also prefer suicidal runs. Is breaks immersion, as you know that if there is an enemy medium Mech with an AC10 it will do its best to close the distance, do as much damage as possible and die. They in no way behave like pilots, who want to survive the encounter.But even these setbacks are not enough to prevent a fan from playing this game and having immense fun with it. In part, this is due to that sensation of piloting a Mech, which is as strong in my late 30-s as it was in my teens. In other part, this is due lack of any meaningful competition in the genre, There are no Heavy Gear, Star Siege, or anytheing else alike. At times I even wish that From Soft take a long pause with Soulsborne and give us another Armored Core game, nevermind how strong I like soulsborne series.A quick note on the game's performance. It's not AAA graphics, but it looks solid enough with no visaul glithces to break immersion during comabt missions. One thing to note is poor ray tracing. On my RTX 2070 (playing in 1080p), RT drops framerate to 20-30 FPS with DLSS, while with RT off, I play at 120-140 FPS easily on high settings. Doom Eternal runs at fixed 144 FPS on  high setting with RT on, and Cyberpunk 2077 play steadily above 60 FPS with RT on as well. Since RT does not bring anything noteworty to MW5, i'd suggest keeping it off and enjoy the highest framerate.

_childDocuments_.review: --If it's on a discount, you might as well just buy everything. Otherwise, at least get the Heroes of the Inner Sphere DLC for career mode. Rasalhague adds other mercenary companies. Call to Arms adds a lot of melee weapons (which, speaking as a newcomer to Battletech, are surprisingly lethal).--Without mods, it's serviceable. Stomping and shooting in the vanilla game is fun, but mech customization is pretty shallow compared to what you can do with just the Mechlab mod on the workshop, and the mission variety can feel a bit stale after a while if you aren't actively planning and testing out builds. A full-price purchase is not recommended if you do not intend to mod the game.--With mods, it's one of the best giant robot games on the market, especially if you're into PvE content. Other than Mechlab, I personally recommend 'vonBiomes' on Steam Workshop and 'Coyote's Mission Mod' on Nexus. Those three mods alone turn the game into a sandbox where even the lightest mechs can be turned into monstrosities of engineering with enough C-bills, some lucky salvage, and a little bit of creativity.--For the love of god, and the sake of your own sanity, download the the 'jumpship animation skip' mod. I didn't think it would bother me until the first time I checked every stop in an industrial hub.--Modded co-op with friends is possible, but not flawless. I strongly advise running similar mod lists to minimize jank. Only the host can use the starmap, initiate and negotiate contracts, view the shop and mech market, and skip forward on the timeline. Story/Career progression is saved only for the host. Jumping to a different system will cancel all changes in progress if one of the other players is customizing a mech.--Make sure to keep your weapon groups simple for any mech you're giving to friendly AI.

_childDocuments_.review: A long-overdue single-player game for the MechWarrior franchise, MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries shakes up the game's usual format with predominantly randomly generated missions, although there are certain hand-crafted questlines here and there. After the tutorial quest chain (which you can skip if you have the DLC, but more on that later) you are sent off to look for a few choice contracts in the nearest warzone and strike it rich with the modest stable of mechs you have on hand. Or die trying. Wouldn't be getting that much hazard pay for nothing, right?The game's overarching plot – or what passes for it – focuses on the exploits of one Commander Mason. After inheriting his father's mercenary company after the latter's death (which is par for the course in the Inner Sphere) he sets off on a quest for vengeance against the pirate group who killed his father, while making a name for himself along the way. Perhaps nothing that stands out on its own, but it's serviceable enough as a plot hook.If there's one thing I think they did especially well for the main campaign, it's that the game pits you against combat vehicles at the start, only gradually introducing enemy mechs from the tutorial missions and onwards. I feel like it helps to cement just how significant battlemechs are in the setting individually. Of course, that effect may lessen once you're up against a bunch of heavies and assaults, but lighter mechs and even the teeny combat vehicles are never phased out among the roster of enemies.The core gameplay loop is simple enough: do missions, get paid, get better stuff, repeat. The negotiation mechanics are an interesting addition with which you can haggle for a mix of extra pay, salvage rights or coverage for damage sustained in the mission. A better reputation with your client means more bargaining power, while bitter hostility with them gives you much less. Extra gear, pilots, and sometimes mechs can be purchased from industrial hubs if you're lucky enough to find what you're looking for, but don't expect a guarantee.After each mission, besides the usual rewards you are able to salvage weapons, parts and mechs from the field based on what you fought and how many salvage shares you bargained for. Salvaging mechs is typically cheaper than buying them from the market, often in less-than-mint condition. Additionally, damage you take in the field has to be repaired between missions, and destroyed weapons have to be replaced from your inventory, encouraging the player to keep the long-term in mind and choose their battles carefully.The mechs in-game are a fairly decent spread of types from the era the game's set in, with others being introduced as the timeline progresses, a detail which I quite liked. They also handle fairly well, though you might want to make sure throttle decay's turned on so you're not still rushing ahead after letting go of the forward key. The faster light mechs have enough speed to make combat feel almost like 2D dogfighting. Jump jets give you another axis of mobility to play with, on certain chassis. Heavy and assault mechs are even able to power straight through walls. It never gets old when you do the whole Kool-Aid Man routine and blow apart the poor sucker on the other side with an AC/20.The actual mech customisation, however, is somewhat lacking. I wasn't expecting anything on par with the sometimes dizzying complexity of MechWarrior Online, but the limited variation of weapon hardpoints between chassis felt restrictive at times. The painting interface, on the other hand, offers a great deal of freedom. Whether you want a company-wide uniform or a hangar full of modern art pieces, it's quick to put a colour scheme together from one menu and apply it to just one or all the mechs in your active hangar. Or even a select few that you specify. Easier than painting miniatures, indeed.Personally, I find that the game truly shines when played co-operatively. Another new direction for the series, up to three additional players can be invited to the game as your lancemates, opening up a far broader array of tactics. Without having to babysit the AI, you have a much easier time in getting one person up front as a scout and another hanging back to provide fire support, for example. It's absolutely satisfying to coordinate as a team against tougher-than-expected odds and just  make it out alive. Even if the repair bill costed more than what the job was worth.AI for friend and foe alike... could use some work, I feel. It's okay, but like many other features in the game, it could be better. The command interface for your lancemates is fairly limited. Attack this thing, follow me, go to where my cursor's pointed, et cetera. I would have liked to have been able to set waypoints for them on the battle map instead. As for the enemies, I feel like they could have benefited from being able to fight smarter instead of charging in like lemmings unless they were an LRM platform. A friend of mine even pointed out to me that they would not acquire targets outside their sensor range, allowing the player to plink shots at them from far enough away without fear of retaliation.While I myself do not own any of the DLC, the game gets  points for being able to play it through joining a DLC-owning friend's session. But based on what it adds – namely the expanded starting options for campaign play and quirks for mechs – I can't help but think it should have been added to the base game as part of an update, especially with the price they're apparently charging for it. As I do not own the DLC, that is all I shall say on the matter.After having played it for long enough, I find myself taking a step back and thinking, "There's so much more the devs could have done here." Committing war crimes in stompy murder robots is all the more fun with your friends, but off the battlefield there's not that much for them to do. They can walk around the ship and the host can give the other players permission to refit and repair mechs, but unfortunately that's about it. There's no way to allow them control over specific duties, like putting someone in charge of buying new gear... although considering how that may make things spiral wildly out of control among certain player groups, that might be for the best.Likewise, the main plot (should you choose to focus on that) could have been so much more. I shan't spoil anything, but once I got to the end it felt rather... abrupt, really. Like a three act play that cuts off after act two. Which was a shame as it left me hankering for more. Assuming that the plot thread does get expanded upon at all, I imagine it would be as part of, what else, another DLC. The other hand-crafted quest chains each have their own little story to tell, but they're still made up of mission types from the same limited pool as the random ones. A greater variety of mission objectives would have also helped keep things fresh, I feel.At the end of the day, MechWarrior 5 is a game that quite clearly has potential, but something about it feels like that potential has not been fully realised. Fairly satisfying gameplay – if a little repetitive – but not without flaws in mech customisation and what felt like a half-finished main plotline. All in all, it's okay at best. Still, I had fun with it. Certainly get it on sale with a couple of friends for the co-op. Mods can help fill in for the weak links, but the same could be said for practically any other game now, for better or worse.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was awesome, and I'm really annoyed I let some of the negative reviews on here dissuade me for awhile. For some qualification, I only played through the base game with no DLCs or mods, and only did the campaign solo, no online stuff, so that's what I'm reviewing here. I have played all of the MechWarrior titles (except MWO) and their expansions before this, so I'm primarily thinking about this game as its campaign compares to the rest of the series campaigns. If you've loved the other MechWarrior games, I can't imagine you won't love this one too.I want to give my two cents on some of the complaints I've seen about this game. First, I experienced almost zero glitching or bugs. I know I'm coming to this game a few years after release, so maybe they've released some bug fixes and took care of the things folks were seeing. IDK, but it was pretty rock solid for me on windows 11. The only bug I ran into was occasionally a campaign mission that was supposed to be available at a certain planet wouldn't show, but saving, popping back to the title screen, and reloading fixed this every time, and it occurred maybe 3 times in my whole play through, so it just didn't bother me.Second, I saw some complaints that the lancemate AI is bad, specifically I saw some mention that pathing is bad, and that your lancemates deal lots of friendly fire to you and each other. I didn't really experience this either, or at least it was no worse than any other game in the series. If you walk right in front of one of your guys during a firefight, I don't really know what you expect to happen. There is going to be _some_ friendly fire. Its not like they don't know you're there and continually try to shoot through you, but you'll definitely catch the odd stray hit if you are all bunched up, especially if you are equipping your mates with weapons that have some spread. I also don't really know why I saw pathing complaints. Telling your lancemates to follow you or go to a navpoint works just as well as it always has IMO. I just didn't experience any issues with either of these problems.Third, I saw some complaints about the story, or supposed lack thereof. I thought the story was simple but good. Its not the Witcher 3 or anything, but it easily met my expectations coming from the other games in the series. There is even a fun twist at the end that I really liked, having a basic understanding of the BattleTech lore and timeline. The voice acting was -- if not quite up to "Deadeye" from MW2 Mercs standards -- solid. One reason I suspect folks complained about the story is because this game greatly expands the nearly-open-world vibe of MW4 to a truly open world with what seems to be hundreds of planets, a large portion of which offer contracts for you to take. Since there are so many more than the other games, a lot of the missions for these contracts are not each handcrafted and are mostly a limited set of generated mission types. To advance the campaign and get better gear, you do have to pick up a lot of these sort of procedural missions, and towards the beginning of my playthrough this did feel a little bit grindy, which I would say is not something I have experienced with any of the other MW games. As I got better mechs and more money though, I thought this kind of play got a lot more fun, it was just that in the beginning having to kill everything in a crappy mech with just medium lasers and lrm5s that was kinda lame. As a result, this game took a lot more playtime to complete than any other MW game I've played. I'd say there was just as much story as usual, but it was a bit diluted by these extra, non-story missions you have to take on. When I started getting some decent heavy mechs -- black knight about midway through my playthrough was awesome -- I was having a good time with these, and by the time I had a couple Annihilators in my lance, I pretty much relished in as much destruction as I could get, story-based or not.Overall, great game and very worthy addition to the series.
_childDocuments_.name: MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries

_childDocuments_.review: ---  THE GOOD ---- The game is enormous. If you want value for money, you cannot go wrong with this. It's not one of those crappy modern games that takes someone around 4 or 5 hours to complete. For reference, I've got just over 100 hours played, and only now have a full lance / team of assault mechs (Yeah I know, I'm a bit slow on this game. More on that in a bit).- Amazing variety of mechs, which all have variants, each with their own weapons loadouts / set ups. One could have a setup for more long range combat, others can be more oriented towards close quarters brawling. So there's likely a mech for everyone. And it's great fun to play around with this.Some mechs can be tailored for certain mission types too. For example, on Assassination missions, I find it good fun to bombard enemies from afar with mechs like the iconic Catapult, and have one or two heavies for backup. It's also handy to have jump jets, because it opens up new gameplay options.On the other hand, if you like to run & and gun / hit 'n run, you could try faster mechs with less armour and weapons on them for quick Raids or Demolition contracts.And contrary to that, you can use heavies & assault mechs where you're basically giant tanks or artillery platforms on legs. Make no mistake though, depending on the difficulty level - usually indicated by tonnage limit on a contract – you might think that using 4 beastly mechs means that you can just steam roll an enemy. But think again. Because the game always has a way of chucking a fly in the ointment, or a "monkey and the wrench", so that you may just end up with some badly damaged mechs by the end of a mission if you're careless. But I like that, it's a good kind of uncertainty where you rarely feel overpowered.  - Fun co-op. Works well most of the time, because you can coordinate and plan various tactics and strategies. I've not had many problems with connecting, but did have an issue where my friend kept being chucked into spectator mode. Not sure why, but it oddly just went away.Quick gripe about co-op though, is that when anyone's a guest in another person's game, they can't earn any C-Bills(in game currency) or salvage. It would have been fantastic if the C-Bills or salvage you earn at the end of a co-op mission could be given to each person to take back to their games, same for salvage. This would definitely be welcomed and appreciated in a future game update.- Really love the vibe of the game, including the retro synthy main menu theme. Mechwarrior 4 Mercenaries was my introduction to mech games WAY back, because I was late to the PC games party, and I loved it. But due to the 4th game being so iconic, this game had some sizeable boots to fill. And dare I say it, it's done it rather well. - Sound effects are superb. The escalating, out of control whirring of a gunship coming down after you laser them out of the sky, followed by a crisp boom when they impact the ground never gets old. One minor gripe I'll add though; the pounding of the footsteps of each mech are basically the same, rather than being a colossal thump when in heavier mechs and a little bump in lighter ones.- The maps and visuals are really immersive and detailed considering the sheer vastness of the game. The graphical settings are all set to high at 1080p, but I don't have an RTX video card so no ray tracing for me. But it still looks sweet 🙂 Landscapes range in size and conditions, from expansive icy tundra, to gloomy arid deserts which resemble something out of the old Star Wars films. Then you have lush, picturesque and tranquil forests(tranquil until you get there LOL), or baron wastelands that are akin to how Mars is depicted in films like Total Recall or John Carpenter's Ghosts Of Mars 🧐Sometimes these Planets can have different weather patterns aswell, including the sort that can cause issues, which includes sulphur or acid rain. This can make your weapons overheat a little quicker if you're too trigger happy. But juxtaposed to that, there might be a blizzard or snow storm on icy levels, and while that does indeed obscure your view significantly, it has a slightly positive affect on the cooling of weapons.Then you have volcanic islands with active volcanoes spitting out liquid hot MAG-MA 😅😛Lava really flows throughout the map too, which can become an environmental hazard, causing overheating or permanent damage if you're not cautious. Very well done that is, and it gives each of the different maps a unique feel. That's hard to do in a game of this magnitude, so props 👍One other small gripe in regards to the aforementioned weather systems: it would have been a nice touch if it was slightly dynamic weather.- Mods. Cheers again to all you mod wizards out there, because there's so many cracking mods for this game, and it's lovely how easy they are to install too. Thank you 😊- Exploration is tip top. It's clear as crystal that Piranha games have done a superb job with the depths and detail of the Starmap. It's really something to behold. And a lot of the names of each star system are like Easter eggs too. Many of them are references to history, films and other games:Altair(Assassins Creed), Argyle(Limo driver in Die Hard haha), Belladonna(Thrill Kill), Tortuga & Port Royal(Pirates of the Caribbean), MCalister(Home Alone), and Romulus & Vulkan(Star Trek).Also, it's brill how the map changes over time, and uniquely for each player, depending on which factions / clans they work for the most as time progresses.Have to say though, at first, the Starmap is so gigantic that it may appear a little on the daunting side, especially to a sort of newbie or very rusty player like myself.That flows into my first real negative point...- The Codex. While packed with info, I don't like it. At the beginning of a game as immense in scale as this, it's definitely worth having a more in depth tutorial to learn as you play instead. I know that the function of a Codex is there to sort of refer back to whenever needed - like on the Mass Effect games - but after completing a very basic tutorial, you're just chucked straight into the deep end, and it feels like you need to read a LOT just to know what to do or where to go like...It felt overwhelming to say the least. And I played the 4th game, so if this is your intro to Mechwarriors, I feel for you. Nevertheless, don't let it put you off trying if that is the case.--- THE BAD ---- The music. Not the quality, but the variety. Gets repetitive fast. To the point where I created a playlist of ambient tracks from other games, including old Mechwarrior games.There's a lot more music in the older games, which is backwards, considering how Mechwarrior 5 seems way larger than those games.- Friendly AI can be bloody appalling!I've not shouted as much profanity for a while as I have whilst playing this. Friendly AI haven't got a clue most of the time. It's like they've over indulged on stupid pills. But enemy AI seem to be controlled by Skynet, because they never miss a beat.One time, using cockpit view and zoomed in shooting an enemy, a friendly mech comes walking right across my line of fire as if they're strolling to a picnic, getting pebble dashed by autocannon rounds and laser fire. Morons! 😡🤬👉Some of the worst friendly AI I've come across, and I've played some right doozies over the years... - Annoying repetition issue. Going up to speak with Ryana after each campaign mission was such an unnecessary chore.Also, at the end of a Raid mission using slow assault mechs, instead of landing right by us, the drop ship decided to land the other side of a f*cking ravine! We didn't have any mechs with jump jets so had to go the VERY long way round. Utter dog sh* t! Royally boiled my p *ss that did! 🤨😠Again, unnecessary frustration. In a game like this, options to choose where the drop ship lands would be awesome.Cheers for reading. Give it a go, it's worth it 😉
_childDocuments_.name: MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries

_childDocuments_.review: After the release of the last DLC I have finally given up all hope of the game being fixed. The AI of this game does not function on any meaningful level and its apparent that there will be no attempt to address it. Do to how bad the pathing finding is your lancemates cant even follow you reliably. They constantly wonder off, get stuck on terrine, take detours that make no sense or my favorite just stop moving and stare off into space. Anything short of an open field just confuses them. They also cant defend themselves, or you for that matter, they have no concept of self preservation, threat identification, focusing fire or engagement range/angles. I'm tired of them walking into my missile barrages, or shooting me in the back with lasers because they dont understand beam duration. I'm tired of watching my lancemates ignore actual threats to shoot at nothing or not fire at all while said threats shoot them in the back. I'm tired of telling my LRM boat to stay at one position for fire support only for it to Leroy Jenkins into the fight on the 1st attack order (even after removing all close range weapons).I'm tired of this game not having basic unit scripting. The AI pilots a Locust the same way it does an Atlas. I'm tired of fighting at a 1/5 disadvantage, having to rely on cheese tactics cause the only way for the AI to be a challenge is overwhelming numbers because the AI doesn't understand the principles of the setting its representing.I know there are basic lance controls like "move here" and "shoot this" but its no where near good enough. "Move here" but shoot at what? "Shoot this" but what range, what weapon, what body part? Mechs in Battletech have roles. Brawler, Direct and Indirect Firesupport, Scout. Not in this game, every Mech acts the same. Walks in a line towards target, fires weapons. Thats it.    I got almost 200 hours in the game. I've tried unmodded and modded campaigns. I love Battletech. I wanted to like this game, but the complete lack of any unit behavior controls just rips the heart out of it. There is fun here but this game is just a glorified shooting gallery with no depth, with other humans its probably much more fun.
_childDocuments_.name: MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries

_childDocuments_.review: I have 500+ hours on the Epic Game version, just so you know this isn't after a minor playthrough.I would highly recommend this game...with mods.Judging the game at its baseline, it is bad. Consider the following:The writing and voice acting is atrocious. Not really something that is too much of a burden for the player, but it is just such a glaring weakness at every point in the game.Very little customization. For a game all about modifying your stompy death robot, the fact that I can't change my armor type, engine, gyro, structure, and so many other things is brutal. Especially a mercenary outfit have all the leeway it would want in that regard. Instead we get very tightly controlled 'Mechs that can only stomach minor modifications until their potential is used up. Barely any fun builds this way and not that much to go with your playstyle.The absolute minimum of "structure" around the missions. What you do doesn't really matter. Neither why you are on a planet or why you are doing certain missions. It is basically all RNG. Even for a sandbox game this is weak.Frustrating mechanics in some cases and horrible AI.The saving graces:Basic gameplay loop is very funCombat feels great, as do most of the weaponsVisuals are mostly excellentSound design for effects and the like is solid'MechsJudgement:Unless you are a die-hard fan of 'Mech games, you won't really like it, since it is sub-par in so many aspects. If you are a die-hard fan of 'Mech games, you won't really like it, since it doesn't offer the complexity that you would expect from that sort of game.Recommendation:Mod it. This fixes most weaknesses. This however does mean that the credit really only goes to the modders and certainly not to the developers. Both DLCs are worse, offering much less for almost the same price. HotIS is decent. Kestrel Lancers has too little to offer for me to consider buying it.As such, I won't give the game a thumbs up. That goes to the modders.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so when the game first came out, I was down on it because it was an Epic exclusive. Then when it came to Steam and I started playing it, I was down on it because the story was really generic and terrible. The characters are one note and completely meaningless. The ship area you hang around in looks surprisingly awful for an Unreal Engine 4 game. And the music is dull, endlessly repetitive rock tracks that you'll hate.But, I'm still playing it and I'd recommend it. Why? Because the actual gameplay is as good as mech combat like this can get, in my opinion. (Keep in mind this is the slower, heavier kind of mech combat) The management aspects for your company are completely reasonable and well-designed. And comparing this build to the initial release of the game, you can see the team has actually been improving it since then.Just take my advice, pick career mode and play for one of the great houses. No we don't have clans yet, they're coming. Just don't play the campaign. It's as bad or worse than the one from Battletech. And I left a really LONG damn review explaining that... Just play career mode. Good luck mechwarrior.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a fun co-op game, get it with some friends.If you play solo, get ready for frustration and save scumming to keep your space money.The game is a solid but bare bone one with easy moddability and good for shorter sessions with your friends who all have their own schedule. This makes for a fun co-op game.However... If you play solo you have up to three lance mates, the galaxies most okayest Lobotomites there are. You can give them commands too but they forget those after five seconds and then continue to brawl it out with the enemy until their last dying breath, if the mission is already over and you are heading to the pick up point is no concern of theirs.This makes some missions outright frustrating to play. Like raids or demolishion contracts where you could make an easy profit if not for their bloodlust.Needs decent AI asap! 6/10 get it in a sale. I wouldn't pay more then 25bucks for it and only if you have at least 2 peeps you can play it with.And yes, all 4 points that are missing is because of the AI.

_childDocuments_.review: I've done 3 full playthroughs of this game at this point, TL;DR, if you like big stompy robots with tank controls, get this game right now, but find a few mods to enhance the experience a bit.On it's own, MW5 is the most "okay" game I've ever played, it has so much going for it and so much going against it, and this is coming from a diehard Mechwarrior fan. I've been playing these games since childhood. This game has so many flaws that are miraculously fixed by mods you can find on the Nexus.Randomized missions are cool but there aren't all that many biomes and mission types. This can be fixed via the mods VonBiomes and Coyote's Mission Pack. Enemy AI is about as simple as it gets, this is fixed by using TT_RulezAI mod.The game is poorly optimized and runs like ♥♥♥♥, even this can be fixed via XenoPax's Optimize mod. So many problems, all fixed by mods. This is the Bethesda approach, I don't want my games busted out of the box, but at least all the fixes are free I guess. The core combat is amazing but everything surrounding it is lacking which, again, can be fixed by just pumping your game full of the latest mods. As much as I hate to admit it, once I did this, the game really clicked for me, its why I put over 100 hours in, I love this franchise and once the gameplay loop gets going I never wanna stop. Needless to say my feelings for this game are rather conflicted. I do recommend it, but I also recommend you get it for a friend since Coop is infinitely more fun than playing alone with 3 braindead AI buddies.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time mechwarrior fan, I can't really recommend this game in good faith. The main story is absolutely awful, the minute-to-minute combat is fun, but hugely repetitive, and there is a HUGE lack of variety in gameplay, missions, and mechs themselves. All mechs feel identical, lacking any nuance or design differentiation. And they are GOD UGLY to boot. Most of the reviews on here say the graphics are bad, but I think the game looks fine. Graphically. ARTISTICALLY though, the game is atrocious. Some mechs look okay, but others are completely unrecognizable from established designs. Its very clear that they had one artist, and this artist apparently has a fetishistic view of generic 2010s sci-fi movie motifs. Random, pointless panel lines. Big chunks of featureless metal that serve no purpose, jutting out from the structures with absolutely no thought as to their purpose. Completely nonsensical cockpit designs. And every single mech in the game has clipping on the level of an original xbox game. These mechs are supposed to be hundreds of years apart, designed by different nations. For different purposes. On different planets. Yet, they all look like they walked out of the same factory, on the same day, ready to be featured in some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 2010 sci-fi action thriller that you'll watch once and never spare a braincell to think about again.Aside from the horrifically generic, and outright BAD art design, the rest of the game features similar issues. The story is nothing. The type of thing again, you experience once, then never think about again. The characters... Well, there aren't any. Its just bored voice actors repeating the same dull unfunny lines. The gameplay is incredibly dull. The same few poorly re-designed vehicles running directly at you like you're playing hoard mode. Mech on mech combat is equally dull. Bad AI just making a B-line to you, only to scrape away your armor, and leave you with a repair bill. The completely generic combat means that there is no difference between light and assault mechs. Lights run fast, but since everything hits you with laser precision, there is functionally no reason to have any light mechs on your team. And at the late game, playing a light mech is actual suicide. Its not like mechwarrior 3 or 4 where you can viably play a smaller chassis, and out maneuver your enemy. Its truly sad that such an amazing, thoughtful franchise as battletech has ended up this way. I pray that someone else gets the licence for this franchise, and makes something worthwhile in the future.I'm actually choosing to add onto this review in reply to some of the comments I've received. Firstly, I'll elaborate on what I think mechwarrior 3 achieved, being that its my favourite game in the franchise. Right from the get-go, mechwarrior 3 tries immerse you in its world. When you begin a mission, the very first thing you hear is the reactor powering up behind you. The sound shifts from ear to ear as it comes to life. Once you start moving, the game grounds you with this incredibly heavy with HUGE sense of momentum. One of my favourite things is piloting a light mech, going full speed into a wall, and slamming into it so hard your mech falls onto its butt. Another thing is the terrain deformation. Firing a salvo of missiles into the ground makes a huge crater. I know that would be technically hard to achieve now, but in 1998 it was mind blowing to see how much impact the firepower of your mech had. Lets not forget the recoil. Cannons recoiled more or less, depending on their placement and the weight of your mech. And getting hit with ballistic weapons did the same. You take an AC-20 round in a light mech, you'll be lucky to still be standing. Getting knocked about in the cockpit was engaging, and made shell firing weapons much more useful.And ammo came at a cost, If your mech begun to heat up into the danger zone, and you kept that mech running hot, your ammo would cook-off. Causing internal explosions. You, as the pilot, had the option of jettisoning your ammo, or risking keeping it inside. Mechwarrior 3 is still the closest any mech game has come to looking like the established lore. The game ripped its art directly from the TRO manuals and novel covers. Staying true to the designs of the original artists, while creating a world that looked the part around it. The voice acting, cutscenes and mission briefings added to this overall sense of immersion too. During the first mission, you get to watch as one of your fellow dropships burns up in orbit. Theres no close up on a big fireball, shouts of the crew, no dramatic music. You simply see it losing its trajectory, before it breaks up into separate pieces, shadowing the challanger shuttle disaster in eerie realism. Finally. art. yes. the 2010s were bad for me in terms of sci-fi. we really lost the design sense of the 80s and 90s, where concept artists were trying to come up with realistic representations of future technology. the works of ralph mcquarrie, steve venters and yoshikazu yasuhiko to name a few. where thought was put into how something worked, what purpose a component served and how something functions on a basic level. all of this was thrown away in the 2010s in favor of mass-market generic art designed to sell toys and look "cool" with zero idea of what something even is. mechwarrior 5 is a prime example of this. mechs that have parts that intersect with each-other during basic movement, jagged pointless grooves and greebles that sever the singular purpose of making something look "complex" having a design with zero flat surfaces isn't more realistic, just because its detailed. quite the opposite. these panel lines, grooves, and intersecting plates and random ornaments shows a fundamental misunderstanding of even the most basic of structural integrity. a design composed of 80% weakpoints isn't realistic just because it looks complex. having huge, bulky, chunky blocks where the original design had deflecting angles and singular armor plates isn't....... good. maybe that would be fine for some designs, but all of them?? to have every single mech look functionally identical, despite the massive breath of diversity in terms of lore, age, and technology???

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to like about this game. Enough, in fact, to overlook the terrible parts of it. I'm going to start with the positives.Quick MWO NoteIf you are expecting this to be a single-player version of MechWarrior Online, you will be disappointed. This is it's own game and that's a good thing. The overwhelming customization options in MWO are not in the spirit of the setting and are absurdly complicated to anyone who isn't a hardcore MWO player. And, with this game, you don't have to suffer the worst part about any MMO: the other people. They're the worst.The Great StuffGiant Stompy Mech CombatIt has plenty and it's fun. This is the part of the game they got right and they nailed it. This is a battlemech simulator and it does it well.Mech Variants GaloreThe devs included just about every mech variant that exists in the lore and then some extras they made up (probably pulled from MWO). These "hero" mechs are pretty amazing but hard to find and can be pricey. That makes it even better when you do get your hands on one. They could even be MORE rare and I would be fine with it. Finding them would be a significant event.Cooperative PlayHoly cow, does this make up for everything this game does wrong. The ability to invite friends to play with as a lance is the single greatest feature of this game. I haven't had this much fun with friends online in a long time. Who needs big expensive mech simulator booths at hard-to-find locations when you can use the Internet! (Ok, I do, but that's beside the point.) And the best part, the only people in your game are the ones you invite. Those other people are the worst. Did I mention that?The Good StuffMaps AplentyThe maps are varied with lots of different terrain features that make battles interesting (or frustrating if you don't have jump jets). They really could use a few maps that don't have so many damned weirdly shaped ridges. What's wrong with an occasional flat plain?? Maybe throw in some heavily forested areas we can giant robot stomp through.The Not-So-Good StuffThe CampaignIt's there. It's a thin wrapping to move you through the Inner Sphere. The vengeance plot is recycled, but it functions. It could have been much more interesting.The LeopardI understand the idea of being able to walk around the mechs themselves and get a sense for their size and grandeur is a neat idea, but in reality it's an annoying time sink. Running up the stairs to talk to Ryana or down the stairs to talk to Fahad is not worth the effort, especially as the dialogue is uninteresting and the models for these characters might as well be cardboard cutouts. They could have done away with all of this and just left us the command interface. It would have been fine. That's where the game happens anyway.Mission BriefingsThey get REALLY annoying after the seventeenth time hearing the same thing. Just once I want to hear Ryana say "It's a demo mission. You know the drill. Good hunting."The Terrible StuffVoice ActingIf you're playing the campaign, you will run into some of the worst voice acting I've ever heard in a video game. Not all of it is bad, though. But when it is it's terrible.Fahad's accent is one of the worst, however if you've read The Mercenary Life anthology by Randall N. Bills, a series which presents the backgrounds and origins of the video games' main characters, you'll discover there's a reason his accent is so bad. But you wouldn't know that if you hadn't read it.The AI MechwarriorsFrom what I can tell, they put all their effort into making the enemy AI reasonably competent and made the allied AI dumber than a box of rocks. While the enemy is focusing fire on my mech almost to the exclusion of the others, my AI lancemates are walking in circles trying to find their asses. Doesn't matter if I tell them a thousand times to attack a target, they spend their time confused about how to drive around a big rock. Or they run up to the target and then run back into formation as if they'll die if they go too far away from me.And don't get me started on how awful they are when you're trying to defend. They do more damage to the thing you're defending than the enemy does. Besides trying to shoot at targets behind buildings, walls, and hills, they will stomp a building flat if they have to because BY GOD they will be in formation. Always and forever. No matter what's in the way. Even you.Lance CommandEven the earliest versions of MechWarrior had far more options for commanding your lance. The ability to select a nav point (which aren't labeled but are referenced by name for some reason) and then order your light mechs forward to recon is the most basic of lance tactics. But you can't do that. Your only option is to send them to a waypoint, but that waypoint has to be something you can point your targeting reticule at. And since the terrain is constantly broken up with hills and canyons, that's a point not very far from you. Pointless. All of that assumes they will actually leave your side, which they don't seem to want to do half the time. No formations. No ability to group your mechs and command them separately. Just attack my target and follow me. That's it. Pitiful.What This Game Needs Going Forward1. More maps. I'd pay for DLC map packs easily.2. More mission types. The ones they have are good. More is better.3. Improve the AI for single player games.4. Better contract management. We should be able to see the actual contracts and negotiate them without having to travel first. Travel costs should be negotiable, too. Contract filtering so we can find the contracts for or against specific factions would be helpful.

_childDocuments_.review: As an old man who greatly enjoyed Mechwarrior 4, I find making comparisons difficult to avoid. So if you're an old series fan like me going from one to the next, hopefully this will give you an idea of what to expect:1) Battlefields are tighter. There are more buildings, rock formations, cliffs, trees, etc. It's much less common to just crank your throttle all the way up and circle your target until it's gone. You need to watch your step and keep from getting stuck.2) Sensors are line-of-sight. You are no longer aware of everything within 1000m--just what you can see. Locks can be maintained through solid objects for a couple seconds (which helps to lob LRMs over obstacles).3) AI opponents invariably want to get close. Like melee-range close. Like use-jump-jets-to-stand-on-your-head close. No more circling you at several hundred meters. No more using 360-degree torso twist to kite you if they're a "ranged" mech.4) Lots of enemies spawn into battles after they begin. You no longer load into a mission with the opfor already on the ground. You fight what's there and then an endless trail of dropships fly within a few hundred meters to rain more mechs on your head.In short, where Mechwarrior 4 felt slower and more deliberate, Mechwarrior 5 feels fast and chaotic. At first, I thought it felt "dumbed-down", but in retrospect it does bring some new depth to its missions. In particular, the more limited sensors and the need to often bypass or escape enemies rather than kill them makes light mechs more interesting. You might spend a mission running past foes using the dense, cover-rich environments to quickly strike soft targets and fade away. You can even (in coop) "share" a sensor lock with an ally to let him fire LRMs at a target from the other side of a hill or a city wall.As someone who always enjoyed lighter chassis but found them difficult to justify, I was pleasantly surprised to find a Mechwarrior title where assault mechs need to be constantly wary of getting swamped in CQB, overrun by faster-moving air-dropped reinforcements, or pounded by long-range artillery while the tactical mobility of lighter weight classes is rewarded.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, I really did. I'm a huge fan of the series since Mechwarrior 2, and the idea of running a merc company like in HBS Battletech but with first-person mech combat sounded amazing.However, this game is not that. It's just let down by so many lazy shortcomings and baffling design decisions. I hate to say it but MW5 is probably my biggest gaming disappointment in a long time.I guess lets start with what it does well: The actual mech combat? Pretty good! Weapons feel like they have weight, there's a good variety of classic mechs, and everything just feels real punchy. Graphically the game is...okay. Some weapons effects are good but LRMs look like something out of a PS2 game for some reason. Weapon sounds are pretty good but the music is all repetitive god awful butt rock that you're going to mute pretty damn fast.But then there's so much bad:The AI is atrocious. Just mind bogglingly bad. If you are going to play this it's  you download the mod that disabled friendly fire from either the Workshop or Nexus Mods. Your lancemates love nothing more than to constantly shoot you or each other in the back. Give a friendly a mech with 2xLRM20s and a couple machine guns? He'll charge in to plink away with those MGs, ignoring that the bulk of his firepower is long ranged, . Friendlies treat squad orders as more of a suggestion than an order. Half the time you'll ask them to form up they just won't, and focus attack orders are often ignored. You can sort of get around it by micromanaging friendlies with "Go Here" orders but why the hell is that necessary? The campaign and missions themselves are just lazy. The story might as well not exist. It's pretty much entirely delivered by monologues from two characters who chill in your dropship and never move from their one spot. Oh yeah the advertised "You can walk around your dropship and talk with crewmates" feature? You can talk to exactly two people: your XO Ryana and your mechanic Fahad at set points in the linear story missions. Neither have any real personalities, they just deliver exposition. You can look at your mechs in first person as well but other than that, that's it. The procedurally generated missions themselves are repetitive and monotonous with little background (even less than HBS Battletech). Without the DLC there's exactly five types of mission: Assassination (destroy these specific mechs), Defense (protect a compound), Demolition (destroy the same kind of compound), Raid (destroy a handful of buildings all over the map) and Warzone (destroy at least X number of units in an area). There's multi-mission contracts that combine a few of these together with no opportunity to repair in-between but...that's it. It gets dull really fast.Then the actual missions themselves are tedious. I hope you like fighting  of Scorpion Light Tanks, J. Edgars, and Valkyrie helicopters spawning out of nowhere, piloted by the Great House Kamikaze squad whose only goal in life is to charge right up to you, blast you in the face once with a medium laser, and die. And the turrets, oh god the turrets. Who the hell thought it would be a good idea to cover the maps with irritating pop-up turrets? It's just whack a mole if the moles had a single AC/2 or small laser. When you do face mechs, the enemy AI has all the issues your lancemates do, but a lot of standard missions dealing with them feels more like an irritation than a battle. Urbanmechs spawning out of nowhere to plink you in the back with their AC/10s, suicidal hordes of Locusts and Fleas. Firestarters jumpjetting all over the place shooting their flamers at nothing while randomly twisting their torso like some terrible dance. Sure  be able to purchase Assaults and Heavies pretty fast given how much money the game throws at you but you'll rarely face them for a big chunk of the game.Maybe once more mods come out they'll be able to fix some of this but as of now this is a definite "Do Not Buy" if you're a fan of the series. Play HBS Battletech for the Battletech feel and the campaign/merc management and just play MWO for the combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I have tried, over and over, to like this game.  I love the lore to mechwarrior, I loved MW3 and MW4, Battletech, and the tabletop.  I cannot recommend this game until something is done about the AI.  It's ridiculous, and laughably bad.I can excuse a few bad decisions on the part of my lancemates, but I swear; they seem content to just walking off into oblivion with no regard to lance cohesion.  Trying to get them to line up and strike your enemies is so horrible that the experience just breaks the game to me.  It's bad when you look at a single light mech coming at you, and you wince because you know your lancemates are going to just muck it up.  I've read guides, watched YouTube videos and did so much research into how to play this game over the last 60 hours, and I can barely get two missions in before my lancemates get two of my four starters cored out because they elected to lone-wolf and run off from the slugfest that devolved into me vs a medium, a light and a swarm of tanks.  Who put together these missions?  Only four mechs vs a legion?  Fire your tactical and intelligence officer, they're trying to get you killed.I've uninstalled this game, and I will be shelving it for a year until I forget how bad this experience is.  Back to Battletech, at least when something goes belligerently bad, it's my fault and not because I relied on a stupid computer to control my allies.  This is 2022, almost 2023; why can't we get competent computers to pilot our allies?

_childDocuments_.review: I first played Mechwarrior 2 when I was 7 years old and absolutely sucked at it. The setting and concepts still burned in my brain and I hoped that one day I'd be able to return when I understood what it was to be a BattleMech pilot.A quarter of a century later and I start playing this game, having spent the past few decades working in IT, stakeholder relations, sales, and business administration just so I'd be able to understand and appreciate every last mechanic. And boy does it not disappoint.The graphical fidelity has obviously jumped leaps and bounds since the 90's, even when I include the rose-coloured glasses through which I view the past. It's absolutely gorgeous and fun and feels like you're striding one of those beasts.But then all the little management mechanics are the cream on top. Managing my crew, my mechs, buying and selling and salvaging and upgrading and factoring in jump times and weather? This is exactly the game for every person who was born to scout on horseback but forced to write asset management software.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't exactly a thumbs up.  Its entertaining enough, but pales in comparison to MWM2, which is pretty sad considering that game was released a quarter century ago.  The basic problem is that difficulty is determined by the amount of badguy spam.  Harder equates to more mechs, more vtols, more turrets.  You'll find yourself fighting entire mech companies and you wont be facing them at your most powerful - there's a weight limit to the mechs you can drop on a given mission.  The why of this is never explained - just, you have to drop with no more than x tons, because....reasons.This makes the Campaign missions an uninteresting slog.  Oh, more mechs.  Oh, they get reinforced.  Oh, here are the Big Bads, and they get reinforced.  And a surprise reinforcement!  It is not admittedly as horrible as fighting two Clan mechs in a damned Savannah Master, but that was at least thoughtful design.  Spam badguys is just lazy game design.The Campaign plot itself is uninteresting - a revenge plot about killing the guys who killed your father.  Certainly lacks the grandeur of MWM2's campaign; oh look, the Clans are invading, and you're directly in their path.  The base game is improved by mods, making this yet another Battletech game that wasn't designed for fans of Battletech.  The mods change this, but that also highlights the game's shortcomings.  There's also a nasty bit of Paradox-like DLC stupidity - you can only play the Campaign mode in the base game, you have to buy a DLC if you want a Career mode.  Shoulda been in the base game.Seems mostly bug free at this point, graphics are ok - it runs around 75C on my older model GPU.  Buy it when its on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is enjoyable for what it is, but can be exceedingly frustrating for what it isn't, which is well designed/programmed.The graphics are NOT up to par for a game released in 2019, but given how long it's been since a proper mech warrior game was released (MWO aside), it's easy to forgive a lot when you're stomping around in a 100 ton assault. What's not so easy to forgive are the number of missteps the game has, that even a few years later, are still uncorrected.  Add to that the laziness of the developer to issue patches with major bugs and then do nothing for months, yeah, it's hard to swallow. Some of the more major issues are mission difficulty swings where missions of the same difficulty can be wildly different in actual difficulty. Drop ship exfil points that are over 2km away from your current position on missions with never ending constant spawn. (If the game can be programmed to have enemy drop ships key on your location and drop mechs directly on top of you, then the same can happen for your own drop ship, which means the developers purposefully did this to add artificial random difficulty spikes to try to increase component loss and damage costs). Variable spawn rates and positions that sometimes have mechs or vehicles popping in only a few hundred meters away (yep, still haven't fixed that either, even if it's less prevalent than it was). Inconsistent spawn mechanics where one mission will spawn waves of 4-5 mechs, 4 or 5 waves, then the next mission, same difficulty, will spawn the same tier of mechs, but give you 2 or 3 waves at once, expecting you to kill 8-12 mechs at the same time.Probably worst of all, and the biggest issue, is your abysmal lance mates that show some pretty incompetent programming on the developers part. The game NEEDS, BADLY, a setting that allows you to turn off friendly fire, because the devs did such a sloppy job with lance mate AI that in many missions, half your damage costs can be attributed to your idiot lance mates shooting you and your other mechs instead of the enemies. Worse is the hit rate where something as simple as an unmoving turret will take your entire lance firing multiple full salvos to actually hit the turret, which normally only takes a single shot from one weapon to blow up, because their programmed accuracy is just that garbage. To top off this horrible bit of mechanics, your lance will literally bombard the hell out of enemy drop ships, that the devs knowingly programmed to be unkillable and take no damage, yet also knowingly programmed your lance mates to open fire on them, wasting ammo and heat in massive displays of idiocy. This doesn't even cover some of the other random stupidity like running ahead of their lance mates into the teeth of multiple assault mechs with the seeming purpose of wanting to take massive damage and lose components or ignoring formation orders to spin in circles or outright ignore enemies that are firing at them to instead lazily walk around as if nothing is going on.So, do i enjoy this game? Yes, when everything is going right, stomping through in an Annihilator with 4 LBX 10 Solids and decimating everything in your path, including one shotting poor little Commandos and Locusts is awesome. Unfortunately, those moments are too rare while dealing with all the other garbage i outlined above. So if you enjoy mech combat enough to be a bit of a masochist, then yeah, go ahead and buy it, but if you're expecting a polished game after years of bug fixes and updates, well, you're not going to get that, because the devs just dont' seem interested in improving the mess, just adding to it with more bugs and issues.

_childDocuments_.review: (MW5) is a first and third-person mech simulation game set far into the future. Mankind has expanded throughout the galaxy for centuries, and split into several warring factions called Houses. In this time of endless conflict and instability, mercenary outfits flourished, offering their services to the highest bidders. Players impersonate Commander Mason, that along with his teammates sets out to become a legendary mercenary..True to the MW franchise, this game doesn't spare one bit of the series' huge 'Mech variety. Dozens of different models, each with multiple variants, will be found throughout the Inner Sphere in missions, markets or as rewards. The same goes for weapons and accessories, which also come in many shapes and sizes. Something new or unusual is always waiting.MW5 manages to balance its combat impressively well. At no point I felt any of my 'Mechs were overpowered, when put through a contract suited for their class and tonnage. Enemies consistently prove dangerous for the unprepared, reckless moves often are punished. High difficulty and multi-stage missions will definitely prove tough even for top-notch teams.From the individual armor thickness of each part, to the paint color pattern, passing through weapons systems, firing groups, accessories and cooling, each 'Mech can be outfitted exactly as players desire, to build a machine that suits their playstyle, or complements it in the hands of fellow teammates. The aforementioned variety of gear and models opens up for endless customization possibilities for each robot.Each quest-line or single contract comes with the chance of encountering new 'Mechs, unit types and weapons not seen before. Thanks to the salvage system, which allows gathering fallen enemy 'Mechs to then repair and use, or eventually sell, progression feels compelling, as something new which can significantly improve one's Lance may just be around the corner.Sometimes, teammates will do just fine on their own - some other times, they won't. Allied AI needs to be constantly babysit with an already restrictive array of available commands (move, attack, hold fire, follow). It goes as far as allies simply not shooting an enemy in range, or going full "suicidal" into a barrage of bullets without any strategy. Also, them getting stuck because of path-finding failures is not uncommon.Co-op is butchered. Players who join someone else's game cannot bring their own 'Mechs, and have no saying in decisions about the mission, salvage credits or loadout. They simply act as human teammates when it's mission time, but otherwise can't do much else. Any progression in co-op (money, XP, etc) is only retained by the Host, with clients left dry.The overall variety of missions only has a handful of archetypes, which themselves boil down to "destroy all enemies in the area" , "destroy this specific building" or "kill this specific target" - that's it. Needless to say, this isn't enough for a 30-40 hours long campaign, with even main missions not steering off this course for the most part. It does become repetitive pretty quickly as far as mission types go.Is mainly performed in the galaxy map, which is composed of hundreds of star systems belonging to diverse factions. Travelling between each costs time and money, however brings about discoveries such as conflict zones to get contracts, industrial hubs for trading / repairs, and even transmissions offering special missions. Exploration on the ground while piloting a 'Mech doesn't have much of a point, except for finding the occasional "Treasure Cache" that however has miserable rewards: the only good destination is the objective.Each 'Mech can be fully customized in an interface that allows changing armaments and allocating systems such as cooling, ammunition, armor and so on as one desires. Many "builds" can be done in this way, experimenting with different weapon combinations is exciting and handles very differently from one to the other on the field. Each robot has a tonnage limit in the equipment it can carry, so a careful balance to not break it is necessary. Pilots can be assigned to each 'Mech, and each of them may be more proficient with certain weapon types or combat styles: choosing the right man for the job is key.Starts with the contracting phase, where players can use points to improve the mission payout, salvage rights (loot from destroyed enemies), insurance for eventual damage and airstrike support amount. These points can be more or less depending on player reputation with a certain faction, having friends can be very profitable indeed. After that is decided, the deployment phase will have players choose 'Mechs to bring on the field (four maximum), with a total deployment tonnage limit to balance things out also here.Plays out in first or third person, in real-time, and often in a chaotic manner with explosions, bullets and debris flying about. 'Mechs have two main weak points: the central torso and the cockpit, when one of these loses all armor and integrity, therefore exploding, the 'Mech is destroyed instantly. Other parts can also be blown away, such as arms or legs, these can cause major damage, disable weapons, explode ammo - however they never are lethal blows. Depending on the approach, it may be wise to weaken enemies instead of aiming straight for the kill. Not only other robots but also aircraft, static defenses and vehicles like tanks will be in both allied and enemy rosters, weaker sure, but much more numerous.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game and most likely always will, but their DLC model is ridiculous. They keep making mediocre campaigns and releasing new gameplay features that should be free updates as part of the DLCs, it's gotten to the point now you need to spend a total of $119.93 USD to get the full gameplay experience.There's also a long running history of the devs rushing out these updates and DLCs with game breaking bugs and other, admittedly less significant annoyances. But they procrastinate on fixing such things for way too long, like we had to wait over six months for them to fix a bug where every ballistic weapon in the game made no sound after they added melee. Modders made a placebo fix, but that only traded melee audio for ballistics audio.I highly doubt they'll change their ways and start making half way intelligent decisions with their DLC releases or taking their time so we're not stuck with some of the most annoying glitches I've ever experienced in a video game, so honestly? Go buy Armored Core 6 instead. It's far more worth your time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: as someone who got introduced to Mechwarrior with the second installation on my playstation back then, this was really a bit of a stroll down memory lane (even though the clans aren't really introduced without the help of mods). The effects are crisp, the graphical fidelity is great and the scope of the battlefields keeps it exciting.The biggest downside for me personally was the very "procedural generation" nature of all missions. I don't like this stuff. It was lame in No Man's Sky and it's lame here. I wished for more handcrafted missions. The results of the randomly generated soul of the game are lifeless characters, uninspiring stories and it all feels extremely detached from the "huge wars" that are supposedly going on in the universe.That being said, this is the ultimate Mech game out there. Your metal giants feel weighty, your shots impactful and every battle has tactical difficulty curves that will keep you sweating.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Due to patches etc i am updating this. Note that my rating number does not take into account mods.I'm a huge fan of the series and universe and i really want to like this game BUT this entry is sub-par. 6/10Lets face it from start Piranha games lacked both the skills and funds to make a game like this with the polish it deserved.Disregarding the controversies regarding the developer and the Epic timed exclusive deal what game do we get?A simplified mechlab to both MWO and previous games.(Edit: There are now mods that alleviate this issue.)A borderline broken AI. (Edit: Mods meke them kinda thick rather then full blown imbecilic)A short lackluster campaign story that is padded with missions that are barely any different from your ordinary contracts, it's repetitive to say the least. But with some good voice actors.(DLC does extend this somewhat but as this is for the main game i do not take this into account)The hanger is a nice idea but poorly executed with barely any point to it since ease of use makes the main menu far more faster and easy to use with the only thing to do in the hanger are the few mandatory interactions with the NPC's for story missions. Multiplayer coop by far is the worst sin in lost potential in that the game gives zero incentive for anyone to join since you don't get anything and there is no carryover or persistency making this a singleplayer or dedicated gaming group game only. It is highly dependent on the host to buy equipment, mechs etc for every pilot and relies heavily on voice coms since they can't do this and are thus forced to basically do nothing while the host does all prep for the next mission. It's a merc game and mercs get payed. In short it is playable and with mod support it has gotten many issues fixed but as it is, it's an unsatisfying reminder of what the series was rather than an actual improvement or innovation. It is playable and is now fun while playing coop but do get it on a discount.
