_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Having clocked close to 100 hours previously in MW5, nothing drastic has changed. PGI sold-out fans to go on another platform to grab their money bag then sell out once they made their profit. Even after nearly two years, the game still has numerous issues with AI, pathfinding, balance and customization, among others. The missions seem to be an endless repeat, just with different characters. As a long-time Mechwarrior and Battletech fan, it is sad to see the lore was not used effectively and instead, MWO was used as a template for simplicity's sake with regards to mech customization. Many of these problems can be fixed with mods, but ask yourself, before you buy it, is it worth all the headaches that come with mod-related issues? Currently priced too high for what you get, the campaign, even with DLC, will put you about 30-40 hours, but by the last 10 hours, it is very grindy. This game is not complete without mods; pick it up from a key reseller like Fanatical for a better price or wait for a sale.Full Review:So before I say anything, I wanted to thank all the beta testers at Epic for this game. I also wanted to let everyone know that I was an original backer of this game but got a refund due to the unacceptable switch to EGS and the ensuing debacle. The radio silence surrounding this game was unacceptable, with long periods of no news, then a sudden delay just because another game will supposedly steal MW5's proverbial thunder. The last time I checked, even now, it wasn't on the bestseller list. There are reasons for that, this is the lowest rated Mechwarrior title historically, and it shows.The AI is slightly better, but without mods to correct the AI pathfinding issues, both friendly and enemy mechs will run in circles around each other until one dies. In addition, pathfinding is still very poor, as friendly mechs still crash into buildings. This makes defence missions very difficult, as the buildings get damaged every time your lance mates run into them. Until you get a mod to fix the spawning issues, it is more of a horde shooter than a Mechwarrior game. Until you get a mod to fix the customization issues in the mech lab, you have no reason to pick anything but the heaviest mech. All of the mechs per class move at the same speed, with few exceptions. Light mechs are supposed to be used to outmaneuver the enemy, but you have no incentive to do so. Medium mechs are supposed to be well balanced etc. You will need a mod to fix the market limitations as well, as some mechs are super hard to find; I could go on.It begs the question that if non-professional modders can do these things, why couldn't PGI do them? The catch 22 now is because PGI delayed the game for so long to steam; many of the modders won't update their mods anymore. It is a huge blow to the game. For the DLC content, the missions you complete to get your mech upgrades are poorly done in some cases. Destroying tracked vehicles was particularly terrible, as only super-heavy tanks count. Some of the missions you need jump jets, but it isn't mentioned in the briefings at all. There are spawning issues as well where only 9/10 enemies show up, and you have to restart your mission as you cant complete it. On launch, even running without mods, this still comes up. Cold storage also didn't work when your saves were transferred at launch, though this was fixed. After all this time, I wonder how all these bugs still exist. There is very little polish, so where did all the money they made from selling out to EGS go? Thanks, PGI.The only thing that saves it is that the mech portion of the game is fun, minus how repetitive it is. More mission variety is needed, and more options overall. I give this game a 6/10. Unfortunately, you likely won't play it after you go through it once; only mods can save you. In the future, I hope another company can do the Mechwarrior franchise right.

_childDocuments_.review: This game leaves a lot to be desired. While it provides the core experience of piloting a giant mecha and smashing things to pieces the title falls short in several places.The core gameplay is satisfying. Walking through a building and watching it collapse feels good and always works the way it should. Firing the weapons and watching them impact enemy mechs tickles the brain. A large enough variety of mechs are featured that you'll always be able to have fun in a quick skirmish or while you're hunting around the Inner Sphere for that coveted mech to add to your lance. The maps in this game are procedurally generated. While this is obvious the first time you see a square little city dropped in the middle of a wasteland, it gets the job done. The variety of mission types is acceptable enough to hold your interest. This game admittedly lacks a lot of the gameplay choices Mechwarrior 4 had throughout their missions leading to a lot of the contracts feeling shallow and repetitive.A lot of the downsides of this game revolve around the poor AI of your lancemates and a boatload of cut or unimplemented features to support this game releasing on consoles. Advanced zoom, a staple from MW4 is not present, Infantry enemies were cut to support performance, mechs do not have separate walk or run animations, third person locomotion does not sync with first person cockpit bob, mechs do not have inverse kinematics to ensure their feet line up with the terrain.It's very frustrating how little control you seem to have over your AI lancemates. You cannot tell them to fire from a position, go to a position if you do not have line of site with it, prioritize destroying buildings (unfortunate as several mission types revolve around this), prioritize a type of unit such as battlemechs, VTOLs, or tanks etc. Ultimately, you're left to do almost everything yourself while these idiot bots snipe at the enemy.This game is saved mostly by co-op and mods. Co-op play is a blast and I've put almost 100% of my gameplay time into this with at least one friend. Several mods either fix or restore features that should have been in the base game. TT_Rulez in particular makes the AI much smarter.While I ultimately would recommend the game if you're a fan of the Mechwarrior series or the Battletech universe, a lot of mech chassis and the entire career gameplay mode is locked behind the Heroes of the Inner Sphere DLC. While I would describe the other three DLCs of MW5 as optional, Heroes of the Inner Sphere feels essential to the core gameplay experience which is very unfortunate as it almost doubles the price of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid Mechwarrior game, though not necessarily an amazing one.In terms of stompy mech action with lots of pew-pew and glitzy detonations, it does a good job of keeping the monkey part of the brain entertained. If you are looking to point a target reticle at something, shoot lasers at it and watch some detonate off, it is a perfectly good time.That being said, the vanilla experience has some significant flaws: Friendly AI is usually moronic and make sub-optimal use of whatever mech you give it (better with mods, more on that later), the missions start feeling pretty same-y\repetitive by 15-20 hours in (your mileage may vary), the universe feels static (your actions don't really change anything in the game universe) and the variety of mech customization is limited.There are two things, however, that can make this game great: playing with a friend (who shouldn't suck as much as the AI does) and mods. A friend that can effectively coordinate with you allows you to take on significantly more challenging missions than when you have the AI derping around. As for mods, everything from mech customization, to AI improvements, to new mission types, and much more: mods can bring it to the table. While this isn't praise for the game developers, it is an element that makes the game that much more involved and worthy of your time.If you don't like modding (or don't like that you need them to make the game truly good) and your friends have failed you in drawing aggro and target selection too many times, the game will be pretty hit-or-miss, so consider your purchase wisely.

_childDocuments_.review: There are tons of mechs that can be kitted out in tons of ways, and they’re all a lot of fun to drive. The campaign is expansive, complex, and reactive, though at times it can also be aggravating and directionless. The mission structure can also feel a little repetitive after a while, but a variety of exciting environments serve to mitigate this. And casually plowing directly through a row of high-rises in an Atlas? Well, that never gets old.8.5/10Some Tips:Get some mods, the game has some issues that can be easily fixed for a massively improved experience.Turn on some level of aim assist. It's very difficult to aim while moving and managing your torso and leg positioning, and even the low setting with help a lot with keeping you on target, especially with lasers.Positioning is incredibly important in fights; you can't just slug it out until you get into heavy and assaults, and even then it's dangerous.Present your tougher sides to targets unless firing. The centurion for instance has more armor on his left arm because of the shield, so you should rotating your torso to present that side towards enemy fire as much as you can.Pay attention to where your components are so you know what to protect and how to position.Ammo will explode if hit by weapons, and take out the section its in. If that's a side torso, the arm attached comes off too. If it's center torso, you die. Don't ever put ammo in the CT.Look for where your targets have their weapons, watch where the beams and projectiles come from. Targeting and destroying enemy weapons is a massive part of combat; don't just fire center mass, blow off arms to weaken them and legs to slow them.Losing a leg cripples you, losing both kills you. Same for enemies.Keep moving, the AI has more trouble hitting you at speed. They are still hideously accurate still though, which is one of the aforementioned issues. Mods can balance this.Lancemates are really bad though and will regularly be worthless, unless you, yes, get mods.I always put a negotiation point into damage costs, and the rest into salvage unless I need a fast cash injection. Salvage will always end up being more valuable in the long term.Check your weapon groups! You don't want to alpha strike (fire everything at the same time) all the time.Specialize your mechs. Focus on close combat and high armor (heavy acs, srms) mid range (lasers and mrms), or long range (ac/2, lrms, ppcs). If you have a spread of different ranged weapons, you're going to be weak at all ranges. Your lancemates can cover the other ranges.You don't always need to max out armor. It helps when you're new and learning positioning, but the best defense is destroying enemy arms and weapons. If you can lose a ton or two of armor and add another laser or missile rack, you will potentially be way better off. Dead mechs can't shoot at you.Don't overdo it on ammo. I promise you you do not need 80 shots on that ac/20.Don't bring what you can't afford to lose. That brand new level 3 large pulse laser is really dope yeah, but if you get your arm blown off it's gone forever. Hope you can find another one! That said, don't be afraid to use your good stuff. Just think about the mech it's going on and the mission ahead (torso slots are usually way, way safer than arms, demolition missions tend to be cqc slogs, etc).Check industrial zones on the regular. They populate with rare weapons and mechs, as well as Hero Mechs. The hero variants are great; always have higher armor and structure, as well as unique perks and bonuses coupled with rare and powerful fittings.Flank flank flank flank. Rear armor is always weaker that front, even if it's maxed. Get behind a mech and go ham on it and you'll drop it in no time. Same goes for you though, so pay attention to your positioning.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechwarrior 5 is a strategic first person shooter in which the player pilots gigantic mechs to assault groups of tanks, hovercraft, and other mechs. The mechs handle well and can be tuned to suit different playstyles. While the combat is generally well done, the player is faced with ever crueler tests of endurance as the game proceeds, not aided by the incompetence of the bot teammates. Overall, the combat and customization are pretty good, but can often be undermined by the progression and mission balancing. It’s decent, and is probably a lot of fun if you can get three or four players together in co-op.You pilot a battlemech. While they vary in size and weight, all mechs are capable of trampling armored vehicles and plowing through buildings. It takes time for the mech to change course, but the torso can be rotated to face a 180 degree area while the legs march along, meaning that your movement rarely interferes with your shooting. The majority of your targets are large to the point that they’re easy to hit even at long range. You, in turn, have a hard time fully avoiding hits.Much of the skill in piloting your mech comes in the form shifting these unavoidable hits across your armor evenly. A mech is defeated if its head, center torso, or both legs are destroyed, with enemy pilots additionally retreating if all their weapons are shot out. What this means is that you only need to deal enough damage to destroy one or two components to kill an enemy. If you’re skilled, you can take four or five times the damage before going down by spreading incoming damage across the whole mech. Combat has a slower, more intentional pace to it while maintaining a sense of pressure under fire.Mechs can be equipped with a number of weapons for combat, each with their own pros and cons. All weapons generate heat that can disable the mech if it hits a critical point. Lasers are typically light and don’t require ammo, generating large amounts of heat instead. Autocannons are heavier guns with a slow fire rate, their range being however far you can lob the shot. SRMs are short ranged missiles that do lots of damage and generate a lot of heat. LRMs can lock on to targets at extreme range and attack indirectly if an ally spots the enemies. Lastly, any mech is capable of ramming enemies and many can punch.While different mechs are limited in exactly what weapons they can bring, there are still choices to be made regarding how much armor and ammo to equip; which armament to choose and how many heat sinks it needs to function smoothly. This culminates in a wall of guns that you can group by range, ammo type, or any arbitrary category that makes sense to you. Shooting works well with a number of different weapons each with their own tradeoffs.The story follows a mercenary company led by commander Mason and their quest for revenge against the company that killed their former leader. While the story is present, it’s just really there to add some unique missions every now and then. It’s mostly an excuse to beat stuff up, and it does a fine job of that.While bot squadmates are better than none at all, they seem to be terrible at aiming, provided they even shoot at the enemies. They can’t be given complex orders, and will normally follow the player if not stuck or sitting completely still. Their only saving grace is that their minimal presence in combat inclines the enemies to focus their fire on the player instead. With this in mind, the game is balanced around the player’s team fielding three or four  pilots each mission. Good luck.Starting from the fourth story mission, a player can host a co-op game on their save file and invite other players to control mechs in their lance. Players, naturally, leap above and beyond the low bar set by the bots, being much more capable gunners and competent tacticians. While players are fully capable in combat, they’re very limited in their permissions outside combat. The only privilege co-operators are allowed is the ability to alter mech loadouts and order repairs. However, they cannot:This system makes decision making a pain in group play. The co-operators need to sit around and pester the host if they want anything at all. While it’s better than bots, it’s not perfect.The company is capable of deploying one lance (four mechs) per mission with its dropship. Once the mechs are on the ground, the player will work to complete the mission objective.Once the objective is complete, the dropship will return for extraction. Reaching the dropship will end the mission, with rewards determined prior to the mission with the player balancing payment, damage insurance, and salvage opportunities.While the mission structure never really changes, missions are kept fresh by a variety of well made maps and a large roster of mechs. Each map offers differing terrain and environments better suited to various mechs and weapon types. Mechs will have different effective ranges, movement speeds, and playstyles. The centurion is reliably average with a variety of weapons and decent armor. The urbanmech is a slow turret that’s only good for trading hits while defending a fixed position. The rifleman is a long range specialist wielding autocannons, distinct from something like the catapult which primarily employs LRMs. Mechs vary wildly in their playstyles and must be approached differently in combat, keeping missions interesting.There is no skillful duel with another master pilot, nor well planned assaults on entrenched foes. Instead, harder missions are only ever longer slogs where the player’s lance plows through one, two, and eventually as many as six full lances on its own. Remember, the player can’t avoid damage so much as shift its impact. Loadout optimization and mechanical mastery can only take a player so far without the capacity to employ any kind of tactics or more mechs.Facing ever crueler odds, quality equipment could give the player a much needed edge in missions. Unfortunately, the player is not able to consistently acquire rarer weapons or mechs no matter how much money they have. That’s all up to whatever limited stock the market just happens to have on hand. With how easily equipment is lost, especially on the player’s mech, it’s hard to justify using rare weapons like gauss guns in real missions. Further, players can’t meaningfully seek heavier mechs with the brute force to clear longer missions. It’s frustrating at times.Generally, the mechs convey a great sense of both weight and power while handling well. The shooting can be quite satisfying with meaningfully different ways to disable foes. Finally, combat is paced slow enough to allow for more strategic play while maintaining reasonable times to kill. Unfortunately, it’s partially sabotaged by the incompetence of the bot pilots and the constant slogs through stacked odds. All in all, it’s decent.

_childDocuments_.review: If I played a game for over 500 hours that I did not in some way enjoy, I would need my head examined. OK, maybe I need it examined anyway, but.....here is my take on Mechwarrior 5.Disclaimer: I am a Battletech nerd. I watched Robotech when it first hit the US. I had the original board game. I still have all the old Tech Manuals. I have played every Battletech game starting with The Crescent Hawk's Revenge to MW5. Unless it sucks, I am going to like a Battletech game.What works in MW5: Mercenaries is the FIGHTS. Jumping into the cockpit of a Mech and blasting things has to be the core of any MW game. It is done very well here. Pretty scenery, varied maps, nice Mech models, exciting weapons fire models that look almost real, smoke, explosions, and the list goes on - all done well. While occasionally there can be a graphical glich (such as a Spider moving one way jumps, lands facing another direction and then kinda speeds off in that direction, then starts moving normally), the player driven combat part of the game is amazing.What does NOT work as well is the campaign/career part of the game. One of the biggest problems is getting enough salvage points to claim bigger Mechs so that you can go after bigger contracts, including taking on some of the harder campaign missions. I cannot count how many times I was 1 or 2 salvage points short trying to claim a nice Mech that once fixed would have enabled me to move on to bigger contracts. I ended up in my second playthrough using a mod that increased the salvage points per negotiating point that made it better, but not great. The tonnage limits on missions I understand were there to make the missions at least a bit challenging, but then why can I only have a dozen Mechs ready for action at any moment? I understand the concept or you have limited space in your Dropship, but this is a giant pain in the ass as it makes doing multiple mission contracts almost impossible. Since repair costs and times are so ridiculous you cannot repair moderately damaged Mechs in time to use them for the 3rd/4th mission and you cannot have 16 Mechs ready to go. Do not even think about taking unrepaired Mechs into a mission as they will get popped in no time. Basically, I had to use another mod to modify this part of the game to make it playable as well. In parts of the game where you have to speak to your crew, there is a pointless setup where you have to run around your ship to get to the crew member just to get a clip of dialog and then you can move forward with the campaign. Overall - fun game, frustrating details that two mods have made much more tolerable. Worth picking up on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I realize I'm late to the party, so I'm probably not adding anything that hasn't been said before.  It is because of past reviews that it took me so long to finally pick up the game.  That is to say, that I came into this game with fairly low expectations, and only a faint suggestion that it had been improved upon in the time since its release.  I am a long time Mechwarrior/Battletech fan, old enough to have played the original MW title, and even the original Crescent Hawk's Inception on the Commodore 64.  Given all that has come before, it is hard to understand how MW5: Mercenaries could have fallen so short of the mark.MW/BT games are rooted in the ability to modify and tweak mechs to build a custom machine that suits the play style of the individual pilot.  MW5 strips out most of the customization options, however, greatly limiting both the amount of equipment available, and what can be installed in any given mech.  While MW5 provides a fair variety of mechs, it's also worth noting how few there are, even after two DLC's, compared to previous titles.  Four or five variants of the same mech only soften the blow of how little customization is offered, and should not be counted towards the total number of different mechs overall.The terrain in the missions is also of a very poor quality.  Everything has a dated feel to it, and would look at home in a game 10-15 years older.  This is a game that offers ray-tracing in its options, and I can't for the life of me figure out why.  There are no bodies of water.  There are only a few models of anything - trees, bushes, buildings, etc., that are just spammed about on maps.  Obstacles come in two varieties: either they are impassable or they can simply be waded through.  Boulders the size of a light mech, or trees as tall as an assault mech, can be waded through and smashed apart without slowing you down in the least.The bases and cities you find are small and disconnected from the terrain or environment.  They are the same regardless of whether they're surrounded by active volcanos, glaciers, or pasteural fields.  Neither are they connected by roads or anything.  It would make some sense if these maps were perhaps procedurally generated, but the maps all appear to have been pre-designed.Combat itself is another issue.  Many of the mechanics of the tabletop or previous MW games have been overlooked.  Staggering or knocking down mechs with heavy weapons is absent, for example.  Heat management, a critical aspect of mech combat, is greatly reduced, so that climate and exterior conditions are no longer observed.  Whether you are standing on an arctic planet or knee deep in lava, you will see no difference in your heat build-up.The AI is quite deplorable - both for the player's lance and the opposition.  The commands you can give your AI lancemates are extremely limited.  I can only order my team to attack my target or follow me, really.  In theory, you can tell your lance to go to a location, but you are limited to only the surrounding area that you can visually see, since the developers didn't provide a tactical map.  This hardly lets you perform any deep strategy, such as sending out a light mech to scout ahead, for example.  Your AI lancemates will crash through the objectives you are meant to defend with the same ease as which they smash the aforementioned boulders and trees.  The NPC's will struggle with pathing and get stuck behind terrain.  Otherwise, they will simply run straight at the target that damaged them last (or most) and circle strafe.The campaigns are not something I have played, so I can't say much about how the addition of a storyline might help alleviate (or make sense of) what this game provides.  I will say that I was not encouraged given how the player starts out being saddled with guilt for their greed and irresponsibility.  I take the word of others who found the original story entirely forgettable, and the DLC to be paper thin.A big part of why I didn't bother with the title earlier was because of the limitations of the multiplayer, too.  I was disappointed to learn that co-op players could only play mechs in the host's lance.  It seemed much more reasonable that they should be able to bring in their own favorite mech.  Also, I found it startling that guest players had no control over their mechs outside of combat, and were forced to play whatever the host gave them.  I've been playing this game with mods almost since the day I bought it, so I can't now tell what has been changed due to developer updates versus the mods I've incorporated.  The only real change I see is that guest players can refit the mechs I give them.I cannot understand why a developer would buy the rights to a title and then treat it so poorly.  They had a long history of titles on which to build something better, and appear to have instead slapped together something worthy of a mobile app.  If they aimed at reviving interest in the series, they have only succeeded in reminding us of what once was.  Certainly modders have made a heroic effort to make the game a passable experience, but they can only do so much with what they're given.  I'm very disappointed to see that the developers have done so little to improve on the game given all of the time they've had since its release.  The modding community has certainly shown them the way.

_childDocuments_.review: Basic stuff first: it's MechWarrior. You've played one before, right? It's big, stompy robots.Everything here is technically competent. The mechs move, shoot, and handle well. It feels comfortable and familiar. The selection of mechs encourages collectors, balancing the books isn't too tedious, procedurally generated maps keep missions from getting too samey too quickly, and customization isn't too restrictive. Good sense of progression as well; when you get your first Marauder or Warhammer, you will feel it. The bones of this game are good.So why don't I recommend it, despite 50+ hours and a stable full of mechs?It's utterly soulless. The voice acting varies between passable and meh. The writing is boiler-plate for a Mercenary title. The villains are faceless. Nothing feels urgent or motivating in the story. If you are not motivated by collecting mechs like Pokemon, I promise you that you will be bored of the story long before you get to the big reveal.Does the DLC save it? I don't know and am not willing to spend the dosh to find out. Will probably finish the main quest just to see if there's some surprise that makes me change my mind, but I'm not hopeful.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechwarrior 5 is a big step up in graphics compared to the Mechwarrior games of the 90s, but feels old and clumsy otherwise. There's a plot, but it's tacked on and stuffed between endless 'rinse, repeat' missions on slightly changing planets. Expect a heavy grind of doing the same 2-3 missions a dozen times in between plot points. At about 8 hours in I still don't have any heavy or assault mechs, and am mostly in the 'middle' weight mechs.Mech customization is in depth, but cumbersome and some quality of life features such as 'compare' between different weapons or loadouts is desperately needed. Being able to rename mechs or give them nicknames would be massively helpful in making you have different loadouts.Ultimately to me, Mechwarrior 5 feels too old. I loved Mechwarrior games as a kid, but I'm dropping this one as I don't feel like another 15-40 hours to see the conclusion of a couple of characters that I don't know or care about is worth the time invested.Unless you're a die hard mechwarrior fan, I'd say skip this one even if you have fond memories of 90s mechwarrior. MW needs to evolve beyond a new skin on old bones.

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to emphasise the viewpoints put forward by many other reviews already in place:The  mechwarrior 5 experience is not particularly good. The mission variety is lacking, the AI is poor, customisation is limited. However, very little of that criticism actually matters. PGI succeeded at two things - the core elements of the gameplay (the models, sounds, and the feel of the mech combat), and some of the most painless and seamless mod support I have seen in a modern game. There are absolutely excellent mods for the game which elevate it from mediocrity to one of the best mechwarrior games you can be playing right now.Whilst there are lots of lists of mods out there and going through all of them would take time, I would strongly recommend Yet Another MechLab which restores customisation of mechs closer to the conditions of MWO or MW4. On the nexus page of that mod is a related suite of compatible mods which I wholeheartedly recommend as a package and is in my view the best way to play. Overall - if you're willing to download some files and drag and drop them into a folder you can turn MW5 into one of the best mech combat games on steam. Highly recommended, and absolutely worth your time.

Types of weapons you can use on a mech are more strictly filtered: it's no longer just a missile hard point, now it's split into Small, Medium and Large restricting your builds quite a bit.4. Can't change the engine.5. No heat vision.6. Much easier to hit the cockpit.BattleTech:1. In this game you get no warning when enemies get detected. Especially considering the fact that the game just likes to spawn them close beside you, this get upsetting.6. You do spend time repairing armor in this game. _childDocuments_.review: Don't miss this game, especially now that it is dropping on 75% off sales (for those of us who still typically wait six months to pay the prices we used to pay for AAA games, anyway). I have been playing the series pretty much since it was still polygon architecture, and this installment made up for lost time by improving just about every aspect of the game from previous versions. Many people dislike the tag-along co-op, but in a highly management-focused game like this one, it is completely understandable how difficulties exist to create a stronger co-op experience. There is a lean towards the management in this game that breaks away from a highly linear storyline and limited mech functions in the fourth installment. This brings it more inline with the board game and deep lore, with dozens of books and a couple of TV shows in this universe or very close adaptations, and allows the player to focus on understanding their machinery, equipment, and personnel needed to attain a high level of success.Playing with AI bots can help remind players that skill does make the difference in success, because bots will have accuracy based on their pilots, which is like a percentage. With the massive cannons and 5-story targets in this game though, even lagging or really bad human players are going to be better AI with a bad pilot. That said, what makes the difference between the success and failure of a difficult mission has much more to do with choosing the right mechs, and outfitting them properly. I was especially psyched by the king crab mech and would be interested in seeing the format move a little outside of the strictly humanoid bipedal format for mechs and into some terapod options, or at least a few new classes of mechs within reason. There is so much content out there and interest in this genre, along with space in general, dozens of novels that probably a large part of making the game is saying no to uncertainty.Addition of the open world star map and freedom to move around can be a little intimidating. There is no indication of where the fog of war is. In early stages where resources are limited, there is no real way to say, this is the right direction, that is the wrong direction. You follow the missions given at first, but later exercise genuine autonomy on your way to massive cash reserves and powerful allies. Developers seem to have done a decent job of balancing the addition of some new weaponry and mechs with this massive universe system, imagine if you had one set of guns and the ammo were on the other side of the universe, after all.Tactically, the game remained largely the same as four, which I say as a good thing. The arena gauntlet missions in that one are still some of my favorite levels of any game of all time. With the DLC, we see flashpoint missions bringing in mercenaries and some split second decisions regarding primary and secondary objectives. Air strikes also create pathways to successfully completing missions in a way that had not been possible beforehand.Finally, one aspect that has always been strangely attractive about this series is the soundtrack and the sound effects. It is always very deep space and methodical; this installment is absolutely no let down. From the minute the drop ship lands and the mechs creak 180 degrees, players know they are back in the MechWarrior world. Like the game itself, the sounds stay true to form, controlled based on a proven formula for success, while also integrating some new elements to take the series out of the  3D polygon-models based arcade hall past (as nostalgic as many players are for that) and firmly into the modern gaming world.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have a passion for commanding towering battle mechs, this game is a must-play, providing countless hours of enjoyment with all the content the game has to offer mods withstanding.🎯 Note: Speaking of DLC's--keep an eye on special offers and discounts; MechWarrior 5 and its DLC's often goes on sale, offering a great opportunity to dive into the world of mechs for peanuts.🔷In MechWarrior 5, you're thrust into a war-torn 31st-century universe, where factions vie for control, and colossal mechs are the ultimate weapons. The game's rich lore and backstory set the stage for an epic adventure as you lead your own band of mercenaries in this tumultuous future. As you progress, navigating the political quagmire of the Great Houses becomes more precarious as your reputation proceeds you for your services. This leads to any number of play throughs as siding with certain Successor State's can change the course of your campaign and lock you off from missions, quest and rewards depending on the side you chose to help. 🔷MechWarrior 5 is a love letter to fans of classic mech combat. It not only captures the essence of piloting these giant machines but also embraces the challenging learning curve and the strategic depth of the genre. Master said mechanics takes time and dedication.⚠️Warning: Newcomers may find the intricacies of mech customization and piloting a bit daunting at first, but once you get the hang of it, it's incredibly rewarding.  For those who prefer a more straightforward experience, you can simplify the controls to play more like an FPS and customize numerous aspects to the difficulty to suit your play style and skill-set. 🔷 In the year 3015, the flames of war continue to engulf the galaxy, and the battlefield is dominated by an array of formidable battle mechs. These towering war machines include iconic models such as the Spider, Zeus, Battlemaster, Orion, Griffin, Archer, Blackjack, Hunchback, Grasshopper and many more, each with their own unique variants, combat capabilities and loadouts. Top of that, each mech has a common, rare and hero variant to collect with hero variants being the most sought after for their special paint schemes, quirks and loadouts that usually make them far stronger than their counterparts. 🔷 With additional DLCs, MechWarrior 5 boasts an even more extensive roster of mechs and variants expanding the total count quite a bit to provide an even greater variety options to utilize and explore during combat.  🔷What stands out with MechWarrior 5 to me is the sheer variety it offers players. Each mission feels unique, thanks to the dynamic mission system and the extensive range of mechs and loadout options available. 🔷You start with a basic mech, but as your journey unfolds, you'll collect and customize more powerful war machines. Your choices in weaponry and equipment dramatically impact your playstyle and tactics.🔷After each mission, you're rewarded based on your performance and the objectives you completed, allowing you to upgrade you to take 'shares' earned to salvage new mechs and equipment which in turn you'll use to enhance your mechs, build new mechs and expand your mercenary company.🔷MechWarrior 5 boasts some of the best visuals you can lay eyes on that bring these colossal war machines to life. The attention to detail in the mechs' designs, the destructible environments, and the immersive world-building make it a visual treat that never gets old. 🔷The game captures the essence of futuristic warfare, combining cutting-edge 3D assets with detailed 2D textures to create a visually captivating experience that is sure to please if you are a big fan of mechs or just really delicious science fiction.🔷The soundtrack of MechWarrior 5 enhances the experience, with a mix of epic orchestral pieces and futuristic tunes. 🔷The sound effects for this game are outright incredible. Guns sound punchy, explosions sound crispy, hot, gassy and I swear I can even hear the air hiss as it ignites from super heated plasma lasers. It's so very good sounding to your ears and will really immerse you in the world of Mech Warrior. 🟣 MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries is a game that truly delivers on the fantasy of piloting massive mechs in a future where war knows no bounds. While it's not without its challenges, the rewards far outweigh the learning curve. The vast array of mechs, customization, and dynamic missions keeps the gameplay fresh and engaging, and the rich universe adds depth to the overall experience.This game is perfect for mech enthusiasts and co-op aficionados alike. It's an immersive journey into the world of mechanized warfare, offering countless hours of gameplay. MechWarrior 5 may have its minor flaws, but the thrill of piloting a mech makes it a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been incredibly hesitant to get this game, since I watched a few let's plays and noticed that the salvage system is kinda BS.  Well it was on sale for 15 bucks, and it looked like some of the bigger issues were smoothed out over the years  - plus that mechgame itch just didn't go away.It's an okay game, especially since I enjoy managing my overhead for costs - but it's quite lazy in its logistical implementation. Unlike in the parallel Battletech turn-based game, if you leave negotiation points on the table you *don't* get any increased standing with the faction you're working with (I know if I was an organization and there was an outfit continually underselling themselves as a valuable asset I'd prefer to hire them vs another group). This is avoidable, until you get missions where you just simply have more negotiation points than there are spots to put them, then you just feel like you're getting screwed....especially in combination with negative modifiers like overtonnage. Which leads me to the next lazy logistics issue: Stripping down your mechs does NOTHING to bring you under tonnage requirements of a job. That's absolute BS. Nigh unforgivable.  I'd like to micromanage my stuff if you're A) giving me the means to do so, and B) instituting punishments for 'going over'.TL:DR  It's a mech game that feels more or less similar to the previous versions, but doesn't quite measure up in a few annoying ways. Still will probably sate your jonesing for mech combat etc  :|

_childDocuments_.review: The first mainline Mechwarrior game in nearly 20 years, but is it good?Short answer is , yes, but it's frustratingly close to greatness.Mechwarrior 5 presents itself similarly to its predecessors. You are in your own personal big stompy robot, and your goal is to wreck other people's big stomp robots over the course of a campaign. Additionally, this is the first time in the series for there to be 4-player co-op.In this game, managing your mechs is just as important as actually piloting them into battle. Bringing the right weapons for the job is very important, but making sure that those weapons stay intact to the end is even more so. Battlemechs aren't cheap. and every bit of damage that you takes will come out of your (in-game) pockets. Mechwarrior 5 is very good at constantly keeping your expenses in the back of your head, and in turn this makes dealing with even fodder enemies very interesting.Like other games in the series, this one comes with a campaign, but unlike the others it isn't the star of the show.'Career' mode is the meat and potatoes of MW5. It's essentially a sandbox mode, where you can travel the galaxy and accept procedurally generated missions as you slowly accumulate your arsenal. This is loads of fun, but reveals a lot of glaring issues with MW5 the more you play it.It's at this point in the review where I'm now going to separate the vanilla experience of MW5 from the modded experience. for the following reasons:There aren't many mech types. You're  limited in customizing each mech. Basically only allowed to change weapons.Every single mission feels like it's on the same map.There's only like 5 mission types, and some are just better than others.The AI is so terrible that it is straight up immersion-breaking.The YAML (Yet Another Mechlab) mods introduce a wide variety of new mechs, and mech variants.YAML also unlocks the customization and gives you full creative freedom over your creations.VonBiomes mod injects an absolute crapload of map variation that is sorely needed. (DLC does this too)VonBiomes, DLC, and CoyoteMissionPack add significantly more mission variety.And last but not least, playing co-op or using TTRulez_AIMod2 will give your teammates a brain!In short:

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games you just wish was better, exacerbated by lots of poor design decisions that unnecessarily draw out game progression. Like so many games these days this just feels unfinished or rushed. This is more like an engine/platform for a base game that has been left to mods to finish/create.A lot of great ideas, just not well executed. You will see from Lets plays etc that you cannot just jump in to games and expect to have fun, prepare for lots of fiddling around in menus that are just not intuitive and learning lots of meta in what is good or the game will be heavily stacked against your enjoyment.You will spend more time dealing with game crashes from balancing mods and hunting through menu's than enjoying the game. _childDocuments_.review: Crush tanks underfoot in your 100 ton monster to a great and hard hitting soundtrack and fight in dangerous battles against powerful adversaries, then cry because you lost the arm with your only gauss cannon and ragequit. A great game, kinda lackluster main story but enjoyable repeatable gameplay and a great coop system. The kind of game you can pick up and play just to wander around the galaxy, building your personal team of your most powerful mechs and outfitting them with the best weapons you can buy or scrounge (and then try to keep them in working order between missions).Mechwarrior 5 is a departure from the usual linear story focused campaigns of previous entries and takes place prior to the Clan Invasion, allowing you to explore the universe at your leisure and perform randomly generated missions as well as side questlines (that are better written than the main campaign which is a simple revenge plot). But you're not here for the plot. You're here for stompy mech action, and this game lets you get your fill. Random mission generation is well made, allowing for missions that are simple but enjoyable. Don't think of the random generation as repetitive. Instead think of it as just a way to casually play without feeling tied down to the story. A casual and fun way to get back into the game even after finishing the story and side content and just play a bit. This game has excellent mod support with a built in mod launcher and a great modding community. It's highly recommended to play this game modded. In particular, it's recommended to get the YetAnotherMechlab mod to bring the game experience in line with MechWarrior Online.

_childDocuments_.review: They have this absolutely BRAINDEAD game design where it spawns ENDLESS waves of enemies. No matter what. So you can't take your time on missions and clear enemies - because more and more and more will spawn. It's absolutely retarded.For example, a small pirate group is guarding an outpost they captured on a planet. Your job is to go in and damage their base beyond repair...okay cool.You go in, kill 6 tanks 2 mechs and 8 defense turrets. Cool, should be done with enemies - it's a small pirate group right? WRONG, they apparently have 6 more mechs, 20 more tanks, 10 more helicopters, to send at you within the next 5 minutes. Every time you clear a wave another one mindlessly spawns.So this pirate group apparently has an ARMY of mechs and tanks and helicopters to send into you until you die or you leave the map in a hurry. It's not realistic, it's not fun, it's bad game design, it feels lazy. Why not build in some kind of logic that just spawns in the appropriately sized amount of units based on the enemy strength, background, mission difficultly? Then when the enemies are dead, they're dead. You can still spawn stuff in like a quick reaction force coming in to defend, but it should be like 10-15 min to arrive and they shouldn't spawn on top of you.Anyway, I wish I could refund after learning this.

_childDocuments_.review: Ratings: 3/5First off there are a couple of annoying bugs unfixed since launch such as music overlapping together and flamer animation being ridiculous and weird (it somehow is also the most powerful weapon in-game)The AI is also quite bad, friendly AIs will frequently wander off into bundles of enemies, walk in front of you as you're shooting and generally need to be baby sat and given high armour + long range weapons because they have no sense of self-preservation. Imagine having 3 Leroy Jenkins in your squad.The UI could be a lot better, the modding community definitely shows how it should be done. In Vanilla, pertinent info at a glance is missing and there's no mass sellThe levels are all hard square box arenas, most of which have infinite waves of respawning enemies that kind of detracts from the universe if you think too much about it, and the enemies are like nameless mooks in an action movie, their job is to run at you and die. Vehicles and flying craft are basically ducks for you to shoot down, and Elite and Green mech pilots don't act differently or behave smarter, they both run at you and die like lemmings, difference being Elites have higher hit percentage. There is very little in the way of tactics; it's just jump in the arena and bash it out like in Serious Sam.Also, what I'm missing from MW3 and MW4 is the lack of stabilisation mechanic so you can knock mechs down, something that should have been part of the melee update.MW5 to me feels very arcady, I had hoped it would have been like the gritty, realistic old original MW5 trailer, (the one with the Warhammer shooting down a building to take out a Jenner and taking cover from missiles and AC by hiding behind a carpark)   but it was not to beUltimately it's still a fun rompy-stompy mech game. It's not as arcady as MechAssault but it in no way scratches the gritty, hardcore, realistic mech-sim itch that I've had forever

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good so far (only 13 hours in). The early game can be a bit frustrating since your options are so limited. However once you start unlocking better mechs with more options, the game really starts to pick up. As many other reviewers have stated, the ally AI is... kinda dumb. You will dread bringing a full lance of mechs to defense missions. Also, if you give them a mix of different-ranged weapons, they will charge right into enemies' faces to get shredded by their AC/20 autocannons. To mitigate the headaches your lancemates will cause, consider only giving them mid-to-long range weapons and slower mechs that will sit back a bit. This keeps them from charging into point-blank range with enemies who are optimized for short-range combat. It also means forgoing the full complement of weapons at times--though this lets you pack on more armor while you're at it. There is some RNG in the game--market inventories are somewhat random and special deals pop up from time to time that might give you a really broken OP mech--like a cheap hero unit Urbanmech that you can fit with both a PPC and Heavy Rifle to turn it into a mobile sniper or a ready-to-go assault mech kitted out with all sorts of fancy toys. These events are semi-random with their contents and can have a huge impact on the difficulty of missions. If you like big stompy mechs, trying to create an ideal team of fighters with limited resources and options, or the Battletech universe in general, you've probably already bought this and my recommendation means nothing to you. For those who like action games but want something that will stress their resource management skills a bit (both in and out of missions), then this might be worth picking up at the $30 price point it's currently at.If you prefer faster-paced action or don't like slogging through fairly repetitive missions, then this might be one to avoid. The mechs are relatively slow compared to the sense of speed you get with the average FPS title and the campaign mostly consists of: Going from dot to dot on the main map, Picking out missions, and Doing them over and over again to earn money and salvage. The reputation mechanic can be a chore to balance when missions for your preferred faction are either limited or locked in higher-level zones that you can't work in because they're too far away or you just don't have the gear to survive missions there. It would have been nice to choose a starting allegiance so you could be dropped off in your preferred faction's turf.All in all, I enjoyed this game, it adds some interesting wrinkles into mech customization, but it definitely isn't for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: I have both mixed feelings and high hopes for this game...What the game does deliver, is good. The graphics are awesome. The sounds of the weapons and explosions are just right. The controlling of your mech even emulates that of this games mighty predecessors. Plus, I personally enjoy the campaign style. Fly around a galaxy at your own disclosure, and kill the people you wanna kill for money, mechs, parts, and respect.I like these things. Now, on to the things that suck.So, customization of your mechs is what I really loved about the series. All of the possibilities for even just one mech were nearly staggering. I could spend a half hour simply tuning up the perfect mech for me, and have a blast doing it.That is almost non existent in this game. The customization has been watered down to paint, and total armor points of the limbs of your mech. And thats pretty much it...There are no more omni hardpoints. There are slots for things and that is what you will put in them and like it. Not impressed with the weapon selection either. Very basic things, for your very basic, cookie-cutter mech. You can find upgraded versions of these basic things that make them marginally better, but the base weapon variety remains lackluster. Especially when first starting out, the game seems almost like an MMO grind-fest. Fighting the same 3 tanks and same 3 mechs on each planet you raid with the same few lasers and missiles you've had since day 1, for much longer than you'll want to... I doubt you will be playing this for hours at a time by yourself.Then almost out of nowehere, hero mech's for purchase start popping up. More enemy types begin to rear their heads in your direction, and the game gets a little bit better after all. The base game feels underwhelming, but is a solid platform for modders to build upon. I truly hope the MekTek guys take a shot at this one...TL;DRDecent game, good graphics.Repetitive gameplay at first, gets better.Watered down Mech customization.EDIT:After sinking a couple hundred more hours into the game over the years I can say I truly do recommend it. Now that workshop mods have entered the field, it's a no-brainer if you're a fan of the series.I hate myself a bit for saying it, but the DLCs flesh the game out a whole lot better. Honestly some stuff the game should've had from the beginning, (more weapons, maps, mechs, mission variants) but also really cool things that hadn't been done before (melee weapons, organic interactions with rival merc units, stealth missions). Before you say "Well i shouldn't have to pay more just to get a full game.", trust me, i'm that guy too. At this point you're getting a really good game for $30, with enough mods to keep you entertained for hundreds of hours as well. Seriously: clan mechs, maps, camos, weapons, UIs, entire game parameter changes, and even the mighty MWO style mechlab... just a few clicks away with nothing but the base game.Now wait for one of the frequent 50% off sales and get the full game, all the modding goodness it comes with, and all the DLCs for $60? Well my friend, you just picked up a great game for a great price, and will indeed have your money's worth.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechwarrior 5 is a game in which you are put in the shoes of Commander Shep... I mean Mason. Mason is a lifeless husk of a human being, with 90% of all of his contributions being "Roger that" in any given dialogue. He is the definition of a blank slate character, I guess we're supposed to connect with him and give him a personality other than "Mercs killed muh dad" but he rarely ever says/does anything. This game isn't about the characters though, it's about good ole fashioned stompy robot mayhem.As far as the giant murder robots are concerned, the game itself is pretty fun. I'd call it a "tactical shooter" in the sense that yes, it's a shooting game, but it's a lot less about dolphin diving and abusing an MP7. It's more of picking which target has offended you the most, and then putting as much firepower (or carefully directed firepower to specific parts, great for salvage if you knock the legs off a 'mech) on them to make them reconsider their life choices. DLC TIME:Heroes of the inner sphere is a pretty cool DLC, the beachhead missions are exactly what they sound like. Think Normandy landing, but a thousand years in the future and replace the M1 Garands with Pulse lasers, replace the squishy meatbags with Ferro-Fibrous nuclear powered walking deathtraps that annihilate everything and the entire time you're getting shelled by artillery. Hectic, yes... but once you get the pacing down it's awesome. More mechs, more weapons... overall I give it a (420) "Nice!"Legends of Kestrel Lancers is a phenomenal idea. On paper. Why do I say this? Well, the damned DLC crashes my game if I try to open the options. OK, let's turn the mods off. Game still crashes... OK. Re-verify game files... Restart game with no mods. Hey the options opened! I guess I don't need to see what button is assigned to melee attacks. Apparently these were added with this update, but since the game does not function in it's current state I can neither confirm nor deny the existence of said punchability.  Why are there like 5 keybindings that are blank? Not "The hotkey for this particular function is not assigned" I mean nothing. Strangely enough, I can set buttons on these blank options, but without the game telling me what that button now does, it's pointless. Long story short? This DLC appears to be rushed as it completely broke the game. That is sad, and the developers should step on a lego for their shameful display. I do however have confidence that they will get this DLC fixed. Up until today the game only crashed when I did something outside of what the game expects (Changing values that aren't meant to be changed, certain mod combos... etc...)Side Note: Can we get a patch that when you change the currently active mods, you get the option to restart the game instead of having to close it out, wait for steam to realize "Hey, this game isn't running anymore" then click on the game, choose your launch option and go from there? Or better yet make the game only load mods into the engine once the actual "game" portion starts, Rimworld style. It shouldn't be too difficult to make a new set of "Main Menus" and have them completely separate from the game engine. MWO's approach to starting it's game may even work, the login box is just that. A login box, and after you sign in the game engine loads proper.Now to get the rest of the crap out of the way. The graphics are good enough that I can identify what I'm looking at and enjoy looking at things. This isn't Daggerfall. As you can tell, I'm not terribly picky about graphics. However, the scenery is pretty good looking and nearly everything in this game is destructible in some form or fashion. Can't see that Locust you blew a leg off because he's hiding in a forest? Burn it down with lasers and find him.The sound design is explosive, chunky and mechanical as all get-out. Mileage may vary depending on weapons used, or if you have any mods that alter sounds. I like it. The little details here really shine, mechanical whirring (different sounds used for different mechs too) when you twist and yaw your torso, the hum of a nuclear reactor spinning up as you increase throttle, the KA-CHUNK of a new AC20 round being reloaded. Daddy like. Voice lines are constantly (Seriously) repeated. There is only 1 version of a voiceover for beachhead missions. Every single pilot in the inner shpere says "Glad you took care of that AA installation! I heard you could use some backup..." in the same voice. I'm willing to overlook the voice acting as it doesn't detract from the game, it just doesn't add anything to it.The story is basically non-existent outside of "Make the people who killed your dad cadavarific." I'm also not surprised that Adam Jensen asked for this. Trust me, that will make more sense when you play the campaign. Ryanna (your 2nd in command although she functionally runs the ship, she's very akin to Otacon from MGS) is your typical fountain of exposition and designated question-mark-over-the-head quest giver. Fahad (your mechanic) does one of 3 things. Complain, fix 'mechs and complains about fixing 'mechs. Otherwise he stands there in all of his British voice acting posh.Overall: MW5 is quickly becoming a staple for me, even if this latest DLC is the proverbial kick in the nards. If you like blowing stuff up, stepping on tanks, intentionally putting 11 lasers into a cockpit took cook an enemy pilot or even building 'mechs, this game is for you.P.S. Comstar wishes you a wonderful "Pay your HPG bill, dummy"

_childDocuments_.review: As somebody who played Mechwarrior 2/2:GBL/2:Mercs, 3/3:PM, 4/4:BK/4:Mercs, Mechcommanders 1 and 2, and was involved in the Mechwarrior community for years back in the golden era....  This is an acceptable giant stompy combat game.Take command of your own mercenary company in the 31st century. Choose where to go and which contracts to accept, while being careful who you offend or favor since your reputation has a big influence on your contract benefits. Prepare for each mission by outfitting yourself and up-to three team mates from your pool of owned mechs and customize their weapons and upgrades. During battle, choose the right weapon for the right target at the right range while managing your heat output and your remaining ammo. Stay moving to avoid taking focused return fire. Follow your waypoints and complete each simple objective (generally some variation on "kill or destroy this"... battlemechs are not subtle) until you're given the go-ahead to leave the area. Between missions, weigh your contract pay and battlefield salvage against your repair costs, crew salaries and travel expenses. Shop for new gear. And try to make enough C-bills to retire on a quiet private world some day.Mechwarrior 5 Mercenaries follows the template of previous "Mercs" entries in the franchise by having each mission be detached from the next by a loading screen, but damage to your mechs and equipment is persistent. Armor and structure must be repaired, blown ammo bays can remove a limb utterly, weapons that get hit too many times will need to be replaced, all of which has a cost in time and C-bills. Pilots are your most valuable asset and gain skill over time that allows them to inflict more damage and receive less, but they can be wounded or killed if they take too many hits to the cockpit or are forced to eject during a mission. Your finances never get especially complex, but there is definitely a strong sense in MW5 of some victories being very, very expensive.You can bring your human friends as lance mates, coop works reasonably well however coop clients can only use equipment from what the host owns and do not get to keep any money or loot for their own later use.  Coop clients will generally need to have the same mods as the hosts for anything that affects missions or gameplay, but not cosmetic things like HUD reskins. This is not an online-focused game, drop-in matchmaking is not a thing, you will need to specifically opt into creating a multiplayer session and having people join if that's what you are trying to do.In terms of systems: This entry introduces the concept of weapon levels, which significantly increases the value and variety of loot. Instead of finding a medium laser, you can have a medium laser in six different levels of quality and there is a noticeable difference how well top shelf equipment performs as they have better damage, range, muzzle velocity and heat output.  A rare high quality weapon from the fallen days of the Star League can be worth as much as the rest of the mech, so maybe try not to have that side of your mech shot off.Mechlab configuration is less flexible than in previous games, you can only put weapons onto hardpoints that exist in the original mech design, which again: increases loot variety because now there's actually a reason to pursue having each variant and some mechs are just canonically better than others. For example you might rebuild or buy a Crab 20 from anywhere, but the far more rare and valuable Crab 27SL variant has an improved engine that lets you pack in bigger guns or more heatsinks. There are mods to make outfitting more flexible like previous titles, but personally I appreciate what the designers were going for here and it greatly extends the amount of time you'll be able to play and keep finding new and interesting salvage.Missions are a mix of hand crafted and randomized. There is a primary story line which tells a rags to riches story of revenge. At any point you can also choose to go off task and do missions which can either be small side stories or randomly generated. Crafted missions have unique dialog and map layouts, while there is an infinite supply of randomly generated missions that the game assembles from map tiles. This idea dates back to Mechwarrior 2:Mercs but it works FAR better here and the random missions feel like a worthy game feature. It's essentially like a marriage of Instant Action with your persistant cash and inventory. A challenging and profitable twist for veteran Merc commanders are "campaigns" of 1-4 randomly generated missions, where once you accept you are locked in without being able to stall for time to repairs. You can abandon a campaign, but it's going to hurt your reputation. Better have spare mechs to be able to power your way through.Visually this is the best looking Mechwarrior game by far, which you would expect since the previous entry in the series was almost 20 years ago. Mech models are more detailed and more mechanically convincing than ever before. The amount of detail in the maps sells the scale and sheer destructive potential of a battlemech better than ever before. The map design is a great mix of wide open vistas where you can plink at enemies from a kilometer away if you have the weaponry for it, and twisty cannons where SRM volleys and heavy autocannons level opponents in seconds.As many things as Mechwarrior 5 does well,  there are some others that hold Mech 5 from being truly great: - The story is 'meh'.  The personality and activities of your lance mates and staff are not fleshed out like Harebrained's  "Battletech" does and it makes things feel pretty lifeless. Aside from their voice chirps your pilots are completely anonymous. You can walk around the inside of your dropship but there is really no point in doing so.- While the game's map evolves according to Battletech's official canon timeline and its politics, you have no influence over it at all. No matter how big or how powerful your mech company gets, it feels like you have no lasting impact on anything. There is no "home turf", you will never make friends in any great houses, you will never be able to pull into a port where people love you or hate you.- The music is a mix of meh and good. It takes its cue from MW2:Mercs and MW4 in being mostly slow metal that fits the vibe of stomping around in a huge war machine with some more introspective pieces out of combat. It's not bad, most tracks are just forgettable.- AI of your team mates is kind of derpy. Sometimes they'll get stuck on a rock and not be able to figure out how to get around it. They also like to walk in front of your line of fire, and have no self preservation at all so if you notice them about to get destroyed then you'll have to take the initiative and tell them to move somewhere to the rear.- As diverse as the battlefields of MW5 are, I would still welcome more variety. For example you never fight any dropships at all, while dropship assaults were featured multiple times in MW4. Turret defenses are always pathetic and walls are easily destroyed, in contrast to past games where turrets could be fierce and trying to find a way into a base to take out a power generator or control tower as a weak point was worth your time. There's also no aerospace fighters. A mod exists to add infantry but it just amounts to guys with small arms occasionally taking shots at you so not really impactful.Overall it's a fun game with some rough or lacking areas. I get the feeling that MW5 was made with a very specific budget of time and money, and they had to make hard choices about where to prioritize spending. The combat is great, the graphics are oustanding, the randomized missions are in the best form of this feature the series has ever seen, but world building and personality has taken a back seat.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried. It just sucks. Its not fun. I felt myself wishing I was playing Battletech, or MW4. They throw whole armies of tanks and VTOLs at you, which would be fine if the radar wasn't broken. You can't detect enemies unless you have line of sight. This is extremely annoying since enemies are constantly spawning behind you without any warning and you don't know they're there until you're taking damage. I've even seen enemies spawn directly in front of me.    The last straw was finishing a mission, being told it's time to extract and then getting shot in the back by a lance of mechs that spawned in part of the map I'd already cleared. To make things worse the map design is hot garbage. There's absolutely no attempt to make the missions feel like they're happening in real places. Every level is a box of prefab terrain pieces. When you look at the map you can literally see the edges of each square chunk of prefab. It's awful. Career mode is locked behind a DLC. Don't reward developers for this predatory behaviour. I installed YAML and its associated mods hoping they would fix the game, but they mostly added new content I'll never see.Unfortunately this game is a huge disappointment and I'm glad I got it on sale because it wasn't worth the cost of entry.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the worst game in my library that I can't bring myself to stop playing. The graphics aren't very good considering it was released in 2021. The AI is dumber than a box of rocks. The maps tend to be way too big or too small. The voice-acting is adequate at best. There is a bunch of missing content that got cut during development.Yet despite all this the core game-play is fun. The progression from starting with a handful of ♥♥♥♥-tier mechs to slowly working your way up into the most mythical and deadly mercenary outfit in the inner-sphere fielding hero mechs out of legend is addictive. Tweaking your weapons load out and finding rare weapons and equipment to give you an edge and then going out and smashing cockpits is 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: MechWarrior 5: Mercenaries

_childDocuments_.review: Spent a few dozen hours when it was exclusive at The Pirat- errr... the Epic Games Store. Back then, it was an unpolished turd that made me want a refund. Enemies spawning behind your back, braindead AI, weirdly outdated interface (the dropship was physical space which you had to walk to the different areas, something that would have been cool in 1997, but wears the patience thin nowadays) and boring gameplay.It has become a much better game since. Quality of life has definitely been improved, and gameplay feels better and gives incentives for exploration with the possibility to find rare weapons and monetary incentives. As for the game itself, it's an update of the Mechwarrior formula. It remains a mech sim, meaning that there's an emphasis for preparation and loadout management. Systems are damaged independently, which gives you flexibility in the tactics you adopt against your enemies. Weapons have a tier system, but finding the better ones is a rare occurence and losing them is a big hit. The loadout is somewhat shallower than in older games, as every weapon uses the same amount of slots. Combat itself occurs in procedurally generated terrains. In my opinion, this is a cop out which makes every terrain feels samey, but it gets the work done and allows for some intense fights. Combat is fun and flexible, and your loadout will make a difference.Graphics are ok. The environments can be reduced to rubble (and preventing them from becoming that in defensive missions can be oddly satisfying), and look good on my laptop's 2070, but they are decidedly dated by 5 or so years (think early PS4 graphics).The managerial aspect of the game is more iffy. It will force you to think in the long term, but there's not a lot of variety and company growth can be slow, locking you in a simple loop of fighting one or two contracts, retreating back to an industrial hub for R&R, explore a bit for new equipment, and go back into the fray. A bit shallow, but serviceable.The story is one of the worst aspects. It might as well not exist, and there's none of the campy zero budget charm of previous Battletech entries. But you should know this, and it is not a deal breaker by any means.In short, a flawed but overall worthy addition to the Mechwarrior franchise. It won't blow your mind, but it won't disappoint you either, and delivers on its promise of a throwback mech simulator experience.

name: WHAT THE GOLF?
detailed_description: Sure, it has ‘golf’ in the title but that’s about where the similarity to golf ends. WHAT THE GOLF? is at heart a comedy game with puzzles, challenges and loads of surprises. Okay, so there’s a bit of what you might recognise as golf in there but loads more of what definitely isn’t! Confused? Excellent! Try Sporty Sports!, It’s Snowtime, A Hole New World or one of the hundreds of other incomprehensible levels, featuring toasters, hot dogs, office chairs and a multitude of utterly random objects. Come back every day to play new courses and win a bunch of more or less useful prizes. Feeling inspired? Create your own silly level with our level editor and get it out there in the world. Grab your clubs (string of sausages, frozen rubber glove, it doesn’t matter which) and tee off into a hilarious anarchic world. Share your screen with a friend via Steam Remote Play Together and spread the crazy. To be honest, so do we. And that’s the beauty of WHAT THE GOLF? A game made for people who hate golf, by people with no clues about or respect for the game. Let’s play!

_childDocuments_.review: nice little golf game for people who hate golf and for those who don't.Whenever you think you got used to this game's shenanigans it throws another curveball. While playing the campaign I oftentimes found myself giggling about the unexpected new silliness the game would throw at me.Therefore: Would recommend
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE GOLF?

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just a truly unique experience. Each of the levels is often short, has several difficulty levels, and are often wildly different from one to the next. It's always a fresh adventure into this game, while being incredibly easy to pick up/put down, and introduce even non-gamers to. The newest update has brought about a fun new UI for the main menu, and the newest Among Golf update is yet another breath of fresh air into this game that I was honestly not expecting to see. It was fun and exciting seeing new levels and adventures available to tackle, and old favorites to revisit yet again.The party mode and daily challenges add a lot of fun replay-ability that even younger kids can pick up and have a blast since the controls are entirely joystick + 1 button to operate. But don't let the simplistic controls fool you, the physics, differing objects, and whacky situations will keep friends and family alike well entertained.
