_childDocuments_.review: I've played a bit of the free demo, liked it, and played a bit more of the game, and I Like it!And I recorded my progress with Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos, please watch if you prefer a more audio/visual format, or just want to get a Feel for the controls and Gameplay: It Feels Good. 👍 Note: The video starts off in the demo, but that is fine, because progress unlocked in the demo is kept going into the main game! OMG! Such an incredible feature that I hope other games emulate.Rogue Heroes is already leading the way in innovation and player focused design! No wasted time here!Anyway, Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos is an Indie, 2D, Action RogueLite all about bringing back the bright SNES Glow of Action RPGs, only this time, with Multiplayer, even Local Multiplayer!Yep, Rogue Heroes is offering both Local and Online Co-op, with up to 4 players; though you can always just go solo if you wish. There are Massive The Legend of Zelda: A Link to The Past vibes to Rogue Heroes visually,  though gameplay wise, the influence is more The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords. These are 2 Very Good Influences to Have! And The Retro Glow of the old age is present here as well, presented in Pixel Graphics with a Beautiful Bright pallet that takes you right back to the early 90s era of console gaming goodness. I deem Rogue Heroes a Zelda-Like! It is Decided!A Zelda-Like with Procedurally Generated Dungeons and Meta-Progression, with Class unlocks and Village upgrades. Cool.Speaking of Meta Progression: It is in the form of gems, which you collect in the Dungeons, whether from beating down enemies, finding them in pots and bushes, or as loot in treasure chests. These gems are used to build structures to upgrade your village, and unlock the ability to upgrade your stats, like HP and Magic at the Clinic, Sword Attack improvements like damage, attack speed, or crit chance at the Forge, or to boost up your tools at the Tool Shed; stuff like that.Make sure to use most of your Gems after you die, as much like Cheron in a different Highly Influential Rogue Lite Action RPG, the Dungeon consumes all your gems when you enter, Rogue Legacy style!Interesting. But Why? I Bet there's a story there.Maybe the Dungeon, as both the original earthly Prison of the evil Titan, and now the Corrupted Seat of its Power, is somehow able to reabsorb the Gems on your person?After all, you did take them from the dungeon, and like, knows like. Perhaps the gems are the shattered, fragmented remains of the monsters of the Titan, which are of it, or at least, controlled by it. Maybe, as it regains Gems, it grows Stronger, retaking the Power it once invested into its minions. I'm Imagining T-1000 style re-absorption of separated parts here.Maybe, if it gets strong enough, it breaks free, rampages across the island, and eats your village!And now you must make haste to rescue the shattered souls of the consumed villagers before they too are consumed by the vile Titan's Fury! All while avoiding the Giant Awakened Beast! OMG! 🤯Speculations as to the final destination of the Gems aside, there is even more to like about Rogue Heroes beyond its Retro Pixel Art Beauty, and Meta Progression Its Gameplay is Great. The land itself is an Open World, letting you Adventure around, Exploring, Fighting enemies and discovering Secrets. Fun. In Contrast to the overworld, the layout and contents of the Dungeons is Procedurally Generated, and Changes every run, think different monster locations, different rooms and connections, different loot, traps, stuff like that.Combat-wise: The combat is Fast and Fun.Stick and move, manage your stamina, block with your shield if you like, and use your character's special ability, the default "Hero" ability is a charge. I also recommend using the tools you find in the Dungeon, like the Grappling Hook to hit from a distance, the Boomerang to Stun, The Wand to quickly Burn Em down from a Distance, and the Bomb Bags to bring the BOOM!I really like its intuitive Stamina system: how it shows visually on your character how exhausted they are as they fight for their life. YES! Display information on the character, Dead Space style, not stuffed way up in the upper Left corner. My eyes are on my character and their immediate environment, so don't pull my eyes from that. Excellent UI decision, though I wish they did the same thing with the Hp as well. Perhaps they will at some point. Anyway, in addition to all that Old School Goodness, and Great RogueLite Gameplay,  Rogue Heroes has Full Controller Support, with support for Mouse and Keyboard control if you wish, and will be released on the Switch as well! In short, if you are looking for a Fun, RogueLite, ZeldaLike Action RPG with Co-op, Fun ARPG Gameplay with a bit of challenge, you have found your game. Give the video a Glance to be sure?

The character you start with (unlike Zelda games) isn't the final character you will be playing in terms of basically EVERYTHING. That's because you unlock upgrades to your character(s) (and their gear)... by spending gems you get within the dungeons. Some of those upgrades include faster and wider sword swings, greater endurance, harder hits with more crits, etc etc.This game also has a town-building feature which is sort of fun.Anyone that's a fan of the Link to the Past era Zelda style should give this a go. You can't go wrong at 20$.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't believe the fake reviews.  This is one of the most broken and buggy games on the entire steam platform.This abomination is why developers should spend at least an hour or two QA testing their games before releasing them. Going to list just a handful of them that I encountered in the past two sessions playing it:*Since everyones camera angle is tied together, if one person lags a bit when going through a transition point all players will get stuck repeatedly going back and forth between the two points.  The same applies for houses and shops.*Enemies positions are client side and will occasionally desync between players, thus people will be fighting entirely different enemies or nothing will show up at all for others.*Some transition points are completely broken, for example there is a cave near the waterfalls that you need to go through to get the power gloves, yet it sends one player through normally (and makes their screen black till they alt+f4 out) and the rest of the party all the way across the map to the snow biome where they get murdered from the Tier 4 enemies.*Spells and projectiles do not cast towards the mouse, but rather where the player is facing, and even then not where the player is facing all the time.  For example, casting a firebolt to the left trying to hit a zombie yet it decides mid flight to go straight up.  Same issues when using the controller. *Players all share one camera, so if someone goes afk it stretches the camera out all the way to where the rest of the team cannot see one foot infront of them, in a game where things generally kill you in three hits, this is not ideal. Ghosts also pull the camera where they move, so if a player is just dead and bored it makes the game hell for the rest of the team.*All players are forced to be in the same room, even though we have encountered bugs where we were able to explore separate rooms on our own.  The bug proves that it's unnecessary and also is frustrating, this is similar to issue #1 except in dungeons, occasionally you will break off from the rest of the party and just be going your own way.  This seems to happen if someone alt tabs out or is in a menu when transitioning.*Bosses are unbalanced and stupidly inconsistent with the dungeon theme .  For example, in the graveyard is an 8000 HP boss and all he does is just a weak easily avoidable fireball attack, then lets the players hit him, and repeats till he dies.  His HP implies he's suppose to be tough, but he is simply just a time waster.  Dungeon 2 hints throughout the entire thing that the boss is going to be a two headed snake or something but instead is just a dancing mushroom that takes 2-4 damage per hit for seemingly no reason, and is just a damage sponge for the sake of being a damage sponge.  Dungeon 1's beetle was fine, but the entire dungeon hinted at it being a tentacle monster of a sort.*Players will DC out mid dungeon fairly often just because of how broken the game is, and they cannot rejoin until the host goes all the way back to lobby,  and their gems are not saved on disconnection.  So the rest of the party will have the full dungeon loot yet the person who DCed will come back with 0.*Trap damage is very inconsistent.  In one floor arrows will hit for 50, another will hit for 200.*Early-mid game every class other than just straight up melee is totally useless.  For example in our play I was hitting for 200x3 dmg three hit combos with the thief while the mage was hitting for like 25-50 and the ranger was around 150, running out of arrows after ten shots.*I really cannot express just how much absolute cancer the shared camera is, it's really bad, especially since it only gives about half a squares worth of vision to players who are near the borders, and enemies will occasionally run off screen and attack from out of viewable distance even though they're only like 10-20 feet away.I am glad I got this game for free, because I would have absolutely hated this if I had to pay full price.  And I honestly feel sorry for those who did have to pay for this garbage.  Literally a $5 game in my opinion, a few dollars more than what they spent on Q&A testing.Also just a fun thing, so in this situation I had four enemies to my right, as well as a bat over there too.  To the south of me, on the other side of the room behind like three walls was another bat.I was facing right, towards the skeletons and instead I shoot STRAIGHT down towards the bat on the other side of the room, which is literally offscreen at the moment.And the rest of my shots ALL went to the wall trying to shoot the bat over there.And in this situationI had an enemy I wanted to shoot on my right and another enemy behind me. I was facing right and I shot to the left.  This happens waaay too often.Amazing.  Truly.

I only played local coop on the demo, but didn't expect all the issues online.If any player views their inventory, every player gets a black screen that says "Another player has paused the game." This is brutal as an accidental spacebar hit goes black screen for everyone. The only menus that do not lock other players are shop-menus.When any player talks or interacts with an object, the text pops up - which is fine. However, it also shows you the controls for what they're using, that being controller/keyboard. So if you're playing on the opposite, then you're going to get confused.Sometimes, textboxes seem to get "stuck" on screen. _childDocuments_.review: This is a good game, there are definitely some things that need tweaking though.  I found the bosses of dungeons to be remarkably easy compared to the dungeons themselves, in fact the only reason I failed to defeat a boss the first time was lack of knowledge of a floor break mechanic on the first one.  It didn't take long to sus out the location of the legendary fish for the final thread I needed at the end of the game.  I feel like the knight thread is vastly overpowered granting far increased defense and attack at the cost of some movement speed which is easily overlooked by it's ability.  I'd like to see more challenge in the endgame.  After just over 30 hours of play, I'm short a mere seven achievements that are more tedious labor than anything else; marking some things in the beastiary, collecting the power spheres, getting the rest of the fish, getting the rest of the shortcuts, hitting 25 in the endless abyss, and a couple others.  At the end of the day, the game is great, don't get me wrong here, but it could be more, there are many rogue-lites out there that continue to offer challenge even well past the end game, I think that this has potential, especially with the Link to the Past vibes that this game gives off.  Mechanically, I found no issues with the single or multiplayer, however I have heard of some synching issues in multiplayer that cause problems for others.  I enjoyed the game, I just find that it was too easy for me to power through it in just a couple of days.  Hopefully the skull dungeon DLC will add some difficult content that will give the challenge I'm looking for.Now the pros and consPros:Puzzles are fun, most offer challenge without being hatefulThe early game is difficult but not so much that it's discouragingI love the building mechanicI love that there are multiple classesThe retro, Link to the Past style gameplay is fantasticThe story is solidCons:Mid to late game is too easyClasses need more diversity to set them apart, why does every class have the same sword mechanic?The Endless Abyss could offer far more challenge being a post game dungeonSpeaking of the Endless Abyss, adding a prompt to enter the final boss fight there would be nice, I've found myself walking into that fight multiple times now accidentally having not done as much as I wanted in thereI've heard that fishing is difficult, I find it to be the opposite, I didn't even realize the rod could be upgraded before I had caught the legendary fishOnline multiplayer could do without sharing the same screen spaceI feel like some of the tools have 'one off' usesOverall I would rate this game a solid 7/10 right now, it definitely needs work, it stands as a solid introduction to the rogue-lite genre and I would definitely see the younger crowd enjoying the play, but in order to keep the generation that looks at this and says "Link to the Past style Rogue-Lite?  Sign me up!" entertained, it needs to have more challenge and be just a little more hateful to the player.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put about seven hours into this game (all single player) and I think I'm done. There are so many minor annoyances that I can't continue.There are so many cheap ways to die. It makes me think of Spelunky, where you can be going along just fine and then a combination of things can kill you really quickly. In that game, you can always see how/why it happened and learn from it. In this game, rather than being a learning experience, it's just frustrating. Get poisoned? It happens easily, and you'll die quickly. Your health will drain away while you can do nothing. The rooms may not be randomly generated, but you do see the same rooms over and over. In the second dungeon, I'd clear one room, advance a couple rooms over, and be faced with the same room as before, with the same annoying puzzle to repeat again.In the overworld, the map is designed poorly. When I'm in the upper-left corner of the map, trying to find my way around this swamp, I want to look at the map continuously. But each time you close the map and reopen it, it resets itself to the middle of the overworld, not remembering what zoom level you had it at. Each time you have to zoom in again, and manually move the map to where you want to see. It sounds minor but it's really annoying.Why is there no music? At all? Enemies are hard to see, your health drains quickly (despite me upgrading it quite a bit), stamina drains quickly. It all makes you feel really weak, and each upgrade is so minimal that it doesn't feel like it makes much of a difference.The game's saving grace, and the only reason I didn't quit it much earlier, is that you get to keep all your currency on death so that you can spend it all on upgrades. So there's no real penalty for death, other than annoyance and wasted time.I played this game exclusively on Deck. I got it on sale for $7.50, which for seven hours I guess is okay. I had some fun with it but I think I'm done. It runs really well on Dekc. But, it hangs every time I exit it, and I have to then manually close it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game will let players relive their A Link to the Past nostalgic childhood experience, I thoroughly enjoyed it for the most part. However, there are many game breaking problems that ultimately ruined my opinion. The game is desperately in need of further development.  The Endless Abyss dungeon teleport pad in the centre of every floor transition room will end the run instantly with no confirmation message and is easy to accidentally activate. Losing a several hour run for the achievement feels bad.   The equipment selection menu sometimes continues to scroll after exiting the menu.      The farming system is broken, when trees die all tiles used by the 3x3 crop become unusable for several in game days or until exiting the game, except for the single tile which the tree seed was planted on.     The beastiary progression for monsters will randomly stop working for some reason.    Several instances of enemies warping through walls.    Monsters becoming immune to all damage, specifically fish monster in swamp dungeon will become immune when stunned and damaged until after the stun ends.     Player unable to attack or receive damage from monsters. Picking up a world space item like grass or stone fixed this.     Audio (overworld, dungeon, and boss music) stops working. A fragment of the boss intro music kept working then abruptly stop which was arguably worse than if it were just silent.   Unable to track specific power sphere collection progress to know which area of the map to search, This should be added to the menu display.

_childDocuments_.review: The only good thing are the dungeons.I have 30 hours in this game, and it is horribly unbalanced to the point that the only class worth playing is the Knight.The second area cannot be accessed at ALL without the knight, because there is a stretch of mud that is barely too long for any other class to jump across. There is no lore. No conversations with NPCs in the town you've built, and the town itself has some bugs. If you built the farm and didn't get a watering can, too bad. Same for the fisherman - you might have the items, but he won't give you the rod.There's also way, way too little direction. You need a compass for a new area? It'll tell you that, but that's it. Guess where it is? On the complete opposite side of the map somewhere you've probably never passed by, and no NPC has information to help you at all throughout the entire game. You built a town, but they only stand around. If you're stuck, you better be okay with watching the singular play-through online that doesn't explain anything, and plays as a knight. For a game that is trying to take notes from Zelda-like series, it is unbelievably lackluster in the lore/NPC interaction department. There is nothing to do, and no tips or aid from any NPC.And if you want to play it for the dungeons, it is rather fun. But don't get your hopes up about the bosses. The final boss doesn't even have music, and its arena is unbelievably tiny. It's genuinely not worth your time. This game is NOT finished, it had no business being released like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall 5/10TL;DR - Town building and world exploring is fun, but combat is primitive, frustrating, and without balance due to several reasonsThe Good:- Town building is fun! Making houses and buildings to progress your power feels rewarding- Exploring the world is fun and can feel very rewarding to find hidden pathways and solve puzzles for passagesThe Bad:- Upgrades are too easy to max turning basic weapons into artifacts of legends. A basic wand can turn from 8 dmg to 154 dmg after spending money from one single dungeon run. The Ugly:- Combat (which makes up at least 50% of the game) is honestly frustrating.  - Contact damage is an old school form of damage that should not be present in current games in my opinion. Enemies with spikes dealing contact damage makes 100% sense, but an enemy with no weapons and make of just bones bumping into me dealing 50% of my life makes 0% sense.  - Enemies run wildly and unpredictably making "learning" a strategy nearly impossible for most enemies  - Ranged weapons are either snipers fired with pin point precision or a blunderbuss where the target can stand in front of you and not be hit. I have fired a wand from point blank range only to watch *both* projectiles stray to the left and right of the target.-Coop is glitched very often. I find myself fighting opponents that are invisible to my coop partner.Overall, this game suffers from the idea that difficulty = fun. The artificial difficulty of unpredictable enemies and contact damage make playing 50% of the game frustrating. Great idea, poor execution.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I think the game is a notably entry for what it tries to do, and is perfectly enjoyable in its own right. The world is complete and mostly fun to explore, the secrets are tantalising and often rewarding, and the freedom to build differently or play with friends is great. I just can't help but feel like the game fell short of its full potential and stumbled with polishing the final product.If you know Zelda: Link to the Past, this game is a love letter to that game and  inspired by it. But, it takes a new approach with its town-building progression and randomised elements and classes, and offers a fresh experience with a slightly different combat system and challenges, and ability to play solo or co-op.If you don't know Zelda: Link to the Past, it's a top-down action-adventure game with a combination of overworld exploration and dungeon-crawling. The overworld and some dungeons are hand-crafted, while some dungeons are procedurally generated. There are some puzzles to solve and secrets to find, and plenty of action combat to be had. You'll be collecting gems from dungons to upgrade you character and build up the central town, which serves as a path of progression parallel to your finding of new tools with which to overcome new obstacles.While I recommend this game to fans of action-adventure games, I have to comment that the game doesn't represent a flawless entry. The bugs are infrequent and never really broke the game, but they do exist, most of them related to the movement system in the game. Ice physics sometimes have a weird memory of your momentum, and I've jumped to a space seemingly between the upper and lower layers where I couldn't interact with anything until I jumped back out. The balance of the game also seems to jump around a bit. It feels like the bosses from dungeons added later in development are on an entirely different difficulty curve than the bosses in the main dungeons. These issues don't ruin the game, but leave it feeling incomplete at times.

_childDocuments_.review: Design decisions work against eachother resulting in clunky & unintuitive gameplay.Poorly optimized, and constantly stutters on a 32G RAM & 5.3 Ghz Computer.You have tiny melee range, and just barely more than enemies, which isn't a problem until you realize that the sword will thrust you forward into enemies and damage you. Back peddling and micro-spacing every rat and skeleton is not fun nor rewarding gameplay.Traps are just darkened tiles on the floor and will almost always hit you when you trip them. They're easy enough to avoid, but are virtually invisible in darkened rooms.The point I'm getting at, is that Rogue Heroes doesn't provide instant deaths like a lot of modern "Hardcore" Roguelikes, but will whittle down on you with chip damage from many unavoidable sources, and will instead frustrate you until you'll want to just throw yourself into a trap to end the run prematurely. Generally a frustrating, tedious and unrewarding experience. I'm sure the Developers have learned their lesson from this game, considering they've went on to make the Blasphemous series.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10 (Long story short) Rogue Heroes: Ruins Of Tasos is a great multiplayer/singleplayer adventure Zelda like game where you go through dungeons and upgrade your hero to go deeper through the ruins.My takeaway: I had so much fun playing Rogue Heroes: Ruins Of Tasos that I completely lost track of time playing it with my friends. The premise of the game is simple- you have a hero you can customize and in which you can choose and change from multiple different classes, you go through the ruins that consists of multiple dungeons, level layouts, and puzzles, you collect in game currency to upgrade the hero, and you keep going this way until you finish the game and discover all of the ruins. There’s multiple sidequests and a few things you can do to kill time like simplified farming, selling, collecting, getting monster data, and power stones. I never had a dull moment playing this title and never ran out of things to do until I eventually did.That being said- the game isn’t without faults. Multiplayer can be glitchy and would periodically kick my party out resulting in having to go back and restart from the main menu. Sometimes my friends would have to restart with no progress saved on their character which would be very frustrating. The game doesn’t hold your hand when it comes to the monsters and puzzles so you’ll have to figure out a lot of the combat and mechanisms by yourself. You also have a long list of tools that they don’t make it easy to switch between; I’ve spent a lot of time either having to pause the game for everyone or keep switching between different tools. I also really like farming and this game does it in a way that is simple and entertaining but the reward for the work just isn’t there and it serves as more of a time waster.Overall the game is great for what it is in its current state- an adventure dungeon game. It’s pretty clear it wanted to be more but in its current state it’s very difficult to care for the characters or even know why everything around you is going on. For what it is, it is well worth the time and I’d recommend it to anyone who isn’t expecting the sun and moon from the title.To see more reviews like this one come support me and follow this curating page! I’d really appreciate it!

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like classic Zelda games like Link to the Past or Link's Awakening? Do you like random dungeons and other rogue-lite elements? If the answer to both is "yes" then this is your game. It trends to be more difficult, largely because the monsters tend to be super aggressive along with some iffy hitboxes, but some of the traps and rooms are rather excessive as well. Once you overcome the initial difficulty, it evens out more but still requires you to pay attention constantly. The game looks excellent with good sprite work and animations. The sound effects are likewise good and help the gameplay along. The music is pretty forgettable, unfortunately, but it's not exactly a dealbreaker. Overall, really good game that gives you a classic Zelda gameplay with some new twists and turns. I haven't tried multiplayer, but it seems like it'd be a unique approach as well.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is to 2D Zelda what 20XX is to Megaman XIt's a fun indie approach to an old classic franchise and I LOVE IT!!!This game is basically 2D Zelda in all but name, there are a lot of staples from that franchise here and they work more or less the same as they would in a 2D Zelda game. The big change is the temples, because this is a Rouge-like game the temples don't have a set format, they change every time you enter them and that is really where the challenge lies in this game.The game may only have four temples, but trust me it's going to take you awhile to beat the first one. You're going to have to try a few times and probably die a lot in the process. But each time you die you take the gems you earned and you upgrade yourself getting stronger. Eventually you'll beat that first temple and move on to the others, taking what you've learned and applying it to the future.Between the temples there are side quests to do just like in Zelda and those side quests tend to have useful rewards for completing them. The over-world map is fun to explore especially once you start getting upgrades that let you start entering new areas. The enemies come in many different varieties and some will require thinking outside the box to beat them. This game has taken a lot of the elements from 2D Zelda and added some of its own allowing for a nice indie game that shines on its own.Some of those new elements include the class system. You can swap out different classes at your house and try them out to see which one you like. For me I enjoy using the knight as his higher defense makes completing the temples easier. The thief is also a good choice for exploring the overworld due to his fast movement. Another new element is the fact that you can upgrade your town. That's something you'll want to do as soon as you can, as upgrading the town gives you more options to upgrade yourself. I like how you can choose what buildings go where and that each building grants some sort of benefit to you.I don't know what else to say other than if you are a fan of Zelda buy this game! I think you will enjoy it for sure and definitely get your moneys worth!

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game.  Gets lots of the aspects from Zelda.Rogue-like, you play as long as you can until you die.  When you die you get gems to upgrade your character. After the first dungeon you'll find yourself going through the game very quickly.  I beat the second dungeon on my second run through, and I beat the third, fourth, and final dungeons without dying.There's a few fetch quests, travel back and forth looking for specific items to unlock areas of the game and equipment, but now that I've beaten it the only thing left to do is see how far I can make it in the endless dungeon.There are a few bugs in the game, specifically collectibles that you can't pick up, as well as some areas you can't reach because they aren't finished.  Hopefully the developer releases an update soon because it's been almost a year since the last patch notes, and there's three remaining areas on the map I'm itching to get to.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you enjoy puzzles, dungeons, combat-heavy class systems,town-building, and farming? Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos has a healthy footing with all of these.Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos is a 1-4 co-op rogue-lite RPG adventure game with farming simulator elements that was developed by Heliocentric Studios. Although this two-person team worked on smaller projects for Xbox Live, in the past three years they have released two of their own games together on Steam. Rogue Heroes is their most significant project. Joshua Grump is the programmer and sound designer, and Brandon Weatherbee is the artist and level designer.GRAPHICS 8.2/10Rogue Heroes’ 16-bit pixel graphics look fantastic. Each class has distinguishing features and each jump dash and blink is exceptionally animated. The world gives off “Link to the Past” vibes and features frozen mountains, boggy swamps (that you can drown in if you aren’t carefully paying attention), and my favorite area, a volcanic region (which made me nostalgic for “The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Seasons”). The overworld submerses you into a well-tied-together atmosphere. Each area has its unique type of terrain, enemies, and plant life. Abilities and spells appear nicely as well. Rogue Heroes’ dungeons are exciting at first but slowly become monotonous as the art style doesn’t change from the first dungeon to the last.SOUND QUALITY 8.8/10Sound quality is one of Rogue Heroes’ best features. The immersive music and sounds made me feel completely engaged in each area. Everything has a specific sound. Each primary weapon has its own slashing sound whether you hit brush, boxes, enemies, or anything else. Enemies have their distinctive cry. Traps in dungeons have a neat sound. Every arrow shot, every bomb dropped, and every gem and pot falling from the sky all make stepping on a trap button worth it. Completing a dungeon was my favorite because of the mini techno beat during the victory screen. The score and sound effects are never disappointing.GAMEPLAY 9/10In Rogue Heroes, you aren’t merely a dungeon diver. There are eight different classes to choose from and each class-tree gives you a different play style. Rather than simply hacking at the enemy (even though that seemed to work best), there are some challenging runs for the more difficult and engaging classes. The mage and ranger have very low defense but are more agile. I did this playthrough as the knight which gave me maximum protection and maximum damage (a "quality build," if you will). As a knight, I could eat everything the enemies, traps, and bosses had to offer. Aside from classes, there is also a level-up system that provides additional abilities. You are also able to switch classes at your leisure. The main currency in the game is gems that are only obtainable by delving through replayable dungeons. Gold is another currency, but it’s only for opening locked chests. Gems give you the ability to build your town which is required to level up damage, health, stamina, tool damage, and buy other classes. There is a great deal of content packed into this game and it makes you want to max out everything so you can through the infinity dungeon with unlimited floors.CHARACTERS 7/10The characters felt reasonably simple without story character building; most side character missions are completed early on and don’t seem to change anything. Most NPCs are shop and store owners, giving you goods, upgrades for gems, and unlocking threads for classes. As the main hero, you do not speak and there is no story for how you came to be. Each area had a seemingly important NPC, but they mean nothing after completing the dungeon as you progress. Each new location has an NPC that gives you an idea of what’s to come or what you need to do to provide headway into each area. NPCs fit their role and include the region that you are currently in.STORY 6.7/10Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos' lowest point is the immersion of the story. The tale is rudimentary and uncomplicated. You are the hero of this quest, and you must defeat each boss in the dungeon to collect coins to unlock the final dungeon. You can altogether skip to the final dungeon due to a teleport pad that takes you directly to the final boss. I was disappointed because I expected challenging puzzles and dynamically powerful enemies inside the last dungeon leading up to the final boss. Yet the final dungeon is simply an infinite dungeon, and I understand why it’s crafted this way. The are sidequest fillers are in this game to progress further in each region, but you can complete them without doing certain overworld side quests. I never felt like I was saving anything or anyone, and it eemed like no one was ever worried about the looming evil of the final boss. The main story is relatively short and can be completed in only 7-8 hours.OVERALL 7.9/10If you want something focused mainly on dungeons, puzzles, and combat, this is the game for you. The sound is perfect and the gameplay is fantastic. I completed the game by only maxing out my damage. I was unstoppable. The characters don’t include much lore, and the story is a bit watered down. However, Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos will hook you with its combat system and you will stay for the never-ending dungeon. Although dungeons are the focus of this game and the farming is minuscule, I was impressed by this game’s extraordinary ability to implement this niche mechanic without making it the only thing to do in the game. Replaying this game solo doesn’t necessarily appeal to me, but I can see myself having a great time playing this game again with up to 3 friends and spelunking through the final dungeon.  All-in-all, this is a great game to play with friends and is an excellent dungeon crawler rogue-lite.

_childDocuments_.review: On paper, the base concept of the game is good, having a hero (or two with coop), several classes, a rogue system, and some puzzles to go through various dungeon.If fun at first, you quickly realise that the game is pretty much grind til the end because it fall short on several aspects :- The classes are not good. The differences lies in passive damage changes depending on the class, and on a difference in the type of dash you have. That's pretty much it. And there's only so much type of dash you can do, and at the end of a day, a dash is a dash, making the classes not really unique (even the Druid the supposedly new class is just dash fever fest 2000).- The UI is correct at best, and awful for some things. At the end of the game you have a lot of "tools", and having to go through them over and over again to switch from using that one or this one is really annoying. You have shortcut but they still require heaving handling of the controller, making it hard to switch from one thing to another. It's even more a shame that most of the tool are useless in most situation and could have been put on a "separated list", you need 3 to 4 tool in quick access no more.- The game loop is a totally repetitive : get gems, upgrade, rince, repeat (fun fact : we did a run near the endgame where we gain almost as much gems that the entirety of our playthrough). And the rest also falls a bit short. The exploration is always to go through convulated ways to get from A to B, and the puzzle offer very little variation in the dungeon. The dungeons are mostly easy, and once you have the patterns, the boss never provides any real challenge (worst being the final boss that we completely destroyed).All in all in terms of roguelike, even with the coop aspect that could have been fun, I wouldn't really recommend this game as a first pick, but more in sale, and if you already played the others of the genre. I, for one, wouldn't really play that one solo (since there are serious contenders like Dead Cells, Rogue Legacy, Hades, etc...)

_childDocuments_.review: "Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos" is a handheld (Nintendo Switch)/console game that's also been put on Steam as a bit of an afterthought, as it's very much designed for the handheld/console gaming audience.  It's a mediocre ripoff of Legend of Zelda (but not really, it's markedly different in a lot of ways apart from ripping off the idea) where you just run through procgen pixelcrap "dungeons" doing top down console-esque brawling.  There's some lightweight RPG elements, but this is a true RPG as much as I'd be a Jeep Cherokee if I had wheels. On the upside, the game does feature customisable controls and resolution, so at least some of the basic, minimum requirements have been met.  Unfortunately there's a number of other technical defects and shortcomings which contribute to the game being difficult to recommend to gamers.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.To make matters worse, while lazy, low quality pixel "art" has been used, making the game look bad, many elements of the game aren't done with pixelcrap... which accomplishes a couple of things.  First, it shows the developers perhaps could have done better and they knew it, so that's a major screwup.Secondly, it destroys any hopes the developer had of creating a "retro aesthetic" as their excuse for the lazy pixelart compromise... It looks completely inauthentic from a retro gaming perspective.  Visually, this is a hamfisted mess, a dogs breakfast of bad visuals, and this kind of laziness and poor quality should never be foisted on gamers.While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.The game features no proper level design or game/story flow/plot, as they opted to try to use samey repetitive procgen algorithms as a substitute for adding such content to the game, to avoid doing the important job of level/map design.  As a result, the game doesn't actually have any content worth mentioning, just endless, boring, repetitive, soulless algorithmically generated sameyness.  Developers must learn that procedural generation is not an acceptable substitute for content.Because this is designed for handheld/portable gaming appliances, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the low power handheld gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the mobile game developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for low power handhelds forces upon a game.  While this might run well on a Steam Deck, we must remember the vast majority of gamers here are gaming on PC.Some of the defects in the game can be attributed to the choice of using the video game library/engine, Monogame.  It's rarely used, because it's arguably worse than construction kits like GameMaker Studio, RPGMaker and Clickteam Fusion, but it's also much harder to work with.  Despite this, Monogame has very limited capabilities, which go some way to explaining the poor quality of the game.  Just as you can't make a silk purse out of a sows ear, you can't make a great video game if you use a terrible engine.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?"Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos" has the preposterous price of $20 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.For comparison, the $20 asking price for this game could get you games like "Monster Hunter World", "Wolfenstein - The New Order" or "Kingdom Come Deliverance".  No pixelcrap is worth $20. If developers want to get paid the same kind of money as real game developers who know how to do graphics properly, they need to learn how to do graphics properly.

So much grinding that it proves this game is shallow and by making people grind they would stay/play with the game longer.  It only ruins a good game.  The walking/running animation is really bad.  Looks like he's bending over back and forth.UPDATE 1It's all about the gems.  Solve lots of puzzles and get to remote places just for more gems.  Game should've been called Gem Lord or Lord of Gems.  Grinding to increase your life/hp doesn't matter because the enemies will damage you accordingly anyways.  Its so stupid and pointless.  If you have 100hp max, enemies damage you 25.  If you have 1000hp, the same enemy now damage you 250.  "eye roll."You do not get weapons per dungeon, but you can buy them off the bat after unlocking the stores.  I have used nothing but the hook for combat.  UPDATE 2Beat the game.  There is NO ending movie or anything.  Just a black screen with rolling credits.  Game returns to the town.  That's IT.  I don't see the difference in the sword that I received.  The game is decent but it leaves more to be desired.  Zelda, A Link to the Past was/is perfect.  Zelda was fullfilling. _childDocuments_.review: Yes, I'd recommend, hesitantly, though. See, the game itself is a decent little Zelda wannabe. The art style is pleasant. The music isn't anything special, but it's not bad. It's... Just kinda there. And that's the biggest problem I have with the game. There's a lot of really half-baked ideas that are just... There. Not sure if this was a kickstarter game, but the game reeks of someone lazily including promised features in the most bare-bones way possible. There are several classes with very minor differences, they all play essentially the same. There's a weather system and day/night cycle that doesn't seem to actually affect anything. None of the NPCs even acknowledge it. There's a farming system which is extremely generic (rainy weather doesn't even water your crops!) and it's pretty much a waste of time, as all you get for doing it is gold, which has almost no uses. There's a fishing system, but really nothing to do with the fish you catch aside from put them in a fish tank. The potion makers interface seems to hint that there was a system to brew potions from different ingredients, but you have all the recipes from the beginning and it doesn't let you experiment. There are odd and unique rocks spread around the overworld. There's also someone in town who is clearly into rocks, as his whole house is covered in them. I *thought* there might be a connection between the two, so I bring one of the special rocks to him. He doesn't care. There's a tavern that just kinda sits there. The tavern owner acts like he might give you quests. He doesn't. There are 2 currencies, gold, which is ONLY used for opening chests and buying a couple items from a random vendor in dungeons, and gems, which buy all your upgrades. You can only find gems in dungeons, so exploring the overworld feels like a waste of time. For some reason, the game takes away all your gems when you enter a dungeon. The only real collectible item are these 100 orbs that let you keep a small percentage of your gems when you enter a dungeon, which is practically useless, as the amount they let you keep is negligible even if you collect all of them, and you're probably spending all your gems on upgrades before you enter, anyhow. So it's not a bad game, really, it's just frustrating to see all these half-assed features that clearly didn't get the time, thought, and effort they needed.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I got this game in the Humble Choice.Main takeaway:There are positives and negatives. I think the positives probably outweigh the negatives. But for $20, this could use a little more polish and bug fixing. It's a bit hard to recommend at $20, but maybe on sale this can be a pretty fun little co-op game to play with a friend. While I believe it supports 4 players coop, I don't think it's actually practical due to the choice of 1 locked, shared camera.Things I liked:The graphics, music, world design, level design, and procedurally generated dungeons are all excellent. In a lot of good ways, this feels like a modern take on the familiar SNES Zelda formula. I'm pretty impressed by the procedurally generated dungeons because we never encountered a "soft lock" due to finding keys out of order or anything, which is sometimes a problem in 16-bit games from that era. I liked the money system. Being able to keep money you earn even if your run fails is kinda nice so you don't feel like you lost all your progress. I like the perks. I like that almost all the tools and weapons had some kind of upgrade path. I like that each class has a skill/perk tree you can invest in.I like how the town works. You get to purchase new buildings with different uses. For example, one building is for upgrading your stamina skill tree. Another is for upgrading weapons, or classes, etc. And you get to manually choose where each building goes, so you get to customize the layout of your town. I really enjoyed this design choice and it made me feel like my decisions for my town mattered.Things I'm a bit neutral on:There are like 8 or so different classes. I like this, in theory. However, magic does not seem to be a viable path. And neither does ranged combat. So basically, my coop partner and I each chose different classes (Knight for me, Ranger for him) but both of us ended up using only the sword as our weapon because the skill/perk upgrades for the sword are SO MUCH better than the ones for bow or magic that anything besides sword simply wasn't viable.Lots of "tools." But too many tools. There are several tools which are redundant and should just upgrade to from base model, to +1, then +2 with increasingly improved effects. For example, there's a hammer for hitting rocks. But there's also a boxing glove for hitting rocks. And all the tools live in 1 tool bar, in which you can only access 1 tool at a time. So by late game, when you have 15 tools, you have to cycle through them all in order to find the one you need. And as you get new tools, the tool order changes, so you can never really memorize the distance between different tools in the toolbar menu.Things I did not like:The toolbar hot menu does not function correctly on gamepad. I was able to set up tools on the different hot menu locations, but trying to cycle between them in-game didn't work.What is the point of farming? We tried this a little bit but it really felt like an afterthought and didn't actually ever earn us enough  currency to feel necessary vs simply farming dungeons.Sharing 1 locked screen is super bad. Especially because if 1 player opens a menu, the other player gets stuck looking at the menu and can't move until the first person closes the menu. Does not feel good in a modern game. 2 player coop felt kinda bad with this, but 3+ players felt really awful. Our 3rd friend quit after about 20 minutes because this was so poorly implemented and annoying to share one screen all the time.The bugs. Early game there weren't really any. But by mid game we were experiencing some bugs, and by later/end game we were experiencing constant bugs. One of the most egregious was in the endless dungeon in the main town that you finally access in late game. There was 1 level in this dungeon that we kept encountering that had a broken staircase. The stairway was textured into the game, but it was not modeled correctly so you couldn't take it up to the other area of the room, which meant you literally could not complete the room to progress. Every time we encountered that room (at least 3 times), we just had to quit out and end our run, which was frustrating.Another weird bug that comes to mind: while both of us were swimming, something glitched out when switching between screens and my character was able to walk on water. Which was slightly amusing at first, but obviously wrong and I wasn't able to fix it without quitting the run.--I would say this game starts out feeling like a 7.5/10. By mid game, with increasing bugs, this probably drops to a 6.5. By end game, I think it's a solid 6/10. I was pretty excited to just end the game and be done by the time we beat the final boss. I'm still going to give this a recommend, because I think they did some cool stuff with familiar genera, but hopefully this dev can do more bug testing and fixing on future titles so their games are more enjoyable to play throughout, instead of mostly in the first 1/3.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing almost 40 hours, I recommend Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos for gamers that love and miss the top down Zelda classics such as A Link to the Past or Link's Awakening. However, it is a rogue lite game, so don't expect the heavy puzzles of a Zelda game as this game is mostly a fight-a-thon with all of the main villains' minions and monsters.PROS:There's a large overworld to explore that contains your typical forest, mountain, frozen tundra, volcano, beach, swamp land, graveyard, and lake areas, etc, similar to a Hyrule adventure. As I said, this game's strength is in appealing to the Zelda fan and it would not be amiss to call this rogue lite a Zelda clone. We have a sword and shield, the hookshot, boomerang, a flute that summons a riding animal, the lantern, the hammer, the fishing rod, bombs and the bomb bag, the wand that shoots ice or fire, spells to quell storms or change the time of day, etc. New or original items might include the punching glove and the extremely underused time wand that shows what the area looked like centuries past and allows our "not Link" player character to interact with the environment as it was in the distant past. The bestiary book is technically new, even though games like Breath of the Wild had one, because this bestiary book is a usable item: you close monsters up into it like you would dried flowers in order to add them to your bestiary. If you add the monsters enough times, you master that monster, however I fail to see how this is beneficial as it seems to not add any extra information or give you any perks, other than getting you one step away from completing the entire bestiary and getting a Steam achievement for it. Cracked walls can be bombed to show hidden caves and passage ways, as we've had in Zelda ever since the first game in the series (well, minus the cracks which didn't come until A Link to the Past). Torches can be lit with the lantern to solve puzzles and reveal hidden chests. One good upgrade on our Zelda lantern is that we can now use it to start brush fires or burn down obstacles in our path. At a certain point in the game you earn a masterful sword of sorts that will shoot out a long range projectile beam of light at enemies if your health is at full. In other words, if you're a Zelda fan, there's plenty to love and be comfortable with here, with a couple new additions or changes. Like in Breath of the Wild, we are given an exhaustion meter that can be upgraded to allow us to do more for longer later in the game. This is important as you don't want to get tired of swinging your sword and get overwhelmed by enemies or drown while swimming. Collectibles and monster drops exist in the game but, except for a couple of side quests or so and making potions, I haven't found any use for the monster drops. The lone collectible comes in the form of power spheres that allow you to keep a certain amount of gems when reentering a new dungeon. The game, unlike Zelda, has two forms of currency: the Rupee like gems and the standard medieval RPG gold coins. You'll need both the progress without hindrance. Gems can only be found in the dungeons, where as gold coins are found everywhere. You'd think the village NPC's would accept gold coins more often but unfortunately it's all gems for the most part. You'll need gold coins to pay to unlock certain treasure chests holding gems as well as the dungeon merchant that offers health potions and whatnot while you're deep in the dungeons. Dungeons cannot be left unless you die, in which case you awaken back at your home in the town, your earned gems in tow to help you upgrade before you face the dungeon yet again. As a rogue lite, puzzles do exist, but it's mostly about fighting your way through until you die or become strong enough to defeat the dungeon. In other words, dungeons are not meant to be beaten on the first try, so expect to die. A lot. Dungeons are generated randomly so that every dungeon attempt is different. There are currently 6 dungeons, although more dungeons may come in the future; we'll get back to this later. The village is an interesting aspect of this Zelda clone because you can use your gems in order to build not only your house, but also vacant houses thereby attracting NPC characters to come live in your village. You also can build a fishing pier and house, a bar, a witch's potion shop, a science lab, a gymn, a hospital, a general store, a sword smith work shop, an tool shop, a thread shop, and a personal farm. The farm gives light Harvest Moon chores as the vegetables can be sold in the market town square for gold coins needed for the dungeons. Vegetable seeds can be found while out exploring the overworld, which cannot be fully explored until you earn and upgrade your typical Zelda tools from the dungeons or the science lab or the tool shop, just as you would expect from a Zelda clone. Some higher end vegetable seeds can also be purchased using gems at the general store. Gold coins can be used mostly in town to buy furnishings for your house. Some of these are functional, but most are cosmetic. You start off with two functioning pieces of furniture, the bed and the wardrobe. The bed passes a day, possibly heals you (I'm not sure, I never tried this), whereas the wardrobe allows you to change your player character class, something definitely not from the Zelda franchise. I have not explored using these classes yet, but more classes can be purchased from the thread shop. They help in multiplayer, I'm sure, but I was not able to do any multiplayer, despite attempting it several times. Multiplayer is both online or split screen local. I stuck to the basic starting player character class as it is the Link-clone standard. Other classes have different changes in offense, defense, and speed and offer a different running move or other ability. The standard "Link" wardrobe offers the Pegasus boot move from A Link to the Past, whereas other classes have invisibility, teleportation, skull rolling, flying via witch's broom or a parrot, a bomb jump, etc. Speaking of jumping, the Roc Feather is sadly missing from this game. The basic premise of the game is to kill the four dungeon bosses in order to gain their 4 coins and add them to the final dungeon ala "Super Mario Land 2: The 6 Golden Coins" in order to access the final dungeon and boss and thus free the land from the villains' curse so the villagers can colonize the continent safely. You are quested, not by the villagers, but by four goddesses who have been imprisoned by the monstrous villains. Side quests will help fill in gaps in story telling, but we'll get to this later. The game's over world features random transitions to night and random thunder storms. Certain stores in the village are closed during night and storms. Sleeping in the bed or using magic spells can change the time or weather and are needed for certain over world puzzle solving. During your exploration of the over world, you'll find abandoned villages, farms, and other human (?) inhabitants who have chosen to live outside of your central village. Some of these characters can be recruited to live in your village to fill one of the vacant houses. The music in the game isn't Zelda tune catchy or upbeat fast, but it is good enough and does it's job. The game feels mostly quiet and I don't feel much need to cut the volume off or wear headphones as to not distract the wife while she's sleeping or working, etc. Sound effects are definitely present even though the music seems calm and quiet at times.CONS:The game is unfortunately unfinished and unpolished as of 8/06/21. There are areas that can be seen but not reached, some underground collectibles cannot be dug up due to bug or error, invisible buildings and objects around the inaccessible mine dungeon, an out of place construction sign for the inaccessible beach dungeon. Fully built town feels empty of residents. Bar does nothing. Bugs. Still, I loved this RL Zelda clone.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I had friends to play this with. Seems it would be amazing with friends!I just solo-completed the story yesterday and through my playthrough, I thoroughly explored everything I could and, got most of it knocked out of the park, so there were very few things to backtrack to or to get some help with a guide.I am down just to the last achievement now, which weirdly enough, ain't even the rarest.The story is simple enough and honestly, wasn't what kept me hooked to the game.It totally was the Link to the Past throwback with enhancements, so my thumbs up.Played through the whole experience on Hard mode (Normal felt like it would be too easy and I didn't feel up to Brutal) and it is a fair challenge until you upgrade damage enough and cut through everything like paper, although for the endless dungeon and the Catacombs the enemies get stronger and spongy as you go deeper.I thoroughly enjoyed the "A Link to the Past" throwback, and while a few things felt like an improvement (Several classes to choose from (although I just played Hero), the many upgrades available, the way you can just swin and much more), another few felt like a total rip-off (bushes, maze rooms in the dark, lamp/torch, rats snakes and bats, and other stuff).I love/hate the Stamina factor. It is a good balance to not have you just mindlessly whacking everything on the spot like you would in ALttP.Rogue Heroes does lack the depth that ALttP would put into dungeon design (for example, how when you get the bow you use it to complete the dungeon and fight the boss, when you get the hammer etc).All of the 4 main dungeons feel somewhat short, while the seem-optional dungeons feel a little bit more thought through or a bit dragged even.I guess some of this is compensated in the fact that the 4 main dungeons appear to be procedurally generated and you get the item at the end of the dungeon (also true for seem-optional dungeon) and it allows you to further navigate the world (as ALttP did), other than that, you get glass items within a dungeon (lose it when you die) to assist you through the dungeon while you don't have the real thing.You don't really lose anything when you die: coin, gems, items (only glass, but you get the real thing as you progress through the game), but you are forced to give up your gems when entering a dungeon, so be sure to spend them real good on your upgrades.Word of advice on this:- Coins are barely used in the game, it is used within the dungeons to unlock chests (which contain gems) and other assists within the dungeon. Coins are easily gathered outside of dungeons rather than within them.- Gems are the other way around: easily gathered within dungeons (no gather outside) and used a lot for your upgrades and unlocking stuff mainly outside of the dungeons.Tavern seems useless in single player.Bosses aren't really complex, I found overall dungeoning and areas putting me through more of a hard time than the bosses did. Boss OST kicks ass though.Talking OST, I SIMPLY LOVE the fact that they used the a couple of free license songs, such as the one in the beach, which is the same for the desert area in Exiled Kingdoms and the one in the fields which is used in some area in Doom & Destiny.In-game bestiary is always a plus, but I don't agree much with their implementation of it, having to smack monsters on a killing blow to get 1st entry of that monster, and again after some kills to "Master" a monster. It is never explained what "Mastering" a monster actually does, so feels like a moot task. You just need 1 kill with the book for each monster entry and to unlock achievement btw - Bosses don't register.I do hate the fishing in this game (controller, didn't try keyboard). It has to be the worst fishing mechanic I have seen to date (and OMG, I played BoF IV, Graveyard Keeper, old school Harvest Moon SNES/PSX, SDV). The only purpose for fishing is unlocking a class and an achievement, and nothing else. You can't eat the fish, you don't use them in recipes, you don't sell them, nothing, nada - actually, just rememberred you can expose them in fish tanks, but really? - Unlocking the class requires 3 different species of 5-star legendary fish, which have better chances in specific spots, which by the way, I got many more of the 5-star legendary fish whatnot than a couple of the species of 3 or 4 star fish I needed for the achievement completion, so that is weird huh.Even with a few of these negatives that I pointed out, I still enjoyed this game pretty much.The asking price is too expensive in my coin (BRL 105,00) and I got a good deal at 90% off, so would advise for the promo.It also features Remote Play Together, which may help to get a coop play going and softening the blow on that price.I guess I may keep this one around after completing achievements and try for a full Brutal playthrough with different classes or as I unlock them and/or try to get a friend onboard on Remote Play.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is unfinished, and a lot of mechanisms were left half-baked, to where I believe this should still be marked as early-access, and I'm annoyed it just got pushed out the door.Just a few of the things:- Tools are half-baked. There's a punching glove and a hammer that both do the similar function of smashing open new areas. The punching glove is barely ever used. Why??- There's stuff like buying furniture for houses that's a half-baked afterthought. I never even figured out how to add furniture or when heroes move into town and to what purpose...and why??- There's an 'under construction' area in the southwest of the map and some other dead ends and invisible walls...are they even planning on finishing this stuff?- Bugs like floors that are incompletable- Fishing and farming also feels like an afterthought. You end up with more than enough money to spend in dungeons, so there's not much point.I think they had big ambitions to mashup Zelda with Animal Cross and Stardew. The base game is fun - building your character, exploring, unlocking new levels...it all just abruptly accumulates to a point where you've unlocked all these things and realize they go nowhere.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this game quite a bit. I'd like to cover some concerns right off the bat that other users have brought up before. As of the time I write this review, online co-op and multiplayer modes are  Local Co-op (or remote play) works as intended from my experience. Remote play works quite well, not much latency if any at all, however trap switches/ tiles become a bit difficult to see at times due to stream video quality fluctuation. YMMV. Online multiplayer works now, however there are currently some shortcut/ progression issues that can occur. For instance, if one user has certain areas unlocked, they can become unlocked if playing together. These small bugs aside- I would recommend buying the game for it's co-op experience currently.I've only recently discovered this game, but to my knowledge it has been around for a few years. Some users are upset and claim the game is "mislabeled" in regards to it's state of development. I have been around many EA and Indie games and rarely does a title grab my attention like this one has. I think it has a lot of potential to grow, regardless of how the game is "labeled". I try to look at these things at face value, considering some AAA games have been released in the past few years in abysmal fashion. Over the past few weeks the developers seem to be addressing everyone's concerns- and actually promptly implementing said features/ fixes. At the moment, some classes fall a bit short in terms of gameplay, but these are being adjusted as well, and some classes have already seen drastic changes. I would like to see alternate hairstyles and beards, or other braids. Different colored/ tiered (stronger) shields, or have them change shade along with your save badge color. The ability to deconstruct buildings would be nice, perhaps a small % return on gems instead of just deleting the building outright? Also, for multiplayer since the hero's home is replaced by the "hub", a new building like a club house, or a complete redesign of the "hub" would be nice. It is unfortunate you cannot customize your house while playing co-op. The dungeon's difficulty scaling with more players could use an increase, as it becomes a bit easy on some floors with 2+ players. Some puzzles sometimes get repetitive, I hope for more map layouts in the future. Talks of a potential map editor and steam workshop integration seem promising. I am still in the beginning stages of the game, but I am satisfied with the amount of content that I have to explore, give or take a few locations. I am happy there are more areas that will become accessible later on.I was actually on the fence about purchasing this game, with concerns of broken co-op and a unfinished game. What I got was a pleasant surprise, and it will definitely have me coming back for more. The developers swiftly crush bugs and have been working on balancing the game, and that's really nice to see happen so quickly. The game is a lot of fun, but you could potentially get lonely if you play by yourself. At the end of the day, I would rate this game positively, and recommend picking it up- especially if you can nab it on sale.tdlr: Co-op/ multiplayer works, some progression bugs, game is good. Buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game.  I love the idea of a co-op Zelda-ish game.  But the game is miserable and grindy to play.  It's difficult in the least satisfying way possible.  If you play slowly and carefully it's generally pretty easy.  So yeah, you play methodically and chip enemies down in a slow, dirgelike rhythym... as the joy of life slowly fades from your body.  But eventually you get bored.  This is inevitable: the enemies have tons of HP (at least with your starting sword) and it's a roguelike so you have to do the same rooms again and again.  And when you get bored you'll try to hurry - try to get an extra hit in on a boring bloody rat who is absolutely uninteresting to fight.  And when you hurry a bit, you'll find that the boring bloody rat's hitbox is a little larger than it seems, or sometimes he won't be knocked back the same way, or the "exhaustion" mechanic means your sword won't swing - and the dumb rat will hit you for a huge chunk of your starter HP.  And so you'll be frustrated and careful for a while, until you get bored again.  Then you'll not properly scan the room for tiles that are one shade darker, and eat another chunk of health to a stupid trap.  Or you'll try to get across one more section of spikes than is safe because you don't want to sit there for another cycle, and the partner you're playing with definitely doesn't want to stand there for another cycle... And then you'll die and realize you have to grind through all that again.Or or or or you'll quit playing and you'll just be saving yourself sadness, because whoever designed this game wants something very different out of a game than I do.

I've watered them 3 times and came back to dead plants. Maybe my nonexistent green thumb carried over to the game.)-Glitching through walls with reaper. I used reaper and glitched hard in a dungeon. Game instantly crashed. (Don't glitch the game)-Fishing. Oh lord fishing will take a minute. The buttons to reel in the fish are weird to do. But keep trying you'll get it. _childDocuments_.review: Decent 2D Zelda clone that is heavily inspired by the series and more specifically the Four Swords games.  Roguelite elements are also included in the games dungeons with plenty of permanent progression to increase your power and durability as you progress.I currently offer a lite recommendation for the game as it could use some bug patches and content updates/changes to be worth the full price.  Primary issues are listed below.- Online coop desync/bugs- Encountering the same rooms in the randomly generated dungeons too often.  One time i had a dungeon which literally had four of the same large rooms on a floor.- The game is far too easy, especially once you start obtaining a lot of upgrades.- Endgame endless dungeon isn't very enjoyable as it lacks boss encounters and has too many repeated rooms and limited challenge.  It might pick up if you can get extremely far in, but it takes far too long and there are no checkpoints.- The different classes don't feel different enough since at the end of the day the sword is your primary and most powerful reusable tool, which makes whatever class has the most sword damage seemingly the best choice.If the online coop is patched up, then at the very least it will be a fun Zelda-like experience for a group of friends that would be an easy recommendation.  Even if the dungeons can sometimes be a let down with repeating rooms, the game also has a handcrafted overworld to explore and enjoy.  Extra activities like farming and fishing help too, even if they are simple tacked on features.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Heroes Ruins of Tasos will no doubt be a controversial game. Doing something different isn't always going to be clean cut and creating a roguelite game that surrounds itself in Legend of Zelda (specifically A Link to the Past) design mechanics is no easy task. There are going to be plenty of people that will adore it for its charm and creative design as well as its polished fundamentals. Other people will harp on the cosmetic bugs, broken online multiplayer, and under delivering on some of the games features. The game does have its charm, and it is far from a disaster, but the truth is that it could have used more time both in bug cleanup before launch, but also is design. Many of the features feel like they were tacked on as after thoughts and were not well thought through on how they would impact other elements of the game. In the end the game feels like two games in one, and both of them are decent.Overall, I think this game won't be for everyone, but personally, I enjoyed it and recommend this toad for anyone that understands its warts. Sure there are things in this game aren't spectacular, but it was fun to play none-the-less, and succeeded in keeping my attention for the many hours I played it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the best games I've played in a long time. However, keep in mind that I'm an age old Zelda fan and A Link To The Past is one of my favorites, in which this game was largely inspired. The pixel art is awesome, the story is simple but great, the other characters all serve a significant role and most importantly this game perfectly blends the methods of a Zelda game with the Rogue-lite formula. This game in some cases may be even better than many Zelda games because it has very fun and unique puzzles that are extremely creative. Plus, the replay value is off the charts. Starting as a regular swordsman but eventually unlocking several more classes, items, and abilities which will keep it fresh for a long time. Also this game has somethings that are not randomly generated, like the over-world, meanwhile inside each dungeon its randomly generated meaning each time you die, you have to redo the dungeon or parts of it but its never the same one twice. This game is fun alone, but really thrives with at least one other friend. Finally, the boss fights are fantastic. Many games have over scripted bosses or they're super easy and just have giant health bars. This game doesn't waste your time with scripted bosses, they're classic. They come at your with their attack patterns and only hold back with just enough time for you to hit it after it wreaks havoc on you. They're crazy funAll that in mind, if you don't like rogue lites, RPGs, or Zelda games. This may not be for you. I'd suggets being a fan of at least 2/3 of those. Cheers!

_childDocuments_.review: We got the game on sale for a few bucks, so by default I think I got my moneys worth out of it. However it felt like I experienced the two polar opposite ends of the spectrum with this game: some really fun multiplayer shenanigans with my friend that pushed us to keep playing AND THEN frustration from the game continuously glitching out to the point where we had to edit our save data to recover all the spheres that magically disappeared from the inventories. The base game has a lot of potential but it's obvious the developers stretched themselves too thin just because the amount of half-baked ideas. Yeah technically the game has farming, but it super barebones and provides no real benefit besides money which gets obsolete later in the game. Classes don't feel balanced at all, some movement abilities are clearly better than others, plus the small stats don't make too much sense. This game could really benefit from some QoL changes like a minimap that updates over time with new areas and collectibles you've already collected. Unfortunately while looking up stuff on the Steam forums, it's pretty apparent this game is dead as there have been no updates or even communication from the developers on the state of the game. For the sale price, I think it's worth a quick look with friends since a 2D Zelda roguelite with multiplayer sounds fun, but for $20 you can find better singleplayer/multiplayer experiences. Very conflicted with this review, because I think I can recommend it since we ended up finishing it, but your miles will absolutely vary.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a whole bunch of great and miserable aspects combined. Sadly, there is too much frustrating stuff, which ultimately leads me to this review.Let's start with the great:- you have the option to change classes at will and are not bound to one after choosing. the classes are not too different (often the only changes are speed, attack and magic as well as a small ability)- the dungeons are a lot of fun, the bosses are cool too- exploration is amazing. you unlock different things along the way that make it possible to get into new areas. going back to a biome you've explored before often still ends in new findings- both palyers end up with the same amount of loot from dungeons, no matter if or when then die- when purchasing something that is for all palyers, everyone can chip in, which is a nice idea imo- leveling up is great, you have many many skill trees to upgrade and can freely choose what you want to put your money in- there are quite a number of side quests to doWhile this all sounds pretty good, it's put into perspective by all of the game's flaws:- if you play with controller, your characer will often still follow the comands when you are in the inventory, which is a HUGE annoyance- the map is sometimes weirdly split into screens and you keep jumping between two "frames" because this slip is so awkward- the game is a BUGGY MESS in general- it happened to us that after a "frame" switch, we suddenly were not able to interact with anything. we were able to walk through anything, couldn't deal nor take damage- we were often teleported to a completely different part of the map when we exited a cave for some reason. this happeend more than once. because we were not supposed to be in that biome, we were not able to exit naturally and had to restart the game in order to  keep playing- quite often, you don't really know what to do or how to do it. you are given tools and have to learn by accident what you can use them for. or you have to go somewhere, finally make it after solving an environmental puzzple of sorts, only to realise that you can still not continue.The bugs are honestly what annoy me most. some of them make the whole gaming experience and especially the multiplayer very frustrating. as a game that is pretty much meant to be played as a multiplayer, that is disappointing.
