_childDocuments_.review: I don't play many roguelites because they often are stupid fustrating hard. Rogue Heroes doesn't really have that problem.At first, the first dungeon is ridiculously hard, since you are a squishy nobody that is whacking away with a stick. Traps pretty much 1 hit you, you are getting battered around by skellies, etc. But once you beat the first dungeon....the rest of the game goes downhill. Each of the 4 dungeons are 3 floors. Roughly take 45 minutes to clear a dungeon (depending on level) while solving all puzzles, and clearing every room. After I beat the first dungeon, I was able to beat each next one within one full try. It took about 3 hours to beat the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and final boss. You are just way overpowered and get so many gems that its just now about how fast you can clear it, not being careful anymore because it doesn't matter anymore. If the first dungeon was a little easier, and the rest of the game was a bit harder, this would've kept up with the increase in your power as well. Unfortunately, it doesn't and you end up being a one-man army really quickly. Also, there are several classes but I don't know why you would use them? I chose Knight, because looking at the shop, it has the most upgrades available. More upgrades = more power. Also, the bow and staff is really annoying to aim. Some of the enemies move too fast to be able to use them effectively. And the auto-aim thing is a bit wacky. I only used the staff and bow when I had to for traps/puzzles. Don't get me wrong, this game is fun, but there is just such a disconnection between challenge and reward.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really fun and I do recommend it. The combat can be satisfying if you like hack and slash combat. Some of the classes are viable, others show up way too late to care for. The game can be rather easy in the dungeons and gems are given away so frequently, you would hardly have to grind after your first few attempts at the first dungeon. The puzzles are very similar to A Link To The Past and it makes me want to go back and play Attp and A Link Between Worlds. The problem is, the game is hardly a rogue-lite. It's more a dungeon-pillaging puzzle-adventure game with some rare stat modifiers and 2D Zelda. Everything else is pre-planned. No luck involved. If you die, it is likely your fault and has very little to do with what your build becomes in a dungeon. But it is incredibly easy to overcome by pumping more gems into your combat and health with some rare circumstances where you need to buff a certain tool (eg. bow and grappling hook). The second half of the game is pretty disappointing. You get some really great dungeons early on but after main dungeon 2, you get some puzzle dungeons with challenging bosses (losing in these dungeons is awful since you have to do all the puzzles again) and your standard dungeons which are easy to breeze through. You also get a lot of the tools around the 2nd dungeon. The reward for the 3rd dungeon is completely useless and there is no reward for the 4th major dungeon. My recommendation to the developers if they decide to release an update is to add something that will be useful for shortcuts . For example, how about an axe to cut through annoying trees or maybe something to climb up mountains to speed up the exploration process and last-minute side quest cleanup. Yes there is bugs. I've had to restart my game a couple of times due to soft-locks. They do not destroy the experience but it does break up the game's flow. Still, I recommend it because it can be fun. I mention the negatives because you should know what you are getting yourself into and temper your expectations. Either expect a super easy "rogue-lite" or a Zelda clone where you could power up your character using standard RPG levelling mechanics. Also, the frogs are awesome and I wish they were used more.

_childDocuments_.review: The basic game loop is fun! Explore the overworld, find a dungeon, try to beat it. Fail to beat it? Go back to town, upgrade your stats, and try again! Eventually beat the dungeon, which unlocks a new item, which you can then use to explore farther on the overworld, eventually reaching a new dungeon.The graphics are cute and fitting. Nothing felt out of place. The sound effects were generally good as well.The overworld itself was fun to explore. There were lots of varied locations, and even though the secrets were generally obvious to find, it was still satisfying to hunt them down and get the rewards from them.There were a ton of different things to upgrade, and the different upgrade trees were cute to look at and explore.Some of the game mechanics felt superfluous. The game had a town building minigame, which mostly involved placing various buildings in various slots around the town. It was cute, but placing a building one place instead of another was just thematic. It was weird placing down a building in a random spot, not understanding what the building was going to be when placed. Several times after placing a structure, I had wished I had placed it somewhere more convenient, but didn't know until it was placed that it would be some building I want to visit often. Ultimately it just made walking back and forth to places in the town slower than it had to be for no real benefit.There was a whole planting / farming mini-game thing that felt entirely useless. My 2 friends and I played through literally the  game without a single crop growing. It seems more designed around singleplayer, where time might pass more often whenever you sleep, which it didn't in co-op.And on that note, there were several other things that didn't quite work so hot in co-op.- Pickups being individual meant we needed for farm 3x as many things to complete the varied "collect stuff" quests (Almost every single 'quest' ended up just being "I need 20 slime balls" or "I want 30 fangs")- Screen transitions were slightly awkward in co-op. If any one player walked off the edge of the screen, it would teleport all players to the new screen. Understandable, but very often jarring. Someone might accidentally walk off the edge of the screen, for example. Or it was purposeful, but then someone else immediately walks back to the previous screen because they were pressing the wrong direction. There was no delay or warning for these transitions, so it caught us off guard several times.The difficulty curve of the game was very poor. We beat the first dungeon after perhaps 5-6 attempts. It was fun, challenging, and the boss was mechanically interesting and relevant. We beat the second dungeon after only 2 attempts, the first attempt ending prematurely because of bugs. The dungeon was a breeze, and the boss's mechanics were irrelevant and we just ignored them. We then proceeded to beat the 3rd, 4th and final dungeons on our first try without even a hint of effort expended. They were just too easy. Or, perhaps we were too strong. Two sides of the same coin. It got really boring near the end because we were just so incredibly overpowered compared to the enemies.The balance of the different upgrades and things were really off as well. My friends went for a sword-based build. I went for a grappling-hook based build. For exactly the first dungeon, I felt like my damage was relevant. I maxxed out the entire upgrade path and never did any relevant damage again, because the sword upgrade tree was much deeper than the grappling hook upgrade tree. Understandable, I suppose. So for the next 2 dungeons, I 100% maxxed out my wand & magic pool. My friends were nearing the top of the sword tree at this point. For comparison, they would deal around 300 damage a hit, 3 times a second, with a 50% chance to crit and hit for 800 or so. Worked out to be around 1000 dps. With every single possible upgrade spent to improve my magic, I could deal around... 30 damage a second. For some later enemies, I could literally expend my entire magic pool on a single enemy over 20 seconds and it wouldn't die. My friends would one-shot them with a sword. This was WITH me using the mage class with it's assorted magical bonuses. Repeat this same process when I tried to level up bombs instead. They just didn't hold a candle to the basic sword weapon in any regard. But, on the plus side, they did self-damage so I died a lot when using them! A fitting end to the saga of "trying to make anything that isn't swords work in any capacity."Also, co-op was exceptionally buggy. It would work great for half an hour, or maybe even 2 hours, but then it would desync. And once it desynced, it was not likely to recover to a playable state, so we had to restart the session to have all of us be able to play again. Additionally, even when it didn't desync, it handled latency / lag very poorly. I know that lag isn't the game's fault, but I feelt like an acceptable outcome for a poor connection is to, say, pause the game until it recovers. Or have the lagging player sit on a wait screen. It's not really an acceptable outcome to have someone lagging be able to pick up a crystal pickup on the ground 500 times because they are lagging, and suddenly get +80,000  gems. Or, like, to be unable to kill anything in the entire dungeon, because while the host sees ever enemy dead, the client doesn't, and they just die to invisible unkillable enemies. Or like... when a screen transition happens during lag, the lagging player (or maybe everyone) appears inside a lake and drowns. Or inside a wall and is stuck. Or the screen transition never happens, and the game is softlocked. It wasn't unplayable, and obviously wouldn't be an issue in solo play, but it was a huge factor in my enjoyment of this game.It's a fun game, and I would recommend it for fans of games in this genre. However, if you plan to play online multiplayer and have low tolerance for constantly restarting your game, or other random bugs, then steer clear. The difficulty curve is not smooth in the least, but it didn't ruin my enjoyment of the game as a whole. Despite the bugs, it still seems more enjoyable with friends than on your own.

_childDocuments_.review: You know, making games is a difficult endeavor. I considered (and re-considered) this fact many times during my hours spent with Rogue Heroes.Quick lead-in before I give a litany of criticism: It's a nice pick-up-and-play, 4-5 session game to jam through with a group of friends. Many pieces of the game are wonky or outright multiplayer-hostile, but there's a special kind of bonding that can occur when you support each during times of adversity.If you have a group of friends that are looking for a fairly casual, low-commitment game to play (the folks you'll have a good time with no matter what you're doing) this is a good pick. Perfect for the off-season of an MMO raid team, for example.Now, to get into the chunkier feedback:It's got a lot of rough edges. It's almost always clear what the game's going for (since it's so clearly built in the vein of classic Zelda games) but there are a lot of little details that got missed in the process. Like how blocks don't get pushed in discrete, 1-unit chunks, there's no the subtle magnetism that vacuums you to be even with bushes / pots / blocks you interact with, the (lack of) readability of which ledges you can (and should) leap off of, that kind of stuff.There are also new, exciting issues unique to this game with no parallels to classic Zelda. A lot of these are situations where the game mechanics are a bit self-sabotaging, especially in multiplayer play. Things like:The game's not all negatives, though (I'm even giving this a positive review!) so here are some good points:It's definitely an odd one, but I enjoyed the block of time I spent with my friends in this game. Enough to give it a slight thumbs up. Grab it on sale, and have a good time!And, you know, I get it. Making games is hard, and they got this one across the finish line. That's an achievement few can claim, so don't be afraid to take some pride in that.

_childDocuments_.review: Many of the negative reviews of this game are completely false. In regards to co-op bugs, I can't speak to, I play solo. But I almost didn't buy this game from some of the complaining about solo aspects of the game: i.e. puzzles can't be completed, unpolished dungeons, unbeatable situations, etc.... But most of these reviews also call the game easy. Clearly not that easy. Look, if you're looking for some souls-like super punishing hardmode game - this isn't it. If you want a fun, Link to the Past (if you're like me and grew up playing Zelda on repeat, you'll love this), semi-challenging but not too punishing (anything too difficult - gems are easy to farm, you can easily scale yourself up past each dungeon and easy mode them) puzzle game: this is very worth it.I love that it's pretty casual, I have found a couple of minor bugs in terms of being able to climb something I shouldn't be able to, or jumping and suddenly landing in a different spot not quite where you should be. None are game breaking. None have stopped any of my runs. And the stuff people are saying about solo mode bugs - totally false. There are some genuinely challenging puzzles but I'm in the 4th dungeon now and haven't run across any puzzle I couldn't do solo - though admittedly some are very frustrating and time consuming (one especially in dungeon 3, but I'm convinced there's any easier way I haven't thought of yet).Bugs about co-op - sure, maybe, I dunno, everything else people are whining about... well, guess the game isn't as easy as they thought if they couldn't complete the puzzles on solo. ;)

_childDocuments_.review: very fun game if you are a fan of old school zelda. upgrading inventory is a great mechanic, though the sword will dwarf all the other items in terms of damage. enemies don't really get complicated, they just kinda get tankier and dish out more damage. personally I think the trap damage got ridiculous but that was about it. Stamina system I don't mind except that the sword just doesn't let you attack once you hit half stam. having the class ability be separate for the stamina bar was a really good choice though. Maybe if there was an easier way to switch between magics I would have used it more. you have to go into the inventory menu to change with spell you are casting. but was still really fun to sword and board the game. Ranger to me felt like the best class. It has a high base speed and the dash ability gives you iframes and recharges very fast. I didn't even bother with the bow mechanics. it was honestly fun enough to dash into enemies and slice them up instead. the aiming for the bow and the spells can be wonky at times. it will target enemies that are not close to you when you have enemies coming right at you.Grappling hook was my go to side arm. Not only does it help traverse the world, but it doesn't have to target enemies it just moves in a straight line. not much damage just like the rest of the items but it felt more consistent if i wanted to attack at range.I like that the main dungeons were more roguelite. _childDocuments_.review: This game is basically "what if the Zelda franchise was public domain and someone re-made Four Swords but also fallen into the trap of traditional RPGs and quantifying every possible stat while putting the focus into traversing randomized dungeons". And it's fairly decent.Having completed the main portion of the game and still having some collectables to look for, my general opinion is that this is a serviceable "Link to the Past clone" for the most part. There are some obtuse things you're supposed to intuit along the game and (currently) it's possible to sequence-break yourself into softlocks, meaning that you'll make that save game impossible to complete. This is avoidable if you don't go too deep into the upgrades to unlock something which will make you sequence break (like swimming stamina) or just focus on doing the main quest as a priority; I'm just saying it so you can prevent yourself from losing your time investment.The main focus, as I stated in the beginning, is clearing dungeons. There isn't that much in the way of difficulty beyond learning enemy attack patterns and finding the class you're most comfortable playing as, since each plays slightly different from each other with the active "movement skill" and percentual distribution of damage (to them and to enemies) as well as movement speed. Keep in mind that faster classes are generally frailer but easier to use when dealing with some timed traps and dungeon room objectives.One of the main gimmicks, the multiplayer component, is something I haven't experienced at all. Sufice to say that at worst you're going to get desynchronized with other players, but at best you're getting the full experience. Dungeon puzzles take into account how many players are in the game and it should be obviously much more interesting when another human being is controlling your progress by being cooperative. There's a local multiplayer mode, but haven't got anyone I could test that with either.The negatives? Personally, I hate the fast cycled sub-items for a specific reason: in dungeons, you can technically select items that you will NEVER have a purpose to use (such as crop seeds). If I'm cycling from the hammer to the hookshot, why would I ever want to pass through the seeds...? One less item to cycle in dungeons would also mean faster swapping and encouraging usage of all your resources more. The game also has a few bugs here and there, but nothing major aside from the sequence-breaking softlocks, in my experience.I'm going to recommend Rogue Heroes because I'm all for someone else taking a shot at classic Zelda titles with multiplayer, since the official source refuses to make them. It's a flawed game but possibly a shiny gem in the genre. No idea how updates will change the game in the future (currently I do see potential to do a bit more with what there is, but again: I haven't completed 100% yet, so no clue), but it's still a good game and significantly better than a few that burned me in the past.

_childDocuments_.review: You start off by exploring the map for the first dungeon. Once you get there, you proceed through a random collection of rooms to get to the boss. There are three floors per dungeon and four dungeons total, but there is a lot more to explore in the world outside of the dungeons. Within the dungeons themselves you can obtain temporary tools (glass) that you will lose when you die or finish the dungeon. You also find gems which are exclusive to dungeons that can be used to "buy" more shops in town which are then used to buy upgrades for your character such as increased health, magic, attack power, attack speed, character classes, permanent tools (not glass), etc.Beating each dungeon will also give you another permanent tool like the hook shot or bombs which are used both in dungeons and in the overworld to get more treasure. Other character classes can be unlocked which give different offensive, defensive, and speed stats. Each class also has their own secondary ability. The basic class uses the Zelda-like pegasus boots charge. The thief class can turn invisible and run fast and so on.The game can be played completely solo or with up to four players. I played mostly two-player with my brother. The game supports both local and online. We played online with two copies of the game on two separate computers in two separate rooms in the same house. The game ran fine online most of the time. There were a couple times where the game desynced and dropped one of us from the game.If one of you dies, the other player can pick up your skull and take it to a revival statue (multiple found in each dungeon). All gems that are picked up by either player are given out equally among all players. This is great because it avoids the problem of fighting over rewards like in Zelda Four Swords Adventures. Also great is that spending gems back in town is done on an individual basis. Each player chooses how they want to spend their gems. The shops purchased for developing the town can be bought with pooled gems. Each player will volunteer how many gems they want to create these new buildings. Playing with my brother, there weren't any problems splitting the cost of these. Note that only the host player will advance the town in their game. Guest players will get to keep all the upgrades they buy for their character, but will not see any of the town developments if they load up their file solo afterwards. This is not a problem because they will be powered up enough to take on dungeons on their own if they want. All player will still earn achievements for beating dungeons at the same time, and will earn personal achievements like defeating X number of enemies separately.As of March 31st the game has been updated to fill the entire world map. There are three new optional dungeons that end with their own unique bosses. However, these dungeons are not randomized like all the other dungeons. these are more traditional top-down Zelda-like dungeons with unique puzzles. They are only one floor each, not multiple floors like all the others, which makes them much shorter experiences.This is a very fun Zelda-like action adventure game with great multiplayer. There is also a free demo, so go try it before you buy!Please watch this for further demonstration of my review points and about the community experimental build.

_childDocuments_.review: The game basically feels like a 2D Zelda in terms of control/abilities, but it turns out deliberate level design is an important part of what makes those Zelda games work. The "rogue-lite" aspects of the game just don't serve the Zelda gameplay well. In a proper roguelike, the game stays compelling because each run has the opportunity to be unique. In Rogue Heroes, dungeon runs aren't interesting because the player's set of abilities is too static. You might pick up some buffs to your stats, but you won't acquire anything that would cause you to adopt a different strategy. The level design of a Zelda game doesn't mesh well with the roguelike format either. Many rooms in a dungeon will feature puzzles. The puzzles in Rogue Heroes are fine, but you're going to encounter the same puzzles multiple times if you run a dungeon more than once. Repeatedly solving the same puzzle isn't a fun experience.Aside from these fundamental structural problems, the game isn't finished. It shouldn't have been released as a 1.0 in the state it was in. The character class descriptions suggest the classes have abilities that they simply didn't have at launch. At least some of it has been updated since I finished playing, but it was pretty frustrating to play as a Mage and find that my magic wand wasn't anymore effective than it was when I played as the base class. There are also large areas of the map that are pointless, but the game doesn't tell you they're pointless, and in at least one case it actively leads you to believe that there should be something more happening:-There was a sidequest to find a lady's husband-I found the dude-I was rewarded with a key to some kind of crab dungeon-After beating the final boss of the game, I went to the crab dungeon. The key opened the door-Inside the crab dungeon was a small room with another door-I couldn't figure out how to open the door. I thought there must be something I'm missing. Obviously this door has to open somehow. -I scoured the world trying to find whatever other ability or key I must have missed that would allow me to progress.  I resisted the urge to look anything up because I assumed it was some kind of puzzle and I wanted to solve it myself.-After probably an hour of this I give up and check the discussion board on Steam. It turns out there's currently no way to open that door. Ok, sometimes games have cut content or they have areas that are plants for future DLC, that's fine. What's not fine is leaving that sidequest in the game. Block off the area of the map until the content is done! Don't give me a key to a nonexistent place! That's ridiculous. So yeah, that really soured my experience. Even if I put that aside, I wouldn't recommend this game. It's not terrible, I had a mostly ok time with it, but you can do a lot better than mostly ok.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn on this one.  This is not super far from being a "do not recommend", but if it's pass/fail, I give it a pass.  If it's cheap, get it.  Link to the Past mechanics cloned (and barely altered), turned into a pretty shallow but cute rogue-like.  They do puzzles well.  They do upgrades ok.  They do NPC's poorly.  A lot of the quests in town felt like the devs assumed they'd be fun just because they were there.  A lot of them weren't, they felt forced, although they did make the town feel more fleshed out.  Your character moves fast, which is fun for exploring, but makes combat feel unfair at first, until you get used to the fact that it's just jarringly quick.  Other than those god-awful dive-bombing birds with impossible to read movement patterns, combat is something that you can work with and get good at (seriously devs, take that enemy out of the game or fix it, it sucks)The different classes basically all feel the same.  I think this game would have been better with fewer classes with more meaningful differences.  As far as I'm concerned, the only three classes in the game are Hero (balanced), Thief (fast and weak), and Knight (slow and strong).  Using the other classes felt like being punished by having to invent my own reasons to use them, and not being able to find them.I think the devs had a pretty strong priority of getting the player right into the exploration, combat, and dungeoneering as fast as possible, and they did a good job with that.  They handle death really well.  It's enough of a setback that it feels like it matters, but you can boomerang back in really effectively.  It felt like they were working from a checklist of "things a good game should have", and just dumped a whole bucket of that stuff in without consideration for fleshing it out, tying it in to the rest of the game, or making it feel like any of it mattered.  Despite that, I still had fun, but not as much as it feels like I could have had.  I can't bring myself to call it good, bad, or forgettable.  It's more fun than it should be for how hollow and perfunctory it is.  Go in with mild standards and you'll have a fun little romp.

_childDocuments_.review: Zelda meets Rogue Legacy.  It's one of those games that is just really frustrating to play, but you really want to beat it and progress.  I'm not sure if I can recommend it, but I kind of do recommend it if you're looking for something to scratch an itch of a Zelda or rogue-lite game.Each "run" you are adventuring like Zelda.  You go into a dungeon, traverse it until you get to the boss, and defeat the boss to defeat the dungeon and continue on the story.  You collect gems which are the currency to buy stuff to improve your subsequent runs so you keep the gems when you die and then get reset back to the beginning.  The bad part is that the upgrades are just +2% damage or +5 health or whatever.  Very incremental upgrades.  There's a lot of upgrades too so it makes the game **very very** grindy.  This is why I probably wouldn't recommend it (at least for me).  I do a run and die from some BS trap while I'm talking to a salesman in the dungeon.  It feels like I'm just pounding my head against a wall and there's only a piece of paper put in between my head and the wall every 5 smacks of my head.  There's not an easy difficulty either.  There are some things that you just can't avoid in the dungeons and everything hits hard.I think I got it on sale for $2 a bit ago.  I would **definitely** recommend it for that price.  $20 though?  Ehh, not really.

_childDocuments_.review: 29.5h (100% achievement, finished the game)  No (some might be grindy depending on your playstyle). Yes (34 achievements). No. is a top-down action-adventure game that can be played by up to 4 players in both local co-op and online co-op. It offers 4 main dungeons and several smaller ones, with the main dungeons being randomly generated each run. That being said, the game is completely playable solo, and this review will be based on that.- 4+ dungeons, with the main dungeons being randomly generated each run- Infinite dungeons for those who want to keep on playing after finishing all contents- A lot of things to do: side quests, secret areas, and others- Grinding might be needed to progress at the beginning- Exiting the game equals dying; your last location won't be saved- Unable to zoom the map fullyIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 uses pixelated visuals in a top-down view. The layout looks similar to  games with their rocky cliffs, square-shaped dungeon interiors with bricks, and other objects such as bushes, pots, and rocks, although it still tries to make them look different. The map size is bigger, for example, with more bushes that you can swipe in between. Moreover, the tileset is also changed based on the terrain, modifying all of the objects to match it. The enemies also try to follow suit with their recolor versions despite being treated as the same enemies.The story is only told at the beginning. However, it can be hard to follow since the game auto-advances the dialogues. Luckily, it only serves as a premise to the game - you won't miss anything if you don't know about it, especially since there is nothing more to the story even after you finished the game. is an action-adventure game at its core. You have an overworld that you can explore with your trusty sword, which you can use to kill the enemies. Killed enemies won't respawn until you reenter the area, making it easy to mark explored spots. The game is pretty much linear - you might have some optional areas to explore, but most areas are only accessible until you progress the game.Enemies have different attack patterns, and it's your job to figure out how to beat them. Learning how to kill some enemies without taking damage might seem tough at first, but most of them will be easy to beat once you know what to do. If you are still having trouble, you can upgrade your stats to kill most of them in 1 hit.Upgrades need to be purchased. Unlike Zelda-like games that allow you to power up by finding items, you need to have enough gems to purchase a stat increase instead. This forces you to grind if you are not good enough, although this also means that you can cheese most bosses as long as you are willing to grind. On the other hand, I like seeing the town getting upgraded after you purchased some building upgrades.As I said before, the main dungeons are randomly generated. Both layout and traps changed each run, and puzzles might need to be solved differently based on your starting location. Moreover, there are a lot of rooms available in the mix, making each run feel different. You need to redo each dungeon several times just to find all rooms that the dungeon has to offer, and playing the game after knowing all rooms isn't going to bore you out since there are still some slight randomizations in the rooms, whether it's from the enemies or the exploration to search for the area exit.The game seems to not know how many keys you need. Clearing a room will net you some reward, which often has a key that can be used to unlock a door. However, I always find myself having more keys that I can use. This might seem to be done as a precaution in case people can't solve some of the puzzles that have the keys as a reward, but I just find it weird that you don't have to explore every room to finish the dungeon because of the spare keys.You need to restart the dungeon from the beginning if you die. Since dungeons are randomized, it's obvious that you can't pick up from where you left off. However, dying in a dungeon will allow you to keep your gems, which can be used to purchase upgrades to make you stronger. The same gems can also be kept if you manage to finish the dungeon, although it might be hard to do without investing a few upgrades beforehand.You won't be able to keep your earned gems if you enter the dungeon. This seems to be one of the "roguelike" aspects that the game has. You need to use them all before you enter each dungeon, or risk losing them. To be honest, I find this feature to be useless - it just forces you to use all gems before entering a dungeon. Losing 400 gems won't matter if you can get 10k gems afterward.I finished the game in 29.5h. The game can be finished faster if you just rushed both dungeons and enemies. It also has a lot of things that you can do: there are side quests to complete, secret areas to explore, bestiary to finish, and many more. As for the difficulty, the game isn't hard as long as you are willing to grind. Some puzzles in the dungeons might take some time to figure out, but most of them are simple enough. If you are stuck on some, there are a lot of spare keys that you can use - you are not forced to complete every room in the dungeon to finish it.I got soft-locked when I tried to do the endless dungeon, forcing me to abandon my run to exit from the area. Moreover, you can't save inside the dungeon. Loading your save will also respawn you to your home, which makes it feel as if you are dying. This prevents people from playing the game in short sessions. Lastly, the map still looks blurry when zoomed to the max, making it hard to figure out everything.Despite its roguelike tag,  doesn't feel like a roguelike at all. All it takes from that genre is the randomly generated dungeon with some upgrades in between. Your currency might be reset upon entering a dungeon, but you can always use them before entering. You might have to reset the dungeon from the beginning, but the game offers a shortcut to go directly to both the second and third floors once you manage to reach and unlock them. The game will try to make everything accessible no matter what, allowing you to finish the game as long as you don't mind grinding if you suck at it.The game feels more like a solid Zelda-like game with some additional features. You can fish, expand your village, plant crops - there are a lot of optional elements, which don't take time to finish. You only need to spend a few minutes at most, allowing you to focus on the action-adventure elements. Exploration might feel unrewarding since it will only offer you collectibles that don't help much with the game, but it's still fun to do if you like to explore everything to its fullest. If you enjoy Zelda-like games and don't mind having to focus on upgrades instead of finding secret collectibles, make sure to buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another indie roguelite that didn't need to be a roguelite.Randomized dungeons are the meat of the game. Unfortunately they're just a slog for you to retry several times until you harvest enough resources to get mathematically good enough to clear it. Nothing significant is different about each run; you neither receive new experiences from repeated attempts, nor do you gain mastery by studying specific challenges. It's just there to spread thin content over a longer playtime.There is good handcrafted content to be had though! Exploring the overworld and bespoke dungeons used to get between the randomized ones is rewarding and well built. Specific rooms you always find in dungeons have good puzzles that are satisfying to solve the first time (though you'll be repeating them many more times than is welcome). This could have been a solid, brief, linear experience; the devs are obviously fans of the genre and seem to know how to conjure Link to the Past magic when they put their minds to it.I feel like lots of games like this (Towerclimb, Scourgebringer, Children of Morta) aren't confident enough in what they're actually trying to do; they're worried about the quantity of content they're delivering and not sure that just the quality of it will  make sales. Adding roguelite elements is an obvious way to pad out a smaller game and make the player spend more time with each batch of content. Making a good roguelite means making a good loop, though; the game needs to actually be about dying and retrying, needs to be about the core mechanical gameplay that the player will be interacting with for hours. A Link to the Past was not fun because its combat was good; it was fun because of the giant world to explore, the constantly shifting context of the enemies and environments, and your evolving and expanding toolset with which to interact with both of those things. Repeating content works against all of those goals, and unfortunately Ruins doesn't offer up anything compelling to justify why you're repeating it.All that said, it's dirt-cheap and has local multiplayer. If you're a megafan of the 2d Zeldas and need a little romp with your friends, it might be worth trying it out.

_childDocuments_.review: So we get quite a few of these co-op adventure games each year. Just a few months ago we had The Survivalists, which I did end up enjoying and recommending despite its issues. Now we’ve got Rogue Heroes, the next contender within that very genre, and let’s just say that it also is not without its issues.This is a game that will have you going through procedurally-generated dungeons and taking out a bunch of enemies within – along with the usual loot and roguelite progression. However, this is also a co-op focused game and if you’re playing it as such, you’ll be doing a lot of combat with your friends scattered about the same room. This is where the problems begin to appear.For one, there’s contact damage when touching any enemy. That’s not bad in itself, but this is on top of the fact that every time you hit an enemy, there is a pretty sizeable knockback. So, as my friends and I quickly discovered, you’ll be taking a lot of damage from someone accidentally hitting an enemy at just the right angle to send it hurtling towards a teammate.There’s also the extremely limited attack range – enough so that you have to almost be on top of some enemies to actually be able to hit them. This is remedied a bit in that you can upgrade your attack range in-between runs, but even after spending most of my jewels upgrading it, it’s still pretty close and the fact that most enemies move around a lot means you’ll be doing a lot of accidental contact damage to yourself while trying to line up attacks. And the hitboxes definitely don’t help either. They’re not all bad, but there are definitely a few that are larger than their sprites would suggest.You have your one basic attack, a secondary slot for a bow, wand, or other item, a class-specific ability, and that’s it. 90% of your combat is going to be pressing the same basic attack, so you’ll need to be close to enemies even if you’re playing a completely different class. Imagine my disappointment when I unlocked the ranger only to discover that you’re not even given a bow and have to find one yourself in the dungeon only to then realize that it does about the same damage as your basic attack but with the added negative of running out of ammo.The combat really just isn’t satisfying until much later once you’ve got a bunch of upgrades backing it up. It’s the opposite of something like Hades or even the recently released Skul: The Hero Slayer, where the combat is immensely satisfying right from the get-go and only gets better from there. The fact that there are so many mechanics that actively harm co-op players doesn’t help either and honestly it wasn’t until I played the game singleplayer that I was able to beat the first boss.The combat is not even my main issue with the game - the bugs and technical issues are actually more of a problem right now. Rogue Heroes is a co-op game with both local and online options, but n actual play, only the local co-op works - the online co-op unfortunately makes the experience almost unplayable. That is because there is a massive desync issue, with each player seeing something different on-screen and never quite being synced up.Treasure chests only appearing for one player, HP and item amounts differing depending on whose screen you’re looking at, and even entire puzzles that flat-out don’t work for others because only one player can see the interactable objects – it’s pretty bad across the board. One of the worst examples being from the first boss fight. I would hit this weak spot to stun it, only for my friends to ask me why I haven’t stunned it yet – as the fact that the boss was stunned did not appear on their screens.For what it’s worth – I did reach out to the publisher and was told that the desync issue was being worked on. However, I was also told that each desync was a standalone issue and to fix they would need specifics of when and where each happened. Given that this happened to me dozens upon dozens of times, it might be a while before all of these desyncs are cleared up, but at least the team is working on it.I also had an issue where my HP upgrades disappeared entirely until I upgraded them again, an issue where my speed as a ghost was permanently locked to the speed I was moving at when I died, a sound bug where the knight’s leap ability would play the wrong sound effect, and even the game’s revive totem straight-up not working and consuming my friend’s skull – leaving me unable to revive them.I didn’t have any crashes or fps issues – it ran perfectly at 1440p and 60 fps, although it unfortunately cannot go higher than 60. The controls are also fine both on controller and keyboard and mouse, the latter of which can be configured. The only issue I have there is that the controller has the ability to automatically attack in whatever direction you hold the right stick, whereas with keyboard and mouse you have to constantly click to attack.Boring and unsatisfying combat is one thing, but being a co-op game and not having functional online co-op just doesn’t do it – and that’s just one of the technical issues. The graphics, music, and roguelite elements are at least nice, although not enough to carry the experience. I really hope the bugs and such can be fixed up in the future, but it will likely take more than that for me to come back to the game.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: While the roguelike formula doesn't exactly work PERFECTLY with the Link to the Past game mechanics, it is a solid game for what it is. A lot of the overworld aspects and side quests are nice, and sometimes are even more engaging than the actual dungeons themselves. While the roguelike aspect of the procedurally generated dungeons is nice, I also feel like that is where some of the game's design falls a bit flat. The puzzles generate based on the items you have in your possession, so if you don't have a hammer for instance, you won't get puzzles that rely on use of the hammer. Unlike LTTP, the item you get from dungeons is gotten at the end after clearing the boss. It's a sacrifice that had to be made to ensure the procedurally generated dungeons work, but also robs that satisfying feeling of progression and meaningful puzzle solving a lot of the LTTP dungeons had. The only real mandatory puzzles are for boss keys, and the rest are usually just for extra gems for upgrades. All in all, the game is solid, but the core gameplay loop does get a little stale after a little while due to the roguelike nature getting in the way of the consistent well thought out dungeon designs that drive that feeling of meaningful progression like in LTTP. Having more static puzzle rooms like those that house the boss key generated throughout the dungeon (for example key rooms having static puzzle layouts), putting some items in guaranteed rooms in a dungeon you'd need to find in order to gain access to the boss door (for example needing the grapple hook to clear a chasm in the room with the first dungeon boss door or something), just a bit more consistency to the dungeons to make exploring feel more meaningful rather than just optional for grinding gems would have probably made for a more solid experience. Multiplayer does help make the game more fun than solo, but it doesn't fix some of the issues due to some of the concepts that could have used a little more polish. Overall, definitely worth picking up and playing if you have some friends and enjoy the classic LTTP style gameplay (works with remote play together so only one of you actually needs a copy), but you might need to take a break around the halfway mark so things don't start getting a bit stale and come back to it with a fresh mindset.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Heroes is exactly as advertised. It feels like Zelda and it’s a roguelite. It plays and looks like how I remember older Zelda’s behaving. The overworld is the same every time, but when you enter any of the main dungeons, the layout changes every time, as with all roguelites. In the dungeon, you earn gems, which can be used to buy permanent upgrades for your character, again, as is pretty standard with roguelites. However, the balance does seem to be off in that gems were extremely easy to get. If you’re playing this game as a roguelite, you will be disappointed as there really is not much reason to enter a dungeon after beating it and most dungeons can be beaten in a few tries. By the end of the game, we were blasting through everything without much trouble at all. This probably can be fixed by just not spending your gems or choosing to play the game on a harder difficulty. On the other hand, playing this as a Zelda knock off is a lot of fun and the randomly generated dungeons was a nice touch. They still contained puzzles as you would expect in a Zelda style dungeon, although none of them were particularly difficult to figure out.Something that was difficult to figure out at times was where to go next. A few times we got lost trying to find how to get from the dungeon we just defeated into the next dungeon, especially towards the end of the game. Navigating the vast number of items was also really bad. Manually cycling through 10s of items takes too much time and I found the quick access wheel to not work great most of the time.It’s really nice that you can play coop with friends, but sometimes that is a bit buggy. It’s also really annoying how any time anyone opens their inventory or does something similar, it pauses the game for everyone. It would also be nice if we could all explore on our own, at least within the village where we upgrade our characters. Being in the middle of browsing a shop or selecting an upgrade and having a friend leave makes you leave as well, which gets annoying fast.Overall, Rogue Heroes is not the most polished game, but it’s still a lot of fun, especially with friends.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game with a great concept -- marrying The Legend of Zelda with the rogue-light death-and-power-up model -- but a few downfalls in execution.The core gameplay is solid; you explore a constant overworld, and venture into procedurally-generated dungeons to fight monsters and get loot. Then you die, revive in town, and spend your crystals on stat boosts so you can do better next time. There are eight character classes (all but one of which are unlocked through play), but they're not massively different; they have different stats and each one has a special ability, but the basics of gameplay don't change. There's also a whole bunch of stuff to do on the side, and this leads into one of the game's main weaknesses.Other than the core dungeoneering, the game's systems are pretty thin. There's a farming minigame, but it's almost entirely bereft of content; you dig holes and plant seeds, then you water them, and you can sell the crops for gold -- which currency is almost never used. There's no challenge and no long-term goal, merely a daily "water the plants" grind for money. Fishing is even worse; the fishing minigame itself has inexplicable controls, and completing the fishing quest requires endless grinding for three rare spawns.The overworld is fun at first, but it seems like the developers ran short of ideas as they went along. The initially-accessible area has lots of paths to explore and secrets to find, but the later areas are much more linear and plain. Worse still, there are areas of the world map (and one accessible dungeon) that are still entirely unfinished, either unpopulated or populated by obvious placeholder mobs, complete with "under construction" signs. There are landmarks identified on the map that cannot be reached. This is not an early-access game, mind you; it's been in full release for almost a year, and is in version 3.0.Still and all, gripes aside, the core game is a lot of fun. If you like the Legend of Zelda, and you like leveling up, you'll have a good time with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: There's very little to do outside of the four main dungeons, virtually all of the other interactions in the overworld seem to be puzzles that always reward you with a spherical (a collectable that allows you to further invest in your class skills) or some sort of fetchquest. The dungeons themselves are enjoyable, but when a player dies (and it can happen easily and often), they're often forced to sit out for 5-10+ minutes until the surviving players can bring their skull to a shrine to resurrect them. Often times players will die in a way such that their skull is stuck in a small area and can't be brought to a shrine at all for the rest of that run. This forces the players to have to decide whether to exile that player indefinitely or restart the run. The mechanic itself has some promise but it's poorly implemented as-is. Some of the dungeons have soft locks that will end your run by locking you in an area you can't leave, so your only option is to self-destruct to end the run.The town buildings/interactions all basically amount to different upgrades, and certain types of upgrades (health vs damage vs stamina etc) are arbitrarily separated into different houses so you have to coordinate with your friends to make a circuit to spend your gems after each run, which can be kind of a chore because  you all have to visit each building together rather than splitting up.The devs are very much done with the game; do not expect any bugfixes or patches. It was fun for a short bit with friends. Get it on a major sale if for some reason you don't want to play Four Swords.

_childDocuments_.review: Many modern games have a crisis of fun - they are technically impressive, but they heap on layers of stupid garbage that you don't want to do and which isn't fun (10 minute opening cinematics, season passes, obtuse crafting mechanics, and other generally Ubisoft crap). This game is different. They have studied the work of gaming's Classical Masters and paid attention to their teachings. They have gazed upon the pixelated Sistene Chapel that is Zelda: A Link to the Past and have applied its lessons admirably.The gameplay in Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos is immediately engaging and fun. The controls are tight, the combat and puzzles feel rewarding, the exploration provides plenty of "aha!" moments, and even when you die you feel like your dungeon crawl was a worthwhile endeavor. Above all else, this game is FUN. It remembers what this medium is actually about, and it doesn't stand in the way of a good time. Highly recommended.

You can pitch in together to build the town, or hoard your gems for the development of your character’s skills and other attributes. Playing with friends progresses the town a lot faster than if you play alone and it also makes the experience with going through the dungeons a bit better (when you die). But that being said, due to the limit of visibility (since you share the same screen with others you’re playing with), sometimes doing a dungeon run solo may be easier honestly. I recommend this game just for the fact that it is one of the nicer and friendlier games that you could play with friends. _childDocuments_.review: Eh. This is a weird one.**Coop**+ Some rooms require cooperation to solve puzzles which can be cool- The game pauses if only one of the player pauses the game. It's very disruptive when you just want to check the map or do other stuff in the menu- Some puzzles are very boring and repetitive- You can get soft locked in some dungeon rooms- Sometimes will desync. Nothing too bad while I was playing tho, mostly enemy positions but they most of the time are doing the same actions on both screens. Didn't happen too much.- Bombs are useless because other players always catch them accidentally. It's a mechanic used for some puzzles. Can be fun at first, but grows old fast.**Story**- Basically inexistant.- Sidequests feel empty. They exists but have no real meaning / rewards...**Combat system**- Stamina system is bad. Using your sword will use your stamina, but there's no point for that because the enemies become invincible a couple seconds after receiving a hit. You also have less attack speed the less stamina you have. Some other weapon also use a lot of stamina along with ammo, so your kiting capabilities are limited AND if you kite, you won't have stamina left to attack with your sword.- Weapon level up: A lot of them cost a lot and feel useless. For instance, your sword starts with 100 units of range, and each range upgrades increases it by... 1 unit. There are similar upgrades for attack speed and other weapons. Since  enemies in dungeons deal so much damage, you mostly need to upgrade your max health...- No balance at all. Overworld enemies are super weak. Dungeon monsters are super strong compared to the overworld... Enemies deal much more damage and have more health. - Dungeon bosses deal almost no damage and is much easier to beat than almost any small enemy in the dungeon. Their attack pattern can be interesting, but you receive so little damage that you end up just tanking most of the hits.- You get so many regenerative items by slashing plants or destroying pots that it removes a lot of the difficulty in the game.- Character class system is pretty useless: They have nothing that make them feel too unique, only 1 simple ability and base stats are changed+/- The traps. THEY'RE EVERYWHERE!!! Be ready to develop trust issues**Sounds**- Only ambiance music. I feel like another kind of music would have been more fitting+ I guess sounds effects are good**Graphics:**+ Actually pretty good. Of course almost all the graphics are based on / inspired of Zelda: alttp, but I liked it.- Tried to be a Zelda: alttp clone with online capabilities. Feels like the devs changed their mind halfway and decided to add every systems they could think of. In the end, most of the systems feel wrong.- Difficulty is very unbalanced- Combat system is based on stamina and is disappointingI really wanted to enjoy the game but it just felt wrong. Still found the motivation to finish the game with a friend.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Heroes is a playable, competent game with good fun to be had with friends. It's by no means a great game but it is not a hard recommend if you've got a couple friends you want to spend a bit of time clearing dungeons with.The Good -- Lots of potential progression to keep each run feeling valuable for a long time- Gameplay is solid- There's enough game chaos to create lots of fun, interesting moments without being overwhelming- Music and sound never got old- Large open world with lots to explore. There are gates but it didn’t feel overly restrictive most of the time- Dynamic puzzles that change depending on the number of players was neat- Scratches the Zelda-esque itch with some of its own variety and uniquityThe Bad -- The game does not evolve much after 3 or 4 hours. Advancement is there but its mostly just increasing stat points.- Pause menu is shared, even across online multiplayer. If one player wants to change their inventory selection or check the map, it pauses all players. This can end up being very frustrating and our group tended to just stay out of the menus as much as possible, even though that gimped us on occasion.- Classes are only vaguely different. Superficially, each class has a different ability and strengths/weaknesses but, realistically your upgrade path will do significantly more to define your play style than the class you choose.- Farming is mostly useless considering how big a deal the game tries to make the mini game. By the time we had the farm and all the requirements to actually use it we were half way through the game and once you have the farm it takes FOREVER to grow and sell your crops. Needing to individually water an entire field every time you return from a dungeon for a couple coins every 6th dungeon run was not at all worth it.The Other -- Exploration was fun but generally underwhelming. The main collectable is an item that lets you keep a percentage of your gems when you enter a dungeon (you have to give up any remaining gem currency each time) and, after collecting around 50 of them, we were only at 17-ish percent you get to keep. And, since its use it or lose it, you're always going to spend as much as you can before starting your next dungeon. Since you'll always start your next run with <200 gems, 17% at the end of the game only equates to keeping 20-30 gems which is less than the drop from a single enemy. Feels like the collectable needed either no in-game reward to just be a side thing you could do as an achievement or a much more meaningful reward like +17% more gems collected.- Quests can be confusing. We constantly had a quest to 'craft a shovel' even though we had already crafted a shovel to use the farm but we found there were places in the world that appeared too dense/thick to dig. Never could figure out how to build the shovel the quest wanted.- Keyboard remapping wouldn’t stick. Change a couple of the commands to use additional mouse buttons but they would only last through that session, restarting the game reset the keybinds.We did enjoy the game and played to the final boss but have no real incentive to continue playing. $20 for ~15 hours of co-op gameplay isn’t bad if you can excuse some of the game's shortcomings :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is actually fun, the puzzles are there with some puzzles being more reaction based and some requiring a little bit of thinking. In solo, the game functions as intended.The main issue most players may come across is the multiplayer that is definitely enjoyable but also comes with a potential game breaking bug. It can be avoided but with the irony that the multiplayer of this game works best when the host of the game has computer specs that isn't too powerful.If the host has a PC with powerful specs, the game will have a high likely chance to encounter the game breaking bug for clients that joins the room.The bug occurs upon exiting certain caves, the game will teleport all players to the top most left corner of the map. While the clients will be stuck with a black screen, the host would be able to move as usual. However, this comes in variation as sometimes it will teleport the players to some inaccessible parts of the map leading to players being stuck in the middle of nowhere. At this point, if the host closes the room or the game, the clients will recover from the black screen. If this issue occurs, it's best to get any of the clients who had a black screen to host the game instead.Probably has something to do with computers with powerful specs loading the map faster than the clients, which lead to the bug.Overall it's an enjoyable game, the different classes has it's place in the team, beating up mobs and bosses with friends as a team is a plus so long the game breaking bug is worked around / resolved in time to come

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a beautiful 2D pixel-art world and has a lot of potential for being a good co-op game (main purpose of getting it) but with some issues I experienced while trying it alone first, I ended up refunding the game. Their are reviews that had longer playtime and have a better perspective of other bugs/multiplayer issues, but focusing on only what I experienced in my short time playing. (sorry for a long list, but hope it helps) If at least some of these bugs were fixed then my recommendation could change, but for now this is my take on it.1. When attacking, the direction you attack is inconsistent. Although it appears you attack in whichever direction you're facing (which can be an issue on its own depending on the game/how it is implemented) it sometimes attacks in completely different directions, and if you are moving by pressing 2 different keys (ex. pressing W and D to move North-East) the game will randomly decide which of the two directions to attack, instead of in the direction being moved every time, which for me is a personal game killer of not having full control over attacks in a game that focuses on attacking enemies. And although the game is sort-of designed to be like this where only WASD are directions to attack in, enemies can attack in all directions most of the time, which is the main reason I'm pointing this out.2. Stamina regen rates are very inconsistent. Whenever you attack and deplete your stamina, the game randomly decides if the stamina will regenerate within 1-2 seconds, while other times it seems to take as long as 5 seconds before it even starts to refill, which is a very odd bug.3. In the dungeons, sometimes a puzzle to be able to access an area/treasure will be designed so that if you are not careful and/or once you activate something, you can be effectively soft-locked out of an entire area of the dungeon, losing access to possible rooms/loot. I am more forgiving of this issue because dungeons are generated as you play, but is still an issue because if it can block you off from things in general, that means their is a chance the dungeon layout will just block you from continuing, effectively ruining your run.4. _childDocuments_.review: Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos is a great game, and one I would highly recommend to anyone looking for a short puzzling adventure game. It brings back memories of Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventure. However, to call this a roguelike is misleading. The only roguelike aspect in this game is the layout of the dungeons. Everything else in this game will be the same every time you play it. The art style brings a lot to the game. The classes all have cute outfits and enemies designs are fun. I have played this game both multiplayer and single player, and both of these modes have various pros and cons to them. The single player is very nice to quickly access your inventory, change out runes or potions, check the map, access quests, and generally has a faster-paced play. That being said, playing with 4 people is a much more enjoyable experience. The different classes feel like they should offer a lot of versatility to how one plays the game, but they do not unfortunately. Some, such as the mage and the reaper, feel like they are just strictly better than others, given that their ability allows them to avoid all damage. It would be nice if the different classes had more unique aspects. The same can also be said about the weapons. After having upgraded the bow, bomb, wand, grapple hook, and sword, only the sword is a viable weapon. It does far more damage and has no limited ammunition or mana cost. There are a number of problems with the game though. The mage can clip through walls sometimes, making it impossible to progress. The fire boss will die to the fire vents in multiplayer, which is entertaining to watch, but makes the dungeon anticlimactic. If a player leaves the match, they cannot join back in without restarting the whole lobby.After having completed this game, I was left wanting more. More side quests, more to explore. Despite the problems I've mentioned, it is a lot of fun and a game that I would recommend to all my friends.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to start by congratulating the developers on making my current autistic obsession. I've wanted a multiplayer Link to the Past for years, and I'm overjoyed to finally have it. Nintendo did make a game that fits that description, but I've never played, and you probably haven't either, at least not with multiplayer, since it required you to have as many GBAs and link cables to hook up to your GameCube/Wii for that number of people playing its multiplayer mode, including player 1. Rogue Heroes has local and online co-op for up to 4 people right away. It also a variety of different classes, several different weapons inspired by some of the more iconic items from Link to the Past, like the hookshot, bombs and wands, and procedural-generated dungeons. It's worth noting that the individual rooms appear to have been deliberately designed, while the enemies, items, certain details of the puzzles and the overall layout of the dungeons are randomized. Conversely, its overworld appears to be entirely designed, even down to enemy placements, and has a number of secret chests with special upgrade items hidden in plain sight to reward thorough exploration or behind item-oriented progression gates. There's side quests given by charming NPCs, many of which become available based on how much you build up your town. This game has a lot to do.All that said, while the game is extremely fun for me, there are some important criticisms that might sway you one way or the other. The minor criticism I have is of the music. It's all royalty free stuff, which tells me that the devs couldn't afford a composer to make the whole soundtrack, but the tracks chosen lean more toward being "atmospheric," rather than exciting and adventurous, which might take the wind out of some peoples' sails, since the music is such an important part of a Zelda-style game's appeal. The major criticism is how the game feels like it was designed around multiplayer primarily, and then adjusted haphazardly to facilitate single-player runs. It's hard to describe the feeling of playing by yourself in detail, but, basically, a lot of the puzzles that felt clever and team-oriented with 2-4 players are still used in singleplayer but often take longer to execute the solution (a lot of pushing blocks onto pressure plates, for instance). There's also no mechanic to replace the resurrection mechanic available with multiple people. In multiplayer, if someone dies, you can pick up their skull and take it to a special shrine to bring them back. As far as I've seen, there's nothing like this in singleplayer, which makes playing by yourself even harder, since one death is an immediate end to your run. I haven't personally been too frustrated by this fact for it to affect whether I like the game or not, but your mileage may vary. It's worth noting that there are bottles in this game that you can fill with potions, which can alleviate the difficulty.The tl:dr is that the game is incredibly fun with 2-4 people, but falters a bit as a singleplayer experience (though not enough for me personally to stop liking it), and the music is boring.  Update! I've figured out how to change the in-game music, and it was much easier than I initially thought. You simply take whatever music you want, convert it into .wma format using a wide variety of tools that can be found with a quick google search (I've been using . After that, you rename to the new .wma file to match the name of the specific song you want to replace in "...steamapps\common\Rogue Heroes\Content\Audio\Mp3", and you're done. The new audio will replace the original song, play based on the same triggers and automatically loop. To test this, you can replace the file "Music - Juniper.wma," which is found in the previously mentioned folder. This is the name of the song that plays over the start screen. Some quick warnings: if the new audio file you're using isn't properly formatted and the original audio file is missing, the game will crash on startup, and I recommend that you make backups of the audio files you plan on replacing before doing so. the biggest problem with this method is that the audio files that're being replaced are named in ways that are not helpful for intuiting the context of where the song will be played in-game. For instance, the song "Juniper" plays over the title screen, "Arid Foothills" plays while in caves and "Morgana Rides" plays while exploring the first dungeon. I'm considering making a proper guide explaining all of this once I beat the game.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr; This is not a "stay away from this game" recommendation. From what I've played so far, it's not a BAD bad game. It's just a bit... all over the place? Considering it's pretty cheap when on sale you can probably get enough bang for your buck before it bores. It's got nice art, the music is meh, and the core gameplay is okay. That said, it also feels unfinished and empty. I hate overly long reviews because who's gonna read them anyway. But to list some of my gripes in more detail:- I'm not sure if it wants to be a roguelike/lite, a zelda clone ("inspired" by Zelda is understating it, it basically rips 80% of the gameplay elements from it), or a dungeon crawler. - Most dungeons are procedurally generated, with a set of rooms that is chosen from for each dungeon. But the puzzly rooms just feel tedious, because it's just a bit of back and forth to press switches. Especially after you have completed them earlier already they're just boring- As said: it feels unfinished and unpolished in some places; for example, the town is much larger than the amount of stuff you can build, and most of the skill "trees" just contain multiple of the same items to inflate how fleshed out they are (the shovel upgrade tree just consists of like 6 "dig X% faster!"...). I'm not even sure what the point is of the whole southwest area, it's just a lot of empty space and an optional dungeon.- The "farming" minigame is extremely tedious and unnecessary.- Overworld pathing is frustrating at times. - The amount of grind counters is excessive (destroy X rocks! shoot X arrows! kill X {monster type} monsters! etc.- There's an annoying bug where enemies may "spawn" into the wrong elevation of the level (like Zelda it's got an upper and a lower level). In order to kill them you need to be on the same elevation, At least one run I had to abandon because an enemy spawned wrong and I couldn't kill it and I needed to kill all enemies to unlock a door.

_childDocuments_.review: I have not experienced the online co-op issues many are reporting. I have played mostly singleplayer and some co-op over the internet utilizing Parsec without any issues in that regard. This game satisfies a simple 2D zelda-esque itch pretty well. Playing it co-op make sit much more interesting as you run around with your friends through the overworld and dungeons with a generally bright and clean art style tying everything together. I do think the game is well worth the cost overall and recommend it for a reasonably fun 2-4 player game if you're doing couch or steam remote play/parsec co-op. That said, I have a few small criticisms.1. All the classes are sword wielders. Magic user, witch, thief, ranger. You're using a sword as your go-to weapon. Your class may modify a sub-weapon when you unlock it but those subweapons require ammo or mana to use and just are overall weaker than swinging the sword as a high damage melee class.2. After the first dungeon, the second dungeon is comparatively difficult to get to. You'll be doing a lot of quests back and forth to and from a swamp to town to get items and leads on where to go next until you finally manage to do some minor dungeons to get to the next big dungeon/shrine. This is okay, but it's very different from all but walking out the first gate of town into the first dungeon, so the pacing is a bit off in that regard.3. The subweapons are unlocked pretty quickly for some, and obtusely for others. You'll get a wand, boomerang (you never use this in my experience) and bomb pretty quickly. Other stuff will take longer and you never really need those items outside of the grappling hook which is required for puzzles. Need a bomb for a puzzle? The game provides unlimited bombs nearby, so why get bombs on your own?4. Incremental leveling and shop building. You have to spend your gems to unlock shops and homes in town, opening quests and upgrade trees. Unfortunately, you're going to be farming a TON of gems. Upgrades are in the realm of 1-10 points of things early on, like 1 sword damage or 5 health. You unlock more trees for higher amounts of these things but the upgrade trees are very flat and plain and not at all entertaining. You aren't getting new abilities so much as getting 0.5% better with each unlock.

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game. It feels like the developers were Link to the Past fans and thought, "I want more of that, but be able to play with a few friends." The progression feels much like that, I'm having fun exploring the world with each new item I'm able to get. And grinding the first dungeon doesn't feel grindy because of the procedural generation. So it's fun to go back to that same dungeon again and again to build your inventory and expand the town.Being able to work on your character in single player and then join or invite friends is a strong point of this game. I don't mind hopping into a friends game to go back to one of the first dungeons to solve the puzzles and clear the rooms. The dungeon bosses are just difficult enough to make the fight exciting without being a slog. When two of your mates have died to the boss and it's down to you and one other, and the teamwork pays off, it's satisfyingThere are a few issues in the co-op mode. A little jank. But I wouldn't say that makes it unplayable. There have been some trees and bushes invisible to some players, and a couple spots impassable by one or two of the players in a group. But it gets reset when another player can just go to the next part of the map and the teammate is automatically teleported there. I found it only a minor inconvenience and I do hope they try to resolve this with a future update. None of those same issues seem to arise in the single player.I've seen far more broken multiplayer play in AAA game titles. This game is well worth the time and money to play IMO. Forty dollars well spent for me and the other copy I bought for my partner.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was $20. I would say it is worth that price.It drew me in with its Link to the Past aesthetic and gameplay and it tickled my nostalgia bone very nicely. So if you don't mind spending $20 for several hours of gameplay and enjoyed Link to the Past, this game is worth it.I will say I am a little disappointed though because before I bought the game, I believed there was more to it than there actually is. I saw the classes as something that would be fun and exciting to play with, but nope. Classes might as well be aesthetic choices because they only provide some intensely minor bonus to one thing and change your dash/run mechanic a bit. The starting guy is the best character until you get Knight, then it becomes the best character because its passive is the most useful (he takes less damage). That about sums up the classes. I had initially imagined how fun it would be to play a Witch or Mage casting spells, but none of that really happens or matters. There are no spells really, just a wand item that everyone gets through play and anyone can use and you just choose between Fire, Ice, or Missile plus two others that really serve no purpose in combat. They cost magic power to use and no one has magic regeneration, so there really isn't a point to being a mage or witch because they don't really offer anything that you can't get as a Knight. The broom ability was kind of cool, but it only lasts 2 seconds and has a looong recharge time and honestly it wasn't needed because the only traps it actually lets you avoid are the obvious floor spikes that are trivial to avoid anyway. It doesn't let you fly over fire or ooze or anything else on the ground, it will hurt you anyway.I also believed that each dungeon would be procedurally generated for unlimited play and that isn't really true either. They layout seems to change each time, but there are only so many rooms in each dungeon and you'll very quickly see them all and know how to complete them and how they work, so it doesn't really have unlimited replayability and I found that disappointing as well.It's a nice little game that had the potential to be really outstanding but fell short of that. But i'd say it is worth $20, and definitely worth getting if it ever goes on sale if you're a fan of Link to the Past.
