_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic and surprisingly fun to play. I see a lot of negative reviews, so I'd like to counterbalance that with my perspective on the matter.First and foremost, I absolutely love co-op couch games with a shared screen option. I play this game with my girlfriend, and we are both fans of Zelda. In terms of look and feel, this game is clearly an homage to the SNES version: A Link to the Past, which I used to play endlessly in the past.I consider this game to be a well-executed casual multiplayer Zelda look-alike with a lot of Roguelike elements. The game offers a delightful dose of retro hack & slash action. It is fun playing together with friends (or in my case, my girlfriend) on the couch, exploring dungeons in a well-designed world, building a village, and even doing some farming and fishing. It's an easy-going game.Multiplayer on one screen works really well. The shared screen option has been well thought out. You are forced to play intuitively and make decisions together. The screen moves smoothly with each player, and when someone goes off-screen, everyone is teleported to the same starting location. A neat detail is that puzzles are seamlessly adjusted for a game with 1 to 4 players. If someone dies, the rooms change to fit the puzzle with the new number of players.Occasionally, you have to wait a bit for each other's selection screen, like when brewing a potion or placing a weapon in your quick-select wheel. However, these moments are few. I can imagine patience wearing thin if your partner takes ages to spend gems in the village while you wait. Luckily, we don't have that problem because we play a style where we shop around aggressively and quickly make all our purchases. We don't bother meticulously calculating how to optimize our character's stats. Because that's not really necessary. Sure, you can theoretically build up your character, and there are plenty of upgrades available. However, for us, it's perfectly fine to enter a shop after a dungeon and without much thought, boost our stamina, weapons, or strength and continue playing.In that regard, it's essential to know what expectations you have for the game. After the first dungeon, I let go of the notion that it would offer a complex challenge where we have to finely balance our characters to progress further, as in Vagante (a fantastic Roguelike Co-op). Its just a simple game, at some point we increased the difficulty, but we still rushed through the game, slaying all creatures, discovering secrets, upgrading our characters, and yeah… having a blast!Of course, I also notice the flaws and missed opportunities. Additionally, many players encounter bugs, which is naturally frustrating, especially if you can't proceed and lose progress. Fortunately, I haven't experienced any of that so far. My most significant criticism is the lack of a quick-select option for various potions and the different runes in your staff. I'd also prefer to see 3 or 4 super well-balanced characters instead of the current 8 or so characters without much added value.The variety of monster movement could use improvement, and I miss seeing monster strengths and weaknesses in relation to all available weapons. It's as if the basic framework and complete artwork for a unique Rogue-Zelda-like game are in place but not entirely matured. There seems to be a certain lack of depth. Did the developers need an extra six months or a year? Or... perhaps the game was intentionally kept more straightforward? Maybe it just doesn't have to match the immense amount of finely balanced roguelikes on Steam.All in all, with the right expectations, the right nostalgic fondness for old SNES games, and a friend or partner to play with, this game is definitely worth it. It's clear that a lot of attention and love were poured into this game. The world is imaginative, the gameplay is smooth, and the music is great. I just really enjoy this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this as an action roguelike to play with my girlfriend. There was way too much of an emphasis on puzzle solving than I expected. _childDocuments_.review: This review is done purely from the perspective of single player (only thing i got to say about multi is that it is buggier then single according to other reviews)Short Version:A fun, roguelike rpg style game that is similar to zelda: a link to the past (except you use your gems/rubies to upgrade your character). In order to keep upgrading your character you need to build your town (which you also use gems for and other things as well). BUT, you will encounter some bugs here and there as a heads up.Longer Version:A fun roguelike that is very similar to Zelda: A link to the past except unlike in zelda, you upgrade your character in a more traditional rpg style type way with the gems you find (your currency as well) is used to upgrade your character/build your town.That being said, there are some features that are in this game that are not very common to the roguelike/lite genre.Such as here they are (along with some extra info): 1. When ever your character hits an enemy, your character takes a step forward, and since contact damage is a thing in this game, you must becareful not to just spam your attack if your close to an enemy.2. There is stamina in this game, as such, after a certain amount of weapon swings, you will tire and attack slower until you just wont be able to attack until you let it build back up again (both blocking and attacking with your sword which all classes do takes up stamina).3. The artwork for the game is somewhat deceiving. Their is no sexes in this game per say. No clear definition of male or female. One could argue that when you change to a certain class, you change sexes to match eg, knight makes you male, witch makes you female ect. But id say your character is just a unisex sprite at the end of the day, neither being male or female. This feature may matter to some, and to others it wont, just tossing this timbit of info out there in order to cover every base i can for a proper review.4. The bugs. You will encounter bugs in this game. More so in multiplayer as opposed to single player but they are there in single. Patch's are few and far between and the game is done in terms of sales (not even in the top 8 pages, last i checked i checked the top 13 and didint see it anywhere), as such, dont expect any bugs you find to be fixed in a timely fashion. They are patching the game (most recent june 7th that fixed the  catacombs bugged that prevent you from even really giving it a solid go, the cata is one of the games 2 infinite dungeons as a heads up, this patch took them 2 months and a bit to do but also brought some more bugs with it lol but at least nothing game breaking from what ive seen so far), just not often.5. This game is also a bit light on the story side. Again to some this might be an issue, to others it wont be. Their is  dialogue but nothing i would classify as an in-depth story with lots to read.6. This game can be played with either a controller or mouse/keyboard. The keys for mouse/keyboard can be rebinded easily enough, however rebinding the controller keys is a nightmare that can only be done via controller layout (and even then it doesint exactly work properly via this method, it is possible to really royally mess up the controls for the controller via this method and have no real way of resetting it back, spent a good 2h on it myself and managed to somewhat get what i wanted rebinding controls this way, you have been warned, dunno if its cause i use a logitech controller with xnput or what, but damn what a nightmare lol)7. Also, sometimes, the game will have VERY small plateform's with a stair leading up to it with enemies waiting for you, depending on the class and what resources you have access too, it can be VERY hard to not take damage sometimes depending what type of enemies are on so said platform (the catacombs, the games last infinite dungeon can be VERY ugly for these types of situations).8. You can choose from a couple of different difficulty settings and change them on the fly and it will take effect off the bat (or should at least). So if you having difficulty, you can just pause the game and lower the difficulty on the fly (im not sure if this applies to the catacombs since i know it records what difficulty the game was on when you die, thus i dont know if it locks the difficulty, havent tested it yet)9. There is no new game + feature in this game.Other then that, the last question that needs to be answered is "Will i get at least 1 hour of fun/entertainment/gameplay for every dollar i spend on this game". To that i say, if you pay full price for this game, you should most likely even if you skip both infinite dungeons. If you give both infinite dungeons a go, then for sure. Game costed me around 20 bucks (bought it on sale) and after using some guides to find some of the power sphere's (another way to upgrade your character, there is lots and some are not ease to find) and giving both infinite dungeons a solid go, i ended up with 32 hours in the game by the time i was mostly finished with it. i definitely got my money's worth and suspect anyone into games such as this will as well (and if this game isint for you, assuming you didint spend alot of time trying to rebind your controls like i did, you will easely find that out with in the first hour and 45 mins of game play and can just get a refund).Over all, i give this game, a 7 out of 10 and definitely recommend but it might be wise to wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: 5 hours in, and I simply don't get the hate that this game gets. Being a fan of the older Zelda games, including the original and A Link to the Past, I can honestly say that this is the best ALTTP clone I've ever seen. It initially seemed a little too straightforward of a game - the first dungeon is discovered very quickly, and bears a fairly punishing level of difficulty. I died a lot trying to complete it. I didn't get a whole lot out of it at first, but the third floor started to feel more like a proper Zelda dungeon to me, as I was starting to get a good grasp of the mechanics of the game.The real magic started while trying to get to the second dungeon - the world opens up more, and getting to the dungeon is a proper puzzle in and of itself. This felt SOOO much like ALTTP, and was one thing that really hit the mark of a proper Zelda game - you go questing about before you can even reach the point of getting to a desired dungeon, and it hit all of the nostalgia marks just right. I forgot that this wasn't a Zelda game at that point. Playing this with my kiddos is an absolute delight. I always wanted to play Four Swords, but never found people to play it with. This scratches that now decades-old itch beautifully. The lovely thing about it is that the game plays beautifully whether single or multiplayer. Every now and then, I run into a puzzle that cannot be completed by one player alone, but it seems like those are few and far between (that, or maybe I just don't have the right items or abilities yet). I haven't experienced almost any of the bugs that so many players have reported. I saw a bit of a bug where running along the corner of a wall yielded some glitchy movement in one specific spot, but I haven't had a single issue since. Playing with my kids hasn't yielded any issues so far. On the note of multiplayer, the developers did something REALLY smart with players who have died - their ghost can possess pots and plants and throw them at enemies. They can also trigger traps to keep you from getting hurt, or as my son did, alert me to traps on the floor I didn't see.  Even if it takes a while to revive the other players, they can still interact in a meaningful way with the game as a whole. I loved that my son could still play, even though he struggled to not die. All in all, I really don't get the poor reviews this game has gotten. I enjoy it quite a bit, and perhaps that's all that matters.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game. It's like a mix of zelda world exploring with roguelike randomized dungeons. Both the world exploring and the dungeons are well done. While I do recommend this game, I do have a few gripes. My first gripe is please, Please, PLEASE, make it so that you can pause the game or open your inventory in coop without forcing your coop partner(s) to also pause their game. There's no reason for this. All it does is automatically make you a ♥♥♥♥ every time you want to look at the map, because doing so prevents your friend from doing anything. They only thing you can do when your partner is in their menu is open your own menu, which then prevents them from doing anything when they are done with their menu, and it's just an endless cycle. The coop elements otherwise work great for the most part. Both the host and client can perform most actions, and moving off a tile automatically moves the other players to the next tile, which is already way better than many coop games. There are a few minor glitches/desync issues in coop but nothing game breaking. The most annoying one I came across is that some achievements don't unlock properly if you play as a client.Next, a fairly large issue with the game right now is balancing. Generally in a game like this you would expect to jump into the first dungeon and immediately be completely obliterated by the enemies, because you don't have any upgrades yet. You then play the dungeon a few times, get gems to purchase upgrades, and learn the enemies better, and eventually unlock the second dungeon. So far, this is all exactly how things play out in Rogue Heroes. The problem starts after you beat the first dungeon. Basically, at that point, the game stops being hard. You would expect the second dungeon to be hard again, until you level some more, and so on for the third and fourth dungeons. But after my friend and I beat the first dungeon, we beat every dungeon thereafter on the first try, often without even dying (if your coop partner dies in a dungeon you can revive them at a revival totem). Even the "endless dungeon" that you unlock after beating the game is extremely easy, and only gets easier as you purchase all the upgrades (although I have to admit I'm kind of glad of this, because otherwise getting the "reach level 25 of the endless dungeon" achievement would be a huge pain in the neck). The balance isn't so bad that the game ceases to be fun. The dungeons are only part of the game (the rest is exploring the world map). But I do hope the devs can improve it. I don't think it's a fundamentally broken aspect of the game. I really think this can be fixed by just tweaking some aspects of the progression. Finally, the game feels somewhat unfinished. Actually, I think it's unfair to say it's unfinished, because the game has a lot of content and you can get to the end of it. The problem is that the devs seem to have had a lot of ideas that didn't really go anywhere, but they still included them all in the game for some reason. There are tons of mechanics/items/etc in the game that either do nothing or are at best are used exactly once. This leaves you feeling very confused about what something does, until you finally realize that the devs just never fleshed that particular thing out. I would love to see some of the ideas actually fleshed out, but I would also suggest to the devs to just remove the things from the game that don't do anything. I would honestly rather see the devs focus on polishing the things that do work (and in particular, fixing the balance issues and coop glitches I mentioned above, or cleaning up the inventory system). There are already plenty of things in the game that are fleshed out. It's really bad to add half baked stuff to a game. Either flesh it out completely, or don't include it at all. All these things do is confuse the player before they figure out they don't actually do anything, and disappoint them when they do.For example, at one point you get a special item that changes the layout of the world. But, unless I missed something, it's only ever used twice: once immediately after you obtain it, and once in a single randomized dungeon room. I was rather expecting the item to change the world map, and maybe force you to re-explore some areas that you previously couldn't access. But instead all it does it clog up your already difficult to use inventory (which is itself only difficult to use because you have to use the scroll wheel to scroll through 20 different items because actually opening your inventory to select something would PAUSE your friend's game, but I digress). There are dozens of similar instances of this, which I'm not going to enumerate here.To be sure, I do recommend this game, especially for coop. But if you play it do be aware of these issues. Don't over-grind past the first dungeon, because the game is already easy enough at that point. And be aware that if you come across a item/mechanics that confusingly doesn't seem to do anything, it's probably because it actually doesn't do anything. The game is still new, so with any luck, the devs will patch the issues I mentioned.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a 'meh' recommendation here. I'm going with a thumbs down in the most tentative, mild way imaginable. This game has fantastic potential, but there's a lot holding it back.  Visually the art style feels more like it's going for Earthbound instead of Zelda. The lack of deep shadows and brighter highlights on objects, characters, and enemies lends to the world having a bland flatness to it.  Certain tools have alternate visuals, while others don't. The world itself feels like it should be large and vast, but it's mostly trees and hills forming linear paths through areas.  I spent most of my time wishing there was an audio mod to put something catchy from A Link to the Past just to try to give some actual energy to the score. There are no catchy tunes, the music is just as subdued as the visuals, sadly. The good thing is that it IS just subdued, nothing will be grating your ears. It's just not stand out or catchy.  There are a few core gameplay elements. Each is a solid foundation, but doesn't reach the point where it needs to be to truly stand on its own. The class system lets you get threads for different cloaks to become a different character class. Unfortunately, the game doesn't give you much documentation on what each secret little feature a class has. On top of this, there isn't enough mechanically different in those classes to make them stand out as a unique play experience. Outside of different stats, the only thing that changes is a special ability button which is just a movement ability, and a few passive abilities. (The Ranger is good with bows, Mage cases spells cheaper, Reaper auto-crits after a certain number of kills) . The problem is that in most cases your standard sword and shield will be so good that there is no point in using anything BUT your sword.  Changing a classes default weapon, even just aesthetically, would help give a more unique feel. In general the buffs each class provides needs to feel tangible or provide a distinct mechanical difference. Maybe give the thief two knives that he can stab instead of a sweeping sword, or make the knight's shield a tower shield that can reflect projectiles automatically.  Allowing players to power-up their classes the same way that everything else is built up would allow for builds to be made would help diversify each class from each other.  There are some redundant tools, and some tools that are used fairly often. The lack of a quick selection wheel or even a favorites wheel to let you quickly pick tools on the fly is something that needs to be added, badly. The boxing glove feels pointless when the mallet can do the same thing, the lens of truth stand in is only used about 4 times, whereas the hook shot is used in just about every dungeon tile set at some point. Magic spells and arrows may as well be the same thing with different colored sprites.  Diversify what some items do while giving different mechanics to them. Make bombs clearly go up and over things when thrown, instead of having it be vague. This way players always know what they can throw over an edge, and what will just hit a railing. Make spells each do something different. Fireball is fine, but why not add in a spell to clone your character for a bit, or an AOE repulsion shield that vanishes after it hits a certain number of enemies. Specialized Classes and their tool of choice should absolutely feel like an outright superior option to the basic sword attack.  Rangers should be able to fire a fan shot of arrows, or a super shot for example.  The only point to exploration is to tidy up a few side quests to flesh out your town, and to find places to dig so you can gather more stones. All the stones do is allow you to keep a percentage of your gems when entering a dungeon. The problem is that it's totally counter-intuitive to do that. In any circumstance you're going to be powering up your character after a dungeon anyways, so you SHOULD be going into that dungeon with next to no gems. Other than that there are hints to a story in the world here and there, but beyond a few quick romps in very brief caves or dungeons the world feels dead and devoid of incentive to explore. Some very minor tools like the boxing gloves can be used in only a few areas and are world exclusive, but there should absolutely be more to discover than that.  The stones need to have an actual purpose that could be tied to player power progression, or unlocking secret areas in the world that lead to unique cloaks, cosmetics, tools, or lore. More areas should be created to flesh out the story of the world and add in extra personality. Use more design assets than trees to shape the layout of the world while experimenting with other methods of moving around. The frog whistle was an absolutely brilliant concept that made the swamps stand out from everything else, it made that biome feel incredibly unique.  There are only 4 main dungeons with a fifth 'endless' dungeon. In comparison Zelda: A Link to the Past (The game this one feels most inspired by) has 12 or so dungeons, each with their own tool, mechanic, and theme. The problem is that the developers banked so much on repeated treks through the same 4 dungeons that it lost the plot in terms of why Zelda Dungeons are so fun to do. In the end you can break down a dungeon's purpose into 4 goals. Get a key, get a bigger key, Get from Point A to Point B,  or get gems. Dungeons (outside of the endless one) are only ever 3 floors, Even by the time you get to that third floor you may be pretty bored of where you are after your third or fourth trek through the same tileset.  There need to be more dungeons and more tilesets. New dungeon mechanics and puzzle mechanics, and more goals than just those same four goals. Setting dungeons up so that they dynamically create obstacles that need to be overcome in the same way the puzzles change dynamically based on the number of players could add some extra flare. Maybe one part of the dungeon is flooded and it needs to be drained by a series of puzzles in another area in the dungeon, for example. The bosses also need a complete redesign and rework, both visually and mechanically. Very bare bones with multiplayer actively gouging out a lot of the story scenes as well. You miss the entire point of the plot if you start the game multiplayer for the first time. There are no major story beats that change the world or really make your adventure seem like an adventure. You just go to four dungeons, beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of some very very bland bosses Fun fact: I played the game entirely in muti-player and after entering the final dungeon accidentally went right in to fight the final boss without even knowing there was a dungeon component attached. We just went in, beat the final boss, saw credits, and that was it. The only reward is an unpredictable energy attack from your sword. It only fires out sometimes, so it's not even useful as a combat tactic. Sometimes it's the first slash, sometimes the fifth, who knows. Beyond that and just a "Hooray, you did it" type of ending summary, that's it. The game was on sale for 14 bucks so i grabbed it. I played about 13 hours, so that was about a dollar of enjoyment per hour. Based on the price of a movie, it's entirely worth it at that price. But there's nothing making me want to come back to the game and keep enjoying it, and that's where the rogue-like elements of a game SHOULD be doing their job to keep you pulled in and playing. Sadly , Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos just leaves you thinking "What's the point?" and moving on to the next game.  I'm looking forward to what the devs can do in future updates. But for now, i'm done.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR version: Fun but buggy; wait for a sale or until the bugs are fixed.I had a lot of fun playing this in co-op online.  There's a lot to explore and several dungeons (monsters & puzzles) to complete.  The first dungeon was seemingly the hardest from starting out.  The bosses at the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and endless were easier due to upgrades unlocked.  (You get the upgrades from gems; the gems you get from completing the dungeons.  It's easy enough once you've completed the first dungeon once to run back through it and just farm for more gems for better upgrades.  Once in endless I got to floor 25 and stopped (got the achievement and it was getting late so I stopped playing).  One thing I did notice was that the levels of the monsters in endless mode on the floors stayed the same (at 120).  The only levels that continued to increase were those of the snakes in the pots (did increase each level).The classes behave in a similar attacking manner - you'll be using your sword for most of attacking purposes.  All the classes do have a different jump/rush ability for fast travel (goes on cooldown for a short bit afterwards).  There are a lot of tools to switch between.  I do like that there is the option of selecting which 8 you use the most and programming that to a button for easier access.  Some of the tools are zone dependent and I wish there was the option to hide them from the tools you'd scroll through in zones they aren't used in at all.One minor annoyance is that when one person opens their menu it will not let you continue playing if you are in co-op mode.  It will just tell you that another person has the menu open.  It's great if you just want to pause the game, but you need to open the menu to check for things.  Having it pop up each time can hinder game play.While playing in online co-op we encountered a lot of bugs.  Some were pretty amusing, others kinda annoying.  Below are some of the bugs encountered:-Entered/exited a cave and came out in a different (unvisited) zone.  (Not a big deal, able to get back to where I was at.)-Walked on water instead of climbing up to an area that should have been accessible to climb up to while swimming.  (Game breaking - was unable to continue in the current state aside from just running around on water.  It was amusing to watch but ultimately had to quit the game and re-enter from town to fix the issue.)-Glitched into what seemed like a different layer of the dungeon floor (was running around in areas I should not have been able to access; since it was online co-op the other player was able to go into another room and pull me into that room.  It's not game breaking in co-op but would be in single player).-The shovel will not work on certain areas of the map in the current state.  There are areas marked where you should be able to dig, but the shovel just makes the noise that you cannot dig there.  (Game breaking in the sense that you cannot get all of the achievements to 100% this game.  If you don't care about the achievements, then this isn't of concern, as it does not affect being able to beat the dungeons or final boss.)Ultimately since I did have fun with it I would still recommend it, but with all the bugs in its current state I don't believe it is worth full price (half off, sure).

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the game, but my recommendation comes with a condition/warning attached. There is a steep difficulty curve, because game resembles classical ones and combat requires precise positioning and stamina management.There are 2 permanent upgrades and unlocks in the game that make consecutive runs easier.As you play you get stat upgrades, unlock secondary weapons (incl. ranged weapons) and classes.Upgrades are unlocked by playing the game and "upgrading" the world/village, which I thought was a very nice touch. I don't dislike the generic "get a magical mcguffin to unlock upgrade menu and then select a trait you want to learn" type of design, but working to hire a blacksmith and buying weapon upgrades from them just feels more organic.There's some open-world exploration in game and (at least early on) the world feels sizable, but it's mostly gated behind dungeons (so far only feature in game that feels very artificial). Sadly I found nothing of value in areas I had access to, which is disappointing. With that said, there IS a place you can go at the start of the game where you will get your butt kicked by super high level monsters. Kudos for that! I hope more games do it.You get access to basic attack (same for all classes), block, special action (class specific) and secondary weapons, which makes most classes feel similar. Special action does make a bit of a difference, but it's hard to use most of them with precision the game requires, so special actions often end up being niche utility skills, rather than a combat skill that changes core gameplay loop.Combat feels like that of a classical game, where position and precision matters as much as knowing enemy patterns. I felt it required a little too much precision early on. What I mean by that is you will take some time to adjust fighting against basic enemies, and once you do they are not a real threat, BUT it's still very easy to screw up with more than 1 enemy around. Combat rarely feels unfair, but when it does, it's because there are multiple enemies to fight and they don't leave much of a window to fight back (especially early on). Attacking one roots the character in place for a brief moment, which leaves them open to damage. This issue gets better later in game, when ranged secondary weapons become available AND character upgrades reduce the difficulty.Just to be clear, I didn't play this co-op, so I will not rate it, but I did buy it with co-op feature in mind. This game is definitely not designed to be a co-op experience. Game is mostly split between exploration and combat. A lot of gameplay is exploration and some of it is combat. Exploration of similar game in co-op just doesn't work, apart from few puzzles, unless everyone is following one player. Combat is outright bad for co-op, as most monsters get knocked backwards AND have contact damage, so 2 players can't reliably hit from same side and they can't surround it. You can't both fight the same enemy, unless both of you are ranged or want to chase it after every hit.Despite being released this game is still in development(at the time of review). There are a couple of bugs in game (they break achievements) that have only been fixed in beta version. The problem here is that you need some technical knowledge to transfer your save back from beta to main game. As of this review the bugs are at least 4 months old. Also there are few areas in game that are clearly meant to have content, but are instead blocked off, which is supposedly for future update content. Game being developed further is a huge positive, but it's only a pure positive to people who play it AFTER it's finished, and a small negative to people playing it now.To summarize I am having fun with the game, and I certainly see the audience for it, but it's a niche game and I think most people will not like it.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, this game is not a finished product by any stretch. The fact that it's not listed in 'Early Access' when there is an in-game dungeon with a sign out front that literally reads 'Under Construction' is frankly deplorable.I wanted to recommend it—it's a generally fun game and the combat feels good, but there is just so much left to be desired, and this game doesn't even come close to competing with its competitors.In fairness, the concept of a roguelike open-world RPG is very well executed. Venturing into a dungeon becomes a procedurally-generated roguelike experience, while the overworld remains a traditional 'Legend of Zelda' or 'Metroid'-like experience, with all the trappings of such a game, for better or worse.The art and graphics are also fantastic, even if somewhat cliché in their genre. It looks, at face-value, like a high-quality game.Unfortunately, a number of very core features feel tacked on and meaningless, like shallow gestures with no substance. This includes the "story," which is so generic and tacked-on, it honestly feels like an afterthought.But the classes are the worst example—the game advertises a great number of distinct and varied classes to play, but they are anything but. Each 'class' is just the same generic swordfighter with slightly different stats and a different dash/leap.This is exacerbated by the fact that the secondary items like the bow and magic wand feel absolutely terrible to use. You can aim them freely around you, but there is no targeting reticule, making it extremely difficult to aim the weapons and use them precisely.So even if the Ranger and Mage get bonus damage with said items, it's rarely worth the effort, and just using the sword is going to be the default experience no matter the class.There are a number of other shallow, tacked-on features too. The farming mechanic is almost completely useless, offering nothing but a way to earn a currency which is very rarely used.The fishing mechanic is unlocked more than halfway through the game and does absolutely nothing to the wider game—no experience, no currency, no NPC favour, just a single achievement.The town-building mechanic is almost entirely pointless too. The NPCs that move into town may have a quest here and there, but there's no relationship or faction system, no dialogue besides a single generic line for each character, and no real incentive to actually invite NPCs to join the town at all.In fact, the game is so clearly unfinished that even after buying every building you can, and inviting every NPC into the town that you can, there are still empty, vacant plots of land that you can't do anything with, which just feels cheap, and a little bit frustrating, since it would seem, when you first start the game, that every single plot will eventually be filled.Regarding the actual dungeons, the core element of the gameplay loop, the bosses are dramatically and almost absurdly easier than the rest of the dungeons.There are also not enough varied rooms for the procedural generation, and you will constantly run into the same rooms over and over, even two or three times within a single dungeon.Extremely important mechanics and interactions, like the ability to cut down shortcuts with the sword, burn piles of wood with the lantern, and throw pots at switches in dungeons, are never explained, and can leave the player feeling extremely frustrated and confused at their seeming inability to progress further.And finally, and possibly most frustratingly at all, because the game is unfinished, it's very hard to tell which parts of the game are inaccessible at the current point in the story and which parts are actually not done, and can't be explored.Ultimately, this game needs a lot of work. In it's current state, it feels like half a game, and it should have never been published outside of Early Access.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is super fun and I recommend buying it. It scratches the itch for top down zelda action. It has a bunch of heroes, great puzzles, and a grind mechanic that keeps you gathering and unlocking. But it's not perfect. 1. You save up gems to unlock something, and then have to find something before you can use it. Which feels ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Examples: I keep finding a place to brew potions in the dungeon, ok here's a shop that makes elixirs I'll save up the gems to build that...oh they make potions, but they don't sell any bottles. I have to save up and UNLOCK a dfferent shop first, then save up and buy the bottle, then brew the potion. AND this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ train of unlocking X things to get 1 thing happens all the time. I have a fully upgraded farm, that's probably really useful early game to make $ I bet, but I've never found the watering pail. So why let me unlock a farm and hide the tool I need? Why not just give me the F$%$!^! tool and let me find a better tool! Sorry it's just really frustrating design. 2. Tools feel really weak, you have to spend a lot of gems to upgrade the damage/speed/rate of your tools, but you could have just spent those gems on your sword damage. Which uses no ammo and you always have, so if you love the feeling and power of the bow/bomb/boomerang in Zelda sorry it's not going to feel as good here. 3. You can't really access the dungeons in any order. You have to get the tool from 1 dungeon to even get to the area around the next dungeon. I mean that's Zeldaish, but there's only 1 dungeon you can access (afaik) at the beginning. And so you will GRIND and grind that dungeon to level up your stats for a long time, and it's gets boring fighting the same enemies and solving the same room puzzles (in a different order, but the puzzle is always the same). If they fixed those points above, make the game more openy less locky it would be amazing. But they combined 2 unlock mechanics (gem spending and tool finding) in a way that clashes rather than improves the experience. So in short how to avoid this in the future:1: Give access to more than 1 dungeon the player can experience and beat from the beginning. 2. Give the weak tools quicker and easier. (especially if it's tied to a building you can buy like elixir and farm)2b. Be careful with nesting unlocks behind unlocks, done wrong it can kill the feeling of reward. 3. Hide and let the player find upgraded powerful tools (which you could also apply the gem upgrades to).FInally:The controls feel greet! The hero abilities are fun and different. I wish each hero had 2 abilities instead of 1 but their great. And whoever did the map design, dungeon designs, and puzzle designs did a really great job!

_childDocuments_.review: If you would like to play a Link to the Past ripoff but with really terrible tweaks and simply not fun mechanics, this game is for you. Throughout my 12 hours of online gameplay, I experienced constant bugs, layer issues, desyncing of gems and health, and so much more. This game boasts of its random procedural generation, when it is really the same 12 tilesets but in a random order each time you enter the dungeon. The bosses were not a challenge at all.  Almost everywhere an enemy is able to get stuck on a different layer, making it impossible to kill them.  In the span of 12 hours, my game got soft-locked 4 times, due to lack of design effort on the dungeons. There are only about 8 items, and all of them are literally from the Zelda series, but are made to look like they aren't. The soundtrack consists of three songs that play regardless of where you are at, and sound just like - you guessed it - ZELDA. The hit registration in this game, is just awful. I would often take damage from things that weren't anywhere close to me. I suppose the art design was alright, but was just very uninspired. Overall, not a great experience. 1/10

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, 16bit Zelda combined with Roguelite sounds great and in general, the game captures the oldschool feel quite well. Especially the combat and visual style are spot on and will take you back instantly. However, if you play online coop, the camera system ruins it because all players share the same screen and the camera only zooms out so far when players are spaced out. If you wander off just a little bit, everyone else will get stuck on the edge of the screen and hate you for that. Not so great in a game where most of the fun comes from exploration... Also, if one player enters a house like a shop or another room inside a dungeon, everyone else has to follow and gets teleported there instantly, no matter what they were doing at the time. This also means that if one player interacts with a shopkeeper and another player leaves the shop, the purchase of the first player gets cancelled and he's being teleported outside as well. I understand that a system like this was all you had back on retro consoles, but I don't understand why this is neccessary in a modern online coop where everyone could just have their own screens.If you are a die hard fan of oldschool Zelda and/or Rogeulites and not planning to play coop, this might be for you. Everyone else, be warned...

_childDocuments_.review: Bugs and online multiplayer issues aside, I'm still disappointed.It's simply a messy experience. The way obtaining equipment works isn't very well explained, and you can both craft and purchase the same gear by accident (wasting money or materials in the process). I could purchase gear in the store while my co-op friends could not (with no explanation as to why). In contrast, other elements are obnoxiously over-tutorialized. There was more than one death that resulted from the stupid tutorial window that repeatedly pops up for skulls blocking the action. More than the tutorial windows obscures the action. Numbers and explosions and particle effects in multiplayer games are so numerous that it's hard to follow what's going on. In a roguelike where every hit hurts, it simply became a frustrating experience to play. After 4 hours, all of my co-op partners were done and had no desire to play again.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Heroes: Ruins of Tasos

_childDocuments_.review: Overall an enjoyable experience but there are a few critiques.The game feels incomplete.Some areas simply can't be accessed which makes me suspect DLC later down the line.Rather than hide this area it has been walled off with objects and scenery, one such easier being mired with invisible walls.This added with quite a lot of bugs some of which soft lock and others that full lock does add to a little bit of frustration.Bosses are way too simple. This is more of an opinion but it would be nice to see different attack patterns and harder to dodge attacks.The only time I perished to a boss was due to bug that rooted me to the floor.Audio.I appreciate this isn't a selling point for many but I have to give the audio a really low score.Every sound or piece of music has been used or heard in some form or another, having no sound at all as the credits roll was also a bit jarring.Gameplay.While not necessarily a bad or good thing if you titled this under another Zelda game you may not know the difference, especially with the level design, items, weapons and some of the sound effects.Was a little on the nose in places.With these points being said there is a lot of fun to be had here.The procedural dungeons up the replay value, multiplayer adds another layer of watching your friends die to a trap you've just set off, and having it be a more roguelike zelda style game isn't a bad thing, just needs that little more polish!With a small team of 2 I think Heliocentric Studios have made something entertaining and fun, even with my gripes I would still recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is WAY BETTER than it has any right to be. This takes Link to the past, Stardew valley, and Crosscode, then drops them into a blender and forces them to make love as they splash into a beautiful new amalgamation. Is it a triple A game? Nope. Is it smooth and responsive? Yes! Is it a roguelike? Barely-- Its closer to an rpg that has respawns than a rogue IMO.Has:Combat-Magic (Find spell "runes" while exploring to equip a new spell and spend mana)-Swords (Everyone gets one! fast and consumes active stamina)-Bows (Bows are chunky, slow, and satisfying!)-Hookshot, hit-them-with-a-book, punch them with gloves, etc.Exploration-Zelda style overworld-Quests and puzzles-Nooks and Crannies-Tons of environmental challenges-Swim around inside frog mouth!Village-Farming-Fishing-NPC quests-Pay the carpenter to build houses, workshops, etc-Minigames!Progression-Dungeon currency (gems) is used for upgrades, which you get from going into a dungeon. You drop all gems when you enter a new dungeon, so try to spend em all.-Gold is used for consumables as you unlock things.-Exploration will earn you things like the power gloves and farmtools, but unlocking most things is a quest or dungeon reward. While in a dungeon, you can get temporary versions of things.Doesn't have:MicrotransactionsRomanceEasy difficulty (Only normal, hard, and extreme IIRC)Overall, while still a teensy bit janky and derpy, its a loving homage to Link to The Past and is honestly fantastic. 8.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a challenging roguelike game, this sadly ain't it.The beginning of the game felt awesome, avoiding enemies and traps because they did a significant amount of damage to you. By the 3rd dungeon, without excessive farming, the upgrades make you too strong, to the point where I truly didn't care if I got hit. Some class abilities also give you many ways to skip mechanics altogether.If you loved A Link to the Past this might still be worth getting on sale, completing it once, and then calling it a day.Do note that the online has also been very buggy for a lot of users, especially when playing with more than 2 players. I played the whole campaign with a nearby friend online and had fairly minimal de-syncs. Maybe we got lucky ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Heroes is a otherwise very solid Zelda/Rogue-lite mashup marred by several technical and design issues. So, first thing first, be aware of what your getting with this game. The state the game is currently in, is not what should be considered a finished state. There are a number of quite severe bugs in both single and multiplayer that somewhat ruin the experience. Many of the bugs that existed at launch have already been fixed (1 week after launch) which gives me hope the remaining issues will also be fixed, and this recommendation is based on that.The core gameplay in Rogue Heroes is solid. It's fun, and the controls, audio, and graphics are all very satisfying. The challenge is fair, and the grind isn't too terrible, so it's easy to simply level your way past any obstacle that your skills can't handle (which is the lite part of rogue-lite). Playing in the overworld or any of the dungeons brings back memories of the best of the 16-bit era of Zelda games. So, with that out of the way, lets dive into the issues that still need to be addressed.On the technical side the worst unaddressed problem currently (at time of this review) is a network de-sync problem that makes the online co-op mode at best a frustrating experience, and at worst unplayable. Slightly less breaking but equally annoying when using steams play together feature to stream local co-op the audio is often horribly distorted and very loud leading to a physically painful experience until the remote players mute the games audio.On the design side, there are a few choices that are going to be much harder to fix as they'll require some re-evaluation of core gameplay. First, there are the power spheres. These are effectively collectibles, and finding all of them currently represents the primary end game activity in the game. The problem with them design wise, is they're utterly pointless. As you collect them, they allow you to retain an ever increasing amount of gems when you enter a dungeon (where normally you lose all unspent gems), but that's an utterly pointless effect. By the time you have enough power stones to where the effect is noticeable as more than a rounding error you don't actually have a use for gems anymore. Considering you'll likely have "beaten" the game by the time you have even a quarter of the power spheres (unless you've been going out of your way to specifically hunt them down), and also likely have purchased literally everything you can buy using gems, being able to retain more gems is utterly and completely useless.Secondly, there's the lack of end game content. There are 5 dungeons, and a final endless dungeon in the game (the devs are working on adding more dungeons though). Beating the 4 of the 5 dungeons (the 5th is optional and unlocks one of the classes) unlocks the final endless dungeon which is effectively the end of the game. Beating those 4 dungeons will take somewhere in the ballpark of 10 hours or so the first time. Once you know what you're doing it's probably doable in as little as 5 or 6 hours for most people. The endless dungeon is, honestly rather pointless. Yes you can keep pushing deeper and deeper into it, but there's very little point to doing so. Aside from an achievement at level 25, you get nothing by going deeper, and the dungeon doesn't really change much either. It's just the exact same thing over and over again against slightly stronger enemies for resources you have no use for. Rather than an endless dungeon, a new game+ mode that increased the difficulty of the original 4 dungeons probably would have been a better design.

_childDocuments_.review:
A dark evil stirs beneath the once peaceful land of Tasos Deep within the four Great Dungeons, the ancient seals that hold the Titans at bay are gravely weakened and their minions have unleashed terror upon the world.

The Goddesses who forged the seals long ago have made a desperate plea for a band of heroes to come forth and save the people from a terrible fate

Rogue Heroes is a 1-4 player classic adventure game with modern rogue-lite elements. Team up with friends to combat procedural dungeons, explore an expansive overworld full of secrets and take down the Titans to save Tasos!

name: Neon Abyss
detailed_description: Combining furious run ‘n’ gun action and deep, roguelike mechanics, Neon Abyss pits you as a member of ‘Grim Squad’ – a task force set-up by Hades himself to infiltrate the Abyss and defeat the New Gods. Death is not the end as every time you die, you’ll find yourself more empowered than before. As you progress through each dungeon, random item drops will be key in helping you infiltrate the Abyss and these passive effects can stack between every item. With no limit to how many can apply; a wide variety of combinations will make each run unique. With each run, you will be able to unlock new rooms, items, bosses, special rules and even new endings! This means each dungeon is unique and expandable, being tailored to your own specific playstyle. Hatch and Evolve Pets If you need some company on your journey into the depths of the abyss, or just some additional firepower or assistance, eggs can be found which will turn into a random pet that has a special ability and will evolve the longer you survive. Mini-Games Take a short break from slaying minions and take part in random mini-games that will also bag you some loot! Jump into Piano Performances, Meditation Challenge, Dance Competitions, and more – staying alive just got a lot more interesting!

_childDocuments_.review: I gotta say, I really enjoy this game a lot. There's times I've found myself letting time go out the window and end up going for "just one more run" and wind up playing for several more hours.As someone who's played a lot similar styles of games, I was pleasantly surprised with Neon Abyss. The gameplay, the music, the replay-ability all hit's the right notes. It's really easy to just get lost and keep playing. I really wish I had discovered it sooner. If you like other games such as Streets of Rogue, Dead Cells, Fury Unleashed and other similar rogue-likes, you'll find a good home here.The amount of combinations with weapons and items can be absurdly OP. What I enjoy most is that no two playthrough is ever alike. Item drops are randomized and there's plenty of variety.One thing I would like to see maybe implemented, is a way to remove an item you might get in a run. There's been a fair few runs where I'll find something and if you're not playing as Amir or have an ability to see what you're picking up, you can completely break a build. That said though, there is a wikia out there that can alleviate this. It's really the only con that I can think of. Seriously, if you like Rogue-Likes, this one is for you.

MANY.☐ There are pretty many☐ I didnt find one myself this far☐ It's okay☑ a fewFun:☑ It's never getting boring!☐ It could get boring after many hours☐ Its gonna get boring after a few hours☐ It isnt fun from the beginningStory:☑ There is one, but its actually endless☐ Yes, and it's good☐ A little bit..☐ Yeah, but it's bad☐ No, not really☐ It's just multiplayerSkill Level:☐ Join eSports and come again☐ Normal Gameplay☐ Hard to learn, hard to master☑ Easy to learn, hard to master☐ You just need 2 handsSearch time (only if it's multiplayer):☐ You find a match immediately!☐ There is a short wait time☐ Around 1 minute☐ Long wait time!☐ You'll find one in 30 minutes if you're luckyCommunity (only for multiplayer):☐ it's hard typing "gg" in the chat without getting called racist☐ people are pretty butthurt☐ there are some nice people after all☐ pretty nice community in total☐ you feel like you're in a church when playing this gameDevelopers:☑ Still releasing frequent updates☐ They could be more active☐ The game is finished☐ They ruined their own game with the updates☐ This game has been completely abandonedPrice:☑ Worth buying!☐ Only buy it if you have spare money☐ I would wait for a sale☐ No, just dont buy it.This game is quite the chunk. I for myself am a huge fan of rogue-likes, it's my favorite genre. Now, the kind of music I really like is darksynth and cyberpunk-style. Additionally, I really like pixel graphics in games as long as they're not too pixely.Now guess what this game has to offer. Yes. It has really nice graphics, evenly balanced between pixel and smooth textures, it has REALLY REALLY good music, which you will notice once you start up the game and play for a bit. (music is cyberpunk-style, like the whole game). It's also a rogue like with a really cool concept that basically lets you expand the dungeons you'll enter while you're in the hub. I'll talk about that later on.Like I said, the graphics of this game are really good. It's one of these rogue-likes where every item you pick up sort of gets plastered onto your body, like Risk of Rain. For example, Enter the Gungeon doesn't have that feature (still a good game tho). And as soon as you get a lot of stuff and a good weapon, oh boy, you will have your fun. Your eyes too.The sound is really good. This sounds brutal, but the hitsounds and the sounds of your enemies dying are really good. I like the little pop.As every roguelike is, it's hard at the beginning, but as soon as you get the hang of it, you're fine. It gets really fun.Now, a bit more about the system and concept they're going with. So, after beating a boss, they drop these little yellow pellets. Those can be spent on different things between runs. So basically, between runs, you're in the hub, also known as the "bar", where you can exchange them for characters, items, and whole new rooms that can show up in your dungeon. You can buy a fishing room, gambling rooms, reward rooms, and much more. As soon as you bought them, they can always show up in your runs, which is amazing. Also, there's a band playing sick music on the stage in the hub and you can dance along. Best feature.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the funnest rogue-like games I've played for a few reasons: huge weapon and items inventory that makes tons of unique combos possible, a fun roster of characters with their own unique abilities, a normal difficulty that doesn't make you suffer but keeps the game play moving and fun, and the fact that after 18 hours of play I'm still finding new game modes, secrets, abilities, rooms to unlock, and more! Oh, and the art! Neon Abyss's aesthetic is everything. I can't get enough of how this game looks! Does this game have a strong story to follow through? No. Does it need one? No. It has a premise and that's enough! If you want a game that's easy to pick up, fun to play through and has endless play through potential while also keeping the casual gaming vibe, this is a great game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: It's basically Binding of Issac with guns. A few enemies are pretty much the same and a few power-ups and familiars as well. Even the evil and non evil paths are pretty similar. That's not a bad thing I just wish it had as much content as Issac. There is basically 3 paths to take; Evil, not evil, and normal. (Not the right terms but still.) That's it. A daily challenge and some single player challenges would make such a big difference and make me more likely to keep coming back. I haven't unlocked all the characters yet but I feel like there isn't really a reason to. I beat the game just fine with the basic characters. Bosses need way more health too. They die way too fast so there isn't much reason to learn the attack patterns. Button remapping is crap. I can't rebind anything to any key that isn't a letter on the keyboard (no ctrl, alt, shift) I can't rebind the melee button. Hope you like F as melee cause that's all you get. Oh you like F as the interact key well guess you gonna be stabbing, dropping mines, etc on a lot of doors instead of opening them.No controller support is a weird choice. This would be a fantastic game to get nice and toasty and just recline and look at the pretty lights.Overall I would say I got my moneys worth. (I had more fun with this than I would at an arcade for the same amount of money) This just has the potential to be a MUCH better game with very small tweaks. Idk maybe these complaints are known and it's harder than it seems. I'm no game developer what do I know.

That being said, it feels a lot like it was trying to emulate The Binding of Isaac and it doesn't get anywhere close to the level of replayability that game has. Still worth a buy if you're looking for something to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so undeniably broken that it isn't even funny. Counter intuitive power UPS with no way to disable one of the two, power UPS that are just horrible to begin with, and a broken user interface are just scratching the surface of the many flaws. _childDocuments_.review: This game is one that I’m always coming back to. For a game where a single run can go less than a half-hour to finish, it’s replay value is really good. The variation in items and builds makes experimenting not only fun, but almost necessary. I will admit that there are some balancing issues that could still be addressed. There are single items that can just halve the difficulty of your run, and some things that make no noticeable difference, or sometimes, make things harder. However, this is addressable in-game due to the item, enemy, and weapon customization available to the player. The devs are pretty good at addressing player concerns, and new content is still on the way. Overall, if this game has shown up in your recommended list, or if a friend says they think you’ll enjoy it, I recommend giving it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: f you ever wanted something in the style of the Binding of Isaac but had no interest in crying poop demons to death, this is the game for you.  I give it a solid 4 stars out of 5.Long form response: Being a side view action roguelite with platformer elements, the core gameplay feels distinct enough to stand alone as its own thing, but the item and upgrade collecting elements feels very similar to BOI -- with the notable exception having documentation that's mediocre at best.  Want to know what an item does without collecting it and possibly ruining your entire run?  Hope you have a second screen with the wiki open, and that the wiki actually tells you what the item is and does.  You could also buy the DLC characters and play Amir, but there's no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason that you should need to buy an extra character to access a mechanic that should be the default gameplay.Red Hearts and Soul Hearts become Hearts and Shields, and each one can be raised to a maximum of 8, which is usually an improvement over BOI's hard cap of 12 total hearts.  Flies are replaced by Sprites of varying types.  Familiars still exist, but instead of being immortal slackers who take the place of one of the useful items you might have acquired in their steads, they hatch from (and evolve through) magic eggs you find scattered about which hatch at seemingly random intervals -- and are subject to some forms of damage.  You've still got a pretty similar assortment composed of "bum type" minions who pick up items and might give you different items in their place, attacking minions, and random garbage that floats around you and might block something once or twice if you're lucky.One of the things I really appreciate is that instead of accumulating random items that completely redefine how your attacks work, Guns are all a separate pool from items -- but still benefits from items that give extra bullets, more damage, etc.  You absolutely can fill the entire screen with bullet spam if you pick up the right combination of items and the right gun.  Many of the guns have charge attacks or charge elements to their attacks, which is basically terrible to try and use with an analog stick, but you might like them if you play with a mouse and keyboard.  Many more of them don't.  Gone are Angel Rooms or Devil Rooms that you might semirandomly get after a boss fight, with no reliably accessible way to influence what appears or whether there's anything at all.  In their stead, there are Wisdom Rooms and Violence Rooms which you can access by rarely taking damage and consistently taking damage respectively.  You'll end up playing both ways several times if you want to clear the entire boss roster.Overall, it's a solid entry in my library.  I picked it up a few months ago, and still pick it up periodically when I'm in the mood for something that will offer surprises without requiring me to learn a new game.

_childDocuments_.review: Offensively boring and stale. This game really gives off the vibe that somebody watched the "American Gods" intro and was like, "Damn that would be totally epic if I made an entire game styled after that!". But much like the show they forgot to add anything interesting after the initial start and you're left with a bunch of half-baked ideas and a slog that equals to nothing satisfying. The enemies are boring, the levels are samey and badly designed, the weapons are all awful and gimmicky, the characters are one-note, blank slates, the bosses range from either pushover to annoyingly spamming and tedious, and holy ♥♥♥♥ the readability/visibility of your character is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ non-existent when everything in the game is some form of neon vomiting all over your screen all at once. Also who's the 200 IQ dev who decided that your character should throw grenades based on which direction you're facing instead of where your crosshair is facing? Just play Gungeon/Nuclear Throne instead for fun gun gameplay or even Undermine if you want some really hidden/underrated roguelike that's decent.

_childDocuments_.review: What grabbed my attention and I assume yours as well was the way that this game looks. It's a beautiful pixel art style and it looks even better in game. Water reflections and light ambiance make the game look amazing. I run this at 1440p at 144fps and it is . Neon Abyss has an art style you'll be thinking about for a while and I hope other developers take note because I'd like more games to look this good.The sound is great but more importantly the music is too! Usually I end up turning off a game's music in favor of my own but not with this game. It has an upbeat & vibrant feeling to it that I really love.Of course, the gameplay is arguably the most important aspect of a game. Right? Story can be an argument but as this game hardly has one, I won't even talk about it. The gameplay itself is very fast paced. Item and Weapon combinations can be extremely rewarding. Sure, you can get to the end of playthrough with decent items and good skill but having an OP build that you lucked out on can be just as fun, if not more fun. After every boss you get a special currency to level up and unlock Items/Weapons. I have only ~6 hours played so far but I am enjoying it and will definitely try to 100% the game.Not being able to save mid-run and come back later is  inconvenient. Each run can take quite a while to finish and this makes it to where you can't play this game in short bursts. But my main problem with this game is that it doesn't do anything innovative with the genre. If you've played any roguelite game in the past, you have seen pretty much everything in this game. (Besides the beautiful art style)Some of the main complaints from everybody else are that the levels don't feel unique, I agree with that. Another thing is the English wording. Some of the tooltips sound awkward and some just seem completely wrong. Lastly is  easily the grind. In ~6 hours I've only gotten like 7 or so skills in the skill tree? I like a grind but there's definitely a thin line between a  and a . This game definitely leans towards the grindy side. At this point, it'll take me a while to finish the game. Luckily, I'm having a lot of fun.I know I spouted a lot of negativity towards the end but I still think this game is . If you're already into roguelites and aren't looking for a big innovative change to the genre, I guarantee you'll have fun with Neon Abyss.

_childDocuments_.review: Roguelikes live and die depending on the addictiveness and enjoyability of their core gameplay loop and Neon Abyss simply fails to capture the "magic" of its contemporaries.I am usually not a fan of judging a game by comparing it to others. But Neon Abyss takes such heavy inspiration from games such as The Binding of Isaac and Enter the Gungeon, that comparisons are unavoidable and I am sad to say that Neon Abyss falls short of its forefathers in almost every way. Lets get into the good things first: The game is beautiful and the Soundtrack is fitting and quite catchy, though it gets repetitive quickly.   The Gameplay has the potential to be up there with the best that a Roguelike could possibly offer. Shooting is very satisfying and the movement feels fluid.I'll get into how the game doesn't utilize this promising framework further on.My very first run was very enjoyable, the music had me bopping my head and the bossfights seemed very interesting.But the scepticism set in when I beat the first "final boss" on my very first run. I am not here to show off, I am in fact not very good at all at 2D games, it took me many hours to not have my ass handed to me in Cuphead for example. The game is simply that stupidly easy. The "challenge" comes in the form of grinding.The gameplay loop consists of getting a useless run, either dying or painstakingly finishing it over the course of way too much time once or at most twice and then getting an op run. So while you will have an entirely unrewarding and slow experience two thirds of the time, the remaining third consists of equally unrewarding runs, where nothing even remotely poses a threat. The only thing stopping you from playing through the entire game on the first good run that you get, is an arbitrary barrier to your progress, in that a run unavoidably ends once you beat a "final boss" that you haven't defeated before. Once you reach the fourth "Manager" or so you may only unlock further bosses by spending a very scarce resource that you only get by defeating previous bosses. And so the grind begins. This resource is the only way to permanently "progress" in the game, by granting you the ability to unlock Upgrades, Features and even characters and it is incredibly time-intensive to come by. This grind doesn't get any more exciting considering that I got bored of the repetitive enemies on only my second run. The "variety" in the form of bosses seemingly fleshes out the game, but they are all so incredibly unthreatening and boring in terms of their attack patterns and defensive options that they quickly melt into the colorless mass.Finishing a run usually takes a little less than an hour for which you are handsomely rewarded with around 20 points, which equates to maybe 2 permanent upgrades in the very beginning. To reach these permanent upgrades you will have to spend half your points on single use "Trial Items" though, so permanent progress isn't even guaranteed. Through these you'll often be left with the prospect of getting even less of a challenge on your next run aswell as not being able to afford anything permanent such as characters or straight up upgrades. So you play for around an hour, upon which your run is forcefully ended only to progress by about 1% in a skill tree to make the game even easier, although it is already basically impossible to fail. This is what this game considers its gameplay loop and it isn't really a loop, but moreso a straight line. I know what you're thinking, but let me assure you that simple damage and health rebalancing wouldn't fix the issue, because the system is inherently flawed. The game is not designed in a way that will ever allow you to feel like you "get it" and know how to reliably avoid all damage. Not receiving any damage is moreso a product of killing everything and anything the game throws at you immdiately. Even on my very first run the fights were usually resolved by immediately clearing out every room and basically facetanking the bosses, since the game absolutely drowns you in health and shield drops. Neon Abyss copied the entirety of BOI's framework without realizing or emulating what made it satisfying in the first place. The inherent difficulty and rewarding nature of the gameplay loop, perhaps even the obtuse story that creates intrigue. Neon Abyss has none of this and it feels like you are dripfed progress simply by breathing. Let me clarify that I didn't go into this expecting a game that would be able to surpass the likes of BOI. However,  having played and greatly enjoyed Undermine among other (obviously BOI inspired) roguelikes, I expected to get my moneys worth in the form of a satisfying, well rounded first "playthrough".Instead I received a promising first impression and the feeling of complete and utter emptiness after every completed run.I somewhat enjoyed my time with the game and I may even play it again, however I can't help but feel like I'm wasting my time whenever I play it.If you simply want to experience what the game has to offer and you enjoy leaning back and not really thinking about what you're doing you might still enjoy this. I didn't though.The game didn't offend me in any way, and aside from a few nitpicks there aren't many things that will immediately stick out as bad or annoying, but I simply cannot recommend a game that fails to motivate me to play it further even in the slightest.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't recommend this game in it's current state, although it is a decent timewaster for what it currently is. The game feels and plays really smoothly, has pretty aesthetics and all, but aside from that, it's very bland at it's current state. Neon Abyss tries to use wacky weapons and 'infinite' item combinations as a selling point, but in reality just about all the guns are worse than the stock one, and the items are generally just slightly faster firing rate or more damage. There isn't a whole lot of enemy variance, as you go down the levels in each run all that changes is that they start doing contact damage and just get more HP. There isn't a whole lot of enemy variety either, and changing the difficulty of the game just makes enemies take a little longer to kill. One of the biggest issues is the upgrade system they use, you get multiple pages of skills to unlock that cost these boss token things, and you only get one per boss takedown. The prices of the later upgrades are so exorbitant that it would take multiple full game clears just to get a few on a page filled with many, so it becomes a grindfest (not even a fun one at that either). I'm gonna try to stay optimistic for the future of the game though since it just released, hopefully they will listen to people's complaints and address them to improve on the many issues currently present in it. All in all, I really can't recommend this right now, wait for a sale or after some future updates hit that fix things if you really wanna bite the bullet 💜

_childDocuments_.review: It's a shame I have to leave a negative review, because Neon Abyss is a game I really wanted to like. Right out of the gate, though, it feels slow, quiet, and uninspired. I found a lot of QoL issues in the demo, but figured that build's about 8 months old, so that's not really too much of an issue- but save for one, they're all still present in the base game.Within 40 minutes of playing, I found the following problems:The trailers will have you believe this is a fast paced, Gungeon-esque game, and I was hoping this would scratch the Gungeon itch, but instead it just makes that itch worse. Instead of taking the positives of Gungeon (its humor, polish, core gameplay loop, balance) it seems to take the negatives (visually busy design, pacing, pre-update slow backtracking) while offering almost nothing new to the table. Babies are a neat concept, but even they aren't completely polished, and that's the game's only standout factor- I had a baby that split into about 10 zombie babies, and it was never explained why- I had to go to the pause menu to figure it out. I never saw the actual health of the zombie babies either, and the item text implies it would just continually split itself, which I figured wasn't right, and sure enough they all died a few seconds later.I feel like Neon Abyss doesn't know what it wants to be. It wants to be Isaac, it wants to be Enter the Gungeon, but what it lacks from those two games is staying power. I put this in the same category as Steredenn and Wizard of Legend, where they're games I really wanted to like, but out of the gate i saw pacing and polish issues that I just can't overlook. I'm willing to overlook problems with a game if it's fun, because no game is perfect, but Neon Abyss... isn't fun.A game being derivative is okay and expected in today's industry. Monolith, for example, is one of my favorite roguelites, and it's just about one of the most derivative roguelites you're going to find. This is derivative for the wrong reasons. Where Monolith takes existing ideas, iterates on them, and seamlessly integrates them together into a cohesive experience, Neon Abyss feels like it's taking existing ideas, throwing them in, and praying it works, and the way I see it, it doesn't work.I think this game has the potential to be good, but it's going to take a lot of changes. The game, overall, needs faster pacing (at the very least optional like in Gungeon) and needs to be able to stand by itself, as well as a lot of quality of life iteration. If i found this many gripes in 40 minutes, that tells me there's probably a lot of others, too.
