_childDocuments_.review: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Darkside Detective is bringing back the classic indie flavor of out-of-the-box thought processes and storytelling, mixed with a fantastic yet simplistic style of gameplay.Hey, kids . . . remember back when indie games weren’t shy about creating weird game designs and stories?  Well, it seems like Darkside Detective is trying to bring that weird awesomeness back with a more refined traditional style of gameplay.In this game, you get to play as a desperate Police Detective trying to solve cases that are out of the scope for most cops; cases that require a bit more open-mindedness and belief in the extraordinary. Well, I am talking about Ghosts, Realms, Demons, and everything creepy in between. The game is all about looking beyond the scope, looking for nitty gritty details, puzzles that require keen attention, and so on. The game is a bit on the dialogue-heavy side, so if you’re not into that, you have been warned. But I must say that dialogues in this game are very well thought-out; charming, witty, and clever. The game obviously is not serious, but it’s kinda funny to see it tries to create some form of tension.Plot: Ah! Twin Lake City is a beauty of a place cursed with a demon infestation (along with a variety of otherworldly creatures). As the curse starts to affect the city more and more, the demand for someone with skills to deal with this kind of infestation grows. Here’s where our protagonist, Detective Francis McQueen, comes into play, specializing in dealing with all the otherworldly drama. Case after case, Detective McQueen takes on the toughest of the tough. Until that one ill-fated day when, while working with his longtime partner Officer Dooley, an unknown event occurred and Officer Dooley was sucked into a different realm far away from human contact. Having running dry on leads, Detective McQueen starts looking for new leads to discover the whereabouts of Officer Dooley. Taking some time off his official duties to dedicate maximum effort to Dooley’s case, McQueen manages to pull Dooley back to his earthly realm.As the days go by, more and more such mysterious cases land on the floor, and who better to manage them other than Detective McQueen.Gameplay: The game doesn’t mess around, with just a brief glimpse of a short yet fantastic animated storyboard which pretty much sets the tone for the first case... There are currently seven such cases, and I am very much hoping to get some more.Each case takes about 20-25 minutes to complete if you’re not in a rush or you’re not paying attention. This is fair enough, considering how well the game has been scripted, and combined with its simplistic gameplay, it’s a win-win situation.The cases sort of progress episodically; when a case comes by that’s slightly spooky, McQueen gets called in for help.As you interact with NPCs on each case, you start to gather up all the necessary information at a snail’s pace. Most interactions are pointless with little information to be collected, but immensely amusing to see NPC’s trying to create some false tension, or making unfunny comments, being jerks to each other. And here’s where the star attraction comes into play, the gameplay itself. Simplistic point and click style of gameplay, full of witty dialogue and nothing much to do other than to go back and forth in scenes to collect items, information, and complete puzzles. There’s a fair bit of backtracking going on in this game, but nothing to get stressed about.  It’s very manageable as you collect information and items from one scene and go to the next to get some more info, while getting the items to interact with each other or with NPC’s. The game features a few unique sets of puzzles; nothing too crazy, mostly items interacting with each other and NPC’s to figure out their purpose. Basically object inventory puzzles, logic puzzles, circuit connection puzzles, etc. Most of the puzzles are either no-brainers or mildly tedious. World design: Darkside displays a fantastic assortment of Pixel Graphics Motion art.  From rooms to streets, everything was pretty much in good shape, contributing to the game's overall charm (although certain things could’ve been improved visually, like the cop car).Music and sound effects: The game features a pretty interesting background tune, trying to simulate some sort of creepy theme; I found it rather funny and enjoyable.I wish I could say the same for the other sound effects; some are okay but others outright disappointing; a little more of something would’ve been nice.Positive: + Fantastic cases to be solved+ Fun and simplistic style of gameplay + No-brainer fun puzzles + Pixel Graphics Motion art+ Enjoyable background tune + Splendid Witty dialoguesNegatives: -  Most dialogues are pretty pointless and distract from the game - Some puzzles are rather tedious- Certain sections of the artwork could’ve been improved - Short game, could use some more casesA super retro indie game that doesn’t takes itself seriously.  It’s pretty funny to see characters trying to create some form of tension . . . well, they tried. 8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: This is everything I wanted out of a second Darkside Detective season.  The first game has a special place in my heart and is among my favorite adventure games.  It is a great series for newcomers to the point and click genre.  If you are not familiar, Darkside Detective is a spooky comedy developed by a small Irish team featuring  a straight-laced detective and his lovably dim cop partner as they investigate supernatural disturbances in and around the fictional city of Twin Lakes.I use the term "season", because Darkside Detective is broken up into distinct standalone cases, making it perfect for popping in and out at your leisure over a long period of time.  It's great for streaming, too, if you are into the Twitch scene.  The first game launched with six completed cases, and every few months the developers dropped a new case, bringing it up to a total of nine.  It appears similar plans may be in the works for A Fumble in the Dark.In DSD2, the boys are back, and the game's current six cases take us to places like a haunted carnival, a demonic wrestling match, and a perfectly normal nursing home where nothing at all strange is happening.Fumble in the Dark is an A+ continuation of the magic formula used in the first game, but with improvements across the board.  The writing is just as funny (if not funnier!).  If anything, the art has gotten even better.  The six currently available cases are a bit longer and more varied than the average case from DSD1, and it feels like Spooky Doorway made conscious efforts to improve puzzle design as well.While the original composer from DSD1 did not return for the second game, the new composer Thomas O'Boyle had big shoes to fill and did a phenomenal job in maintaining the feel of the original game while putting his own spin on it.If you are new to the series, go ahead and buy the bundle with both of them.  Just do it, and thank me later.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this is one of the games that made me wish steam had a more neutral option for reviews.That said, I definitely didn't enjoy this game as much as the first one. I'd suggest playing the original Darkside Detective if you have any interest. And honestly, frankly, skipping this one. I enjoyed it, but the puzzles in this game were a lot more of a pain in the ass than the original. In the first game, I wouldn't say I hit any major stumbling blocks in solving any of the cases. Most of the logic made sense, things were well foreshadowed in their use, and the layout of puzzles did a good job making sure you didn't have to backtrack too much.This game definitely is a step down in puzzle design. Several steps down in my eyes, honestly. There were multiple points in this game where I ended up completely stuck with no idea how to progress. Multiple times where I felt like I was pixel hunting for something that wasn't properly signposted, or a lack of context clues left me with zero idea how to proceed. I had to look up guides at points for over half the mainline cases. I don't like referring to guides if I can avoid it, I'd much rather solve puzzles in games from, well, within the game. Generally when I'm looking at a guide it's because I feel the game has failed in guiding me or signposting what it expects from me. For that reason, I can't really say this succeeds as a sequel to the original, which I never ran into that issue with.As for the actual story in the cases, it was nice. Good follow up to the original darkside detective. Good continued building of the setting. Jokes still quite amusing, and the tone of the game bang on to the original, props for all that.All that said, be warned the puzzles in this game are a step down from the first if you are going to get it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: The pixel art is awesome and the atmosphere was interesting overall. However, unlike the first game, half of the cases had annoyingly-hard puzzles so much so that after trying numerous combinations for a long time (without any progress), I had to watch walkthroughs to find the solutions. And some of the dialogue was unnecessarily long, boring and cringey. Had I not bought the 2 games in a bundle, I'd refund this game after the first hour with no regrets.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Oh my god, I love this game so much.  I want there to be a series of these things so that I can never be without them.  Not only are they hilarious, well, wait a second, the humor is both character based (Officer Dooley is wonderful as is his friendship with Detective McQueen) and situational, and also I think Irish, but the puzzles are genuinely fun, clever enough to be satisfying, logical enough to be satisfying, not so hard as to leave you clicking on every damn thing everywhere looking for clues.  My whole family gathers around the laptop in bed to play it, which is cozy and delightful, and my kid quotes Dooley, which means it is probably also educational. BUY THIS SO THAT THE SPOOKY DOORWAY PEOPLE WILL THINK THAT MAKING MORE OF THESE WILL KEEP THEM IN BEER MONEY please please please.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an AMAZING continuation of The Darkside Detective franchise. You don't have to play the previous title, but it is recommended as they make several references to characters and events that happened in cases in the first game. This game makes a lot of hilarious references to 80s and 90s games/movies/tv - so older players will very much enjoy the cheeky humor. It's not spooky, but more in the mystery realm.If you enjoy titles such as the Monkey Island franchise, Maniac Mansion, Loom, Grim Fandango - you will absolutely love this! 12/10 for this title. Absolutely worth playing if you enjoy point-and-click mystery titles. I can't wait for a 3rd installment!PROS:* GREAT story that builds upon the previous title and each case* hilarious commentary and cheeky references to 80/90s pop culture* simplistic controls (left mouse button only)* no ability to die* auto save and manual saves anywhere* cases separated into their own segments that builds upon each other* fun puzzles* fitting background music that fits, isn't annoying and is engaging with the gameCONS:* lot of dialogue to read - would have been nice to have it voice acted. Not a big deal for me but could be a negative for some people* some of the puzzles were a bit convoluted (don't forget to click on Dooley as he's a solution to many of them)
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: If you know the first installment, you know what you're getting yourself into. I'm a little ambiguous on that, but overall it's another great game from Spooky Doorway.+Pixel graphic at it's finest+Great soundtrack+Delightfully dark and almost brilliant humor+A tribute to some of the great Point & Click Adventures of yore+Some lovely new NPCs and some of the old ones+Easy achievements and around 10-15 hours of gameplay+Free DLCs+-As with the first game, the focus is definitely on finding and combining things. I would have liked a few more puzzles. There are some, but all are exremely easy.+-As in the first game, the cases are not very well connected, or not connected at all. I know that's on purpose, but some central theme would still be great, i think. At least in some cases.Like the first game, the second one is a must for any fan of the genre. And still worth the money for everyone else. Highly recommended at full price and definitely on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: The Darkside Detective series is something truly special. I fell in love with the first installment so playing this title was a no-brainer. In comparison to "The Darkside Detective", "The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark" is a bit longer, achievements took me some more time and the quality... is even better. Everything you loved is grander in the sequel.You can read many ravishing reviews praising the pixel graphics, the soundtrack but for me, the greatest thing is the writing. It's not "just" the characters that are interesting, likeable; written in a way you're getting invested into their background stories. Not only the cases which are a perfect mixture of intriguing and absurd for you to keep wanting more. For me it's the undeniable talent and wit that made this universe come to life, the attention to detail and writing dozens of clever jokes to put in this game so that every time you click on something, you laugh.I play many point and click games, many detective games too, and this is the one I would recommend to anyone, both enthusiasts of this genre and people who are new to it. Buy it, at full price, it's worth it (or wait for sale and buy both parts of the game).
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: So, there can definitely be too much of a good thing. I liked the first game well enough, but this one just went on for too long. There were too many references to characters that I didn't recall from years ago and the writing ends up being quirky, but not particularly funny. There's also just a lot of repetitive clicking around as solutions open up by clicking on something that you've already clicked on before following some random unconnected event that doesn't really indicate any change. I was definitely dragging myself to finish this.

_childDocuments_.review: Even better than the 1st one! Can't say that about a lot of games. I love moving around in a bigger map and explore. And it's not often you get a game every line is a joke and most of them are actually funny. Yes there are relentless puns but even those are fun. _childDocuments_.review: is a point & click detective adventure game that is a sequel to the first game. While you do not need to play the first game to get into this one, I would recommend that you try to do so, because there are small parts of the story and some jokes that will make more sense if you are familiar with the first game.Your favorite paranormal detective is back in action with 6 new cases to solve in this game. Hopefully the developers will add to this game, as they did for the first season after release.Playing as the detective investigating the supernatural occurrences, you will be using the usual point & click actions of finding items, using items, talking to NPCs, and also solving mini-puzzles, etc. The game follows the classic formula.The graphics are in simple pixel art, making the game feel authentic. You should be able to use a controller too, but I did not try that.Most games have progressively increasing price tags when a sequel is made, but not for this game! The price stayed at the same €11.49/$12.99 base price as the first. This is definitely a fair price for this game. If you like the first  game, you will love this one too. _childDocuments_.review: The introduction of Detective Francis McQueen and his sidekick, Officer Patrick Dooley, in 2017’s comedy horror point-and-click, , was an unexpected delight. The strange and kooky world of Twin Lakes didn’t take the ‘horror’ bit all that seriously; it was much happier indulging obscure film references and finding innuendo .And we were all the better for it.The sequel, , is much the same, only bigger and carried off with a confidence born of its developers knowing they’ve crafted a winning duo, milking it for all it's worth – albeit a little too much at times.There are six cases for McQueen to solve, starting with bringing Dooley back from his entrapment in the eponymous ‘Darkside’ – a ghoulish mirror of Twin Lakes, which is inhabited by a menagerie of monsters and spooks. Some of them are nice, even friendly. Most aren’t.Dooley’s time in the Darkside forms the rough backbone of the narrative, with most of the cases you need to solve in some way related to this endearing and wonderful idiot. In one particularly memorable episode we take a trip to Ireland to visit the Dooley clan, who reside in a magnificent castle (one of a few striking pixely vistas; the game is often very lovely to look at).The cases themselves are of a decent length and do a solid job of poking fun at the illogical logic of the point-and-click, whilst slickly evoking what makes them great – the bizarre thrill of combining items in obscure ways, often without quite understanding  it matters. In this respect I reckon  is more challenging than its predecessor, although there’s the odd silly and inexplicable puzzle that’s difficult to solve in a logical way, even by the game’s standards. But then it wouldn’t be a point-and-click without ‘em, would it?As much as I love the genre, though, it’s not  gameplay that attracts me to it. Much like the first game, Twin Lakes is a wonderful place to spend time in – and such a brilliant locale for point-and-click adventures. It’s full of quirk and character, with every interaction, no matter how small, helping to expand the game’s world into something truly eclectic. Somewhere so far beyond the horizon of supernatural silliness that you can’t help  find pleasure in it.Its immersive qualities owe a great debt not only to the writing, but also Thomas O’Boyle’s stellar soundtrack. He couldn’t have crafted a more ideal set of tunes to go along with McQueen and Dooley’s adventures.It’s been a real kick spending the last few nights in unhinged retirement homes and haunted funfairs (and their Darkside mirrors, ).Which I suppose is weird when I don’t actually find  as funny as most people do. Sure, I always had a smile on my face, but it never quite had me laughing hysterically, which is where I feel I ought to be with its brand of comedy. That may be because it's working overtime to be funny, forever in pursuit of the joke whether there’s one there or not. I think writing-wise that’s a mistake, and it’s something that held the first game back, too. A pause is a valuable tool, but  games aren’t sure where that is, or even which joke or pun is best. So it goes for broke, never quite hitting the highs it wants. It’s a pacing issue.But that smile it elicited never wavered, in part because McQueen and Dooley make for such an enjoyable pair and are the perfect window into Twin Lakes. They charmed me back in 2017 (or whenever it was I played the first…it’s possible it was later, but whatever!) and charm me still. But I think I want them to win my , and the writing will need to find a better balance to do that.With a seventh case to be unlocked at a later date there's still time to do that, and the strengths of  are such that I’m already anticipating the inevitable third game. Spooky Doorway have set themselves no limit on what supernatural shenanigans can manifest in Twin Lakes, and we should be grateful for that.Originally published on .

_childDocuments_.review: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark is a sequel to The Darkside Detective, being a funny point-and-click mystery game with pixel artstyle. It takes place about a year after the first game, and Det. McQueen is trying to bring his friend Officer Dooley back from the Darkside. Like before, there are 9 cases to solve, actually 11 since case 9 is 3 smaller cases, and each of them pretty longer than the first game. In total, the sequel is almost double its length.Gameplay is identical to the first, and so is the Gravity Falls-like funny mystery in small town vibe. The humor is kinda better, I think they're funnier and more meta, like one time a Bloodwolf tells us to leave a positive review (which of course I did) complete with a *wink wink*. The levels are also bigger, more varied, and also more creative with the events going on, like time travel and digital worlds which makes the cases in the first game feel pretty tame by comparison.If you enjoyed the first game, you'll most likely enjoy The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark more. It's the same, but better and longer yet managed to stay fun and not monotonous. If you're a fan of the genre and looking to play this duology, you should play the first game before this since there are many characters and references to events you won't understand if you skipped straight to the second title.

_childDocuments_.review: While I didn't find this second outing for Detective McQueen and Officer Dooley to be quite so compelling as the original,  is another excellent point-and-click adventure. Puzzles for the most part have solutions that make reasonable sense (though there's still the occasional instance of 'moon-logic' making it worth having a guide to hand), the detailed pixelart is used to good effect and the writing is excellent throughout. _childDocuments_.review: A Fumble in the Dark is a solid follow-up to the original Darkside Detective. It’s not so much an iterative sequel as an additional set of cases; it’s the exact same point-and-click mechanics, same art, same characters. Yet I didn’t enjoy it as much as the first one. The developers seem to have upped the difficulty of the puzzles; most are fine, but there are a few that are particularly complex and obtuse, and required me to hit walkthroughs to progress. I also found it less funny; I can’t tell if this is because the jokes aren’t as sharp, or if it’s simply a result of the fact that a sequel is inherently less surprising than the original, and familiarity is the death of comedy.These complaints aside, it’s still an amusing point-and-click, crafted with love, with a nice episodic structure to break things up and free episodes added post-release.

_childDocuments_.review: (AFitD)is the sequel to the excellent  and takes you back to Twin Lakes, the 34th most haunted city in America, and into the role of Detective McQueen. Six more cases will see you solve puzzles in places like a warped funfair, a psychically possessed retirement home and a druid's castle in Ireland. takes place just after the end of the first game and expands on a lot of the characters and themes from it. Thankfully, it doesn't do that stupid sequel trope of re-calling the events or attempting to detail anything from the prequel. It just picks up the baton and runs with it, as all sequels should, in my opinion. This does lead to the game being totally unwelcoming to newcomers. If you have not played the first game, you will have absolutely no clue who anyone is or what's going on.As for the writing, it's still brilliant.  cases go into the finer details on characters and go to strange new places. The dialogue is still sharp and witty and the game uses its large ensemble cast to flesh out the city of Twin Falls really well. We even leave Twin Falls and America in some of the cases, with one taking place in Ireland. Marking one of the few times in gaming that a level set in Ireland has been written by Irish people, this case is easily the best in the series. The main characters of McQueen and Dooley are both given much more backstory imbuing them even more a sense of life than before. Dooley's, in particular, is explored in great depth, and he's fast becoming my favourite character in any game ever. His swings from absurd levels of idiocy to astounding clarity are never jarring and fit perfectly with his goofball side-kick character. His general cluelessness is the basis for a lot of the humour and it's so well done that it never gets old or repetitive. Gameplay is the standard point and click adventure fare. You explore the rooms, pick up items and talk to everyone you can to solve puzzles and progress the story. As with the prequel, there's no moon logic puzzles and most can be solved with a bit of lateral thinking and some time. That said, there are one or two that will have you thinking for a while on the solution, but it's through genuine challenge, and not because you don't happen to think along the same lines as the writer. The main difference between  and its prequel is the length. Where DD could be cleared in around four hours, that would only get you to the end of the third case here. There's still no dying in . While this didn't ruin the game for me, I felt it undermines some of the more dramatic scenes. For example, there's a scene where you're stuck in a box that's filling with water, the music has changed to create a sense of tension, but you've all the time in the world to escape as the water level never rises. It makes no sense to construct a scene to evoke danger, only to erase it right at the start. It didn't ruin any of the scenes for me though, but it did leave me wondering about why that was done.The graphics are the same as in the first game, basic but functional, although a little more effort has gone into making sure that items are more defined than in . The character models are all well done, and the background art sets each scene up nicely. There's much more variety in the backgrounds than in the previous game.The music score is not composed by Ben Prunty as with . The composer here is Thomas O'Boyle, and his score is just as effective. Simple and unique, each track suits the area it's used in perfectly. It doesn't distract from the game and sets the tone nicely. The  which doesn't clash with the comedic elements of the game. The game still lacks voice acting and can get oddly quiet at times due to the lack of any environmental sounds.If you enjoyed , then this is more of what you love. If you didn't enjoy  then this is more of what you disliked.  is a superb second entry in a series I hope runs for a long time. For the most part, it's pretty much identical to the first installment. It does require the player to have played the first game to know what's going on and I'm still convinced the only thing preventing this series from becoming sensational is the lack of a good voice cast.  cements the  series as a staple of every adventure game fan's collection.

_childDocuments_.review: I have just completed Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark, and what can I say? It is another rare sequel that learns from the first installment and creates an even more enjoyable experience.The first game was already fun, perfect for a relaxing evening. This game brought back all the fun characters from the original, introduced even more hilarious dialog and references, and added engaging interactive puzzles; nothing too brain-destroying to make a minimally frustrating experience.Things I liked (in no particular order):- Those chunky, bright-colored pixels - they are positively charming.- The music. It is cheerful, cheezy, and spooky. Also, prepare for a glorious song!- The characters. If you loved them before, you will love them even more now.- The puzzles. Some were more time-consuming than others, but nothing that took too long or offered much frustration, and they were all fun.- The stories in each case. Each was entertaining and brought unique sets of characters and puzzles to solve.- Delightful bonus cases! After the main story, there were three bonus cases.- The game was longer. I clocked up around 18 hours.Things I did not like:- Nothing. This game was fantastic.Thank you for giving me a week's worth of evenings relaxing and playing this during a stressful time. I appreciated it.Devs, thank you for your hard work, and I am excited for any future installments of this unique and wonderful series!

_childDocuments_.review: In this sequel, we once again play as the dynamic duo, Detective McQueen and Officer Dooley, who have more paranormal cases to handle in a world that is full of silliness and doesn't take itself seriously. The gameplay is a simple point and click that anyone can jump into and get a hang of. We interact with objects in the environment, talk to NPCs, and use stuff from our inventory when the situation suits it. It's pretty much the same as the gameplay of the first part of this series, except each case is longer and some puzzles are noticeably harder and might require an occasional glance at a walkthrough.Visuals take a form of pixel art, again just like in the first game, and the overall presentation is very user-friendly. It is too much of the same as the first game and it's too simplistic to stand out too much, but it's a decent way to pass time and get some silly laughs. _childDocuments_.review: [Early review, will update.]A Fumble in the Dark is excellent. As with the first Darkside Detective game, it's a funny, heartfelt point & click adventure about police work in a moderately-cursed city. The game is structured into self-contained cases, with each case taking about an hour and having its own locations, items, etc., but you'll see plenty of recurrent characters. Puzzles are generally inventory-based, but with some clever set pieces as well, like a devilish telephone switchboard. What separates this game and its predecessor from others in the genre is just how  it is. It's well-written and genuinely funny, without any of the sarcastic edgelord humor that this genre often has. As an adventure game, it hits the right level of difficulty for a fun but thoughtful playthrough: in general, there's little sign-posting about what to do next, but the puzzles are also logical (by the standards of a cursed city, anyway) and you can pretty much always work out what to do next by just thinking through it or paying attention to dialogue. You'll feel very clever but also won't have a migraine.  In comparison to the first game, A Fumble in the Dark doesn't reinvent the wheel but it also doesn't sit still. It's a bit more polished and practiced in a lot of facets. The pixel art's a little more vibrant and eyecatching, the writing's gotten a bit sharper and funnier, and the production values generally seem higher. In sum, it's exactly what I was hoping it would be, and will easily be on my list of top adventure games in 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: – Point-and-click mystery solving and mini games that are fun and not too hard– Lots of humor– An adorable friendship– Cute pixel art– Overall cute and fun, and this one hit me in the feels more than the first!*My actual playtime is about 8 hours. I played this elsewhere but now have a Steam copy too.*This is going to be less of a review and more just me rambling about my feels and specific things I loved. If you’ve already played and loved the first game, all you need to know is that this is just as great, with more of the same gameplay and humor and friendship, and you should play it! If you’re still not convinced, you should know that you also get to see McQueen’s butt (which, let’s be honest, you’re probably a little disappointed that it’s not Dooley’s, but McQueen’s no slouch). 😉 And if you didn’t play the first game yet, you can read my review for that one.There is one potential technical problem, which is my only negative. There seems to be an issue with save data getting deleted. It happened to me multiple times, and I found some other people mention it online too. If it does happen to you, the best workaround I could figure out was to play each case in one sitting and check the Spooky Doorway website FAQ to learn how to unlock all the cases. That way, you can at least move on to the next case even if your previous cases don’t stay marked as “solved.”Now, moving on to my thoughts about the game and story. Warning, there are some spoilers ahead that might ruin some jokes or emotional impact if you haven’t played this sequel yet.There are even some extra jokes if you check out the game settings/options.The launcher I used says I played for 9 hours, though probably half an hour to an hour was spent replaying and trying to fix the save issues.Anyway, another fun game!(May not include everything)– Not accessible for blind / visually impaired players or screen reader users.

_childDocuments_.review: A Fumble In The Dark is a perfectly cromulent adventure game, once you turn off the ghastly music.I bought this a while back after not hating the original game. Kept trying to play it, could never make it through more than an episode at a time because the music is literally painful to my ears. Normally I stick with a game's original soundtrack to try respect what the developers intended, but in this case the music just pushes my every button. It's that kind of deliberately dissonant "spooky" style that sounds like someone randomly mashing on a cheap Portasound whose pitch bender got stuck. It's the worst. So I turned it off, cued up something good instead, and suddenly the game got much better.And yet it remains an unremarkable 7/10, same as the first game. The dialog is mildly amusing. The puzzles are absurd, but most of them are signposted well enough. The graphics are what they are, decent enough pixel art. The characters are fine. They're forgettable. And that's the biggest problem with the Darkside Detective series. I don't care about anyone in it. Don't care about their city. Not particularly interested in anything that happens. It's all very wholesome and pleasant, but it never feels like there's any stakes, there's no real conflict, it never feels like anything you do matters. Each episode just comes across as arbitrary set dressing around a handful of puns and puzzles instead of an actual story. If you want some inoffensive point and clicking where you don't need to think or care too much, it's fine, I suppose. Just turn the damn music off.

_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal adventure game with genuinely funny writing. Could not wait to get this and play it when I saw they released a follow-up to the first game (also out of this world) and I was not disappointed. Builds off the great small area adventure gaming that you had in the first and gives you more to explore and transition between.  Cannot stress it enough though, everything is just quality here; art, music, presentation, puzzles, and most importantly, the writing. Go get this and bleat for us all!
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty good sequel. I loved the original, and while this game is longer and more complex it also has less heart, somehow. The biggest drawback is the inability to skip over repeated dialogue. The humor gets really labored really fast when you have to click through multiple dialogue screens over and over again just to see if anyone has anything new to say (which does happen). Still recommended if you enjoyed the first installment, and/or old school games in general.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: A great game with a whimsical setting, excellent comedy writing, and decent puzzles. It also solves one of the main problems of the point-and-click genre: moving characters from one point to another. This is usually boring and a waste of time. But here, thanks to the minimalistic and creative screen design, you can fully focus on the story and puzzles without unnecessary movement.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: This is a humorous throw-back to old-school adventure games. You are a detective for a dubious 'Darkside Division'. You are tasked with investigating supernatural crimes with your oblivious partner. The game is delivered in 20-30 minutes episodes, each connected through running gags and characters to the previous. The puzzles are fairly simple, though you may need a walkthrough on occasion. By far, the best part of the game is the humor -- this is not a serious detective game. More like a buddy comedy with puzzles!This series has rekindled my love of old-school adventure games and I can only recommend you buy this along with the first. You won't regret it
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the first game, you'll probably enjoy this because it's more of the funny point and click antics from the first game.If you haven't played the first game you should probably play that first? but also I highly recommend that game to point and click enthusiasts and also enthusiasts of fun.Waited to finish the game to post my review but I don't really know why because it's not like there was any point during my playthrough where I expected this would be anything but positive.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: The unique, hand-crafted pixel art style makes this game special. The jokes are very well written and have been perfectly integrated into the story. Not a single joke feels forced, it's all naturally good humour.If you like point & click adventures in general, this one should be the next on your list (after you played the first game, of course).If you're still sceptical, try out the free demo version and see for yourself. It will give you a great first impression of the whole experience in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: The sequel is just like the first game.You get 9 full cases to solve: 6 main and 3 bonus.The writing and humor are still the only selling points of the game.The low resolution pixel art is truly getting on my nerves by now.The dozen of point&click MOON logic puzzles is just not logical or fun:combine a bottle with a toilet and you get an AK47... who would have guessed.(using guides is a requirement in such moon logic games)Combining all this and the game gets pretty tiring, I fell asleep multiple times and even using guides each case was a slog.Fumble in the Dark is a decent game but not fantastic.Great if you liked the first game, but not the best in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Very decent sequel. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely wonderful follow-up of the original! As some other reviews have mentioned, definitely play the prequel first! This game  offers the same energy and auras in a twist (attempting to avoid spoilers because the game is quite story-rich).You are solving puzzles and mysteries in point and click fashion with some differing difficulties in each level. _childDocuments_.review: I'm mixed on this one, but I'm glad I bought it and glad it got me to re-play the original.On the one hand- I absolutely had to go back and play the original again for a solid number of the jokes to land or the plot to make sense. And on top of that, I actually do just feel like the sequel is more guilty of impossible Point-and-Click Puzzle Moon Logic than the original, and that was already the first game's biggest failing.And yet, as I play this game, I keep seeing characters show up again and getting a big stupid smile on my face because I adore them, and I just know that they'll be there for great jokes.This game is still a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ riot, even if I have to spend time looking at guides to get through the cases, finding out that my pixel-hunting skills were off-base, or I didn't remember some weird turn of logic I was supposed to use. Those annoyances are worth it for the jokes. This is a game where you usually have a sidekick or 3 following you from screen to screen, and it's absolutely worth your time to check what they have to say at every step. A more cleanly-designed game might use those points to give you hints to the more challenging puzzles, and I do kinda wish they did, but I also don't want to miss out on all the beautifully stupid dialogue that's gone into this game.I strongly recommend going to the first game and playing its demo first, which is just its first (and best) case. If that seems like your jam, the first game is a riot, and this one follows suit on delivering more Darkside Detective Nonsense, and I means that Oh-so-very affectionately.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I'm a big fan of the point and click genre as well as the first game. I was very excited to play this title when it released, and I'm already loving it. From the humor, the soundtrack, and just the overall presentation, it's an absolute treat. It picks up at the end of Season 1, but has a recap at the beginning so playing the first one is not necessary (but like, seriously. You should do it anyway.)  Highly recommended title to anyone who might be curious. The puzzles are brain teasers, but not impossibly challenging, the NPC's are a delight to talk to, and the humor and writing are top shelf.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark does not disappoint, it builds off what Darkside Detective 1 was, and continues to be a hilarious game with several puns, meta-jokes, fourth wall breaks, interdimensional portals, bears, embarassing memories, a cladly clothed Dooley, and much, much more. _childDocuments_.review: A really fun point-and-click puzzle game with some excellent writing. The game's off-beat sense of humor also got quite a few genuine laughs out of me. A strong recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderfully funny adventure game, with entertaining puzzles, charming characters and full of (often quite obscure) in-jokes and references to the adventure game genre and horror/sci fi media. A perfect break for a fan of the Darkside who needs a light break from the heavy stuff and are ready to laugh at beloved tropes and conventions. The game does not solely rely on meta-humor and sci-fi references - don't worry this isn't Rick and Morty - and you can have quite an average IQ to figure out the puzzles, as long as you embrace Adventure Game logic. It does at points reach levels close to "fake-moustache-made-of-cat-hair-and-glued-on-with-honey" (*cough cough* bubblegum *cough cough*) but it's played with a wink and if you ask around enough you should be able to gather enough hints to decipher the moon logic without reaching for a guide. And you don't mind clicking around and trying a bunch of different combinations in this game, because the writing and flavor texts are delightful. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Apart from the same winning dry humor of the original(s), Fumble in the Dark now has 200% more fourth-wall-breaking, and a degree more charm that I don't quite remember being there before: There's still plenty of back-and-forth banter between the duo, but now a sort of budding caramedrie that we get to see as McQueen trusts Dooley with his life at several points, and lets him put the finishing touches on several cases , and Dooley for his part is more generally helpful and friendly, but retains his classic dunderheadedness that gets them into all sorts of misadventures, but naturally in part also due to McQueen's own nerdy, relatable antics.For those new to the series, Darkside Detective is just as advertised, a witty puzzle adventure with not-so-straightforward, ofttimes unearthly solutions to mundane problems, but everything coming together in the end for a satisfying playsession each episode. Certainly worth the price for the playtime you get out of each individual episode (currently there are 8, with a 9th seemingly in the works), plus replayablity in finding all the secrets in each, and who can say no to a weird, winding story with returning references & characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Good sequel. Playing the first two cases took me four hours - that's with talking to everyone and exhausting every dialog option, examining every hotspot and extra backtracking to make sure I didn't miss anything. Your mileage may vary.Still pixel art, somewhat streamlined adventure game but this time you're given more freedom to roam around, backtrack, and wonder what you're supposed to do with a given item.Minor quibble, I did find a minigame involving a map to be unintuitive: you're supposed to examine all locations for certain clues like a phone, but you can't examine a location unless you "cross out" all others first. In a process of elimination, you'd expect the exact reverse.Controller support is good, I was able to alternate seemlessly between the mouse and an Xbox controller, which is always appreciated.I found the writing a bit better, with more jokes landing for me - although I found the fourth-wall-breaking ones to be very hit or miss. However, compared to other titles like Gibbous: A Cthulu Adventure or The Book of Unwritten Tales, there are considerably less custom lines when you try an item on something you're not supposed to. Given the aforementioned games are voiced and this one is not, it's a pity the devs didn't double down on this aspect. It would've given the game a lot more charm.The main characters are parodies but are still likeable, the music is good and the pixel art well done, and you still run into incredibly wacky situations. Verdict: play it.

_childDocuments_.review: This was such a disappointing sequel. If you liked the concept and the demo, play the first game. This sequel only has hints of the old humor and it drags on and on in many ways. They're in stark contrast from each other. Also, I wouldn't be playing a detective/cop game if I wanted to see everyone dog pile on the protagonist for their career. Where's the humor in that? Why would you make a detective game if you hate cops so much? Of course that's not the only thing that's propagandized. So if you don't like smug, condescending as*hats that posture they're the voice, judge, and savior of the people they harm, then I'd say to avoid this game. _childDocuments_.review: The Darkside games follow a pretty straightforward path. Weird mystery, goofy jokes, point and click puzzles. Its not aiming to be more than a short fun time and it excels at what it does. Still, the first game struck me as a bit mean-spirited and cynical in its utter disinterest in (even outright distaste for) a wider narrative.That sensibility is still present here, but its more polished and refined. The already tenuous 4th wall completely drops in Fumble in the Dark. Characters bemoan that they don't love the archetype/obstacle they have to be this episode, but push through for the sake of the puzzles. The puzzle designer shows up to get angry at the idea that McQueen would want to skip the puzzle she worked so hard on. So on and so forth. It feels more like actors going through the motions than a goofy world. You'd think it'd get tiring, but it ends up swerving back around to endearing somehow.I think what really makes this work is the shift in McQueen and Dooley's dynamic. They were a classic serious downtrodden protag/goofy sidekick team, with McQueen often the brunt of being treated as a fool and a loser by his "friend" Dooley. Because the 4th wall is almost nonexistent, McQueen and Dooley develop this new dynamic where they both know their roles and thrive in it. The dumb jokes are more for the other's benefit than the audience's. When their usual back-and-forth starts back up, there's more affection to it. Its the Sam and Max dynamic rather than a sadsack hero and his dumb friend. The rare moment the game tries to be sincere, its always focused on McQueen and Dooley's friendship rather than some big threat. It adds a much needed dose of heart to a game series that I enjoyed but found a little hollow. Its just a sweet game about solving puzzles with two goofballs pointing to something weird and going "that's stupid. Let's go make fun of it together."

_childDocuments_.review: I completed all the cases in the 1st game which I found decently entertaining overall (despite some real flaws).On this second game, I uninstalled after 15 min as soon as I realized tedious puzzles will be par for the course in this one (and no, I won't grab a guide this early into the game).I've played just long enough to draw the conclusion that this 2nd game shares the same flaws as its predecessor (but doesn't have the excuse of novelty from the 1st game), including:- Too much blablablah, sometimes funny but often tedious- Inappropriate music for the atmosphere conveyed by the game- Extremely minimal staging which is a serious flaw for a P&C game- Items becoming "pickable" at some arbitrary future point in the gameThis game presents no tangible improvement over the 1st game. _childDocuments_.review: Can't say I am amazed.Yes it's funny sometimes, but also a lot of the riddles seem really stupid as in "I know what you want me to do, and I should be able to do it, but I am also obviously missing a totally arbitrary in-between step that serves no purpose except to get you stuck".Which is something I personally despise in P&Cs. It is a bit longer than the first installment, but overall the quality of the episodes is really all over the place. Some are excellent and fun, others are just stupid and boring.Overall I'd give this game a neutral rating, but steam forces me to give a binary +1/-1 rating, and overall, for the full price, I'd recommend against it. But I'd say, if you really like P&Cs and feel a bit parched, get this on sale. It's "good enough", if you will.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10This game has the good aspects from the original (simple interface, nice pixel art).Unfortunately it has a lot more of the bad aspects too (horrible jokes, many illogical puzzles, absolutely moronic characters).Dooley is totally useless as a partner. Unlike other games where partners provide useful hints or information, Dooley is purely there for comedic relief - making annoying dad jokes and puns. Blind playthrough of the whole game took me about 10 hours, and I cringed at some of the ridiculous puzzles. For example, at one point you need a crank/handle and the solution is to take it out of a painting. And near the end of the game, you have to increase the volume of a speaker by drawing a number higher than its maximum output. WTF."A Fumble in the Dark" is aptly named because a lot of times I felt I was really fumbling around cluelessly, just mindlessly trying inventory objects on everything.

Almost every character is another variety of Peter. In fact, the entire world is Peter. Your character is special though because you're the Meg in this world. That's the other half of the jokes btw.As for myself... I don't really like characters like Peter and I especially hate being forced to be Meg. They made the right choice to not give you any option in the game, because I know if I was given an option to kill certain characters or to destroy the entire world I'd do it with no hesitation. And then there would be no other games... because I would had made that choice with the first one already soooo... Yeah, good on them.I recomment it if you buy both games on sale, don't want a serious game, enjoy jokes that go "Haha so weird/dumb" and just wanna play a chill but distracting enough game that has some Halloween vibe to it as you wait for the Halloween sale to finally arrive.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful point'n'click quest, a strong representative of it's genre. While the puzzle parts may seem a bit weak and easy for someone who's into more "brain-breaking" kind of stuff, I find them perfectly fine for an easygoing pace of this game. _childDocuments_.review: The first one was really charming and I loved it.  This one I can't recommend.  It boring and uninspired.    First of all, it doesn't have the charm of the first one.  Instead of delightful and creative music, I'm two hours in and its looping the same ugly track.  The story is bland, the puzzles don't make sense like they used to, and I find myself bored which never happened with the first.  The dialogue has grown exponentially in all the wrong ways, and the jokes just aren't cheesy funny anymore, they are just... bland.And second, I've clicked on about 8 things and it references the evils of capitalism.  It's not just one character doing this, either.... which makes it all more apparent its some soap box point the creator wants to rub in your face.  You know what, a healthy middle class and some upper class are the only thing that keep roads paved and schools and welfare funded.  Healthy competition allows for the tax base that allows for these things.  Why am I playing a pixel game and getting lectured that "capitalism is the only legal form of theft?"  Socialism is theft.  Socialism takes money from people and gives it away to those who don't, or won't, contribute.  Communist governments have seen their people starve time and time again.  Communism = We must achieve equity in making everyone dirt poor because there is only so much to go around.  (while the elites still live like elites)       Capitalism = We can make, create and produce more guys, and everyone can work their way up.  Even our poorest don't starve. I wish I had returned it but I am past the mark to do so.  I want to get Dooley back, but I don't know if I can even stand it.  Its so boring and insulting on top of it.  What a game about spooks and supernatural stuff that trashes the west and bashes God over and over... Man I hate this game.  I'm done with this company.  Nothing like the first.  I do NOT recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: After having played and hated the first game, my expectations were low for this game. While I can say that this was better than the first, I can't say that it is good. Story-wise, I liked that it actually had some follow-up from the first game and subsequent cases for a while, but after the first three or so, it went downhill. The "action scenes" felt like they were supposed to instill tension but fell flat on its face.Humor-wise, it has even more unfunny references and meta-humor than the last game, which is saying a lot. That said, the few jokes that didn't fall into this category were a lot funnier than the average jokes from the original. But every time I laughed at a good joke, I cringed three times from yet another quip about how they're in a video game.And since I waited until the 9th case to write this review, I gotta say... it was a huge letdown. It was way too easy to solve to feel satisfied. Not to mention it felt rushed, between the constant reuse of characters and other assets (even if you don't count the people in the stands at the baseball game, the number of reused characters far outweigh the original ones) and the spelling and grammar mistakes found throughout, such as one character redundantly using the word "the" twice in a row.Disappoint me once, shame on you. Disappoint me twice, and I won't play whatever third game this series decides to release.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a lot of point and click adventure games. Some of them are good, some of them are bad, and this game is solidly in the latter category.The game is basically a "homage" to the sort of "weird but not necessarily horror" genre - stuff like Twin Peaks. It doesn't do it in a good way though, more of a "Hey, remember Twin Peaks? Huh? Huh?" kind of way. Not to mention that genre's already oversaturated with better games - Thimbleweed Park for one. I played the first of the game's seven cases, and it was just.. bad. It's difficult not from a "this puzzle is actually difficult" perspective, but from one of bad signposting and overall bad game design. There's a puzzle early on where you have to find three things and know where two of them are. You find a mysterious piece of paper with an address on it. It's not hard to figure out the paper has the location of the third thing... only to get the third address as a location, you have to use the paper on a completely unrelated item. I had to look up a guide specifically to figure this out, because I had no idea what the hell the game wanted me to do with it.I grabbed the other two items with relatively little difficulty, and then went to the final puzzle - which involves moving pegs with wires on them to form patterns. This puzzle was where I dropped the game: again, not because it was difficult, but because it was just poorly designed. You see, you can't simply pull the wires out and re-insert them. You have to move them over each other - which is not at all hard to do, just extremely tedious. At that point I felt like I'd had enough and refunded the game.The writing also isn't great. It's trying to be funny, but just.. isn't. At all. I'd say avoid this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: "The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark" is a text adventure game similar to old LucasArts adventure games like The Secret of Monkey Island and Day of the Tentacle but with a kinda lame supernatural detective shtick instead of any kind of interesting topic, leaving us with decades old game-play, pixel-crap "graphics" and an unjustifiably high price tag for the kind of game you can slap together in hours using the Adventure Game Construction Kit (but this is made in Unity, so I guess as well as not knowing how to do computer graphics properly, they also eschew doing things the easy way, having put in a lot of effort to achieve the same thing a construction kit can do). From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  Because this is designed for consoles, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game."The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark" has the far too high price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  For comparison, the $15 asking price for this game could get you games like "Europa Universalis IV", "Grand Theft Auto V" or "Dead by Daylight".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.  There's also thousands of free, superior quality games on Steam.
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Edit to add: The developers of this game, Spooky Doorway, are the best.  They just added the first of three planned free bonus cases on Christmas Eve.  I played it as soon as it was available, and it was great fun.  They did the same thing with the first Darkside Detective, adding completely free a series of bonus cases well after initial release.A lot of (sometimes minor) characters from season 1 of The Darkside Detective make return appearances in this second season -- it's cool they keep building out the world like that -- and to refresh my memory I started going back and replaying episodes from the first game while going through this one.  And I enjoyed them so much again that I ended up replaying all of them in random order.  That ended up making me feel as I finished this game up (except the, at this point, unreleased bonus episode) that the second season wasn't quite as good as the first.  But that's a very high bar to try to reach, since I loved the first season.  Main comparative downside for me was that it seemed like they aimed to build out longer episodes with more challenging puzzles, which was a good direction to take a lot of the time, but it was a bit marred by what seemed to me to be some excessively convoluted, directionless puzzles and moon-logicky item combinations that you needed to make and some cases of excessive backtracking through the larger environments trying to find something to interact with.  I don't want to sound down on Fumble in the Dark at all, though.  I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys humorous point and click adventure games.  It's again got top notch writing throughout.  The wrestling case in particular was my favorite from either season.  It's so stupid, but I still crack up every time I remember your antagonist in that episode being called 'The Overgiver.'  That's one minor example of The Darkside Detective games being rare gems in being comedic point and click adventure games that are actually really funny instead of just annoying and even rarer in being games that incorporate parodies of other pop culture that is actually creative instead of just being the usual 'hey remember that thing, this is a reference to that thing you remember, how about that!'  Within the confines of the super crude pixel style, it also looks really good.  Pixel art is often (most of the time probably, actually) just used as an excuse for lazy, crap art and graphics, but Darkside Detective (another example would be the two Last Door games) shows that when developers actually care about what they're doing and put in the effort it doesn't have to be that way at all.  Music and sound is also again excellent, and I suspect that not having voice acting is the right choice.  Bad voice acting is much worse than no voice acting, and indie P&C voice acting is usually bad.[empty edit for Steam awards badge]
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: After enjoying the original Darkside Detective point & click adventure game so much, I was looking forward to this sequel. And it has the same pixel art (crude but nonetheless very expressive), the same funny dialogue interplay between the characters, the same episodic format, and the same mix of achievements for game progression and for odd, easily missed interactions.But... for me, this game was good but somehow not as special and enjoyable as the first game; I've been trying to work out why. Perhaps I played A Fumble in the Dark too soon after the original - certainly I laughed out loud much less in this game. In both games I needed some help from the various excellent guides for the easily missed side achievements, but whereas I worked out nearly all of the puzzle and plot solutions myself in the original game, in this one I found myself stuck much more often; the solutions, when I found (or read) them, often seemed more contrived or "stretched out". This is reflected in my play time - each game had six core cases and three bonus ones, but the first game took me almost exactly half of the time of the second.And that, I think, answers my question about why I preferred the first game - it was more tight and lean, with every action in the game understandable, purposeful and oddly logical (even if weird!), and no sense of "padding". I ended the first one happy and satiated, and hoping for more of the same another time; I ended this game with a slight sense of "job done" and relief.So, in summary, this is a good game, but the first one is extra-special and that is the one I would recommend to anyone trying these kind of point & click games for the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: It plays a lot like a mobile game, in that you only need the left mouse button but it's a fun little adventure.The game, like its predecessor, is made up of a bunch of mini adventures or episodes.This means you'll never get stuck for long since every episode only has about a dozen screens.The graphics are great for what they are.There isn't a ton of music, but what there is is good enough that it never gets annoying.And the same goes for the sound effects, the game(s) are a good example of doing a lot with little.The gameplay is fairly standard adventure stuff, grab objects and combine them to solve problems.There are also some fun minigame puzzles, but very few of them.The story/stories are fun and funny and really the whole game has a bunch of jokes in it.Would I recommend it?If you like point and click adventures and don't mind the simplicity of the mobile origins, definitely.The characters, dialogue and story are a lot of fun and it's not too bad with the adventure game logic.Most puzzles have a logical solution and there is often a hint in what the characters are saying.

_childDocuments_.review: Return to the spooky world of Twin Lakes, a city so full of paranormal tomfoolery that it once had its own Spooky Division Police Force. Once again, follow Detective McQueen and his faithful (unofficial sidekick) along their quirky encounters with supernatural forces, from Darkside rescues to Sun restorations to  even escaping the clutches of a crazed clown gameshow. Along the way, encounter the vibrant cast of characters and phenomenon that makes the world of Darkside Detective a whimsical place.Like its predecessor, DD:FD is a point-and-click game spaced out into nine cases. Each case is largely self-contained, with occasional callbacks to previous ones. Most of the charm from the first carries over into the next, with some witty quips and zany antics here and there. I liked the passive worldbuilding and the nonchalant statements of nebulous logic. I especially liked how the last bonus case let us play the game as members of the supporting cast, getting their perspective on the crazy paranormal phenomena plaguing Twin Lakes.However, while I enjoyed the first game, I feel like this one was a step back:- There were multiple times where I was having difficulty following the game's logic, whether it involved where to go next or which items to use to get the next one. I was fine for most of the game, making the few places where I stumbled exceedingly annoying. - The game had an annoying habit of making progress lock out backtracking, making me antsy about missing some flavor dialog or achievements.- They could have toned down the meta commentary humor. Sometimes it felt like they couldn't go more than five sentences without "oh this is so wacky, thank goodness this works somehow" or "Wow, searching trash cans again, so silly". I enjoy third-wall breaking, but there needs to be some restraint.- The last case didn't really feel all that climactic. The first game had a city spanning case, with multiple locations needing to be revisited. No case in this one gave that same grand-ish feeling. That being said, it was still a fun time. I think it's worth the $15. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: I complete the first Darkside Detective so I mostly new what to expect. Despite that it took me a while to get use to the series again. Graphics are intentionally very bad. I don't mind pixel graphics but in DD they are so low resolution it can be hard to pick out what parts of the screen are items that you can interact with.It also took me a while to get used to the humour. Once I got used to the style of humour again I began to appreciate the game more.The puzzles are mostly reasonable. _childDocuments_.review: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark is not only a great point and click adventure game; it's a very good sequel to the first game, now the story. It has been a year since Patrick Dooley was taken and trapped in the darkside, his best friend Francis McQueen desperately searches for him stopping at nothing even when the darkside division have been disbanded.But that will not stop him in finding his best friend, especially when Twin Lakes needs them when in Twin Lakes Spooks are spooking, cultists will be a cultisting and ummm monsters they monstering? Well only these two are capable of stopping the tide of terror with one fumble at time.Okay the likes, the story like the first game is really good with plenty of great twists and turns and plenty of good moments from comical to cool to even badass, all wrapped up in a story that doesn't take itself too seriously. They are also plenty of great callbacks to the previous cases of the first game from the item description to certain returning characters. The story also does a very good job with its commentary taking a lot of jabs at plenty of people, it's not subtle but it is quite enjoyable. The comedy like the first game is very good, quite well written with a good use of puns, innuendos and funny descriptions, some jokes didn't land but there were a lot of other jokes that certainly had me laughing. The characters are still really good and quite interesting even side characters and NPCs both old and new are quite well written with so many people to like, from the main characters like Francis McQueen and his partner Patrick Dooley to side characters like the bloodwolves and Raxa, to new npcs like the Sea Hags. The gameplay is still pretty fun it's your standard point and click game with picking up items and combining them, but there's also plenty of good and well balanced puzzles with a nice sense of exploration. The puzzles are really good and very fair while still quite challenging, just takes a good bit of brain work. The pixel graphic art style is still really good with plenty of great details with a great use of colors, even the more dark and somber colors have a nice sort of brightness to them, it’s all very well detailed and even better than the first game and the first games graphics were really good. The levels are still quite good and very diverse with so many nice little details that make the whole world feel alive; there are also plenty of great call backs to works of horror from the classics to even a few modern ones. The music is very good with plenty of nice tracks to listen too.Okay the dislikes, like the first game I would say this is perfect but there is one or two bugs like there's this one bug in the game where sometimes for some reason in the dialogue box you can't click on any of the different dialogue choices, but that's easily fixed by pausing the game and unpause it. Then there is this one bug, although truth be told it was more from my end, basically if you have a virus protection the game won't completely install no matter how many times you verify, luckily the good team at spooky doors helped me and I made a little tutorial in discussions on how to make sure all the files get downloaded, so future players know what to do.Now that's all done The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark is not only a great point and click adventure game; it's a very good sequel to the first game, with a really good story, very good comedy and really good characters. So if you like the first game you're going to love this game I highly, highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: It falls into the sophomore adventure game slump of padding out its content with needless puzzles that add nothing to the game at large except a longer runtime, but overall this is a really silly, fun nod to good ol' pointing and clicking. Future games could do with a lot less returning characters, as it makes the otherwise cute stories a nonstop regurgitation of "oh, it's that person you met for two seconds in the previous game." In a way, that seems to be a deliberate poke at the genre, but the whole game leans on it as hard as something named Monkey Island.That said, this series is an absolute must-play if you're looking for a lighthearted breezy adventure game broken up into very manageable chunks.

_childDocuments_.review: - Visual design is, of course, the same as the first game. Lots of appealing pixel art throughout- I don't know if it's just that I was paying better attention to the music, but it feels much improved this time. There's no real theme or genre to it, but it's all pretty good. The best tracks usually drop when the tension ramps up- Like the first game, the story unfolds as a series of sorta-connected vignettes. Unlike the first game, there's a consistent thread running throughout the narrative that nicely ties everything together. It mostly pertains to what happens in the aftermath of the first game, so be sure you've played the prequel before trying this one out- This is a marked improvement from the first title. My biggest complaint was the lack of a metanarrative to hold the story together, and that's nicely addressed in this game- The humor is still pretty good. This title is maybe a little funnier than the first game, but it's a close contest- As before, the writing/dialogue is superb. I love how well fleshed-out everyone's personality is. You can tell the writers put a lot of effort into this game- It's a point and click adventure game without may innovations on the basic formula. You'll wander around, investigate clues, pick up items, combine those items in humorous and unexpected ways, and inch the story along as you figure out each puzzle- I understand that it's an entrenched genre trope at this point, but I still feel like some of the solutions are really unintuitive sometimes. I wouldn't have naturally figured out to combine decorative bunting and a garden gnome to make a grappling hook. Frustration-induced item combining is more-or-less a prerequisite for plot advancement- Probably not going to return to the game, but only because I 100%ed the achievements. The chapter select menu made this much easier- Except for the graphics (which are basically identical to the the prequel) and the writing (which is still very good), just about every change made in this title is an improvement. It's really nice to see a developer build upon and evolve a series with a simple concept, carefully ironing out the wrinkles and refining their formula- The game ran perfectly on the Steam Deck. Basically just like the first one, but with several improvements. More of a good thing is always a good thing, so buy with confidence if you liked the first title
_childDocuments_.name: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark

_childDocuments_.review: Darkside Detective 1 was an unexpected joy - it was an indie adventure that didn't try very hard to impress you with fancy graphics or deep plot. Instead, it just had two very charming characters and spun them off in several episodes to hilarious effect. But the main reason why the first one worked so well was seeing how the friendship between McQueen and Dooley grew. Which is precisely the issue with the 2nd one - their friendship doesn't really grow much anymore. In a bid to franchise this game, they decided to make it closer to a sitcom, but honestly it doesn't quite work. Aside from the lack of progress in their friendship, the jokes are laid way, way, way thicker this time - and the verbosity is honestly overkill. Less is more, and the attempts at jokes in the 2nd one became way more groan-worthy than in the 1st. The addition of some weird moon logic doesn't help. But honestly, one thing they can do is to stop the characters from repeating themselves when you click on them, especially since sometimes the text is multiple pages long (see: verbosity issue). The game still has its charm, but it is clear that less is not more. I'm gonna give this a 6/10 - more like a so-so for me, but not bad enough that I'd give it a thumbs down.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent fun! A classic-style point & click adventure with excellent writing, witty dialogue, and some enjoyable in-jokes, references, and easter eggs. The game is well made, runs as it should, the only issues being a few spelling mistakes in the text, which do nothing to spoil the fun. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: The Darkside Detective: A Fumble in the Dark is everything a sequel should be: bigger, longer, and more ambitious, but still absolutely hilarious.Mechanically, this game is as voluntarily primitive as the first game. Even for a point and click adventure game, it's very no-frills - the character are static in every scene, there are no walk cycle, no voice acting and very few special effects. However, like the first game, that doesn't matter, because it is all about the humour. I was so happy to delve back into this world where everybody is completely loony and weird, but nobody sees it as anything out of the ordinary. It's another absolute riot.Like the first game, A Fumble in the Dark is divided in a number of different, independent cases, like an episodic tv show. However, unlike the first game, these cases are much longer - each one took me at least an hour. This has pros and con. The pros is that the cases are richer, more complex, and more diverse. The cons is that it remove the "bite-sized, play on your break" aspect of the original. It's not a dealbreaker for me, but it could be for you. So yeah, if you want more of one of the funniest point-and-click game ever made, buy this!
