_childDocuments_.review: I'm not even half-way through the game, yet, but it has been great so far and ticks a lot of boxes for me, personally.The Nightmare difficulty (the game's recommended default) is rather brutal early level and you WILL end up wiping and restarting, but that leads to increased power and steady progression through the Remembrance system which grants passive bonuses through subsequent Recollections (runs). Not being able to regenerate health through normal means adds a good level of difficulty and decision making, as the tough choice to sacrifice valuable Daughters in order to overcome the next difficult fight and progress further makes each success rewarding. Sacrifices also provide excellent power boosts to the recipient Daughters and you can always bring back your favorite ones later.That said, the grind to progress may not be for everyone. I'd still recommend trying the game on Nightmare first and then, if you still find it too difficult or frustrating, try the Dream difficulty which adds passive healing (50% recovery) for Daughters each new day and a free Resurrection Token at the start.The combat mechanics are fairly intricate and can take some getting used to in order to get the most out of your skills and the dynamic timeline, but it feels really good when you manage to set up and pull off devastating combos that turn the tide. The boss battles can be absolutely brutal and a single mistake or miscalculation can lead to defeat. Bosses can feel overpowered or downright unfair at first, but once your own power grows and you learn their mechanics and what to watch out for they aren't too bad.There are only 5 Eras, but with the difficulty and rogue-lite death loop there is enough content to fill quite a few hours. As far as the Synapses go, there are a couple really difficult ones that can be costly and tedious to undertake if you aren't properly prepared. I'm looking at you Rescue mission... Others, such as Hunts are typically simple and straight-forward. My only real gripe is that there are a fairly limited number of Synapse maps which can get a little stale after a while. It would be nice if there was a greater variety of maps as well as more initial random spawn locations on each. It would also be nice if we could choose the formation of our Daughters when spawning into a map, to allow for more tactical positioning at the start. It seems like every boss fight my Shieldbearer starts way in the back, so I have to spend a turn or two simply moving them into range, which can be a bit more painful with certain Traits like Ethereal Flame which lowers movement range.The art style and aesthetic is perfect for the bleakness of the world and the character designs are amazing and quite polished. While there may not be a huge number of enemy types, I feel that the number isn't lacking. There seems to be a good mix of different types (melee, ranged, elites, etc) with their own skill sets and mechanics that add a good amount of complexity to battles. I've seen many reviews stating that the story is lacking, but it is actually unlocked through progression. This makes a lot of sense when you think about how the game is based around unlocking memories through recollections and remembering events. The lore is unlocked in bits and pieces, like a puzzle that takes time to unravel. The story that I have unlocked so far is actually quite intriguing.The soundtrack is absolutely amazing. When I first started the game, I found myself sitting in the menu just listening to the music for a while and checking the credits to listen to that song for a while longer. The music for the first boss was excellent and the transition into phase 3 of the fight fit so perfectly. Truly well thought out and executed.All in all, I am really enjoying this game and I wish I would have found it sooner than I did. A very solid 9 out of 10 for me and highly recommended to anyone who likes dark fantasy, souls-like difficulty, rogue-lite progression and tactical turn-based RPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: An XCOM-like isometric tactical game set in a dark, gothic, post-apocalyptic world with an interesting visual style. Nightmarish creatures are roaming about and only the Daughters, clones of a great female warrior, can lay those creatures to rest. Aside from the usual XCOM-like features, such as isometric grid movement, action points determining what we can do in a turn, and squad-type missions, Othercide offers some of its own unique features too that spice up the gameplay.The overwatch feature is taken to the next level with a variety of skills acting as interruptions or reactions. Interruptions allow a daughter to counter an enemy attack on an ally in range, while a reaction can cause a daughter to have an additional action, depending on what triggers the reaction (e.g. an enemy coming within melee range getting automatically hit, etc). Daughters come in 3 classes in the beginning (+ a 4th class that becomes available partway through the game), each one with their own strengths and weaknesses. New skills can be unlocked at specific level ups, and at each such instance, we can choose one of two skills to go for, so there's some variety in builds even within the same class.The combat operates on a timeline system, where turns are dynamic. Enemies can be pushed back along the timeline so their turn comes later, and likewise allies can be boosted forward on the timeline to take their turns sooner. Some effects from abilities can also last for a specific duration amount or trigger at certain points on the timeline.Lastly, the game has a recollections system. If we fail at any point during a campaign, we can start over from the beginning with unlocked bonuses, tackling the same challenges with more advantages on our side. Some of these bonuses do allow us to skip past certain eras if we don't wish to replay them, so it's a nice mechanic. Can feel a bit grindy, but adds an interesting twist on the campaign progression.Generally, the game is challenging and we're almost always outnumbered, but there are many ways in which we can tackle these challenges. It's a very rewarding experience. Boss fights are also well-designed and fun. The only part of the game I disliked is the final boss, as it felt like a cheap difficulty spike, intended to force you to grind more.The story is mainly secondary to the gameplay and provides a nice backdrop for the conflict. The grey and red visuals also do great at enhancing the overall experience. There are some really amazing music tracks in places too, such as during the boss fights. But there are also some annoyingly jarring tracks playing during regular missions combat encounters. A great, challenging, tactical turn-based game that shows quality all around with only a few drawbacks. For a more in-depth review and a gameplay video, check here:

_childDocuments_.review: The enemy AI is terribly inconsistent, both with regards to rules previously implied or established, and with prioritization. In SRPGs, being able to predict enemy movement, or at least movement possibilities is fundamental to how you place your units. Beyond the movement, enemy bosses seem to have moves that ignore the rules of combat. Having a gunner on standby waiting for "The first attack an enemy makes" only to have them not fire when the boss uses an attack, seems to devalue the class even further than it already is. The game isn't all bad. The mechanic surrounding preserving HP over time is interesting, especially as it plays into some of the more powerful abilities costing HP. The aesthetic is a bit edgy, but it's consistent throughout and has a unique draw. Overall the game would be a fine time sink if it weren't for the aforementioned issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Too frustrating for me, but I'd say give it a shot if it looks good to you.This is not a bad game. The artstyle is nice, you have to be smart about the way you approach everything and the game as a whole feels well thought out.But - you have to be some sort of masochist to play this game, which I am not. And this is coming from someone who played Dark Souls way into NG++. Damage received in battles is permanent and if you want to heal a character, you have to sacrifice one of the same or a higher level. If a character is dead, she is taken to the cemetery where you could theoretically revive her, but the necessary resource can only rarely be obtained. Restarting the game is part of the game cycle and gives you a certain resource you can spend on bonuses, but it also makes all of your characters die. Interesting concepts for sure, but also extremely frustrating, pressuring you into "voluntary setbacks". This game makes me feel like a little more successful Sisyphos. You create characters and level them up only for them to die by the enemies' hand or by yours in order to heal another character. Then you create new characters to fill the gap and everything starts anew...I don't intend to put 50 hours into figuring everything out and leveling a few characters to the max when I could learn everything so much faster if the game was a bit more forgiving.

_childDocuments_.review: Why not? Cause few features that are key in the game are hidden during times where they are most useful.You can upgrade your active skills with modifiers that drastically change the gameplay.aaaaand there is no way of viewing them during combatThe fact that due to (otherwise cool) stylistic choices all daughters look very similar and if left to random generations their names start repeating themselves pretty quickly is unfortunate. Same goes for special traits that are important stat modifiersCan you view those stats and write them down on a piece of paper before a mission? yup. But no one will. Nor should have to.It's like having a game about parkour with a wallrun you use all the time  but to use it you need to press 1+alt+leftarrow+del at the same time. They promised to fix it. Time will tell.Then there's the repetitiveness. I know its the nature of such a game in some regards, but the voicelines, classes and maps are seriously samey or straight up "the same". You've got only 4 classes. The enemies have a decent variety, but - again - having a style that brings it all down they could have flexed those creative muscles just a bit more to come up with more content.And again - style and visuals - when you apply those mods to your skills (just one per skill) it shows as a red gem put into a socket. Now get this: all "gems" look the same, regardless of what skill they are used on or what modifications they represent.And same goes for icons of active skills you use. They are bland (arrow, clock etc) and represent the TYPE of action it belongs to (instant, delayed, reaction, boost). So five funky slashes with a sword can have the same icon as AoE done with a pistol. lameness incarnate.Aside from that the order of attacks and changing intiative is key, so having (and being able to read and distinguish) those icons on the timeline is also crucial. I still haven't figured out how to tell the difference between my delayed action from enemies delayed action.How can you go so wrong where there's so much potential and already so much there?  This is quite close to "recommend" but sorry, no cigar.--------------------The devs get major point for responding to comments and even answering to this negative review.So I'd like to quickly point out that I wouldn't bother with reviewing if there wasn't a lot of good stuff about Othercide. Intersitng combat mechanics and refined, bold visual style being the monst noticable ones. I also like how a lot of lore is suggested (not unlike in Darkest Dungeon) which allows for everyone to create their own associations with what's given. That makes the whole world seem a lot bigger and fleshed out without overburdening the player with bs facts to memorize. That and the mentioned style are signs of an experienced storyteller and craftsman. I like how you can tell that there was a particular vision behind Othercide. And creators set out to achieve that vision. Just that is refreshing in 2021 when 99% games are just bland spineless rehashes of s**t that's been done 54123 times already. I just wished that nothing stood in the way of enjoying that vision.I believe in you Lightbulb Crew:D All the best!

_childDocuments_.review: Othercide is a grim, stylish, turn-based strategy game (a la XCOM, but smaller) with roguelite elements seamlessly baked in - I specify that it's seamless because the roguelite portion, which forces you to sort of lose in a forward direction and gain bonuses from your failures, fits so well tonally with the presented story.The story itself is simple but satisfying, and a bit esoteric, as it is primarily told through codex entries, limited dialogue, and to a lesser extent, the environment itself. It never feels forced on the player, but it (like the rest of the game) wins on the style front.As for the combat gameplay, it primarily revolves around managing the timeline, which is an action-economy initiative order shown at the bottom of the screen while in-mission. You plan your moves according to who is on the battlefield, and while the initial learning curve can be sort of brutal if you're not cautious, the play smooths out relatively quickly. For the most part, it plays how one might expect - you attack enemies by spending your action points to use various abilities, and try to avoid attacks from enemies. Enemy movesets are available to you in-match and in the codex, though at times their descriptions feel incomplete. There were a few instances during the game when I had to open the wiki to confirm something after an enemy seemed to break a rule previously stated by the game, but this was uncommon enough not to be too bothersome. Overall the gameplay was satisfying, and I enjoyed setting up combos between my units using their reactions and such. Pulling off a slick play in Othercide feels really good.That said, the game started to drag a bit for me at the end as repetition took its toll. Luckily it didn't overstay its welcome, as a full clear (campaign completion (on the intended "nightmare" difficulty) + 100% achievements) for me took between 30 and 40 hours - hard to give an exact amount because I left it open a few times when running to a store or making food. Oops. I'll also say that perception of Othercide's difficulty seems to vary person-to-person as the other reviews I've read speak about the challenge in inconsistent ways, but I found the difficulty to be comfortable. It was tough at times, but never insurmountably so.Current full price is $30, and I don't know if I'd have bought it for that (I picked it up on sale), but I would've felt comfortable spending $20 on this game. I really enjoyed it, I'm just picky about my cost-to-playtime ratio.My overall takeaway is this: Othercide is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool. If you like turn-based strategy and the visuals doesn't seem too fatiguing for you, I'd definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is coming from the perspective of someone who has never played a game with a turn-based combat system. I definitely made a gamble when I bought this game, not knowing if I'd enjoy it. Even as someone who enjoys games like Dark Souls and Elden Ring, I was still thrown off at first by the difficulty this game provides. However, I consider it a good thing.I find it incredibly satisfying to learn how to use the daughters in tandem with one another to effectively navigate through combat situations that I found rather daunting when I first started. You can learn how to play the game through trial and error without reliance on outside sources such as tutorials. It is fair difficulty: when you fail, you know it's your own fault, and you learn for the next run or encounter.The art direction is fantastic, the music is consistently on point, and both the voice actors and writers did an impressive job on this game.Overall, even in my first few hours of getting my ass handed to me, I am enjoying this game and would recommend it to anyone looking for a challenging turn based/roguelite game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels actively unpleasant to play. - VOs consist of a sobbing woman repeating the same lines over and over again. Atmospheric? Maybe. Except that you hear the exact same line every single time an enemy type spawns. The first act alone consists of maybe 60-odd enemy spawns, 40-odd of which are chosen from TWO enemy types. - It's really buggy. For instance, I have a Blademaster that can't be viewed, and freezes the game if I use her.- It models itself as a roguelike, but lacks any of the random elements of a roguelike. Skills, 'equipment', and traits all drop based on prereqs.- The only way to heal a character is by sacrificing another equal-leveled character. That's kinda cool, except it forces you to play painfully conservatively. Also makes survival missions ridiculously brutal, when a full mission of enemies spawn right on top of the escape zone.- The above also means that you basically have to abandon your run the moment you kill a boss. Which matches the 'all hope is lost' theme, but it also means you don't feel the sense of risk that should come with permadeath.- It lacks QOL features such as viewing enemy-threatened areas.- Complete lack of customization options. This means all your Daughters are basically just templates.- Lack of meaningful choices. The only real choice you ever make is on the skill tree. There are no options to specialise a character into something, or to remove a trait.

_childDocuments_.review: Stylistic and a lot of fun with plenty of challenge. The aesthetic is pretty good, the gameplay right up there with some of my favorites like Xcom. Definitely a difficult game, but the way they've built it, you are expected to face tough fights and eventually lose a few times, getting stronger through that as well. Has a couple bugs that I hope will eventually be patched, such as the all important initiative bar having issues where the graphics will not line up properly, and has a fourth class of characters that can be entirely missed if you kill a certain boss to quickly (The Maid. I recommend playing it out slowly, since I cleared the game before even realizing there was another class at all). I plan to follow the production company to see what else they might be capable of making. Overall, a really fun game worth the money if you like difficult tactical games (Xcom, Fire Emblem, etc) but, as with most small studios, there's a few bugs to work through.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not usually a fan of turn-based games or strategy playstyles, but after beating the game last night I have to say that it was a super rewarding experience. For reference, I finished the game in 17 recollections (re-dos. basically when you lose, you restart the game but can revive your old units. I did this 17 times.) and 5 or 6 of them were done on purpose to raise units with specific traits that are locked in level ranges. The last 2 bosses were disappointingly easy (probably because of my grinding) and I was able to reach and beat the final boss without skipping the other bosses (fighting old bosses becomes a strategic option).The game starts off very difficult because your controlled units are low level with skills that seem too risky to use or who's main use is to deal damage, since controlling the battlefield isn't too important so early on, however the need to rely on tactics based on the strengths of each unit, risky or not, becomes rapidly obvious because of the ever ramping difficulty of the game. Othercide tells you from the very beginning that defeat is part of the game, and unless you're a genius master tactician, you will not be finishing this game in one play through let alone even 5. And this is where the satisfaction all comes into play: attempting to finish Othercide in as few attempts as possible will provide a unique challenge to players looking for one, while taking time to build up your units will yield an incredible sense of progression as you will obviously notice how much easier certain enemies and bosses become when you learn proper strategies and level your units.The story is told vaguely by mouth with short cutscenes but is really fleshed out by reading the codexes and enemy descriptions. You could say it's souls-like in this sense because you need to put some effort into reading the lore. The story is simple and concise; short enough so that reading it all the way through is in no way a chore, yet long enough to create a complete story. You could compare it to a 100-150 page light novel. Overall 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Othercide is great in theory, but the experience is just awful. The good:Stylistically, the game is pretty nicely themed with that Black, White, and Red style. The Daughters you create are really cool and it's super interesting the way they degrade and such as they battle on. The trait feature with how you randomly gain super powerful buffs depending on what happens in your battles is super cool. The music also gave me like.. heavy early 2000's campy rock tones and I loved it. Also, it's not as difficult as most people say it is. In fact, once one of the classes hits 15 they get a skill that just all-kills the entire board apart from bosses.The Bad:Firstly, You cannot heal your characters without sacrificing one of equal or higher level on the normal difficulty. This kills that character AND changes the trait token you've given to the one being healed through previous sacrifices, which means you're often looking to only sacrifice Blademasters to heal to maintain their damage fragment. Secondly, the only way to revive a dead character is with a credit coin from either A: Restarting from the beginning, or B: Doing a rescue mission. If you do a rescue mission in the final act of the game, the pistol corrupted type enemy will almost always snipe your escortee and fail the mission. This game also massively encourages only 1 style of play to be successful - Ambushing Alpha-Strikes. Since you cannot heal, you often want to keep your character out of the enemies movement bubble so that they have to come to you first, wasting their turn, then pouncing on them and hoping you're able to kill it, otherwise it will be in range and hit you with permanent damage on it's next turn.  So many turns and time is wasted waiting for monsters to tell you they're going to spawn, then spawning, then moving, then you counter. It's a massive waste of time. Also, Boss monsters talk to you during regular missions, often repeating the same voice line over and over again. At one point a boss said "No, No, Memories hurt" 6 times in a row to me with no other lines inbetween.The Ugly: Right away, I'm putting this game as not recommended solely because of the last boss. It's massively overtuned often getting to attack your characters 10-15 (TEN TO FIFTEEN) times between each of your characters attacks. It also can swap places with any of your characters, and then cause them to explode for roughly 20% of their health. He also has a skill that just kills one of your characters. No tactics, no planning, no avoiding, just "Hey, she's dead now." It's definitely a killable boss, but it feels AWFUL and after asking your players to play through the game as many times as needed to be strong enough to get to him, this fight is just terrible. I was often doing one attack and then minimising the game to do something else while the boss took his time doing 6-8 minutes worth of abilities back to back. You don't want your player to be bored in your games climax. So all in all, I would say pass on this game. You're not missing a lot. If you do think you still want to play it get it on sale. I don't think I would ever play it again.

_childDocuments_.review: A rough gem. You should play other games in the genre first (XCOM, Darkest Dungeon, Into the Breach), but Othercide has its own merits and is within a sidestep away from standing against these giants with an expansion or sequel.Pros:- Obviously the art style is incredible. Original and beautiful from concept to execution. This is one of those games that I fell in love with from the title screen.- The gothic, lovecraftian aesthetic is on par with the best. The sense of hopelessness is thick in the air- The tactical complexity is very engaging and rewards smart play. When you understand how enemies and abilities work encounters that seemed impossible can be played through without losing a single HP- The sacrifice mechanic fits very well and forces you to consider every decision carefully- Sisters look bad ass and you will grow to care for them- The audio is top notch. The soundtrack is creepy and tense, the voice acting and sound effects are great. The reaper sounds still make my skin crawlCons:- The game is designed to be played through multiple runs, but it lacks the content to be interesting after one or two. With only 4 classes (3 for half the game) and not that many base enemy archetypes. Also the duration of a single play through is very long and some of the repetitive encounters could be cut down- The UI is buggy and slow to update to input. It often displays wrong information that can be run ending in a game as punishing as this. Do not trust the UI and always double check before committing to an action!- The UI lacks important information. Skill upgrades (memories) are not visible at all in descriptions in game, even though their effect can be as important as the skill itself. Duration of effects like root is not displayed. Character codexes can't be viewed in battle, forcing you to remember that enemy 1 targets lower HP, while visually identical enemy 2 targets higher HP

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really cool tactical turn based game, feels like a hybrid between XCOM and Darkest Dungeon. The music is great, the atmosphere is awesome, and the strategy can be great. I am definitely looking forward to playing more already, but there are a couple things that the developers really need to address to make this game a 10/10.First, there NEEDS to be more level/enemy variety. I had been playing the game for only a half hour when I started a new battle and immediately recognized the same map/enemy location from a battle I had fought earlier. While taking my time in the earlier eras, with 6 hours in so far, I have had ONE mission that was not the generic hunt mission type. I have had to quit and take a break from the game multiple times just to make the fights feel fresh. Even just enabling enemy placement to be random would be a HUGE breath of fresh air. Second, and immediately following point 1, there needs to be some more ability variety for the Daughters. At the moment all of my classes have been built the exact same way in the cookie-cutter pattern I think suits each class best, and the only real variety to each Daughter is what level they are. This is ESPECIALLY bad when paired with point 1, as not only am i fighting the exact same battle again, I am usually clearing it in the exact same ability order I did the first time.Maybe make the ability you get on level up random instead, anything to add a bit more variety.Third (and this is more a Quality of Life) you are able to change the name of a Daughter when they are first "born", but as soon as you pick their class, you can never again change their name. I've had to remove multiple "dead" characters from my graveyard just because they shared the name I wanted, and sacrifice other characters because I didnt like their default name.Fourth, why do ALL of your characters die whenever you reset lol? Getting wiped by a boss, alright maybe, but just resetting to train? Having to completely trash your roster just to go back to the earlier battles to grind kind of defeats the purpose. Either that, or there needs to be a faster way to earn Resurrection tokens. Very early on, you get a perk that allows you ONE Rez token whenever you reset, which means you can essentially carry only ONE character between runs. At this point, I have been playing for over 6 hours, just taking my time and grinding slowly, and I have never gotten a second resurrection token in a run. Maybe they are easier to get in later eras, but then why would you need them when your default un-nameable characters from the start of the run and other new chars are all level 10+?Definitely hurts the "getting attached to your soldiers" concept that we all loved from XCOM, especially in the early game.Let me be clear, I definitely enjoy this game and I do recommend it to anyone who enjoys rougelites and turn based strategy games. I also understand that this is a brand new game and things may be changed around a bit in the coming months. But I really hope that the developers see this review and think about a couple of these changes, while not a developer myself, I cant imagine most of these (such as allowing re-naming or letting enemy placement be random) would be terribly difficult to implement. With just a little bit of polish, this could easily land as one of the top 2020 games of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: The hybrid of Fire Emblem and Darkest Dungeon, but with a pure female playable cast, set in a Gothic Victorian era. It's a very fun concept and I love the setting. I wasn't keen on the lack of colours at first, but it quickly grew on me the more I played. Made it to day 18 on my first run, so it's likely on the easier end for rogue likes when compared to Binding of Isaac, Our Darker Purpose, Darkest Dungeon or Dead Cells, but that doesn't mean it's actually easy, The game can and will punish you relentlessly if you don't master the timeline system and make the most out of your skill combinations and sync your daughter's moves to cover each other. 2 or 3 hits and you've lost a daughter, so a nice learning curve with steady difficulty, but still not the hardest rogue like out there. The music is also awesome. I'd give it a 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: More of a 'meh' or 'it's ok' than a real thumbs up. This is really one of those games that makes me wish steam had that option rather than the binary because I don't dislike this game but I also don't love it.The main reason for this is the roguelike format. Now I enjoy roguelikes for the most part but here it really feels like a way to pad out the game more so than anything tied to story or progression. It's as if they decided that four classes and five bosses wasn't enough.The thing is, I think it is enough, or it would be if there were a little more tactical depth to the gameplay. The XCOM reboot games only have 4 classes as well but they make the best of it having mechanics layered over them, like the cover system, the research, the choice of equipment. In Othercide there's just kind of ... nothing.The dynamic timeline system is the only really interesting part to the strategy layer in my opinion, and that's done really well here, but it isn't enough to make up for the fact that each class only has one role to play on the field. Sure you can pick between two abilities at each level milestone, but they are not created equal and some are just plainly more useful then others. So the repeating of sections (thankfully you don't have to repeat the whole game because once you encounter a boss you can skip straight to their section on resetting your playthrough) just became a bit tedious for me and I really felt I'd seen everything by about the 2/3 point. I get what they were going for with the whole 'fight against hopeless odds' thing but I feel like there must have been a less repetitive way to get that feeling across. Add to that the weird 'permadeath but not quite' system where you can bring back high level units between runs but can't heal them without sacrificing an equal or even higher level unit and I found that progress slowed down so much after the halfway point I eventually just lost all motivation to play.Game looks spectacular though and the soundtrack is a standout. I dunno what genre you'd call it, some kind of metal? But it hits different when the lyrics start during the last phase of a boss fight. Would love to see a sequel or successor.

_childDocuments_.review: Found it to be frustrating as far as tactical games go. I wanted to enjoy it but I found the game to be too lacking in UI readability and feedback.- The aesthetic is very cool but everything ends up looking very samey and its hard to really understand the battlefield at a glance, having to constantly zoom in and click on things just to remember what they are. Definitely not a good game for people with eye sight trouble.- Lots of information that I would love to know is just not present in the UI for a game of this ilk, like just a number for how far enemies can move.- Speaking of movement, the lack of grid makes it annoying to judge distances, and all you get are weird bubbles on the map to show how far something can go.- Other things in menus are seemingly absent, like the AP cost of your actions when upgrading them.- The timeline is a neat concept but like everything else, hard to gauge, which is a problem since its a core concept. Furthremore, icons on the timeline are sometimes incredibly vague, showing you SOMETHING happens in 30 steps but not what will happen or even who is doing it without clicking on things.Further less significant problems include- Really annoying, pretentious and vague dialogue that happens constantly during a battle. The game really loves its "Plague" theme and wont shut up about it.- Dull music.- Nothing to get you invested in it other than an extremely vague premise and the rogue-like mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: , a strategy roguelike, with an interesting ahestethic that isn't limited to the skin deep anime waifus.I'll elaborate:The style is achieved with a black and white palette with a small tinge of red that focuses your attention to details in order to highlight the character and enemy design.The design itself from the enemies to the envirnment is esoteric yet familiar mirroring the world the lore paints.Lore is unlocked through the gameplay in the forms of logs you can read, they are not necessary to enjoy the title as a tactical game, but it enhances the experience.The game itself is grid/turn based with a focus on Action Points management, giving you the choice between using just a small ammount of them to get the next turn sooner, or use a lot of them to make a lot of actions but having your turn dealyed by a lot, and the balance weights on this, turn order and how much you can or cannot do to not be caught with your guard down between turns.The roguelike part comes in the Recollection System, with each run you'll accumulate a certain resource that when you get a Game Over, you can use to permanetly power up your charachters for the next one.There are 4 playable classes in the game, each covering a certain niche that can learn abilities and augment them with modifiers that you'll find during gameplay.With the exception of a couple of VERY unbalanced abilities I have nothing but praise.I got it for the style but I got a lot more out of it, very reccomanded.

_childDocuments_.review: A challenging turn-based tactics game that pulls no punches, but don't let that intimidate you. Othercide's main gimmick is its Initiative timeline. Instead of a static turn order like other turn-based tactics games with set orders, Othercide uses a dynamic timeline where both your army of Daughters and the enemies will move up and down. The further up the initiative you are, the sooner you act. Both Daughters and enemies have abilities that can either pull allies up in the timeline, or push enemies back further down. This will be your saving grace, as manipulation of the timeline is critical to a successful mission, and often means the difference between life and death. Of course, chances are you'll soon find your Daughters defeated and the run over. However, this is not the end; far from it. Whenever you finish a run, you unlock Remembrances; powerful modifiers that can greatly increase your odds of survival. These can include additional damage buffs to specific enemy types, starting with higher level Daughters, or even starting a run with a previous Daughter resurrected from the dead. Every time you fall is another chance to get back up, stronger than before.Othercide's other unique trait is healing: there is none. Not in the traditional sense, at least. The only way to regain health to an injured Daughter is via sacrificing another Daughter of equal or higher level. And as a good amount of abilities cost a small percentage of health, even your Daughters who have never been touched by enemies will soon find themselves on their last legs. This becomes a careful balance of Daughters, managing who keeps around and who must be sacrificed to save another. Those sacrificed also pass on a powerful trait to those they heal, adding another consideration to the mix. For those who find this daunting, you can opt to enable "Dream Mode", which will restore a Daughter's HP at the end of the day instead, allowing for a much more casual approach to the game, with less stress on balancing all your Daughter's HP.Visually, I think Othercide may be among my top prettiest looking game. The monochrome world occasionally interrupted by the splatter of crimson blood and the bright red scarves of your Daughters, which also double as a dynamic HP bar, is captivating. The enemy and boss designs are also equally fascinating and disturbing. The soundtrack also does a wonderful job of bringing the entire game together into a gritty, dark world, where it is up to you and The Red Mother to carry on the last spark of flame in this dying reality.

_childDocuments_.review: Greetings Always!  Today I’ll be reviewing “Othercide” a turn based tactics game with some interesting roguelite mechanics.  I believe this is a first for the tactics genre and along with a very distinctive art style game definitely stands out from the crowd but the question always remains; is it worth your time?  Let’s discuss.Our Journey into Paradise:  Before anything we have to discuss the atmosphere of this game.  Probably one of the most beautifully, high contrast style I’ve seen in a long time.  The only real colors used in the game are black, white (shades of both) and red with some light uses of yellow in the eyes.  Yes, this does create some issues were things tend to blend into the surroundings but it makes the world feel otherworldly and immediately makes the game stand out.  The sound effects and audio lines are all well done, if a bit repetitive and I will say that the music is largely forgettable (except for that pickup on the main song).  The dialog of the story is cryptic and creepy as well as engaging and all of the voice actors did a stellar job; especially the Mother and second boss.  The game also does a great job aesthetically at making the characters attractive without overly sexualizing them; though not opposed to the ‘waifu’ aspect of other games this one keeps the designs attractive without making it the goal to be sexy what you are left with is less Bayonetta and more Sucker Punch.  This was gracefully achieved without making the characters ugly (which seem to be a common thing as of late) but coming off as more stylized than fetishistic.  Although this is where the uniqueness largely ends that doesn’t mean the rest of the game is bad per se.Wait…where’s my Overtwatch:  At the core this game is a tactics game, which means you command a group of characters (your daughters) in a turn based battle against your enemies.  Your daughters level up, gain new abilities but the game also has an interesting trait system where the daughters have a chance of gaining modifies based on how they perform.  If one of them is constantly dying she may get injured or maybe another daughter will see her sister constantly dying and become apathetic to it.  But the gameplay is fairly basic outside of that.  The game is also fairly brutal in regards to taking damage as the only way to heal is sacrificing another daughter and enemies do a considerable amount of damage.  This leaves the game feeling more like a puzzle than a typical tactics game.  The last major part of the game is that you aren’t really meant to clear it in one passing.  At some point you will need to reset the progress; using shards you collected to turn on modifiers for the next game and either train new daughters or resurrect old ones.  Even after beating the game you can continue to reset and try new things; giving the game a high level of replayability.Grind, baby, Grind:  There are a few bugs in the game or at least UI issues from my perspective.  Selecting a target can sometimes be a chore, as the game is missing a lot of the shortcuts that most games of the genre have and I had to deselect and reselect things to get actions to complete.  Managing memories (items) in the game is also tedious and in dire need of a better layout.  You can’t discard or prioritize memories and even the sorting function resets every time you leave it.  The class balance is also off; the sword and gun classes are just so much better than the other two due to their mobility and range.  It also doesn’t help that there really isn’t much difference between multiple daughters of the same class even with the trait system.  Many times they didn’t feel different and when they did never in a good way (mixing up who had which ability).Overall, this is a good game if you like tactics games.  You may find the base gameplay to be a bit basic and once beaten I feel no real drive to keep playing (even though I can) but it is a solid game for the price and the story is enough off the path to be engaging so I’d recommend you grab this if you can.  Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hilariously imbalanced, whether it is enemy ranges (enemies can spit farther than you can shoot with your gunslinging sisters), healing (you can't heal, but enemies can), higher bonuses for equivalent abilities (your "tanks" generally gain somewhere around 180 armor when spending health, whereas equivalent enemy sisters gain somewhere around 1300 armor, and don't spend any health), and some enemies can root you from basically halfway across the map. Couple that with the fact that on any mission other than hunts (which have a set amount of enemies) you'll generally be outnumbered and spammed by enemies on the magnitude of 5-7 times of your 2-3 sisters you are allowed to bring (for some reason, some missions only allow 2, while others allow 4 sisters. Why? Who knows. Artificial difficulty, instead of allowing a general amount like 4 per mission.) The other thing the game doesn't tell you is that enemies can't attack the first round or the round they spawn in, unless they spawn immediately next to you or are within range of a ranged ability (like an infested's spit attack, that can _reach farther than your bullets_).There are some wild circumstances that can occur due to enemy spawns that fall into one of two categories - tedious or mission-ending. Bright soul escort missions typically end with hordes of enemies spawning at the far end of the map once you get the bright soul out safely, but before you evacuate your sisters. Unfortunately, the option for 'fast gameplay' is still slow as molasses, so you're stuck watching 10 - 15 new enemies scuttle toward you each round, despite the fact that they won't get close to you before you evacuate. It's tedious and annoying, as you feel like you're wasting time just watching the horde slowly crawl across the screen while you wait for the turn to come to evacuate.The other example, mission-ending, is frustrating as hell because there's not much that can be done - you're basically hosed due to an unlucky spawn. The enemy in this case is the maggot, which as mentioned before can root one or more of your sisters from literally halfway across the map. For reference, your gun-toting soullingers can only shoot _6_ tiles (they should really look into loading their cartridges with the proper grain, because those bullets really aren't going anywhere near a reasonable distance). The maggot, even when it's just one by itself, can root often enough that your melee sisters will never be able to move and close the distance with it before its damage from the root goes off. The range on that root needs to be significantly reduced, either that, or soulslinger gun range needs to be increased (keep in mind, even enemy curse witches, cultists with guns, can shoot further with their weapons. Why? Because F*CK you, that's why). Granted, this is a rare occurrence, but it's a tediously annoying RNG spawn that can easily end a mission, let alone a run. The most recent issue with this was during a survival mission, where I had staved off the hordes thrown at me. The evacuation point appeared and I moved my units within 1 turn of escaping. Of course, a maggot spawned and from its little corner halfway across the map spammed roots that prevented my sisters from escaping. The range on the Grasping Mandibles (Seriously guys, _20_ tiles? Nothing in the player's arsenal even has half that range. Nothing. That's just idiocy), needs to be reduced. Add on the delayed damage and you are basically stuck until your characters die. This can easily be balanced with one of several options - 1) increase the delay time on the action; 2) do not allow maggots to spawn in certain mission types; 3) reduce the root time by 1-2 rounds so that you are not permanently stuck in place. But hey, glad to see they added _cosmetic DLC_ for your disposable, useless units instead of considering balance issues. In addition, when any given unit is debuffed there is no way to tell how long the debuff lasts and what exactly it does - for example if an enemy roots one of your characters you have no idea how long it lasts and how it might affect that unit's statistics. That's just poor provision of information, and the devs should consider amending this to be more informative. That's not good game design, and is clearly intended to screw you over by simply withholding information.The developers claim they review and collect suggestions but I'm sure they simply ignored the complaints about this game, which are consistent across negative reviews, and they haven't modified much of anything in terms of balance. Enemies still spawn in hordes, they still get more range and better abilities without expending health, and the maggot still exists, 20 tile ability and all, untouched.

_childDocuments_.review: Some excellent turn based boss fights; but meh trash fights that become a grind.It almost feels like the game was designed to be played ironman-style (in which case it does a very good job walking the line of very-hard-but-never-impossible). But then perhaps the devs lost their nerve, and implemented the recollection system.It gives you massive buffs when you lose for the next run. The result of these is to make the trash fights trivial grinds, and it's the weakest bit of the design. The fact as a player you're getting better, and also being handed huge buffs, means the game see-saws almost immediately from hard to way too easy on the 2nd recollection.This isn't helped by the really limited diversity of trash encounters. You will see the exact same spawns and maps so often it becomes a tedious job of repeating the exact same moves over and over to flawlessly clear an area, since there's virtually zero randomness. This is okay on the first recollection - the odd misclick or dodge can still mix things up - but once you're buffed up on the 2nd, it feels like a punitive, trivial grind.I still recommend it as one of the better turn-based games, though it's a '7/10' type game for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Verdict - Fans of the genre should buy on-sale.Pros:-Solid customization for your units-some tactical innovations in the form of dynamic turns and boosting-aesthetic and lore are compelling-challenging fights that require a planCons:-a bit on the simple side, most of your decisions will be in limiting your enemy's options, setting up for backstabs and moving just out of reach of enemies-artificial gameplay loop in the form of a not very interesting rogue-like mechanic. can be minimized with the easy mode-some bosses and enemies are very gimmicky-not very many options of units, makes for a predictable setup for your team-not a lot of enemy variety-pretty short game length considering a lot of it will be due to reptition-some levels and modes are incredibly irritating to play through, rescue is a standout annoying mission -- and also the most important mission style in the game.  -massively poor design in terms of inverse difficulty curve.  The first few hours of the game are by far the hardest compared to even the mid game once your characters become stronger-my biggest problem: skills didn't behave predictably, and sometimes wouldn't do anything at all.  modern game design shouldnt require that I read a manual to play the game -- the built-in description should be enough -the boss design is both confusing and unintuitive, with phase changes and % based dynamic interrupting the boss will sometimes just attack 4 times in a row after doing a normal pattern for 3-4 rounds. _childDocuments_.review: Laid in black and white with a hint of red, Othercide is a turn-based tactical game developed by indie developer Lightbulb Crew and published by Focus Home Interactive. This title’s most striking quality is its distinct, minimalistic aesthetic. The game has a similarly humble soundtrack to match with subtle ambient and whispers, disturbed by occasional musical track only in the most extraordinary of moments. Impressive both in terms of gameplay and stylistic choices, the title in question is a bittersweet journey about keeping hope amidst despair.Othercide puts the player in charge of a herculean task of mending a literal tear in reality. The quest ahead is to close the latest chapter in the history of wars against immaterial horrors lurking beyond, bent on manifesting themselves in reality. What makes this conflict special is that for the first time the evil has succeeded in coming forth into existence. Laws of physics gave way to temporal loop, ever re-playing the moment the reality broke. The only way out is to defeat the malign influence behind it all.Frankly, Othercide’s story is by far its least tangible aspect. The meat of the game is a steady stream of increasingly more difficult skirmishes where your ever-growing army of daughters, much like light to balance the dark, will face an army of horrors born from nightmares of a suffering child. Conducted over a number of preset maps consisting of square tiles, the player takes turns to carefully engage the enemy, always striding to deal as much damage as possible while also staying out of the harm’s way. Gradually, you will gain experience, increase your daughters’ levels, develop your favourites and eventually watch them die. Only for the cycle to repeat.Simply put, the core gameplay of Othercide is merciless. Perhaps its most telling mechanic is the characters’ lack of ability to heal. Not only every hit taken by a daughter is there to stay – the only way to regenerate a daughter is to sacrifice another one of the same level. Taking into account how challenging the bosses are, heartbreaking as it may be, your most powerful daughters will fall. Furthermore, failure to defeat the boss immediately ends a run. The only thing that remains is to start over. However, you do come back stronger – with game progress the player unlocks global buffs, such as increased starting level or damage, steadily empowering daughters in preparation for the next milestone (and boss) ahead. With ground rules established, let’s take a look at the daughters themselves. Every run begins with 3 warriors at the player’s disposal – blademaster, gunslinger and shieldbearer – each equipped with a dedicated set of skills. Blademaster is a nimble warrior, excelling in mobility and melee damage; gunslinger provides ranged support with both bullets and buffs; shieldbearer’s specialty is protection and disturbing the enemy. Don’t be fooled by her sturdier stature though, there is no tank in a game where every ounce of damage is permanent. To keep things interesting, every class has 4 skills unlockable with level progression. They always come with a choice of 2, allowing for a diversity among the daughters of the same class.Much like the game’s aesthetic, the gameplay loop of Othercide is plain, yet effective. Characters present on the map take turns to traverse a given number of tiles and attack. Each move consumes a set number of Action Points and the amount spent determines the character’s place on the initiative bar. Careful management of initiative is a crucial aspect of the game as untimely overexerted character may end up exposed and killed in a single turn.Once the player gets a firm grip of the basics, the game becomes increasingly nuanced. New enemies are introduced and later replaced by their enhanced versions with a broader moveset. While killing is an inherent part of every mission, the ultimate objective may be different than plain eradication – timed survival, escort or prevention of a dark ritual; each type comes with a tiny spin to further keep things varied and interesting. Daughters in time receive traits that reflect their performance in battle in form of a permanent buff, and you probably get the gist by now. The devil is in the details.For all the joy of creating a seemingly unstoppable force of daughters and excitement that monumental bossfights deliver, one cannot forget that the player is meant to fail by design. Beating the game requires multiple replays and even if this title does everything in its power to smoothen the pill (going so far as to provide easy mode) it is still hard to swallow that what you’ve meticulously built over several hours eventually just falls apart. However, fitting to overarching theme of the game, this design choice will make some of you drop the game long before the credits roll.Charming as Othercide may be, there are some minor concerns that need to be raised. As mentioned, the story of the game is rather difficult to follow. To truly grasp what transpires, one needs to read the codex, especially the memories – droppable bits of lore that second as buffs for daughters’ skills. Memories are assigned to chapters, alas codex pages won’t be complete until the game is beaten. It’s a worthwhile read though, as it covers the protagonist’s past, providing a lot of context to the events unfolding on the screen. It gives depth to the story, completely imperceptible over the regular course of play. A risky design choice to say the least.Second dishonourable mention goes to minor bugs, still present in the game despite multiple updates addressing such issues. Perhaps the most unfortunate one is how a number of reaction skills occasionally don’t work, especially taking into account they cost total health percentage to use. Another vexing example is consistent issues with red markers, representing the area of the enemy’s attack. They almost never respond to skills moving the enemy away, and often linger 1-2 turns past their resolution, introducing confusion and memory game, particularly to otherwise atmospheric bossfights.All things considered, Othercide deserves all of its critical acclaim. This title is a feast for any enthusiast of turn-based, tactical play. As a bright-red cherry on top, the game’s aesthetic is a delightful application of minimalism, coupled with soundtrack evoking pathos where fitting. Minor hiccups I experienced along the way didn’t deter me in any way from greatly enjoying the game. However, one has to remember how difficult Othercide is. The game, by design, is meant to induce pinches of fatigue and hopelessness, alas those looking for light-hearted fun should steer clear away from this title. On the other hand, those who enjoy their gaming a little rough, and especially fans of the genre, can confidently send their daughters to war.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - fantastic game that has devs that are still actively listening to the community & working on their game as of this review (9/11/20). worth a buy at full price if u enjoy grid-based combat games & also games with roguelike elements (do NOT expect the variety between runs to be on the same levels as games such as slay the spire) otherwise, consider purchasing at a discount i couldn't recommend this game to most players prior to the most recent patch, while i very much enjoy the game, it served a very niche base of hardcore players, and had some horrible balancing issues with the classes that if utilized properly, could allow you to kill every boss before it even takes its' first action. i also felt like the game still has more of a cookie clicker type progression than a roguelike one because of how brutal the first boss was. the patch hit all of these complaints by toning down the first boss, adding what looks like a really fun casual mode (hadn't tried it yet) and also while the exploit is still possible, it's extremely tedious now and entirely pointless given the new casual mode. the game comes with one of the best game soundtracks i've ever heard in a game, many of the tracks are solid standalone tracks. the art, while lacking a bit in variety due to relatively few layouts you play on, is otherwise a great asset.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun and I recommend it IF you're NOT only getting it for "Turn-based Tactics" combat and IF you're okay with fairly long "roguelite" sessions. It is definitely a unique combination of resource management, RPG and roguelite elements and worth a try.With that said I did not appreciate resource management (health in particular) aspect of the game pushed me towards the only viable strategy in combat (which, by the way, almost guarantees victory).  7/10 (8/10 IF you consciously avoid cheese strategies, which game pushes you into).This game doesn't do any groundbreaking graphics or innovative techniques. It picked a style and it went with it. Literally everything else is something you've likely seen in other games, BUT because of unique style and contrasting colors a lot of it pops out a lot more than in other games.Gameplay is fun unless/until you realize what it takes to win the game makes it a fail as a "tactics" game. That doesn't mean it's not challenging in some ways, but it's is not the core "tactics" gameplay that creates the challenge and I see that as a problem.The reason I gave 2 grades to gameplay is this game has 2 difficulties one of them just makes the problem worse.The reason for that is HEALING and to understand why here's some mechanics for default (nightmare) difficulty:In case  you don't see where this is going, you need to keep your daughters alive, so you really can't afford getting hit. The only way to win the game is to rely on cheese strategies. In most cases you just use first turn or 2 to kill whatever you can kill before it gets close and has a chance to attack. When enemies close in you burn through HP skills that prevent attacks from hitting, because sacrificing 5-15% HP is always cheaper than getting hit and losing 30-60%. Your only real choice is if you want to use more actions and delay your daughters actions by an extra "turn" (it's actually initiative system, not turns).In easier (Dream) difficulty daughters get back 50% of their HP each day (effectively after the fight). This can either be a really good thing or a really bad thing, depending on how you play. On one hand you can now comfortably take a hit, so you're not limited to mostly ranged units and/or HP skill spam. On the other hand you can now do the HP skill spam without really worrying about losing HP...There's a lot more to gameplay elements (mostly to do with progression and resource management), which make the game genuinely good, but in my opinion health management and health skills remove all nuance from combat (core gameplay loop), which brings the entire game down.Sessions are 1-10 hours long (up to 2 hours per boss), which slightly decreases as you unlock buffs. The main problem I found with this, is it's hard to pick up for a roguelite. Like you can't just sit down play a session and not touch it for a year, because if you come back in a year, you'll take a while to remember what's going on or will fail the run in a few turns.Obviously, due to long session time, resetting(or losing) a run feels like a massive loss, which I don't appreciate in most games.There's some permanent progression. Namely you get shards based on how many stages you cleared (total) and you can use those shards in each run to activate buffs you unlocked by hitting certain milestones (dealing damage, killing bosses, etc.). If you play it smart, you also get to resurrect daughters from previous runs on new ones.Temporary progression boils down to The 3 above are fairly well spaced out, so despite not feeling particularly powerful individually, they do give a sense of constant growth... These suffer somewhat from previously mentioned healing mechanic, as you have to keep too many daughters and it's difficult to keep track or even notice progression of individual daughters when you need to switch between 3-4 teams of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Just got done getting achievements to 100%. I personally spent hours on some missions, especially boss fights, but a Painslinger/Infested combo and the final boss (he's insane the first time without prior knowledge) were two of the few things that could wipe out my whole team on my first recollection. Also, remembrances make each run a lot easier, and you never lose shards to unlock them with on subsequent recollections. This made my second, full clear recollection a breeze.Gameplay aside, the 1st and 4th boss music is excellent and the protagonist has an interesting backstory you learn more about as you collect "memories" across your missions. It is slightly awkward that we only get "daughters" and there are zero "sons" though, even if it does make sense with the protagonist being female... There's also the noticeable downside of some bugs that ruin gameplay: a moderate amount when the previewed AoE of an enemy's attack stays displayed or becomes displayed wrong when an enemy is pushed (mostly occurs with bosses), and there was one time (and only one, thankfully) that I had a lv14 unit and her traits disappear permanantly into a lv7 unit who couldn't level up anymore in my 2nd recollection.Overall, I really enjoyed Othercide and trying really hard to beat the game in my very first playthrough made me a better tactical RPG gamer.

_childDocuments_.review: Ive not played a lot of Othercide yet, at the time of writing this ive spend 9 Hours with this game.Personally, ive never felt like writing reviews for games, but this one needs an exception.tl;dr: If youre into hard tactical games, enjoy the strong artstyle, or like a story that doesnt tell you all answers from the start, buy this game. and if you dont want to spend money, check it out on youtube, because while not worth your money, it deserves your attention.Gameplay:Othercide is a Rogue Lite, Tactial Game and most would say it is much like XCom, I actually think it has way more similatites to the game Mechanicus, but that game is more under the radar. Othercide is about tough choices and permanence, every point of damage taken, every bad decision is here to stay, this may lead to frustraitio for some and may be a dealbreaker for others, but all failed attempts ontribute to making your next one more succsessful through upgrades that range from stat ups, to the ability to straight up skip bosses.Speaking of the Bosses, ive experienced the first one, and i can allready tell the bosses will be the highpoints of this game, you will need to bing your A-Game, and you will need a strategy that exploits the bosses mechanics. This theme of exploiting machanics is actually taught to you very directly, you can check the AI patterns of all enemies in the in game codex, and adapt your strategies around what you fight. leading to a system that may punish damage hars, but gives you many tools to circumvent it.The only problem ive found is that the gameplay can feel a bit slow, but that isnt even a problem because speeding it up is literally an option in the menu.Art:Othercides defiletly sets its foot forward in the art department, personally i knew this game would be amazing from the title screen and the music that played, the soundtrack, which seems to be either dynamic or very well paced, is nothing short of phenomenal. If youre into Rock or Metal, definetly give this soundtrack a listen, im sure you'll not be dissapointed.the games Black/White/Red colour pallete is nothing short of fantastically exectued. The game feels incredibly alive not despite, but because of this strong art drirection.Story:The story is probably one of the strongest ive seen so far, while the main conflict is pretty straightforward; ie, "white monsters be evil go kill em" what these fights are about and what they actually mean is obsucured form you, but theres enough here to invite and reward you for thinking about what the game is trying to say, it is definetly presenting a story beyond what is happening, i just dont know what yet.I might update this part of the review once i have more context, but this is how i feel about it up until now.In Conclusion:Othercide is a game i that enticed me for its gameplay but made me an instant fan through its Art, Story and Music, and in my opinion, it deserves all attention it can get. While many games shy away from this strong stylization and difficulty, Othercide went all in and succeeded on all fronts. If anythign i just described sounded interessting, and not like the rambling of a fanboy, then go buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Stylish, without a doubt. B&W with a monocolour flourish will never go out of style when executed properly. The graphics can be a bit cluttered and hamfisted at times, but overall the art direction is very solid and certainly one of the game's highlights. Othercide immediately offers a sense of homecoming to players familiar with other great titles like X-Com and Darkest Dungeon. The gameplay is both familiar and rewarding at times. However, Othercide really manages to take the worst aspects of both games without finding many of the redeeming traits hidden in both.Even on the most brutal modes, Darkest Dungeon allows the player to heal units without turning on easy mode or sacrificing other units to do so. In fact, almost every roguelike I've ever played has some sort of limited ability to heal. This wouldn't be a gamebreaker in itself. It's a unique concept. But it's also just the tip of the iceberg. Read on.Despite the many similarities between Othercide and the X-Com series, the obligation of a health cost required to activate most overwatch type skills or counters really shifts the emphasis of gameplay and rewards a focus on proper zoning and active abilities rather than any use of reactive combat unless absolutely necessary. Despite Othercide having made use of overwatch feel like the lesser of two evils at the best of times and into more of a punishment than a viable tactic at the worst of times, this too does not preclude the game from having a solid foundation. Risk vs reward choices typically make games feel more fulfilling once you understand the consequences of your actions.Like most other roguelikes, Othercide is designed around the concept of growth through failure and encourages you to make these tough choices. But instead of just dropping you into the thick of things under-prepared and with increasing odds ever stacked against you, the entire combat system of Othercide seems pretty flawed to me. Or at least, designed with a particularly sadistic intent. Perhaps some players, whether they are self-proclaimed pro gamers or masochists may derive pleasure from this. But, hey.. I chose "Give me God of War" once upon a time too and didn't regret it.There is a difference, however subtle, between having enough practice and skill to be able to play a game near-flawlessly and that game not having the means to do so at your disposal. Othercide seems to be designed with unit loss as a core mechanic of its gameplay - and something about that just doesn't sit well with me. Loss should be anticipated... expected even, but not required. For a game with its emphasis on squad-based tactical combat, having enemies warp into the battlefield at random locations while not being able to determine what type of unit they are or what their movement/attack range will be until they take their turn is just unacceptable. That's the perfect circumstance for overwatch, is it not? Then, it's too bad players have to sacrifice unit health just to activate it. You're basically gambling on whether paying blood to mitigate the chances at paying more blood is worth it or not. I rarely pass on games, so I might not refund it and see if it grows on me. But 1.4 hrs in and the rose tinted glasses are off. Unfortunately, the game ends up looking very black and white to me as a result.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game I've pre-ordered in quite some time and I couldn't be happier that I did. I watched the gameplay trailers a few weeks ago which left me immediately intrigued by the semi-monochromatic, gothic aesthetic and the fluid timeline mechanics. I'm 10 hours in now and just passed the first boss... I'm hooked. The game is a near perfect marriage between narrative and gameplay. Let me elaborate a little bit... Othercide is a game about overcoming trauma and each boss is a representation of a specific traumatic instance that the mother (the creator of the Daughters you play as) and the child (the main villain of the story) have endured. You are essentially battling through what is their collective memory of events involving sickness, grief and, of course, suffering. The bosses, just like trauma, are incredibly difficult to overcome and feel like literally insurmountable walls to your progress. The game actively knows you will fail to manage these challenges encounters right away (who can actually manage their trauma head on anyway??) and encourages you to fail in order to see the best ways to grow forward. There is no growth without sacrifice hence literal sacrifice is a crux of the game. I've noticed some reviewers have seen this as a downside since the game requires you to grind a good bit by consistently axes various Daughters in favor of healing others. I haven't felt this to be much of a negative at all and it only strengthens my appreciation for how well the narrative and gameplay come together. Like no pain, no gain right? You may have to sacrifice a Daughter but by doing so you pass on traits and buffs to the Daughter that is being healed. For examples sacrificing a shieldbearer Daughter will buff another with a health and armor boost thus helping with their longevity in future fights. Like in life, you can't see growth without letting things go. So while I knew axing a few Daughters would leave me with less forces... the Daughters I have left would be much better equipped to fight the boss at the end of the week. After my first two attempts on the Surgeon I resorted to preparing to overcome the encounter like I have my own depression and anxiety... I avoided fighting it head on until I felt I had the true resolve and wisdom to actually overcome it. This meant rebooting the recollection a few times without even attempting to fight the boss. This way I gained more access memories and artifacts to buff my Daughters each time I began the recollection again, so by the time my six recollection came around my Daughters were more than prepared to take out the boss. I also haven't found this game as frustratingly difficult or repetitive as some have found it. Each class is easy to get a feel for and you quickly learn what enemy types they are best to match up against. Also don't listen to other reviews that say to avoid the abilities that cost health... those are some of the most unique and, when used right, can actually help you to avoid losing health. For example, the soulslinger has an interrupting move that cost 10% of her health. She will fire at the first enemy that makes an attack on an ally within range. This move has saved my Daughters' collective skins so many times from taking unnecessary damage since the move prevents the enemy from using an attack (if it doesn't outright murder them). I think many players feel funneled into not using them since in many other tactical games damaging a unit is incredibly counterproductive, but in Othercide it is the only way to progress. I also don't find the various systems of the game to be nearly as overwhelming as other tactical games that involve base building and other systems management. In Othercide the Daughters are the stars of the show and everything is pretty much built around their development/survival. I also didn't find myself as frustrating with having to restart the recollection as I did restarting a save on X-Com 2 because half of my units decided to miss Overwatch shots with 80-90% success rate by firing randomly in the f**kin sky. I also found that the timeline system and combos you can create with your Daughters lead to much shorter mission times. Once you get into the rhythm you can easily clear most missions under 20 minutes and that includes the "Impossible" ones. The only cons I have so far are the number of classes available and access to the various game modes. The three classes offered are quite robust and offer a lot of variation in terms of playability. I just personally wish there was another class or two and hope they add a couple with future expansions. I also think that they could definitely introduce the various game modes a lot quicker. For the recollections I've done so far I've almost exclusively been given hunt missions which is only one out of the three types. Survival has come up a couple times and I have yet to see a rescue mission. This is a little annoying since it is obviously nice to have some mission variety and because rescue is the one mode that offers the type of currency you need to resurrect Daughters as a reward. There is one artifact that gives you a resurrection coin at the start of a recollection but other than that I haven't gotten a chance to earn others which is a bummer when you want to run a roster of specific Daughters. Hopefully this can be changed with a future patch to help make the mission variety. All in all this is shaping up to be one of my favorite games of the year. One with a story that is incredibly timely given the circumstances of the world at large right now. Looking forward to overcoming the challenges of Suffering that lie ahead! 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: OVERALL - Not recommended.I cannot recommend this game, unless it is on a big sale and you want to try the tactical combat mechanics (which I think is the only strong point of the game). Otherwise, this game is skippable.STORY - 1/5I really didn't like how the story was presented.   Basically unless you want to read all the codex, the story as presented while playing through the game is almost non-existent.   Chosen Child, Child is corrupted, stop the child, stop the corrupter.   For the most part I just kept asking why do I care at all about these characters.  I read some of the codex, but it didn't peak my interest enough to keep reading.GRAPHICS - 2/5The "gray-scale + red" (red for blood, of course) looks pretty good overall and I enjoyed the intentional style.  But I found it hard to look at and discern details.   I wish all the enemies had a small color added in for each type too.  I think it would have been very helpful visually if cultists, nightmare creatures, and corrupted daughters all had a small amount of different color. COMBAT - 4/5The tactical combat mechanics are quite interesting.  Definitely the strongest part of the game and why I finished it.  I really enjoyed the initiative system and the choice to "burst" or not.   Also, keeping movement and actions all under one action point system was a nice change from most tactical games.  I felt the game had lots of interesting mechanics, but some could have been explored moreOUTSIDE COMBAT - 2/5I felt the outside combat mechanics had some interesting aspects, but almost all of them needed more refinement.   The memories were a mess.  Trying to sort through them was a pain and it felt like most of them weren't very useful.  Also they weren't always clear what they did.   At least a few of the abilities had almost not choice for memories.   The traits were a pain.   Some of them were really good and others were just ok.  Some were even detrimental.  But since they are all random, there was almost nothing you could do about it.  Sacrificing your daughters worked thematically I guess, but overall I didn't like the mechanic.  By the end of the game the vitae(main currency) was pointless.  I also had so many memories it they didn't even feel like a limited resource except for a few of the really rare ones.UI- 2/5I honestly think the UI on this game was ok, but because of the choices with the outside combat buffing it made the flaws in the UI stand out.  The main problem is you just have no good idea how much damage you're going to do.  The UI tries but there's just too many modifiers.Base DmgEnemy Type DamageSkill Memory DamageArmorFlanking/BackstabbingCrit ChanceCrit DamageThere was also quite a few bugs in the UI when using the inspect on enemies.Games I would recommend insteadBanner Saga 1,2,3Into the BreachXCOM 2Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: The best way to describe this game is Darkest Dungeon + Xcom/Mutant Year Zero. It's definitely it's own beast and it does some new things that I wasn't for sure was going to work at first. However, I find this game to be very addicting. You will get attached to these girls sometimes and losing them really sucks. Death is permanent however it does offer ways as you progress to keep a couple of your favorite daughters as a dedicated team. It's intimidating as you first start playing and there is a lot of math to take into consideration if you want to take full advantage of the Timeline mechanic. This is the perfect game for guys who love to "Theorycraft" numbers and work out the perfect build/team for defeating your enemies.  However, it's not necessary to play the game. So far I'm really enjoying this game and it is a gem that any Tactical/Strategy Game fan should have in their library.
