_childDocuments_.review: I'll give it a "meh". I love TRPGs and the aesthetic of this game looked really appealing so i was excited for it. The actual skill trees are pretty bare bones but the gameplay and soundtrack are solid. I actually really enjoyed myself up until the end and then couldn't bring myself to complete it. The game operates in the same fashion as Rogue Legacy or Dead Cells where the game doesn't expect you to complete it on your first try and it gets considerably easier the more times you play through it. Unlike those games, this isn't a roguelite so your gameplay experience is going to be more or less the same on subsequent playthroughs. This is fine in itself until the final boss where the game requires actual grinding. Before this point, bosses can be dealt with by learning the bosses moveset and changing your tactics accordingly on subsequent runs. The final boss just throws a ton of unavoidable damage at you to the point where you have to make sure you have a bunch of adequately leveled characters in your graveyard with good memories. The game at this point becomes a slog.

_childDocuments_.review: This was the most conflicting hour and a half I've had in a long time. I really wanted to like this game. I have a lot to say because I think this game could have been a masterpiece but, a lot of things are holding it back. I hope that the developers take this criticism constructively and work on either improving this game or making their next game better.The verdict for those who don't want to read: it's not worth the price of admission. Wait until it's on sale or major updates are made to the game.The presentation is top of the line. I love the black, white, and red aesthetic and I think the graphical fidelity of the game deserves praise. The assets are absolutely gorgeous. The models, the animations, the graphical design, the UI, the performance; it's all fantastic. However, the music stands out on its own. It is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ EXCELLENT (it's the reason I bought the game). Clearly there are some talented artists on this team.On the gameplay front, the ideas behind the timeline, the AP/interruption/initiative system are really interesting and I found myself wanting to go back and keep experimenting with the game's battle systems.However... this is where my praise ends.The game has three fundamental problems:* Poor pacing* Confusing gameplay* Abysmal storyAs a whole, the biggest problem with this game is pacing. In the first hour, you will be introduced to so many things you'll eventually ask yourself "why should I care about any of this?" Not only is the game throwing a massive amount of exposition at you, mostly filled with proper nouns like the Chosen One, the Mother, the Daughter, the Veil, the Suffering, etc., but it's also throwing gameplay mechanics at you way too quickly. SLOW DOWN. Let the game breathe! The tutorial doesn't need to introduce every game mechanic in the first thirty minutes. The introduction doesn't need to introduce all of the different elements to the story. Just skip all that ♥♥♥♥! Show me the setting, 1899 or whatever, and go straight to the gameplay! What sucks even more about this is that once you start to understand the systems and its charm, what awaits you is a game that has very little variety. You'll be using the same skills, fighting in the same maps, fighting against the same enemies, all for the goal of reaching the end boss for your run. There's one model for the Daughters (they just have different hairstyles and one of three outfits), and they mostly resemble the Mother, so you'll be seeing the same girls over and over. There simply wasn't enough randomness while I was playing to keep me interested.Then there's the gameplay. Two things are really hurting the game from a gameplay perspective: a UI that values style over substance, and mechanics that are simply too punishing.Firstly on the UI, many of the gameplay terms are vague (like "Remembrance", "Memories", "Inner Void", etc.) Just give it to me straight dude! I'm in a run, I'm going to get upgrades, and I have to manage my party. Secondly, you'll often be wondering what the UI design is supposed to represent. You'll be looking at squares and bars wondering what they mean, what the different shades of color represent on the timeline, how the timeline even works, etc. It won't be until you've permanently lost a couple of Daughters that you'll realize how the game works, which is just frustrating and not fun at all. Also, I had issues understanding what unit was queued up to be moved, how far I had to move to issue certain attacks, and in general the UI just actively worked against me during combat.On the punishing mechanics: this wouldn't be a problem if there was a sense of progression. However while the temporary nature of the game is interesting on paper, in practice it's just frustrating. You'll be killing your own Daughters to heal others. You'll be leveling up other Daughters, just to lose them and then be unable to resurrect them because the game decided to not give you any resurrection tokens.And in general, the early game is way too punishing. It shouldn't be possible for early game mobs to be able to dodge and hit twice. The game should not start with you ZERO resurrection tokens. The game should refund you your memories if your Daughters die. I should always have enough tokens to germinate a new Daughter on the first run. Hell, why did you let me pick the role for my first germination? I would have obviously picked the shield girl had I known she was missing from my team composition. Also, if you're going to design the first run to be impossible, INFORM YOUR PLAYER SO THAT THEY DON'T SUICIDE THEIR ENTIRE SQUAD.And lastly, the story is abysmal. Again, in the span of thirty minutes, you're introduced to the Chosen One, the Veil, the Suffering, the Mother, the Daughters and MORE. Every time a new proper noun was introduced I rolled my eyes. The dialogue was also extremely edgy and cringy. I get it; the game is about a mother's suffering and the evils she has to go through to bring a child into the world when at the end your offspring are the ones who hurt you the most. It doesn't need to be that deep. It's a strategy game. Just stop the exposition, quiet down and show me the game.It also doesn't help that the game pulls a classic Child of Light move, trying to be deep before establishing a cohesive narrative. It just comes across as pretentious. The same comment I made with the gameplay applies here: you don't need to show your entire hand upfront! If you're going to show all of the exposition at the start, make sure it's relevant to the game. None of the exposition changed the gameplay whatsoever. And don't be afraid to give your characters actual names for ♥♥♥♥♥ sake.One of the best moments was seeing the Chosen One holding the Egg, watching the Egg float and grow bigger after every camera cut. I was legitimately impressed by the artistry and it seemed heavily inspired by Berserk. Too bad it was undercut by the horrible dialogue from the Chosen One. I wish I cared enough to keep going to see what the Egg turns out to be.What made this experience even more disappointing for me was the massive missed opportunity. This could have been an excellent game. It almost seems like this game has all of the right ideas but half the execution. Someone on this team knew that the presentation and polish was important, that the gameplay mattered, that a meaningful story mattered, but ultimately no one had the vision to say "this isn't fun" or "this is too far". It's almost like the team was so in love with their product they forgot to put it in front of playtesters. PLAYTEST YOUR GAME. Get opinions outside of your dev team. Next time it will go a long way to making your game truly excellent. I don't believe this game is worth the price tag, and you should probably wait until it's on sale or major updates are made to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I am still very early in the game at the time of this review, but I love the concept and the execution. Roguelite tactical combat gameplay with heavy Claymore vibes that fit perfectly with a Sin City color palette. I don't know how they got the idea to put all that together but the result is great. Now let me explain the description further: Roguelite: Permadeath is a core part of the game. Even if your daughters don't get killed in combat, you will have to sacrifice them sooner or later. The quote unquote "campaign" is short but you will need to start over and upgrade your daughters through multiple playthroughs with persistent unlocks in order to beat it. You will also need to learn how to fight effectively and overcome the difficulty curve, getting better the more you play. In this way Othercide is similar to Dead Cells, Monster Train, Rogue Legacy, and other great games like that with roguelite elements.Tactical combat: Classic turn-based squad combat. Whether you like XCOM, FF Tactics, or Disgaea, you will find something to like in Othercide. So far the gameplay seems to have elements from both western style and Japanese style games. I am only a few unlocks in and the interaction between units can get pretty deep (auras, intercepts, synergy attacks, etc). I can see where this is going and I like it.Claymore vibes: That one is pretty obvious if you know the anime. If you don't and you enjoy this game, you will probably enjoy watching Claymore. But this is not just a similarity in the theme and story. Sacrifice is a big part of the gameplay. This includes incremental sacrifice - giving up a part of yourself to achieve something, or setting off on a path of  no return - and outright offering your life to help another when the time comes. These are core gameplay elements, both during combat and in the campaign meta game.Sin City color palette: What you see in the trailers and screenshots. Goes great with minimal design. Othercide is minimal but not sloppy or unskilled like some indie game graphics are. What is there looks good, it is obviously created with intent, and it all works out great. It also runs on a potato-ish laptop with no real GPU.

_childDocuments_.review: So... we're mixing 'Roguelite' with XCom-style tactical combat now? That could be interesting, so long as they balance the difficulty with the greater time-investment that sort of battle-system entails....yeah, no. It's not a 'hard' game. It's just 'unfair'. Get defeated in a boss-fight, and you're Game Over instantly, even if you have more troops in reserve. Go into a boss-fight blind, and you will lose, because they can only be beaten by highly specific tactics that you probably didn't bring the right team for. So basically, the only way to advance through the game is either with the knowledge that you'll ABSOLUTELY get a Game Over the first time you meet each boss, which is only going to be more aggravating the deeper into the game you get, OR you look up a guide and compose your team accordingly before you even SEE each boss. Which just isn't a fun way to play a game.It was an interesting idea, but it fails in execution. Pass.

_childDocuments_.review: As infuriating as the game can be I honestly believe its one of the best games thats been released recently. At the moment there are only 3 classes to choose from and the combinations you can do tend to be the same ones but as it stands it is a full playable game.  I bought this game due to it being a new turned based game with an interesting art style, and let me tell you I fell in love with its aesthetic. Its simple yet complex and its music is beautiful in a more morbid sense. I really really hope the devs continue to work on and add to the game I feel like even with all its content there is still so much potential for this to become an even better game.  The only negative id have to say is that even though there is  good amount of content in the game im afraid its not quite worth its 35 dollar price point. I bought it on sale and boy what a steal, but I definitely feel 35 is a bit steep. Overall if your someone who loves turn based tactics games definitely at least add this to your wishlist. As someone who grew up on the xcom series the game offers a completely different approach to unit management in that death of your units is essentially unavoidable. In order to keep going and fight and grow stronger, sacrifice is a must. Never have i played a game where death of a unit is so common yet so impactful at the same time, I truly hope to see this game shine. Definitely getting my vote for the steam awards

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I NEVER THOUGHT THIS GAME WOULD BE SO GOOD!Stylish combos, rocking soundtrack, and one helluva of a feel trip. This game is so close to being an art piece, and even with cheesy boss mechanics and obvious stat-check/DPS rush chokepoints, the game is still awesome.At first it starts slow, you get the hang of taking on small groups of enemies, watch as your daughters die and restart the run because you ♥♥♥♥ up. Then slowly you power through with a small group of your most beloved thralls, as you throw them into the fray. This game has psychological horror woven into every part of its macabre aesthetic, and I loved every bit of it. It gave the dark, gloomy atmosphere of darksouls a run for its own money, with a more coherent storyline hidden in fragments throughout the game.The plot isn't anything home to write about, BUT HELL THE BOSS BATTLES. Most battles drone on with the animations and repetitive soundtrack, but your heart really starts pumping when its boss battle time. The music ramps up beautifully as you get further and further into dangerous territory, and its really a rush when you execute mad combos and exploit the living ♥♥♥♥ outta every single mechanic available to you just to outsmart or outplay the bosses and their gimmicks.I'm not one to shy away from a challenge, but the first few bosses did feel cheap unless you learnt to exploit the reaction mechanic and stack your upgrades, but the battles do get better as the game continues. The deeper in you go, the more complex enemy types and movesets come into the picture, and before long you'll be stacking cheesy combo's off the dynamic timeline and feeling like a boss.I honestly love how they pulled off combat for this. Music and artistic vision really come through as you turn your daughters individual talents into a battlefield blender.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, DID I MENTION I LOVE THIS GAME AND I CANT STOP BINGEING IT? ITS ON SALE, GO GET IT!

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an amazing theme and story-telling, but is bogged down by bugs that the Devs seem to have no intention of fixing. The 3rd Boss of the game will basically freeze-lock your game during one of her cutscenes, and this issue has been known over a year and still has not been fixed.Armor buffs basically give double the  value they should, making certain enemies way overscaled in terms of power. Also an issue that's been known since RELEASE. Almost two years later and has not been fixed.There are also many other instances of the game just being completely unpolished. The fact that buff duration does not show up on the timeline or on the enemy information sheet.  The fact that there is no confirmation button for recollections and pressing the "Next Day" button, meaning you can ruin a playthrough with just a misclick. So many examples.This is a rare instance of game where the meat and bones are all there for something absolutely outstanding, but the devs are simply to lazy or are just incapable of updating the game to polish it. The game is basically is a Beta Version, and therefore I cannot recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: So i'm currently up to the fourth boss and I thought I would give a some sort of a review so far. In short, buy the game, Othercide is well worth the price of entry and they've done an amazing job in giving you something a little more unique in Real-Time Tactics and teamwork. Easily the best parts are the art design, music, difficulty and gameplay. I'd love to see a sequel and a few follow up expansions :D I'm not quite finished and I'm still playing but I can easily recommend to join in on the ride so far.Othercide is set in a limbo like world where The Mother acts as a guardian between realms trying to ward off The Suffering from entering the world. As such, with The Suffering and The Child overwhelming her, she sends her Daughters on a quest to overcome The Suffering and help The Child. It's all you really need to know, i'm not a fan of talking about spoilers and prefer recommending something to someone going in blind. Suffice to say, similar to Dark Souls/Bloodborne and Twin Peaks, you get pieces of the story with some of it being implied, some of it through first hand descriptions by The Mother and you see the story through her eyes. You piece together the history and how the characters interact, your mileage may vary how much you like the approach and i'm still curious to see the end.The art style and visuals are amazing, they really do need to give these guys a raise. The Black/White/Red colour scheme lends you a sense of a hopeless, purgatory world overrun by something Lovecraftian. I'm not quite sure if the developers were Devil May Cry fans but you definitely wouldn't be amiss in saying they could be sisters of Dante, all of the Daughter classes and The Mother have a great sense of design. Having said that, even though you can choose the name, you get a random hairstyle and overtime you see changes in their face and eyes, it would be nice to see some more customisation in the future.Gameplay wise, Otherwise is a mixture of XCOM gridstyle combat and a mixture of JRPG combat systems, similar to FInal Fantasy and Persona (in the Persona sense of SP points per turn and paying for health for some abilities with combos encouraged.) You choose a group of Daughters of different classes, you can modify their abilities with Memories (think mods or sockets) and you can give them one out of two potential skills on each milestone level. Each of them fill a roll to a degree but each can become a carry in their own right, many times i've had my Soulslinger (Ranged class) or Shield class roll through monsters like a gladiator in Ancient Rome. The game is Challenging! It forces you to make the best of your tool set from the start and understand the timeline system which you can manipulate, which isn't static, both you and the enemy have abilities that change the nature of your time to act. Understanding and knowing when to Burst or not to Burst (essentially two turns at once) can change the game.Two other gameplay points I would mention, No.1, yes it is true, you don't have a way to heal besides sacrificing something of the same or higher level but you do give that particular recipient a huge power boost and heal her, it really is about making each life count in a way. Should you have a higher level group and you're close to death or have an upcoming fight, you do need to rotate out or change up your members, and progressing through the game, you gain revive tokens, so you can keep a similar team through your playthrough. So the early game can be brutal, took me about four goes on the first boss and I was proud I beat the third boss on the first try, you can refer to your Codex on creature and boss tactics, which is No.2. The game actually has different tactics for different creatures and bosses and how the AI determines their path to victory and who they target. Its quite nice actually, you have to study and anticipate as you go through the game while planning ahead. If you charge ahead going guns blazing through a boss or a new bunch of enemies, you may get wiped quite quickly.Death isn't the end, its even a statement they make after the end of the tutorial. In fact, the beauty about this compared to something like XCOM as you go through the levels, is that even though you may be close or playing with a leveled, but weakened party, if you do wipe or die, you'll come back so much stronger. XCOM can feel cheap taking a single hit and having a team member on hiatus for a long time, in this, it makes you value every choice you make and when to expend your life to save your teammates in battle, just as if it were real to a degree.Thanks for reading! Buy Othercide, it's a great challenge, i've really enjoyed it, I hope you do too. Rating - Buy it :D

_childDocuments_.review: A complex and tricky strategy game, Othercide has a very clear idea of what it wants to be and executes its design perfectly.Whether or not you will like that design is up to you.Othercide is a game about making hard decisions, sucking up the occasional bad RNG, dealing with your mistakes and soldiering on.  There's no takebacks, and the only way to heal is to voluntarily kill off one of your units of equal or greater level outside of battle.  The intention behind this is that healing should be costly, but the effect is largely that you do a lot of extra grinding so that you have spare soldiers you can feed to your favorites.That won't click with everyone.  If you're into quirky, atmospheric games with a strong ludo-narrative link between gameplay, story and design though, this game will scratch that itch.As a strategy game it's very good looking and moody and moderately deep.  There's a lot of effects that play with the action economy, but only a limited amount of comboing as your squads are kept small.  Overall, it's innovative and thematic, but not groundbreaking.  Grab it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Othercide is fairly attractive, and makes the most of it's design choices, but the gameplay is just too repetitive for me. I got Star Renegades at the same time, and found it intriguing that two turn-based games that weren't in the exact same genre were both finding a way to use roguelite replayability. I credit rehashed nostalgia for winning the war between the two games, but I also think the greater variety of personalities, powers, and enemies greatly tilted the balance to the other side. Interested to see more from Lightbulb Crew, and kind of hoping that the concept of Othercide is expanded to hold my interest. In the meantime, I'll be killing quantum robots with beautifully pixelated explosions.

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure, I was both given the game for free as well as paid to play it on launch.That being said, I have no obligations to do anything with this review other than the legal one to mention the above. I love this game. It's an absolutely fantastic tactics game on its own and the rogue like elements are handled incredibly well. The world is dark and twisted and the gameplay mechanics are tied to the same lore for those that are interested. For those that L OMEGALUL RE in chat, don't worry, the game itself is mechanistically satisfying and the boss battles will really push you to your limits. You're gonna be barely squeaking by with an almost dead party if you even make it at all your first few times.It's hard, but it isn't unfair, you need to expect that enemies will be making the best moves most of the time and play around it. I hate in other strategy games where enemies just do idiotic stuff like some bandit attacks your main tank who has counter attack, the game even has a forecast thing that predicts a 0% chance to deal damage and a 100% chance the counter attack is lethal to the AI bandit, and the AI will do it anyway. There's not of that crap in here fortunately.All in all I give it an 8/10, I think if anyone is looking at this like they really want it, it'll be worth it to them at full price, and if you're even a little bit curious, this is definitely one to not miss a sale on.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game. I actually loved it when I just started: it's stylish, the game mechanics are fun, the music is pretty good, and well, I've been looking for a new strategy game to play.The problem is twofold: lack of QoL features, and glitches.The game uses a timeline system. Each time you take action on your unit, they will be able to move again after a set number of time units. You can take extra actions with your unit at the cost of a greater time delay before moving again. This timeline system is the core gameplay mechanic.Now enter buffs and debuffs. Say you apply a defense buff to yourself which lasts 25 time units. Upon cast, you can see in your stats that your defense has gone up, but there's no indication as to when the buff will wear off. Since you're the caster you can probably figure it out. But what about if an enemy has a buff? What about when there's 10 enemies on the field, and 5 of them have buffs, all cast at different times, with various lengths? Keeping track of this yourself is a massive headache and adds difficulty to the game for no reason. As you progress, the amount of statuses you need to keep track of in this way increases exponentially. This is the sort of QoL that's missing from this game, and which adds a level of unnecessary frustration.The next problem I have is with enemy aggro. After encountering an enemy type they gain a codex entry telling you how they decide which of your units to attack. Great, except you can't open this codex mid battle, so you better have it memorized. Also, although an enemy type might always "prefer" to attack the farthest unit, if they happen to be next to another unit they might go for a bite... Glitch or feature? Hard to say, and it makes it feel like the AI is unpredictable, which isn't great in a game where you don't have healing.Finally, the actual glitches. I've on many occasions had AOE attack indicators just not go away even after the attack has finished. They then start to block the view of real AOE attacks, and I have to guess based on my memory of the attack's shape where the safe zones are... yeah. Less frequent but equally frustrating glitches include getting melee attacked randomly from across the map, enemies attacking on the same turn that they spawn (not supposed to happen - or so I think...) and visual glitches of enemies suddenly turning 10x their normal size (mostly funny).That isn't to say the gameplay is all frustrating. In fact, I actually like it. The timeline system is simple enough to grasp intuitively while allowing for a lot of complexity by manipulating the move order of the enemy and your units. But the lack of QoL made me finally quit on the 4th week where my head at last started to explode under the sheer amount of stuff I had to remember.6/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Othercide

_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty torn on whether or not to recommend this game.  I'm a lover of tactics and strategy games, and Othercide has some really positive qualities that make it really stand out in that genre - but the systems outside of the actual combat just kill this game for me.  The initiative and action point system is phenomenal, and I love the different abilities the daughters have.  Every decision point you reach have so many cool considerations to take into account.  You really have a lot of choices around managing resources and manipulating/working around the initiative system.  I've really enjoyed every combat I've played.But then the outside system just ruins the entire experience, with the main sticking point being that your daughters cant heal.  They'll gain hp when they level up, but outside of that, you have to sacrifice another daughter of equal or higher level.  Initially, I thought this was a cool aspect of the game, because you had to consider your actions with even more thoughtfulness.  Because damage is permanent, it means that you can't dismiss weaker enemies that do slightly lesser damage - which means literally every enemy is a real threat.What I found myself doing however, was spending time trying to raise daughters just for the purpose of eventually sacrificing them for another.  This restricted me from actually developing any characters because most of my time was spent managing my roster and figuring out how to keep everyone's level the same so that I could be ready to level up someone to heal another daughter.While an interesting idea, having to sac an equal level daughter just turns the game into this awkward character roster manager thing that isn't really fun to maintain.  While I get that this game is supposed to feel hopeless and brooding and dark or whatever, it just gets boring when my moments in between fights are spent having to manage xp distribution and team composition, just for the ability to heal a character.TLDR:  The combat is incredibly fun, but the progression systems you have to deal with along the way bogs it down and turns the whole experience into an unavoidable chore.  It's not a hardcore challenge or anything... its just boring.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this was a neat little tactics game with a cool aesthetic. It wasn't as in depth as some other strategy games but it has a neat mechanic with the timeline for player/enemy actions. Don't get me wrong, there is still plenty of strategy to the fights and bosses. The game did get easier for me once I figured out what skills work best and can be exploited to take down bosses with relative ease. I don't know how much replay value I'll get out of it. For myself not much, but others may do a run from level one with only so many perks to do a self imposed hard mode. I got it for 20% off and for how much time/fun I got out of it I'd say it was well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: For the price, it's a good game.My Score: 7.5/10Pros:- Amazing boss fights- Actually hard, but failing makes the next try easier- Timeline combat is interesting- Music- Art StyleCons:- Lacks complexity- Repetitive- Last boss feels rushed- Meh storyRegarding  each point:1) The boss fights are great, bosses have phases which makes them increasingly harder as the fight goes on and keeps the fight interesting for the whole duration of the fight.2) The game is hard. While the lack of difficulty setting is a cons, the fact that when you fail, you can come back with more stuff to make it easier is great. When you lose, you restart the game and add "remembrance" points to your pool of "remembrance" points which you can reserve to unlock powerful bonuses, resurrect dead characters or skip bosses. This means that eventually, everyone will succeed at the game.3) Timeline combat mechanic is interesting, not much more to say about it. It's different from other turn based games.4) Great music, especially for the boss fights.5) Art style is great. It fits the ambiance and music.6) Lack of complexity is just that the game is very basic when it comes to turn base combat, beside the timeline mechanic. There is no elevation, no positional advantage outside some line of sight, no crowd control outside of delaying an enemy turn and some displacement, no fog of war and no consumables or limited use abilities beside abilities with health cost.7) Repetitive is basically the direct result of the lack of complexity. The bosses keeps it fresh enough, but the rest of the fights become really repetitive, especially when there are only 4 different type of battles and the majority of the time it's only going to be a "hunt" type which is to just kill everything on the map.8) Last boss is kinda disappointing. The first 3 phases are so easy you won't even take any damage, the last 2 phases change the boss into a completely unfun annoy fest because of the combination of 4 of its mechanics. Firstly, he will counter a melee attack, pushing your character back until you hit a wall or character, every time it gets its turn, which by itself is fine but combined with the rest, it makes it really annoying. Secondly, he gets its turn really fast so you absolutely need a specific trait that reduce the delay between your characters turn in order to actually be able to actually play against this boss. Thirdly, he teleport to your furthest character every turn, making your melee waste most of their turn on moving around to hit the boss, combined with the other 2 points, this is super lame. Lastly, he also delay each of your characters turn occasionally, adding insult to injury. Now, all of this taken into consideration... you can actually just cheese the boss by using one single overpowered ability that basically give you 19 turns on one of your character for free, which is more than enough to kill the boss by just spamming that character's attack on it until the boss dies. It's also possible to just outright kill the boss before he can even get a first turn with a well tailored team like I had on my second time I killed the boss.9) There really isn't any story here. You get a few tidbits to give you the basic of the story theme and who's who, but it doesn't explain much of anything regarding the world and your characters.

_childDocuments_.review: The core idea of the game, aka the timeline combat, is good, but unfortunately there's a lot of basic mistakes that make the game a drag.For starter, all your gals look the same. The sacrifice mechanic would be mildly interesting if you actually remembered who you're sacrificing to save whom. This is not the case here.The biggest flaw is the boring repetition. Three classes that have VERY few customization options is, frankly, a bit pathetic. But what really killed the game for me is when I noticed the fights I was getting into were not procedurally generated. Sure, on paper it's a good idea to ensure that the difficulty is not dialed down or dialed up too much. On practice I'm sick of getting into the exact same fight several times a "week" because the developers barely bothered to come up with 5 differents types. Once you know the drill the fights get really trivial.The UI in general is also frustrating to go through. Some of the boss's skills are very confusing and must be experienced to fully understand. As for the combat and game play it has one of the most refreshing takes in a turn based system. Rather than focusing on chances to hit or micromanaging ability charges and cool downs. Othercide uses an initiative system emphasizing risk and reward. Do you take the extra action to kill an enemy but as a result have your unit unable to move for twice as long? _childDocuments_.review: Othercide is one of those games that edges into the realms of playable more on the virtue of its mood than any element of good or fun gameplay.The positives of this game pretty much solely focus on the cool gameplay ideas and themes. Having to sacrifice units to heal others is a novel concept and has great room for application in the genre. especially when you've nurtured and grown attached to your units. The setting in general is intriguing, if a little edgy and you definitely want to learn more about the world(even if it feels there isn't the deepest story in gaming history going on). The Red Splash noir design is very effective, and definitely works well with the games themes although I can see why it would put some people off who have difficulty focusing on cluttered black and white environments. On the other hand the gameplay doesn't really back this up. Even though othercide is a complicated game it quickly becomes apparent none of the systems involved are very deep. Even the active timeline system, which is a very novel concept in the genre often ultimately boils down to a more complicated crowd control system. Pushing enemies up in the timeline of events is rewarded on this game but ultimately it's no different from more primitive titles where you'd stun an enemy to have it act later, the timeline system is simply more granular and allows for a few other mechanics such as delayed actions and reaction shots.Customisation of your units is very limited, cosmetically and gameplay wise. There's not really much interaction with traits as a player unless you've played the game a lot and are willing to grind good ones out. Equippable buffs are semi randomly assigned and there's a lot of filler garbage that drops(so many 5% crit chance items). You can only assign 1 to a skill and few skills in the early game really interact with each other so there's no interesting gameplay choices here. Even the meta game elements are pretty shallow, there's some useful items you can acquire between runs but there's an obvious heirarchy of usefulness so it lacks choice.There's a lot of people mentioning the game is hard, ultimately I don't think this is true, it's just very stingy with opportunity to learn. The bosses are extreme difficulty spikes in comparison to the default enemies. They also have much more complicated behaviour, way more health/defense/life and tons of mobility. You often need specific strategies to counter them. Meanwhile the attack patterns of the standard enemies teaches you nothing about facing the bosses, it's very bread and butter gameplay, mostly about paying attention to zones of threat and ranging enemies. Compare it to having to play and hour of tic tac toe to be allowed 10 minutes of golf. You'll get good at tic tac toe fast while you're still learning golfs basics.Ultimately I think if you're a hardcore tbs gamer who's really lacking games to play you might enjoy this. There's also the possibility they'll keep developing it and it'll turn into something quite special. The possibility is definitely there. Right now though this is complicated not complex game that doesn't really respect your time and has too many rough edges it's eager to rub against you.

_childDocuments_.review: *Post Completion*Othercide is a fresh breath of darkness. In this title, you engage in one narrative while earning tidbits of another. As you play, you pick up tidbits, like fragments of a stained glass mural; scattered, unordered, pieces missing. Eventually, the pile of glass re-organizes itself in three frames.On the left, the protagonist. On the right, the victim. Above, the end of both, a grotesque, nebulous egg.When you play this game, think back on chess. It has clear rules, the attack patterns of the pieces can be known, and with some experience one can predict the flow of battle and emerge triumphant.I challenge you, new player. Do what I did. Finish the game in 5 recollections. This game is punishing, to be sure, but once you have learned how the pieces move the game changes from a brutal grind to a journey for discovery.*First Impression*This game feels as punishing as X-Com, but it is not.In X-Com, you toil for hours just to get your game going. Then, you miss an 80% chance to snipe that chosen, you party wipe and go downhill from there. In Othercide, you party wipe, take your upgrades and begin again. You are told "You will fail..." thats the same as Xcom. In addition you are told "and that's ok. You must fail so that you can prevail". This game has taken the top rank in my book for strategy games. I'm no completionist, but I will unlock every achievement!

_childDocuments_.review: XCOM Roguelite with a Lovecraftian theme.PROS:- You can tailor combat to your own style and difficulty preferences. Between four unique classes, dozens of mods for up to six attacks on each one, and the Rememberance system that buffs various components of your Daughters, you can make this game as difficult or easy as you'd like.- Between the Codex and in-fight enemy information, you'll have very few surprises regarding what you're about to face. Combat is predictable.- Losses are painful but not devastating, and the Recollection system allows you to "reset" your mistakes at the cost of repeating previous combat.- Between Rememberances and the lack of a penalty for starting a new Recollection, the game actively pushes you towards completion.- Despite the black and white aesthetic, the game is fairly pretty.CONS:- Because the game is only as hard as you make it, taking advantage of all your resources leads to a pretty easy experience. Rememberances are trivial to acquire and equip and, with no penalty for starting new Recollections, you can outlevel the enemies you face from almost the beginning of the game.- Combat doesn't seem to have been balanced around Soulslingers. The optimal strategy is largely to throw a group of 'slingers into the middle of a room, wait for enemies to run at you, then shoot them. Effective, satisfying, and boring as hell.- The atmosphere, while pretty, made it difficult to see the battlefield at times. When everything is colored from a gray pallet and dropped onto a gray pallet, you miss things.- While completely fine 95% of the time, this game can be buggy as hell. Enemy movement not displaying, enemies themselves not displaying, enemy AOE attack ranges not disappearing from the map after the attack fires off, and a few others, make it difficult to count on a consistent experience.Othercide is a good RTS and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys a good strategy game, but the lack of punishment for utilizing everything the game gives you, as well as a lack of replayability, keeps it from being great.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a roguelike and I wouldn't even call it a roguelite. Maybe a better fitting genre would be something like ?✔ there are no options for healing, which frees you from the common trope in tactical games of spending time on constantly keeping your gals at max life✔ customization of active skills with socketable upgrades❔ you can very easily carry over your team across runs, with their levels and gained perks, which is unique in this kind of genre and gives a sense of progression when you effortlessly destroy what posed challenge before. Basically you can play using the same characters most of the time and only spawn others as backup when one dies or you need a bigger team❔ exactly three classes of characters, although quite different from each other. Three is in majority of the cases also you team limit✘ random mechanics (damage range, dodge, crit chance, enemy spawn location) in an extremely health pool-based game (you don't receive any healing in or between fights, unless you play easy mode or sacrifice you other characters of the same power, which seemed mostly pointless - it's even more grind to keep them leveled so they can be used as a health potion)✘ strong incentive to play safe and never let loose to have fun✘ enemies can appear out of nowhere quickly and do massive damage before you can react✘ places where enemies will soon appear block your path. No you cannot run past them, these are random obstacles that can f*** you up. This killed my character once✘ you are supposed to grind perma-progression tokens, for major benefits in future runs, which you get 25 for every combat. And this truly is a stupid grind that you cannot  speed up. You can attack the floor boss sooner... but then you lose out on the easy tokens you could get on the floor from normal combat. On the next floor the fights are more difficult and you still get +25 tokens for each. The best strategy is obvious: grind simple fights, kill your team, start a new run with your overleveled team, rinse and repeat. You don't even get the skipped tokens for killing the boss of the floor. I cannot comprehend why it's like this✘ lack of attack of opportunity of some kind in tactical games annoys me. Enemies can just run past your melee gals, who cares? Well, it kind of exists here, but you pay with health on each use so its strongly disincentivized✘ the game bugged out on a mission, during which each girl has to kill some enemies to score points. Getting all points forces them out of the battlefield. There were no more enemies, no more were spawning and I was missing a single point. So the only way forward was to abandon her. I found reports of this on the web and looks like nothing has been done to fix this for years. Maybe it's a design decision and you are supposed to count exactly how many points each enemy gives, but that would make it even worseSo did I want to grind even more to ressurect her just to grind more to kill next boss and then die when the enemies became too strong ( or more likely the total damage I obtained finally caught up to me) so that I can start the entire process again and do the same stuff? NoOh and one more thing for clarity: you could potentially run multiple teams at the same time, thus having backup  ready to be quaffed. This way you can prolong your run. I found this strategy to be much slower for the reasons mentioned above about how the perma-progression: it's much better to have faster feedback loops from your perma-boosts. And you don't have to do the same things  - there is already far too much repetition in this game anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid turn-based tactics game with RPG and roguelite elements. Worth mentioning that even in a genre that is notorious for being difficult, this game in particular is quite hard, even on the "easy" mode. That being said, you are given all of the tools you need to succeed (eventually) and you can learn enemy patterns / behaviors as you go along. Much like other games in the genre, failure is expected and you probably shouldn't get too attached to any set of characters.The main gimmick involves replaying the stages to unlock meta-currency, and unlocking specific uses for said currency that make the next run stronger. You'll become objectively stronger through those means, and subjectively the game becomes easier from improved knowledge. Fortunately, once you reach the boss of a chapter, you can skip right to that boss on your next playthrough, so progress within chapters can feel slow at first, but you'll get to a point where you can comfortably chunk away at the earlier levels to buff up your characters and retry the boss.I mentioned earlier to not get too attached to any characters, but that's a bit of a lie. You can actually resurrect your units between levels, and they even persist in the resurrection pool / graveyard between playthroughs, so if you want, it's certainly possible to resurrect the same "core" between cycles. Since units gain traits based on their participation in battles, this is almost a necessity as you continue on.The difficulty is pretty spiky, with each chapter increasing in difficulty by a significant amount, and each boss being a suitably challenging end-cap to make sure you're actually ready for the next chapter (spoilers, you probably aren't). With those spikes come troughs though, and I'll say that in my experience character levels and knowledge make an enormous difference in power levels to the point that you will be trivializing earlier content faster than you'd expect.As for non-gameplay elements: the screenshots should be enough to communicate that this game has a morbidly gorgeous art style, evoking some grotesque imagery in its boss / enemy design, and even the levels feature some horror elements in the design like oversized corpses forming a landscape in a dull void. You'll either love or hate the art style / color choice, but for me personally I couldn't get enough of it. The daughters look a little goofy by comparison though, and I wish there was a way to randomize the looks or otherwise customize their appearance some. The game also features an excellent soundtrack which it makes great use of to build tension and communicate the weight of some heavy moments e.g. boss fights, phase changes, and "strong enemy" spawns.Overall, a very good game if you enjoy XCOM and the like. Minor gripes include achievement hunting being a bit of a grind-fest if you're going for 100%, and somewhat of a lack of replayability once you've "beaten" a run. To me, it's better to think of the game's progression as taking roguelite elements rather than that the game as a whole is intended to be a roguelite. That is, there's meta-progression and repetition, but the overarching game doesn't seem like it was intended to be something you play through over and over once you beat the final boss. Frequently goes on sale and very much worth it when it does. If you're a fan of the genre, give it a try. If you're new to the genre, be prepared for a very difficult experience with a high learning curve and not much in the way of forgiveness, and honestly I'd suggest playing a more simple / easy TRPG before this one to see if this type of game is for you. If you're not a fan of the genre or have played games like XCOM, Darkest Dungeon, etc and didn't enjoy them, this probably isn't going to win you over unless you're a massive sucker for the art style.

_childDocuments_.review: I think I never played a game before where 4 hours felt like 40.Best analogy I can come up with is: it's like when you're trying to climb a ladder and at some point all the steps ahead of you are just broken. And to fix it you have to jump down the ladder because for reaching that height someone dropped you the missing steps on the ladder at that point. Then you can climb up there again until you reach such a point with missing steps again. All you have to do is jump down again and pick up your new steps...It's so blatantly obvious that someone was having this idea of the progression mechanic in this game and in order for it to get used they needed to enforce it somehow.What this game is trying to sell as "tactics" is a bad joke. After 4h of gameplay I can totally see the points @Nombly made with their review.I just had gotten a couple of gals to level 2. It was day 3. I did a mission rated as hard before with 3. I read that doing rescue missions gives you the opportunity to resurrect one of your gals in case they die. I went in there with 3 gals. The level spawned literally 20 enemies in my face. It was impossible to do. Abandoning the mission kills all your gals in that mission too. Cool. I'm definitely coming back to this experience. Not. The game tells you it wants you to fail. And come back and try again. Ok cool but you just showed me that there will always be situations where there is no problem to solve for me because it's just a setup to fail. Why would I come back to trying to solve a puzzle that's just unsolvable for me at that point in time? You really expect me to grind to a point where I realize I have to start over just to solve that specific challenge the next time around - maybe?Games, especially very difficult ones, should be designed in a way where the player has multiple ways of solving a problem. Not plenty of problems that are all solved in the exact same way.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I really like the game. The gameplay itself is great. Exactly what I want form a turn based strategy game where you have a squad of fighters. A lot of people compare it to Xcom. It's no surprise then that I will also do that (You'll see I have played a lot of Xcom 1 and 2).Visually, a lot of people like it. See the screenshots and trailer to see if it's your thing. Personally, it doesn't do much for me both negatively or positively.Audio is great. Sound effects, voice acting and the music as well are all fine. However, the voice lines do get repetitive pretty quick.Tactically, the game is similar and does scratch the same itch as Xcom. However:- There are only a few classes, and not many skills per class. Basically, you have less tools. Also, because there is no elevation mechanic, and no cover mechanic, and no items to bring, it's a lot simpler.- Therefore, a lot more important to make correct decisions. It does get hard if you just mess around. There is "dream" option, but if you struggle with X-com or similar games on normal difficulty, you're not going to like this. Or at least you're going to die a lot.- The timeline mechanic is actually GREAT and it allows for more planning, tactics and tricks then simple turn-based. Wonderfully done.Now, I do want to debunk some things:- I see a lot of people claim "grind grind grind" for heals. This is not (entirely) true. Basically, git gud (no joke). This is why your decisions are important. IF you screw up too much, or IF you play "casually", you will lose a lot of health and your daughters WILL die because you can't heal them.- But I played the game for the first time, and I reached the first boss the 1st round, the third boss the 2nd round, and I'm doing quite well in my 3rd round where I'm sure I'll at least reach the fourth boss (there are 5).- For every boss you kill, you can get 1 resurrection on ALL your next campaigns. And you can get resurrections throughout the whole game (if you don't skip parts). I've just done the third boss and I've resurrected both my A-teams from the 1st and 2nd campaign. You CAN (without grinding) make a perfectly healthy, strong team of the daughters you're attached to.Now there are some negatives as well. First of all the UI seems not be tested properly. EVER.- In the beginning it feels super clunky. Oftentimes you have to click multiple different buttons where there should have been no need. ESC doesn't work to cancel. It opens the menu screen. (cancel is C).- Numbers on the UI are wrong. They don't show all boosts or debuffs. Just base stats/damage.- Some things are not in the UI at all. A lot of stats of your units (traits, equipped buffs, etc.) can't be seen or found anywhere when you're inside a mission. Some of which are really important, such as "does 40% damage buff on adjacent units" and such.- Instead of giving tooltips, the game makes you press every skill and every unit to check what they do (and then you have to cancel out again).- You do get used to it, but it's the main problem with this game for me.Repetiton:- The game is, luckily, not that long. I am still enjoying but I can see that if you have played through fully, you're done. There is no reason to restart unless you're REALLY enjoying it. But there is no higher/lower difficulty, no new units to discover, no this or that choices, no nothing that can result in a different type of campaign. They're all the same.- EDIT: The final boss is quite the pain in the ass and a pretty unfair. Luckily, if you die to the boss, you can restart AFTER the previous boss so it's not that bad (you don't have to repeat the game). But damn... that guy made me mad a few times.Devs:- I've seen a lot of messages on the forum of devs saying "we'll look into this or that" and they never did. And then they abandoned the game without getting rid of the kinks.Is it worth it? In the end, yes, if you LIKE tactical games AND are at least somewhat skilled at them, you'll enjoy it. If you're not that skilled, or you want a chill game, don't buy this.The game does provide a well thought out tactical system with interesting units and possibilities. By the time you've seen all of it, you're probably just about done with the game anyway. I would guess 25 hours or so? (EDIT: Turned out to be 35 hours) Which is reasonable for this price. Basically, it's "fun till you get sick of it".I'm not sick of it yet, so I'm happy to say I got my money's worth.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello o/ This is my first time trying to do a review so I apologize in advance for my poor english and if my rumbling is incoherent. Othercide is a really cool game so far for me (I went to the 4th boss), but it's not for everyone, even if you love turn-based tactics game. The game is really hard, but the difficulty doesn't come from stupidly hard ennemies with inflated stats but from the fact that every mistakes you make matters. The only way to heal a unit is to sacrifice an other on the same level or higher so you have to avoid to take any hits as much as possible. If a unit dies in combat, it's gone forever, unless you use a precious token to revive it which are only obtainable after doing a Rescue mission (I only got one mission after playing 17h so I don't know if my luck is bad or if they are really scarce) that are quite difficult (I got stomped on the only one I got) so you shouldn't rely on it to much. You can also buy some with a special currency (more details latter) but know that one token is unlocked in the shop after discovering a boss for the first time( one boss = one chapter and you have 5 bosses as far as I know).The key to victory and to avoid unecessary restart is knowledge and how you use it. If you go blind for maxium suffering and pleasure, you'll have to gather information as fast as possible and test it in order to  understand how the IA of the ennemies work (the Codex give you a general idea of that to help you), how their skills work and how yours work aswell. It's important to remember these key informations to progress smootlhy into the game.Regarding the gameplay in itself, it's fairly basic with a timeline to show you the turn order, when the skills are going to active / up to when they are active etc...You have 3 starting classes and an other one you'll unlock after progressing in the story that receive a new skill at level 3 5 10 and idk since my highest level is 11. Each timer you earn a new skill, you'll have to make a choice between 2 abilities that are most of the time quite usefull so it's up to you to decide, regarding your main comp, you play style etc...Now I'm going to talk about one of the core mecanic of this game: when you die to a boss you have to start from the beginning ( you can chose to do so without dying but Idk how it works since I never chose that option). The game is encouraging you to fail in the way that every time you clear a mission ( that isn't a boss mission) you'll get 25 points of a special currency. When you restart, that number will be added to your current pool (which starts at 0) and that will allow you to buy numerous bonuses that will help you to progress. In my opinion it's a double edge sword because if you fail a lot, the game will look borring after dying over and over if you can't assimilate the game's mecanics. But it also serves as a motivation to do your best every time and it adds tention to boss fight. You have to put efforts into the game to truly enjoy it in my opinion. Regarding the art direction and the music, it's black and white with a hint of red for some key elements. The music isn't the selling point of that game(you still have a few bangers) but it serves its purpose and add to the heavy atmosphere of the game.Now I'm going to talk about some of the negative aspects of the game. Firstly, the game lack some polishing. It's a common occurence to have some UI issues when you have a lot of traits / skills / characters. The targetting system may decide to be a ***** on some occasions which can be quite frustrating and it lacks some QoL. For exemple you can't name a character after seeing what it looks like (it's dumb but I find it meh), you can't sort your characters, you can't chose the position of your units at the beginning of a mission. These are smalls things I thought it was worth it to mention them. Also after doing missions of the same category in the same chapter, you may found that some of them are the exact same. For some people it might be a deterrent to "do the same thing" but in my oponion it's a good way to see how efficiently your skill is progressing. To conclude, I'm would like to apologize  again since It's my first time trying to do a review. Also sorry in advance for my poor english. What I wanted to convey through my rumbling is that Othercide has a lot of good points and is truly enjoyable but only if you put the efforts to learn how the game works. The game expects you to die and will "reward" you for that, but it's up to you to do the very best to progress as far as possible to make your subsequents tries smoother with the knowledge you'll accumulated (especially for bosses).  The game will reward you if you can gather datas and process them fast and will punish you for your "mistakes". It's up to you to learn from them and grow stronger so that you can clear the game before getting burned out (which fits the theme of game nicely ngl).

_childDocuments_.review: With the action point system, tactics wise its way better than any other turn based strategy game. In this review I will be comparing this game to Xcom since it is a very common and known tbs game.The amount of different choices one can make in Othercide is quite limited and also a lot less forgiving. This makes this game seem more like a chess puzzle where there might only be one good move or at most a few decent ones and making a wrong one will heavily hinder the continuation of the run. Where as in Xcom and other tbs games things happen turn to turn battle to battle. This makes these games more like a simple board game where almost every decision you make is equally good and you have much more flexibility due to the slight rng (putting all your guys into cover and save scumming until your shots hit, doesn't really matter what you research in base / build since its all good and you will have it all eventually).While the amount of options at the beginning of the game might seem limited. Later on your sisters will get stronger and as a result open up new skill sets which heavily compliment the skill sets of other sisters.The only way to move forward and get stronger is to have a good deal of your sisters perish (However its okay to get attached to some sisters since you can bring a few of them back from the dead. Where in Xcom losing your best squad will probably spell defeat and halt or at the very least put a huge screw in your campaign.The repetition of losing and starting from square one with slight bonuses and a bunch of sisters in your graveyard might feel repetitive to some. But that's because Othercide is a roguelite, its not meant to be played for extensive periods of time, you play one run and do another later on.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game, accompanied by elegant artstyle and intense boss battle (really gets your adrenaline running).Gameplay - turn-based roguelike game (similar to x-com); fairly difficult during the first few playthroughs, it can become a grind if you keep losing, but you can tune up the game speed to hasten the process (wouldn't recommend it as it might ruin the mood for the game). Music - The atmospheric gloomy music is pretty good, but I'm particularly fond of the bossfight soundtrack, really gets your blood-boiling. On that note, each vocal soundtrack is addressed to a particular character(s) in game, which means it gets more meaningful once you completed the game and listen to the soundtrack again. Story - The story of the game can be slightly confusing at first, but once you go through the codex and read the entries, along with the cutscenes of the game you will understand it eventually. It's not a long story, but it is heartbreaking and hauntingly beautiful. Voice Acting - It's good, not really an expert here but it's good. If I'm not wrong the Mother's voice actor is the same as the Firekeeper in DS3. Overall, I give it a 8.5/10 at the moment, mainly because its lack of replay value and some game-breaking bugs that have been encountered by some players (like seriously If I had encountered the same bugs I might stop playing for a while). Will give it a 9 once the bugs are fixed. Definitely recommend buying it, can be a bit pricey but I do think it's worth every penny. Kudos to you, Lightbulb Crew (but seriously please fix the bug ASAP).

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR: Buy Othercide if you recognize this genre/family of genres and you like these kinds of games! If you like games along these lines and you're just not sure if it's worth it (the $30+ price tag): IT ABSOLUTELY IS! Especially on any % sale.Now for people that are newer to this kind of game: rouge-like, turn-based, difficult, strategy games (this is the family of genres I was talking about) I ask you to please read a little of the following to see if you might love this game.First I have to disclose that this game is exceptionally hard, it's designed to be this difficult. You need to be willing to endure the punishment and the difficulty without ending up being peeved is basically the relevance of what I am saying. Though before you decide the difficulty is a turn off, I want to say that the mechanics are not complicated necessarily and the game is not "BS" that is not were the difficulty comes from. The "difficulty" is more relative to what one might expect from a game in general and even a game in this genre. Othercide is unique in a awesome way. There are many situations were you are not expected to succeed. You cannot win in every scenario and I will get into this further in the review. The game also makes this very clear and it works into the story and lore of the game in an excellent way.If you buy the game I hope you enjoy it and I think it is extremely enjoyable if you can appreciate the mechanics, the difficulty, and how beautifully those 2 things that make up the game-play work with the lore and the story in the game. I just don't want anyone to buy the game, not like it, and leave a negative review if their only reason for disliking it is that they did not like the punishing brutal system the game has. Because I think the brutality is partially what makes the game very special. I understand some players just don't fancy this style of game so while I want to recommend the game, cause I like it a lot, I also want to save players like that the trouble and the money. I'll be starting with were the difficulty comes from. The game like I said is designed to be very hard. The game itself explains this quite well. "Some of your daughters will die" or some variation of that is an idea/phrase repeated often. First you need to understand that Othercide is a turn-based strategy game and it's like a rouge-like that is played in "Runs". You build up your strength from learning the game (of course) as well as unlocking new stuff in your runs by making progress further and further into the game. The "difficulty" comes from the sensation of dying and losing. But like I said the game is based on "Runs" and you build on yourself, your failures, to do better every run. There are some cases were you literally cannot play it well enough to win at your current strength. By failing you gain more resources at your disposable for the next run. There is a mechanic were when your daughters die they go to a "Cemetery" and they can later be resurrected at a price (in another run if you want). The price is a moral one, you can do rescue missions to save an innocent life and after you save them you can either set them free and receive a useful resource or you can sacrifice them to bring back a fallen daughter. Also the only way to heal a daughter is between missions and it requires you sacrifice another daughter. It's worth mentioning you can also create new daughters and each daughter needs to be leveled up. If you actually read this far I recommend watching the trailer and reading some other reviews if you haven't already because it will help you understand what the heck I am talking about. Anyway choices like this are among the many interesting mechanics in the game. Daughters are effectively like clones and are disposable. It really fits into the story and makes you feel the struggle of what the main character is trying to achieve all by themselves. It really is you against the world. But by these mechanics make some daughters permanent even when they die. Any levelup progress is saved when you revive them. So you can pick certain daughters to bring back so your run will be stronger then say when you first played and had all level 1 daughters. So this "difficulty" mainly comes from people not enjoying losing and dying. But it's also really fun to lose and lose and lose because in Othercide, what does not kill you permanently makes you stronger.As a final series of little notes I just want to say again that the game is super cool the story is super cool and I will probably edit this review later to make it more concise cause near the end I starting going off about the mechanics because I want to share it with people and I hope it can encourage them to experience it for themselves by getting the game. Many people already mentioned in reviews that the Music is excellent and the atmosphere is good so I focused on the parts people did not go into too much detail on. But I wanted to bring it up because yes the music and the visuals are super well done and the style is real. Lastly someone mentioned that the levels are repeated a lot. That is because if you fail completely the run restarts and you go back in time. You can still revive dead daughters and stuff but it makes it so that you do the same levels again. This helps you master strategy for certain levels and you unlock more buy getting further into the game/story. It's like a time rewind ability, you can do the same task again but now with more knowledge.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a few minor interface tweaks I'd make, but overall this game comes out massively in creditFor a start, the game does a lot to keep things simple. The abilities revolve primarily around dealing or avoiding damage; you don't have to worry about things like different damage types, resistances, attack speed, things like that. The abilities are pretty simple to understand; you target an enemy, it takes damage, you target an area, enemies in it take damage, you dash to an enemy and it takes damage. There's no complicated formulas to understand for your stats; armour is flat damage reduction on damage taken, damage bonus is flat damage increase on each hit, dodge chance is chance to dodge a hit. All this adds up to you being able to very much focus on what you're doing and not have to worry too much about how it's all working under the hoodDespite having pretty simple mechanics, there's actually a lot of depth to the strategising, and you'll probably go through several iterations of suddenly realising why something is more viable than you originally thought it was. You can mix and match sometimes in ways that the community will often discourage you from doing, because when you find what's working for you there's a lot you can do to commit to it. Because there's something of a learning curve I'd recommend first playing for a bit on Dream mode so you can get used to the mechanics, but do play it on Nightmare once you've got the hang of it, because without the sacrifice mechanic you are missing a big part of the gameplay experienceEnemy behaviours are described in the codex, you are free to see the description of an enemy's abilities, you can see exactly when on the initiative queue enemies will take their turns, hovering over an enemy shows you exactly how far it can move. Altogether this means that the game is never throwing you a curveball, you're never going to be blindsided by not knowing how the enemy AI works or what they can do, it gives you all the information to make an informed decision so that your victories and losses are never based on luck, but effective strategising on your own meritsThis game is especially good if, like me, you've been having trouble committing to a game for long at a time. I hadn't been able to do more than about half an hour at a push in any game before it started to feel like a slog for quite a while and I was really worried that games were going to have to stop being part of my life. This game has fixed that for me. Not because it's just so good it renewed my addiction (although it is crackerjack), but because each mission can be wrapped up in about ten or twenty minutes. I can sit down for a gameplay session and do a mission or two before I get bored, then close the game still ready for more. Often I'll come back to it again later that day, so I've been managing to get a lot more playtime than I have for quite a while. It's a game that doesn't require a huge time commitment on your partSomething I personally like, although it might not be for everyone, is that this game adopts the Dark Souls approach to storytelling, i.e. the sequence of events is fairly straightforward, but understanding it will require reading item descriptions. If you don't follow the story that's okay, it isn't full of twists and turns that require careful attention, it's a simple sequence of events contextualised by worldbuilding revealed through item descriptionsThe use of a timeline as opposed to the more traditional stack based model for the initiative queue is an interesting mechanic which allows for a much more dynamic take on the turn-based strategy genre. The requirement to sacrifice Daughters in order to heal each other is an interesting mechanic as well, making you really think about what you're doing, and the fact that sacrificing Daughters not only heals the others but actually improves them adds another dimension to itThis game is described as having roguelike elements and I think it's important to keep that wording in mind. It's not a roguelike, I wouldn't even call it a roguelite, it HAS roguelike elements. It has permadeath of a sort (you don't really have "your character" so when Daughters die that's not necessarily game over, but you can fail a run and have to restart). An era could be thought of as being like a level, with a series of rooms (represented here by synapses), some of which are optional, and a boss at the end. Don't go into this expecting a huge amount in terms of the roguelike experience, this game isn't trying to emulate roguelikes, they just picked a couple of the features they thought served the experience well and used themI really like a lot of the aesthetic choices in this game. The monochromatic visual style is great, helping to create a feeling of despair but not hopelessness, with splashes of red thrown in as if to signify that the Mother and her Daughters are the return of colour to this dim and desperate world. The form and function of the characters has clearly had a lot of thought put into how it's supposed to make you feel (e.g. how Bright Souls are curled into a foetal position, glide slowly as they move, and dissolve from view when they leave, creating a feeling of them being meek and fragile beings). The fact that your units are all female allows them to be referred to as "she" and "her" rather than "they", which makes them feel a little bit more personal; I don't know whether that was intentional or just a happy side effect of an aesthetic gimmick, but given that this is a game that relies heavily on sacrifice and acquiring traits to make the Daughters feel unique, I think it's brilliant. I do also like that the Daughters are all female; it's not a massively deep gimmick, but at least it's something to add a little bit of flavour to it, rather than leaving them feeling like Generic Faceless Army. The Daughters also aren't sexualised at all, there's no bikini armour, huge breasts or seductive poses, similarly there's no attempt to use them being female as commentary about men vs women; it doesn't feel like it's being used for anything, it's just a neat little quirk. I like the naming conventions for the Daughters as well, they're all given names like "Celeste", "Temperance", "Harmony", I think it fits the aesthetic style really well (although you can rename your Daughters if you don't like those names). Sorry for rambling here, I just really love it when aesthetics get proper consideration and this game has done that in bucketsAll in all a solid pick and I'm very glad I got it, it was worth every penny

_childDocuments_.review: I almost fell in love with it from the moment I got to the main menu. It's not every day a game greets you with a metal song, and a really good one at that. With a cool animated screen in the background, too.Stylistically, it's awesome. I can't help thinking of it as the Dark Souls of XCOM-likes. Grim, oppressive setting. World stuck in an unnatural state. Undead bosses with some lore. No colors except black, white, and red. No healing except through sacrifice of daughters (your units) of equal or higher level. Although levelups restore some health by the amount your max health goes up. And if you die after reaching a boss, you can go straight to him on your next run, no need to complete any other levels to get back there.Othercide is a roguelike with progression "checkpoints". The further you get, the more items become available to you that can be activated at the start of every loop, but each costs a special resource that is earned by beating levels across all runs. With that and the ability to resurrect your daughters from not only current but also previous runs, keeping their level and acquired traits (but not upgrades), you can bruteforce the game to a degree, making some things easier. I barely ever had to farm, though.Compared to XCOM, it's obviously much more about melee combat (though you and enemies have ranged units too) but there's a couple of other things that stood out to me:1) It's a lot less balanced. Some things enemies do are stupidly broken. The same goes for the things you can do. Swing at the enemy 10 times per second, anime-style? Sure, why not - completely possible with the right setup and just as deadly as it sounds. When enemies did similar things to me, I must admit, I quit out to fool the autosave (it restarts the level if you do). Just saving time, you know. Oh and yes, no manual saves obviously, since roguelike.2) As you progress through the game, you get items that let you spawn new daughters at a higher starting level. And resurrection tokens can only be earned by completing rarely available difficult missions or from unlocks at the start of runs. So in early game it's exceedingly hard to stick with the same daughters instead of swapping them out. And later on, you'll probably just want to progress already. Point is, I found it hard to get attached to any specific units. Maybe if you play the lategame for long, though... but I dunno what's there to do after beating the game except senseless farm.

_childDocuments_.review: This strategy game generally doesn't allow you to plan ahead.  It is constantly spawning enemies directly on top of you and enemy telegraphed ranges suddenly change when it reaches their turn, if you can even get the sticky, clunky controls to display the range in the first place.  If you don't 1 hit KO enemies they will take off 1/2 your health on their turn which might as well kill the character because of how inconvenient healing is.  In my 7 hour playtime I never once had an opportunity to heal a character.  Either the characters are too high level for you to have extra's to sac, or they're too low level to warrant spending resources on healing them.   The nail in the coffin was when I finally made it to the first boss and he had an auto counter for melee attacks that makes 2/3 of the classes literally unplayable.  It does this with no warning before the fight and if you chose to do all the fights like I did you might have spent 4 hours on your run just to get there.  This sums up to a game where you just slog through missions until you get big enough numbers to ignore the game entirely.  An overall very frustrating experience.
