_childDocuments_.review: I'd really like to give Per Aspera a neutral rating if steam allowed it. The fundamental issue is that Per Aspera is a wonderful piece of visual art, but a very weak game. It does the former so well it almost overwhelms all my issues with the later, but not quite. tldr at the bottom.Per Aspera nails the aesthetics of terraforming like nothing else I have ever played. Slowly seeing the Red Planet change as the icecaps melt, your structures expand, and life is introduced to the once barren landscape is a beautiful process. The planet has a sense of majesty and wonder to it that constantly reminded me of the feelings I got reading Kim Stanley Robinson's Mars trilogy (which the devs obviously take a lot of inspiration from). Lots of old science fiction ideas are wonderfully translated into a form that could only really be achieved in a video game. It's a work of art.That's also why it's so painful that the actual gameplay that drives this spectacle is so weak. Per Aspera is a supply chain logistics game where you need to manufacture increasingly complex goods and make sure those goods are delivered to the places they need to be, allowing you to progress the terraforming process. The closest reference point I have is probably the Anno franchise, and despite it's planetary scale Per Aspera does mostly feel and play more like a city builder than anything else. It even has a simple real time tactics mini-game in the same way that Anno does. There are two problems though. First, there's very little complexity to the production chains. You produce basic raw materials, a few tiers of basic refined and manufactured goods, but very little beyond that so there's little serious challenge or escalation to that part of the game. Secondly this is a logistics game where you have no control over the logistics. Goods are moved across the map autonomously by bots who shuffle them from building to building. It's incredibly inefficient and unintutive. You have extremely little control over the flow of items and what control you do have often feels more like an exploit than an intended design feature. Some of this is poorly communicated mechanics, some of it is poor design. This is frustrating in the early game, but excruciating in the late game. There is a late game tech that allows higher volume and distance transport routes, but this felt like something bolted on to stop the system completely grinding to a halt. The lack of control in logistics is also why there are no complex production chains, they would be impossible to produce with any consistency. Choosing to play on hard was a mistake that made this whole process slower and more tedious than it would otherwise have been, but didn't add any meaningful challenge. Finally the game treats Colonists in a very strange way. Colonists are what produces research, more colonists means faster research, and certain techs are gated behind getting to a certain population of colonists. But there's something about the game that makes colonists feel completely superfluous. They produce research, but other than that they play no role in the game. Unlike many similar games I felt no intrinsic satisfaction from growing the population or doing a better job supplying their needs, they were just another currency. Once the research tree is completed you can actually get rid of your colonists, they no longer do anything except place more pressure on your production network. Also overshooting your terraforming goals means nothing. I was expecting the final part of the game to involve balancing the terraforming processes you've set in motion so that temperature or atmospheric pressure don't overshoot and make the planet unlivable again. This doesn't happen, overshooting effects nothing and is not acknowledged by the game in any way. It leaves the simulation feeling hollow at the end.The main campaign is pretty good. It certainly has way more polish than you normally see in city builders, even big budget ones. In particular the voice acting is very good and elevates some of the material. Unfortunately the pacing of the campaign is pretty bad (probably made worse by playing on hard). For example early on you are given the option to nuke the ice caps to accelerate melting them. This is a cool idea, but I never got to use it because the icecaps had entirely melted by the time I had met the requirements to do this. I don't know if I was warming the planet to quickly or reaching this goal to slowly, but either way I don't feel like I could have done much to reach it faster because of how little control of the logistics you get. Later on I would have the opposite problem a number of times, where there would be some story beat that implied urgency, only for the associated mechanical goal to take months or years to be met. It would have been funny if it wasn't so tedious. The main campaign is let down by some weak world building (for example we never learn if it's normal for AI to be self-aware in this world, or if this is a special quality of the terraforming AI you play as, which makes it hard to know where we stand in relation to the rest of the characters). The best writing and world building is in the mini-narratives that can be uncovered through archaeological exploration of older mars missions. These are great, but it's extremely annoying that half of them can be covered by rising water. The DLC supposedly fixes this, but it's a really obvious flaw that should have been addressed in the base game. Really whatever strengths the campaign has are weighed down by the core game play not working as well as it should.tldr: Read Red Mars, it's amazing. Consider Per Aspera if the book grabs you for the beautiful depiction of a changing planet, but keep your expectations for the actual game low. Don't play on hard, it only makes the game more tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: Starts out really fun and the tutorial is reasonable. However when you try and establish a second landing site things get almost impossible. _childDocuments_.review: It has some problems, but its still a good choice if you like the concept of Mars, colonizing Mars, changing the surface and all that without becoming too abstract.I mean, its still based on typical production lines like aluminium, water, carbon and all that in typical scifi-esque facilities.The most abstract part is the usage of drones, which is possibly what leads to the three major problems it has:1.) Performance. It can tank quite fast and a lot due to what is going on. A lot of this possibly comes from:2.) Transportation becomes messy and inefficient fast. The priority logic isnt there, you have a ton of untransported goods you need, because your transporter moves stuff it rather shouldnt. Even if you set up your priorities correct, it might be they move stuff they arent allowed or outright bug out and drive in circles, which leads to a massive load on performance after some time.3.) Productionlogic becomes rather confusing after some time. You place down so much stuff and your "base" becomes so big wit ha gigantic and super-messy network due to the roadsystem the game has to create roads automatically. A cool tech, but not good for a good information flow to the player.Look at some of the screenshots that show a zoomed out (screenshot 4 and 8 on the store page are showing it well), to see how messy some networks become. And managing all that, is as problematic.Besides that, it has everything necessary to get a good "Terraforming Mars" feeling.Especially the presentation is unique and super nice to look at. It gets the theme across very well.On top, its still fun, is challenging, has a story that is intruiging.However, considering the negatives, i would say, get on sale.It had regular sales down to at least 50% and 30€ is def. too much. For like 15-18€ its a good pick.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good colonization game.  I am a big simulation fan--city builders, factory builders, tycoon games, etc.  Also RTS games.  I got 30 hours out of this one.  If you go into this expecting a colony sim, you'll be satisfied.  One especially nice thing is that there is a pretty clear "you beat the game" point once you have terraformed Mars, completed the story, and achieved 1 million population.  Don't expect too much from the RTS element--but it luckily does not detract from the colony sim part.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A bit on the fence on this one but I don't think I have the conscience to dislike a game I played for 6 hours on my first session. This game really suffers in a few areas. Early on you'll be overwhelmed by science jargon in your research tree, you'll also be given options for water collection. This will lead to confusion because the game doesn't tell you that you won't have access to water until much later on when most of the map will become flooded and most of your buildings will be destroyed if you don't account for it.  The rate that this all happens is determined by the amount of chemicals you've created in the atmosphere, I still haven't made sense of how to look at these levels and know what they mean. I love the science jargon but not without a tooltip to dumb things down.Micromanagement Hell - Really, the level of torture here seems intentional. You'll have to track down the tiny icons to find the building you're looking for if you want to try and make sense of why something isn't being produced at the rate it should be. You have the option to a massive list of your buildings by name but that's basically the equivalent of giving the player access to the game data as if it were an excel spreadsheet. There was a lot of answers I found by googling but a handful I couldn't find. Road upgrades for example. You have to click the upgrade button on a building, than click another building and all roads between the buildings are upgraded. Found that one out by accident.Despite all those gripes and offences I still plan on seeing where this goes, cuz I'm all about what it's trying to accomplish

_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: As it is now, I can't recommend the game, tedious is the only word I can use to describe it.Your worker/hauler units are a big part of that, they have a set lifespan, there's no way to repair them or even see the life they have remaining, and if you don't micromanage them and something else takes your attention away for a while, a large number of them could just poof out of existence while you struggle to bring your workforce back up which is very hard to do while you have such a small number of units because...The priority system is horrible, there are only two priorities to set in a game where you are making dozens of things that depend on each other, not only that, but the priority system is shared between production and building, so if you want to say, prioritize a chain of raw resources to make components to build workers, everything will get done at the same time, workers will go half-way across your colony to extract resources to bring to a solar power plant on the other side of the map and completely neglect your worker factories while you number of workers continues to dwindle.For a story focusing so much on terraforming and bringing life to Mars, the human aspect of the game is entirely overlooked, colonists are a glorified research point generator, you can starve them, get them killed, or treat them the best you ever have and nothing changes aside from a single number, it creates a really damn strong sense of ludonarrative dissonance.There are other things I don't like about the game like the combat, which is entirely without a tutorial (protip, you can move your units by clicking on the number circle) and is more simplistic than even the most basic RTS games so far, enemies blob you and unless you have more than them, you lose, there are no tactics. The performance is not very good, the game is slowing to a crawl and I'm only 5 hours in. Building icons are huge and overlapping, the UI is unresponsive, you can't select multiple buildings at a time.If the game can get some patches to address these issues it could be a lot better, the game has a good bit of potential, but as it is now it's just frustrating to try to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I played the free weekend, but won't be back. I wanted to like this game - being on the lookout for a good 'base/empire' builder in a while. Sadly, this is not it. The gameplay is tedious and some of the building strategy amounts more to puzzle solving than actual well, building. For example, you can get 'hard locked' at times because the building that produces aluminium requires aluminium... there are (thankfully) ways around this but not without spending time staring at the screen while in 16x speed.One kudos for the optimization of the game - I played at a steady 120fps with a 2080rtx throughout, and 32:9 is supported natively. Story-wise, the game starts strong and hints at "there's more to this than meet the eye" but ultimately disapoints as it's just an excuse to go from objective to objective. Ultimately, it's extremely slow paced, has a fairly clunky UI and didn't captivate me to want to make a purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A fresh take on colon sim as not yet seen before, removes all the fancy stuff in favour of much larger scale and faster pace. In a successful colony you'll build hundrets of buildings with emphasis on micro-management and logistic/economic but not too heavy emphasis to make it complicated so that you can focus on expanding out. Also the most scientific approach to Mars terraforming I've seen in video games so far. The entire map is a detailed height map of the Mars surface, with proper captions of mounts, craters, seas and the remnants of the historic Mars missions that you can go investigate.Throughout 5 phases starting with bootstrapping you'll utilize many currently investigated approaches to establishing a habitable Mars, starting with melting existing ice on the poles by a way of your choice, from building an orbital mirror network to deflect sunlight onto the poles, nuclear blasts on the poles, creating black particle dust in the atmosphere or simply importing greenhouse gases from the earth or creating them in factories on Mars from local chemical resources.Each phase presents you with goals of certain atmospheric pressure, water level, CO², O², N² %, and then % of surface covered in bacteria and/or greens and a working dipol-magnetosphere.I throughouly enjoyed it as something I havent played before. Currently there is a multiplayer coop campaign for up to 5 people in beta I hope to find the time to dip into.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly well done resource management game.The mechanics of how your building network organically grows around the planet are fun, and turning the red dirtball into a blue/green marble is quite satisfying.  While I found the AI’s inner dialog a bit preachy and angsty at times, the campaign story is a lot better than I expected and is a good complement to the game play.Overall, definitely a recommend if you enjoy city-builder games with a sci-fi flavor.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable title.  There were a few things off with the game but it was mostly fun. The logistics were a bit bizarre, but I got the hang of it. I think the most immersive breaking parts of the game was  The story would sometimes seem rushed or inconsequential. The main dialogue between you and the other characters followed a logical progression and was interesting. However, there were many times when it was out-of-place or just cringe to further some emotional arc. And you, the AI, would become grating at times with constant interrupting self-pep dialogue. The most frustrating part was the inability to filter out which buildings I was looking for. Sifting through hundreds of buildings to find one is awful. This QOL feature is sorely needed.Even though I enjoyed terraforming Mars, it felt lifeless. Surviving Mars did a much better job at making Mars feel alive, though the terraforming physics were more enjoyable and detailed in Per Aspera. In general, it's a good game. I recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a "realistic" (or at least plausible) terraforming game, which is rooted in science but without the boring bits, look no further! Per Aspera is a city builder at heart, but with the goal of changing the face of Mars forever. This means that not only you have a clear objective compared to standard city builders, but that the game slowly changes the more you progress. Mechanically it works pretty well and, except the rare frustrating occasions, it is 'smart' enough that you don't have to micromanage too much.The terraforming part adds a nice complexity without being too overwhelming. No magic knob that makes the planet habitable in three seconds, but one of the most complete and scientific approaches to the topic I've ever seen (with some licence in the actual timing, shortened for game purposes).The campaign is (at least at the beginning) mostly a way of making you follow the steps with some added flavour: you don't have to expect big events or cliffhangers (at least in the early game), but nice enough to provide some pacing.Not for those who want quick-and-fire games, but for the others it's absolutely worth it if you like the concept or city building.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: A one-of-a-kind Mars terraforming city-builder where you don't have to micromanage traffic!Pros:Easy to jump straight into gameplayIncredibly immersive story narrative with meaningful choices and multiple "endings"Mistakes made early in city planning are not penalized later when working to improve the overall cityscapeLess than 2 weeks old and already released 2 quality-of-life patches and a roadmap to further improve gameplayIndie developer is attentive to community's requests (hence the 2 QOL patches)Cons:May appear minimalist to more hardened city-builder playersCon removed with Update 2Camera took some getting used to (zoom level determines what information is displayed, which may be a personal preference problem for me)
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: There is a whole lot's of ups and downs to this game. But overall I did enjoy my 12h marathon stream session with it :D.The ups: - The story telling is doing a good job. You make decisions that seem to affect the late game (can't and won't confirm this hence spoilers) - The interface is clear enough for you to understand what needs to be done and fix it. - It runs smoothly on my linux box :D. - Terraforming is a nice visual experience.Cons: - The economy game play is broken to bits. There is no incentive to play optimized. Just spam whatever you need and daisychain botstations to your next destination. - The story telling sometimes does not keep up with things happening at the moment, - Terraforming does not feel like a task, just click a decision, get the resources, next stage.The cheeze: - Spam infinite resources by building new landing sites. Yeah, abusing this can net you disgusting base results.Eventhough I will not pick it up again for another stream (unless some significant updates have been done) I can still recommend this game, as it is the correct price for the correct experience :D.Have fun and don't spoil the story for other people ;).
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent minimalist Mars colony builder with some excellent story notes. A breath of fresh air in the city building/Mars colonizing genre. Among this games many fine points including an excellent UI and story/character development not often found in these types of games the excellent voice acting stands out as a particular high point.

_childDocuments_.review: While I've enjoyed my time playing the early stages of this game, I found way too many frustrating setbacks that stacked up so high that it makes me hesitate to boot it up again.The game is very much city-builder-lite. You're managing the gathering of resources, colonists for the research trees, and long-term goals to eventually terraform Mars. You don't have any sort of budget to keep in mind (aside from building/unit limits) so the most consideration you will have in placing buildings is putting them close enough to other buildings and having the electrical bandwidth to power them all. As someone who's not the best at this kind of genre, this is nice. It's really satisfying seeing my bases expand and potentially build new ones on other parts of the planet.The story itself has been pretty compelling as well! Not to dive into any spoilers but it's a story around an AI (You) building the necessary tools to aid in the mission of terraforming mars and diving into its many mysteries while the AI contemplates their own existence and purpose. Very existential stuff. All voice acted too with great performances which is a plus.My problems arise when you get to a big enough base that keeping track of everything becomes nearly impossible both visually and technically.Hope you have good eyesight, because once your base is big enough, good luck looking for anything specific because the icons representing buildings and what resource they generate when zoomed out are SO TINY that I spent most of my time  at the screen to find the specific resource mines I want to place new factories around or buildings I want to shut off to save power. Some icons are far too similar to each other, how am I supposed to tell the difference between a solar farm and a battery? I can't, they both have the lightning symbol and a background that blends in with the white outlining of icons and roads. Sure I can click a resource from the bottom row to highlight factories and mines that produce/use them, but all that does is create a two thin white lines around those buildings The problem gets exacerbated when you have more than one base. That bottom row of resources also gives you graphs that show you the rise and fall of productivity for each item on a global scale. Overall, this is great for micromanaging what factories and resources to focus on! Number go up and green is good and all that. This immediately falls apart the second you build a second base. Want to know if that second base is being self sufficient? Nope, when you select that bases "district" menu, all you get are flat numbers of its inventory, no graphs. That district has 0 computer chips in its inventory? could that be because they're all being used too quickly to notice? or are they not being produced at all because of some other problem (such as power, another thing that is hard to spot because of its tiny icon over the building)? who knows! Does my second district generate enough food/water to support their colonists long term? Maybe! the first district is inflating the numbers of my global scale that I don't know if district 2 is on the rise or decline.Overall, I see some glaring flaws in this games UI design that it feels too much of a chore to power through to the later stages where I will need to rely on the information the UI gives me to properly manage everything rather than eyeballing it.Dealing with combat and my swarms are the bane of my existence, its like herding cats. For one, it's so annoying switching between swarms when I have to right-click MULTIPLE TIMES before I can select another swarm less I accidentally redirect the course of the currently selected swarm to merge with the other.I hate that as soon as a swarm fully wipes out an enemy swarm, it returns back to base immediately on its own with no regard of other enemies around them. I have to keep a close eye at every encounter to make sure no one leaves the fight early, leaving my buildings wide open for the slow-ass towers.It's also annoying not being able to assign groups of swarms to readily intercept any oncoming swarms, it all needs to be done individually. This then circles back to the frustration that is selecting and deselecting units.It's also frustrating that merged swarms don't split up when returning to base. Each Hive tower holds 100 at the start, but never readjusts themselves when a swarm returns with more than that. Leaving some towers understaffed and underprepared for the next invasion due to the swarm unit limits. This then leaves to more annoying busywork readjusting them yourself.Overall, I feel that this game should have just left out combat all together and focused on its base-building aspects and simulation. It all feels like an afterthought.

_childDocuments_.review: I was enjoying myself. I made a whole big base. it took a long time. but then I saw that the way to win quickly is to make another big base, just like the first one. and another. and another.Research fluctulates wildly, and there's no way to find out why it does that. _childDocuments_.review: It's very satisfying to paint Mars, first blue, then green. And the early and mid-game both have that 'just one more turn' feeling, where you're making decisions and pushing to balance everything that's going on and having on. The campaign is interesting, has solid voice-acting, and rewards multiple playthroughs with different dialogue and three different endings. But it starts to drag in the end game phase, where you're either repetitively building the same sets of buildings, or waiting with the game on 16x speed to progress research or complete a special project or for your scanners to find a particular resource spawn. The combat also feels like a very unnecessary addition to the campaign and left a sour taste in my mouth whenever I had to interact with the system. Definitely worth a full playthrough though, despite its shortcomings.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't the best thing ever, but it is still really nice to play sometimes.- Everything looks nice and makes noises.- It isn't really a complex game where you do crazy production lines, but that doesn't make the game worse.--- The devs did fix some stuff so that the game is actually playable and isn't frustrating, and they seem to be doing content updates as well, so the game can still become better than what it is right now.- Basically, every drone has to know how to navigate all of your base and does all the calculations on the fly, so the game gets very cpu-intensive after midgame or so.- Sometimes they can't move that one resource piece at all even though the building it should go to is prioritized and is literally right next to the resource unit. Just like the framerates, this stuff usually works fine for the most of the game, but gets worse towards the end of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Art in this game is fantastic, and the whole experience was very addictive, watching oceans form and land turn green, then get populated with animals is so good, even if towards the end of the game it involves a whole lot of waiting. The story in the campaign helps make the long time spent waiting a little less dull.Maybe I was not playing it right, but the limitations on resources and the need for constant expansion makes things difficult to optimise, I think the feeling is more or less that I am relying on RNG to get me a limited resource that I know I will run out of again. Though without those limitations there would not really be any gameplay other than waiting/setting up new outposts. Game has lots of issues, I would recommend trying it if you enjoy grand strategy type games, city builder games, and enjoy mars as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This is a real good and balanced colonization game.  It has repertitive elements like any game of this kind.The complexity increases smoothly and you won't face any nasty surprises.The techtree is straight forward and well balanced.As always one may find it too complex, one other may miss endless ressources. I do neither nor.Let's compare it to other games. The campaign is well narrated and does its best to make the AI setting of the story feel real. There are rare dry spells, but overall the story is omnipresent. This has been done much better than in Surviving Mars. The difficulty and complexity of Surviving Mars can be hard, while Per Aspera plays like clockwork. Is it worth buying?You may check some "how long to beat" sources. I have not regretted it, but would have been very happy if the logistics were more complex and the consequences of planning errors were punished more severely. In the end, though, it's a question of what type of player you are, and I would recommend the game to anyone from beginner to advanced.Cheer, Chaly
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, but I understand that it won't be for everyone.I wholeheartedly recommend it if you like high concept games (Last Federation), for example.Don't let it fool you that this game is in city builders, it is closer by a lot to Factorio.There are a number of annoyances that I hope will get addressed in a Quality of Life patch.I would love to be able to upgrade all roads centrally, turn on and off spaceport/elevator projects. reassign hotkeys, have edge scrolling, reorienting the camera.But these are minor annoyances to me, the vision of this game shines through all of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Some neat ideas hamstringed by a lack of usability and a DLC that should've been packaged with the base game (and feels very tacked on, to the point that I found it hard to use and placement of things obnoxious.) Just totally lacking in QOL it feels like, and hard to believe anyone played through this QA wise and didn't notice these things.As of the time of writing:- No bulk orders for delete, upgrade, disable, etc. with a building cap makes for a frustrating experience. Very annoying to try to replace/disable old sections of the world.- Constantly kicking up to the Orbital layer just to manage space missions can get annoying. On top of that no methodology or display on what's a repeated or single time mission.- No automatic deletion of old mines that are empty- Research system has some neat space options, but mostly just feels like a lack of convenience improvements that instead just add more weight to the game as it goes on. Very little simplification as you proceed or things that make the gameplay smoother. A lot of later game is spent just.. idling for that next building that's just better than your previous (and some of which you can't just upgrade into or are a pain to upgrade into.)- Resources have no actual uniqueness, they're just different colored cubes that all kinda act the same except that produced versions require a different set and there are hot spots on the planet. Uranium being the only exception.- Certain aspect ratios actually lose portions of the UI, I was playing a 16##x10## resolution and noticed there were sections of the screen and UI half-cut off.- (DLC) Due to the nature of flooding in the game and the constantly rising sea levels you must constantly keep moving your ports and shipyards and any water-adjacent buildings. This makes the entire Blue Planet DLC an annoying experience as the ports are already fiddly with placement, the boats seem to path globally and waste tons of time, and any increase in water level will require you to reconstruct everything.Story mode was good, concepts are neat, art is great, just.. fails on the UI/gameplay front. I hope future patches fix a lot of the QOL issues.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Conceptually, I really like Per Aspera; a 4x-like experience with a neat sci-fi story should be right up my alley. Unfortunately, the 4x layer of the game is very shallow (despite appearing quite elaborate) as certain mechanical guardrails make it very difficult for you to 'lose' no matter how inefficiently you lay things out, and so it really only serves as a means for you to kill time in between story beats. If you're looking for a rich sci-fi strategy game, stick with Endless Space 2.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I was dubious about this game, mainly due to the "mixed" feedback, but was pleasantly surprised. I'm an avid player of resource management/city builder like games, Anno., Factorio cities skylines and the like.The story - This was one of the best parts of the game, really enjoyable to find out the back story, supported by the great voice acting. The game did a great job of drip feeding you with bits of the story to keep you immersed, yet not overwhelmed.Graphics - Simple and lovely. There's an amazing simplicity to the graphics, but with the ability to zoom all the way into minute detail seamlessly from the orbital view.I've heard a lot of complaining about the logistics in this, game, I actually found these worked reasonably well. I seemed to get a recurring issue where my worker factory constantly produced one more worker than I had capacity for, which appeared to happen once I had scrapped a previously built worker hub and then replaced it. Whilst improving the prioritisation feature with logistics wouldn't go a miss, I'd say this is far from broken.The beginning and Mid game are great, supported by the story and resource management of the game, whilst you slowly start expanding. The daisy chaining of worker hubs, did get a little monotonous as you progressed through to the late game. Being totally honest the late game is lacking somewhat and is in definite need of additional content to keep the game from becoming a "fast forward on 16 times" until oxygen drops below 30% affair. The last 30 or so years really dragged as research projects took a very long time, and the story content had all but dried up. The natural disasters never caused a problem, so could do with having more frequent ones of those. I terrafomred Mars, yet the only difference I noted was the melting of water. I would have loved to see grass land, and forests actually visually appear on the planet and I just felt a little cheated that the world did start to pop into life. I think a real wasted opportunity to expand the direction of the game, and introduce gameplay mechanics, like balancing plant and animal life, as you introduce the uncovered cities (which took around 8 years to unlock and then didn't get used as mars was "tarraformed").To conclude - great game, good concept, lovely graphically, engaging story, and despite what the negative comments say, I think well worth the money and totally playable. There needs to be a focus on end game, because after all of that, I felt a little flat when I finally hit year 75 and the credits started rolling!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I'm 15 hours in.This game is trying new stuff in the 4X genre and I believe it works. Many of the complaints raised in negative reviews seem to be because they're playing the game wrong, you can't just play this like you'd play any other 4X game. It needs a bit more planning.The story is engaging, which is rare in games as these. The speed is fine, the economy is pretty hands-off so you can speed through parts you don't want.The terraforming part needs a bit more refinement but adds something unique. People I've seen complaining about the terraforming are basically just chucking rocks at the planet, something which you're warned off will have bad results. The combat is simple but reasonably elegant, basically you're just pitting economies at each other. Graphics are fine, the UI is clear (people complaining have not found the building menu I believe). Resources being finite forces you to keep expanding, which I like, most games like these just let you get a god level economy before you go handle tasks. The only thing I'd like was some way to turn buildings you're using into just conductors for energy/roads; I get that it's done this way to force you to keep expanding, but at some point I have like infinite energy because that's what you build to get places. So maybe that after 10 years of use you can just turn buildings into husks or something.

_childDocuments_.review: I played hours upon hours of this game, always excited to see what would happen in the next stage of terraforming. The hours are not on display since I first tried it out from the account of a friend, for about a day, but sadly, my excitement blinded me and it was after I had paid for it that the mess this game is struck me. I'm studying physics so I've really been looking forward to something that would scratch the itch I got for terraforming Mars, and hopefully with some sense of realism and actual numbers, that a certain other game failed to do.-The monumental let-down is that you terraform a barren planet end up with a beautiful Earth-alike scenery, with forests and a ocean plus some lakes. However comparing that to the first few hours of the game, where you create your first human habitats, you need to supply them with food and water. You collect water by mining for ice deposits, and you process food in a factory that inputs chemicals ( a raw resource you also mine for) and water and produce food. Makes sense when nothing can grow outside of some kind of enclosure. However as you progress, you melt the icecaps, introduce greenhouse gases, you terraform the planet and end up with a temperature of 16 Celsius maybe more, an Earth-like pressure around 1 bar or 1 atmosphere and a very similar concentration of O2, N2 and CO2 to that we have here. AND YET not a SINGLE thing changes about production. You still mine ice. Near the equator, heck there are even ice deposits under the water, and not a single way to filter that to for consumption or any other way. The greenery is also there just for show, you can build "biodomes" that spread radiation resistant lichen and then move on to more complex flora and eventually fauna, but you never grow a single plant to feed your colonists. It's all about getting the chemicals from the mine to the food factory.-The other huge problem is that the logistics are atrocious. You place down a worker hubs, and you produce worker drones ( tracked, not flying) from a worker factory. One worker per hub and roads are auto-generated between buildings when you place them down. Good and simple. However, each worker hub, generates its own 'sector", even if two of them are as physically close as the game allows, they will create a new sector and except for fetching and depositing resources to the immediate neighboring sectors, the drones will never leave their sector. There is absolutely no way to redraw these sectors, or tell the drones where they are needed, or an order of priorities like "1. building materials, 2. production resources 3........"and mind you this is a game about colonising a planet where you eventually are forces to exceed 1000 buildings and driven to expand outwards because raw resource stockpiles/deposits hold finite amounts of the resource. So as the game progresses what starts off a quirky but functional once you learn it, system for a city/planet builder, turns into a cursed mess, with building materials getting stockpiled on some random solar or wind farm, drones maniacally transferring the same unit of carbon up and down between two buildings, on a road, or worse, in a hyperloop connection ( the means of for long range and quick transportation of goods) rendering it completely unusable since only a single unit can be transferred at a time. You end up having to place buildings in opposite sites of the planet, yet the logistics algorithm is borderline functioning when you are confided to 1/30 of the surface. You are the most advanced AI in existence but you cannot tell the drones you supposedly control how to behave.I could go on, but I feel these alone give enough information for anyone reading to stay away. This game is a builder and terraforming sim and it does the first horribly and the second only on a cosmetic level.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Just ignore the positive reviews that has less than 5 hours.I also loved it at first. The storyline interactions are quite well written.Sound actors are very good, and the game gets you, you think you will love it, you think its just your kind of game.Then you get to mid-late game. Here are the problems:1 - Resources: Small patches everywhere, distributed randomly. You have to expand practically all around the planet just to survive. There is no improved mining tech that gives you access to bigger patches of resources or different ways of getting them. Tech helps you mine only faster, thats it. Which is pointless since even the largest patches are mined quite fast.2 - Tech tree: It basically plays with numbers. Completely fails to give you different build options as you progess. You basically build the same tedious base over and over and over.3 - Roads: You cant just connect two of your bases with roads. There is no such option. You always have to grow your base to connect to the other one. No flight connection, no bare road connection. This means if you want to get to that farther mine or research outpost, you have to build all the buildings you have in your main base in a line, so the road doesnt get destroyed by lack of maintenance in 5 turns. This is incredibly annoying. %80 of lategame is about building long lines of bases as road replacements. 4 - Depots: Tech doesnt give you bigger resource depots so you have to build 3-4 depots together. And you have no control over what they collect. Its just random. Drones basically distribute resources anywhere they just randomly like.5 - Logistics: In lategame, drones dumb down. Although you have the superspeed hyperloops and road upgrades, and tons of drones all around your base, some buildings take years to get build. They just refuse to get the resources to that building. You just wait at 16x speed. 6 - Drones & Maintenance: In lategame, somehow drones refuse to supply for drone worker factories and maintenance buildings. This should results in an ALT+F4 almost in every case. Because you end up without any drones to carry stuff, and maintenance stops building maintenance drones, so your base dies in front of you eyes and you feel an excruciating feeling of lack of control. Your base dies in front of you, after a 6 hour playthrough, and there is nothing you can do about it. Overall: Dont BUY. Its very annoying, and even if you play for the well written story, its very likey that you will ALT+F4 and uninstall, and come here for a rant.

_childDocuments_.review: My review for Per Aspera is... that it's alright.The highlights of the game is definitively the story writing and voice acting. I definitively enjoyed playing a more personal version of the typical AI protagonist, and the relationships between the characters are believable enough.Terraforming Mars is definitively also good compared to competition. A lot of details goes into getting temperature, gas composition, and water levels to a certain amount, and there are quite a lot of ways to do it in the game, which gives you a lot of headroom to get everything you need to do just right.HOWEVER - The logistic part of the game is... painful. Let alone the Blue Mars DLC that you somewhat need to access the resources that become flooded in the late game, the AI (the irony isn't lost on me) that handles resource transfers is pretty unoptimized and even dumb at times. The only real way to make things work is to have tons of worker hubs to carry stuff around and use hyperloop to get anything further than 5-7 buildings moving. There's tons of moving parts, which I do appreciate, but it seems things get snagged, goes into a loop, and eventually even had a memory leak for me where the game ran calculations until my PC Crashed.The combat was also evidently an afterthought. You get drones, you send them, numbers vs numbers (and towers underfoot), and eventually it dies out. There's no real strategy or tactics, and even the research tree, while nice, is made so that you can't soft-lock yourself by not doing any military upgrades.All in all, a decent time. I'd play it if you want a chill terraforming mars experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing visually and technologically and is quite the innovative take on city building to planet building. But my biggest pet peeve that makes me shake in anger is the workers... One of the most important things in the game and instead of doing what has been prioritised (and yes everything else has been shut down apart from power and I have more than ample resources to construct the building or task) and instead of doing what they need to do they just deliver random materials to shut down or non essential buildings or tasks for no reason.I love the game for its features but this one is mentally killing me, in a patch is there a way to get the workers to stop whatever else they are doing and prioritise a single task? that can only be active at one time? Please those lil guys need help.

_childDocuments_.review: I came to this game looking for a Mars terraforming simulator. I'm sorry to say that this game doesn't scratch that itch, although it probably comes closer than any other game (except Terraforming Mars, but that's too abstracted to really count).I suspect that the developers might view this game as being about the narrative, with terraforming Mars as more of a setting. Unfortunately, although the story has some good parts, it's also let down by the fact that it's very easy to trigger parts of the story out of order and have characters act as though certain things either have or haven't happened. I've only had one play-through, but I strongly suspect that there is basically one meaningful choice in the game -- this is very much an on-the-rails experience and not so much choose-your-own-adventure.The gameplay is ultimately pretty rudimentary. I had hoped to dig into logistics and production chains (love Factorio, just to give you a sense of where I'm coming from), but they end up being fairly shallow. I could imagine optimizing the process, but the UI doesn't make it easy and ultimately there just isn't a need because it's so straightforward. I played on medium difficulty, so it's possible that optimization is more crucial on the hard difficulty but honestly that just sounds really tedious.There is a "military" component to the game, but it's even more shallow than the terraforming and the best I can say about it is that the AI is bad enough that you can get through it pretty quickly.I really wanted to like this game. I still do! There is a lot of room for improvement, and the devs have certainly said that they intend to keep working on. Frankly, I'm not sure this game was ready to leave early access -- the core game loop is there, but... it's just not that fun. Hopefully they make enough changes that I can recommend it, but until then save your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera: A worse factorio.Aspera is a very weird game. It hires big name VA's like Troy Baker to prop up the story of asentient AI that is colonising mars. Yet, between the weird simping of Elon Musk and just general vapidness of the story. e.g. every so often,, unprompted and in no way correlative to gameplay you get asked oooo am i alive questions. And its like, i dont know you, i dont really care honestly. If you are going to have a sentient AI, dont just have them question their sentience, do something, make a gameplay purpose, decisions, or at the very least make it interesting. Anyway, very ignorable plot aside (just use sandbox imo). What is the gameplay of Per Aspera. Its kind of like factoro. There are resource nodes around the planet. So you extend your conlony to reach them, with a weird mix of buildings. it says in the tutorial worker hubs are the best bridges (as your colony must be connected by roads). yet after a while it becomes an absolute chore because you need power to your worker hubs, so you build a power building every so often, then they need maintence, so you build a maintenence hub inbetween the two, then you need to protect them from the enemy so you build another military hub, and it just becomes an absolute mess because you have to slosh through the inefficient UI, all to get to a single resource node. But let's say you get through the AI, you have the resource what next? well, the workers take it to a factory where it's processed, and.... that's it. Thats the entire logistics gameplay loop. The only way to improve it is one click improve roads, and the only stoppers are maintenance and enemeies, all a matter of just having the right buildings in the radius. There was never a time when i had to think about any of my placements.  After you realize this, it becomes deadening. There is no solution to logistics. There is no massive transport bus or cool research. There is only one road, and it leads not to Rome but to annoyance. Researching new tech is also kind of a chore. it's based on how many colonists you have. The number of colonists you have is limited by research. So do you either research things that will actually kind of assist (like faster roads, which as aforementioned, are the ONLY logistical improvement) or do you research more colonists for the ability, to do more research? There is no game changer where it's like, you can refine a good twice or thrice to create a better end product. The only research there is is more amount of buildings you can place, yes it is capped, or more colonists. Tl: Dr, Per Aspera has an ignorable story. It has an extremely shallow gameplay loop especially compared to other factory sims, and the progression it has is extremely shallow and never feels rewarding.Buy Dyson Sphere Program, they deserve your money.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game, UI could be a bit better like its annoying having to go into the menu to select each individual mine you want to place, they should make it so you have a centralized "mine" button, having the type automatically switch out depending on which deposit you click as especially once you reach tier 2 mines it just exasperates the problem of just having to change out the selection all the time and its just annoying. You cant even place mines without the deposit at all so there just no reason for the selection to work the way it does, the game kinda tries to play as something its not. Just pretty anti-user in some areas is all like another thing is if your buildings ever die all the way you have to scout find them and press repair on each individual one even if their under a matience bot sector like what was the point of making the things if their not gonna rebuild the gaht dang buildings when a meteor hits them (which is often) and man dont even think about upgradeing your roads it takes years to connect it all, i have no idea why they dont let you drag select all the roads you want upgradedI also just find the Narration a little weak so far with your choices not correctly bouncing off future convos which was sorta one of the main points the game tries to strive for... like i tried picking the options that were "pro nuke the poles" as one could say but then the AI you play as has a whole monolog about "man how am i gonna tell them i dont want to do this" despite the fact i had literally just said i was going to do it like. Mabye it picks up later, im still again just hitting tier 2 afterall but man, thankfully the gameplay satisfies my monkey builder brain greatly and the atmosphere of it all is really nice so its thumbs up worth the time i put into it even if its not perfect
