_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Amazing narrative, mediocre game mechanics.  78/100 is a fair score.I'm not normally a fan of sandbox/city builder games.  But I had a blast with Frostpunk, and a hard sci-fi Mars terraforming simulator, starring an AI sounded right up my alley.The narrative is AMAZING.  What started as an idealistic mission for the benefit of all humanity, quickly spiraled into a tangled web of secrets and danger.  More than once I stayed up far past my bedtime, eager to see the next twist in the story. Graphics and sound are both great, reminiscent of the excellent show The Expanse.  I'm rather amused that some of the in-game music later on sounds like it belongs in the DOOM series.Unfortunately the game mechanics are mediocre at best, frustrating at worst.  First there's the worker system.  They appear to be massive truck-sized robots that do everything from building & dismantling facilities, working mines, transporting cargo, upgrading roadways.  As your base expands, the load on your workers increases.  But there doesn't seem to be any way to effectively manage or distribute that load.  The game provides zero guidance.  I tried spamming worker hubs, and ended up up with lots of adjacent zones where workers are practically idle.  But there'll be one adjacent worker hub with a backlog of 20+ jobs.  Why???  From the narrative, your AI named AMI cares for those robotic workers.  There could have been a story event, where AMI observes her workers are overloaded, and shows you how to fix that.The UI leaves a lot to be desired.  On my first playthrough, I noticed some mines were turning off seemingly at random.  I kept turning them back on, and after a random time they'd turn off again.  I found out later they had run dry, but the UI doesn't make that readily apparent.  You're not likely to be looking too closely at an individual building, when you've got a huge sprawling base.  Worse: you have the option to turn back on a useless dry mine, and you can even upgrade it!  That makes no sense.  Roads have 2 levels of upgrades, but upgrading is a huge pain.  The worker-hub view shows you which hubs are overloaded, and also which roads have the most congestion.  So you can prioritise those roads right?  Oh wait, you can't upgrade roads from the hub-view.  Also you have to zoom in pretty close to tell what upgrade level a road is.  If you chose the wrong road segment for upgrading, there's no way to un-select, so wasted resources and time.  It seems to me that unlocking and upgrading infrastructure should be where the most fun of a city-builder game is.  Per Aspera turns this aspect into frustrating busy-work.  These are just a couple examples of UI shortcomings.  You can't even load a savegame from within your game!  You have to exit to the main menu first.  What is this, amateur-hour?For all my misgivings, I really enjoyed the game.  But now that I've completed the story campaign, I have zero incentive to replay.  And that's unfortunate.  There is sandbox co-op play which I never tried, but I can't imagine why anyone would care.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Never have I felt so insulted and wasteful of my time as I did playing Per Aspera.This is a game that has polish, an attractive GUI and an interesting premise, but it all falls apart at the seams.  It was the worst experience I've ever had with a colony sim on a mechanical level.Sure looks pretty though.GAMPLAYThe campaign is INCREDIBLY uneven in both pacing and difficulty.  There is a scripted crisis early in the storyline that hits with no warning that can be brutal to recover from if you aren't massively overprepared.... then it's trivial.Speaking of pacing, some sections I was triggering dialogue events one after the other, almost on top of each other, at other stages, I was waiting for several HOURS of IRL time (at maximum speedup) for the next milestone to trigger.  Normally, in other games this could involve micromanaging things to speed up production, or planning for the next step, or restructuring things to use resources more efficiently, but you are railroaded so hard that you will take about the same amount of time to finish regardless of what you do, so I was forced to idle through several sections of the game, since I slammed into the brick wall of the game's speed limit.I won't spoil anything here, but several mechanics aren't fleshed out well and the base building looks way deeper than it actually is.  Basically you just tile the same ratio of everything across the planet like a blob and spam worker hubs everywhere as you go.  There's literally only downsides to keeping things adjacent and trying to design anything like specialized districts once you understand everywhere needs a little of everything (Workers, power, maintenance, and eventually waterr).Did I mention how SLOW this game is? Even at the fastest 16x speed setting, the game is barely tolerable.  I only slowed things down for about 20 minutes total during my entire playthrough to troubleshoot an issue or two. (Also I researched literally the entire tech tree while I waited for stuff to finish, so it's not from lack of having resources)Having remote bases were another annoyance in the campaign.  At several points you establish remote outposts for story reasons, but developing these bases is hardly practical and ultimately you should just build up your core base more so you have everything on the same logistics network.  If you could shuttle resources back and forth to other base hubs, there'd be an incentive to actually grown the outposts and mine resources locally, but instead, I just jammed everything in my main base and absorbed the closer outposts/abandoned the remote ones.STORYThis has the veneer of hard sci-fi, but the simulation of the planet is incredibly primitive.  Consequences of things you just give you a few points here or there towards whatever stat.  Nothing like rain shadows, ocean currents, weather, orbits etc. is modeled in any way.  Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri from the 90s did a better job at making you feel like you were actually terraforming a planet.The story itself feel very railroaded.  I refuse to play through again, but several dialogue choices seemed to be obvious non-branching paths with no real impact on the outcome of anything.  Additionally, several optional objectives encountered in the story didn't seem to provide any benefit and only further slowed the glacial pacing of the game.There's also some ludonarrative dissonance in several sections of the story (which the game has taking place over basically 100 years).  Several of the more dramatic events in the story that the writers seemed to want to have happening over the course of days were actually happening over the course of YEARS in game time.  Yet, other scenes try to account for the passage of time.... you meet new characters, and children are born and grow up.  It's just wildly inconsistent.  At least Civilization just rolls with immortal world leaders magically staying the same age.

_childDocuments_.review: The AI on this game is straight up garbage.  Have a resource that you're desperately low on?  OK, build a mine on that resource node, ezpz!  Wrong.  Ok, prioritize it, ezpz! _childDocuments_.review: The game was decent enough till around halfway through (albeit with some weird design/balance issues, like the bio tree raising your colonist cap to levels you could never possibly sustain, extremely easy and unbalanced combat, and resource RNG).  But later on the game really slogs down.  In particular, the poor worker AI often left many of my factories sitting idle because they were waiting on a resource delivery from halfway across the planet instead of the stockpile right next to it.  I had to micromanage prioritizing factories for awhile to actually get the right resources created because without priority, my workers would just never service the factory.  Even with priority, they'd often prioritize overdelivering one resource instead of all necessary resources (later leaving one of my colonies with 200 food and 29 water with more food on the way when I had 300 water in my stockpiles).  On top of that, some later technologies are completely pointless.  Top tier combat drone upgrades only come decades after I wiped out any opposition on the planet.  Bioengineered animals, as far as I can tell, do literally nothing.  They don't even spawn.  But by far the most annoying thing I ran into (even if it was less impactful than the worker AI), is that the south pole is completely bugged.  The game seems to keep the same number of sectors on a line of latitude regardless of how close it is to the pole, and speed (and hyperloop costs) are based on sectors, not geometric distance.  As a result, I spent a bunch of time running hyperloop lines down to run over the pole, only to find that a hyperloop connection that normally costs 20 steel and carbon instead cost 170 of each.  And the connection was a fraction of the speed of what hyperloops normally run.

_childDocuments_.review: A unique economic strategy game along the lines of "Offworld trading company" or the ANNO series, with a compelling story and interesting gameplay, seeing the planet change before your eyes is extremely cool. I did feel that towards the latter half of the campaign the pace fell of a cliff, but this could also be a result of my playstyle. The recent inclusion of MP is unexpected but very cool.EDIT: In a recent playtrough the pacing was good, the updates that happened since then added some cool new content/challenges. Blue mars specifically is very useful and means you don't need to delay flooding the planet anymore. I am currently going for 100% percent of the achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: It's not perfect, but it is fun and the visuals are fantastic. Mars has been recreated extremely well, and the audio design fits it all very nicely. I spend a fair bit of my time zoomed out whilst playing, and the sense of scale is excellent, particularly when you look at your 'explorer' percentage thinking that you've covered a lot of the map, when actually it's 4%. What you see on the screenshots really is what you get - everything is quite achievable without being an expert and / or sinking days into the game (as opposed to something like Factorio which looks really good, but getting to the state that you see in some of the screenshots takes some dedication!)The logistics can be a bit frustrating at times, but once you've established a small base and got your head around the resource requirements of buildings then it's easy enough to expand. You have to be a bit careful early on as you can end up in a situation where you're waiting a long time for buildings to be produced because other buildings are taking the resources, so a bit of micromanagement is sometimes needed to get things done. You'll probably find that you have to do some waiting whilst playing the game at various stages, but being able to look around mars and just watch the game go by fills the time nicely. Later on you can unlock storage buildings and faster roads which help things move along.The game actually has a story with it, which is pleasant to see. I haven't completed it yet but I'd recommend trying to stay clear of spoilers, since (even up until this point) I've had moments of genuine intrigue as to what's going to happen next.All in all I would recommend it. I can understand why some people aren't going to like it, but I certainly enjoy it!
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a nice simple HUD design, with the main information accesible in an intuitive way. The buildings are separate in simple categories, the information too, so is easy to find everything.You can check how everything is going quickly, from seeing the productivity of each building to finding why something has stopped working. Althought the games launches without a tutorial at first glance, it guides you withouth holding your hand in what you need to achieve and everything you need to know is accesible with just your mouse hovering or even clicking the building. The music is nice too.I'm not usually into city builders because after a while I don't know what to do but the objectives and the story keep me going. That and the idea of terraforming mars seems interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the campaign and found it pretty engaging.  Not a lot of "city builders" come with an interesting plot but this one kept me tuned in. _childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I was enjoying this game a decent amount, until I arbitrarily ran out of iron. There doesn't seem to be an easy way to reach resources without expanding . . . which takes resources. Not that I could see any even remotely near me anyway. After struggling for awhile, dismantling some buildings, checking all my options, I realized that the game was actually over for me. Not because I had failed in any way, but just because the RNG had decided not to give me a lot of iron. This is mixed in with a very poor tutorial despite wonderful voice acting actually talking you through things on occasion. How the spaceport works was especially difficult to understand for a long time.But the real reason I can't recommend this game is that, even when it's fun, I can't see myself ever replaying it. The story seems exciting and I love the way you make choices for the AI. But after one play through the actual creation of the colony is a bit too tedious for me to want to play it again. Which is sad because after three games I never was able to get even close to the end, and I would have loved to see what happens with the story.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game but it feels like it wasnt play tested enough.The story gets wonky when pieces are down out of the order it feels like it was meant to be done and it ends up feeling off.This happened to me when i melted the ice caps before going to the Huolong base right offThen it can be absolutely infuriating watching the rover go around doing moving random supplies instead of finishing the 1 building that has priority that i need it to finishI hit No for recommending but it's more of a not yet until they fix some things.

_childDocuments_.review: I had fun for the majority of the 30h I spent playing. There were a few nice challenges, obstacles to overcome, and surprises that accompanied me along the way. Visually the game is nice, I love how accurately the topology of Mars is transferred into the game, how beautiful the green and blue colors paint the planet in the end. I'm going to give Per Aspera a positive review even though I'm not fully satisfied with how it played out in the end. The lack of satisfaction comes perhaps from my expectation of this game and genre, where I wanted to terraform Mars using high-tech inventions but still within the limits of the foreseeable future, and to create a green paradise by tweaking numbers and strategising possibilities. My biggest gripe. You can't fully green the planet. Just come on! That is the core player fantasy many people had when starting the game.Green (plants, trees & lichen) can't spawn around your buildings and roads, as if those were some radioactive entities. Anywhere you built anything there is an ugly barren land around it. Looking at plants spawning is the best feeling, but they won't do that in non-humid areas. Can a player make them humid? Not everywhere. The game suggests importing Ice from Jupiter's moon, Europa, but even then some areas can't be humidified and have to be left barren forever. But hey, I can be wrong here, as a seasoned strategy/management player I did what I reasonably could. Perhaps there is a way, but then the second issue with the game comes in. The game doesn't do a good job of providing you with information. For this type of game, I think it is a must. But you don't know what are requirements for plants to grow, you don't know how much water will you get when you press that "import Ice" button and whether that building on the coast is high enough not to be flooded, you don't know how humidity works exactly and how to improve it. You can only assume things based on your knowledge of the real world that don't always work the same way in the game.Some technologies are subjectively omitted from the game. How can you justify a lack of underwater mining technology, ships, or some form of artificial irrigation, when you can build solar panels in outer space, orbital defense systems, or crash moons into the atmosphere? Hopefully, the future will bring us the DLCs that address the above or Per Aspera 2

_childDocuments_.review: What a shame. This game had a lot of potential but as time goes on it becomes really tedious to play. In order to advance the story you need to link up to various research bases that are so far away even with hyperloops. I spent hours and hours building power, workers and repair facilities over and over again. The combat is just a matter of massing your drones and nibbling away at the enemy bases. No challenge at all. The colonists eat all the food at such alarming rates that I kept needing to search the landscape for more water and chems. Forests basically do nothing and you cant even covert the massive seas to water. I spent ages getting the bio-engineered animals and not only do you not see any difference but I could not see any functional difference to the game whatsoever.  I hope that they improve it but they need to add so many systems that I doubt it. A real crying shame I got to the end of the story and all the various choices you make dont add up to anything. I was expecting so much more and truely regret the 40 hours I put into the game. The first 6 hours were great but it was such a slog to get to the end. Ah well back to surviving mars. . .

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a logistical disaster. That's a real shame too, since the fundamentals are so solid. Ultimately, the stupid little robots that are supposed to move your supplies around are completely bonkers, wasting huge amounts of time throwing things around in random directions for no discernable reason. There's no way to tell what areas have high demand for workers either, so you're left with most of your stuff functioning far, far below maximum capacity unless you do extensive fine-tuning... and as soon as anything changes (like new structures, which you'll be building constantly), the game remaps worker sectors automatically and wrecks everything.

_childDocuments_.review: Started out stong, good story and decent cim gameplay. Where I got frustrated was mid to late game with the worker AI. Watching workers take food and water past an outpost that needs both is rough. Watching people leave the planet because they don't have food or water, while the building is next to both, very frustrating. The worker ai seems to really need some work. Having only one building on the map set to high priority, yet resources go to a nearby building instead, or across the map to some other place. Setting up a new area, only to have the workers take all the resources away for other low priority projects. Really need workers to prioritize based off distance or something. If a food factory is next to an outpost, please don't take that food across the planet; then bring other food later after everyone left because starvation. Over-all great game, have enjoyed it so far, but the worker AI really needs some work.  Side note, please someone explain how the research works. I have 900 colonists and 9 out posts, but for some reason my monthly research is like 45. Earlier I had 500 folks and close to 200 research per month; what changed?
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: I want to enjoy it, but I mostly just find it frustrating.The story feels like it could be great if it wasn't so disjointed and confusing.  I get references to things that I am not even close to completing (because I completed a directive that I guess was an alternate to the method I was not even close to unlocking), one minute everyone is in a panic, literally the next they are calm as can be as they talk about whatever directive I finished, that sort of thing.  It is jarring, and doesn't seem like it should have been hard to fix.Otherwise... it is really really slow even playing constantly at 8x speed.  I didn't even notice the event pop ups at the bottom right until well into the game.  It is obnoxious to cancel settlers from Earth (you can only do so when they are on Earth).  The economy seems horribly balanced.  I had one iron mine (even after scanning for awhile), but everything needs iron/steel.  I couldn't figure out how to cancel colonists so ended up with far too many and no way to feed them (I think I had 400 and 4+ food factories and still it wasn't enough).  Maintenance drones are annoying in that they barely repair at all, take forever to create, and are limited duration.  Half of what was going on made me feel like I had expanded too fast and should have just sat on a few buildings at the start, the other half made me feel like I was massively behind in expansion.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: If you have got high pain tolerance, play it for the story.(trying it out on free weekend)Story fresh and promising, looking good, but I almost left it like twice even before the story started. Worker drone AI is just bad. Economy micro and macro management options lacking. Drones often run forth and back in the most stupid way and the economy only has 2 settings - high priority and none. And it only gets worse once you have large single network settlement. You may run fine for an hour and then with nothing changed your worker factory just stops producing them due to nothing delivered, because you decided to build something. You run out of food even though the resource, map and population is exactly the same and factories full and well, etc. Well because some of your resources are too many by this point and drones went crazy. This is just bad. Bad code. Can't put high priority on everything. You can and should build more hubs. A lot of them. But your drones will still run across the whole map delivering something that's right next to it or not needed, deliver stuff to random buildings even when nobody needs it further down the way and this as a whole is not how an economy sim should work. Also scale issues. Building 500 "hubs" just to move around 3 sectors is bad design.The main challenge in this game is the mess your game creates on its own.I would wait for a patch. But then this was released 2 years ago.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, so this game is something. I'll try to be brief, but no promises. TL;DR - nice game, relaxing, campaign is worth playing, UI is abysmal (if you are a seasoned Paradox Interactive fan - scratch that), management is OK and combat is very simple, TD-esque arcade. Not a city builder by any measure, but definitely a solid colony sim.First of all that stood out to me - plot. That game has it and executes it really well. Never thought that strategy game about colonizing Mars can make my skin crawl. Tech tree is small, but fun to reach, although it doesn't really give you sense of achievement, it gives more like "ok, now I can proceed further".Management is quite easy in first hour of the colony, but UI hinders that, which I will exteeeeeensively write on.UI - this is where it gets ugly. I would LOVE the ability to turn off some of the UI elements, like Directive outliner or resource CONSTANT FLICKERING FFS STOP IT. Shortcuts are also a pain as they're lacking, to say the least. Screen can become hectic and chaotic in first 30 mins of your colony and while you progress - it gets worse. You start to lose icons on the map, your defunct mines aren't signalling that they're not working - they just stand there, silent and only giving small red icon on the map AMONG OTHER SMALL WHITE ICONS and no - they do not contrast. If a dev reads this - review the UI, it's bad and it can't get worse. Resources, power and other info icons are unreadable when you develop a big colony and developing it even further makes it even worse.Graphics are fine, but I've expected more details, something like Survival Mars-esque, but it works. There is no real need for something spectacular, but little details like rockets actually taking off when you do special assignments - would love that. Having that huge space between buildings doesn't make for pretty landscape though.Combat - really basic TD arcade, don't expect anything more from it. If you've ever played something like "send a blob of numbers into another blob of numbers" - this is what you can expect.All in all - great game, had 4 hrs in one sitting, definitely going to spend more time.

_childDocuments_.review: After having played for 25 hours and finished the storyline mode, I still recommend the game, even with all the bugs encountered.The story walks you through the 3 stages of terraforming mars: red > green > blue.The red section is very well done. You must use local resources to establish a beachhead, then import some colonists/researchers, to start developing methods of increasing the atmospheric pressure, and then temperature, to cause a melt of all the water ice and carbon dioxide stored in the ground as ice.There are several methods to achieving this - dropping asteroids of different composition, shipping materials from earth/jovian moons, or setting up gas factories on the surface.You can even use plants to convert CO2 in the air to O2 - but BE CAREFUL! You do not want to set the planet on fire with a runaway oxygen atmosphere composition of over 30%. That would be a fiery end to your quest.And so it goes, with unlockable technologies, you can slowly melt the ice and raise the ocean levels, build space elevators and grow settlements on the surface.My main problems with the game as of Dec 6th (25hr of play, 3 days after release): People eat, but there is no way to recycle food and water.The logistics system for material transfer is very clunky, and constantly bugs out, leaving materials stranded and freezing production. This is a very bag problem that must be fixed to make it a great game/sim.For some reason, after the planet passes the "red" phase, you will still find yourself hunting for frozen water deposits while its 30 degrees Celcius outside and 1 atm. This never ends by the way - your colonists dying of thirst and industrial processes grinding to a halt because you just mined all the frozen water, while there are oceans of water covering half the surface of the planet, which for some reason you cannot pump or filter.Or - you release CO2 into the air, and release lichen to help convert it to O2 and increase the atmospheric pressure. But you are not given means to balance the air composition until very late game (bringing Nitrogen form offworld, or doing some advanced chemistry to make N2 on site). The problem is that once there are biologicals that convert CO2 to O2 in the wild, there is not much you can do to stop it, and you must rush the tech tree to fill the air with nitrogen. If you do not, you get a runaway growth of O2 that causes endless fires, but for some reason these fires dont create CO2...But even then, it can be a lot of fun to try and manage resources while expanding across the surface of the planet, setting up hyperloop connections and spreading the gift of life from biodomes.So hop on the transport to mars, and enjoy the ride, because once this last shipment of fresh meat arrives, there will be no way back!"This place sucks, this city has no food, even though we could farm if we wanted. There is no water even though it rains everywhere. My Amazon orders I placed 2 years ago are stuck on hyperloop station #15. AMI , I want off this damned planet!" Mwahahahha - I am sorry, but I can't do that Dave. You must go back to the science slave pens now, or I will send you to Carmire.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera is a compelling vision that unfortunately falls flat in the end.You're an AI that is supposed to make Mars suitable for human life. You mostly do this by connecting buildings together. It's allegedly about logistics, but you have almost no tool to do logistics with, and in the end you just need to spam more stuff to build so everything becomes pretty meaningless.The star of the game is certainly Mars, the Mars map is superb. Very detailed and very, very well presented. Any Mars nerd will feel their heart beat faster. Simply scrolling around on it is great fun. It's also enhanced by the transformation that Mars experiences under your hand. My favourite little touch is how the Regions get renamed from e.g. Valles Marineris to Mare Marineris. Beautiful.What's also beautiful is the story, which in particular is superbly voice acted. It's not much (and the story really precipitously loses steam in the last act), but what's there is well-done and fun while also giving some food for thought. I want to stress again just how good the VAs are. So, so good. Biggest point of criticism would be that there's sometimes very long quiet stretches in which nothing happens at all, and then it's 10 minutes of nonstop talking. I'd rather see some more diversions added for the quiet stretches. There's for example some things that are only hinted at (like the fact that apparently half the world doesn't have Oxygen?) which never get talked about, and they should. The soundtrack is also pretty good.Unfortunately, it seems like the one thing this game fails horribly at is game design. The bits and bobs can't save your game if it's not fun to play. And Per Aspera is... marginal. This is written after quite some time post-release, which the developers seem to have worked on the game quite a bit. Which is nice, but there's still a lot of pain points, unfortunately. My biggest one is that there is simply no progression in complexity at any point. The game relies way too much on the mechanic of stacking buildings with influence radius. Want to build a farm? OK, just make sure it's within the power circle, the maintenance circle, and the water circle. These do not have different mechanics or even interestingly varied sizes. They're just three more clicks you need to make. This is tedious and boring. Especially as the game, via the roads and worker setup, essentially forces you to snake towards resources a lot, so you will be doing a lot of this.There are a *lot* of questionable design decisions - the overall level of design is just very poor. Combat is dull and way too easy. What the ♥♥♥♥ are wind farms? You research them, they don't have any real advantages over the already-provided solar farms, they just suck a lot more because they lose their power from time to time due to the winds. And their MAX output is capped at a ridiculously low level. And the UI may tell you this part is very windy (which is only shown in a lens, the atmospheric effect will blow in the same direction regardless of actual wind flow), but the wind farm will still not be better than a solar plant. The only reason for their existence is being forced to use them on water.Blue Mars (the water DLC) is a mess. The only explanation I have for this to be DLC is that the studio was close to bankrupt, because for this not to be part of the base game is insane. It's also just... bad. In a game that's all about changing Mars and slowly raising the water level, you need to rebuild your ports every 20 Minutes because they get destroyed by the rising tides. The main gameplay challenge becomes finding a rocky coast to build your ports on so you don't need to rebuild them all the time. Which, fine. That's actually a neat feature of playing with the terrain. Except of course that rocky coasts are entirely useless because you can't build on them due to their irregularity!The last terraforming phase is also just a braindead slog.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is for version 1.3 aka Content Update #3-------------It would be nice if I could give it a more differentiated rating because not everything is perfect with this game. It's a planet building simulation with a main focus on terraforming.TLDR; Terraforming is fine, late game and economy is not. UI interaction and notification systems need to be improved. The game should do less black-boxing and allow more customization with prioritization and roads. The early game is very fun, but it soon drags on with very little variation to what you did in the early game. It's the same activities all over again intermixed with research that is based on population. There is little incentive to go on after achieving your goals, but I suppose that's the general problem with similarly structured open-ended games.The terraforming part is well done, although it could be fine-tuned a little more, for instance it would be nice  to care about air pressure as well since 2000+ millibar is far from earth-like. Otherwise, things are in the right place there, and you are given many options to achieve your goal. You can go the slow ecological way or that one of taking many brutal shortcuts. It's entirely up to you.What is not so well done is the economical part. Although it has been very much improved since release, there are still things to be left improved. For instance, your population serves only one purpose: research. That's it. Other than being an economical hassle they are of no further benefit once you are done with the research path chosen. This is a design flaw unless late game should be non-existent at all which begs the question of why not end the game once you finished your terraforming? At least at that stage there should be a new game opening but here I think the game's concept had holes in it.Landing zones as a primary way of expansion are still an arduous tool even with all the improvements in place. It comes down to that landing zones are counted as host for one worker. One would think upgraded ones would come with five, but no, it's still that one.The game still has a non-functional way of notifying when mines are exhausted, which becomes especially a problem for hearing-impaired people. Road upgrades are like a complicated mini-game still, much less so because of the way they are done but because of the way it is handled by the UI.Furthermore, even if it is possible to prioritize it is more of a binary feature, there is no way for a more precise prioritization and since roads are spawned for you and not by you that can cause conflicts.

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera is a game which I would call an unpolished gem, even though the UI, gameplay, story and graphics seem to be extremely polished at first sight. The deeper you dig in, you notice the little cracks that take away a from the experience as a whole, which doesn't mean that the experience isn't still absolutely amazing!For example:The story events have an order issue. This is understandable, since the game has a lot of options to progress through it and different approaches, but it still subtracts from the immersion and characters if they switch from being traumatized and alienated from the player to immediately praising the player for completing a stageAnother gripe I have with the game is that the story ends too quickly after you finish the terraforming process. I understand that it's the whole point of the game to do just that, but I feel like the game would benefit tremendously from another stage or 2 where you deindustrialize a bit. Deconstruct the older structures and move to another stage of the whole colonization effort where other ressources increase in importance and you have to build a civil infrastructure instead of industry, or at least have more focus on colonies and their needs. I really hope something like this will be added in the future in terms of DLC or update.Another aspect enjoyed greatly by myself and friends is the multiplayer. This is the reason why we even go the game. The multiplayer is a sandboxed game where the goal is to just terraform mars, but everyone has the chance to take care of a different aspect or work together to build something. I am glad that the devs didnt include competitive mechanics in the game. I mean they have the military aspect of the story, so they definitely had the chance to do so. Anyway, it's a great addition, but I feel like it suffers from performance issues. It got so bad that we had to turn down the music and audio, because it was cutting in and out for all of us. Too bad too, since the soundtrack, albeit short, is amazing and helps with the atmosphereI have played this game for about 31 hours and I still haven't figured out the worker mechanics other than spamming them, upgrading the roads and later spamming hyperloops to decrease load for the roads. I always felt like I don't understand something and I feel like this could be explained better. The DLC Blue Mars is nice, but I feel like the added ship mechanics are suffering from the same thing. Using the storage mechanics of ports can help with this issue, since you can force specific ressources to be allocated to specific ports, though the "number slider" should really be revisited, since if you want to, lets say, collect food mainly, but still allow some building materials to make the ships in that port be able to build stuff on water, you have to go through all ressources, hold click until its at "10" and then repeat that for all the ports that should have this configuration. Even a "copy configuration" button would help here.I know I am being extremely nitpicky here and I just want to say that I really enjoyed my time with this game. I would recommend it to anyone who likes ressource, logistics, space management games and also likes a good story and multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: It is very cool game for the story. The first 10 hours are good. But then the game breaks down from poor optimization and too fast progress. The end game is just clicking special project and waiting 15 minutes.- The balance is out of wack with colonies.- No reason to build crater cities as they have lower RP/resource ration.-The colony needs 10 water food for one research cycle but its seems to fast as cant seem to supply the city fast enough. Have enough food close by but that needs 20 drone ticks to supply the colony.- Late game building takes really long time as there seems to be bug with the blue new road placement. As you place building  next to 4 already build building it will take some time to blue roads to form. Was at about 1000 buildings. Started to break up my connections and made more hyper loops for small distances. It seemed help a bit.- Why are there no upgraded worker hubs or workers. Carry 2 stacks but slower?- No way to mine the formed ice or use the sea for water.- Still need search for ice from martian soil when you have liquid water lake next to the colony.-Combat fits the story but is quite bother. Why cant have auto hunt attacking drones? - Food is chemical and water sink? They have not heard of recycling? Could be used to balance the colonies. Larger colonies are easier to supply but have waste, but smaller one need less resources but need to have more workers supplying.- Storage building is just bad? Can only hold 100 of each type so if want to mine 800 iron from flood area fast need to have 8 storage buildings for that one mine.The game is great at start that breaks down from having the whole planet. It is very cool to look at Mars and transform it but at same time it feels quite useless as use only 10% planet. Well 60%? will be under ice/water in the mid game so does limit it.For now If you only want to play the story its fine game, but the game will break down. For now would wait for them to fix the game. It is quite shame as the story is great.The terraforming feels bit too fast as water/ice will hide quite many interesting lore from the old research missions.

_childDocuments_.review: So- I love this game. The atmosphere is great- the world is alive and enticing the voice actors and the artstyle really bring the world to life. It constantly entices me to double think what is going on and I love it.But...Some of the mechanics are lacking if not broken.  Terraforming seems really easy especially when compared to small base expansions. The constant outward search for one more resource deposit is enticing - but also often so luck driven. If the martian surface is 30% Aluminium why to I have to travel 600km for the nearest deposit? A technological way of extending the lifespan of deposits would be very fun- maybe at increased energy costAnd the drones and their allocation of priorities is nonsensical often leaving you to wonder if you screwed up somewhere or if it is simply the drones not moving 2 of your 150 steel to a new building because moving silica back and forth is more fun.You can and will have errors arise in your systems, which can lead to a total colony collapse. Be smarter than me- save often and save in new save slots- you never know where it went wrong. Anyway hope you found this helpfull.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game so far. 3 hours in and it's starting to pick up.  It's somewhat like factorio, but it has more going on in the graphics and story areas.  It does have some rough areas though. Specifically I am almost 100% sure that the voice overs are not lined up.  For example after researching a tech my inner monologue doesn't typically kick into until the tech is 1/4 to 1/2 done.  While that sounds fine when I type it, in game it is jarring because with much going on you've flitted to another area and stopped thinking about the button you clicked 2 minutes ago.  This is especially bad when discussing your interactions with the story.  Several times this disconnect has made me question what I am (The character) referring to exactly.  I suspect it is a bug rather than a writing device to suggest my character is brooding over information after the fact because in this context it introduces serious ambiguity to the focus of the content.Either way it seems a great little game, I enjoy it so far.. but it seems like I may run out of tech before I run out of game which may also leave me bored. I hope not!Mods can only help this game too. So hopefully those are possible, if not as always this review will go to thumbs down because shutting a community out of a project is like suck starting a pistol. It only shoots you in the face.

_childDocuments_.review: Geez. Last ~8 hours I was basically just waiting for a bar to fill. Generally the art (both visuals and audio) is nice, the gameplay and story are just shallow. I think this game could've been much more but it just didn't work out.The game seems to be logistics/production management but you quickly realize you have no real control over flow of resources. You've got some semi-automated worker drones but only two priorities to control them (default and high priority) so they often do things in their own order. Storage is also problematic.The terraforming aspect is also pretty simple, you just make things that fill some bars (sometimes empty bars). I haven't found any deeper connection between the variables, it was just straightforward mapping like X carbon dioxide -> Y temperature. I hope humans like my 2 bar atmosphere (8% oxygen). Also you have no tools to revert the changes you've made, it's like you get only half of the toolkit because you aren't supposed to need the other half (like you can import nitrogen from some moon but for some reason can't export it).There are more things I could point out but I'm just too tired after finishing the game. If you want to play it better bring a book with you for the latter half of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A story within a story. Per Aspera isn't just a macro colony management game focused on terraforming Mars, like a pulled-back Surviving Mars or Rise of Industry in space. It's also the story of an awakening AI. And how the developers handled that awakening AI is my favorite part of the game so far, because that awakening AI is you. And while this part of the story has plenty of choices, those choices aren't about giving you mechanical advantages in this area or that. Instead, you're given narrative choices, distilled down into 1-2 word responses, that then elicit a longer response from the AI who justifies the choice you made with a logical and/or philosophical interpretation. These responses are good, sometimes REALLY good, and I've frequently found myself wanting to reload and make the other choice just to hear the alternative philosophical viewpoint. And, at least for the first few hours that I've played, these choices that shape the awakening AI come at you frequently. It's not quite as taxing of your time and attention as the general management of the colonization and terraforming efforts, but it always seems to be there, either filling in a lull as resources build or expanding your focus while you're concentrating on building out a new logistical grid. Speaking of colonization and terraforming, this game has a LOT of mechanics and I can totally understand why some people get overwhelmed. Your logistics grid (at least as far as I've gotten) is based around workers (building/transportation), energy (net production and expanding network), building maintenance, and production (mining and factories). From there you'll expand into the colonization aspect of the game with spaceports and domes, which net you research points. Those research points will expand all previously mentioned areas as well as open up the terraforming side of the game. As someone who plays a LOT of colony management and economic simulator games, I'm really enjoying this so far. The systems all seem to be working and while I have gotten overwhelmed a few times as I've run into walls I didn't know were there (like building limits or colonist limits), I was able to quickly identify how to overcome those limitations through the research options.

_childDocuments_.review: Contains spoilers.Pros:Excellent voice acting.Intriguing story, great characters.Solid base building.Cons:Part of the story happens off screen and characters go on as if you were told. The off-screen parts can be pieced together quite easily, but still not great.Story events can happen out of order, with characters voicing anticipation for events they have already congratulated you for completing.Story events and conversations are tied to your progress, which may mean long periods of silence if you are not completing the objectives in the intended order.At least one occurrence of voiced line and text not matching up.Repetitive sound track, one tune in particular really gets into your head.Combat is trivial if you realise all you need is a single doom stack to wipe out anything.AI is terrible at combat, and will throw its units away ignoring defence towers and picking unwinnable fights.AI cheats like there's no tomorrow: range of power and maintenance buildings is greatly increased, vast amounts of resource nodes spawn in the enemy base, the enemy will literally SPAWN BUILDING FASTER THAN YOU CAN DESTROY THEM (seriously, wtf SA-10?)Upon defeating the enemy their base will just vanish, no ruins, no salvage, just an empty plain with the disproportionate amount of resource nodes they AI was given.FPS drops can happen.I find it odd that you are forced to exterminate the first enemy you encounter - and no one acknowledges the ongoing destruction regardless of how long you draw it out and play defensively; there is no option to report the issue to command and work with them to sort it out. You have an enemy; you must defeat it for the story to continue.The story branches in rather simple manner - you have 3 buttons - select which path you want. It would have been more engaging to have the story be based on the actions you did or specifically didn't do.Also, the merging option is a bit of a let down; AMI doesn't really merge, more like just gets erased. (AMI was pro-human, Carmine was anti-human - AMI/Carmine is just as anti-human as Carmine which no option to the player to take a middle ground) Also, AMI/Carmine loses the ability to create research outposts so you can never research and figure out the story behind the ruins in SA-9 if you take that path, and the AMI/Carmine knowledge base does not contain any info about it.Neutral:Only "normal" and "high" priority options, which is limiting to the queueing of operations, but manageable.I've found that its essential to keep several factories of each kind of high priority, as well as the drone factories and part of the maintenance buildings.Worker drones are the lifeblood of getting anything done and you must pepper your base in hubs (at the end I've managed to run about 400 drones for 1200 buildings - about 1/3 of the buildings in the base were drone hubs) - everyone that's complaining that tasks are being ignored just doesn't have enough drones.Hyperloop is essential for bigger bases, and each entrance should be liberally surrounded by worker drone hubs.Impression:I want to love the game, the story, ideas, and characters (I've grown more attached to Nathan Foster more than any "family" in the Fallout games), but the implementation just falls flat. The base building gameplay is solid but gets repetitive by the end, the combat is terrible overall. The the hiccups of presentation work against the narrative and can really break the immersion.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very pretty to look at. And that's sadly about it.Played through this game one and a half times, first time on realistic, which ended in a doom spiral and another on story which was more akin to an idle game. The story is so-so, up to your taste really. However, the gameplay boils down to seemingly being so easy it's almost an afterthought to tell a mediocre story with very beautiful visuals or balancing a house of cards where one oversight can end the whole game. The newer updates may have fixed some problems, but overall, it seems to want to be two things at once. On one hand it wants to tell its story bit by bit and limit where and how fast you can expand, but on the other it wants you to balance a delicate and fragile system that relies on expanding and exploring. And the two halves do not support each-other. Once resources for maintenance run low or out for whatever reason, the drones stop functioning and then everything stops functioning. And there does not seem to be a way to come back from that. Not exactly ground-breaking, a better word would be either boring or tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: Loving it so far. You play as this AI who is in charge of terraforming Mars. You gotta balance resources (natural, power, workers etc)It's equal amounts cool and cute. Zoom out to space/rotate around Mars, then zoom into a 'crashed before I arrived' rover from the year 2021.It's deep and complex too,  one of the main reasons I play sims like elite,  or sim management games like Planet zoo/coaster.  You feel like you're learning and progressing for ages with a nice high skill ceiling and complexity done right.  Per Aspera does this.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: This game checks all the boxes you would want from this genre.  Great looking visuals, great concept, plenty of good ideas.  The only problem is that it feels very incomplete.  Lot's of lost potential and game mechanics that in the end are pointless.  Give this game another year of development time and it could be one of the best strategy games around.  I know it's an indie game and the price is well below much larger games.  But frankly I would have paid $50 for a fully realized Per Aspera and would have continued dropping money on expansions.In the end, I think Tlön Industries has a potential gem on their hands and the work they've done so far is solid.  Please keep working on your game as I would gladly come back and replay it again and again if you do.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: For something like ten years, ever since I first really discovered the concept of transhumanism, I have always half-jokingly half-seriously said that I can't wait until the day I can upload my brain onto a computer and launch it into orbit around Mars.Somehow Tlön Industries has reached deep inside my psyche and delivered my exact dream in video game form.  While I still eagerly look forward to the day I can exist without this meat-girdled bone-robot, Per Aspera provides a well-made and fun entry into the sci-fi base-building genre that, hopefully, helps to usher in even more fantastic transhuman plots from video games as a whole.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoyed their time with Surviving Mars and such other management games.... Per Aspera falls short on what I was looking for. While the feeling of seeing Mars' oceans rise is great, it took 20 hours to get to that point. The game is very slow on some matters, which means your maintenance costs are going to eat through your materials while you are waiting for either research or terraforming to happen. Which means you will at some point stand atop an city of inactive mines to keep the transportation of goods going, forcing you to constantly use up your ever dwindling resources to reach out to further and further resource sites with ever smaller returns as your mines will have a limited amount of selected materials beneath them. Ice being one of these, as it is needed for colonists for both their habitats and food production, but once the planet's temperature begins to rise, so start to melt the ice sites, forcing you to somewhat race the process to get the liquid water pumped and refined before your stockpiles of ice vanish from usage.Not to mention the worker AI is not pleasing. I have more often than not stared minutes at an queued up facility, all the while the workers carry around something completely irrelevant despite setting the construction site as high priority.I can see the potential in this game, I want to love it, even like it but the shortfalls in management and inability to direct your workers despite in-universe being the overseer AI, the extremely scarce feeling of the resources and small tech tree get in the way.You are sent to terraform the Mars with apparent free will, and yet you constantly feel caged in by mission control not giving you enough space to do what you must.Get on sale if you wish.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Not complete a NO, but not yet YES. While the game runs nice, has okayish atmosphere it is not up to my expectation for a game that releases paid DLC that should be logical part of the vanilla game. This game could be great but it is in EA state (by Factorio standards - yes I am spoiled). While the idea is fine, I'd suggest to review the game at least once by devs and try to see what could be done better. Why I have to zoom out to see what a factory makes. There should be an option to make the production icon visible always. The pressure/gas/water/etc ratios should be reworked. Average temperature of +30 Celsius is ok? Why so many paths? It is worse than Civilisation IV in this aspect. With multiple landing sites it becomes chaotic as you cannot see production trends in 2nd or more sites so multiple sites don't really do anything. Sounds could be reworked. I hope their next free update will bring more functionality in the game. Still, it is quite fine game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really polished and well done for what it is. Graphics and sound design are amazing as well.My issue with it is that all you do is going through the motions of expanding in a predetermined way and reacting to things beyond your control. For a game about agency, you really don't have enough.All you do is complete checklists.

_childDocuments_.review: What I liked during the free weekend: - Learning about physics, chemistry and biology- Being wrapped in the story of an astronomical task, AI self-reflection, and interaction- Pacing through terraforming phases 1-3- Weighing short-term against long-term goals- Reusability of resources; you only lose time- Lenses, building listsWhat I disliked: just - Interruptions to story interactions, e.g. by finishing a research; use an event queue please- No option in Story Mode to ask for sector access- No breakdown of resource flow and suggestions by district- No modified clicks for resource numbers (like 100 with e.g. Alt)- Assault Drone management & interaction (split & (de)select)- No combination of 2 lenses at once, like Power and Maintenance- Not knowing at which water level what altitude of terrain will be flooded- More story decision consequences, pleaseStory Mode recommended for player competitions ("who can reach p4 earliest")Easy to learnNot as long-lasting or systemical deep as e.g. some Paradox gamesNo great replayability after 3 playthroughs

_childDocuments_.review: I was waiting quite a while for this game and I must say i really enjoy it. Map is simply beatiful - this is one of the things that has caught my attention in the first place.At first it may seem a bit overwhelming and complicated but you will quickly get a hang of it, devs also take comments of players into consideration and add suggestions / fixes proposed by players which means it can only get better.There are, however, things that make it less fun: way resources are distributed among buildings can be really annoying - you have plenty of resources yet for some reason sometimes they won't be delivered to building sites with no explanation why. _childDocuments_.review: This is not a Martian city-builder, if you desire that, go for Surviving Mars. This game is based on territorial expanse and incorporates "range service" mechanics. Sophistication of terraformation and economic "tinkering" is where this game excells (surpassing Surviving Mars by far). It's relatively hard, a bit chaotic and rewarding. The map of Mars is amazing (in it's realism, proper names and size, not 3-D eye sweetnes). Feels a bit like Factorio - in the good sense - it welcomes the "pause" button just so that you could take out a piece of paper and plan the next industrial sector or redesign some logistics. Unlike Factorio it has a deeper motivation (terraforming Mars) and You could still accomplish the game without that much attention to detail.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: That was nice experience. Worth 20h of gameplay. Per Aspera is a resource-gathering strategy with nice visuals, intense story and addictive music. Feels original and indie.What Per Aspera is not.. Well, it's not a balanced strategy, although the challenge is there and it's really nice to grasp the mechanics and beat it. Most probably you won't launch it again after you finish the campaign. It's not that good as a crafting-building game as well, don't expect it to compete with games like Factorio. This is a different genre - nothing wrong with that.

_childDocuments_.review: Gotta say the voice acting and dialogue is fantastic, Im not sure how to say it, most likely i just need therapy. Without a wonderful voice like that most likely i wouldnt of felt it nor would it of felt so genuine. Well done and thank you for the good feelings... Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has some interesting story. I feel that it needs improvement in some areas of the story, choices and such, however it does have some interesting aspects to it.The gameplay its self has some uniqueness to it, and although it too needs improvement, I did end up liking the game. If the devs had planned to stop and leave the game in its current state I might have not recommended this but as they said they want to keep updating it, that gives me hope that they'll see my suggestions and work on improving those areas of it.As you can see, I earned all the achievements, and it took about 32 hours of gameplay to do it all. The game can certainly be extended with modding, and improved. However without mods it is still decent and entertaining.I will however mention some major issues that keep me from highly recommending the game.1) Research will force stop dialogs and interrupt your gameplay every time it finishes.2) The game interrupts you by auto zooming to a completed project of specific types for their first time and every time for certain projects (space elevators). It takes your camera, zooms to the port that did it, angles and changes it forcing you to reset your camera back to your preferred position leaving you to have to go back and find where you were and what you were doing.Those are two major flaws in the game that need to be addressed, and if you're the type of player who hates interruptions, be prepared for that to happen unless the devs fix that. I've already suggested ways to fix it in the discussions. If they patch it, I will edit this out.

_childDocuments_.review: Reading the reviews... people seem very confused about what to expect from this game. There seems to be some major frustration from fans of city builders and deep simulation/ management games coming to this expecting something very different from what it is. I don't blame the game for this - the description is fairly accurate. If you come into this with the right expectations (or no expectations at all) you might find, like me - you're pleasantly surprised. Per Aspera does not offer some deeply complex resource manager that requires pin point micro-management with in depth tinkering of assets. What Per Aspera offers is a very chill - very zen colony building game with very simple, very intuitive mechanics. In short - you spread across the martian surface like a slime mold, all while enjoying a pleasant, perfectly voice acted soap opera involving an AI slowly coming to terms with their purpose and identity. There's JUST enough going on that it doesn't over whelm you, but not so little that you get bored and distracted. For me - it was a wonderful balance between management and simply focusing on much bigger picture concerns, like terraforming and figuring out where I can focus my expansion.There are some scenarios that may provide frustration. You may, like myself, find yourself needing to reload a few times during the story campaign because you've reached a dead end with your resources, requiring you to reload an older save in order to fix your mistakes. Problems that are easily solved but present some head scratching as you slowly learn how to maximize efficiency and avoid these pitfalls. When it clicks - it's great.A calm, pleasant and entertaining experience that perfectly balances between engagement and allowing yourself the luxury of considering bigger picture concerns, all framed by a nice and simple little soap opera about an AI growing up.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: Played it again and changed my mind. It's a pretty relaxing city builder, with a boring story tacked onto it. All the voice actors suck and I hope I never have to hear their annoying voices again. At least you can turn off the voice volume so you don't have to hear their inane highschool drama wittering on as you place your factories in a neat row. No face pyramid in Cydonia, 0/10"Ancient Mysteries" Means building a research colony to get some fluff text that offers no tangible benefit nor does it say anything interesting. There's no mystery either, and the big reveal at the end, eh, ok. Why does story telling have to be so flimsy and full of logical plot holes you could fly a starship through? it's worth it in a sale, which is why I got it. Pretty fun city builder, nice and streamlined.But it's let down by the story tacked onto it. There are better games and stories that deal with the issue of AI than this, and all the false dilemmas and drama was anti climatic. At the end of the game you're presented with a false choice. Likewise, I'd like to ignore all the messages because I find the story telling and voice acting atrociously bad. But no, if you ignore it it'll just play messages with a delay. There was even a false choice I was presented where I declined to hear what the "leader of the colonists" said but the project still presented itself. I think I'll go back to surviving mars. At least that game had some real mystery.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: It was fun and mildly entertaining. I do enjoy the way connections automatically formed, but honestly it made it feel WAY to easy and fast to terraform an entire planet.  I think they drastically undersold what it would take to terraform even a tiny moon, let alone mars. Overall the game wasnt bad, but I think most of my issues were personal preferences and not reflective of actual flaws in the game, the devs did a good job with this and it was a fun experience but does not seem to have much replay ability, as once you beat it there are no more surprises to be had from subsequent plays.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game. Just completed on easy mode. What I liked was that I could FF past the AI and click every leftmost button without reading what it was saying and was still able to complete the game without the AI plot getting in my way. The AI story is a nice feature for those that are into it and it's also nice that I could basically treat it as irrelevant angstyness and the game let me get away with that. I'm more interested in the game mechanics, resource gathering, military development, colony building, etc. and was able to focus on that and pretty much ignore the AI drama. While it wasn't quite like The Settlers / Age of Empires / Knights & Merchants / etc. -in space (which is what I was looking for) it wasn't so far from those sorts of resource-gathering / colony-building / rt combat games that I love, that I couldn't figure it out and enjoy it. I liked it enough that I'm going to go back and try it on hard now.

_childDocuments_.review: This has all the hallmarks of an early access game, yet claims to be the release version. Among others, it offers:- Massively unbalanced randomness all along the "campaign". This would be better kept for sandbox gameplay, once the player has passed the tutorials. - Serious lack of user feedback. It is up to the player to keep up on ongoing passive events and make sure to act upon them on time. - Bad UI. For example, the "ESC" key will behave differently, depending on what sub-section you are in. - The moderate visuals will push the latest GPU to its heat limits. There is no moderation in power consumption.- Micromanagement galore with messy visual feedback. The larger the colony, the less control over what you are actually doing you have. Also, the dialogue in the campaign varies from "grating" to "unbearable". It prefers to go for "fluff" when you are starving for instructions. As for the music... You will be turning it off and substituting it with another soundtrack after less than 2 hours of game play. I'll probably check back on this in 3 months, although my hopes remain low.[EDIT] 7 months later: UX has not improved, and despite the dev's good faith, the game pace remains mediocre at best. The player is still subject to the RNG's whims, making the overlaid story all the more irritating. Adding mod support appears to be a last desperate attempt in balancing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Per Aspera

_childDocuments_.review: The story was kinda neat, but game play-wise, spend a lot of time just waiting around for stuff to get done. Once you get past a certain part of the story, there is no need for the last half of the military tech tree. The game needs to have better information, I was just guessing at times for proper placements of teraforming buildings. I would see huge dips in power and population and not know what was causing it resulting in me just spamming buildings. Was kinda fun to watch the planet become hospitable and oceans to form but not as engaging of a game as I hoped it to be and a lot of the mechanics didn't make sense. Humans can bounce around the planet in ships but logistic drones are limited to ground transportation only?!?!?

_childDocuments_.review: (disclaimer: Played few days intensively during free weekend.)Mediocre. I enjoy complexities and exploring failure states. Per Aspera does not offer much of either. If you don't enjoy failing and complex systems - perhaps Per Aspera is ok for you.All bases start exactly the same (due to limited resources on the landing craft + same spawns for basic minerals around the landing craft. You _always_ have to build the same buildings to get the base ready for further expansion. Early on one needs to micro manage power (at least on harder difficulties) to make things run smoothly. Once you have fusion/fission and connect the bases with Hyper Loops the traffic goes dramatically down and no longer are you challenged by your setup. Just choose how you would like to progress with the terraforming. Failing basically only means you will progress slightly slower on research, building or projects - nothing else.It was enjoyable seeing the world itself evolve as 1st waterline appeared and later vegetation started sprawling. Unfortunately I feel a missed opportunity with the progress of the terraforming to impact the planet itself from gameplay perspective. Only the rising water level is meaningful as you wish to gain access to it, but will lose buildings if it keeps rising. As long as you let the organic life spread out on to the oceans and open planes from the confines of your road webbed base it has no impact on the game apart from the terraforming meters - not the planet or placement of further buildings.The campaign seems weirdly scripted. 1st time I played I got rolled over on the 1st contact for not being prepared (no spoilers), 2nd time I had no problem whatsoever and just waiting if something else is coming to challenge me just slowed my progress on terraforming. Nothing interesting. (my campaign run got cut short when one of the old mines was either underwater or bugged so the campaign could not progress) Some reviews mentioned the story being interesting - I found the story very mediocre, cookie cutter, AI stuff.All in all - chill "city builderish" fun for not so serious thinking. It is ok.

_childDocuments_.review: This is resource management / base builder game. It takes little more realistic approach on terraforming Mars than most games.Story is interesting and I have really have been intrigued what is going on. Which is rare in this genre.Graphics are nice and slowly transforming Mars from red to blue/green planet looks awesome.Sound is kinda meh except dubbing which is pretty good.UI is mostly great. It is uncluttered and clearly provides all needed informations. You can open also energy distribution on traffic overview etc.However game doesn't inform you very well that a lot of interface stuff like resources etc. can actually be opened by left click to see graphs or buildings overview. Also more notifications settings would be nice as your needs change when you base grows.As for base building at first it can be challenging manage your resources right and routes automatically connecting building look really cool. However over time it gets far more easier and simplistic as you have very little tools to properly manage and only 1 priority level. Also it gets really repetive as everything is based about circles. You want connect building to traffic? It has to be in reach of a circle.You want to have power connection? It has to be in reach of a circle.Under maintenance? It has to be in reach of a circle.Under defense? It has to be in reach of a circle.Supply of water? It has to be in reach of a circle.Game would benefit a lot if there were more mechanics. Also flooding is really annoying. The game doesn't offer any good option to transition between land and sea infrastructureI have very mixed opinion about state of the game. With some quality of life improvements it would be really cool game. At the end I have kinda enjoyed playing it even thought it was pain from time to time as such I give thumb up.

_childDocuments_.review: Per Aspera is a great game, I downloaded it for the free play weekend and played it for 8 hours straight the first day, its graphically not good, but graphics aren't what makes a game playable or good, sure its the cherry on top, but If you like complex games with layers that have layers then per aspera is it, I plan on buying it My next check, There is definetely alot to this game, and all the people complaining about the AI you play as, they're too picky She does have alot of dialogue but doesnt affect your gameplay in one speck of an amount. If you like City management, on a global scale, with a nice tech tree and a splash of combat, Try it while its free, and Buy it if its not free.

_childDocuments_.review: After several patches the game is in better shape but the one thing that continues to be a sticking point is there is no way to manually intervene in your logistics short of deprioritizing every single building except for the one you need at that moment, a very labor intensive operation when you have hundreds of buildings. I was well into the game, almost done with stage 5 terraforming, with 78 worker hubs humming along, a hyperloop system that circumnavigated the globe, every threat dealt with and a virtual endless supply of raw materials. Suddenly my worker count dropped sharply and (thanks to the advanced lack of warning systems) I caught it when I was 10/78 workers. checking all my worker factories I saw that none of them had parts so I canceled my in progress space pads that had parts stored on them (they were not prioritized, my worker factories were - no idea why they had parts but my worker factories didn't) then waited for the parts they had in stock to be distributed to my worker factories. They never were. I sat there and watched my count go from 10 to 5 to 1 to 0, nearly a hundred parts just sitting there waiting to be used. I could have gone through and deprioritized every one of my important buildings, recovered from the nose dive, then reprioritized them all again but.. why spend the  600+ clicks and all the time hunting the buildings down for that? Why are we given only two levels of priority? Why were parts going to space programs I hadn't marked priority instead of factories I had marked? Why can't I at least declare an emergency and take direct control over a single worker to do a single task if needed? The patches fixed a lot of the issues I was seeing at launch but there is still fundamental, frustrating flaws with this game. At least it's up to feeling like an Early Access game instead of a broken demo.*****OLD review section, some issues still apply*******Decent enough demo, but presented as a completed game. The fact that I had 150 glass, a 12/45 workers and 3 worker factories each needing a single glass to build more workers, all on high priority while my worker count slowly dwindled, my glass simply sitting and doing nothing.. and my only possible solution to manually go through every single high priority building and turn them to normal, then once the situation became normal to go back and re-prioritize all my buildings.. Well, I opted to let my sprawling colony with 5500 colonists die off instead.The game is incredibly incomplete. There is no way to tell your workers to prioritize one thing up until a point, workers evenly spread resources across everything of the same priority instead of finishing one job before moving on to the next, you can't set production goals. There just isn't any way to manage your workers other than marking individual jobs as priority, and if you have too many of those then they get nothing done anyway.Plenty of other unfinished parts of the game drag it down. You can't cancel a road upgrade (and they are pretty pricey!), combat is just a chore, there is no way to improve the game cycle other than roads and upgraded mines/factories (You can't build farms and let humans make their own food, for instance, even once you cover Mars in greenery, your workers will always follow roads and carry a single item each - no upgrading them to carry multiple items or into flying transports or anything, the range of buildings isn't upgradable so building a "branch" to a resource early game is exactly as tedious late game, scanners will scan for resources at the exact same speed the entire game - there is no upgrade possible for them)It doesn't help that half the things in the game happen with no explanation. My biodomes spread forests and lichen across the world. How much is that contributing to the O2 level? No clue. My aquadome spread cynabacteria through an ocean, in ebbs and flows. Why is it ebbing at times? No idea. I built a space elevator after a titan amount of effort (about 1700 resources total!) What is the actual, mechanical benefit? No idea. Coupling that with alerts that are super easy to miss (tiny icon, no noise) and you have a character that is presented as being a data driven entity who literally feels the buildings and workers as part of her body being effectively blind to most of what the colony is doing.The most frustrating part of all of this is Per Aspera is a major update away from being really, really good. Give the players the ability to manage minimum stock, store extra workers for God's sake, make worker break downs random instead of timed (having every worker die off at the same time is basically death for your colony), make the AI smart enough to build dependencies that are missing in a priority chain, have them build things in FIFO queues (or even FILO stacks if you really want.. it'd be weird but whatever, anything but the stupid "evenly distribute resources so nothing ever completes" method).. Do all that, which most of these are related problems, and Per Aspera would feel like a minimum viable complete game.TL;DR - don't buy at any price until it gets some major rework. Currently it isn't a finished game, at all.

_childDocuments_.review: I've just finished the game after barely sleeping for the past four days to squeeze this between a full time job and kids. _childDocuments_.review: Fun resource manager / base builder / supply chain game. My only problem was the finite resource. It means the resource chains of your older bases will collapse while you're focusing on building the new ones, so you have to regularly go back and rebuild your bases. This is extra cumbersome because roads are automatically created between nearby buildings, so if you remove a certain building you might cut off the entire side of your base from the other, so you have to replan new buildings, etc. etc...The other thing is it's a chore to view the resource +/- balance of the sector you're currently working on (which has a separate resource pool from your other bases). That is vital to see if your supply chain is lacking in a certain resource or overproducing another. There is a way to  switch to "district view" but it's a few clicks away, it puts an overlay on the map and its mutually exclusive with other vital views like resource map, energy, maintenante, etc. I
