_childDocuments_.review: These are my first impressions of the game, remaster and the PC port. This is not a review.Destroy All Humans is a series that has evaded PC. Given the work done with this remaster, I'd say it's a crime we never got these games sooner. This is a game that plays like a dream for what it sets out to do. Controls in the remaster are fluid, environments are great and gameplay is varied and fun. The voice acting and general writing is very notable and the overall "fun factor" is just up there. While the franchise hit its stride with Destroy All Humans 2. The first game, especially with this remaster. Is very much worth checking out!Basically, you're an anti-hero type alien (Furon) named Crypto that sounds like Jack Nicholson. You run around and harvest humans for their strains of Furon DNA that has been apart of the human DNA strain for centuries. Furons can't reproduce except for cloning themselves but the strain weakens after each cloning. It gets so bad that it effects intelligence, and even a clone of Crypto was captured back on Earth because of it. So now you must harvest humans for their stored Furon DNA and rescue the Crypto clone all the while you control the human populace and make sure they aren't alerted to your presence. This is while government agents are trying to stop you during the games wonderful missions which have you using all kinds of abilities and tools such as anal probes, lightning guns, flying saucer death rays, body cloning, brain harvesting. Good stuff. Great dialogue and voice acting backs it up too with some intentionally strange and eccentric performances from the cast.There are some problems. Voice audio sounds a bit muffled in the cutscenes. Sound bytes also repeats often within the game when you're zapping humans and they yell the same things over and over again when they spot you. The game has its share of glitches in the press pre-release copy. I've seen the same trucks in the same spot spawn in hovering 3 feet off the ground. There are some performance hitches when starting a level too. There's also the issue regarding the art style. It generally looks nice but the character models vary. They look a bit too much like plastic dolls sometimes and their jawlines would make Chad Thundercock blush. There's also the obligatory, awful-looking Unreal Engine 4 particle physics that look like blinding neon lights. They look awful and I don't know why every game has this problem in this engine.From what I've played, this is an excellent remaster despite flaws in the original release and the remaster itself as it improves the original significantly from what it was. Destroy All Humans 2 is still a much better game and I really can't wait for Black Forrest Games to get that one out as it improves so much upon the original. If you haven't touched the series, I'd definitely give this version a look but you might be better off waiting for a sale or the sequel as it's just that much of a better game. If you liked the original, absolutely pick this up as soon as possible. You won't be disappointed (except maybe with the character models, then again the original was pretty hideous too).Thanks for reading! I have a full video right here if you want to check it out:We also have a curator page if you want some more recommendations: Have a good one!

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans!Originally released in 2005 for the Xbox and Playstation 2, Destroy All Humans! takes place during the 1950's in the middle of the Cold War between the United States and the now defunct USSR, DAH! uses the time to explore rural, urban and suburban and provide a satirical commentary on uncle sam military propaganda, red flag paranoia, and communist hysteria that took root in the United States throughout the entire Cold War.DAH! Doesn't just poke fun at the US of the time, it also cracks at 50's B-Movie Sci-Fi: Take - The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951), It Came from Outer Space and War of the Worlds (1953), Them! (1954), Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1957), and The Fly (1958). You view the game through the eyes of a Furon, a stunted blue-ish alien similar in description to the supposed Roswell Grey's, named Cryptosporidium, clone #137. Your goal on Earth is 2-fold: Find out what happened to your predecessor - Crpytospordium, clone #136 -  and harvest human DNA strands stored in their brainstems to resequence your species' DNA which has become degraded from eons of cloning after they rendered themselves infertile from over use of nuclear weapons.The game is filled to the brim with highly exaggerated, flamboyant borderline offensive stereotypes and cliches, interwoven into every possible aspect of the game: weapons, enemies, story, dialogue, settings, locations, and art style. While the old hardware of the Original Xbox and PS2 cranked out just enough displayable polygons to sell what the devs were aspiring to create, the overhauled graphics amp an already outrageous game up to 11, and it is absolutely glorious.Before you even touch down in rural American, somewhere in Mississippi if I had to guess based on the map, your handler and lead scientist on the Furon DNA resequence project, Orthopox, clone #13, is already barking orders at you, Crpyto, and he does so the entire game. The two seem to share a love-hate relationship, with 'Pox being interested in furthering mission goals and the invasion of Earth while Crypto begrudgingly follows his orders, anticipating the next time he gets to vaporise a family of 4, or knock down a couple city blocks.Very early on in the game you start butting heads with the Military and some shady organization called "Majestic" which is totally not the CIA, I swear. On top of local law enforcement, and any civilians you encounter, there is a lot to shoot at. The missions of the game follow a set plot, but you're encouraged to free-roam the current locations to complete challenges, recover collectables, just plain old explore and blow stuff up if you so please. Progression of the game is locked to missions, the more missions you complete the more hardware you've given to Destroy All Humans!Your on-foot arsenal consists of 4 weapons: The Zap-O-Matic, a deliciously over the top electrical discharge weapon that can chain to near-by enemies. The Disintegrator Ray, a very stereotypical weapon for hostile aliens that reduces whatever it kills to ash. The Anal Probe, which does exactly as you think it does, connects to the nearest anus and then proceeds to blow that person's head off. And lastly, for when all else fails, there's the Ion Detonator: A grenade launcher that instantly vaporizes all infantry and most vehicles in a single shot.However as a highly evolved Furon, you get access to a full suite of mental abilities including: Telekinesis, Mind Reading, Brain Extraction (Similar to the Anal Probe), Holobob which allows you to blend in to your surroundings by imitating an individual. Forget, Distract, and Follow. As well as Transmog which converts props you find in the map to ammo. And a bunch of contextual specific powers which I won't get into.And your highly advanced interstellar civilization has a hole pack of hardware built into your space suit: A full-on Jet Pack, Hoverskates, Shield Generator, and Dash Jets.And no Alien invasion game would be complete without your very own FLYING SAUCER. Oh yeah! Complete with a Death Ray, Sonic Boom Generator, and Quantum Deconstructor, you can be levelling entire city blocks in just a few shots with any one of these. It also has repulsion field, and abduction beam, and transmoger for ammo recovery just like you do on foot. Wow its almost like the game wants you to use the tools its given you to have fun. Revolutionary concept I know, but its something I feel many modern games have forgotten.A full set of upgrades exists to make your arsenal improve as the game progresses, for you to choose as you see fit. Some missions require you to be stealthy or avoid hard contact with local law enforcement, while others just have you murdering everything in sight as you so choose to do. The upgrade progression is tied to DNA collection, of which you get DNA by... what else? Harvesting human brains, extract and anal probe as much as you can. But the fun doesn't stop there, every mission gives you a sum of DNA upon completion, and each mission has a series of secondary objectives which aren't critical to the completion of that mission but will reward you with more DNA upon success of the operation.Spread throughout the locations are a series of drone collectables which reward DNA for their recovery, and as the game progresses, challenge missions which are entirely optional, are unlocked at each one of the locations you discover and explore that grant you even more DNA based on your score in them, up to 3 Stars. Races, Rampage, Abduction, and Armageddon challenges will gift you bonuses, and the ability to complete them is some-what locked off behind your progression through the upgrades. Upgrades effect your Saucer, weapons, mental abilities, and your suit. So every aspect of your arsenal improves as you move through the game.A personal recommendation: Upgrade the Zap-O-Matic as quickly as possible, it is all round the best and grab the S.K.A.T.E upgrades as you'll need your hover skates to achieve 3 stars in the challenge races.A thorough player is rewarded with ample DNA for upgrades, bonus skins for Crypto that you can wear at your leisure, and a complete set of concept art for you to browse through which details the graphics overhaul the devs put into this game. There's also a complete handbook that unlocks entries as you encounter new and strange things, all of which have comments from the game's 3rd Furon character: Gastroenteritis, clone #999. He has a much bigger roll and appearance DAH! 2.Crpyto is voiced by the J. Grant Albrecht who done VA work for a huge number of video games, while Orthopox is voiced by the legendary Richard Steven Horvitz, most well known for his iconic Invader Zim. And oh boy these two have an absolute ball playing their respective characters, they do the vast majority of the meaningful talking in this game, along with majestic agents, and the occasional military hard-ball general.The original soundtrack and main furon theme focuses on the more eerie side of science fiction, similar to the original Alien, or certain parts of the Independence Day score. And while certainly not the highlight of this game, its soundtrack compliments the gameplay and cutscene well enough, definitely not a detractor. The Furon Main menu theme though, is both frightening and mysterious in a sci-fi typical score you'd expect when dealing with aliens.For everything this remake wants to do and achieve, it succeeds in spades. There's content here you wouldn't get buying the typical 60 dollar base version of a modern "AAA" title, and on that alone Destroy All Humans! is worth the money their asking for it. If you pre-ordered the game you get access to a bunch of Deluxe skins for Crypto that you can choose to wear, otherwise you have to purchase it as DLC.Obviously a thumbs up from me, and more importantly, I need a DAH!2 remake now like yesterday.Destroy All Humans!One giant step on mankind.

_childDocuments_.review: For lovers of the other games, it's a great wrap-up to the series instalments. And it's cheap.Older games, like Destroy All Humans (2005), offered a great amount of playability, story, current graphic standards and many enjoyable game mechanics. Though a game as old as DAH hasn't maintained its playability as a game title on it's own.This remake sees Destroy All Humans as the game it could have been if it were made this year. As a player of the old game you'd think "I wish the game let me do this-", and the devs saw that.

_childDocuments_.review: *Possible Spoilers*The game is worth it. There are few games that exceed in value for what they cost. You get a triple AAA experience.  The maps, story, and missions are great but what really makes the game stand out is the ability to free roam on each map. You can use your ship or go on foot. Free RoamThe game provides a fun and amazing way to level up your abilities outside of missions by earning DNA points. You can just go around causing mayhem on humans, cars and buildings if you want or test new abilities/weapons. All maps have 4 specific "trials" that you can complete during free roam to earn points as well. All four trials are fun. MissionsDestroy All Humans! has a great story and the missions are fun. Their are optional objects throughout missions which give you bonus DNA(points). The character you play is a clone and the voice acting is great for your character. It sounds a lot like Jack Nicholson. There are some real funny moments in the story and it is very enjoyable. Weapons/AbilitiesThe team did a great job coming up with different abilities and weapons. As you progress you unlock powerful versions of abilities and weapons which makes the game more fun and allows you to go back and complete challenges you didn't get 100% on. Now, you have upgrades for both your ship, weapons and character abilities. Some of my favorite abilities is Brain probing but with the upgrade that makes it jump to other attacking NPC's. It is an easy way to grab lots of DNA when you are at military bases with soldiers in big groups. The S.K.A.T.E ability allows you to do a dash and then basically like roller blade around lol. When upgraded it becomes a power ability. The death ray on the space ship is like a classic weapon pulled from a alien movie.  I would highly recommend you play the game. A++++There seems to a small bug were if you read a humans mind to much, the audio playback seems to revert back to a default audio recording which I suspect is from one of the game creators. It doesn't happen all the time but once in a while when I read a mind you notice the voice change from Jack to some regular guy IRL at work and it sounds like a programmer! :) Besides this, I have not come across another bug. I wouldn't even consider this a bug as it doesn't diminish the game play at all.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really weird game, that's both smarter and dumber than it ought to be. It has a very, very dark view on 1950's America (well deserved, but still), and will without question require a 'trigger warning' for anyone with Political right-leaning views who can't laugh at themselves as it has a very dim view on that side of the aisle. That aside, it is fun, although the common review complaint: too many cutscenes (skipable or not) is a major problem, probably the biggest problem; it really breaks the follow of the game and is jarring at times as you go from in combat to totally peaceful, in a new location, in a cutscene. The gameplay is solid though, and the ever expanding inventory of classic sci-fi/B-Movie/Shlock Alien movie weapons (including an anal probe because of course it would) makes it feel varied in how you conduct yourself. It is interesting the game included both a stealth approach system (scanning and wearing a human's apperance) and a 'loud' approach system, although I feel as though the missions themselves could have done more to encourage either approach as most seemed geared, or outright forced, in one way or the other. It's clearly an older game in both feel and fun and I'd recommend it with the caveat to remember that many of the problems mentioned above are borne from more than 10 years of game development since the base of this game was made that has refined many of the concepts in it.

_childDocuments_.review: To start what is this game at its core. Well its a fun non serious arcade shooter with crude but effective humor. Is it childish at times with its humor? Yes very much so. It also pokes fun at Cold War paranoia justified or not. But it isn't preaching anything political to anyone just poking fun at everything that moves.How about gameplay is it good? It is fun that is what it is. It doesn't stand out for any amazing mechanics nor are any of them top of the line but they work together to give you a enjoyable gameplay loop. All weapons are viable with the only real outlier being the starter weapon being somewhat op. The telekinesis and other mind abilities are probably its strongest gameplay feature. Stealing brains to refill shields faster? Pretty fun idea. Transmuting random stuff into ammo? Honestly one of the more fun ideas out there. Throwing NPC's around like wrecking balls? Honestly hilarious especially since many have lines for when they are grabbed. Probably the weakest point of gameplay is the saucer but it is still fun especially making ballistic cows with it.Graphics are fitting is the best description. They are nothing to write home about but there is a great deal of charm with them. You can tell its origin was the early 2000's but a very nice coat was put on it.Story well it isn't terribly special. Its there but don't go expecting anything much beyond poking fun at the past and explosions. But that isn't really the selling point of the game.Characters are honestly great. Crypto and Pox play off each other amazingly. The Majestic agents are amusing. And the other minor characters are funny.Overall it is a fun experience. It is a great cleanser from more serious games or something to play while in a bad mood. If you can get it on sale it is a great choice.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine GTA but there's an unchangeable HUD cluttering your screen with a bunch of game controls all over it and objective text over your screen that NEVER GOES AWAY during missions because you can't remember 1 or 2 simple objectives and simple controls.and nothing can be removed from the HUD in the game settings.Very annoying. Incredibly immersion breaking.Look online at the remaster game HUD and then look up the OG game HUD and you'll seethe OG HUD is incredibly clean by comparison. And thereby much better at keeping your immersion in the game.The OG game HUD was very clean, there was ABSOLUTELY ZERO reason to add this much clutter to the remastered game's HUD.After doing a tutorial, I don't need the game to have the game controls, objectives, and optional objectives, pasted over my screen THE WHOLE TIME during missions.Just tell me at the beginning of the mission and if I forget, let me pause the game to read them.I'm a long time Destroy All Humans fan but unfortunately...I can't recommend this game until there's a game setting to remove absolutely unnecessary game controls, and objective text from my game HUD screen while I play missions.If this is fixed, I will change my review to positive.

_childDocuments_.review: Barely a yes. It's an old game, the graphical update is nice, but of course nowhere near current standards. Gameplay works surprisingly well though. I encountered almost no bugs, once I almost got perma stuck in a wall, another time the game crashed, but auto-saved and let me continue from there.A few times I found it frustratingly vague what to do. Like that you can only land your saucer at a very specific spot. Or how to "electrocute scientists". And the final boss was just... meh. It's an incredible difficulty spike, not because the boss is super hard, but because every boss in this game has 3 health bars, and the last two bosses have incredibly high hit point pools, while you can not replenish your shields manually, you just have to cower in fear and hope nothing hits you, otherwise no more shield recharge.Playing on foot is simple, saucer controls are a bit annoying. Upgrades should be focused on you and not the saucer, since there are only 4 or 5 levels out of the 23 where you can even use it. You can revisit an area, once you've cleared the mission associated with it, to find more upgrade resources, challenges, etc. if you want to.If you don't, you'll basically get 7 hours worth of entertainment AT MOST for 30 bucks. But those 7 hours are 95% fun. Who doesn't want to be the invading species for once?

_childDocuments_.review: this is a really good remake. Like.... Really good. I wasn't a fan of Spyro's remake but this feels fresh somehow. _childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely wonderful remaster, and I've had an equally wonderful time playing it. The first time I played this game is when I was an idiot kid, and didn't know how to beat video games. Now, I've finally had the full experience, and it's been awesome. You play as Crypto, an alien invading earth to gather information on the humans, and ultimately destroying them. It's loaded with dry humor, action, and challenging trials. It's short, easy to get the hang of, and a damn good time. I love the humorous Cold War theme the developers were able to capture, as well as their unique art style. Although the maps are small, everything feels full of life and color, and there's hours of fun to be had. There's not much to add to this review with a pros/cons list since it can be summarized pretty quickly.The remaster has updated the graphics and added achievements, so now it looks prettier and you get points for juggling humans in the air. It has all the same humor, the same cutscenes, and the same dialogue, it just looks better now. The controls are easy to use, the UI works just fine, and all in all, it's functionally wonderful. Throwing humans 200 feet into the air literally never gets old.As far as downsides? A handful of times, the game lagged a bit and crashed once (but that might be because of my laptop). The game is also fairly short, but who cares? It's a ton of fun and it doesn't drag itself out.All in all, it's a short game, with a tiny bit of replay value, and it's a damn good time. I'd recommend this game to anyone, especially if it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: There are not many games that can have unconsenting anal insertion as not just a scene, but an essential gameplay mechanic, and sell that as comedy *correctly*. From this perspective, Destroy All Humans has a certain elegance, but your mileage may vary. It is, in its own admission at the start of the game, from a different time: the mid 2000's, where there's at least three poop jokes, one catsuit-ed female assassin boss fight, and a reminder that the Overton Window for acceptable language marches ever onward (granted, those calling you a "midget" don't serve much purpose besides immediate target practice and brain collection).Gameplay wise, it's solid, though another carry over from the era is a bunch of collectibles that aren't worth tracking down. You don't have the widest array of guns, but they're satisfying to use, all serve a point (mostly), and the game doesn't drag on long enough to want for much more. Still, I tuned out for 20 minutes just blowing up every building on a map, then working through the remains in a human-harvesting rampage, all without any real objective or goal to drive me forward - which is probably the best seal of approval a game like this could ask for.

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans! is a remake made with love – it improves on almost every aspect of its predecessor. With revamped graphics, sweeping QoL changes, more abilities and upgrades, and creative bonus objectives, the game manages to provide the old-school arcade-y charm in a new package that nostalgic gamers crave for! However, sticking closely towards the limitations of the original stop it from moving ahead and becoming a classic in its own regard – some campaign missions that perhaps felt fresh 15 years before, will not appeal to certain modern audiences.If you are looking for a fun comedic romp packed with action, destruction, subterfuge, and an astonishingly enjoyable UFO – Destroy All Humans! is something that you cannot choose to miss.

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans! is a very faithful remake to a cult classic from 15 years ago. The graphics have been updated for 2020 to give it a very cartoonish look and create some hilarious caricatures for humans, the humor remains intact, and the gameplay mechanics have been improved. If you are a fan of the original or are longing for a classic Xbox/Ps2 game, definitely consider picking this up. Fairly simple with a little more depth than just "We're here to kill since we found this planet". The Furon Empire has sent their new clone soldier Cryptosporidium-137 (Crypto) to collect Furon DNA which has been encoded in humans since ancient times. It is needed to be collected so the Furons can live on for eternity (and for reproductive issues). Fine enough story and the title of the game says the rest. You get some nice humorous interactions from Crypto, his leader who is basically a toned down Invader ZIM, and the humans of course.This is where the game varies and I have a hard time recommending it to people who are expecting something real modern in terms of action from the popular games of the past few years. The devs display a message in the beginning of the game that paraphrased comes down to "remember that this is a remake of a 2005 game and everything is still intact". You quickly get used to Crypto's mechanics of telekinesis (PK), zapping rays, jetpack, abducting people in the saucer, even anal probing for brain stems to replenish shields. It's very arcade-like and there are really no real challenging objectives unless you choose to do the "Optional Objectives" (highly recommend). However, there are two things that might shatter expectations for anyone new coming in.  Granted, you are free to explore levels in the endgame but it's not all connected. Furthermore, the missions in here can get real repetitive or just plain boring at points. My least favorite involved escorting a truck with a *very special package* through a terrain that was kinda hell to do the Optional Objectives. If you aren't a completionist for this game, everything will be fairly easy save for 2 missions. There is a lot of repetitiveness and even questionable choices for missions like "why aren't I doing this mission in the Saucer?". It might be off putting to anybody looking for variety in the missions and I can't recommend it to anybody who is expecting huge variety and complex action. I'd advise you to play the demo. Overall, I like the improvements with the mechanics from the original as now I can levitate an object/human while probing another if I please. It's still the gameplay you know and love if you are a veteran. There are challenges and races for areas if you want to have more difficulty with this game. The graphics is the real major thing updated from 2005 and it feels more than just a fresh coat of paint. I love the human designs with them looking like caricatures of their roles. Farmers look hilarious with their billy bob teeth. The mayor looks like a lazy slob in a suit. Army men have underbites. Just fun designs set in a 1950s America. The aliens look great, the environments are nice, and i believe it achieved the look it was going for. Audio is pulled directly from the 2005 game and there are a few audio issues I experienced in the later half that I hope gets patched. Sometimes after killing some humans, I'd hear their voices linger around a spot like it was the audio for them getting zapped. It only happened in the last 2 areas for me, but it threw me off a little bit. For the most part, this game ran smooth with my 1060. Only having some minor hiccups or stutters in the Saucer areas in the last half of the game. However, during the final part of the game, I did crash when I was supposed to restart that final part of the mission. Hoping this can get patched out ASAP as many players will die from this part and it's the finale. Overall, aside from these things, the game ran well with really no drops in frames or assets being blurry trying to load in. This is a fun blast from the past that veterans will surely enjoy and has improved upon the original in every way. For newcomers on the fence, I'd say try to watch some gameplay videos  or play the demo before making a decision on buying to know what you're getting into in terms of repetitive missions. It's a nice 7hr game that only had a few low points for me, but that is probably an issue at the game's core rather than this remake. Hope to see a remake to the sequel in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans Remake was a nice addition to my collection, but the gameplay itself left a sour taste in my mouth after playing it for several minutes. Here is my list of nitpicks that I've noticed so far.- Using any of Crypto's telepathic abilities (besides Corvex Scanning) can interrupt and expose Crypto's current disguise. In comparison to the original game, you were allowed to use your telekinesis, brain extractions without having to deal with your disguise automatically failing, but you still had to scan to maintain the disguise. This change was one of the biggest flaws IMO that really limits the gameplay, enjoyment and adds more challenge over the fun aspect (especially during exploring mode which is one of the best replay value options you can have in this game}.  - Ragdoll physics from this remake looks a nicer upgrade, but there is no flailing when you levitate someone in the air. They just stand up like a stiff board (dead or alive). One cool addition would be the hats and guns falling off than it super glued onto their hands/head. On a side note, compared to the original Destroy All Humans, the bodies were remained in whatever pose they were and it would have some weight while in the air. Plus I think the ragdoll joints were better overall in the original than the remake because the legs were hard to spread apart and usually stayed close to one another. It felt like I play moving around jello.- Telekinesis in this remake has a better visual, but the control of objects felt weightless (there was barely any delay of air movement when moving them left , right, up, down). Another flaw was the ability to target and throw the levitated object at an NPC or NPC to NPC. In the remake, you can do it, but often it's impossible and usually it would miss the target that you're trying to aim at.- Personally, I didn't dig the cartoony scheme of it all. I liked the one from the orginal more, some of the humans look uglier, but they definitely got THICC-er and that would be one of the good ones, but also bad since there wasn't a lot of variety besides the same clothes with different patterns.

The enemies are incredibly easy to defeat with some very easy cheese methods of defeating them on top of that - for example, psychokinesis can launch a group of Majestic Agents into the stratosphere, without an issue. The abilities are very easy to level up and honesty I don’t recommend you do if you want a more challenging experience. Secondly, the missions are fairly simple, there's maybe one or two which are kinda challenging and they are the ones which don't really involve fighting. Would have seen some original missions.Thirdly, the probes (collectable items), there is no incentive to find them all, except to have additional DNA to level up abilities. I would have liked to have seen a Easter Egg or at least a Steam achievement considering how easy the rest are to get. Most of the time I have spent playing this game was looking for these, so sucks it was really for nothing except seeing every part of a very well detailed map. Overall, I would recommend buying and playing the game, just don’t over level and find new ways to make it challenging.

_childDocuments_.review: "Don't get mad, get sadistic."- Crypto In recent years, many developers have attempted to successfully revive dated but beloved games, demonstrating that well-known titles can still be relevant in the contemporary era. One such game is Destroy All Humans, a faithful remake of the iconic 2005 experience that offered endless hours of fun and pure enjoyment. Although it was a welcome addition at the time and was unquestionably adored for its quirky humour and chaotic tone, its greatest strength has since turned into its greatest weakness, as it doesn't make much of an effort to improve upon the original formula. A Furon saucer is struck by a military test rocket in 1914, causing it to crash into Area 51. Later, an undercover group known as Majestic captures the Cryptosporidium 136 passenger from the flying UFO, which ultimately results in its demise. Twelve years after those events, Cryptosporidium 137 is sent to Earth to find his brother and complete the remainder of his mission. Harvest DNA and bring down the US government in the remake of the legendary Alien Invasion action adventure.Whether it's 2005 or 2022, the ability to wipe out our species while blaming the communists makes one genuinely smile. In Destroy All Humans, you play as an alien that not only despises the human race because of their primitive nature but also wants to put an end to their own existence using cunning planning and reliable weapons. This is a genuine change that I personally find refreshing, in contrast to other world-saving stories where the hero tries to save the day. The remake faithfully captures the original game's feeling; as a result, the writing and cast remain the same, bringing back the old reliable controversial humour. Personally, I find the story intriguing not because of its content but because of its execution. The well-placed puns intend to satirise the beliefs of a bygone era where communists and aliens, for example, were portrayed as the reason for every possible misfortune, while good American patriots were saving the day. While the remake retains some of its unique mechanics, there are some changes that improve the overall experience. For instance, the combat feels fluid and is not restricted by a cumbersome lock-on system, and the controls have been greatly simplified without lowering the quality of the experience. The same can be said for the enhanced animations and the newly distinct interactions, which add another line of defence to Crypto's arsenal of destructive tools. Anal Probe, I'm looking at you!The remake greatly improves on the environment's capabilities over the original by including a large number of interactive objects and NPCs. Despite the fact that some areas at first glance appear to be familiar, closer inspection reveals numerous texture and variety differences that give the places a distinct vibe. The original title's flat fields have been replaced with more detailed, polished buildings that add much-needed depth to the environments. Incoming projectiles, hostile NPCs, police vehicles, side quest markers, and other details can all be seen by Crypto from a great distance and are not covered by a blueish fog thanks to the generous size of each map, which includes rendered distance. The combination of the aforementioned elements results in an intriguing world that cries out to be explored.Despite its potential, the game limits itself to twenty-three missions that can be revisited through the main menu. These missions are divided into six main environments, each with its own set of challenges and collectibles to discover. The main missions also include optional tasks that lead to additional DNA samples, an in-game currency you can use to purchase different weapon upgrades. After completing your first mission in each zone, you are free to roam that world and engage in some exclusive tasks or just obliterate as much of the environment as you like. There is a wide range of missions available, from infiltration to kidnapping, where you will either need to operate covertly or guarantee the demise of everyone who gets in your way. With this kind of formula, execution is the only problem. During your playthrough, you will be introduced to a respectable number of abilities that can control minds or simply cause explosions; however, some abilities are not properly presented, causing a lot of confusion about, for example, their radius. Such inconsistencies, particularly in covert missions, can lead to failure because you don't know whether a disguise change will be noticed by the NPCs from a certain distance, jeopardising your cover.As previously mentioned, Crypto has a very diverse collection of tools at his disposal. In retrospect, combat is divided into two thrilling modes: the alien form and the saucer form. Since you will be on the surface the majority of the time, Crypto is outfitted with a variety of absurd skills, such as telekinetic powers, lightning-shooting weapons, and more. After completing certain missions where Crypto is urged to experience their destructive power, all of those skills and weapons will become available for use. You can boost their effectiveness and efficiency by using the DNA samples you've gathered on your adventures. Last but not least, Crypto is also able to use his jetpack to either reach high places or traverse the land in a quick, more cultural manner thanks to the advanced alien technological breakthroughs. The saucer is very entertaining and equally destructive. In order to cause chaos in every situation, the vehicle is equipped with laser beams, sonic weapons, atomic bombs, and more. Similar to Crypto, the UFO can be improved in the mothership; however, it cannot alter its skin or design.Each sequence's emotions, from the subtler to the more intense ones, are effectively captured by the animated facial details. The reworked animations and cutscenes do an excellent job of fusing the comedic and graphical effects elements, and the textures show to be a huge improvement. Not to mention the various details you will learn from the altered environment, like strange vibrations coming from cars parked in obscure places or protests in front of significant construction sites sparked by prior events. The only thing that seems disturbing to the eye is the character model chosen for the depiction of the NPCs, as they do not mix well with the seemingly cartoonish look of the environment.  The sound design is without a doubt the game's shining point. Even though some of the original title's elements have been used in a more polished way, Grant Albrecht and Richard Horvitz's flawless performances continue to blow my mind. Additionally, the crisp sound effects for both abilities and weapons enhance the experience even further by satisfactorily capturing the impact of each explosion and fatality. Destroy All Humans represents a giant step forward for remakes as it flawlessly fuses contemporary graphics with a freshened gameplay aesthetic. However, the only aspect that significantly lowers the overall experience is the lack of consistency. Although it is a faithful remake, the writers might have preferred to give the script a little more polish rather than play to nostalgia given that it is aimed at a much more demanding playerbase.

_childDocuments_.review: There's no denying how much a big player Pandemic Games were back in the 2000s. Bringing us the original Star Wars Battlefront series, Mercenaries, the criminally underrated The Saboteur, and of course Destroy All Humans! I admit in modesty that when I was a kid I didn't really understand the humor too much due to being a bright-eyed 6-year-old, but I do remember a lot of the pivotal moments and all I can say is that this remaster translates everything from the original 2005 release near flawlessly, even going as far as adding a cut mission to mix it up a little bit. I also have to commend Black Forest Games for keeping a lot of the original jokes and subject-matter in the game. Furthermore, I also need to praise how every character model is stylized in a more cartoony manner this time around, completely doing away with the realistic depiction we got back in '05, hell even some of the more graphic sound effects were changed to be a little goofier.But my biggest praise for this game is how Black Forest overhauled the destruction in this game. My biggest memory from the original was seeing the unlockable concept art depicting your death ray cutting a building in half and now in 2022 it's pretty much a reality with building flinging debris in every direction when they are hit, having smoke and dust engulf the surrounding area, buildings collapsing into dozens of different pieces, and trees and grass become scorched when struck with a death ray. It's just these little environmental changes that make this remake feel like a more fully realized project and I feel that the original team would have tears in their eyes seeing how their product was reanimated and reinvented with this remaster, and honestly I feel like this remaster should set an example for a lot of companies on how to do a proper remaster.

_childDocuments_.review: So... Destroy All Humans! Remake. For those who don't know, this game is back from Xbox and Playstation 2 days. It plays kind of like Saints Row 3 and 4, more or less 4 because you can fly and do crazy amounts of damage. All things considered, I'd rather play a DAH game over a modern Saints Row game. This series has a huge cult following and for good reason, it's one of the funnier games out there. A lot of the jokes in these games would never be allowed in today's clown world. Just know that this genre of game is a bit dated and dying because of horrible flops like Agents of Mayhem or Crackdown 3. The whole game can be completed in just a few hours and 100%'d in less than a dozen hours. So for old players, how is it?This team did a great job remaking this game overall. They made several changes to fix issues the game had in the original version. The best improvement was the addition of the mission select menu. In this remake, you're able to play any mission in the game with all of the upgrades you could have had unlocked at that part of the campaign. If you remember, that was a huge issue with DAH and games like it. It's one of those old games where you get the best stuff in the last 10% of the game and then have no time to actually enjoy it because the game is over and there's no missions left. They also streamlined and simplified a lot of the controls and mechanics which helped and hurt the game in a lot of ways.This remake has a handful of glaring issues. For one they've oversimplified some of the mechanics. If you recall in the original game, each NPC type had a different value of Furon DNA (upgrade currency) in their brains. I believe civilians were 10? Cops were 25, soldiers were either 25 or 50, majestic was either 25 or 50, and then scientists were 100. In this version of the game, all brains are worth 25. This means the whole mechanic of trying to salvage the brain of a living NPC goes out the window. In the original game you got the most points possible if you extracted the brain of a living NPC. If you killed them, it devalued their brain. This was a mechanic because of the Furon mind ability to make heads explode and the probe gun. They were harder and riskier to use on live targets, because they left you open to taking damage. Therefore, in this game it doesn't matter if you save or kill them, making the probe gun virtually useless until its maxed out due to it's slow firerate.Additional issues with the game include balance and performance. The performance of this game is pretty solid for the most part, but it does have occasional stutters or lag spikes during hectic fights or on bigger maps like Capital City. The race challenge in particular is more difficult on Capital City due to these freezes. Others have reported they had trouble with the final boss due to stutters. As for the balance, I don't know what's wrong. I don't know if it's because I haven't played these games since I was about 10-12 years old and I got better, or if I'm getting DAH 1 and 2 confused, OR this remake has somehow changed mechanics. Overall, I never died and I only had my shields pop for the first time in the entire game during the final missions. I think in the original you had to use the abduction beam to harvest brains from people in the UFO, but in this game you can just mash a button from down the street and have their brains fly to you. This greatly decreased the grinding time in this version which I guess is a nice quality of life feature.On a final note, there are more positives than negatives with this game. I was actually quite surprised to see this is one of the better remakes/remasters in the last few years. I would put it up there with Resident Evil 2 Remake. They do a great job staying with the old game, making it look decent, and even fixed the whole upgrade/NG+ thing. I think the $30 price is worth it just because this is a good game, but new-gen players will be upset with the amount of content for the price. All of that being said, I hope to god these guys get THQ Nordic to hire them for a DAH 2 Remake.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm highly sceptical of game remakes, but this one may of just sold me on the concept while making me realise just how little fun I've actually been having with ostensibly excellent games in this past generation. They took a clunky and awkward game that suffered development challenges and dated quickly and transmogrified it into a highly relevant and fresh feeling sandbox that appeals to even someone like me who has grown to detest the sandbox genre. The move away from a more desaturated and realistic artstyle as in the 2005 release toward a colorful and exadurated world was an inspired choice that absolutely sticks the landing once you get used to the shift and only serves to amplify many times over the satirical caricature of 50s Red Scare Republicanism, Police brutality, Nationalistic Jingoism and a culture of childish ignorance that the game's light-hearted and more-relevant-than-ever writing is all about.This has instantly placed itself in my top 10 of all time, if you think you'd be into it. Just get it.Now I just hope that they capitalise on this incredible momentum and continue the franchise anew while making everything after DAH 2 non-canon //---------- [Long form thoughts] ---------- //I played the original games in my childhood and absolutely fell in love with the concept but always felt the execution fell far short to the point I'd never recommend them.THQ's decision to have the devs pivot away from a destruction and chaos focused game to a Character focused stealth game had clearly strained the final product almost to breaking point in places, some of the publisher's influence was great, originally the Furons were all to have english accents but I'm very glad they ended with the excellent cast that they have... however in the end Crypto for all his warmongering energy felt fragile, weak and incredibly clunky even 15 years ago with the gameplay railroading the majority of your gameplay time into a frankly terrible stealth system.Not so in the remake, they have seemingly achieved the impossible by maintaining all of the original mission design fundamentals while totally re-balancing the systems and mechanics from mobility to upgrades to turn Crypto into the legitimate alien war machine he's billed as (Destroy All Humans was picked as the name before the pivot to stealth iirc) Stealth is now smooth and fun in it's own right and feels like a fun method of approach rather than a mandatory survival tactic in the face of a clunky combat system.I tend to be cautious about the concept of remakes - though I appreciate the benefits such as keeping old games relevant, and the cheaper cost of development owing to already having the whole blueprint for your design laid out in advance... I simply worry that they'll be used as a quick money maker while distorting or outright destroying the artistic intent within the original. Ratchet and Clank's 2016 remake saw that world become the very Celebrity Obsessed, Cynically consumerist and broadly marketable movie tie-in cash in that the original PS2 games had set out to pointedly mock. I cannot describe how glad I am to see that Crypto and Pox did not have to suffer the same fate, but rather experienced an upgrade more true to the designers intent than even they were able to achieve in the original release - This is what a remake should do first and foremost and I hope the industry is taking some serious notes.I get the sense the developers really loved the chance they had been given and genuinely cared about making the best they could with the IP within their budget, down to reworking the tractor beam to the spiral version from the original games' box art, having the Furon cloning tanks shown aboard the mothership (Originally intended to be the first games representation of save files) and obviously the fact they reconstructed cut missions that never saw the light of day until now.They absolutely nailed it, the biggest critiques I have are really fairly petty, things like how the saucer no longer sparks aflame as it's health wears down or how the Mothership backgrounds are now flat illustrations rather than the modelled and connected interior spaces that helped ground the original in a sense of place despite being a quite lonely invasion of one scientist and one soldier against the world.I couldn't really ask for more, once again I only hope that this team is given the opportunity to bring their talent to a true continuation of the franchise so it can continue to make good on those ideas it had fallen just short of for the last 15 years.P.S.If I were to ask for more, Please make Big Willy Unleashed and Path of the Furon non-canon. 1 and 2 were always a little too lonely, I want to see the Furon empire return and I want to see them be every bit the psychopathic space warmongers that nuked Mars. Make it happen THQ Nordic. You'll have a day 1 preorder from me.

_childDocuments_.review: A classic 6th gen game remastered with a fun new art style. This game is an irreverent favorite of mine and still mostly holds up in the modern age. If you're a fan of the new, more cartoon-like art design, then the game looks fantastic from start to finish and runs really well even on modest PC's. Crypto's arsenal of weapons are still satisfying to use and destroying buildings in the saucer is still a blast (literally).    However, much of the gameplay is pretty dated and you should know that going in. Expect mindless wave defense missions and little variety or depth. When it comes to bugs, there are a few minor ones that are mostly benign, but sometimes do hamper the experience. It's mostly things like missing textures or looping sound effects, but I did once have a bug that forced me to restart a challenge mission. Not the best experience in that regard.    Still, Destroy All Humans is a great remaster of the original game and totally worth the price that I paid for it (~$7.50). I'd definitely recommend it if you want a good 10-20 hours of casual fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this remake is everything I could have hoped for and much, much more. It honestly brought a tear to my eye the first time I launched it because of all the memories I made playing this game as a kid. Aside from the nostalgia factor, this game is an amazingly faithful recreation with a few new tricks up its sleeve like a couple new PK abilities, a new mission which was cut from the original game, and new upgrades among the countless other improvements and additions the new engine provides. This is technically the third time I've purchased this game (PS2, PS4, and now PC), and I don't know what amount of times I've played it all the way through, it's at least 15, so if that doesn't tell you how much I love this game I don't know what will. I think this is the one game that I can say I will probably be playing until the day I die because it just never gets old. I was extremely optimistic about this game when it was first revealed, and my expectations were blown away because while I absolutely love the original, it definitely shows its age and this brings it into the modern era. Overall, I couldn't recommend this game enough to anyone who either wants to relive their childhood with all the nostalgia and none of the aging gameplay mechanics or has never touched this series and just wants to have a good time. I genuinely hope that this is only the start of a new beginning for this series because this truly is the most fun I've had in a long, long time. So, thank you to the developers at THQ Nordic and Black Forest Games for allowing me to relive some of my fondest childhood memories, I am forever grateful for that.

You’ll get about 10 to 20 hours of humanity destroying fun, and then you can move on. Trust me, taking your maxed out UFO to destroy Washington DC is VERY satisfying.There are some uneven difficulty spikes, and the story is just “meh”, but I didn’t really care. I bought this game to blow up entire towns/cities, and set thousands of humans on fire. This game lets you do that. Not much more to it than that, but if you got the itch, this game lets you scratch it.

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans 2 was a childhood favourite of mine. Having missed the experience of the first game all those years ago, this remake was an opportunity to relive the enjoyment of playing as a dry and sarcastic little "green" alien and his arsenal of endearingly sadistic weapons, but now with the privilege of modern graphics and more precise controls. I can't comment on how this holds up as a remake, but the essence of the series, the game play, the atmosphere and the incredible physics based chaos which ensues from violently throwing rag dolls into a crowd of people remain and take me back to how I felt as a kid. This is exactly what I hoped it would be.
_childDocuments_.name: Destroy All Humans!

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans 2020 is great, just like the original. If you've played the original and liked it, then you'll love this one. The voice-lines are unchanged I'm glad! Crypto's tone is just perfect, and I couldn't imagine it being "re-done".  This game is comical, and trys to not take itself to seriously so it's silly-fun. It's set during the "red-scare" in 1950s U.S when anyone and everyone who wasn't like you was a commie! If want a couple hours of just goofy fun then this is for you, if you want a game that has a deep story and heartfelt characters then you'll most likely want to find a diffrent game.

_childDocuments_.review: It was a lot of fun to play this old classic again. Graphically this remake is stunning, in terms of landscape, effects and so on. The new custscenes likewise are a great improvement in terms of camera work and dynamic visual story telling. However, sad to say that it's not a 100% faithful remake of the game. The art style is the most obvious change to those who played the original, as the remake is cartoony, whereas the original had a more "realism" based look for the characters. Some missions/maps take place in the day where originally they were night (which story-wise makes more sense in some cases). I do admit I prefer the original style of the effects for Crypto's powers, as well as the original HUD, and menu screens, but this is mainly taste on my part. Some mechanics have been altered (some for better, some for worse). Example is camera work, the jetpack, and lock-on being good improved features, however the game has also been neutered in some small regards mechanically. For example, melee attacks from enemies are not in this game, the original game had enemies kick or push you over if you got too close to them, in this game the enemy NPCs don't seem to know what to do for a few moments when you get close, and is something that can be exploited. Likewise, in this game you can't be run over by cars, in the original game running in front of a car could get you knocked down and a lot of health would be lost.The game has removed the need for DNA to be collected to move on to the next mission, something I am split on, for it allows for smoother gameplay and removes tediousness, but at the same time I appreciated the old mechanic for it made players spend more times in maps to explore and appreciate them more. (But this can be still done by free choice of course).Another small change is the removal of the concentration bar for Crypto's powers, meaning PK is unlimited. Something I can't make up my mind over whether I think it's better or worse for the game.As for other changes, quite a few lines have been cut from this game, not only in cutscenes, but also from various NPCs, from speech to mind reading, some seemingly for no reason. So overall I can say there are pros and cons to this remake, but it still retains the 'heart' of the original, but I would have liked a more faithful remake. So I recommend it for people new to the series, younger generations would certainly like it for what it is, but if you're looking for a 100% faithful remake as someone who enjoyed the original, I couldn't fully recommend. It's only by a thin margin that I do hit the "thumbs up" for this review, for these changes don't impact the overall "larger" experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot add anything more than all the other comments have added.  This is a wacky/silly shooter game from the 200X's. The dialogue is funny at times, plot is contrived, and the game play is serviceable. I rarely grew bored while playing this game outside of challenges which are *mostly* fun not counting random difficulty spikes. The remake aspect is mostly visual and judging by the bonus concept art you unlock you can tell this wasn't a shameless cash grab but a genuine attempt to recreate the original's glory.I was able to get 100% achievements and collect everything in the game besides probes [screw that crap] and while I enjoyed my time I most likely will not play it again for at least another few years.The sad truth of the matter is that in terms of game-play the game is a product of its time, being outclassed by most games that have been released this last half decade. This game is fun but not worth the $30 unless you played the original and only experience joy through the sweet hit of nostalgia it can bring. Get it on sale for 66% off if you want a time-killer that is fun if not a bit forgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll freely admit it, the original Destroy All Humans! is one of my all time guilty pleasures. There’s something cathartic in embodying a 1950’s stereotype of alien invader and laying waste to puny humans without a care in the world. Imagine my surprise (and joy) when I heard that THQ Nordic was going to publish a faithful remake of this Pandemic Studios classic this year. I HAD to get my hands on the game, and that’s why here I am, letting you know what I thought about this Black Forest Games/THQ Nordic collaboration.The first thing that hit me when I fired up the game was how much prettier everything looked. The original game wasn’t exactly cutting edge, but it worked well anyway, because it wasn’t the kind of title that takes itself seriously, so the somewhat dated graphics were more charming than anything else (think Deadly Premonition, but running at playable frame-rates and with far less bugs). This remake, however, looks a lot more like a current generation release, and if that wasn’t enough, the team at Black Forest Games chose a genuinely excellent art style that perfectly fits the 1950’s B-movie feeling of the game.So, what else is new? Besides a very noticeable new coat of paint, this remake features a bunch of quality of life enhancements designed to bring a 2005 game up to 2020 standards (mostly). This means that, while the basic flow of the game remains unchanged, the controls have been updated, and our character can now use different abilities at the same time he’s firing his weapon, something that you’ll agree with me that it’s a very important update, if you played the original. Oh, and there’s a brand new mission that was cut from the 2005 release.Speaking of abilities, all the favorites return, and look and feel better than ever. Our hero Crypto can use telekinesis to move objects with his mind, Holobob to become a facsimile of a human in order to infiltrate highly guarded areas without raising suspicion, mind-wipe guards, force humans to follow him and do his bidding, and other niceties (such as popping out their brains and scooping them up to upgrade our arsenal). Playing with all of these abilities never gets old, and as I’ve said before, it’s a lot easier to manage than it ever was in the original game.If mind powers aren’t your game, then you’ll be happy to learn that Crypto’s superior Furon technology is as good as you might have remembered. Our little grey man can jetpack around the place, zap people with an electric ray, turn them into dust with a disintegrator ray, anal probe them, and blow them up with a big Ion Detonator. Doesn’t sound like much? I’d disagree, but if that’s your line, then I’d also like to point out that our little Furon’s arsenal can be upgraded with all sorts of interesting perks (even letting us surf around the place with the jetpack, for instance). Believe me when I say that by the end of the game, my Crypto was a veritable force of nature, spitting out rays, evading rockets, sending them back the way they came, and transmogrifying tanks into ammunition for his Ion Detonator.Of course, a big arsenal is nice, but doesn’t mean much if we don’t get a chance to use it. Thankfully, Destroy All Humans! is all about using our weapons and abilities, and while the mission design often leaves a lot to be desired (it’s one of the few parts of the game that weren’t updated in this remake), I can’t say that I didn’t have fun blowing up helpless humans and moving from set piece to set piece. Most missions involve a relatively short stealth sequence, followed by skirmishes with the local humans, short platforming segments, or all out chases. From time to time, the game breaks out the big guns and lets us control Crypto’s flying saucer, blowing up houses like there’s no tomorrow, and generally being a nuisance for the poor Army boys that want nothing more than to bring down what they perceive as a Communist threat to their American way of life.Once we’ve cleared a mission, we’ll be able to return to the play area where it took place, and engage in several types of challenges (that will unlock gradually as we progress in the game’s campaign), or just zip around the place, causing mayhem, scooping up brains, or finding hidden items that will reward us with upgrade points that can be spent either upgrading Crypto’s arsenal, or his flying saucer.As expected from a game set in the 1950’s, there’s tons of references to the Cold War, and the writers did a pretty good job with the constant barrage of jokes that bombard the player, even if some of them are a bit outdated nowadays. Of course, while we are talking about jokes and writing, we should take a moment to highlight the vocal performances of the two main characters, Crypto and Orthopox, since the actors playing them (J. Grant Albrecht and Richard Horvitz) did a marvellous job. Crypto sounds like Jack Nicholson at his craziest, and Orthopox is always majestic and aristocratic, even when sending us to do the most unbelievable things. This is another aspect that didn’t get an update in the remake, and I’m very glad that this is the case, because I can’t see anyone else pulling off performances of this caliber for this kind of game.Going back to the gameplay, the one part that I am not glad that wasn’t updated is the stealth, which can be quite grating, as it’s often non-optional, and it usually forces the player to follow a rigid path, doing specific actions with no room to improvise. I am aware that this is how it was in the original game, but honestly, I feel that this remake could have taken a page out of the Resident Evil remake book, and reworked the stealth segments entirely. Missions failing instantly because of finicky and under-cooked gameplay mechanics will never be fun (though thankfully there are checkpoints you can fall back to when it happens).Other than that, I don’t have many complaints about Black Forest Games‘ job here. Destroy All Humans! (2020) is a faithful remake that captures the joy of the 2005 original while at the same time looking and feeling like a modern game. If you are a fan of Pandemic Studios‘ output, then I’d say that you owe it to yourself to pick this gem up, as it’s a perfect tribute to the kind of games they used to make.

_childDocuments_.review: Kicking it to the past you pathetic humans! This is a game that is a throwback to the era of well made PS2 classics redefined for a modern era. _childDocuments_.review: There's challenges, side-missions, equipment-upgrades to grind for, and a campaign. But that campaign is just extremely basic and cliché, and doesn't really offer much of anything... Honestly, all you do the entire game is play around with your gear and kill humans/buildings. That's why Destroy All Humans is best described as a Sandbox. This gameplay can be fun at times, but will get very repetitive. The campy nature of the game did give me a few chuckles here and there, though at the same time it can get  cringy as well. Overall, the entertainment is just too short-lived, campy and limited. I feel like there isn't much reason to keep playing. Well, except for maybe finishing the campaign and achievements if you're a completionist (like I did).I also want to note 2 other flaws I came across. NPC's are just copied and pasted way too much, causing you to come across the exact same farmer/wife/whatever and their quips hundreds of times in the same mission. Also, I found the psychokinesis ability to be rather finicky and non-reliable. When I want to throw a target into another, it often just drops it mid-air like a limp ragdoll, hardcore face-slams it into the ground, or just plain yeets it off far into the distance.So even though Destroy All Humans can offer some fun moments and has decent gameplay, the game's basic and repetitive nature, extremely campy campaign and real lack of purpose keeps me from recommending it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really excited for this game when it came out, but I waited for a really good deal on it because I've become accustomed to disappointments.  Anyways, this was not a disappointment!  I was really happy to genuinely feel nostalgia as I remembered some fun parts of one of my favorite games growing up!I remember the gameplay being awesome, and that's how this game is too.  There were a couple missions where the difficulty spiked unexpectedly but not a huge deal.  Just had to hit retry and lean forward.  I'm only 8 hours in, and it's really great so far.Well done with this one.I don't really remember the old game enough to comment on improvements or depredations.  I can only say I've only encountered one bug and it is extremely minor.This works very well on controller too.  The lockon mechanic works very well.I also noticed some lines in this game referencing other stuff, but I don't remember if they were lines from the original game (and hence other media is referencing this game) or if they were created as references to other media in this game.1. Rick's recipe for "dark matter" appears in one of the newspaper articles!2. "Don't get mad, get sadistic", which I recognized as a voice line for Viegar in LoLI'm sure there's even more I'm not picking up on.  (If anyone's curious, I got this in a humble bundle; $14 for this game and a handful of others.  It's probably worth the $30 price tag but things go on sale so often, why not wait a bit?)

name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead
detailed_description: Special Edition JOIN OUR DISCORD COMMUNITY About the Game In Iratus you find yourself fighting for the forces of darkness in the role of the titular necromancer—Iratus, recently freed from his millennia-long imprisonment. You control an obedient army of the living dead, with skeletons, zombies, banshees and many other unliving warriors. Create your soldiers the only way a necromancer knows how: from the body parts of your slain enemies! Expand and improve your underground lair. Strengthen your servants by researching secret rituals. Explore the twisted corridors and underground catacombs, and battle against lobotomized miners, greedy dwarves and corrupt mercenaries. Aid Iratus in his quest to recapture and eclipse his former power. Lead him to conquer the forces of good and unleash an eternal kingdom of death upon the world! The sheer variety of tactical and strategic options makes Iratus a true treat for any ardent fans of the roguelike genre. Play on the side of evil, embodied by the necromancer Iratus! Expand and improve your underground lair. 19 types of obedient servants: zombies, vampires, skeletons, mummies, banshees and many more! Craft minions from the body parts of your conquered enemies. Advanced combat system: to win you need to know both the strengths and weaknesses of your troops and enemies. Iratus can kill his enemies not only by magic or claw but also by draining their sanity! Each minion has six unique abilities for a total of nearly one-hundred abilities for you to command. Four talent trees that alter the way you play: Alchemy, Magic, Ire and Destruction. Roguelike elements: minions that die are gone for good and the game saves automatically, making each choice irreversible. Detailed 2D graphics and a gloomy atmosphere of dark fantasy. Various difficulty levels, satisfying every type of player from novice to hardcore. Iratus himself is voiced by the voice-acting legend Stefan Weyte, famous for his performance as Caleb in the cult game series 'Blood'!

And kill everyone in his path.So far the game has only 3 dungeons but its already super good gameplay. And completely worth the time and investment to play it early. With time this game will only get better and its already very good. A must buy for any big fan of a tactical rpg gameplay. GL HF

_childDocuments_.review: For me (and many others, apparently), comparisons between Iratus and Darkest Dungeon are inevitable - so let's start there. DD's moments of frustration are what actually pushed me into Iratus's cold embrace as Iratus delivers a deceptively similar combat loop, but the whole game is less frustrating and more akin to popular deck-builder roguelikes such as Slay The Spire (except you are gruesomely collecting body and armour parts as opposed to cards). As a matter of fact, Iratus seems to be like a lovechild of those two game: combat loop resembles that from DD and map progression is almost exactly like that from STS. The overall feel is closer to STS however, as DD offers a very different atmosphere and a much deeper overall game loop with more risks and a more satisfying progression, but also potential for much more frustration.Now that I got those comparisons out of my system, let's talk about Iratus on its own merits. The game is pretty tight with a number of cleverly interlocking moving parts which fit together nicely such as body part crafting, tomb-improvements, mana spells, wrath fuelled abilities and of course your army of undead minions. All these elements can interact with each other, enabling interesting combos which reveal themselves over the opening few hours of the game. The artwork and atmosphere are mock-grim and enjoyable, but nothing to write home about. The body-part economy is engaging and well-balanced. The game can be challenging, but on the normal difficulty setting, should prove quite manageable.Recommended when discounted as a chill and lighthearted, relaxing yet engaging filler.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: Addictive game and quite a decent amount of content for Early Access. I do like playing as the undead rather than the normal band of heroes, and there are enough elements to the game to keep you interested - strategy, turn based combat, inventory & resource management, crafting, levelling up yourself and your minions, and more. Am really looking forward to seeing what they add to the game in the future, with hopefully an even bigger roster of different minions to recruit.If you like games like Darkest Dungeon, Dead In Vinland, Deep Sky Derelicts and that type of game then you will enjoy this.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: While the comparisons to Darkest Dungeon are valid, Iratus offers a more accessible experience. Beyond the usual cries of 'OMG GIT GUD' when it comes to DD, it's a monster of a game to get through knowledge wise. The systems in Iratus are more streamlined, and navigating the map is a simple click-this-node affair. With planning your route being a key point to hit the loot you want / need, and picking your fights with elites. Planning combat is a key part too. For example, you don't want a party based around dealing stress damage facing off against a group that is mostly immune. Every unit thankfully has at least two different attack types, so you're never ENTIRELY screwed, but it's a nasty surprise on first play! ( Not that it happened to me, honest. >.> )A good, solid game with it's own style for someone looking for more / similar to Darkest Dungeon, but possibly too easy for folks who have broken that particular title over their knee.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty solid game to be honest, didn't expect to be already this much refined given the early access tag.Very few balance issues that can be glanced over and some fun strats, for example (Banshee|Wraith|Mummy|Dark Knight) dropping all enemies to 0 sanity in 1-2 turns (there is much more variety allowed in your comps here than in Darkest Dungeon, where a Jester and Vestal are almost always required for harder/farmstead missions).Hopefully this game gets a more accessible mod support in the future and a bit more ironing out from the devs (Talents trees don't many sense, after a Stress talent you find one that gives Attack, you have to get a talent that helps you upgrade more building to get one that buffs your minions -- Some enemies on hard mode are way too strong, notably Swordsman, Berserker and Bard, especially the Bard who can heal AND stress heal for half the enemy resource bar each turn)
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: At times like this I wish Steam had an "Okay" rating. The game is fine, it draws extremely heavily on it's inspiration, Darkest Dungeon, while not necessarily a bad thing it at times feels like a knock off, as DD just feels better in almost every way. That being said, if you enjoy Darkest Dungeon's combat I would recommend trying this as it expands upon it in some ways with greater customization of heroes/minions.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a perfect roguelite experience, but pretty good overall.+Lots of different minions with lots of different abilities, items, artefacts and talents. No run need to be exactly same.+Feeling of permanent progress when you unlock new minions to use and enemy entries in humonarium.+Fights are a comfortable challenge, if you know what you're doing.-Some things are too good, even on higher difficulties (Looking at you, Finger of Death). Instead of modifying strategy against specific enemies, you'll end up spamming the one tactic that works everytime. Then you have to resolve not to use it at all in the next run simply for the sake of keeping things a challenge.-With lots of things being too good, lots of other things are too bad. Many useless abilities can be upgraded to include handy effects, like moving an enemy or removing all blocks and wards, but too many damage abilities simply have "increase x damage" or "increase y damage". -Runs tend to get a little boring on 4th floor and upwards.Did you know you can upgrade a part inside a minion with digger souls? I didn't.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend the game. It has great potential and exciting atmosphere. The creature skills are interesting and the gameplay is fun. Visuals and sound are descent. The crafting system is adequate. However, it is unfinished at this moment. It feels that it lacks the depth to keep me playing it for more than 20 hours. I would personally like to see more options - more creature levels, more items per creature, more items per hero, more hero skills (especially passive ones). Also, developers don't know it but these games have multiplayer potential in co-op style. Also the game is hard in the wrong way. I would like either an option or skill to get more information about your enemies (especially bosses) or withdraw. I saw others complain about this too. Unless you attack a boss in a specific way you will not defeat it. This resulted in me losing my 10 strongest creatures against a mediocre boss that a beat with lvl. 1 creatures afterwards. A way to skip turns and get the benefits will be nice. This game will benefit from some sort of repeatable meta mission system with improved rewards.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun to play actively, also fun to load up and play a couple rounds here and there while working.  Run in a smaller window and alt-tab between meetings, etc.  Graphics are great, voice acting is solid, good depth in the various minions.  The map path choices start to be more important as you increase in difficulty.  I've been playing on both Windows and MacOS.  Super stable and performant on either platform.  Zero crashes.My play time is a bit skewed as I idle quite a bit, but I've played through 3 times, each on increasing difficulty.  The hardest difficulty, which I'm at now, actually has me thinking about restarting and hoping for better fight outcomes and random drops.  The previous difficulty was challenging, but I never really felt in danger of having to restart.  Recommend continuing on after the tutorial on easy mode just to get a sense of the game and easily explore the various team comps to see which you enjoy most.Comparing it to Darkest Dungeon:  Less grind, less negative RNG (no character insanity, for example).  I can get a bit more attached and reliably spec out the minions.  Some might find Iratus a bit less gritty and challenging than DD, but, thinking back on the two, I think part of the challenge of DD is simply tolerating the RNG frustration.  I find Iratus more fun and enjoyable.Cons?  at least up until the last difficulty, I feel once you hit a certain tipping point, you're pretty much unstoppable unless you consciously screw up.  This can make the large maps somewhat unnecessary.  Would prefer a more noticeable scaling during each level.  Course, then again, I'm getting my ass kicked on the first run of the hardest difficulty, so maybe I should calm down on that scaling idea.Overall:  Great asynch, lightweight gameplay that scratches that RPG character building dungeon crawler itch.  Recommend.
