_childDocuments_.review: Alright.Iratus.Another "Darkest Dungeon but you're the bad guys' game.The fact I can say "another" both pleases and confuses me.Anyway, the core Idea, the aesthetics and world is great and the voice acting and humor made me want to keep playing.Customization is just fantastic as well and I love the many ideas for minions and their flavor, iratus himself helps this a lot.It also tries to, like most of the othet games of this caliber, to build it's own gameplay loop.But alas, just like the others this is where it also falls off.To me this kind of game needs a really solid base loop to keep me caring and engaged.But this also has this puzzle-ish feeling.Instead of fighting weaker enemies you still shouldn't underestimate as one bad move could turn things around, these are hulking behemoths.The second you leave the mines the game just turns up to overdrive and turns from fun challenge to not too fun and frustrating.Xcom, Darkest dungeon and so on.They have one thing in common, while they can feel unfair, it adds to tension instead of actually taking away.You spend time with your people and once you inevitably lose them you usually blame yourself (and the bad rng).But you know you COULD have done better.That's where this game turns frustrating.It baits you into thinking you can do as you wish and to have fun, customizing your squads and trying out wacky combos, but as soon as you do it stabs you in the face and kicks you while you're down.The way missions work and the forced pace don't do it any favors here, but I suppose it didn't want to copy darkest dungeon too much.Take the one man army build.It is fantastic, funny and works amazingly if you use the right minion and get the item.But then suddenly the game says "nay" and just robs you of the core on the next floor and spits in your face.You have a stress build? Here are berserkers they will now one-shot your entire team instantly.I get it.It's this odd puzzle-ish keep your team mixed up idea.But why.You allow me to customize and do as I like really, so why make enemies hard-shut down a ton of playstyles.It really, really limits replayability and variety, sadly.In a way I wish they'd have went heavier on the darkest dungeon but you are the monster side of things, but all these games seem kind of scared to really do it. Instead they all try to force as much as they can this "heroes are broken, try your best to not die by hard countering them" approach which ends up playing like a chore and making me not want to come back while darkest dungeon is a game I still install every other month for wacky adventures.Freedom in your stupidity with these games is key and you need to have choices to make what happens really feel something, but the choices in iratus just end up short in too many aspects sadly.I think there are a lot of people who might enjoy it, but in the end it just misses the mark, keeping me mainly interested with the top notch presentation instead of the mediocre gameplay.Disappointing because I feel that it could have been darkest dungeon but with a mighty fine twist to make it unique and interesting if it wanted to be, instead choosing an oddly overpopulated niche and ending up feeling suprisingly uninspired gameplay.I just don't recommend it because I feel that it just won't be fun to a lot of people as it's not what you expect it to be.But if you do enjoy the gameplay I do actually whole heartedly recommend this, as iratus is most likely the by far best in it's weird niche.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game fervently, it takes a lot of the elements of Darkest Dungeon and really stands on its own feet. I can see myself investing countless hours into this game, but unfortunately the game suffers from incredibly skewed boss fights. Not, "Git gud" fight, but instead incredibly random RNG fights. An example I can recall very vividly is that of the inventor, and his 10% luck that crit 9 times of the about 12 times he used his 4 tile electrocute. Not only does the RNG seem so aggregiously skewed, but the fight doesn't seem to have been playtested either (this is an early access I'm aware) as whenever  I've put a fair amount of time into this game already and plan to put in more, but it is painful to literally throw wave after wave of perfect parties that should handle the physical damage/soak rush that this fight requires just to have the Inventor spit on my corpses. I'm not a game developer, but I can tell from the countless corpses thrown at this guy that he is incredibly overtuned, and even the streamers that I watch that are Darkest Dungeon veterans have stated that they believe the boss "wasn't playtested" or is "overtuned." I want this game to do well, and will continue trying to beat him, but I only have a surplus of so many corpses before the Inventor will have drained the last of my will out of me. TL;DR I recommend the game, but to those looking for a more casual experience with a Darkesst Dungeon feel, this is not that. The game will beat you down and keep you down. If you like a challenge, with bosses that have unique mechanics, this may be your cup of tea, but this game won't hold back. I have a fair amount of time in this, and Darkest Dungeon and believe this to be a solid entry, if a little skewed toward the RNG.EDIT: It is worth noting that the Devs have now released a balancing patch that is designed to address some of the issues with the game. When I have the time I will be attempting the boss again to determine if the changes have made a big enough impact!EDIT2: I have faced the second boss, and even with just level 1 Lost soul, Dark knight (x2) and a Skeleton, I was able to defeat the boss with only losing the Skele and Lost Soul. The change has definitely made this boss less of a headache! .

_childDocuments_.review: Iratus: Lord of the Dead is an excellent turn based strategy game. If you ever wanted to lead your own army of undead against the forces of "light", this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Kinda like Darkest Dungeon, but infinitely better. The resource management feels like actual resource management, you're thinking about your overall journey through the complexes you're moving through instead of just a single dungeon instance, but the management is done in such a way to never make you feel awful about the choices you have to make regarding it, they just feel risky or interesting.The combat isn't heavily reliant on RNG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and while there is some out there, the odds you're expecting are more-or-less the odds you'll be getting, and they can be easily mitigated and worked with. Building up your base, character levels, and master level gives you an actual sense of growing power, while also maintaining a good amount of enemy threat, instead of Darkest Dungeon's nonsense where it feels like your grinding is entirely worthless. I feel like the only reason why this game didn't take off like a shooting star was because it came out after DD and the animations/sounds aren't nearly as crisp and satisfying, but even with that problem the entire game ultimately is much more so overall. Great game, thanks for making it guys.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is 1000% worth it. The time I've gotten as of now (without finishing one, let alone the three difficulties) is crazy. The game is a constant dripfeed of resources and there's always a new creature being unlocked, slowly but surely. It's that progression and evil tone that gets this games hooks in FAST. I'd gotten 9 hours in before I realised I should farm insanity off of my enemies to unlock X character. Then I can collect X to unlock X character and so on and so on. You're always grinding, it feels great. The two complaints I have, which is rare given my tendency to dislike things, is that their needs to be more creatures, that are variety. A lot of the mobs unlocked are good, and unique with how they attack, but are relegated to "not as good as X" or "doesn't fit this slot" (Looking at you third party position, seriously where are the DPS?) there are a few good unique characters that play like no other such as The Mummy and The Headless Hunter, with the first focusing on curses and making opponents 'unlucky' and the second with pisspoor accuracy (tends to happen when you're lacking a head) but good damage and stun chances, I just wish there were more characters like that in the game. The combat is juicy and there's no BS hit chances to sully your fun, if my character had good enough accuracy I was always hitting my shots asides the aforementioned Headless Horseman. Battles constantly feel fun and the variety of enemies means you have to shake up your team comps a ton which is great, it leads to a lot of natural gameplay and testing of what works and what works for something else. Some enemies have a lot of armour, so heavy hitters or magic that dispells or negates armour is great, while others have physical wards, which can take three galatic explosions before they break meaning you need a stress composition. Then there's mental resistance which stops said stress attacks, and requires a mix of multi attack moves and good AOE. Overall an amazing game, I bought the supporter pack and Necromancer DLC as well, simply cause it's so fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Decent bit of fun, I'd certainly recommend it. Voice acting is great and the combat systems are fun to interact with. The ending makes me want a sequel. Every bit the reverse darkest dungeons it looks like.Do temper expectations a little though as balance isn't great, just get a werewolf or 2 and normal mode, the only difficulty you can play at first after quiting the tutorial will crumple so it's opening warning about difficulty seems a bit unwarrented. I still have no idea what happens if you lose all your guys in a fight. Many units seem a bit useless when the alternative is an unstoppable force of slaughter. Game is quite forgiving for losing units, often getting the brain back to shove it in a newer, better body power leveling a fresh body to keep up. If you wanted something relatively casual this would be it. Hopefully the higher difficulties will offer some challenge that can withstand a werewolf just slaughtering everything with life steal. Levels could be a bit shorter too.Never did figure out how to change spells, so most of my talent points were pointless. Hopefully just me being blind as out of the lower 2 tabs of spells I was stuck with, only the bite that removes 2 block was ever worth casting, just feeding into the werewolf auto win.I did still nearly binge the entire game in one sitting despite my complaints. It is fun though needs some polish.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I'm going to start out by saying that even though I don't recommend it, this game is still decent for what it is.The problem I have is there is no real substance to the game. It's fun for about an hour, but then it just.... drags. Nothing really has any impact to it, from the way the minions work to the sound effects. It also seems like there are minions that are just flat out not that good outside of niche cases, and others that are just flat out too strong (Mummy and werewolf come to mind)Another issue is there's nothing to break anything up. It's always, fight-grab something-fight grab something until the boss and next level. Look at Darkest Dungeon if you want a good example of how to do something better than what I just described.The items and potions are also rather use and forget. Nothing is so interesting you go out of your way to use it so it just seems more for preference rather than whats good.If this was early access, and there was another half a game coming out, I'd say absolutely go for it. _childDocuments_.review: My reviews are very scarce. I rarely find a game where I want to put any time toward a review. But DAMN this one deserves some more support.Darkest Dungeon + Slay the Spire. Except.... You're the bad guy!I've played a toooonnn of roguelikes, and this one is top tier.I came home from a rough day at work. Didn't want to play games, or stream, or talk to people. But i forced myself to throw this game on stream.I was chatty, happy, and engrossed for over five hours. I had to pull myself away because the game is that good.The visuals are fantastic. I LOVE the color palette overall, and the attacks and movements are fluid.The diversity between the enemies and the classes is pretty great as well.Randomness of map generation and how your *parts* turn out keeps the replayability value high. Not to mention every combined part gets random attributes.It fixes a lot of issues I had with Darkest Dungeon, and its amazin as far as roguelikes go.I've been playing on medium and the difficulty feels just right, especially for learning all of the mechanics, items, and abilities (there are a lot).My only very slight gripes with it are1 - the economy. Parts feels a bit too scarce, and I feel like the harder difficulties will be brutally unfair on 95% of your runs.2 - Architect Tokens.... Are a bit hard to utilize due to the parts feeling too scarce.3 - Lack of support units (healers mainly) I haven't unlocked many yet, but out of 7 classes, only 2 have a heal and both are self heal. One of which is an ultimate ability, the other needing a sacrifice.But honestly. Those are really minor compared to the abilities, class paths, items, artifacts, part diversity, branching paths, decisions, graveyard building and management, crafting, visuals, talent tree, and more.And they EVEN HAVE A HALLOWEEN EVEN ALREADY. Devs are on top of their game.Again.Darkest Dungeon meets slay the spire meets RPG (kinda), where its your job to be the villain and destroy the world.100% FFFF yes.

_childDocuments_.review: to be evil.Straight up, this needs to be compared to the other major game in the category of turn based, cruel RNG, dungeon crawl.  If you like the other, this one feels enjoyable too.  It feels like there is a bit more on the irreversible decisions on the skill tree.  At the same time, levels and control of the "what is available at a given time" feels like you, the player, have more control over the game.  Even though the RNG can be without mercy (how many  times have I seen the 1hp opponent sitting there), that control  gives a bit more to the ability to not blame just the RNG.The pathing of the game is a one way determined march to the exit.  Instead of the "follow step by step though the map" it is instead "room by room with no going back".  Again, this allows for more planning and less cursing of the RNG.  And its important to consider the entire map as one moves through the level.As I said, its good.

_childDocuments_.review: I would say a solid 8 out of 10Graphics are good - effects are viscreal without being over the top.Audio is good - they nailed the voice actor who does Iratus as a exceptional delivery.Game-play is ok - There could be some more apparent explanation of how some things work - like the tutorial should explain how to check a units special features. Also you initially start off with a very limit range of units to develop. The pacing for some stuff feels off (like architech souls)Balance is good - You have to really stop for a second and think of how your units interplay with each other; then realize what weaknesses a encounter may exploit and how you can compensate; this is best reflected by the fact that Iratus can cast spells into the combat to balance it out. One thing that seems Off is the randomizer; I miss way more then I should which leads me to believe that the accuracy/evasion system is a bit out of wack.Tip - make a unit that your not attached to; send them into first time encounters with new enemy types so that you can see what dirty tricks might be used.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game. Exactly like Darkest Dungeon except... not nearly as good. The balance of game play is awful. There are certain enemies (Flamethrowers and The Inventor Boss for example) who can wipe all your hours of hard work out in minutes. It's very frustrating. Unlike DD which is a somewhat rewarding frustration. You can adjust your gameplay and find creative ways to avoid these crazy swings, but overall, it's just too annoying. I went back to play Darkest Dungeon after a couple years, and I was blown away by how polished it is. It makes Iratus look bleak in comparison. This game is solid, but the balance kills it. Also, it needs more variety in spells, cosmetics, and dungeon exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: This is what happens when Guild of Dungeoneering and Darkest Dungeon have a love child. You play as the undead hordes vrs the humans, and can cause stress damage to them, rather than the other way around. Just as it warns you in the start, this game can be very unforgiving. What I particularly like about this game is it's crafting system to create new minions, very innovative at it's core, but some touch-ups would do it some justice. _childDocuments_.review: The comparisons to Darkest Dungeon make sense, but do not do justice to the depth that Iratus offers. The units in this game, both friendly and enemy, are very well designed and the balance feels great around your units. The possible synergies between your units is extremely wide and the game rewards you for understanding your opponents capabilities and bringing a lineup to each fight that punishes those weaknesses or counters their strengths.Unlike Darkest Dungeon, where you take a single roster through a series of largely unknown encounters. In Iratus, you bring a roster for each 4v4 conflict that decides whether or not you make progress. Each conflict, with very few exceptions, matches you against a strong cadre of enemy units that can very easily squad wipe your team if you prepare or execute poorly. You are rewarded for good choices, and quickly punished for imprecise play or poor planning.The "campaign" does run similar to Darkest Dungeon to the extent that it builds in a really good space for error. You WILL lose units and there are comeback mechanics to help you continue, but resources are finite and limited and you will only be able to suicide your units for so long. The flexibility is strong enough to allow you to learn from your mistakes and make corrections to your strategy, but not strong enough to allow you to keep making the same mistakes over and over again.Overall, this game is easily becoming one of my favorites and this comes from a player with a deep love for Darkest Dungeon, Battle Brothers, and other turn-based RPGs. A must-play if you like the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a good game, Iratus has an interesting sense of humor and the art style will probably grow on you.Its a early access game so these things may be improved on. At the moment however the game is just unbalanced beyond belief. You can really see that the devs put the effort in to make the characters kits work together, and integrate the magic system into the combat. However in practice the game does not deliver on balance. As you go up in floors, your damage increases due to better parts marginally, however the enemies become much stronger. In damage, defenses, resistances and most importantly evasion. Enemies that get much tankier should not scale upwards in evasion simultaneously as this just causes situations where a miss will cost you dearly and RNG will be allowed to skew the results of any particular run. The game has a very intuitive interface, but its rather confusing at first because it requires interaction with the art presented rather than just menus.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are someone who enjoyed Darkest Dungeon, then you may perhaps find Iratus to be enjoyable as well. I did not enjoy Darkest Dungeon, mostly because I do not find walking at an excruciatingly slow pace to be a stellar gameplay mechanic. I had hoped that perhaps Iratus would clean up some of these issues, and I was correct, but somehow it still fails to impress. They have packed so many RPG elements into the game, and have failed to polish a single one of them. The core issue is quantity over quality. Iratus has a skill tree, relics that can be equipped, buildings that can be upgraded, individual stat upgrades for each undead, two relic slots for each undead, upgrades for each individual skill for each undead, potions and alchemy. All of this is crammed into the game, and yet, none of it feels like it makes a meaningful impact on gameplay. Stat boosts are miniscule at best, skill options for the creatures you control don't provide legitimate opportunity for differentiation, buildings are nearly pointless, the relics are lackluster at best and occasionally bordering on completely useless. It feels as though the developers really wanted to make a certain style of game, but had no original ideas or unique mechanics with which to flesh it out.Overall, Iratus is a bizarre parody of itself. It is a dead shambling corpse of a game cobbled together from stolen parts that probably saw better use in their former life.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was an extreme disappointment. I played Darkest Dungeon and enjoyed it. Although the random chance is unfair and extremely aggravating I naively believe other game's would learn from it. Although, the randomness is less annoying because of the lack of customisation for units and the game generally tends to be easy. Don't enter this game with the mindset of "necromancer simulation" it's just Darkest Dungeon with expendable units. The game is generally quite ugly, units have uninteresting designs besides the bone golem and the void knight. And the fighting feels very unsatisfying. The expendable nature of the units stops you from being attached to them and the game loses tension. But the units can only be grouped as high as four. Interesting unit compositions comprise of. [Lich, "various ranged units", "various melee units", "expendable skeleton or high ward shade" ] or maybe the classic ["buff", "ranged", "melee", "tank"] due to their general blandness. How Thrilling! My point here is that the game has a very low skill-ceiling and other than the lich ( a unit that hurts your friendlies but does massive damage) or something like a headhunter with items that increase stats for empty spaces in a one man team. The game rarely lets you take advantage of your own wits. Also, the main character (Iratus, the necromancer) isn't interesting in the slightest. He makes for a trash protagonist and only serves to make your game more annoying with quotes that repeat over and over. The units are also uninteresting with names as fun as "skeleton" they all look the same unless you pay for a DLC ( These are very benevolent developers, you see) and some are simply terrible. whereas the lich is simply one of the best and the void knight's prot makes him the best too. units such as the banshee serve as slot-fillers and units like the bone golem have abilities like "self-destruct" because you are never going to use this ability and we needed to fill an ability slot.  The villains are also extremely generic, this makes the plot even less interesting. _childDocuments_.review: If I were to score this game I would probably give it a 5.5. It is not a terrible game in any significant way but it lacks a certain something to keep me interested. It is Slay the Spire meets something else (not really sure what -- some weird monster trainer/dungeon master thingee) except there is no deck building aspect. Instead you need to make minion armies and choose paths in a somewhat linear fashion. Once you learn what lies ahead of you, your choices may have more meaning but it feels very much just like a grind with no real pay off in the end. The buildings that you can build in the graveyard seem largely a bad idea (you sacrifice creations to enable most of them) with low to insignificant pay offs but they are luckily not forced on you. So you can opt to just not enable them. That you are forced to do the cakewalk difficulty before moving forward means you may find its replay value rather low while not being particularly challenged. I don't usually feel that way about this kind of game but it seems rather bland. The artwork is fine and the UI is great (No serious hiccups or gotchyas.) The game crashes fairly often but since it also saves often that's not typically a problem. Just reload and keep going.I suppose unlocking some of the "higher" level creations could be an end goal to help drive your grind but for me after completing the first cakewalk I didn't really find the game very enjoyable. Nor was the 2nd difficulty level very challenging either.  As a game that lists itself as dangerous and frustration inducing I found it to be neither really. The few times I lost a creation they were easily replaced. The only downside was figuring out how the creation died (each time it was a one-hit kill by some freak critical that sped by too fast to be properly registered.) But not really a frustration or obstacle. I never felt concerned for resources or even when fighting that my creatures were ever threatened. With all this negativity you might wonder why I thumbed up the game. The answer is mostly because of Steam's horrendous binary rating system and to be fair I did not hate playing it. It is entertaining to some degree though not my cup of tea story-wise. Playing the "bad" guy is fine but if it's just a clown show it becomes not very interesting, to me. You might find the story the best part. My recommendation is buy it on sale, and try it for yourself. If you get 10 hours+ out if it, it was probably worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfrozen’s  is one of the greatest tactical rogue-likes one can enjoy right now; one that surpasses the titles it pays homage to in almost every way. The road to getting rid of anything that breaths with your necromancer is filled with a series of challenging battles, with an enormous amount of depth in the mechanics on offer, and with a heavy dose of resource management thrown in as well. The challenge will test your mettle, as mistakes are rarely accepted, and failure is part of the recipe. It suffers a bit from a lack of content, and a slight dose of repetitiveness, yet the gameplay is so much fun that you’ll keep coming back to it no matter what - not to mention that the visuals are so beautiful that it makes staring at corpses and apparitions quite the enjoyable pastime.

_childDocuments_.review: update: first review was written at 3.8 hours. I'm now a little over 13 hours in. My opinion of the game has improved with more playtime. My tl;dr remains unchanged, but some of my criticisms were heavy handed.My advice is not to compare this game to Darkest Dungeon. It has elements in common, but it's not trying to be a clone. It's a substantially different game. The combat style, narration, and town view make it hard to avoid comparisons, but do try.I'm still not ready to recommend the game. It's not bad, but I just... can't recommend it. If you want a game that revolves around your ability to study myriad customization options to find synergy, this game definitely has that.My new top criticism is this:- UI makes study & comparison of relevant build, squad, minion, and resource details extremely cumbersome. This could be greatly improved with an additional, spreadsheet-like UI pane to serve as an all-in-one HUD for your various resources, minions and other build choices.==============tl;dr: Min-maxier Darkest Dungeon without the tension. replaces moment-to-moment choices & uncertainty with lengthy build planning & overwhelming predictability. Feels like all rules and options have to memorized from turn 0 in order to get any useful effect out of the individually-minor customization options.==========I bought Iratus after reading some reviews claiming it features the tension from Darkest Dungeon while also offering a greater degree of choice. In both cases I'm finding to opposite to be true. Where Darkest Dungeon gameplay mixes moment-to-moment reactivity & self control with easy-to-learn, hard-to-master rules, Iratus provides a mix of lengthy, up-front rules memorization and build planning followed by a long period of predictable slogging, waiting for your build to come online so you can have fun.+ talent trees allow you some customization+ minion skill upgrades represent a choice between utility flavors+ customization options likely hide some truly broken builds/strategies for those who enjoy that+ UI is clean, responsive, and easy learn, remember, and use- most choices feel too small to be worth the time it takes to make them- the most important choice of Darkest Dungeon - whether to push your luck - is completely missing- even upgraded minions feel disposable - no emotional attachment- less choice in dungeon traversal - branches feel interchangeable and samey. no backtracking, no consequences for a longer route, no cut-your-losses/live to fight an other day options- 'town' upgrade options extremely underwhelming early game- legacy mechanics have no place in this genre, yet here they are. Unlocking minion types requires achievements that will span multiple play attempts, meaning your first several runs feel even more like just grinding out that optimal build to come online hours and hours later.(retracted) - narration is entirely uncompelling * narration grows on you after a while(retracted) - soundtrack is elevator music * a more dynamic track would be nice- UI/UX is functional but clunky. Navigating the 'town' is an artistically disguised back-and-forth through nested menus. UI layout is borrowed from Darkest Dungeon (not a problem) but the UI workflow makes this a poor design choice.

_childDocuments_.review: Iratus Lord of the Dead takes Darkest Dungeon, turns it around and end result is better game in overall. Being in receiving end of dread and insanity is not as fun as inflicting them. Though Darkest Dungeon is still worth it as an experience, just finishing it might feel like a chore after playing Iratus. What both share is the line based combat. Both sides have their characters in a line and abilities are based on the position. So positioning the minions right really matters. Layout most likely won't static during the fight as some minions have abilities that move them around. Which might prevent other minions of using their most useful abilities as they might end up in wrong place. There's also multiple damage types, which means that knowing the enemy helps as you know their weaknesses and abilities even before the fight starts. Which means you can plan ahead better. There's humarium that you can use to look that information up. It won't be filled up right away though, you have to collect randomly awarded tokens, which means that in order to unlock the whole thing, you have play the game multiple times.Despite of what the game states of minions not being expendable, it's still somewhat forgiving. Minions will get experience and raise their level, but levels are mostly based on the brain (quality of parts being the other factor). Plug in high level brain to fresh minion and you'll get quite many levels and access to customizing abilities right away. So if you lose a minion, you should be able to create something close to the previous one if you don't lose too many of your minions. Good stuff will eventually run out and only thing left is parts for cannon fodder. Keep losing even more and you'll run out of even the bad parts.Between the fights you have multiple ways of improving things like using alchemy and artifacts to get and edge on next fight. If you have the Wrath of the Necromancer DLC, you can also brew potions. Most of the things will consume your stock of parts, so you have to balance things a bit in order to keep current minions alive or have enough parts to create new ones. Different minions are constructed from different combination of parts, so having stock of everything helps. You might also have to heal your minions in mortuary, so they will unavailable for next fight. Which in turn might mean that you have to rethink your tactics and come up with new potential synergies. Unless you have spare of same kind minion of course.As Iratus is kind of reverse dungeon crawler (you are climbing up from a dungeon instead climbing down) there's a dungeon that you have to traverse. Implementation resembles Slay the Spire as you choose paths from already revealed map. So choices do matter as you can plan your route beforehand. You can only change your direction in intersections, so once you commit to a hallway, you'll have to go through it. You'll also have to move always forwards toward your goal, so exploring whole dungeon is not an option.Sound and graphics deserve special mention. They really make it extra satisfaction of lashing out dread and damage to the opponents. Low health is really visible on the opponents (unless the damage is inside). Add over the top narrator to the mix and it gets even better.Minion types are unlocked via multiple ways, but the unlocks are permanent. So there's few new minions maybe for three playthroughs. Especially because few minions are unlocked by finishing the game with certain difficulty. It doesn't matter if you have played these line based battlers (there must be proper term, but I haven't seen any), Iratus is better to the competition by large enough margin. If you totally disliked Darkest Dungeon, you probably won't like this one either as main mechanics are so similar. But in all other cases, Iratus is worthy addition to your collection.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Original review from early access is below, I've tried playing the game again since release and found the developers did a great job creating methods to rebuild your units up to fighting strength. Among other aspects, the ability to retreat in a battle going south, getting minions at comparable levels to your current party during certain map events, and the fact unit training building actually lets minions gain experience faster than map battles, all allow you sufficient wiggle room that even a spat of bad luck won't prematurely end a campaign.Game has enjoyable setting and has fun combat mechanics with enough units to make finding new synergies rewarding.OLD REVIEW:The game has a lot of potential, but it seems to be suffering from two competing design strategies taken from Darkest Dungeon and Slay the Spire.The former game, Darkest Dungeon, emphasizes the expendability of your units. Making defeat a constant spectre of any dungeon run depending on how strong your units are. This isn't problematic however, as the game is setup such that you can return to old dungeons with fresh units in case a string of defeats has set you back to nearly square one. You're never railroaded into continuously more difficult encounters in case you've had a bad string of luck.The latter game, Slay the Spire, emphasizes the indispensability of your unit. You have to achieve victory in every single combat up to the final boss lest you need to restart the game entirely. This isn't problematic either, because there's not much setup or time invested into any one run. The game is also balanced such that with a little luck and enough knowledge of game mechanics you can put together card combos that make defeat nigh impossible.The problem with Iratus then is that it tries to emphasize the expendable and replaceable nature of your units in a game setting where defeat is very unforgiving.I want to recommend the game, and again: the game has a lot of potential, but I think the developers need to figure out a way balance the gameplay design such that a string of defeats won't leave you resentful of the fact you're being forced to progress in a losing scenario. Where quitting and restarting the game is actually the more viable strategy compared to seeing things out until the end.

_childDocuments_.review: So I want to open by saying that this game is a lot of fun. Minions are entertaining, artwork is grand, and you can blow through hours fine-tuning your teams to be the ultimate hero-killers. I love Iratus, and have been waiting on it ever since it was first announced. But there are a few serious issues with it in Early Access that may or may not be dealbreakers for some people who enjoyed Darkest Dungeon. I do hope that some of these issues will be fixed in future, but as they are now, they add unnecessary problems to the gameplay.----------------Stress. In Darkest Dungeon, Stress worked as an extra statistic that forced you to attend to the mental health of your party.If you didn't take care of it, characters that you had worked on for days and days could just keel over dead, making the player panic and rush to fix severe mental scarring in a hurry. In Iratus, Stress amounts to little more than an extra health bar that MOST enemies have, that claims to give debuffs and insanities to enemies, but seems to have a negligible impact outside of the occasional backstab done on its own teammate, and the damage done is so low that I might as well have just done the damage myself. Also, Battles are random, certainly, but there are minions that ONLY affect the stress bar, but enemies that don't have one at all that can just appear out of nowhere. So if you have a couple Stress minions, and a couple physical minions, half your Alpha team just went into the crapper as soon as a golem or elemental shows up. I sincerely hope that this is fixed in a future patch, and that sanity becomes a MUCH more important feature, but as of right now it has little to no point outside of adding padded time to an already drawn out combat.Story.Why is it that every time a game claims "Embrace evil. Be the bad guy!" they always feel the need to make the 'heroes' just as bad, or comically bent? I'm an ancient, forgotten evil on a pissed-off rampage. The first thing I see? Mind controlled slaves, villainous taskmasters and corrupt dwarves. If I'm to be evil, stop giving me 'good guys' that are written to be just as bad! Greedy diggers cracking open my tomb is one thing, but after 30 fights with corpse-robbers, insane mages, drugged slaves and malicious mercenaries, I'm seriously starting to wonder if I'm actually the bad guy here.Iratus himself.Holy crap the guy yaps like an old woman on a long distance phone call. Every spell, attack, ability, and so on, he has something to add, and it's usually something he's added a gajillion times already. There's only one line of dialogue per spell that you can cast, and he belts out the same line for each spell, over and over like a busted phonograph. I've heard the words "How about a little tingle up your spine?" so many times that the captions are burned into my eyelids. He seriously either needs to ease up, or some more lines of dialogue should be added to give him some variety.The backpack.Explain to me why we need a bar at the top that counts our resources, but also need to see every single non-stackable instance of those resources in a bag when we're trying to find a single piece of gear? I have pages and pages of skulls, but one single Etched Bone. We don't really need all that clutter, do we?The Dungeon.Darkest Dungeon was a good game, with custom heroes that you could work from rags to riches under your own power. Iratus tries to have the same, but lacks a key feature that we desperately need. The random dungeon. If we can't go to grind materials and levels, what is the point of having these minions level at all? Without the ability to go back and grind, necessary resources become harder to get, and thus, if you have one bad run or glitch, it can essentially outright end a game. I don't mean we need some procedural generator for content or anything, but the ability to go back and travel the paths we didn't walk down in the existing dungeon might be nice, rather than having several paths on a procedural map be locked off forever, meaning that the game put in all that work for nothing at all and might as well have just given us a linear corridor for all the good the randomized design does..To the creators of Iratus, I want you to know that this list of complaints really is a love letter, and that I have already burned through several hours of gameplay with the intent to play a lot more. I want it to do well, as it really is a stellar Early Access game. It's fun to lay traps, set up combos, murder dudes with zombie cannoneers and evil spells. But some aspects of the game are just... not as fun. I hope you don't take upset at this review and I look forward to the day when I can flip around and say "BEST GAME EVAR!".Love,A Huge Fan

_childDocuments_.review: New and unusual character skill trees and synergies.  I like games that go out of the standard box, and this game does that.  I think they tried to stretch out game play by forcing you to beat it once to unlock a couple extra characters, and then beat it again to unlock the hardest difficulty.  I don't think the game will interest me long enough to beat it 3 times.  I just completed my 2nd stage in my first run, so we'll see.  I'm curious to see if simply turning up the difficulty will be enough of a challenge once I learn the patterns.The other thing I'm questioning was the decision that opening up characters in one game file opens them up in all game files.  Its still early for me in my first run through, so maybe the game would be impossible if you didn't have all the characters at the start of the harder difficulties, but it would be interesting to take different paths to different characters in subsequent run-throughs.  Easy mode is very easy so far.  A couple times I sent in a rookie team against a big fight to scout it out and they win anyway.  I had to retreat out of the fight before it ended in order to make sure my big boys got the xp from the boss fights.  The ease of the game makes me want to turn up the difficulty, right away, but the hardest setting needs to be unlocked.I'm not nearly far enough along to give any full review, but these are my initial assessments.

_childDocuments_.review: Bottom line, Iratus does the best job of any pseudo-Darkest Dungeon clone of scratching that itch if you're looking for more Darkest Dungeon (1, to be clear).  There is a variety of monsters for different group builds (more than you can hold in the main roster at once, in fact), some clever ideas with the economy (you build your monsters out of parts that you get from enemies, use those monsters to upgrade buildings, and can repurpose parts for alchemy, although I do think the Diggers Souls currency needs something else to do once buildings are upgraded), and some good production value with the voice acting.It is held back by some very rough edges with the UX.  Some have already pointed out that the subtitles for a voiceover overlap the x button on a lot of windows, and there's a lot of clunk with what you can do, where.  You can store buildings in a training and health recovery building, for example, but can't set up your party without first going to a particular screen and dragging them back into the roster.  If you open up the character screen AT that particular screen, you can't see items you can equip or upgrade your monster with.  And you can't open up the character screen at all from the dungeon map screen as you try to decide where to go and who should go there.  Your main roster is at the bottom of the screen, and is divided into several different groups so you could have different cohesive parties, but since you only use one at once, and take everyone with you, this seemed like a needless feature when there are so many other QOL issues that get annoying after awhile.The animation is another thing holding Iratus back, for me.  It's paperdoll based, though obviously a high production version.  But it lagged the sound design and I never felt like the animations brought much impact.Finally, I think the non-combat gameplay will be in an uncanny valley between a more simple roguelike and a true campaign.  The dungeon map is really a Slay the Spire style branching path; you can't go back, you can't return.  You don't make any choices about which dungeon to attack next and have no goal other than getting to the end, and if you meet an encounter that proves difficult, there's nothing to do but keep sending monsters at the exact same encounter until you either win or run out of resources to make more.This can work, and is the vogue for a lot of game design these days, but a single "run" in this game can still take 20+ hours.  At that length, I think implementing a more fleshed-out strategy layer would have been a proper choice (I've also said the same with games that are more obviously built around the rogue-like experience, like Legend of the Keepers, but the game time there is such where you could see the rationale behind the choice).  Giving players a choice about whether to attack the dwarves or the mercenaries next, maybe to hunt for specific parts for specific projects or party build ideas, with specific objectives that could be achieved in a shorter play session, I think would have made the back side of the gameplay loop more engaging.But far as the combat system goes, there isn't a truer replication of Darkest Dungeon out there (that I've played anyway).  All characters have different attacks from different positions, monsters start with the base version of all abilities unlocked (with a choice between two different upgrades available for each), and, if you have the resources (including brains, which determine the monsters level) you can have fun building different compositions as you like without needing to grind them up (although since grinding isn't really an option, this could be considered silver lining).  Others have pointed that the game does really incentivize just leveling a few monsters to stay ahead of the difficulty curve, and I agree. This seems like an oversight rather than a conscious design decision, and could be remediated by either tweaking how monsters level or, again, adding a strategic layer that allows you to return to lower level opponents to try out new builds and level monsters that have fallen behind.  But this wouldn't even be an issue if a run in this game was only designed to last an hour or so and then start again like a proper roguelike, because then you could just try a different build.Got off track there, but returning to the combat, of course this has you play as the monsters.  You don't preserve sanity, you attack it (which if you decide to really focus on it, can be a lot of fun).  And other than the above, most of the changes will either be to your taste or not: whereas DD has a cartoony art style and a dark mood, Iratus has a style that looks more middle school "dark and edgy", masking a sense of humor to match.   It's a good game, not great.  Gets in its own way in a lot of ways, but if you're looking for what it's offering, it's worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, I have only played for 1.5 hours up till now, but I have serious issues with the art design of the game. The idea is good, and I want to like the game; but it feels like a flat, boring, unpolished Darkest Dungeon and HoMM2-Necromancer-town rip-off. Iratus' graveyard is a cheap copy of the Necromancer town in Heroes of Might and Magic 2. The colors of the game are too bright, and thus feel contrary to the atmosphere that is trying to be built. There is a total lack of unique atmosphere & story & suspense. The music is generic and boring. Even the fonts are boring!! I cannot really tell which font it is, but it is really disturbing to see Arial fonts hovering over minions in a battle. (Check out the alchemy table in the promotional images as a case in point.) The heavily-muscled necromancer looks more like a dead Conan, and not like a terrifying necromancer. I will probably play and finish this game, but it is really hard to get past the poor quality of art direction. The developers seem to have spent more time in developing mechanics than the actual content, and even then it is basically a DD rip-off! I would normally see no problem in a game focused mostly on the mechanics. (take FTL and Into the Breach as brilliant examples of this. Still they have a certain color palette, and style that feels unique.) What made Darkest Dungeon work was not just the brilliant idea behind it, but also superior voice acting, writing and art design all of which contributed to the great atmosphere of the game. Really sorry to say this, but Iratus is a terrible sore in the eyes... It feels as if there is no effort behind the game, and as if the developers wanted to make a quick buck from rogue-like and DD fans. PS: And please, please, please, please stop calling every game with a skill tree a RPG! RPG does not mean "a game that implements skill trees."

_childDocuments_.review: This game makes me wish I could give a neutral rating. It's not a bad game, but it's not that great either. There's a ton of tedium between each fight. The enemy diversity tries to encourage different builds, but almost any strategy is going to work. The only enemy that forced me to change strategy was the monks.The game isn't long, but the time I spent getting through every floor felt long because nothing really different happens. The most interesting nodes you can interact with are the mini-quests, but even those boil down to "Have a specific minion you wouldn't know to bring" or "Do an extra optional fight for rewards". It's a ton of choices with lots of micromanagement, and not enough pizazz. You even have to re-select the group you've made every time you open the map. It's a ton of constant small choices, and nothing feels like a significant choice.The strengths the game has is actually the fact that you can make almost anything work. It's fun making a Boiling Blood Werewolf or Lich and having it solo the world. This is fun enough to carry the game pretty far, but not enough to totally save it.Overall it's extremely mediocre. It's a ton of constant tiny decision making without any impact, but at least the massive number of choices means you can play around with tons of builds.

_childDocuments_.review: The world is doomed.  An army of undead is coming to wipe away all of life.  One by one.  Can anyone stop it?  Certainly not you.  In fact...you're the one leading the army of undead.Chop up your enemy, collect their parts, and make them your friends.  There are four difficulty modes of play.  Cakewalk, Normal, "Good Always Wins" and something else I haven't made it that far.  Cakewalk is basically a mode to get yourself familiar with the game.  Then there's the second difficulty setting, which is basically, "Ok...I know what I'm doing".  "Good Always Wins" is basically you saying "C'mon, make this a challenge" and the game saying "Sure thing".  I haven't been able to open the last difficulty setting yet, but I'm guessing its the game saying "Got milk?  I'm making cheese!".The game requires understanding how to make the most of different abilities to form a strategical squad that works well together in both offense and support.  There is no "perfect" squad either (once you think you've found one, the game will throw a curve ball...except on cakewalk). What I liked most about this game is that I got to play a necromancer, leading an army of undead and conquering the world, rather than saving those pathetic mortals who don't appreciate it and send me on pointless missions anyways.  Being evil wasn't an accident.Tired of always being the "hero"?  Great game.  Still want to save princesses?  Maybe not for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this game sits in a weird spot for me. Darkest Dungeon introduced me to this genre, and maybe it set my expectations too high for the rest of them. I enjoyed this game, it was fun, I played around with a handful of the characters, and I liked that there were set goals to unlock all of the different units. I didn't find a need for 80% of the units, I found a layout that worked for me and it carried me through the game and I only ever lost 1 major minion. I was able to immediately replace that minion thanks to the OVERWHELMING forgiveness of the starter difficulty. But that leads to the downfall of the game for me. I enjoyed the content, it took me 10 hours to beat the game, and it was 10 hours of relaxed enjoyment. So I sat through the rather disappointing end and started again on the normal difficulty. Despite having access to 1/4 or maybe even 1/5 of the items and resources I was able to clear the first area and am halfway through the 2nd area in 2 hours. I've experimented with different units and more volatile setups, but I quickly came to a rather disappointing realization.I was bored. The difficulty doesn't effect the types of enemies you come across, or their move sets. So even though I had less to work with, I only had to manage units better instead of strong-arming with the same 4 units. I saw everything before already, so I knew what to anticipate, how to counter, and how I wanted to build troops. There isn't enough left for me to explore in the game to make me want to spend more time beating the exact same thing again, and so I won't.So I've grown bored after 12 hours, which is more time than dollars I spent on the game, which makes it worth buying on sale, but I honestly think I would have been disappointed had I paid full price.

_childDocuments_.review: So Iratus is an interesting game. I came into it thinking it would be a game similar to Darkest Dungeon and played it as such...which led me to not enjoy the game at all! Once I realized I had to approach the game completely different from DD, i.e. not getting attached to characters AT ALL, in fact there is a minion with a super strong heal built around sacrificing your other minions, I started having a ton of fun.The game is HARD, borderline cheap in some cases but if you persevere there is a rewarding and challenging game that awaits you. Contrary to what many people say every minion is viable, not sure about the Ghoul as I haven't unlocked it yet. Not every minion is as good as the next but I think that is what makes the game interesting. I found a lot of enjoyment in figuring out OP, in my opinion, combos or going all in on good body part rolls. The former gave me a lot of strategizing through multiple playthroughs and the latter let me come up with strategies on the fly (and let me try minions I wouldn't normally use).Enemies are HARD, harder than DD in my opinion. They are unforgiving and can feel cheap at times, however, if you approach the game from a Necromancer's point of view, i.e. minions are expendable, you will have a lot more fun. Once I embraced this mindset I enjoyed overwhelming my enemies with numbers rather than super elite units (which you can still get, it just requires sacrifice of other units to get there, for me anyway).The TLDR is to approach this game with an open mind and devote time to master it. If you do you will have a great time!My only annoyances so far are the following:1. I want more ways to effect enemy stats/actions (not just stress)2. The Ghoul is WAY harder to unlock than the other minions (if not explicitly trying to unlock it)3. More ways of retaining your high level parts after a minion dies would be nice and help when a party wipes. I get the game is supposed to be hard, but it should just end the game at some point when you lose enough parts because it feels like an exercise in futility to use base part minions to try and get past the super hard fight you just lost to.Additionally, I really love the art direction of the game! I'm really looking forward to the new levels and enemy/minion content!I only mention my 1st point because I enjoy debuffing more than I enjoy doing direct damage. But the design for synergies is really fun. I particularly like Wraith, Shade, Banshee, Vampire as a party ^.^. I really like how much insanity effects the game. It gives interesting mechanics as well as just flat debuffs. Very well implemented in my opinion!Overall I think this game is great and a welcome addition to the genre! Definitely going to keep following this game and looking forward to updates!

_childDocuments_.review: SHORT REVIEWThis review is for the Wrath of the Necromancer Edition which includes the DLCs as I bought it as a bundle.  The comparisons to Darkest Dungeon are unavoidable but don't think of this as just a Darkest Dungeon clone, it is actually a much better game than Darkest Dungeon.PLOT:  The plot is pretty standard fantasy fare.  An evil necromancer has awoken from his imprisonment in an underground complex and is sending forth hordes of undead to destroy the world and the forces of good must rally together to defeat him.  The twist with this game is that you are playing the evil necromancer.COMBAT:  Its a 4 vs 4 tactical combat game.GRAPHICS & SOUND:  The graphics and sound are very good but where this game really excels is the voice acting for Iratus himself which is absolutely superb and really sets the game apart from many others.REPLAY VALUE:  Very Good.  Its a roguelike with 4 difficulty settings ranging from Cakewalk (Easy) to Eternal Harvest (Very Hard).ISSUES AND BUGS: The game runs “straight out of the box” and appears to be bug free.ACHIEVEMENTS AND TRADING CARDS:  Full integration with the Steam platform.VALUE FOR MONEY:  Average at full price.  However, it's definitely one to put it in the “wait for a discount” category.  Its not an old game (only just over 2 years old at the time of writing) but even so it comes round on offer regularly and with a big discount at which point I rate it as excellent.  (It was 80% off in the Steam 2022 Summer sale and was on a similar discount about a month before the sale and again a month after the sale.)LONG REVIEWWhen reviewing Iratus Lord of the Dead it is impossible to do so without making comparisons to Darkest Dungeon but it should not be thought of as purely a Darkest Dungeon clone.  At the highest level it is darkest dungeon in reverse with you playing the bad guys and making the heroes go insane.The gameplay is more streamlined than Darkest Dungeon with much less micro management involved.  Effectively items/trinkets are a one time allocation (once they are assigned that cannot be unassigned although they can be overwritten).. There is no “equipping your party” and no “inventory management” involved so the level of micro management required is significantly reduced.The elements of grind and randomness that plague Darkest Dungeon have also been removed.  In Iratus you probably need to develop 2 parties (you can do it with 1 but probably need some back-ups) as opposed to the 4 required in Darkest Dungeon and the brains offer a way to bring new minions in at higher level without having to grind them up from the start.  It also feels a lot less random that Darkest Dungeon.  Darkest Dungeon suffers from a “there is nothing you could do about that, the RNG just hates you” feeling.  I'm sure Iratus has an RNG in the background somewhere but its far less intrusive.Iratus also has 4 difficulty settings as opposed to 3 in Darkest Dungeon  I would say the game is easier than Darkest Dungeon as effectively the 4th difficulty setting (Cakewalk) is at the lower end of the scale.  This addresses the biggest problem with Darkest Dungeon and that is that the game is just too ****ing hard!All in all Iratus Lord of the Dead is not just a Darkest Dungeon clone, it is actually a much better game than Darkest Dungeon.Generally I'm not a fan of DLCs (they are often just a blatant cash grab) but the ones for this game aren't too bad as they actually and contain a reasonable amount of content.  The additional skin sets strike me as rather pointless and are probably best avoided.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, we're all here hoping to get some more of that Darkest Dungeon fix, don't deny it. This review will probably contain many references to DD, but the developers pretty much brought it on themselves.The Premise is pretty much exactly what I'd want out of this kind of game - You're the big bad ascending from his tomb after 1,000 years to wreak havoc and go for World Domination attempt 2, Electric Boogaloo. You build up your army from bits and bobs taken from your slain foes, nice Necromancy delivering all you need for your minions. A feature I particularly like is that these parts (Bones, armor, flesh, ectoplasm, etc.) come in many levels of powerful, and slapping them on a minion means they get more stat points. So you can start a level 1 minion with some really decent stats if you save up, or upgrade some of your longer-standing ones further. More on leveling later.The Minions themselves are quite varied, certainly visually. Werewolves, many types of Ghosts, all flavors of flesh amalgamations, some magical constructs, and more. Having a look at the trailers will tell you the sort of beasties at your disposal. Unlocking new ones feels rewarding because not only do you have more options, you *want* to play around with this cool new monster. The designs are fantastic and it makes me very happy to see the Developers didn't cheap out and make things a reskin. It really makes you feel like the Big Bad Evil Guy with his horde of nightmare creatures.Their abilities fit with their themes and usually have fun names to boot. All of their abilities are unlocked from the start and are only restricted by unit positioning, unlike in DD where you could only equip 4 but also had to worry about positioning. I'd say that this is primarily because combat has a lot more shuffle - your minions and the enemies are often moving positions of their own volition and in response to attacks. Having limited ability slots would mean you'd either have to choose one ability to work for each spot or just be screwed if the shuffle puts you in a tight spot. Though in DD you could have a character move instead of using an ability, in Iratus you have to use a spell to move someone 1 space, and you can only cast 1 spell per round of combat, and there's a dozen better things you could be doing with that spell instead of moving so it feels like an odd decision from Unfrozen.Let's get into combat a bit more. Your minions are slaughtering people, and people generally have two bars - Health and Sanity. They also have varying kinds of resistances to physical, sanity, and mental damage. In addition, there are Shields and Wards, which will tank any 1 hit from their corresponding source (Wards pull double-duty for magic and sanity damage). These can make the first rounds of combat something of a slog as you put out attacks just to wear down their blocks unless your minions have abilities to bypass them. Now, your minions can get these too, which levels the playing field somewhat, but it still feels slow from it.Stress damage is a nice addition to the combat instead of restricting things to mere health damage. It make sense thematically - we're the BBEG after all, and our minions have no such concerns for sanity, but all the squishy mortals do. Rather than trying to stab a particularly tough opponent to death, you could stress him to the point of having a heart attack, drive them insane, make them flee in terror, or just turn on their allies. However, like in DD, there's a chance that they may become inspired under the pressure and become a bigger threat. Higher difficulties increases this chance of Inspiration, but certain trinkets can negate this entirely and guarantee they'll never become so.Trinkets are part of your Loadout. Iratus himself can be equipped with artifacts in certain slots that grant bonuses of varying quality. Like a sickle that boosts minions if their combined party is low-level, or a cloak that permanently increases minion damage if they land killing blows on enemies. There's also that trinket I mentioned which disables enemy Inspiration, which makes dealing Stress Damage a really effective option for dealing with multiple enemies - just let them weigh each other down and it'll all go smoother. There's also Minion artifacts - they have 2 slots and you can't pull them out - once it's spent on a minion, it's stuck there. Some combinations of equipment and minions can feel quite unbalanced, like ones that deal percentage damage to health and sanity of enemies every time that minion uses an ability. I like to slap it on my riposte minions to whittle down the whole enemy squad.On the topic of unbalanced are Spells, but first comes Leveling. Iratus' minions level up from combat while Iratus levels up all the time. As minions level, you can boost some of their stats like damage, evasion, adding wards or shields, so on. Iratus has some standard RPG trees in 4 disciplines that basically boil down to Resources, Buffs, Curses, and Damage spells. When you level up, you get a point, as well as some boosts to your Rage and Spellpower. Spellpower does what it says on the tin while Rage allows minions to execute special moves in combat. For some spells, Spellpower means more damage or boosting, but for others it means cheaper casting. There's a spell called "Fate" which guarantees the next attack from a minion will be a critical. This is very powerful and useful for your hard-hitting minions like the Werewolf or the Zombie. And then there's the Bride who has a dedicated attack that does way more crit damage than normal, so you just hit her with it and let her chomp healthbars by half.This all may sound like the game gets easy once you learn the tricks, really it's more that you HAVE to learn the tricks to stand more of a fighting chance, especially on the harder difficulties. You have 16 minion slots in your squad bar, and it's because you should expect your minions to be getting pretty well hammered or killed. Now, this is to be expected - they're your minions, dying is in the job description. It also sort of forces you to try out squad variations and new minions you acquire. You have to really learn your enemies' attacks and skills to help keep your minions un-alive. Some enemies can utterly wreck your squishier dudes if you don't negate stances or take out certain foes first. Playing intelligently and planning your turns out will keep you going, but remember that you're still going to take losses. Keep at it, and crush the mortals beneath your feet.The final thing I'll touch on is the "Story" not that there really is much, and that's a problem for me. Darkest Dungeon's story was all-pervading; it was in the descriptions of characters and buildings, the explanation of bosses, the state of the manor and hamlet, and the foes you faced. The Ancestor's narration constantly gave more insight and meaning to everything you did, and by the end you felt like you understood everything that had happened. "In time, you will know the tragic depths of my failings..." he says. Buuuuuuuuuut that's not here.Iratus' goal is to rise from the underground and try to take over the world. The most "story" you get outside of that is 2 cutscenes near the end and some brief boss text walls. Iratus still narrates like the Ancestor does - in combat and as you expand your base and create minions, but it lacks the same depth. What I mean is Iratus just sort of talks smack or gives a comment on his thoughts. He never expounds on how mortals have changed and advanced, memories of some of the areas, allusions to these battles you're fighting being like ones of old, none of it. There's no sense of discovery or wonder to it, of getting to know the narrator and his story. It just feels lacking. His voice acting and lines are good, very good, but just lacking.Overall, this is a fun and interesting game with mechanics hard to find elsewhere. Support Unfrozen - they did good work and I want to see more from them.

_childDocuments_.review: Iratus Lord of the Dead is an interesting take on the classic party of 4. It has a home base for you to upgrade, minions can be created using parts from slain foes, talents that make future battles easier, and much more. Every fight you need to consider your team composition as well as whom to upgrade over others. In general, if your team comp sucks/bad matchup your units are likely to die. If you want keep your units alive longer consider how to best approach each enemy type. This is especially apparent on Good Always Wins where even a good team comp can be squashed due to improper leveling or maybe a mistake in talents. sometimes enemies will just crit your dudes for all their health even if your evasion percent is at like 60%+. I highly recommend this game if you want a challenge which will require you to think about your actions.If you came from Darkest dungeon then this game shares similarities with it but is way more simplified than darkest dungeon and you'll understand the jist of iratus quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: When i opened this game, i saw a familiar message, one claiming this game to be brutal, with many setbacks, and an extremely brutal campaign. A mantra held high by the likeness of Darkest Dungeon, a truly brutal game that took me 100+ hours and did indeed cause me to recoil in horror as i lost my team many MANY times.This isn't anything like that, in fact this might be one of the easiest games I ever played.I spammed reaper scythe attack to get past all the levels easily without fail, up until the 3rd boss who had an AoE attack. After that i lost a monster every now and then but i could immediately get  a new one buy putting a brain into the same type of monster.Resources where so plentiful i basically got to have everything right at the beginning, which really hurt this game roguelike feel.At 30$ its really pricey.Theres an option to turn off "cliche voicelines".... the voicelines are like the least cliche thing about this game, the characters look like they are from a shoddy mobile game. + The plot is actually good, like really good, not as good as Darkest Dungeons which is the exact same concept and price, and just WAY better, but its good.This game has some really neat cutscenes, but again, not as good as darkest dungeon.Basically what im saying is this is an overpriced game that has a pretty direct competitor that is actually worth your money. If your on the fence about this game, just do yourself a favor, get Darkest Dungeon. Its ACTUALLY hard, way better designed, way more fun, better animated, has non cliche voice lines, and as a bonus, you dont spend most of your time allocating stat points.yeah i should have mentioned that, i spent MORE time spam allocating stat points than i did playing the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: Any of the higher lvl difficulty is a cluster ♥♥♥♥ of RNG save scum. sadly you'll have to use mostly the same team everywhere too because most of the minion don't scale well into higher difficulty and will become a hindrance.Boss have a very few viable option, anything else is dead before the fight even start. and because a run is so long 10h+ and you can lose it to a single bad crit RNG it's not worth playing (well save scuming help wit that).Balance aside, the art/voice are really cool, so you'll probably have fun for the first few run in lower difficulty, so if you have nothing else to play or got this one in a bundle you can still get a few hours of fun out of it before reaching the eternal harvest of boredom point.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game, I had a lot of fun playing this one!It's great to play 'evil' once in a while since it opens a whole set of different opportunities.From the very start, the voice actor of Iratus does a remarkable job.Each and every voice line is spot on, perfectly delivered with a lot of witty comments.This, combined with the music, pulls you into it from the get-go.The game starts with a very nice tutorial that step by step introduces you to the different concepts.Afterwards you can either continue on the starting difficulty or re-start on a higher difficulty.While at its core the game is a turn-based, tactical rogue-like, it brings with it a lot of features:Different minions all with their own abilities and skill sets, upgrade options, gear for your main character, gear for your minions, talent trees for your main character, spells, alchemy, ... name it and it's in the game!I really liked the fact that you had to unlock minions by doing certain tasks. It makes you try different things to get the next unlock.I played the game on the 'More Pain!' difficulty which is the 'normal' difficulty and spend 16hrs on the playthrough. After this you unlock another set of minions, so this opens the path for a higher difficulty which I will definitely try out!The game plays extremely fluid and responsive, I didn't have a single glitch or issue playing it.The devs are also very active, providing continuous support, a new expansion and free content (Werewolf minion, which is awesome!).Two thumbs up on this one, I highly recommend it!Update:I continued playing the game on the next difficulty level, 'Good Always Wins' and again had a blast!For this run I used 'Fallen Dhampir, Wraith, Mummy, Bone Golem'.The graphics and animations are really nice, there is a lot of eye for detail.A multitude of minions to choose from, figuring out Team compositions, which skills fit well etc is really fun.In many cases I found myself saying "one more battle" which is a good sign :)After beating that difficulty you unlock 'Eternal Harvest' in which there are 5 tiers.Before starting the first tier I got myself the DLC which adds more minions, an extra level, potion brewing and a whole set of different minion skins.For this playthrough I used 'Fallen Dhampir, Reaper, Black Widow, Abomination' and again had a lot of fun.Even on this run I had several new ideas on yet another Team composition, so I'll have to keep going!
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: This game is tough, you won't find yourself grinding, that might make things a little more bearable. No you'll cling to life trying to survive. materials are rare, the choices you make and your upgrades early on make a big difference. Punishing game play make this a rewarding challenge to over come. Don't expect to plow through this quickly, you'll be chipping away at this game for a long time while you slowly learn to master the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: This is a gem among games that look and feel a lot like Darkest Dungeon.Cheesy lines and lighthearted writing make it easy to enjoy playing as the bad guys in what feels like role-reversal from a typical roguelike. You unlock and create various classes of undead which form your combat parties, are used to unlock/upgrade buildings and can even be straight up sacrificed for loot. My biggest gripe with Iratus is a lack of freedom from what is, minus a few route choices, a fairly linear gameplay loop - beat the game with increasing difficulty levels while carrying over unlocked classes. There isn't any "free time" to grind or play around outside of progressing directly to your next objective. This will hurt the game's replayability for me in the long run as I progress to higher difficulties.A great, solid experience that you'll get a decent bit of gametime out of before it becomes stale due to the linear nature of the game. Lots of classes to mix and match, lots of items and parts to customize your characters. Until you realize this game doesn't really have farming, backtracking or grinding and have to limit yourself for the sake of resource management. Could be better but worth every penny at the current price.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: Iratus: Lord of The Dead is a breath of fresh air! After the huge success of Darkest Dungeon, there’s been a lot of attempts at creating a dark, gritty, hardcore, roguelike with tactical elements. Permadeath, getting attached to characters, and being surrounded by complete stress is what this niche is about. There has been a lot of mediocre titles recently that have tried to emulate Darkest Dungeon, but I truly feel that Iratus: Lord of The Dead actually stands a good chance of surpassing it. Iratus, though in Early Access, shows a lot of promise with it’s insane polish. Graphics are detailed and animated well. It’s a very dark atmosphere that fits the setting. Gameplay is good old tactical combat with you taking four units per encounter to take out enemies. Level them up, modify their stats and skills, and combo your way to victory. The most exciting part for me is the ability as a Summoner to be directly involved. Equip yourself with gear and spells to change the tide of battle. Choose talents to increase bounties or improve your spell power. This game has that air to it. It will be another classic. Definitely play it.Thanks for reading! If you’d prefer to instead watch gameplay then I’ve provided the link to my First Look Gameplay Impressions [Mabimpressions] for Iratus: Lord of The Dead here:

_childDocuments_.review: I've only got 7 hours on this game.I purchased it because of a review I read that said it was "deep"I really cannot collaborate this sentiment.The gameplay is pretty ok. Very "Darkest Dungeon" without the atmosphere.The artistic direction is where I feel this game really  misses. It really FEELS like a mobile game ported over to steam. The voice acting hints at a bit of humor and self aware criticism. The art assets feel very generic and uninspired. What I really dislike is the ambiant soundtrack and classical music score used in the game. It is absolutely trite and uninspired.  any one of these things would not kill this game, but all together. It all adds up to product that feels kind of low effort. Is is a Bad game? No. (the mechanics are solid if uninspired)Is it a Great game? No.Is it a Good game? _childDocuments_.review: Iratus: Lord of the Dead is a challenging game that is still in early access as of my review. I wanted to put some hours into not just it but the community before I decided on my recommendation.I recommend this game to people who:Enjoy a challenge and learning from your mistakes.Like having many choices in group composition and enjoy searching for that "perfect" team.Want play the bad guy and send your minions to DESTROY!Have fun with games that have some micromanagment of buildings and unit upgrades.I don't recommend this game to people who:Want full sessions that finishes fast. (The levels can be somewhat long but you can leave and come back from a non battle screen without penalty.)Like to steamroll content.Have no patience for losing.Are looking for a fully finished and polished game.Yes, there are unbalanced parts (It's still in Early Access) but the Devs have been great so far on patching out bugs and balancing gameplay as we play and give them information to work on. They have been active on the Discord where they listen and have commented on suggestions and bug-reports or just popped into chat to say hello.There's still content to add and the roadmap (currently visible on the news page here on Steam) shows just how much more content they're working to add to the game.The Discord community has been a helpful and relaxed bunch who are more than willing to answer questions and often brag about their favorite team compositions.This game has kept me playing from the start with it's darker tone and challenging rogue-like gameplay and it's only getting better as time goes on.I recommend you give this one a look.
