_childDocuments_.review: Iratus is the rare indie game that takes inspiration from better known games, but actually manages to develop on that inspiration rather than lazily plagiarize.  The inspiration from Darkest Dungeon is particularly obvious, so much so that it immediately invites comparison. This is something the developers themselves acknowledge. However they rebut the claim that Iratus is a DD clone by pointing to the greater tactical depth of DD and added mechanics.  And while the differences aren't exactly night and day, after 12 hours of play i have to say their statements ring true. Iratus offers a much deeper roster of potential minions than DD, as well as far more tactial options to help your minions directly in combat. Additionally theres a much greater enemy variation as well, and the means though items to replace high level pawns which die unexpectedly.  In short, Iratus builds of the core gameply of DD but very subtly removes a tremendous amount of the grinding and lack of control that made DD frustrating.  I would go so far as to say that on a gameplay level Iratus is the better game. My only real criticism of the game is the Art Direction which, apart from your pawns which are pretty beautiful, tends to be either ugly, generic, or basically stolen.  A lot of the later enemies look like they were plucked directly from warhammer fantasy. But i guess art is subjective.  All in all Iratus is a tremendous freshman indie game from a studio i want to see more from. It's core gameplay is familliar but fun and challenging.  I hope the Studio finds it's own distinct creative vision as they move forward.

_childDocuments_.review: Iratus LOTD is a turn-based, troop-management roguelike RPG where you lead undead minions from the depths of your subterranean prison to the world above. For a roguelike RPG, Iratus is more RPG and less roguelike which I personally like. The core of the game is leveling your units and going to battle against scores of baddies (or in this case, "goodies"). Unit build customization is in between average and complex. You can select their stats, skill types and accessories. Other mechanics include base upgrades, alchemy, talent tree and artifact customization for Iratus (you).PROS+ Deep RPG elements and unit build customization.+ Lots of accessories that change the way a unit plays.+ Good variety of units. Large variety of enemies.+ Spell effects are very nice and impactful.+ Lovely art style. Some forgivable anatomy issues.+ The dialogue and voice overs are fantastic!!!+ You can name your units. Very important because...CONS- Units only have 1 skin!!! Unless you buy the DLCs.- UI seems floaty and non-interactive sometimes.- The "wait" command for units didn't work for me.- In-battle dialogue causes unnecessary delay in actions.- And the biggest CON: Replacing high-level units is a little too easy. When your unit dies, there's a good chance that a "brain" will drop after you win the battle. The brain will have a level at or close to the level of the unit that died. So if my dead unit was lv 35, the brain drop will be lv 35. I can create a new lv 1 unit, plug the lv 35 brain into him/her, and now I have a new lv 35 unit. Often, the dead unit drops some of its upgrades and OP accessories which help rebuild the new unit almost identically. Further, in your battles, brains would randomly drop matching the high level of the enemies. So I just stockpile brains and never have to fear losing a unit. It makes me feel less attached to a unit and feel less bad when they're gone. Granted, I played at the second to the hardest difficulty. Maybe I will change my tune at the hardest game mode.Don't let these cons deter you from buying the game. They are easily overlooked with the fun I had. Iratus gets an 8.5 from me. Very good addition to my library which I see my self replaying. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is brilliant.We play the bad guys and contrary to Darkest Dungeon it's the enemies who have to deal with both their sanity and health.The way it's done though makes the game unique and very fun.For the combat itself, there are 3 types of damage, stress damage, magical health damage and physical health damage and it's possible to kill enemies with just health damage or stress damage. These aspects coupled with many other mechanics like stances, the very different minions and enemies make team building and the battle system excellent and very interesting elements of the game.Some of the strategies I tried for example were stress damage team based on moving enemies around, very defensive AOE stress damage team, curse based team, physical health damage team, magical health damage team, etc... There are many possibilities but note that higher difficulties significantly reduce the number of viable teams. The difficulty is another aspect I like compared to Darkest Dungeon when I first played it, overall Iratus is less frustrating since you can play easier difficulties first to learn.Things outside combat are also well done like the talent system, artifacts, "crafting", base building, etc... While simple, the map system is interesting and allows to plan a route based on what's needed so there is a soft strategic layer to the game. The story is very basic and doesn't matter that much in this kind of game but the atmosphere is good. The animations and art style look great. Iratus' voice repeats the same lines quite quickly but is cool nonetheless.If you liked Darkest Dungeon, Iratus is definitely a must have. If you never played any of these 2 excellent games, Iratus is probably the most forgiving to begin with.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral option, the game isn't bad by any means, but it feels a little shallow.  I would possibly recommend it, when on sale and not in early access.    When I got to the last boss, with my main forces wiped out, I figured I would lose.  Nope, beat the final boss, and still had my four minions.I agree with other reviews, that the starting minions are fairly weak compared to the ones you unlock.  I actually beat the game on my first play through, using mainly the starting minions.  Half way through second play through, I have unlocked most of the minions now, and the game is significantly easier.I'm also not a huge fan of a majority of the spells and minion .  They either feel too insignificant, or they do more harm than good.  Of course there are exceptions, but I'm referring to the majority.  I also don't like that the minion stat upgrades are tied to the upgrade skill.  For instance, if you want to choose a skill that increases the damage of said minion skill, the stat upgrade that comes with it might be for health, where as the alternative choice, might increase the spells area or duration, but give you additional stats in attack.I give it about a 6.5/10 at this point, a passing game score, but again, not one to break the bank for.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Darkest Dungeon, you'll probably like this. If you have a thing for necromancy and playing the bad guys and like turn-based combat, you'll probably also like this.This game draws obvious inspiration from Darkest Dungeon and doesn't try to hide it. The premise is basically Darkest Dungeon but you are the evil necromancer and instead of having to manage stress for your own party, it is YOU who can deal both physical damage and stress damage in order to defeat your enemies.The game doesn't quite have as much polish or depth as Darkest Dungeon, however. One example would be how the abilities for your minions develop. All abilities for each minion is already unlocked, but each can be upgraded in two different exclusive ways. On the surface this is an interesting idea, as you must choose between two roughly equally good upgrades. In practice, however, the upgrades mostly change stat values instead of offering any unique gameplay mechanics.The progress system does feel a bit weird, you have to essentially accomplish in-game challenges (trigger insanity 80 times, deal 750 damage to your own minions, etc) to unlock new minion types, but once you have them, they are unlocked for all future runs you do.  It effectively means you should just play through the game on the tutorial difficulty and unlock all the minions you can before starting a "real" campaign where you have access to everything. Part of me wishes there was a per-run progression needed to unlock each minion type each campaign.Overall I really enjoy the game and I'm a sucker for any game that lets me be a necromancer.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished my first playthrough last night. I'd love to say it comes highly recommended, as the thematics go well towards a DD clone that lets you take the role of the monsters terrorizing the human adventurers. But there's many things lacking overall. Getting each creature type can be a slog, and in a game where your unit options are everything you'll probably be starting new games just to get all of the monsters unlocked, which drives the fun down a tad when you should be playing through start to finish instead. The WotN DLC is helpful, but perhaps too much. The item selection is poor, be it for Minions or Iratus himself, and you begin wishing some things were better than they are for varieties sake. The Graveyard gives you essential boosts, but equally lacks variety, and your upgrade path will depend on what your team is doing. There's great satisfaction to be found in the Sanity damage mechanic, causing your enemies to die of fright rather than damage to their HP, but some enemies are immune to it so building strictly for Sanity damage can be problematic. I'm sure that with mod support it would open up, but that seems lacking as well. Possibly a lack of interest in the base game? It would improve with a NG+ option too. I hope that if this gets a sequel it does well, because the foundation is solid and the game would scratch that itch folks have for a DD type experience that's not as ballbusting. The execution just leaves one wanting in a few ways by the end. Good as a time waster, I suppose.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright we already know this game is a lot like Darkest Dungeon on a core level. What you're probably asking yourself is "what can I do in this that I can't in Darkest Dungeon already?", so I'll summarize it for you.-Play as the Darkest Dungeon itself with your goal being to piss on the Hamlet instead of trying to rebuild it.-Have the stress system on your side where the enemy is the one trying to roll against afflictions at 100 stress and dying to heart attacks instead of you (and yes, stress builds are a thing and are perfectly viable depending on the enemy).-Assume direct control in combat with a mana system that lets you personally blast the enemy with cheap magic spells from the safety of your home. (There's even a wine skeleton spell for stressing everyone on the enemy team)-Manage the health of your monsters because they don't heal between fights by either sending them to the morgue for their version of a relaxing vacation, or performing dark alchemy by taking whatever organs, bones, or trash you have laying around your house and distilling them into funny zombie beer.-Control an army of undead who are both willing to play as a team and step right the hell over one another in a desperate power-struggle for your affection, such as the ghoul who can cannibalize her own team for health, or the Bone Golem who is willing to explode and die for your sins at a moments notice.-Equip items like burning blood and cannibals jaw to a Lich to create a miniboss that will have the enemy screaming in eldritch horror as they are single handedly wiped out by a funny floating skeleton who gets absurd stat bonuses for being alone on the field and whenever an ally dies.-Cry when your favorite monster gets nuked because there's no death's door mechanic, only suffering, but sigh in relief as you're able to get a new one up and running so long as you have an appropriately leveled brain you can place into it.-The zombie has a gun.If any of that sounds interesting, then you should give this game a whirl. It's really good. Flawed in some aspects, like enemy variety is kinda shallow and there's currently no workshop, but I'd say it's still a really fun experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: 7.8/10Very solid but not astounding. I'd recommend it if you're in love with turn based strategy the likes of Darkest Dungeon (hereafter referred to as DD). Consider waiting for a minor sale if you don't enjoy this kind of gameplay with a bit of difficulty.Gameplay: 7.5/10Kill the enemy squad. That's 90% of the experience. A colossal proportion of the smaller features and mechanics at play here directly influence your ability to kill the other squad. If you're taking advantage of Steam's refund policy and trying this game for 1 hour and 59 minutes, make sure you're enjoying this.Outside of combat, there's some sort of economy to grow and manage, roughly similar to XCOM's basebuilding, where you invest resources gathered from combat to improve your combat performance. For better or for worse, it's not too deep, though.When your units level up you are able to upgrade their abilities, but this system is surprisingly lacking. You have two options for each ability, and 90% of these total options will either upgrade the Primary effect of the ability (doing damage, doing stress damage, healing, etc.) or it will upgrade the Secondary effect (buffs, debuffs, effect duration, etc.). There are few times you're going to find an upgrade that opens a ton of new strategies. You can also freely upgrade your units' stats when they level up. However, I found that increasing their damage resistance was overwhelmingly effective, as it mitigated the effects of enemies getting lucky with crits many times in a row. I'm sure after playing this game more, I'll find some more interesting stat distributions, but it seems that minmaxxing your units to serve 1-2 specialized jobs is Extremely strong.Between combat, you move through the map similarly to Slay The Spire, where you choose a path that will grant you the kinds of encounters you're looking for before you reach the boss.Graphics: 8/10(?)The character models themselves are very impressive to me, but some of the animations aren't the best. Sometimes, characters will move in such a way that you can clearly see the joints on the puppets in action. On the other hand, some of the animations are simply incredible. At worst, these are Serviceable, and it only goes up from there. Although, it can look pretty goofy when a character who moves like they're in the game Barotrauma is casting a spell.Story: 3/10There's none. You're a necromancer trying to take over the world. That's about it. I didn't buy this game for the plot and neither should you. I didn't factor this into my final score, but it was worth mentioning. Despite the lack of story, the tone of the game is very consistent. Iratus narrates your experience the same way The Ancestor does in Darkest Dungeon. It adds some character to your quest.Sound: 7/10The music does its job well, both in combat and out, but it's not winning any awards. As I write this, I can't call to mind any song from the game, except the battle music of two of the worlds you travel through. After about ten hours of playing, I had switched the music off to listen to a playlist instead.The sound effects aren't super consistent with the in-game source. It's very strange. The "Dark Knight" character has one specific sound when receiving damage that makes him sound like a whiny zombie that's tripped on a ladder and fallen over. The same character has a different pain sound that makes him sound like a demon laughing menacingly when he's struck. The "Miner" enemy's primary attack sounds like he's aggressively zipping shut a zipper, while he swings a pickaxe at you. I've used these two examples because you start with a Dark Knight, and you will fight a Miner very early on. These examples will be easy to find for someone looking to experience this game and still be able to return it if they like. I'd say about 15% of the sound effects are strange like these.Overall, Iratus is a decent game, but I doubt I would ever put more than 200 hours into it.

_childDocuments_.review: Overview:In Iratus:LotD you assume the role of a necromancer up to no good. You will assemble a roster of undead, selecting from roughly a dozen or so (more with unlocks and DLC) undead creature types. From this roster, you select 4 creatures (possibly including duplicate creature types), and engage in 4v4 battle turn-based battle ala Darkest Dungeon (i.e. battle position matters). Your roster will level up, allowing the allocation of stats (with options differing by creature type) and the selection of enhanced abilities, from your core of 6 per creature. Each creature may hold two items, which may not be removed once placed. Similarly Iratus (i.e. you) may equip 5 items, though these may be swapped in and out. There is also a tech tree for Iratus, allowing the casting of spells (one per round) and the accumulation of battle passives. There is also a minor base building aspect. The game is a rouge-like taking place over 5 levels. Each level is comprised of various branching nodes (think Slay the Spire) but each level is much larger.Your individual creatures may permanently die, though exact replicates may more-or-less be created using "brains" you acquire, which basically let you create a creature from scratch and level it to the specified level (often higher than the creatures you have been leveling the entire game).Summary: For full disclosure, I played only once, on the 'cakewalk' difficulty, and it was unsurprisingly super-easy. I still found the mechanics (battles, creature creation, base building) mildly engaging for a time, but sadly grew bored with the gameplay about 60% through. Not necessarily because the game was on easy difficulty, but mostly because I just got bored with the fighting. Though I can't comment too fully since I didn't play on a proper difficulty level, the fact that you could lose a high-level monster to permadeath, and then create a better one immediately soured me somewhat. I think some of the enjoyment is to be derived from team-building, but this aspect just wasn't enough to keep me engaged. I also thought each run was much longer than it needed to be.You should be able to get this for under $10. It isn't quite like DD (nor is it as good), but if you like that kind of turn-based fighting you may give it try. Overall, I must say I was disappointed, and was hoping that I could get more playtime out of this title. But on the whole I don't regret by purchase or time invested.Overall: 6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: In this game you play the villain as a necromancer hellbent on ruling/destroying the world. You raise a team of undead minions and use them to destroy your enemies throughout various dungeons. The dungeon contains multiple paths containg various events culmunating in a boss fight which you have to route for yourself depending on your priorities not unlike slay the spire. The minions in this game have each 6 abilities (of which at least one an "ultimate" move). Depending on the position of the minion in the formation, the minion can use a subset of these abilities. You can customise these abilities as you progress throughout the game. Addtionally each minion has a specific spread of base stats and a set of which you can upgrade them with a different cost. Finally you can accessorize with items which give them an extra bonus. This make each minion unique , gives them a role(s) and even some synercy and anti-synergy. However they are not inflexible at all. How a minion plays can change drastically even during the same playthrough. Finally You can customize the necromancer as well with perks and artifacts which either gives you spells to use in combat or passive bonusses to complete your formation.The combat is very fun, the enemies are quite distinct with unique roles. They are dangerous enough that if you are not carefull can wipe out your team. That said most have them an element of counterplay to them. This means that with the right minion choice and good tactics, you can shut them down. This also applies to the bosses as well. They are more powerfull sure but they are not without weakness which you can exploit.If you however make a mistake and lose a minion it is not the end of the world; the game puts in a mechanic that allows you to recreate a minion and train it up instanously. So you don't need to grind up a supbar minion. They are not disposable though these instant level ups are not limitless and you still lose some of the rare resources (like items or special parts) you invested in the minion. the game strikes a good balance in that regard. So all in all, it is a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’ve been looking for something that does the unthinkable by taking inspiration from titles like FTL and Darkest Dungeon while offering a comparable, if not superior experience, Iratus: Lord of the Dead may be the next big hit for you. It combines large-scale party management, branching advancement paths, and a dark setting to create something that’s quite familiar, but also fresh in many ways, that stands out from the many clones that seem to have flooded the market in recent years.Iratus: Lord of the Dead has you taking on the role of the revived necromancer himself as some unfortunate miners happened to dig just a little too deep. As you grow in power and push ever upward in your struggle to reclaim the world as your own undead playground, you’ll travel through locations like the mines and the catacombs as you encounter a plethora of not-so-do-gooder foes that will attempt to subdue your growing power and influence.Though you’ll start off facing off against less impressive foes like slave miners and simple stone golems, you’ll eventually be facing off against powerful heroes that just won’t quit. Lucky for you, you have a variety of tools for the job and whether you slay them all with brute force or terrify them to the point that their heart gives out makes no difference. The enemy variety is truly impressive, and I’ll leave the rest of that for you to encounter on your own without spoilers.Although you begin with rather modest capabilities in the form of low-level minions, as you progress, they will gain experience and improve. They’ll gain stat points that can be used to improve everything from their damage output (physical and magical) to their dread (stress damage) to their evasion, durability, and health. They’ll also be able to upgrade each of their six basic starter abilities into one of two superior options.Many of these offer significantly different specialization and grant plenty of customization opportunities for tailoring your minions for specific tactics. For example, one of the minion types that you start with access to, the skeleton, has a move that allows them to take a defensive stance to reduce incoming damage. When upgraded, this move can either reduce even more damage or it can cause any that attack it to suffer a retaliation that deals a noticeable amount of stress damage. This system allows you to build each minion in a different way, sometimes even changing up their role entirely in some of the more extreme situations.The number of minions available to you is impressive considering that each can already be specialized into differing roles. You’ll only be able to create a select few at first, though the others will unlock as you reach certain milestones. New creatures aren’t recruited in the old-fashioned sense either; they’ll have to be created through the use of body parts collects from your fallen foes, such as bones, hearts, and flesh. Each minion requires four specific pats, though differing tiers of rarity for these offers attribute bonuses that make them far more powerful.This means that they with a selection of all purple, ultra-rare parts, a new level one monster will begin with as many stat points as if they’d achieved level twenty-five! Fortunately, parts can be replaced and destroyed so you are able to upgrade your long-standing minions that have survived as opposed to creating new ones entirely, though death is a part of the game so don’t grow too attached to them all the same! New parts are always coming along, and the second deaths of your servants aren’t disasters, only inconveniences that need to be corrected.Iratus joins in on the party by gaining experience as well. Though he never enters the battle directly, his levels grant many spells that can be used in battle as well as abilities that grant passive benefits whether you’re in combat or not. These abilities are divided into four skill trees that can be built upon: alchemy, magic, ire, and destruction. Alchemy focuses mostly on improving your out-of-control capabilities by increasing the number of body parts that drop as well as making their usage more potent and efficient.Magic tends to be a mixed bag of spells, some aiding you while others complicate matters for your foes. Ire offers buffs for your minions by improving their capabilities in a variety of way, assisting in them bringing the hurt to your enemies for you. Finally, destruction is what you’re probably expecting; it specializes in directly slapping around your foes with significant damage potential. All of these paths are balanced well and which trees you choose are likely to differ based on your playstyle.Combat is incredibly fulfilling in Iratus: Lord of the Dead. Every battle feels fairly unique as the combinations and synergies, even among your enemies, is impressive. I never really found myself to be bored at any point, and on several occasions I found myself losing track of time and playing for over four hours in one sitting. For those who have played Darkest Dungeon, it will feel familiar in many ways, but there are several differences that make it stand out. The most game-changing of these is the stress mechanic that attacks the minds of your foes instead of their bodies.In Darkest Dungeon, your characters suffered stress while the enemy did not. In Iratus, this is reversed as you’re the monsters this time around. Other than that, you have a wide variety of minions with plenty of abilities to synergize with and countless foes that will force you to swap up your go-to strategies to overcome them. Don’t send in a party specialized in causing fear when your enemy’s party is composed mostly of constructs, for example.Iratus: Lord of the Dead is an excellent title and one that I highly recommend to any who enjoy the rogue-lite feel of those who have come before it, especially Darkest Dungeon. I’ve been keeping my eyes open for something that could truly compete with Darkest Dungeon instead of simply copying certain aspects of it, and Iratus has exceeded my expectations in nearly every way. Although I struggle with making a strong claim on either of these games on which is the superior experience, I believe that Iratus: Lord of the Dead may be the one that has finally dethroned Darkest Dungeon and that’s no small feat to be sure; it really is a must-play title for those who enjoy the genre. I can’t praise the game enough for having an excellent variety in both wicked minions and pesky living foes that will keep you engaged and playing long after many of its competitors would have you shutting down to play something else. Give it a try and I doubt you’ll be disappointed!

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, you can compare this to DD. That is what it is, a DD clone. Only you play on the side of the bad guys. But that is too simple, too easy. This is not a write-off game. I love DD and have logged many hours on my computer, on my ps4 and even on my ipad. DD is a better game. It has that certain IT factor. That being said, I have to say... Iratus: Lord of the Dead is more fun. The vibe is a bit more tongue in cheek without being too obvious. I love sitting in the set up room of the game and having Iratus  standing there, quipping on your choices. Each of your minions (more open while you play) have a talent tree of skills and a tree of attributes you are able to customize to your style.  The characters are more whimsical and fun. You have archers, zombies with rocker launchers. banshees, ghouls, warrior undead, etc. The whole thing seems more forgiving as well. You will lose minions, but it isn't so drastic when it happens. You are able to train more minions quickly via upgrades you earn while playing. Overall, I really like this game. DD is a classic and we wouldn't have this with that, but Iratus gives DD a run for its money.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It's a good game - probably the best darkest dungeon clone I've played. However there are some issues that make it hard for me to recommend currently. For 45 bucks total w/ the dlc, it's a hard sell. But if you can grab it for 20 bucks or so then it's definitely a must get.  The DLC definitely feels required to get the most out of the game, as it adds more enemy and boss variety which the base game is sorely lacking. The true ending is locked behind the DLC as well, which really really grinds my gears. It's a bit of a pet peeve of mine when companies (indie or not) add DLC that really, really should of been a free update to the base game. Hardest difficulties are just not that fun, and this is coming from someone whose done a few blood moon runs on DD. A lot of the minions just aren't good on harder difficulties and the way they scaled the difficulty just isn't fun to go through. Certain mechanics just don't scale well on the harder difficulties. _childDocuments_.review: is a villain-centric  clone that does enough things right. Will it knock your socks off? No. Is it better than ? No. Is it challenging…diverse and interesting…replayable…make you really  about how to win? Yes. I’m 100% sure you will find things to be disappointed in, but the devs invested enough in the right areas to make it worth my time.It’s inescapable.  looks, plays, and feels exactly like a  for  If you’re tired and frustrated with reading review after review comparing this to  I’m sorry.  did it first, and did it better. I didn’t find anything……to make me say you should play  over  so I am just going to focus on how  is different.All that said, a good clone can be a breath of fresh air while keeping the gameplay, mechanics, and atmosphere that you fell in love with.  definitely does that.Things that  does well includes diverse units to build your team. I have only finished two complete runs and found good uses for most of the units. That said, unit balance feels like a bit of an issue. Some units are clear favorites…and others are like…well, would you ever really take a ghoul over a werewolf for your elite squad of undead hitmen? No, you don’t need to know anything else to answer that question.I also really enjoyed how  took the concept of sanity and turned it on its ear. Instead of another way for your dudes to die, it’s a completely different way for you to approach combat. All units have some physical and sanity-based uses, but it is pretty clear each unit will do much better in a team that focuses on one type of damage. You  be rewarded for a grab-bag of physical and sanity based attacks. Enemies only die when you deplete their health  sanity. Having separate physical and sanity-based teams will be very useful.As you move through the dungeons, you will know exactly what you are up against next. AND you can change which team goes into the next fight. Instead of being rewarded for building a balanced team that can handle the entire dungeon, you are rewarded for having multiple focused team comps. Your total team size is very limited, though. You do need to think through your builds and options when you add/remove units from your team, and you need options that are useful against the enemies in your current dungeon.One thing I did not like was the “meta” progression. More than half your units don’t unlock until after you have “driven 50 enemies insane.” While I understand that from a “learn the game in steps” perspective, it feels too limiting. You can’t even build a strong sanity damage team until after you have unlocked everyone…which more or less requires you to successfully complete a run. So, half the game isn’t even there until you complete the arbitrary meta-challenge.Voice acting is pretty good, but writing and world building is was not. It goes beyond cringeworthy. Reading unit descriptions, I can tell the writers were trying to tell a joke…but it comes off as a tired, poorly executed trope that just makes you turn off the TV.Finally, there isn’t much diversity in gameplay. Once you have completed the game, you know exactly what to expect. The challenge won’t be in “how to beat the enemy”…the challenge will be in building a new team from a different set of units to finish the game…or just do better. I read another review that discussed how they tried a team made up of 4 Specters.  An interesting idea, and turns out it worked pretty well.So, if you enjoy playing around with unit/party compositions, and trying to min/max the game,  has some decent offerings. If things outside of immediate gameplay are important, this will not likely be a game for you. Even all that said, I can’t imagine myself playing  for more than 100-200 hours before I will wake up in the middle of the night, cold sweat, screaming “why didn’t I just play more ”

_childDocuments_.review: You like Darkest Dungeon?This game's better than Darkest Dungeon. These enemies are more specialized and more unforgiving than you'd find in Darkest Dungeon, so you have to consider how to counter play the teams you will go up against. As a result, you cannot lean on the same tried-and-true party compositions in Iratus, you have to learn how to play many different styles to succeed.Make no mistake, this game isn't just a cheap Darkest Dungeon knock-off. It's aiming to be a full-blown competitor with fresh new ideas. Fresh new ideas that work.(To be fair, this game does lag behind Darkest Dungeon in art, but then again, Darkest Dungeon is a prettier game than most others out there.)

_childDocuments_.review: I have been loving this game and though it still needs work I would recommend it to people who enjoy roguelikes. That said the main reason I am writting a review is because I saw in another review that the devs read these (major kudos for that) and respond and there are a few things I would like to point out as someone who has played the game for a while now and give my two cents.Though I acknowledge the need for the lich cloud changes I think the way it was addressed was wrong, you could have a similar results by halfing the amount of stress damage done and kept the fun of the shuffling strategy which was far far more fun to use than any other strategy I have tried out so far, the strength of roguelikes is that it is single player and that can allow for insane combos and one of the two biggest distinctive features of iratus is traps (and stances) so you should have some strategies that showcase these.On the subject of strategies I have also been trying to make other comps work and the ignision comp has been specifically hard to make work. The fact there is no decent position 4 ignition minion coupled with 2 of the bosses being effectively immune to this makes it hard to make a decent ignision comp. Focusing your ignite effects on one target with brides makes the guy die to the direct damage far before the burn damage matters and spreading it with zombies makes it obvious how underwhelming stoke the flames (one of the few spells that is made to compliment this comp) is for only affecting one target rather than everyone.The scarcity of healing makes the 75 wrath healing talent mandatory to have and rush for all comps and discourages using your wrath abilities unless it either ends the battle or cost less than 25 so you're still over the 75 threshold if you had 100 at the start of the round. I understand the concept of the game is supposed to be that the minions are replaceable but with the high costs of making a good team at the moment plus the trinkets being lost you cannot win if you lose members of your A team to a couple of crits. On that front I would suggest you get back their parts after they die but them being damaged and costing a few parts of the same type to repair (saving costs on getting purple parts to remake your minions makes it less impactful if they die which was the original theme) and if you did win the fight to be able to retrieve the trinkets since you usually don't have too many of them and many have effects you just cannot use and are only there for the flat bonus. I understand that this makes it harder to get a game over but as is you hardly ever get a game over as is, you have a bunch of level 1 minions with only gray parts in buildings and sending them to die would be a waste of time so you would usually just delete the save once you're out of brains so it's more complex than what it seems.On the subject of the map I would like to be able to see the enemy comp without having to go there and sacrifice a minion so I can choose my path based on which elite I am hunting for my humanorium collection, I have done 7 runs just trying to get the elite trader, defensive pylon and elite bard and they have either never showed up or just refuse to drop their token (looking at you defensive pylon).Finally I would like to ask the devs how do I get the infected and the different minion models since I have bought the bundle with the dlc but I don't have these and I would like to ask the fans if anyone is doing an ainz ooal gown model for iratus and making the nazaric guardians as minions, I cannot be the only one who thought of that while playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: well completed tutorial and more pain difficulty  (2-4). I can say it's worth the money, and pretty well done especially for a new company. If you like games like darkest dungeon this is definitely one you will enjoy.  22 unlock-able minions with no limit to how many of each you can use. all having their own unique skills, and special passives, along with a 1 out of 2 choice to upgrade every skill. Upgrades for base stats of damage, dread, armor, accuracy, crit, dodge, ect. alot more customization to each minion available which is very nice. Items for your minions along with items for yourself, unlockable spells, and passives.        I can say i did lose a few of my minions even in the more pain difficulty. but not enough to make it really difficult, which is good for a lower difficulty. _childDocuments_.review: It's a tough question: would I recommend this game to "other players". The answer is Yes, I would recommend this game to people who are looking for a "Light Strategy" game. But no, I wouldn't recommend this to people looking for something akin to Darkest Dungeon, since I felt like this game really didn't have enough depth.  Caveat: I played through this on "More Pain!" difficulty, which is considered the "Normal" difficulty. It's entirely possible that the game is balanced better on higher difficulty. However, after a 15 hour slog through the Normal difficulty, I find myself with very little incentive to play through it again. Also, if your game is not enjoyable on the default setting, I feel like the default setting needs tweaking.Once I stopped trying to actually be strategic about the game, it became ridiculously easy - that is, once I decided to stop worrying about the Sanity mechanic at all, and just build teams around beating enemies to death, I basically was on cruise control from the second floor until the end of the game. Sure, I might lose a minion, and very rarely two, in a battle or two, but I could just throw a new brain into a new minion and keep moving, so I never really felt the loss at all. I built a team that worked and then didn't need to change members ever again. I didn't need the Arena or the Mortuary at all, and Digger's Soul's became essentially irrelevant pretty quickly.  Artifacts were mostly an afterthought, I played through a lot of the game without even realizing they were there. Crafting in Alchemy is bland and boring, and Distillation with a full graveyard means full heals between every battle.So, maybe the game is better-balanced up at third and fourth difficulty, but this one didn't give me any sort of "feeling of accomplishment" (thanks EA), even when I cruised my way up through the final boss. I will set this game down for a while, and if I come back and try the third difficulty and enjoy it more, then I'll change this review. For now, the game itself felt so bland that I don't want to jump right back in - more like a mobile game than an in-depth PC game.

_childDocuments_.review: Balance all but dies after the first dungeon. The devs have made one crucial mistake: the block and ward are too strong. It seems like the guy designing player units figured that out, you get no abilities of the sort from units within the first two dungeons. Near the end I got a lost soul unit, which is able to offer a block+ward (buffed ability) at the cost of the unit doing less damage for two turns. The guy who designed the enemies didn't know this.So what makes this ability so strong? It completely nullifies an attack. No damage, no CC, nothing. Any unit with this buff becomes a difficult battle.The elite dwarves seem to have some sort of superinitiative, they all went for a single unit on my team and killed him before I even had a chance to act. A level 7 skeleton dies without a chance.I went up against a dwarf with 2 golden axes, when he went berserk he does 80 damage+ enough to do 2/3rds of my tanks hp and enough to oneshot most units on my team.I would have killed him from his berserk state, but to my surprise he couldn't be hurt. He was in the third slot on enemy team, only reachable by 1 unit on my team, he was repeatedly buffed by a potion user who gave him a block and ward every turn and ended up mopping my team.I went back in, and to my surprise the stacking shields remained on the dwarf and to top it off, he quickly went berserk and I ended up in a similar state. I managed to win the fight with 3 units on my team dying. Technically 4 units died if you count the skeleton my wraith summoned.And that was a singular fight.I checked out what spells would be most ideal and found one that gifted me vampires from fleeing opponents.i now have about 7 vampires since I keep getting them from fleeing enemies, they're all I seem to have left now that all my units keep ending up dead.When you get close to the end of the second dungeon, there's a dwarf that can offer a 4 unit buff on both shield and ward, meaning they can block attacks from my team of 4 units. And those wards will not go away until I hit them. The developer who came up with that dwarf is crazier than the man you're playing as.This rng fest featuring wards all over the place make it impossible to enjoy the gameplay. I'll keep going in the hopes of seeing something fun, but honestly? I doubt it'll improve. I thought there were serious balance issues with darkest dungeon, but this game makes it look like easy game. At least when I attacked enemies in DD, it did damage. Here II have to plan my party out on AoE and multiattack on single target.I expect a complete and full balanced game, devs, you're not in early access anymore. I see complaints, a year old, on similar issues that have not been taken care of. There's waaaay too much RNG, unbalanced abilities on enemies and weak abilities on units. Also, it would have been nice to let players know they can unlock units and carry over that unit unlock from easy to harder difficulties in the tutorial. If you plan a difficulty based on the player unlocking units, don't tell them they can exit and play a higher difficulty, your game is not balanced around that.

_childDocuments_.review: It would be easy to write off Iratus as a Darkest Dungeon clone. In many ways it is; a hand drawn dungeon crawler using a customized party of 4 with permadeath and a haunting aesthetic.But in many ways I prefer it to Darkest Dungeon. First, it eliminates the need to grind as there are a fixed number of encounters in the game. Second, it offers multiple difficulty levels to ease people into what can be a very difficult game. Third, characters can be customized in both ability customization and stat distribution. The quirky "quirks" system is gone from Iratus. Lastly, instead of being victims of insanity, you can inflict psychic damage on your foes.The story, art direction, and voice acting are probably better in Darkest Dungeon, but these are all still good here. Most importantly, there's plenty of gameplay depth in customizing your minions, the artifacts they equip, the spells you take into battle, and global artifacts you can use. The DLC is also a great purchase.I liked Darkest Dungeon, but this is a pretty damn good clone.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: The comparisons to Darkest Dungeon are apt, but don't mistake this for a cheap imitation for even a moment.Iratus: Lord of the Dead, admittedly, lacks the same polish of Darkest Dungeon's sound, art and narrative design, and in its current state is distinctly incomplete. It's a little sparse in content right now (notably with only 3/5 Acts available at the time of this review, very little narrative outside of textboxes and few bosses), and there's the occasional spelling error or game mechanic that's not fully intuitive. It also lacks the certain 'character' of Darkest Dungeon, where you find yourself strongly invested in your best heroes that you've dedicated so much time and effort into developing - but then, you wouldn't quite expect that same investment in your undead hordes, either.However, with all of that said, the core mechanics of Iratus are ; quite probably better than Darkest Dungeon in many core facets. Each 'class' is extremely distinct, mechanically deep and with ample customisation options. The game is designed to encourage you to keep changing which creatures you field on a battle-by-battle basis, ever trying new lineups with new synergies and new interactions to try. In my experience, battles in Iratus are more strategically deep and difficult than almost any in vanilla Darkest Dungeon; but there is a certain forgiving element that you can keep trying the same battle over and over again (as long as you have the troops to throw at the problem) and the ability to have your own troops retreat is pretty generous and player-friendly.In brief; Iratus is a take on a Darkest-Dungeon like genre, only focused on providing an excellent, mechanically deep and challenging combat-centric experience at, perhaps, the expense of its main competitor's polish and charm. Personally, I find it an easy, strong recommendation for how well-crafted the core gameplay loop is, and how varied and satisfying the myriad 'class' designs are.

_childDocuments_.review: It might be early access, but this is EA done right. The devs, you cheeky bses you are so smart I will give you that. You took the two most played games of a similar genre at this time - Darkest Dungeon and Slay the Spire, and added your own twist into the mixture - playing as the bad guy. Well played, you clever people, well played.TL;DR. Am I endorsing this game? You can bet your ass that I am. I always write reviews either to tell people that they got good stuff on their hands or to stay away from it. And I can tell you, this is the good ****.So let's start. What's good about the game?1. Involvement.I ragequitted so many times in Darkest Dungeon (DD for short) when I lost a char I loved so much. Even the chance to get it back later on didn't entice me. In this case, we have undead (granted, you can involve yourself, or invest yourself in them by changing their names), but it was so much easy for me. I don't care if they die, or something happens to them, I just keep going on.In this game we get exactly what we got in Slay the Spire. Barebones, but good barebones, so much so to get invested.2. Depth.The game is as deep as the ocean. You can mix and match characters + builds + items + level ups. The options are so much it's insane. It foregoes the stale DD improvement and lets you customize as much as you like, down to the items themselves, while DD was simple % increases. Kudos to the devs, DD 2 needs to learn from them to keep us sufficienty interested and invested in it.3. Gameplay.Quick and fulfilling. The game is prettier than DD and plays as fast as DD and Slay the Spire (STS for short). There is plenty for you to do, and plenty of hours to invest to get good in this game. Even the barebones material now is decent, just as STS was when it launched.The game in and of itself is interesting and involving. It plays the way you expect, snappy. You pick your route, you stick with it and you overcome dangers with what you are given. Based on your way of playing, you can make it easier on yourself, tougher on yourself or steamroll the game if you are really good at it. As things stand, I already see lineups that can beat the game as easily as a snap of a finger.What's bad about this game then?1. As things stand in this early access build, the option menus are stale, boring and bare-bones as heck. You have as much to tweak as in a flash game.2. Lots of content needs to be added in. Meaningful campaign, challenges, sandbox mode, etc. However, I am positive that the devs are aiming high, and that this is coming.3. Tough as nails. Cakewalk??? The devs really need to add a few more difficulties, and change their names. Whoever thinks the cakewalk difficulty is a cakewalk are sorely mistaken. I had top soldiers and still LOST!!!4. The devs are hard pressed to deliver. They have the base, but they also have a challenge to overcome. I can already see builds that will totally trash the game. They have a lot of tweaking and balancing to do.Conclusion.Buy it. Just do it. even in its barebones state, I can see myself dumping multiples of hours in this game. People who have followed my reviews know that I expect a good return on my money. In this EA build, I can see myself getting at least 4 times the amount without getting bored. That, along with the pleasing graphics, the great gameplay and the horrendous challenge I am up against, is enough to merit a purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems to be based on the premise of darkest dungeon, but from the other side (i.e. the bad guy perspective). In general, I find this game more fun than darkest dungeon (and its not even fully released yet). It is hard, and people who say that losing monsters can snowball into making the game impossible to win are correct (i.e. you would have to  start over), at the same time however, there is some strategy here and as i have played, i wipe (lose monsters) far less than i initially did. The gameplay is fun, in part because you can inflict stress dmg (to eventually drive enemy insane, whereby they may dmg each other or do other crazy stuff) or damage their health bar. If the stress bar is at zero, further stress attacks have a chance to kill the enemy. Each of your minions has its own role (some are not really apparent until you get further into the game), but i have found each unit i have used to be interesting, and the upgrade path (through xp your minion levels) allow you to make choices that determine how you will play the match with that unit (i.e. a bit more health or dmg or accuracy etc, you only have a choice of 2 options for each power your minion has but it still changes things up. all in all i like the art, sound, gameplay and general feel of the game. it is enjoyable even in its early stages. Although it is fairly hard, you can choose an easy mode (i played that first to learn the game) now i am on the harder mode and it is a lot more difficult to chain wins and not lose minions. I think this game would benefit from some buffs to some of your units and or include more options for players..i.e. handicap/buff slider for when you start a game (so you can further make the game harder/easier depending on your preferences). Also i think this game could benefit from a general game mode where you can pick 4 minions for a team and get to choose which enemies you would play (it would not be part of the campaign) so you could learn new strategies against various enemies without having to start a new campaign. I think it would be fun and allow people to decide which gameplay style worked for them. Overall though this game is more fun than darkest dungeon, has great art and is enjoyable to play. if you are on the fence i would still buy it at this point, its that good!

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Darkest Dungeon, you are probably here thinking if this is similar, but in reverse.And the answer is, yes..kind of. I'll be comparing the two games, so if you haven't played DD some of the comparisons may not make sense. Sorry about that.The style of combat is a very similar 4v4 where position determines which skills are accessible (but less punishing than DD). You face heroes that you can kill either with stress or pure damage. The enemy and, more importantly, your units, variety is really (really) good. There is less RNG in combat, and both good tactics and team composition are equally important. Team composition might be even more important thatn DD as sometimes you need to deal with enemy buffs, debuffs or dangerous stances. Oh, and no need to bring your Vestal :)In short the combat is awesome, more plz.The only complaint is that it does not have you at the edge of your seat due to less RNG but also no death's door.Units are upgradable in two ways, both available after leveling up. One is improving the stats, the other is picking a special upgrade of their core abilities which may now work very differently than before.You get your units by using parts (like skulls, bone) that you get from enemies. However your units always start at lvl 1 which is a problem when your current highest level unit is 40. Thankfully, you have another limited resource called brains, which essentially levels up the unit to keep pace. Personally, I don't like this mechanic at all. If you lose a unit in combat you need to give it a brain and then spent 40+ attribute points again to spec. Redoing this is the most painful part of your units dying.Your main character also levels up, giving access to some perks and spells, but you can cast only once per round so meh. There are also "town" upgrades, which give you some higher chance of getting loot, or more exp but really nothing exciting.The game is far less grindy than DD (thankfully). Units are more easier replaced, but it's also more possible to reach a dead end due to level difference (although unlikely). HOWEVER, the game takes quite a while to beat. The levels are huge and you have multiples of them. I would have preferred much shorter levels to have more time to experiment with different team compositions.I feel that the first difficulty after the tutorial is too easy once you learn the game, and the next one is just right (with more to be unlocked). However, the issue is that some units are locked and take time to acess. You may only get to use them in a different playthrough so starting right away with the harder one would make it even more difficult.All in all, a pretty good game. It does have some DD vibes but without the exciting moments (will my hero panic or become virtuous? will he survive the next hit on death's door or die). But it's also without the grind. It's tactical and there are many ways to make your team composition. My biggest grief is that a single run takes way too long to beat.Overall, if you liked DD, you'll likely like Iratus. If you haven't played DD but like tactical games, it's still a great pick up!One last thing: The "real" ending is locked behind an expensive DLC. That alone would normally bring a review down to negative, but the story does not really matter here making the DLC just more added content. However, if you really need closure even to an essentially non-existent story, just be warned that the base game does not provide it.

_childDocuments_.review: High fantasy setting along with „hero saves the day” trope is easily one of the most prevalent archetypes of storytelling across video games as a whole. Having seen it milled 100 times over, with a varying degree of success, I always find it refreshing when a game tries to twist this formula. This particular dungeon isn’t your ordinary adventurer’s piggy bank. Here the evil is on the offensive, this unassuming set of caverns is but a staging ground for an undead invasion that will sweep over the mortal world. The player is granted the mantle of Iratus, a master necromancer and the mind behind the nascent undead horde. Create yourself a team of 4 minions and have them carve the way to the surface, one turn-based engagement at the time.To address the elephant in the room – Iratus is overall a decent game, provided you enjoy turn-based combat or have fond experience with Darkest Dungeon, you can hop straight into this title without much hesitation. , one may be tempted to ask. That really takes the long answer, for now keep in mind that Iratus involves several design choices working to its own detriment.Before we can move on to the game’s issues, it’s vital to establish what Iratus: LotD is in the first place. The in-game disclaimer fittingly describes the title as a “hardcore tactical rougelike”. Tactical aspect of the game is twofold. First being the turn-based combat with a core principle of dealing the most damage possible at the least own cost. To further this goal, the player may choose from an astounding variety of 19 minion types, each with a unique set of 6 abilities. Most minions are unlocked through fulfilling specific requirements (e.g. deal X physical damage or slay bosses), both encouraging the player to build a team composition with meeting these objectives in mind and as a way to reward game progression.Every minion also has a dedicated set of stats which can be upgraded as they gain experience. While skill tree does leave room for minor tailoring, each minion type has a single specific role to fill. Said loosely-defined classes revolve around one of 3 types of damage present in Iratus – physical, magical and stress. While the first two deliver severe case of being dead, stress damage is often able to circumvent the enemy’s defences to make them rout or get a heart attack. Take note that while morale is not a factor for your undead horde, when minion’s health hits 0 they are gone forever.Second tactical aspect is the resource management. Frankly, the amount of options available may seem overwhelming at first. Minion creation, base building, Iratus’ own skill tree, alchemy and a comprehensive tutorial to allow player to take all of that in. However, once you start the game proper, it soon becomes apparent that factual management is extremely basic and boils down mostly to order in which you will build new facilities. Time spent in Iratus’ chambers is primarily means to add diversity to combat-heavy gameplay and is at best a second fiddle to managing the minions themselves.The rougelike piece of the game is conducted in genre’s most classical take. Game is divided into 5 areas, each being a set of meandering corridors with pre-determined set of encounters. The player may use an occasional crossroads to alter the chosen path but this is about all one can do to adapt to the current state of your undead army. Hopefully this robust introduction conveys well what makes Iratus: LotD tick. Alas, it’s time to move on to less rosy aspects of the game. You might have noticed how I didn’t bring up the game’s story. This is because the game doesn’t have one, it has Stephen Weyte voicing Iratus instead. Frankly, stellar voiceacting is the only thing that gives the character of Iratus a personality, while also being the driving force behind the game’s slightly dark tone. Otherwise, the game’s lore can be summarised by “world domination”. To make matters worse, this title’s writing ranges from uninspired to miserable – skeleton’s only shtick is being bullied for how unremarkable it is, while some of the enemy lore entries are downright painful to read. On the note of overarching tone of the game, reception of Iratus: LotD artstyle is a matter of taste, however a damned soul sporting a pair of voluptuous breasts feels out of place. Sure, sexy and undead both have their appeal but in this case, game appears to actively contradict its own darker tone for the sake of .Another major issue of Iratus: LotD is the game’s seeming infatuation with Darkest Dungeon. The ever-present narrator with a profound voice, the entire stress mechanic and aspiration to be both extremely difficult and replayable title, seem a little familiar. It has to be stated that Iratus: LotD has more than enough of its own ideas to not be a copycat, which makes this heavy-handed take on inspiration all the more baffling. Especially the game’s pursuit of “hardcore”, almost encouraging a degree of association with Darkest Dungeon, which to me works foremost to undermine the game’s own ideas.This flaw is worked into the core of how Iratus handles game progression. The game clearly is intended to be replayed as the player needs to beat the game on medium difficulty to unlock higher one. Make no mistake, it is a perfectly reasonable design choice, allowing the player to properly learn the game and unlock all the minions first. Initial run of Iratus is a surprisingly forgiving experience. Save and floor restart features provide all the safety net in the world, thus you can experiment without restraint to develop a strategy that suits you most.Having beaten the game once, the player finally can move onto the “hardcore” proper. One may finally gather all the knowledge accumulated throughout the first playthrough and throw it out of the window. Difficulty spike between normal and hard is staggering. With saves gone and enemy damage upped to eleven, rather than capitalise on gathered experience, you are forced to completely revise your approach to the game. Alas, not only your minions drop like flies, easily half of the roster is no longer viable. Playing on hard becomes tedious relatively quickly, especially as you realise that after beating the game once you really have seen everything it had to offer. Is that truly the pinnacle experience Iratus was building towards? Many reviews cite the forgiving nature as the game’s defining positive quality. Further giving credence to the notion, that most players are satisfied with beating the game once and don’t ever bother delving into hard difficulty,  if we were to follow the “hardcore” angle. Perhaps Iratus would be much better off if the developers instead saved the limelight for the laid-back fun it can deliver, especially as it seems to be better suited to showcase the aspects that make the game stand out.Iratus: LotD is one of these games that really makes me wish for a mixed rating to still be available. All in all, it is a legitimately decent title – one I was able to enjoy despite its mild identity crisis. The game can be easily recommended to fans of turn-based combat, if they are not deterred by aforementioned red flags. Iratus’ greatest vice is completely overselling its high difficulty level, which mostly falls flat in comparison to the freedom of the first playthrough. Ultimately, I decided that the game’s reception could benefit from a little of a contrarian viewpoint.

_childDocuments_.review: "Iratus: Lord of the Dead is a well polished, well executed tactical combat game featuring a wide selection of minions to play with, plenty of advancement choice for both those monsters and for Iratus himself (there are many skills and spells to pick from as the game progresses) and many ways to approach each battle because of the large variety of artefacts and equipment to pick from. The character design is exemplary, with unique looking, beautifully animated heroes to fight, armed with thoughtfully crafted sets of abilities that mesh more or less well with their peers and creating challenges of varying degrees to your own minion team builds.The presentation here is top notch. The user interface, suitably gothic, looks great and everything you need is easy to find there. The voice acting from Stefan Weyte is solid and I found didn’t grate even after hours of play. I absolutely love the sound design, art and animation and I give a hearty thumbs up to the shamelessly sexy approach to the horror genre, something I find sorely lacking in the output of western studios in today’s increasingly intolerant, regressively prudish games development climate. The simple combat mechanics are underpinned with layer upon layer of attendant systems that create a varied and exciting game that demands exploration and experimentation, whilst the wonderful variety of minion builds and team combinations will keep fans of this genre happy for many many hours."Please see my full review for eXplorminate.co here:

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, it is too short for the moment. After watching some gameplay videos and researching the wiki, I rushed though the game on Cakewalk difficulty with ease. If I minus the time spent thinking about tactics, the actual gameplay time should be around 5 hours as of this moment. Considering the current roadmap, the creators should have much more in store for the future.For Darkest Dungeons players, if you are comparing this to Iratus, here are my insights:- Iratus has a forgiving difficulty dedicated to beginners: Cakewalk. Not like Darkest Dungeon which is hard regardless of difficulty.- Battles seem to be longer, critical hits occur somewhat more often.- It's less focused on RNG mechanics. Targets are guaranteed to suffer from effects like DOT and moving if they get hit.- Stress mechanic is quite interesting, it is reversed and you can inflict insanity on foes.- If you are veteran DD player and consider that you research tactics, party combos,... carefully, you should have a much easier time with Iratus.- The map is currently quite bland from my view. Instead of a large map parchment, you could replace it with a circular tank that gives Iratus an aerial view on the actual human world and use that as a map instead. The map then should have a more lively look. A paper map is a bit outdated idea in my opinion, so you should have something more mystical.- Easy-to-approach modding mechanics. A game lives long when it has a modding community that constantly makes custom modifications to give it a newer look. Since Iratus is an unfinished game for the moment, I believe this is not your top priority right now. But in the far future when Iratus has received enough attention, making the game easily moddable might be a good move.- Make it possible to fight all battles and interact with points of interest. This should prolong the gameplay and give undead armies more time to gain experience, training and more resources.- Give the option for minions to move themselves rather than relying on spells and the different effectiveness when they move (1,2 or 3 positions). - I don't know if you intend to implement more skins for minions and even humans later, but giving the game a new look isn't bad at all.

_childDocuments_.review: I daresay that I felt this is at least as good as if not a better game than Darkest Dungeon. I got it on sale, super cheap less than 5 bucks I think. It was amazing for the value. A number of negative reviews mention that buffs aren't clearly explained. It's true that the tutorial leaves out the glaring fact of the "feature" buffs when you start the game. Once you take that in it became fairly easy to figure out how to min/max accordingly. The characters scale nicely as you play, and pair well with one another. The game also seems much more fair, in that very few battles (if any) are unbeatable with the cast of characters you may bring. I beat it each progressive difficulty setting, I didn't die or fail on any of them, but the last one was definitely challenging. I used a playthrough that was stress based and physical damage based, each one had their pluses and minuses. Overall a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun twist on the "Darkest Dungeon" style game, where you play as the bad guy.  I like that your minions don't just show up out of the blue, but you have to actually construct and reanimate them from the pieces of your defeated enemies.  I also like that you have to unlock most of them through various achievements, all of which are thematic to the individual minion type.  The graphics are a nice digitally painted style, but it sometimes feels like some of the designs were left over from an Artifex Mundi game, if you know what I mean.  The music does it's job, giving a fitting atmosphere to each of the areas.  The main character's voice work was nicely done, and it sounds like they really had fun making him an over-the-top villain, both in performance and in script content.  As a side note, the "Wrath of the Necromancer" DLC feels like it's necessary for full enjoyment of the game, adding new minion types and a variety of features - like potion brewing - which I found to be fairly indispensable.  The "Supporter pack" DLC is totally optional, but I bought it anyway to support the devs.  When this game goes on sale, you can pick up the total package for around $10, and it is absolutely worth it if you like this kind of game.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I have now completed all difficulties and completed basically everything it has to offer. Its all about strategy in every fight.When I first played this I felt it was too hard. But after putting lots of time into it, and unlocking the many more advanced classes it really opened up and I was able to tailor my abilities to successful runs. I've completed easy and medium difficulties multiple times using different combat styles, team builds etc. If you need tips, Build your Iratus mostly down one path and don't deviate much with his skills each run. Build your party around that path as well. Utilize your defenses, they seriously make huge differences. And look at the enemies, some of the enemies are easier to chop down, some are easier to make weaker. If you focus on a defensive build you can do a war of attrition and eventually they'll just flee where you can either stunlock them in flee mode, or just let them run.Also - Just quit to menu if you are about to lose a battle so hard you are unhappy with how it went and restart the fight. (This strat is very useful on the very hard difficulties where, sometimes, rng will just f you over hard).

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly good game. Similar, but not too similar, to Darkest Dungeon in terms of gameplay, and because of the similarities that it seems to have at first glance, I wasn't expecting much. Ultimately, I'd say that the game manages to stand on its own merits. The base difficulty is fairly challenging, there were a few cases where my Werewolf got one-shotted by Berserkers, which was a little frustrating, but I wouldn't say that it negatively impacts the game, as it does say that you should adjust your teams based on your encounters. My only real complaint is that the Dhampir's unlock requirements are a little obnoxious, and as a result, I had to play through the game twice to get the achievement for unlocking her. I would say that this is poor design, as not everyone will want to play through the game twice to unlock every minion, and it's disappointing that not everyone would get to use her in their team, because she has a really cool design and great gameplay. On the more positive side, every minion has unique gameplay, their own place in your team composition, and great artistic design. Many of the enemies have great designs as well, and backstories/descriptions in the archive for those that are interested. Overall, I'd give this game a solid 7/10. Would be an 8/10 if it was longer, but it seems that it was designed to be played through multiple times.

_childDocuments_.review: Ahhhh, yeah, it's pretty good. It's BASICALLY Darkest Dungeon, but you control the bad guys, though it isn't one-to-one. You can cast spells that affect the fights (think Dungeon Keeper) in addition to giving orders. There's also a little more animation to it (though Darkest's art style is more.... enthralling?). There aren't as many unit types here as Darkest, but there're a lot of cool minions to bust out. I'm particularly fond of the Ghoul and Dark Knight.You have to unlock enemies, as well, which I guess is a trade-off for being able to create whomever you want (so long as you have the parts). You only have to do it the one time; I've started eight or nine new games and the minions never become re-locked, which is nice. I was actually surprised that the expansion's units were available right off the bat. Grateful, too; unlocking a few of those guys really sucked.Uhh.... Your dudes level up over time and you spend points in their stats, and pick an upgraded form of their moves every so many levels. YOU also level up over time, as well, and get access to more spells and passives. It's a pretty subdued system; your units take a much greater precedence than do any of your abilities as a necromancer.I played the Hell out of this in EA, and you could beat the three available floors there in a few hours, but the levels are much longer now. It's pretty fun, overall, but for some reason, despite how similar they are, this can't hold me like Darkest can. Don't get me wrong; I can't play DD for more than five or six hours straight, because it's so stressful, but this...? I dunno; I LIKE it, but it just can't hold my interest as long.I DID just beat it for the first time since its release (fitting; Halloween and all that), and I think I can honestly say, I will never bother beating it again. I'll almost certainly PLAY it, but I was SHOCKED at how much the final zone made the game completely un-fun. Between enemies that hit like runaway freight trains (and it didn't matter what stats I beefed or how high of a level I made my minions; even twenty levels above the area's enemies, which you can do by inserting brains into your minions, didn't matter. Didn't matter if I leveled evasion or defense or armor or block or HP, the Monk enemies would kill level-50-and-change tank units in four hits, and there was nothing I could do to stop them) and enemies that can full-restore the entire enemy party, it was a COMPLETE slog. The secret turned out to be Stress-builds, which, fine, I guess, but it was very irritating to have half of the tactics of the game just be obviated by enemies that felt fake difficult.Plus, I'm pretty sure more than once an enemy bugged out and made the fight basically unwinnable.Obviously, one time through the game doesn't make me an inside-and-outside master, but it took quite a while and gave me a lot of time to experiment with tactics, which didn't appear to make much of a difference.I dunno. This one's fine, particularly if you can get it on sale. I like its concept, and had area 5 been the last one, I'd probably be a LITTLE more breathless in my recommendation, but the endgame area really took the wind out of my sales.I don't mind difficult (I've posted bona-fides in a buncha reviews already, and I'm going to stop), but I hate it when it feels cheap.

_childDocuments_.review: It's basically Darkest Dungeon where you play as the bad guys in a type of Slay the Spire scenario. I think the game is fun, but the difficulty settings feel so out of place. This isn't the type of game that should have difficulty options. You also have to beat the game one time before you can play the hardest difficulty. They should have just gotten rid of the difficulty settings, placed us in the hardest one and let us go crazy.They also allow you to start over combat as many times as you want. I dislike that too. I am not a fan of roguelikes that allow you to reload. It sort of defeats the purpose of being a roguelike.Also a lot of the semantics are slightly off in the way the game explains some things. For example: there is a debuff that says "you take twice as much damage". But that is not exactly how it works. What is ACTUALLY happening is the incoming potency of the enemies attacks is doubled. So if you have 5 armor that blocks 5 damage and an enemy hits you with an attack with a base of 10 potency, you will take 15 damage instead of 10. The incoming potency is doubled from 10 to 20 instead of the damage you receive being doubled from 5 to 10. Fixing the first 2 things would change this review to a highly recommend from a no recommend. It is quite fun, but it requires too much of an open mind for me to recommend it to anyone. I also could never recommend a game that locks the hardest difficulty setting for your first playthrough under any circumstance. That mechanic is video game cancer.
