_childDocuments_.review: This game needs a lot more time in the Oven.There is a lot to say here, so i will try to organize this into sections:General balance:First of all, though, this game is NOT darkest dungeon and is not supposed to be similar to it or compared to.They share the same format (2D- 4 team vs 4 team) and that's about it, they have completely different mechanics in all aspects.Comparing Iratus to DD is like comparing apples to oranges (for the most part).Just a bit of background: I completed the game countless of times on "More pain!" which is the medium difficulty and one time on max difficulty ( although i had many attempts on max diffculty with other line ups).I'm going to list the features that bother me the most and prevent me from further playing this game.The overall balance in this game, and the balance patches the developers release feels like one huge roller-coaster.Minions are either nerfed or buffed to oblivion in every patch. In this game minions have 6 skills each and there are some, like Lich for example that are only used for just 1 skill, the rest are completely useless, this is a flawed design that requires overhaul.Other times there are RNG-based minions that, like Blood phantasm that can either be decent or completely worthless depends on how the dice roll, this diminish strategic thinking  and only promote frustration.You would expect that a minion will have a strong side and a weak side, but there are some got either everything or nothing.For example, Head hunter is durable physical damage dealer. However, he has extremely low base accuracy AND extremely large gap between minimum and maximum damage. this means that he is practically un-usable as a damage dealer and can only serve as a damage sponge.Speaking about RNG, the way the game makes you lose feels cheap, frustrating and leaves a bad taste in the mouth.This comes in two forms:1) RNG plays dominant role in the form of critical hits and misses2) Un-imaginative design - mostly regarding the bosses in the game.I will elaborate:Critical strikes in this game bypass any form of defense or strategy you can field, because they ignore all defenses.There are a good chunk of enemies that has very high base damage and very high crit chance (in the hardest difficulty it can go up to 60-75% chance to crit).Whats more, the game has little tools for you play with in order to stop those crits from destroying your party.Generally, the way to deal with this is through CC, namely either stuns or "turn skips", the former is very scarce (only banshee has a reliable CC) and the latter is non existent as minions skills.Even if you build around controlling your enemies with debuffs and whatever CC you can muster, you have "hit chance" to overcome.Generally that's rarely a thing that makes you lose, but in this game there is black magic that i can't explain.You have a minion with 95% hit chance misses 3 times in a row against an enemy that has 0% evasion.When that miss is a crucial stun, the result is a crit in your face.Those crits are generally out of scale, as an example, a swordsman in the FIRST level, on the first turn can double crit you for TWICE 30+ damage, if he misses he gets a damage and accuracy buff, and he is usually paired with an ally that buffs hes damage even further.You, as a logical decision, attempt to debuff him or stun him ouf this, but he also has 30% evasion to boot. you miss the stun/debuff, he plays and double crits one of your minions two times, each 42 damage , essentially a one shot.Considering how long battles take in the game, more so in hard difficulties, it can generally spiral out of control and you lose.How do you think it feels, when you thought the scenario through, you brought the right tools, had the right plan in mind and lost to random odds that overcame all sense of strategy.RNG is OK to include in a game, but it should NEVER be the dominant factor that decides if you lose or win (unless your just a bad player).Generally i'm a person with a lot of patience but even I eventually raise my hands up at some point, say "screw that BS" and go play something else.Finally, whats even worse is that said enemies, like the swordsman are abundant in the very first level of the game, there are more enemies that have double attack + high base damage an good crit chance or a combination of 2 out of the 3 (notice the pattern?): Miners, assassins, berserkers (2nd floor). But it gets worse, against certain combinations of enemies it feels like you play a lottery rather than playing a strategic "chess game".For example, remember the swordsman? well, how about 2 of them in the front and 2 support enemies in the back line.What does the support do? buff their damage of course, because that's the most creative thing you can come up with.By how much? 30%, and it STACKS. if the swordsman misses with at least one of hes DOUBLE attacks he gets another +30% buff AND accuracy buff (and remember that they also have high evasion).What does this mean? this means that if you somehow don't find a way to debuff them or stun them (assuming you brought the right tools to do that........) one of your minions have a good chance to get vaporized in a single strike, doesn't matter if you stacked armor or block on it.But there are two swordsmen, and they are ALSO protected by blocks and wards (forgot to tell you that as well), which you need to break in order to CC/damage them.There are also elite variant of said enemies, with more stats, more crit chance, more evasion...more of the good stuff.Again, the most horrible fact is that the players need to face such "challenges" at the very start of the game, where your minions are fairly low in level and you have limited tools/spells to play.That's how fun the strategic depth of this game is, and this is but one example, I could write an entire article about other scenarios like this.Bosses:This is where i will compare to DD because what it looks like is the devs took the necromancer boss from DD, copy pasted it 3 times and slapped it in all 3 levels.When done with next to no thought, adds in boss fights serve nothing but creating artificial difficulty.And generally you don't spam them, like in this game.Overall the boss fights are terrible and boring, revolving around going through minions in order to get through the boss, but some of them are worse  than the others:-First bossRNG shows its ugly face once again in this fight, since he can summon dangerous enemies, sometimes 3 at once (WTF? why can't he summon one a time?), after you bothered clearing them, and if you got unlucky, you can get some things like 2x miners (double attack + high base damage, sounds familiar?), the boss, of-course also have an AOE nuke on your entire party to make things even more interesting and a single target weak attack that he uses once in a blue moon.-2nd boss.This fight is actually fairly fair, you just need to bring the right tools for the job (buff removals) (oh, there are also adds).-3rd bossNothing special, again adds, this time they explode in your face and the boss does nothing interesting except casting generic damage spells.The bosses are just bland, they have no interesting mechanics or niches and honestly, sorry for the insult but they feel like they were design by in-experienced minds.In DD, all bosses are completely unique and sport different mechanics and skills.Finally, I'm going to finish with Position control and shuffling:This is another comparison I will make to DD because the same should share the same concept.In Iratus, nearly every enemy has good means to kill you no matter what position he is at, attempting to employ strategy through position shuffling, against the vast majority of enemies is pointless. (I ran out of room to continue this review).Anyway those are the glaring issues for me, i'm going to shelf this game for now until it will get in a proper shape.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Ignore reviews that say this game is unbalanced. Give it a shot!So I've been watching this game for a while now, and finally bought it on sale. I'd seen a lot of reviews go into detail about things that need to be fixed, or keep it from being fun long-term. So buying this was a bit of a risk. However! I love this game! I know there's a disclaimer at the beginning that says this game will be super difficult, but that entirely depends on the difficulty setting you choose. At easier levels, it is possible to play this game casually, but don't expect to not give your moves any thought. One of the things I saw people complain about the most was running out of minions, crafting goods, and other resources late into the game, and feeling like you wasted an entire playthrough. Given the complexity of the resource system - everything forces you to make a choice - I don't see how this is possible. If you consistently ignore the importance of certain resources, you will probably reach a point where you can't continue, but the game is well-balanced and does a good job of sending you clues that you need to be working on things that will keep your undead army balanced. As far as other aspects go, the aesthetic design is wonderful. The voice acting sounds perfect for the genre, and the art style embodies its slightly-irreverent tone. Enemies and minions are varied, and no one of them is exactly like another. Between the minions and enemies, there are no "mirrors" or characters that are just faction copies of each other.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a Kickstarter backer for this project so when it was first announced I thought, 'Hey cool, a Darkest Dungeon style game and you play the bad guy.  I'll take a shot.'  So the game comes out of early access and I was expecting a Darkest Dungeon Clone but a fun experience.  As I started the game it actually seemed the game had some really unique ideas as well, with monster creation and how you could get better stats with better parts and so on.  So my expectation of a better game increased.  But as I began to play I noticed  there seemed to be some big issues with how some of the enemies were balanced to the point of it seeming the devs made the enemies to not be challenging but to outright kill your party no matter how hard you try to strategically play your moves.      I will give one example,  In the third level, there is the Crossbow enemy, a ranged combatant.   Their primary position is the back two slots of their party for their primary attack.  So as a player, I would want to try to get him to the front row.  As you do this he has a secondary attack, some kind of flash bomb, that he can throw to reposition him to the back.  This is fine, except as a secondary attack it can also hit your characters pretty hard and not only can it do good damages it hits EVERYONE in your party and can also critical.  And this is his secondary attack.  As a cross reference, I will use Darkest Dungeon when you are fighting the brigand with a rifle.  You can get him to the front ranks and while he can attack in the front,  his attack is much weaker, not as accurate and if I remember correctly doesn't hit everyone or if it can it is very very weak..the whole move is to get him to the back of the line again.      This is not the only enemy like this where the secondary attacks can be almost just as devastating as the enemies primary attacks.  There is the elf swordsman if you move him out of the front ranks he has a move that hits,,,again all your team with a pretty hard attack to get him back to the front ranks.     Also there are issues with how percentages work as well and abilities of the enemies, there is a normal swordsman who has an evade of 30 but you will miss him constantly,  instead of a 1 in 3 chance to miss ,you will miss him 2 out of 3 times on a consistent basis.  I can even predict when the game is going to make me miss so it will keep an enemy alive so it can get another attack.     Enemies can also go into stances and the game allows them to remain in those stances throughout the battle and still attack without having the enemy use an action to reset the stance.  Your characters on the other hand have to reset their stance every turn and it uses an action.    To me, the game is unbalanced with how it implements the abilities of the enemies.  Especially with the enemies secondary abilities.  I have played Darkest Dungeon a TON and have even beat that game.  And while there are times Darkest Dungeon can pull a fast one on you it is overall a fun fair game.  Iratus however I feel is not and the Devs have added in all these special abilities of enemies they want to attack you with and almost break the game to showcase those abilities.  In other words..it likes to push in cheap hits.     I have went back several times to play as well just in case I felt I was missing something or doing something wrong and I wanted to be fair in what I wrote. But I feel overall that my experience with the game is pretty much on target.     I'm not sure if the devs plan on doing any updates or balancing of the game but I hope so as I would like to play the game more and it be more enjoyable but as of right now it is a pass.EDITED FOR GRAMMAR

_childDocuments_.review: Ever wanted to take on the role of the Necropolis faction from Heroes of Might and Magic games but with the combat system of Darkest Dungeon? Then look no further. We play on the side of evil here, as the necromancer Iratus, and on our path to conquer the world, we have a few scores to settle with the mortal heroes. This is a simple yet fun premise that helps to service the tactical gameplay.The combat is very similar to games like Darkest Dungeon, with our team having up to 4 minions and the enemy team also having up to 4 fighters. The positioning of the characters matters, as some abilities can only be done from certain positions and target specific positions on the enemy side.The number of possible minions we can have is really good and there's a great variety in them. They all fit the theme of undead monsters, such as skeletons, vampires, wraiths, banshees, mummies, and so on. They all have their own unique abilities and can be levelled up throughout the course of the campaign. At first we have only 6 minion types unlocked, but over the course of the game we unlock the others, and these become available forever, for any new games you'd start after this one. This is a nice way to introduce each minion so not to overwhelm the player with too much at once while also keeping our curiosity piqued each time we unlock a new minion.There is a wealth of different combat mechanics here. Aside from simply dealing damage to the enemy HP, we can also drive them insane with stress attacks, as well as lay traps at specific positions that affect any enemy that moves into the positions where they're located. There's also a blocks and wards system. These allow the character to fully resist an attack regardless of how strong it is (blocks for physical attacks, wards for magic and stress). These can be used to buff our own minions, however, the enemies will also make use of them, and the game provides many ways to get rid of these.We craft our minions out of body parts that drop from slain enemies. Each minion requires a specific combo of body parts. There is also a brain body part that can drop, which can raise any minion to a specific level, and hence this allows us to bypass grinding.The dungeons we access on a map screen and can decide which paths to take. There's no backtracking, so we can't go back to grind for items or experience. But since we can see all paths ahead, we can plan our route and decide what points of interest we'd like to interact with. In this sense, the dungeon crawling aspect differs a lot from Darkest Dungeon, because we don't do individual dungeon runs, but rather just go through one giant dungeon and recoup in our lair in between battles with enemy troops.We also have the 'Graveyard' area where we can construct buildings. These have different functions, such as healing minions in between battles or improving the amount of experience that Iratus gains, and so on. In addition to this, we can equip Iratus with various artifacts, and also level him up too and get him to learn new skills, some are passives, and others are spells to be used in battle to aid our minions. The game has 4 difficulty modes, so it can appeal to a wide range of players who enjoy tactics-based games. The game has a nice level of presentation. The environments are crafted beautifully. The minions all look impressive and have fun battle animations. Voice acting for Iratus is also nice and adds some flavour during battles. The music is a little generic and doesn't stand out too much, but it does its job well and fits the theme of the game.I've found myself really addicted to the game and have already played through it twice (on the first two difficulty modes). It has a tonne of strategic depth and a lot of potential to experiment with various team combinations of minions. The amount of enemies is quite large too, so you'd always be facing fresh challenge with interesting battle mechanics that will keep you on your toes. The game's style and combat mechanics resemble Darkest Dungeon a lot, so it often gets compared to it. For the most part, both games have some similarities and some differences, but both offer a deep tactical gameplay to last you many hours. And although there are some people who liked one but not the other, I'd say if you've enjoyed Darkest Dungeon, it's highly likely that you'd enjoy Iratus too.For a more in-depth review and a gameplay video, check here:

_childDocuments_.review: Iratus thoughts. Note that I lean more towards mixed than negative on this title. It's just alright. But after 8 hours, the more the game kinda reveals that it's a long, long burn. Which, I mean if you want a less frustrating, less challenging Darkest Dungeon, go for it. But what you're left with is a very repetitive TBS game that doesn't honest elicit any sort of reaction out of me. So, there are 5 levels to the main campaign and cross a single level at best takes a couple of hours. And until then it's just a slow campaign. I like the general theme of being this super powerful necromancer and you get a decent display of that here, but the spells are fairly boring (or bad). The minions, while varied, have zero personality in combat. So, I feel little attachment or interest in them. They mostly just become disposable corpses. While the game also tries to make you invest into them. Which is just....a really weird design choice. Honestly I think the pacing is just extremely too slow. There should have been quests or missions or just something to break it up but it just goes combat -> get X thing -> combat -> get X thing -> elite combat -> get X thing and repeat till you get to the boss. I don't mind that it has a slower pace but it needs something to break up the pace and add excitement. I may have played on too easy a mode but I'm also not excited about doing a harder version of it. Cause failing that means resetting a level alllllllllllllllllllllll the way back to the beginning and I'd rather not. Enjoyed the theme, enjoyed the narrator and the aesthetic works. But I have no compulsion to keep going.

The game isn't bad if you are looking for another game like DD, but compared to DD it doesn't hold up IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: Very strategic, Very many combos, Very many Options, Meta progressions light and doesnt superbly change the game so far. _childDocuments_.review: It's okay, like 6/10 Main problem for me its too easy Combat is fine, although I beat the game without dlc in 6-7h, I oneshotted some bosses in 1 turn , and yeah that doesn't sound like a good boss design. _childDocuments_.review: A solid little dungeon crawler rouge-like that borrows as much from the CRPGs of the 1980s as it does from more modern games like Darkest Dungeon. It's basically the premise (and some of the game play) of Wizardry 4: The Return of Werdna but with a much more forgiving game to play. That's not to say Iratus is a cakewalk, it's a decent challenge. Wizardry 4 was just very hard. It's got a pretty addictive game play loop. The dungeon is big and there's a variety of ways you can use your very VERY expendable minions to get ahead. The difficulty scales well as far as I've seen. Worth a shot if you are looking for a good time sink.

_childDocuments_.review: I will be the first to tell ya, 3 hours is probably not enough time to get into the game... But I just don't have any allure here. Had this on my wishlist for ages and decided to finally give it a try, but it has simply bored me to the point where I literally forget I have it installed. I don't think about the game when I'm not playing it - I barely think of it when I AM playing it. It simply has no mechanic in it that gives me interest. Gosh I wish it did. If I were bored, I'd play literally any other installed game first, which is probably a bad sign.

_childDocuments_.review: This is genuinely pretty good.It is, by design, sort of a simplified Darkest Dungeon where you play as the villains. Simplifying the formula doesn't add anything new and interesting to it, and it makes the game quite a lot easier (apart from a couple of wild difficulty spikes at certain bosses), but it's sort of fun to just cruise through, wrecking encounters on normal.There's a sanity mechanic, and you can use it against enemies (although you often need to build a whole team around this, and there are some enemies that are immune to sanity loss).Units are easy to create, promote, and swap into and out of your team.Upgrades are easy to come by, and mostly involve waiting to unlock the right type of unit to use as their foundation material.Units have a decent variety of directions you can build them in, and don't cost much to improve.Basically, if you bounced off Darkest Dungeon because of the difficulty, or you want something that's a bit more generic fantasy (although with some decent gothic notes), this should mostly hit the mark. It doesn't have a lot of plot, but the writing is decent and the voice actor for Iratus deserves a medal.This is a solid purchase on sale for most rpg fans---although Iratus is pretty blandly evil, and if you don't enjoy that, playing as him may put you off a bit.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: If you played Darkest Dungeon, liked the basic formula, but concluded that it would be better without all the edgy artificial difficulty, then you'll probably like Iratus. Also, it turns out that driving your enemies insane is a lot more enjoyable than your characters being driven insane. No surprise there. Fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: Great first impression for this. I liked DD a lot, and this is scratching that itch while waiting for a sequel. This is also the first game I've picked up in quite a while that I am actually finding enjoyable (have hit lots of duds lately).It has a sleek look to it and offers a large set of minions to choose from. I like how you can find instant upgrades along the way to get newly acquired minions up to a usable level.Only complaint so far is there is a overly limited way to explore the dungeon. Once you select a path on a fork, you cannot backtrack or even take that path when it comes up deeper in the dungeon. It would be nice if the game provided some sort of mechanic like food from DD that at least gives you the chance to further explore areas.Overall, definitely a recommend if you enjoy turn-base strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: Watched a couple of gameplays and got immediately hooked. the graphics are amazing, the tactics and different strategies are interesting, and the game while warning you that your minions may die, helps you get back on your feet and doesn't punishes you for all eternity. after my first playthrough I went straight to the second one. this is the first game of the genre that I decided to buy, and now other games are dimmed in comparison. highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: The hardest difficulty of the game is simply not balanced. Generally the hardest difficulty of any game is the "endgame" it's where you go after you've mastered the game, built the "ultimate" squad, and are ready for a challenge. Sadly, the hardest difficulty in this game can't be beaten by skill, it's entirely RNG based and it's very likely you will lose, because some of the enemies attacks are higher than you can even get most of your minions HP, IE 1-shot. On the easiest of difficulties you can basically not know what you are doing at all and just breeze through. On the middle-tier difficulties you might have to have some knowledge and have a decent squad but it's still pretty easy. So, that's the kind of game this is. Once you figure everything out the game is ridiculously easy or it just 1-shots you. However, I suppose figuring that out is fun for a masochist.

_childDocuments_.review: Want a Darkest Dungeon lite but think Vambrace: Cold Soul doesn't live up to the promise?  This is it.The selling points that got my attention:- A stress/HP mechanic with affliction/virtue/heart attack on the -enemies-, yes, this time you get to scare them to death!- A decent size of starting roster - 16 classes, 1 extra via paid DLC- An 'unseen' main character with talent trees that can be built to directly affect battles by casting spells, or indirectly buffing your team of minions via passive bonus and effects.  Can equip items for more spells/passives.- Minor town building, think of it like DD town building, but less significance.  Minions get skills via level up, "gears" via drops and crafting, for example.- Speaking of which, each minion is "crafted" by combining 4 pieces of material, each can be upgraded to have better stats and equipped.  With 2 equipment slots, each minion virtually has 6 "slots" for passive buffs.- Easy to mod (for now), if you can read/modify json files (opened in free copy of visual studio or something), you can mod the current classes to a fair extent. - The same type of replayability DD may have, and likely improved if/when class mods are made available.- For an early access product, the core mechanics are in place and no game ending bugs (as far as I can see from forum posts).  Unavailable "areas" notwithstanding, you can play the current three areas from start to finish.- Concerns of balance is kinda moot when you can easily edit the json files and change minion/enemy stats to your liking.  I haven't even looked into changing level up perks beyond stats yet, but that seems feasible.All in all, worth every cent if you want something similar to DD but with enough different mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Iratus: Lord of the Dead

_childDocuments_.review: Played a few hours in early access but didnt find it fun enough to endure the horrible artstyle. Played through it once now after release, and it's a lot better. Anyone looking for another Darkest Dungeon, this really isn't it. The only similarity is in the fights, where it feels very familiar but with slightly less RNG. I'd say the combat is more interesting but the atmosphere, where Darkest Dungeon really shined for me, it isn't similar in the slightest. Neither is any of the elements outside of fighting. Instead of dungeon crawling with limited resources, you're constructing minions, equipping artifacts, managing which minions heal and which train and rebuilding your city between every fight. Which means that the focus of the game is solely on fighting, but if you like it that's not necessarily a bad thing.Bullet list:Pros: - Game focuses on combat, and the combat is fun - Decent amount of characters, most of which are useful and none of which are broken, save for perhaps the Shade - but it does nothing on its own and needs to be built around - Good enemy variety, even if they follow certain archetypes - Has that "just one more fight"-appealCons: - The artstyle in general, for me. This is subjective, but I found Iratus' commentary to be trite. Feels like a poorly made homage to the Darkest Dungeon announcer.  Other than that, every female character being scantily clad, Iratus... Feels like it was designed by, or maybe for, an edgy, very horny teenager with some kind of dead people/monster fetisch.  - The animations in battle are super tacky. Nothing about it sells me on the characters being involved in a life-and-death struggle. Especially the "got hit" animations are horrendous,  - UI in general is a bit of a chore even looking past the awful artstyle. Most things require several clicks even if it's intuitive most of the time. - Story is lacking. Really.  - Lacklustre resource management. Maybe it's better on higher difficulty levels (I played on "more pain" which was the highest I could play on), but never really felt myself lacking anything. Could always play whatever composition I wanted, and if I lost a minion I could just create a new one and keep going. On the other hand, if it turns out to be super hard at higher difficulties, running out of resources would really screw you as you have no way to level things up without winning battles if you don't have any brains.  - On "more pain", I never lost a fight despite experimenting a lot. Barely lost a minion until the final floor, which was a huge difficulty spike. One run takes a long time so I had to invest several hours in something that was barely a challenge before being able to try it out on a higher difficulty. All in all the fighting and the many combinations to try out is interesting enough for me to recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Darkest Dungeon, but you're the bad guy.  Roleplaying a necromancer at its best.  Hard af tbs, but the learning curve is acceptable. name: REVEIL
detailed_description: More Horror from Pixelsplit Funhouse Edition In addition to REVEIL, the Funhouse Edition contains the following DLCs: REVEIL Original Soundtrack: 14 original compositions, beautiful and haunting. Digital Artbook: A look behind the scenes of the game, featuring concept art and inspirations. Black and White Camera Filter: Use this in game for vintage horror atmosphere. Audio Plays: A selection of audio plays recorded with the game's voice actors, more bits and pieces from the world of REVEIL. Developer Commentary: Commentary by the developers to be found in-game, for even more background insights. About the Game A unique, visually appealing, mentally challenging story. Versatile puzzles, unanswered questions, confusing clues and a disturbing psyche demand a lot from both the player and the protagonist, Walter Thompson. Can you manage to make sense of it all? Should you persevere, there is a chance to find answers to your questions. You wake up. You're disoriented. Your head hurts. Things seem surreal, yet familiar. Your wife Martha and your daughter Dorie are not there. Why? Looking for answers, you explore your environment and fragments of memories. On your journey you are repeatedly confronted with riddling tasks, driven by the desire to find out what's going on. What happened last night? Why can't you think of any other thing aside from your days as a stage builder at the circus? As things get crazier and more bizarre, the lines between reality, memory, and imagination become more and more blurred and you realize: there is no going back. You have to do whatever it takes to bring this story to an end, no matter at what cost... 'The feeling of safety is an elusive one. It's not over yet.' In REVEIL, the player is immersed into a world, designed with attention to detail, where the boundaries between reality and illusion become blurred. The setting is an authentically orchestrated environment inspired by the circus of the 60s, which soon takes on surreal features. Get a glimpse into the psyche and the past of Walter Thompson: The impressions become darker, more mysterious, more enigmatic the further you advance. Once caught in the maelstrom of deceptive impressions, memory fragments and mysterious visions, your only option is to dive deeper - in the hope of finding answers to your perplexing situation and condition, even if this hope is slowly fading. The only thing that keeps you from giving up is the will to find Martha and Dorie. Do not shut your eyes to the hints left by the two, but keep them wide open and ... try to not lose your mind. A deeply psychological experience that will keep you questioning everything. Five playable acts in different, carefully designed environments. First-person narrative experience including: Various puzzles and riddles Beautiful and immersive visual experience #madewithunity Multi-layered narrative with psychedelic, biographical and disturbing elements Atmospheric paintings, posters, writings referring to the circus era of the 60s.

short_description: REVEIL is a narrative first-person psycho-thriller game that focuses on story, puzzles and exploration. Find out what’s going on inside Walter Thompson and what his dark past at the Nelson Bros Circus has to do with it.

_childDocuments_.review: This was great in the first couple of hours, then it turned into avoid the monster/entity and retrieve object horror game play which I shouldn't have to be doing in a walking simulator. I was looking more for a story driven and interaction/solving puzzles but not so much getting caught by monsters and having to start things over without any explanation why this is happening. Not the kind of game I thought it would be. I thought this would be more Layers of Fear type of horror, but I guess I was wrong. I think they threw this in just so people would not complain that there's no game play.
_childDocuments_.name: REVEIL

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. Falls short of being great (for me) for these reasons:- Poor final puzzles. After some of the earlier ones, doing the modules at the finale felt like a chore. They weren't difficult or interesting, and didn't match the quality of puzzles found throughout the rest of the game. - Mandatory stealth sections. They don't add much, don't fit with the flow of the game, and the crouching speed is honestly much too slow. - Some unclear plot points. - Ends with no real resolution. The mysteries are wrapped up nicely enough, but it seriously just sort of ends without any flair. You solve a few lacklustre puzzles, open a door and the credits roll. It felt quite rushed and unimaginative.All in all, a strong game with some rough edges. It's not scary, but the set pieces, imagery and storytelling were all very good, as were the vast majority of puzzles. I would love more like this.
_childDocuments_.name: REVEIL

_childDocuments_.review: Visually gorgeous, excellent sound design and a story (with multiple endings) that will keep you on the edge guessing until the very end.I was fortunate enough to be given a pre-release key to review this game so thank you very much to the developers for this. The game is a very good entry into this genre. The story escalates with each chapter building towards the final chapter climax. In my opinion, often these kind of narrative games don't know how to make the ending tie the story together leaving me feel confused and underwhelmed. However, in the case of Reveil I think the developers did an excellent job.The puzzles were quite lightweight, nothing too challenging but enough to keep me engaged. The horror is more focused on atmosphere and pacing, not cheap jump-scares! This is a major positive for the game personally but if you are looking for a jump-scare per minute then this isn't the game you're looking for.  Overall, I would recommend this. Give it a go if you like narrative driven horror games with puzzle elements. I bet you won't be able to guess what is really happening before you reach the end...
_childDocuments_.name: REVEIL

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very lucky to have played REVEIL already and I can absolutely recommend this game.I don't want to spoil the story but I can say the following:The story is gripping from the start and its narrative simply forces you to keep playing! :D I couldn't bear not knowing what is going on. The feeling of "Just one more chapter" is omnispresent!The narrative is cleverly set up and all its twists and turns fit in well into Walter's story. There is SO MUCH to unearth. The logo of the game includes the Penrose triangle and we can find it in many places of this world. The premise of the Penrose triangle is: it is an impossible figure that cannot exist in a three-dimensional world... thus it is but an illusion. Whilst exploring the story, one realizes quickly that things are not what they appear to be - they are illusionary. Walter is an unreliable narrator from the get-go and WE have to find out what really happened in the Nelson Bros Circus. The game is very much story-driven yet contains a handful of well-placed puzzles. The difficulty is balanced in so far as riddles can be challenging, yet they do not frustrate. Visually the game is pleasing. I am a huge fan of the lighting and the uncanny feeling that the player is surrounded by. This uncanny feeling is also supported by a great soundtrack. "The circus" is a theme that was used in horror games, films and literature before, and in REVEIL this set-up also does not disappoint. If I had to describe the setting in two words, I would say "playfully gruesome". I mean this in the most positive sense, I felt truly immersed in this world.Is the game scary? Hell yea. I've had many eerie, jumpscare moments that are again well-placed. You can tell that the devs have a very good understanding of placing them at the right time and have been inspired by games such as Layers of Fear. I was scared, yet I didn't feel the frustration of getting jumped at all the time. The balance was again just right!A lot of times the fear was entirely in my own mind - and that felt eeriely good. The game manages to confuse the players and thus make them feel just as overwhelmed as Walter is feeling.If you like psychological horror games, REVEIL is a great one for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting classic puzzle game with a fresh modern coat that could have been a lot more immersive had the intentional flaws been fixed. * The puzzles within the game are very nostalgic as they are akin to the puzzles that games have had for the last 20 years. Very classic escape room style puzzles. * Immersion is broken because the game keeps taking control of your camera and forces the narrators speech into to your ears every few minutes. * Game is a little short and does in fact feel very indie and for that I would say its consumer price should be $9.99 rather than what it is currently for sale for. Similar to: Layers of Fear mixed in with a vintage 2005 puzzle solver game. Verdict: Give it a go but maybe when the price has dropped a little.

_childDocuments_.review: Reveil is a first-person psychological horror game that mostly takes place inside the mind of protagonist Walter. He suddenly awakes after having a nightmare only to find that both his wife Martha and his daughter have disappeared. Unable to remember what happened, he needs to discover the mystery behind his family’s disappearance. Soon enough, Walter starts questioning his reality and the environments take the shape of his imagination, bringing him into a dark circus filled with unsettling attractions and hostile monstrosities. As you can imagine, this is the classic formula for horror narrative-driven waking sims. For the record, I enjoyed  - although I don’t include it amongst the best horror gaming experiences I’ve had - but I have grown tired of horror games that use the same narrative clichés (amnesia, surrealism, hallucinations, trivial psychology). It was cool when  was the only one doing it, but now it’s getting way too abused in my opinion. That said, if you loved LoF you will likely enjoy this one too, but probably less so.The game is divided into five acts and really doesn’t take long to complete. It took me about 5 hours, including reading notes and looking in every corner for collectibles (there are quite a lot).  But someone who just wants to follow the story might complete it in four hours or less. I can’t talk about the story too much because this is the entire game, but what I can say for sure is that the protagonist talks too much and doesn’t allow you to interpret the story in your own way or to just feel the environment. The voice acting isn’t good either; it felt like the actor knew the lines but not the context of where the action happens (either that or he didn’t care too much). The house sections were great and immediately reminded me of  and . The other (mostly surreal) environments were more linear and less interesting. There are twists here and there throughout the story, but none that really shocked me. The multiple endings depend only on a choice that you can make at the end, so there isn’t any replayability. The one I got was short and felt like a rushed epilogue, and the others that I saw online were no more satisfying than mine. I don’t understand the idea of making multiple short endings rather than one solid ending (especially considering that the game is extremely linear). Why give a choice at the end when there were none throughout the entire game?Being a story-driven game, all you have to do is explore each new location you are thrown into and solve puzzles while trying not to be seen by hostile monstrosities. Some puzzles are a bit more creative, but most of them require that you find a key item and bring it to another place in order to progress (that’s not really difficult even when playing hide-and-seek with the monster). In-between the story you do get some cheap jumpscares and parts where you are being chased by a monster. Again, typical scenarios for a horror game that no longer provide any tension or surprise to someone who eats horror games for breakfast.Now the graphics are really beautiful at max settings. Each location is created in great detail and provides some very good atmospheric moments, also thanks to the great lighting in both external and internal locations. The game performance is also good, only few frame drops here and there, but this is not the kind of game where you need 60 fps or more all the time. I think that Reveil is a game that maybe takes too much from other games from the same genre (particularly ) while not adding anything new or different to the gameplay and narrative structure. Not only is the game short (especially considering the price) and without any replay value, but it lacks tension and except for a few atmospheric moments, doesn’t engage you in the protagonist’s story. It might be worth trying if only for the beautiful graphics and locations (especially if you like the circus), but it certainly won’t be a memorable horror experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I will keep it spoiler free up here, a bit later there will be some spoilers when it comes to the story, but I will leave a new warning before that.-Headphones strongly recommended when playing-First up: How scary is it?If you are sensitive to circus stuff, than it's either gonna be not for you, or incredibly scary.If not, then I would say somewhere between beginner and early intermediate.It has some jump scares, but they are pretty mild in my opinion and tasteful, so your ears are not gonna bleed!The atmosphere and sound design do most of the heavy lifting.+ Pros• Visual art style is fantastic. Especially when the film grain is turned off the atmosphere gets really immersive.• Textures look believable, are not too repetitive and high quality.• The lighting is super smooth and looks amazing. Fantastic work!• Level design is heavily inspired by a few older titles (I think) at times, but I think this is a pro. Well executed and it looks great!• Sound design is fantastic. Music, sound effects (the sound effects are incredibly good btw) and spoken lines are super well mixed, super high quality and elevates the atmosphere up by a TON. I can't get over the sound, it's really really good!• Voice actors do (mostly) a good job. The grunting can sound pretty funny, but otherwise the lines are well spoken.• Story keeps you engaged to keep playing.• Runs very smooth on my weird system. 4080 but the bottleneck (ryzen 7 3700x) doesn't hurt the performance here. Runs well!• FOV SLIDER. As a person who gets motion sick or headaches when the FOV is too low, I greatly appreciate this!- cons• Puzzle difficulty varies a lot between very easy and intermediate. No puzzle is really hard here and there's no option for a separate high puzzle difficulty or similar.• The camera often locks to "interesting things". Only a minor thing, but it feels like taking away control. I hear that stuff is happening, If I would be able to rotate the camera myself it would be way more immersive.• The protagonist talks too much. If you're fast it even overlaps or the voice lines come way too late.• Not really a spoiler, but man the protagonist is not the brightest, let's put it that way.• Some models can have a bit lower quality then the rest, makes it look a bit off. I especially mean the merry-go-round horses, they do look a bit.... edgy? It doesn't have a lot of polygons.• (already got addressed) The tooltips (press c to crouch and stuff) come all the time at certain scenes and there's no way to turn them off....yet. Devs already said on discord that it gets added to the list. Appreciate it!I will type some stuff about the story all the way below, so for anyone who does not wanna get spoiled I do put my final words here already:I highly recommend playing this game if you're looking for a good entry into the horror genre, or if you wanna solve some puzzles in a dark atmosphere and have a story with it.The price quite low. You can about 4–6 hours of playtime, depending on how fast you are.I strongly recommend it. It is really fun to play through, easy to get into and easy to get lost in.Fantastic work Pixelsplit, not only are you fantastic people to chat with, but also devs that seem to keep a good balance between feedback + your own vision.I'm proud to have the fun house edition in my library, as well as the supporter edition of Indoorlands from you. You deserve the support and I hope this game is getting known more.---THIS IS MILD SPOILER TERRITORY---The story:It got advertised to me as a "mindfu**" which is probably accurate for most people. If you're an "old timer" who has a lot of experience, you can piece some things together. The ending is not what I expected, but honestly probably due to the wrong reasons. I was thinking way outside the box here and got misled, the story is way more logical than I hoped. The extra notes in game are not that necessary to get the full pictureThis is only me speaking though. It does present itself as a perfect story for horror beginners though. I liked the story, but it's not reinventing the wheel or adds anything truly unique into it. Still, I really enjoyed it. It was money well spent, and I recommend to pretty much every one of you to pick it up. Great product for a good price!

_childDocuments_.review: As far as short, sweet indie-horror titles go, this is honestly one of the best I've played in years. There's so much to love about what Pixelsplit have created here, it's almost impossible to know where to start.The attention to detail is the first thing which struck me. Everything has been so lovingly crafted, from the puzzles right down to feel and flow of the environments. The use of lighting and color is particularly stunning, and if you have a HDR display, you're in for an absolute treat. The sound design deserves equal praise - from the ambient elements to the soundtrack itself, the immersion was pretty much flawless. And there's some genuine creativity in the mix once you start to understand the broader context of the game world.I did initially have some misgivings about the voice acting. Not because of it's quality, but rather the tonality in the context of the protagonist's experiences. Without spoiling anything, this too has it's place - and the latter parts of the game took some turns I genuinely wasn't expecting.On the performance side of things, I ran this at 4K / max settings on a 3080 Ti and only experienced the occasional hitch when entering a new area. Reveil does have some very brief loading screens between chapters, so while the odd stutter was disappointing, they were so infrequent that it's almost not worth mentioning.In short, the love for what this small team has crafted here just oozes out of every corner of the game. If you're looking for a palette cleanser or just feel like a bite-sized trip down a psychedelic horror rabbit hole, I honestly can't recommend this enough. I really hope this finds the audience it deserves.

I know jump scares are often a main attraction in horror games, but I’m personally not a fan of them so I’m glad they didn’t go overboard with them here. Although there were just enough to make me instinctively curse out loud on occasion, something I’m usually not known to do! I certainly don’t regret getting a ticket to this crazy circus adventure. It may not be the greatest show on earth with only a four-hour funhouse ride, but it makes for a captivating exploration through its protagonist’s twisted dreams and tortured memories.

_childDocuments_.review: I can see the SOMA influences all over this game. It's worth picking up for sure but there are some points where it could have done a lot better:Even the more challenging ones () could't puzzle my brain enough as it was quickly (made) obvious what i should be doing (protagonist's commentary also serves as passive hint system). This game feels more like it belongs to the so called "walking sim" genre rather the "adventure" genre which is alright, but be ready for that.  Subjectively speaking it's not really scary, only sports jumpscares in one bit, thank god, with the excpection of a couple of truly scary sequences (). Unfortunately, it always become predictable to me what transpired in the backstory before each reveal, i frequently found answering my questions with certainty before important plot turns. That has a negative effect to the  "phychological horror" as it doens't allow the story to feel more affective.In the contrary, when it comes to graphics and sound desing, i do believe they are responsible for carrying more of the horror moments.The underlying idea is just great! But certain parts feel weird:a. b.  c. d. ...which duh, it's the nature of the genre, but it is felt way too much most of the times feeling i have to walk from A to B, very little exploration or illusion of openess even, just a narrow walkway forward is how this game felt to me. Compare it to how SOMA or The Vanishing of Ethan Carter or other similar games structured their adventure lines.The 1st stealth sequence felt off mechanicly they just don't add up but also  The 2nd stealth sequence was plain bad. In conclusion this game would have benefited from more solid puzzles, a much better ending and more attention to story. This should also help to bring the overall duration up a bit, 5 hours is on the short side for me and i spent most of it looking at the graphics and taking screenshots.This is not a "poetic licence" kind of game by any means, it's a game about 'wow' story moments and I didn't quite get that. This company is on the right track with this one, especially on the art direction department, im sure if they improve upon this formula the next game is going to be a banger.

_childDocuments_.review: The story on this one finally won me over, but only as I was nearing the finish line. Reveil is a great looking game but it's also one you've likely played before.  As a walking sim goes it "plays the hits" but its kind of a bummer to hear that every hit it plays is just a pale cover of the original.  It's a creepy walking sim with an unreliable reality a la "Layers of Fear." It's a reminiscing story like a dozen games I could name. It has a couple of additional gameplay elements. Logic puzzles being one (pretty decent!) and the other is creeping around without being caught by the scary thing while you hunt for 3 props (my least favorite!). That's it really. It hadn't offered me anything new and just felt like another drop in the bucket walking sim that I spent most of my gameplay planning to ultimately not recommend it.  But then it subverted my expectations in the end. I'll leave it at that as not to spoil things. It's still a mostly rehashing of leftovers but it really did surprise me and left a pleasant taste in my mouth and I kinda of love it now so if you venture in, but sure to stick with it.

_childDocuments_.review: "Reveil," is a first-person psychological thriller that immerses players in a surreal circus environment. The game follows Walter Thompson as he searches for his missing wife and daughter, unraveling a narrative filled with psychological horror elements.Pros:- Engaging Narrative: "Reveil" presents a compelling story that delves into themes of memory and reality, keeping players invested throughout the experience. - Atmospheric Design: The game's visuals and sound design effectively create a haunting circus atmosphere, enhancing the psychological horror elements. - Challenging Puzzles: Players encounter a variety of puzzles that are well-integrated into the narrative, offering a satisfying challenge without disrupting the story's flow. Cons:- Limited Scare Factor: Some players may find that the game leans more towards a psychological thriller than outright horror, potentially lacking in traditional scare elements. - Voice Acting Inconsistencies: The protagonist's voice acting has been noted as occasionally lacking emotional depth, which can detract from the immersive experience. - Short Playtime: With a runtime of approximately five hours, some players might feel the experience is brief, especially given the game's engaging narrative. In conclusion, "Reveil" offers a captivating psychological thriller experience with its engaging narrative and atmospheric design. While it may not deliver traditional horror scares and has a relatively short playtime, it stands out as a noteworthy addition to the genre.Score: 9 out of 10 circus tents—A thrilling ride through a mind-bending big top.

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Beautiful 3d visuals with detailed models, atmospheric lighting conditions and cool optical effects like volume lights and flares.- Decent horror atmosphere with some immersive moments, yet without managing to be really scary.- Well designed world with various places to visit and some surreal sceneries although most of them are based to cliché horror scenes you've seen before.- Despite the overall shallow gameplay it offers two or three interesting puzzles that have some creativity and need a little bit of thought.- Good audio design. It's pretty simple but offers some convincing environmental sounds and many creepy others.- There is a certain point with a twist that saves the story. Although it's a little bit rushed with mediocre build up it manages to give new interest to the game. Some pieces are coming together and the story parts ways from worn horror elements.The bad- Maybe it's intentional, but during its first two thirds the game is pretty boring based on cliché horror concepts like small girls, bloody walls, objects that are moving by themselves and more. Most of its mechanisms are worn too. Deformed places, labyrinths, rooms that change shape behind you after reaching a dead end. We've seen all these several times before.-  The first two thirds of the story is a combination of random events and cryptic symbols without particular coherence, like it just tries to impress the player. Storytelling is also poor with memories and voices at certain points revealing parts of the plot. The final third is more interesting but it needed some better build up.- Gameplay is shallow. You mostly move into a linear path watching horror tricks and a few silly jump scares.- Voice acting performances are not convincing and fail to catch the vibes or the emotions of each moment.

_childDocuments_.review: as a horror game fan. REVEIL, I can confidently say it's a game that truly immerses you in a psychological rollercoaster. The game's features are outstanding:REVEIL offers an unforgettable gaming experience that will leave horror enthusiasts craving for more.From the moment you awaken in a disorienting haze, the game plunges you into the shoes of Walter Thompson, a man plagued by fragmented memories and a desperate search for his missing wife and daughter. As you navigate through a world where the boundaries between reality and illusion blur, REVEIL presents a series of cryptic puzzles and unsettling clues that test both your intellect and your sanity.The game's narrative unfolds in five distinct acts, each set in meticulously designed environments that draw inspiration from the circus era of the 1960s. From the faded grandeur of circus tents to the eerie corridors of Walter's mind, every location is rendered with stunning detail and immersive atmosphere, pulling players deeper into the unraveling mystery.What truly sets REVEIL apart is its multi-layered narrative, which seamlessly weaves together elements of psychedelia, biography, and horror to create a story that is as compelling as it is disturbing. As you delve deeper into Walter's psyche, you'll uncover dark secrets and hidden truths that challenge your perceptions of reality, leaving you questioning everything you thought you knew.But perhaps the most impressive aspect of REVEIL is its ability to keep players on the edge of their seats from start to finish. With its cleverly crafted puzzles, visually stunning environments, and spine-tingling atmosphere, the game offers a truly immersive horror experience that is guaranteed to keep you hooked until the very end.In conclusion, REVEIL is a masterpiece of psychological horror that deserves a place in the library of any horror game fan. With its compelling narrative, immersive atmosphere, and challenging game-play, it offers an experience that is as thrilling as it is thought-provoking. If you're looking for a game that will keep you guessing until the very end, look no further than REVEIL. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Full gameplay: Like some of the other users mentioned, this game is very similar to Layers Of Fear game, if you like those type of psychological narrative games without many horror elements I think you might like this game. Game has good visuals with an interesting story, but unfortunately the gameplay is not engaging even with few good puzzles. You basically just walk from point A to B to progress like many other horror games, although I am not sure if this game considered as horror game or not because there weren't many scary elements in this game. I was able to finish the game after about 3 hours and I think for $20 asking price this amount of gameplay is little short, however there are multiple endings and some replayability. So if you are OK with this price and game style I'd recommend it. Otherwise wait for discount. I liked overall visuals and art style, these type of games like Layers Of Fear have a good and creative way of presenting their story, there are lots of unique visual elements and presentation in the game that I liked. Overall graphics are good but it didn't wow me. One of the negative points for me was lack of body for character, in these games I think having animation for character body adds a lot to immersion. The gameplay as I said is very basic, walking from A to B, solve some puzzles in between, read documents and interact with objects to understand what the story is and progress. You've seen these type of gameplays in most of horror games so don't expect something new. Some of the puzzles I think were fun to solve and I liked them but some were unusually simple. There are some chapters in the game that you need to hide from enemies to survive, the positive side of their design is that if you fail and die you'll get back to a very close point without losing a lot of progress, it feels like it was part of the story and you don't have to start from beginning of checkpoint. Overall game speed felt little slow even with running option, I wish the running was little faster but it's not game breaking. I think story is best part of this game, although it started very slow and felt very boring in the beginning, after 30-45 minutes of my gameplay it got a little more interesting, you start to feel something is not right and become more curious about what has happened to the antagonist. Some of the areas of the game like the bedroom felt repetitive, from story stand point it made total sense to visit it multiple times but from gameplay standpoint it was a little on boring side. There were some other areas that you visit for multiple times and I wish there were more variety to the environment that you visit in game. I think story was good and interesting, however there were some questions that I didn't get the answers for but there are multiple endings while some of them were very underwhelming. Overall I enjoyed the sound effects and specially some of music track were really good. I played on max quality with DLSS on quality mode and was getting more than 200fps. There were some hiccups when entering new areas and also alot of ghosting probably because of DLSS, but overall the performance was really good and game run very smoothly and didn't encounter any bugs during my gameplay. I also have to thank devs for including this save system, although it's not manual save but for this game I think it's good enough, you have list of chapters and within each chapter you can select the checkpoint to start.There are some replayability in this game, as I said there are multiple endings and also there are some collectible in each chapter if you are interested in these stuff.CPU: Intel Core i9-12900KMB: MSI Z690 Edge WiFi DDR4RAM: GSkill 32Gb DDR4 3600MhzGPU: Asus GeForce RTX 3090 StrixMonitor: Samsung Odyssey G7 32" 1440P 240Hz

_childDocuments_.review: Look, if you want to help a small, pretty much one-man-band indie developer, buy the game.  I understand as a dev there's a point where you ask yourself, "Well... do I polish this, and work on detail for the next two years, or just release it at a bargain rate and get noticed by a big time developer with a small game like this in my portfolio?"  He's not wrong, by the way - but the game is far from finished.  It is also far from entertaining.  Here me out:Early into Chapter 1 I fell through the floor at one point in a hallway, and didn't die.  After no clipping, and the screen going black but still having the reticle, I found I was able to run/walk, so I thought it was part of the game, (since you have multiple and sudden psychedelic moments).  Nope.  Just didn't hit a death barrier, and was essentially under the map with no reference in any direction I ran and heard my footsteps.  Time to restart and avoid that spot on the floor while running down the hallway.  There's several more instances not unlike this, where I thought, "Why in God's name am I still bothering to play this?"  Then I would have to restart again, and avoid that spot, or attempt to open the object again hoping it didn't glitch.  It might be petty, but another notable nuisance is movement in general.  The only time you *actually* run in the game, is a forest scene with a Baba Yaga of sorts, otherwise "running" is a derpy, awkward, shuffle forward.  There IS no "running."  The majority of the game you walk VERY slowly, (to extend the very short storyline I presume - as much as a viewer can stand, yet still play regardless).  I cannot emphasize this enough.  You move so slowly throughout the game, it put me to sleep in Chapter one looking for the up-teenth item to leave the area the first time I attempted playthrough.  There are THREE puzzles in the game.  Yes you read that correctly.  One is using a clever little Crytography versus symbology with a laser to unlock a box, the second is opening a puzzle box, and lastly the final puzzle is fumbling at a machine with different modules to get the coding correct for an interface sequence.  The rest of the ENTIRE GAME is TREASURE HUNTING for parts/pieces/objects to escape, (if you like that sort of thing).  Some jump scares, and again poor programming for interactions in my opinion, (at least with an Xbox controller).  This game pulls out ideas from successful stories like Vanilla Sky and Total Recall.  I saw nothing truly original, nor remarkable.  Sprinkle in some Groundhog Day, and voilà! you have Reveil.  I bought the bundle, so I'll have to play through it's semi-sequel Shift 87, but quite honestly: I think this dev paid some YouTubers to "review" and play the Reveil game, then hoped to make a million bucks after working hard on it , (EDIT: Dev replied 5 years)  That's what it feels like, that's how it played, and that's the level of engagement I got from it.  Although, with  (EDIT: Dev replied no AI used) the ability to simply pull all these assets directly from an game engine without having to design any of it now from scratch,  At the end of the day I don't mind paying.  After all, it was as I said, reasonably priced ($24 for both in a bundle).  If you're not 43 years old, and a film studies major, you'll likely enjoy this game and it's twists.  I had a great experience myself with Backrooms: Lost Tape, Pools, or Superliminal - extraordinary games that didn't pull from typical Hollywood tropes; also very reasonable price points that were in my opinion more frightening, or in the case of Superliminal, highly puzzle driven.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR |   REVEIL is a decently crafted horror indie game that focuses on puzzles and some mind messing to create some fun jump scares and a few creepy areas.  At 20 bucks i feel the game sits at the edge of worth it price.  When on sale it is a  well worth it buy if you like horror games with puzzles that won't tax your mind to much and can be beat in one sitting.Full Review. REVEIL is a short horror game that sit's it self on the edge of a Walking simulator with a few minor threats.  A bit like Layers of Fear in that regard.  Though with alot less "death chance " moments.  The story it self is unique with a some fun twists that did honestly have me smiling by the end of the game.  Though it did give me a few good jump scares here and there. Sadly they where to few and far apart. The game focuses more so on the story and events of Walter Thompson. but out side of that i did not find the game overall that scary 90 percent of the time.  The game also has no real threat through most of the game.  The few times you have a threat, it is very easy to avoid. Luck is not really a factor at all with them. The game does also use the "motion interaction" method that Frictional Games (amnesia, Soma) use in their game.  Though i do feel it's not as well implemented in this game.  I had a more than a few moments where it was hard to understand exactly what and how it wanted me to move my mouse. Thus causing things to be more frustrating than immersive overall. Length of the game is also not that long.  A single play session of 3 to 4 hours will beat this game.  It dose have a little bit of a replay value once you beat it to get the endings.  Thankfully once beat you have access to well place Chapter select options so you don't have to PLAY the entire game all over again just to make one little choice to change things up. Overall I give this game a 7/10.  If you like games that mess with your mind a bit like Evil Within, Layers of Fear. And want some Puzzles that where part of old school horror games from the ps1 days.   I feel you will enjoy this game and the story it has.    If your  looking for hardcore horror and jumps cares though like that of OUTLAST style games, This is not it.  It is here to tell you a story and go BOO a few times.   A bit of a hard sale at 20 bucks, but when on sale a worth grab to add.

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid fan of horror games, I'm always on the lookout for experiences that truly push the boundaries of the genre. REVEIL, developed by Pixelsplit, stands out as a shining example of what a narrative-driven psycho-thriller should be.From the moment I stepped into the shoes of Walter Thompson, I was engulfed in a world of mystery and terror. The attention to detail in both storytelling and gameplay mechanics is simply astounding. Every corner of the Nelson Bros Circus, with its dark history and hidden secrets, kept me on the edge of my seat as I unraveled the twisted tale that awaited.What sets REVEIL apart is its seamless integration of story, puzzles, and exploration. Each element complements the other, creating a cohesive and immersive experience that is as satisfying as it is chilling. The puzzles are cleverly crafted, requiring both wit and courage to solve, while the exploration rewards curiosity with haunting discoveries.Pixelsplit has once again proven their prowess as developers with REVEIL. Their previous title, Virtual Rides 3, showcased their talent for creating immersive experiences, and REVEIL takes it to a whole new level. The atmosphere they've crafted is palpable, drawing players deeper into the darkness with each passing moment.But perhaps the true highlight of REVEIL is its narrative. As Walter's past intertwines with the horrors of the present, the story unfolds in ways that are both shocking and thought-provoking. It's a testament to the skill of the writers and the dedication of the development team to deliver a tale that lingers long after the credits roll.In conclusion, REVEIL is a masterpiece of horror gaming that deserves a place among the greats. With its gripping story, clever puzzles, and atmospheric world, it's an experience that will haunt players long after they've put down the controller. If you're a fan of psychological thrillers, do yourself a favor and dive into the darkness of REVEIL. You won't be disappointed.And for those interested in witnessing the terror firsthand, check out my live stream of REVEIL at Rays Sim's YouTube Channel . Join me as we brave the nightmares together!

You wake up. You're disoriented. Your head hurts. Things seem surreal, yet familiar.

name: Jupiter Hell
detailed_description: Do you miss the good old days when games weren't holding your hand? Then you're in the perfect place. In Jupiter Hell - Action follows your every move. When you act, your enemies act. But when you die. You die for good. Jupiter Hell lets you become a hero in a classic 90s-flavored sci-fi universe. It's you and your trusty shotgun (or chaingun, railgun or even a chainsaw) against hordes of demonic and alien motherfu***. All to the shine of CRT monitors. Just like in the good old days. But the graphics are much better. Unlock new perks, test out new builds and try to live through the hell you have ended up in. Every run is different, thanks to the procedurally generated levels. Earn new perks. Build your character to endure what lurks around the corner. If you manage to survive the Jupiter Hell - you can unlock new challenges. It's not gonna get any easier. Quite the contrary. it's gonna make you suffer. Does 20+ years of experience making top-down, cosmic-hell roguelikes sound like a recipe for a hell of a good turn-based roguelike? ChaosForge team, the developer of Jupiter Hell, gained recognition for creating Doom, the Roguelike (known also as DRL.) They built the Jupiter Hell as a spiritual successor to DRL.

_childDocuments_.review: It's just great! Really easy to fire it up and get killing, none of the usual roguelike faffing (though of course there's a time and a place for that). It's shot through with a sense of fun and exuberance. Though I haven't quite plumbed the depths of it yet, I can see that there is also a lot of depth to it with regards to customising your run too. Also  on the run where I got the furthest, my character was ludicrously overpowered, until he wasn't and an enemy one shotted me! _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A 5-6/10 that's just okay, at the moment. IMHO.I hate to say this. Normally people don't genuinely mean that, but I do.Unless significant changes are made, this just isn't worth (near) full price.Is it a bad game? I wouldn't say that.Whether you played DRL or not, this game seems a bit... average.Not bad, but not very good. It's an okay game.Graphically, everything is far too muddy and dark.Perhaps it's for atmosphere, but it just went too far with it.The core gameplay was... functional. However, it became repetitive far quicker than expected.For me, everything became very stale around floor 4.It's possible that mid/late-game mix things up, but I'm not so sure.Sounds are not great. Certain weapons, like shotguns, sound weak.Music is generic, at best, and fails to get the blood pumping.The player character became annoying very quickly. He rarely speaks, but was annoying when he did.I can't think of a better description for the player character than "edgy tryhard ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥."This gimmick can work, and can be entertaining.Something is off about the execution here, though.It wasn't doing anything for me.I won't speak on difficulty, or weapon and enemy balance.As I haven't really played enough to comfortably gauge that.However, I had no issues there. At least on medium difficulty.The inability to unload weapons is a minor annoyance, but nothing beyond that.I must say, however, something stands out with character balance.The marine, as far as I know, is the only class that can't increase inventory size, or number of weapons.This is a massive drawback, that I don't think his improved health regeneration makes up for.If I'm completely blind, and somehow missed the option, then ignore this point.I still can't say this is an objectively bad game.But I just can't call it good.It plays everything too safe, and just ends up being very average.As a result, I can't score it higher than a 5/10.If there was ever a need for a "neutral" review option, it's here.I hope the devs can improve the game, and make it the great game it deserves to be.

_childDocuments_.review: GAME DESIGN:The game has a grid-based, turned-based movement system. You can usually move only in 4 directions. There are three character classes. Each class provides different tools to beat the game. Most of the tools however are available in some way to all the classes which makes the classes not that unique. Nevertheless, I think the game has a well-thought-out and well-balanced character development system.AI:Enemies are very often stupid, which makes some sense because all of them are zombies, monsters, or robots. In a lot of cases you just hide behind the cover and enemies willingly walk out of their covers to be easily shot. Enemies seem to walk towards you when they hear you but when they lose you from sight they weirdly retreat. The AI ​​in this game to me feels quite artificial. I would like it if an enemy could consciously (not accidentally) shoot the explosive barrel when I'm standing next to it.GRAPHICS AND CHARACTER ANIMATION:The graphics are ok however, I would like to point out that:- The lighting is not quite polished in some parts of the game. For example in Europa cave levels light is so strong that you can barely see the items on the floor.- When you for example press the up button and the right button at once it seems that the character is moving diagonally. In the tutorial, they explain that actually, you can move only in 4 directions, and moving diagonally is only a side effect of the animation system and that they're two consecutive moves. I think the graphics should match and accentuate the game design.THE MOOD:The graphical style and the music are inspired by DOOM.In my opinion, the music lives up to the original DOOM score.SUMMARY:Jupiter Hell is a very good classical rogue-like.I have played it for 25 hours and I'm still not bored.The game is still a bit unpolished but it's understandable. It's a very complicated game and it has been developed in a very small team for the last 13 years.It is still in active development and a lot of things will eventually get polished.The game is definitely worth trying out.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Great spiritual rogue-like successor of DoomRL which improved upon its formula and removed some really annoying mechanics (destroying items, giftdropping, unloading weapons...). Now it is its own thing with great variety of difficulties and modes to play at. Biggest improvements are cover/dodge mechanics, more much clearer rules and less RNG depended playthroughs. Also its 3D but that is not really important for game like this (but its nicer to look at at least :) ).Like before each class and individual master traits provide different enough playstyles that can give enough playtime for hundreds of hours. Variety of weapons, items, traits, uniques, monsters and levels is in the sweet spot where there is enough but it is not too much where I know what to expect but it is still variable enough.Majority of times I die (and that can happen a lot) I know perfectly well what I did wrong and how I could have prevented it (usually by hoarding healing items and refusing to use them until it is too late). For me that is most important trait of good rogue-like - I hate when I lose purely to RNG.Highly recommend for fans of tactical games, rogue-likes or DoomRL fans.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic and addictive, but be warned. As fun as it is - and I do not throw this around lightly as it is a stereotype of whiny gamerz lol - this game is *so cheap*. Prepare to die in the most absolutely unfair ways. In a sense, I understand this as it is very common for rogue likes to have huge difficulty spikes (and this game's theme is for it to literally be hell). However, there are times where the game just absolutely bends you  over and there is no recourse. It can be so frustrating, especially after a great hours long run, just for it to end on rng for an enemy spawn, or for a random massive spike of damage from one bullet that flukes and hits you. With that said, this game again is so addictive, and so easy to just pour time into. Diverse character builds, interesting and challenging enemies, a variety of cool locations to explore and loot, and of course the fantastic angry space man voice acting of none other than our "favourite spaceman on the citadel" Mark Meer. If you can stomach the rough patches of difficulty, you will have an absolute blast playing this game, it's a diamond in the rough that is well worth the price!
