name: Unbound: Worlds Apart
detailed_description: What is Unbound? Unbound: Worlds Apart is a challenging, atmospheric and hand-drawn puzzle-platformer set in a universe where all worlds are connected by portals. You control Soli, a gifted young mage who has the power to open portals and control the unique properties of each world - such as inverse gravity, time manipulation, super strength and more. Using these newfound skills, Soli must journey across dangerous and mysterious worlds, each brimming with secrets and challenges. You must use every skill Soli has to defeat a ruthless evil that is tearing reality apart, while learning the shocking truth behind your world’s collapse. Gameplay Your reflexes and twitch platforming skills will be put to the ultimate test in Unbound: Worlds Apart. As Soli you can explore large worlds full of hidden secrets and unlockable skills that open up even more of the map as you progress. Along the way you will meet many weird, wonderful and devious characters, each with rich backstories and dialogue. By completing their quests or listening to their tales of hope and sorrow, you will learn more about Unbound’s grand universe of worlds and the portals that connect them. Key features: 10 different portals with unique mechanics Vibrant and detailed hand-drawn artwork Twitch platforming with new skills to unlock Challenging puzzles, traps, monsters and bosses A rich narrative, world lore and cast of NPCs Hidden secrets, quests and collectibles

_childDocuments_.review: Well, where do I start? Are you a fan of Ori and the Blind Forest? Is Hollow Knight your favourite game? Well, let me tell you something. This is your lucky day! This game has everything you've been missing: the fascinating, cryptic lore of Hollow Knight? Check. Trying platforming and puzzles like Ori? Check. Charming NPCs? Check. Varied and stunning locations? Check. Honestly, this game really feels like Hollow Knight and Ori’s third long lost sibling. And Soli the protagonist is so adorable!About the gameplay and platforming. It’s honestly what I would call *fair*. The game starts with some kinda easy platforming, but it has a really uphill difficulty curve. It gets from easy to really hard towards the end. And by hard I mean Super Meat Boy hard. The later part of the game will really put you to the test. If you’re one of those gamers that really likes a challenge, then the extra content the game has is definitely for you! *flashback to Hollow Knight's buzzsaw level* I’m not telling you how to get it, so have fun discovering that one on your own!I'd say the game clocks at about 20 hours of content if you explore everything and get all the secrets, so you're getting your money's worth. If you're like me and you're still (im)patiently waiting for Silksong's release date, then this game will scratch your itch. Have fun and thank me later!

_childDocuments_.review: Exceptional precision puzzle platformer that will test your reflexes and multitasking to the max. Expect to die hundreds if not thousands of times to complete challenging sections. The side pathways to collect villager's and optional areas that unlocked after collecting them all are extremely difficult (). These optional areas will require you to simultaneously manage portal placement while platforming in near impossible spaces. The game is very forgiving with checkpoints placed after almost every section in the story progression path. The portal mechanic not only is fun and engaging way to solve puzzles but feels unique with every different power. There is no health bar as just one touch to the environment or vicious creatures will instantly k!ll you. You should by no means go into it expecting an experience similar to  or other similar platformer. The game can be completed within 10 to 15 hours depending if you dare to take on the more challenging areas. Overall,  is a unique experience with intuitive and smooth gameplay, beautiful hand-drawn visuals and enchanting soundtrack. [10/10]

_childDocuments_.review: Unbound is a metroidvania only in the loosest definition of the genre. It's a puzzle platformer with generally linear progression, indirect combat via the environment, and light exploration elements. You should by no means go into it expecting an experience similar to Ori or Hollow Knight as some reviewers seem to suggest. If you want something recent along those lines, try Ender Lillies or if you just want a decent metroidvania try Astalon. None of this is to discredit Unbound; its portal mechanics challenge the grey matter in a way those other games don't and there is some very challenging platforming to be had here, especially some of the optional areas that require precise platforming and portal management simultaneously. The art is nice and the gameplay is generally very fluid. The world and story didn't really grab me, as it did with some of the other titles I mentioned but it does the job. Overall, I say it's worth a buy at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: You play as a cute little red mage named Soli, that can use a power to bend reality and defy the physic. Use them as your advantage to defeat creepy monsters that dwell around and solve the puzzles along your way.  It was all quiet and peaceful in the Vaiya, but everything changed when the demon attacked. Soli being one of the survivors and gifted with the magical power to control power from a portal, set a path to find the source of the evil and put an end to it.The story is a simple premise where you fight your way to find the demon that causes all the rampage. There is not much more into it from what I have seen it, no development or buildup along the way. Definitely not the strong suit of the game.Unbound is a heavy puzzle with a tight platformer. Even though Soli is a Mage, he’s not built for a fight. You died with any direct contact with any enemy and hazardous environment. Also, you can’t fight an enemy directly. You must be tricky with how you use the ability to avoid the enemy or defeat them.About the portal's power, you gain access to use that power once you go through the portal, and you lose it if you exit the portal. The game feels like a segmented puzzle world where you can only use what the game dictates to you what power you can use in a certain area.On the bright side, you can find skills like double jump and dash, your daily dose of platforming skills, and that permanent. There are not many skills to acquire and nothing memorable about them.What I like in Unbound is their puzzle really does be challenging my brain. You need to find a way to utilize the power creatively. On other hand, I don’t like how they make some of the jumps is so tight to make it. What I meant by that is you need to get so close to the edge of the ledge to jump to make it to the other end. It is unnecessary and not fun.They have a single side quest, where you need to find missing villagers. There’s no reward to it besides the game achievement. But you can find all the missing villagers you rescue in one area and they speak some cryptic sentences that I don’t get what they mean.The art is great! Especially the enemies, they are intended to be creepy, and yes they do creep me out to the point I don’t want to stare too much at them. But most of the other NPC is similar to our character, a hoodie mage, with just differentiation of size and color.The ambiance music is nice and fits perfectly with the atmosphere of each area. It gave tranquility feeling even in the darkest place.Final ScoreUnbound: Worlds Apart turn out to be heavily on the puzzle side rather than adventure and exploring I feel like. There was a prolog demo at first on the store to get a little taste of the game, but they removed it now. Even though the overalls seem kind of bland and mediocre for me, but the gameplay is pretty solid with great art and a reasonable price. Still a good game if you like to train your brain and mechanical platforming skill.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: I am a glut for Metroidvanias, and Unbound starts out very strong: good flow, pacing, and diverse and satisfying mechanics. But a few hours in the game suddenly and unexpectedly spikes from a well-balanced Ori-like level of difficulty to absolutely bonkers, Super Meat Boy levels of sadism. I'm fine with optional side missions and secrets being extra hard, but we're talking about the main game here; mandatory areas that require preternatural levels of speed, precision, and coordination. it's not fun and it ruins what would otherwise be an instant classic in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Vivi and the Blind Forest was the crossover we didn’t know we needed. Shout out to Wizards with eyes in a dark void for a face, gotta be one of my favorite genders.Platformer/Metroidvanias are my bread and butter, so I’m really digging this games concept. This game feels like it's roughly 75% platformer and 25% Metroidvania. There is some ability gating and you’ll find a double jump and wall jump but this game is purely a platformer with no combat. It's fairly challenging but pretty forgiving and generous with checkpoints. The artstyle is fantastic and each NPC has a unqiue look. Puzzles / gimmicks don't really repeat themselves and you're constantly facing something new and fun with each new area. Portals are kinda original and are really cool/fun. At the moment I’m only about 50% in progress, but gotta say this game seems really polished and fun.Reminds me a lot of Ori and the Blind Forest. Exploration, fun mechanics and no combat. I think a lot of casual players not wanting souls-like but just want to relax will have a blast with this. Both Ori games and Unbound just feel comfy to play. Focused on movement, quick respawns on death, the sorta games that are just nice to pick up and play even after not touching them for a few days or weeks.It’s definitely something to play while I wait for Silksong... 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's interesting to see how the player's skill progress works in this game. Starting in the lamp atmosphere of a colorful world where you can only jump, we gradually come to a double jump under water, followed by a double dash and instant switching of the conditions of the surrounding reality. Competent development becomes one of the main achievements of the game, because it is thanks to him that you begin to feel that the hero is really developing together with the world and you. The story is pretty standard - suddenly the world around begins to collapse, familiar things take on some ugly shade, so the little protagonist has to take the initiative into his own hands and save everyone. An unpretentious, but effective concept, which, although it does not present huge surprises, works quite competently. The fellow villagers hidden in the locations help to reveal the history of the world, each of whom shares interesting thoughts with the player. What's even more pleasing is that finding all the villagers and completing two very difficult challenges associated with this search allow you to open an alternative ending to the game.If we talk about complexity, then here we need to talk about what goal the player sets for himself. Beating the main plot is unlikely to put some impossible challenges in front of the player (with the exception of the final boss), but if you start hunting for hidden fellow villagers and go through tests, then the difficulty here increases significantly. Moreover, in these trials, you begin to meet injustice, which is not at all in the main game, because some of them are senselessly difficult. This is most evident in the segment with oblique bubbles in the forest test, where everything is solely based on luck, and several other examples can be cited. In these hardcore challenges, you begin to realize that double jump in the game works oddly, often triggering from the first press of a button. It is unlikely that you will encounter this in the main game, but it needs to be said about it. The developers' imagination works perfectly well, the variety of mechanics pleases until the very last location, and the appearance of the game applies. Hand drawing looks incredible; the world is saturated with bright colors as much as possible, beautiful smooth animations are executed neatly and softly."Unbound: Worlds Apart" becomes a bright and exciting adventure in the world of platform puzzles, which can both relax the player and challenge his skills.

_childDocuments_.review: It looks, sounds and feels amazing. But let me tell you about the portal mechanic. It, combined with really clever level design - and I mean REALLY clever! - makes for a super engaging experience, right off the bat. To be more clear, 5 minutes in and you're already both using your brain (hopefully) and your portal. It becomes second nature in literal minutes.This is one of those few games where you don't need any kind of tutorializing to figure out how to use what's at your disposal. The moment you get the portal and you figure out how to hop between worlds you naturally transition into understanding everything the game throws your way. And boy does it throw a lot! I let out an audible "WOAH" when I realized my portal was inverting gravity. Unbound will make you think, but it won't make you *stop* and think. You keep going and improvising on the fly, it all flows beautifully together - hard to believe this is the first time these guys are making a platformer. It's beautifully balanced, and the level design is freaking ace.And, again - it looks amazing, every step of the way. You rarely see 2D games developed in Unreal, but I can see why they went with it. They pulled out the big guns, there are particles, godrays, parallaxing layers, soft and diffuse light, glows, mist... You only need to watch a few seconds of footage to realize just how frigging gorge this game is. An enthusiastic recommendation, even if you don't usually play puzzle platformers. It's fresh, beautiful, satisfying, and it keeps going. Triple B: brain, brawns, and beauty. PS: Soli is ADORBS!

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent puzzle/precision platformer that will truly test your skills without being totally unfair, utilizing an awesome gameplay mechanic in the form of reality-bending portals. Definitely something to check out if you want a challenge. Keep in mind that aside from the visuals (and they are beautiful!) and difficulty, this is NOT going to be the same experience as Ori and the Blind Forest or Hollow Knight. There is no combat (you have to use your environment to defeat or get around enemies, no projectiles or weapons), the Metroidvania world isn't as richly detailed, and the story is dirt simple. Keep that in mind if you choose to play. Other than that, I had a lot of fun with this game and I'm glad I checked it out, and I think it's definitely worth checking out on its own merits.

_childDocuments_.review: I've waited until completing the game to leave a review - and I'm gutted it's a negative one.I was looking forward to this game, and I'm really disappointed.  It is very much a mix of Hollow Knight and Ori, except lacking in a lot of areas.  The story was weak and forgettable, I found myself forgetting the point of what I was doing and not at all invested in the game, or even my own progress.Parts of the game can be difficult, but it's a mix of platforming skill, timing and chance...lots or chance.  There's a fair amount of trying over and over, but there's no sense of achievement, just boredom.  I found myself just trying to get through the game because I'd bought it.  The graphics are ok, there's some areas of just walking through uninteresting screens to get from A to B.  I had some glitches after using double jump, I had to double jump again to get rid of the yellow lines.  The music isn't note worthy - I played my own over the top of it.Overall, I'd give 3/5 - it's hard not to compare it to Hollow Knight or Ori as certain functions, game play and even the map are very similar.  Even when I'd finished the final boss I didn't really care - there was no joy in beating the game, no twinge of sadness when a great game comes to an end...just glad it was over really.I'd say if you can get this for a few quid in a sale, then give it a go, or better yet, just replay Ori or Hollow Knight!

_childDocuments_.review: Such a great game.  Solid platforming and great puzzles, and while often a bit difficult, it is very forgiving and never felt stressful to play through.  Unlike many similar games, Unbound has no health system.  You die in one hit.  However, the devs (thankfully) set it up to autosave pretty much any time you are on solid ground, which means you're only really playing one obstacle at a time.  This set up is a massive relief, because while the platforming/puzzles are fun, there are a few that were precise enough that I was happy to not have to repeat.  It also lets you fast travel directly from the map screen which is an awesome quality of life feature.  The game is a metroidvania, but only very lightly.  The backtracking you do is generally very small (opening a gate in your current section, and return to it, etc), and the ability gating usually only exists very close to the spots where you gain the abilities.  The map is great though, and in the end I think this was the right call, because getting too lost and repeating sections in Unbound would be a bit more stressful/annoying than in other metroidvanias.The platforming and puzzles all felt great.  The game often will introduce a new mechanic, and explore it very in depth before moving on.  Passing sections felt extremely satisfying.  A really great game, would definitely recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: I''m about 5 hours in and have been really enjoying the game so far! Pros- Difficult (but generally fair) platforming- Snappy controls- Beautiful atmosphere/cute characters- The world building is great so far!Cons - No way to disable screen shake, I was getting genuinely motion sick after redoing a boss a few times. (This was pretty major for me)- Dash has a weird screen effect that makes it feel clunky and throws off my eyes- Some hit boxes don't match their sprites, especially some spiked ceilings in boss fightsOther notes/nitpicks - Imo it's kind of weird that all the lost villagers just have random phrases when you find them, it makes them feel less like actual characters and isn't very immersive. On that note it would be cool if we could have the stone tablet with what they say with us at all times instead of it being stationary.- in a similar vein, most of the actual characters feel like they're just there to give lore instead of having their own personality. They all talk in pretty much the same way.- Some frustrating mechanics (although they might just be frustrating for me since I'm trash), especially making platforms from fireballs. This seems like a cool mechanic conceptually, but I haven't been able to consistently use it in a way that feels good.- Seems a little weird that the main character has a black outline when other characters don't, Not dramatic or anything, but was something I noticed.All in all, I would 100% recommend the game so far! _childDocuments_.review: Pros:I have played Ori, Hollow Knight and other puzzle like games. But what a refreshing game mechanic this game has. The portals that you can create gives the puzzles another dimension. This is something I have never seen in other puzzle games. The puzzles are super clever and are very challenging. The art is amazing, such gorgeous drawings. Throughout the game you constantly want to draw your portal to see how the world in the portal is drawn, because it looks so different every time. There is no dull repetitive art in the game.Cons:Altho the game is good-looking and the puzzles are challenging, it does feel a bit messy and a bit empty.With messy I mean the structure of the game. There is no sense of anticipation. Which makes boss fight less epic then you want. What I also missed were NPCs that give more context about the bad things that are going on. The game feels a bit empty because you don't really feel a connection to characters. What I personally did not like where the lost travelers. It just not feels rewarding when you find one. When you find one it just speaks out a part of bigger story. But because it takes time to find them you forget what the story was about and then it just feels like random words. Is this a game like Hollow Knight and Ori, No.. But it has the hard puzzles and bosses that they also have, but it just lacks a good constructed story-line. So if you really like challenging puzzles and pretty worlds then I would definitely recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: Play this game for the platforming and the aesthetic (including a beautiful soundtrack). Don't necessarily play it just for the story or exploration.If you're looking for a fun, challenging, yet fair 2D puzzle platformer, then you've come to the right place. Unbound: Worlds Apart has a solid difficulty curve where you'll often be challenged, but almost never faced with something that feels insurmountable. In addition to a well-crafted main route, the game also features a lot of really clever setups scattered throughout, which force you to fully understand the mechanics to get 100% completion. Each hit in Unbound is a one-shot, but it features very a quick respawn time, which is essential for this type of game. Platforming is at the heart of nearly every moment in this game, and they've really nailed it basically everywhere.Just look even at the few screenshots on the Steam page; this game is  Each major area of each world feels distinct, and the attention to detail in the visuals for each scene goes far above what I had expected. Plus, the soundtrack is phenomenal, and is often dynamic depending on your situation. The aesthetic and the platforming are by far Unbound's strongest aspects, and I'd definitely consider them the most important as well.There's no story spoilers here, but I've spoiler-tagged this for the sake of those who don't want even opinion spoilers.One of the top community tags on this game is "Metroidvania," which is admittedly what made me pick it up in the first place. It certainly does contain one of these elements: you collect powerups throughout the game that let you go back and find hidden "collectibles" (). However, Unbound is a very linear game overall, with only very short paths (with the aforementioned collectibles at their ends) leading off the main route. While the environments are incredibly fun to traverse, don't expect to satiate any sort of craving for exploration specifically.So at the end of all that, notice that my review is definitely a positive. Unbound: Worlds Apart was a fun and memorable experience, thanks to its creative uses of its platforming mechanics and its fantastic aesthetic. It took me about 10 hours total to 100%, and the moment-to-moment gameplay firmly held my attention all the way through. If that sounds like fun to you, then I can definitely recommend checking out Unbound: Worlds Apart.

_childDocuments_.review: Is a charming little puzzle platformer, but it has some flaws that really don't resonate with me.- Gameplay is very dull.I've seen reviews compare it to Hollow Knight and Ori, but it's far from those. The only thing it has in common is it's a platformer. It's not open world. But my biggest complaint in gameplay is how utterly slow it is. I played for 3 hours. In that time, I completed 5 maps. Took me 2 hours to get my first permanent ability. Won't spoil it, but it's an ability every platformer ever has. And it doesn't feel good to use, it feels really bland, especially for waiting 2 hours to get *something* to spice up the gameplay. So far, what I can tell is the main gimmick are abilities you get with your portal. And those are fine... except they only persist in specific areas. So far, the majority of the game, I haven't gotten to use the cool portal stuff. So the gameplay is really boring. I know there's a dash ability since the controller menu spoils it, but at this point, I don't care. I doubt the dashing would make up for the rest of the mediocre gameplay imo- Difficulty curveIn my 3 hours of playing, I haven't felt an overall progression curve. Instead, the game is primarily too easy/obvious for me, but has some random spots that are frustratingly difficult. I'm no stranger to difficult platforming segments - I did Path of Pain in Hollow Knight, I've played Celeste, etc. But they just don't feel well designed in this game, and they really stick out like a sore thumb to the rest of the ease of the game for me. Some segments are near frame perfect or require using jump buffer to make some jumps, which is fine... if you're going for a precision platformer, which this is not. And some reviews say it gets much harder, which again, I'm not a fan of for this game. The difficult bits just feel forced and not engaging, and really out of place with the difficulty of parts they're in. I also hoped this game focused more on puzzles - and maybe it does later on, but from my experience, all puzzles I came to, I had to think very little on. Now, I'm not expecting this to have Portal-level puzzles, but maybe I was expecting a little too much from this game's puzzles.- Music & lore are ok, but nothing to write home aboutThis game has the equivalent of Hollow Knight's lore tablets; out of place bits of lore info that may or may not mean something. Not a fan of how they work in this game. They're also not that well hidden.I try to be very lenient with indie games as an indie dev myself, but I just can't recommend this if you're looking for something with progression akin to Ori/Hollow Knight. It's a very slow paced game that doesn't give you much to work with for awhile, so unless you like spending most of the game with jumping being all you can do, I don't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, there is more good than bad, but I found myself frustrated with things more often than I would have liked and for that it gets this middling review. 	This is metroidvania. It's characters are cute and the art looks pretty good in general. I know what I can interact with and thing are distinct from other things. There are a few short animated cut scenes, and although the frame rate on them is on the lower side, they still convey the feelings the game is going for. Nothing wrong with the graphics, but it doesn't stand out to me either.	The music doesn't stand out either, though some parts are very loud. I think they needed to balance the audio a little better. No dialogue is spoken. Everything is text, which is fine by me for a game like this. The problem is, everyone talks in vague terms and I often got bored of the 2-5 text boxes each character had for me before I was done reading it. The small plot is fine in general, but again, not much in this game stands out.	The gameplay gave me issues. The game has a terrible habit of dropping inputs on your jumps. It's really bad when you get double jump and have to combine a second jump with other movement options and then you just don't get a second jump. The game eats it and its gone. I know I lose my first jump if I walk off a platform or fall off a wall, but the game doesn't clearly show when you are starting this movement and I died many times due to this awkward design. Also, having L1 being one type of control and R2 being the other type is just plain inexcusable. It's clunky to have it designed that way when R1 is not used for anything all game long.	The game teaches you how to use the abilities you get, most of the time. Though there was one time that I got to a boss and had no idea how to even hit it because the game never bothered to explain that mechanic. I ended up stumbling onto it randomly because nothing would work. The game would just put roadblocks like that in your way. 	The difficulty spikes really got on my nerves towards the end. You platform through an entire section, learn what the game is teaching you, and then you have to do all of that while not having any time to look at the situation and figure out how to use it. You have to go as fast as possible and even that is just barely fast enough. Some of the platforming sections would be leagues more difficult than the rest of the game and while the game teaches you how to use the abilities, putting them together in these ways would often feel unfair.	Finally, my last gripe is with some puzzles having very confusing requirements to complete. I got lost many times because I thought I needed a new ability when all I needed was what I had, but the timing had to be perfect to get it. Even with perfect timing, it would often not look like you could make a jump or get to an area, but then it works anyway. Meanwhile, I went back and re-explored everything trying to find wheat I missed so I could move on. There was just never a clear path laid out that you need this ability at this point and you gain it during the last sequence. You can just go everywhere, end up with 4 dead ends and then have to go back and find the area that it looks like you can't get to and go that way to find the next ability in a dead end.	It's worth playing on sale, but not unless you are into this style of game already. It's not something that will get you into the genre. For a game that does, try the Ori games, or the classics that created the genre Metroid and Castlevania.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: DO NOT BUY IF YOUR ONLY REASON IS YOU'VE BEEN TOLD THIS IS LIKE HOLLOW KNIGHT! IT'S NOT.I don't want to come across as someone criticising a game because of comparing it to another, that isn't fair. Honestly once I put aside the frustration that I'd been told this was akin to hollow knight and that's why I'd bought it, I enjoyed myself a lot more. It is a fun little game and the concept itself I think is good. I loved the being made tiny mechanic and the changing gravity between up and down was so so so fun every time, that was my favourite part. However I'd not recommend it because I think it was overall fairly boring. For a game reliant on tricky timing, I found the controls were not at all as responsive as I wanted them to be and often felt quite slow. The amount of times I had to redo something because there was no way I could react fast enough with the controls was frustratingly high. I found it very hard to improvise and save myself because of this. Having to redo from the checkpoint and largely follow one set route to the goal. As I saw someone else saying in a review, the sense of achievement is very limited. The most rewarding thing about the game is genuinely how enjoyable it feels to move around with the floaty gravity when the portal gives you control over it. The story is boring and not engaging, it felt very much like set caverns to go through because you're told to, rather than being invested in any reason you're doing it. The characters were all completely forgettable. The only vaguely interesting story moments were the cutscenes right at the beginning and right at the end of the game.You get rewarded with lore for tricky extra platforming if you're into that, but again I did not find the background worldbuilding interesting enough for it to ever be worth it when I got them. I'm certainly not enticed to go round and collect them all. I have seen a few reviews saying the lore and characters were great... they are not!! Don't be fooled.However if you want platforming that is fun and different, and little more than that (it's quite a short game too) then I'd say this game could be for you. However the timing being tricky not just because of precision needed but the controls not feeling as precise as they should be is definitely frustrating. I noticed this the most on the last boss fight (which btw ends quite abruptly after a surprisingly easy challenge which again ruined any feeling of achievement or it being a big moment of victory). As things went on and I had to keep repeating challenges and being sent back to the beginning because of lag it really put a bad taste in my mouth and was a real shame.TL;DR - Only buy this game for the platforming, nothing else. It is short, the controls are slower than I would like, but there is definite fun and uniqueness with some of the mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo of this game a year ago, and thought it had a lot of potential. Perhaps it could be a new Ori. Now, a year later, I could finally buy it and though the game was enjoyable, it is not a new Ori. The game is a lot harder, (think super meatboy) but also a little less polished. I died at least 3 to 4 times more than I died in Ori, and really felt the need to take a break everynow and then. I don't always mind hard games, as long as they feel fair, but in this game not every death felt this way. I guess this is a metroidvania, but the focus is very much on puzzles. These puzzles were smart and good, but not very forgiving. It seems that even if you know the solution, you still need pixel perfect execution to solve it. Still i liked the challenge and will remember some creative parts!I think my biggest gripe is that with this game is that it lacks a rewarding crecendo-type moment (think the amped up grav gun from hl2, or having to back-track through an old section in Ori, but now with the new powers and you finish in a minute a section that took half an hour before), a moment where you can feel REALLY powerful, where everything comes together and after all the work you can feel like superman for a while. In this game this feeling never really comes, so there seems to be a missing pay off for all the work you put in (though a section where the portal automatically moves for you is close to this feeling). All in all the game is good if you like this type of challenging and unforgiving games. The dev also seems to be very available for comments and questions on the steam discussion forums, so that's always nice.Scores: Gameplay: 7/10Graphics: 7/10Sound and score: 7/10Creativity: 9/10Puzzles: 8/10 Story: 6/10Atmosphere: 7.5/10Replayability: 6/10Overall 7.5/10 Only buy if you like challenging games and don't mind dying a lot!

_childDocuments_.review: Though this game can technically be considered a Metroidvania, it’s very light on that aspect. Most of the gameplay involves one-off abilities tied to specific areas, though there are also your standard Metroidvania-style permanent upgrades. This unfortunately leads to the same problem I identified in Antichamber, where it can be unclear if you haven’t thought hard enough about a puzzle or if you literally can’t solve it. It’s also heavier on precision and timing than most puzzle platformers, which I found frustrating in several levels (that series of rotating spiky platforms, ugh).The basic premise is that you can open portals to other worlds, which alter the space around you while they’re open. In practice, this really just overlays a slightly different version of the level, but it works for puzzle purposes. Most levels have you accessing different worlds, with different effects, so it doesn’t get stale.The plot seems to be an anti-colonialism thing but also seems kinda anti-intellectual to me? Basically, Big Academia started colonizing other worlds under the claim they were spreading knowledge and welfare, which… seemed to be true? But then they were too “greedy for knowledge” and did an experiment that screwed up reality, and silenced everyone involved to cover it up. This is all told through optional lore snippets, so it’s a bit unclear. Also, the bad guy is evil because his completely justified anger toward the mages turned him into a demon and now he wants to destroy the world for no reason.One thing the store page doesn’t really mention and that I would have liked more warning on, however, is that the game actually has pretty strong horror themes. The monsters have very disturbing designs, made all the worse by their often being in shadow or only seen briefly, and your character dies at the slightest touch. It’s also really big on jumpscares. Not inherently a bad thing, but I would have appreciated a heads-up beforehand.

_childDocuments_.review: AVOID | LACKING | MAYBE | WORTHWHILE |  | UNMISSABLEUnbound: Worlds Apart is an atmospheric indie game that betrays being boxed into one genre. What this means is that it will likely appeal to fans of adventure/exploration games, those who enjoy metroidvanias, and people who appreciate a precision platforming challenge, all the while not really excelling in any one particular aspects of those genres. By this I mean that, for example, if you bought this game because it is listed as a precision platformer, there are definitely challenging sections to satiate that want, but probably not enough for someone who is looking for Path of Pain in full game length form. Similarly, while the game has metroidvania elements (you obtain abilities that let you access areas of the map you previously couldn't), if you are looking for something akin to Hollow Knight because Unbound is listed as a metrodvania, you are likely to be disappointed. In Unbound, you play as Soli, a mage, who you come to learn more about as you complete the game. The game heavily relies on "gates" that afford you the ability to change your environment after you pass through them (similar to games such as Hue) in your adventures. I quite enjoyed this element of the game and it led to several moments of delight when I realized what abilities I suddenly had access to. Combat was also interesting in this game, as there isn't combat in the traditional sense of the word, but there are boss fights, so there is creativity required as to how those are won. Additionally, there is no health stat, which means that you're either 100% perfect or you die. While this is sometimes frustrating for the reason listed below, it also is one less thing to manage throughout the gameplay.My only real complaint of this game is that it features some sections of precision platforming that are quite difficult. The game frankly doesn't demand them to be fun and there aren't enough of them to really make this a precision platforming game overall. What this means is the game leaves you in a bit of a weird limbo where you have to complete maybe five or so challenging sections, including two that took me a solid 45 minutes or so to complete, as you work your way through the game, and it feels out of place in terms of the difficulty of the rest of the game. Because there is no health stat, you must complete these sections (and others, such as boss fights) hitless. This is particularly frustrating when it's not immediately clear how to proceed leading you to have to redo difficult sections multiple times just to even get a chance at trying to figure out what to do next. Ultimately, it's not THAT challenging, but I wouldn't recommend this game to newer players because of it. I think this is a negative because otherwise the game would be great for newer players, as well as those who want a more laidback, but still challenging, experience.I completed the game in 8.5 hours and then took another ~1.25 hours to do some achievement cleanup.In summary, Unbound likely has broad appeal because it tiptoes into a variety of different genres, but isn't going to make the top 5 list for any one genre for the same reason. While I think the precision platforming sections are too difficult to recommend this game to someone who isn't experienced with them, I greatly enjoyed my time playing.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like they took all that was fun about Ori, put that aside and made this game with whatever was left.Plays a lot like Ori, except you don't really have much character progression. Puzzles are sometimes fun, sometimes annoying. Not because they are hard (which they are, but that isn't a bad thing in itself) but because you'll either have a checkpoint reeeally far back or the checkpoint will be out of sync with the puzzle meaning you'll spend ~5-10 sec every time you die just waiting for a platform to come back. Also, it's mostly hard because you only have 1 life. If you mess up anything, even just touching a leaf of a thistle, you're sent back to your latest checkpoint.Also, game is very short. I fully completed it apart from one achievement I missed, and it took me less than 7 hours. And that last achievement will  be like a 5 minute run to talk to some NPC I just ran past.A waste of €20, honestly.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo a year ago and have since been keeping an eye on this game. I was given a key to try it out and overall it's enjoyable game that's well worth checking out.The art style is lovely. The music works well for the game although it feels a bit more subdued at points.At its core Unbound is a puzzle platformer that grants a few extra platforming abilities as you progress (Double Jump, Wall Climb, Dash) to access new areas and overcome more involved puzzles. It primarily revolves around creating stationary portals to influence the environment to overcome a variety of obstacles. Some blocks may disappear in a portal or platforms may appear. Enemies may vanish (or a more innocuous critter might suddenly become quite aggressive). Gravity might be reversed. Regardless of your powers it's knowing when and where to place portals while platforming, often setting up multiple portals in succession to traverse a dangerous gauntlet. The game has a number of challenging segments but death is a slap on the wrist and there are generous checkpoints. There are no difficulty settings or assist mode, however.There are lost villagers and other NPCs to find in the world from optional areas, and finding enough villagers can open additional challenge areas to try out, so there is some replay value if you want to find everything.Game length is probably in the 6-8 hour range for completing, depending on how much extra exploration you do. I was able to complete the game including the optional areas and find most villagers in about seven hours but I'm not particularly skilled at puzzle platformers so that number may be lower depending on if you're better and/or skip the optional areas.If you're a fan of the genre, I'd very much recommend it. Even if you aren't, it's worth trying out.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to buy this at first due to seeing a full play through posted on YouTube that was only 3 hours long. _childDocuments_.review: Currently 3h into Unbound: Worlds Apart, and I'm thoroughly enjoying it!I first found out about the game through a Steam festival of sorts, where many games had demos available to try, and since then I've been looking forward to its full release. I'd just like to say that I love how the full release has added new elements to it, which was not something I expected. I'd like to take some time to appreciate that, it's a really nice plus, making it feel like a whole new experience :)From what I've experienced so far, Unbound is unique, as it feels like a puzzle game with platforming elements. Having played both Ori games and Hollow Knight, where both weighed heavily on platforming challenges, Unbound is something new that has been brought to the table, where puzzles are the main thing (although who knows, I might feel like it's a mix of both when I get to the end!), and it's a nice, unique and refreshing new twist. It's this that makes me feel like Unbound cannot really be compared to Ori and HK, because of how different it is. Many of the challenges require some thought, mainly 'how can I get there with the skills I have at my disposal'? it often feels very rewarding when you get through a challenge, and it's nice to know that your solutions work. Platforming so far hasn't been too difficult, where most of the challenge comes from figuring things out.  So far it doesn't have frustrating elements where the game resets you in a far-off land when you die, which is something I can appreciate a lot, and deaths are quick, allowing you to just get back on your feet immediately, in a vein similar to Celeste - which is something I like, because it doesn't feel like too much time is being spent on the death animation, and you're free to keep retrying over and over again without it feeling like a drag.There seems to be a slight Metroidvania element to Unbound as well, and I am pleasantly surprised! The game encourages you to return to areas you were previously in , which is something I look forward to! I'm not sure if the path one takes in the game would be linear, , and I look forward to seeing where that goes!Overall I'm loving the art style, music and atmosphere so far. I love the little sounds that are made throughout the world, and it gives a really nice feel to it. I look forward to playing it more, and will try to update my review accordingly. :p

_childDocuments_.review: This quickly turned into one of my very favorite games!Hollow Knight meets Ori with a sprinkle of A Walk in the Dark, this is truly a masterpiece and so much more than I ever expected. I thought it was just another little platform with a  "world-changing" feature and not much more. Instead I got one of the most atmospheric, sweet and well-made games I've ever played. This is an open world gem with everchanging gameplay. The music is wonderful, the controls are amazing and the graphics are some of the best out there - Take your time and really look at the background, both within and outside of your little portal. It is not a super difficult game, but it has some challenging points which fits in nicely with the overall gameplay - Just enough to keep you interested, but not too much to the point of ripping out your hair. Like with every other aspect of this game, the difficulty is nicely balanced.I really have nothing bad to say about this game. I found it a bit odd to see the logo after each cutscene, but other than that, the only complaint I can give is the length of the game - I want more!All achievements are easy to obtain and I played the whole game with an Xbox One controller.Give yourself a smile and make Soli walk instead of running, cuteness overload!

_childDocuments_.review: I like difficult and precise platformers, but this moves from "comfortably difficult" to too hard much too abruptly. _childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: fully recommendation for this game if you like platforming with a bit of Metroidvania in it. I had a blast with it.Pros:- portal mechanic is creative and fun- very good Level design that makes great use of mechanics- good difficulty, only one small optional section I found frustrating- you feel like you have a lot of control over the character; it plays well- fun and challenging platforming (for an ok-ish player)- bosses don't overstay their welcome- cute story- great visuals and art design- tough sections are mostly optional sections- Metroidvania elements are fun too- fair checkpoints (with maybe some exceptions)- good length- some cool puzzles, where you have to think a bit outside the box- you can rebind buttons freely (I played with a controller)- once loaded very short loading times (I had it installed on an HDD)neutral:- no voiced dialogues- the new movement abilities you unlock are pretty standard, but still feel great- I had one game crash during the second phase of the final boss, which made me repeat the first phase again and on some deaths (rare though) the character did not re-appear at the checkpoint again (back to main menu and then continue fixed it without losing progress), else I encountered no technical problems or major bugs and those might be fixed by now (I played the release version)- takes fps limit from Windows' monitor refresh rate setting, limit fps in settings would be appreciated- You can control your character with the left analogue stick and/or D-padCons:- no additional "Reset Portal" button, so you have to double-tap the open/close (toggle) portal button a lot in some sections, which felt exhausting and not as smooth control wise- bosses are maybe too easy for really good players- no icon on map that shows the gates that turn on/off your portal ability (I think)- first phase of the final boss was a bit annoying in partsUnbound: Worlds Apart is a platformer with Metroidvania elements. So the comparison with Hollow Knight or Ori you often read is a bit unprecise, though not completely wrong.Unbound focuses mainly on platforming and some puzzles, but has no real combat (maybe with one/two exceptions) combined with a great art style. The classic Metroidvania "get new abilities (wall jump, double jump, etc) and backtrack to explore new areas that can be accessed now with the new ability" is in the game too, but it's not its main focus and often this is more about optional areas (ofc with some exceptions too). That is however not a bad thing, just to set your expectations right. It's more a platformer than a Metroidvania.The coolest thing in my opinion is the "portal" ability. By pressing the "Toggle Portal" button (standard L1/LB) you open/close a "bubble" (Portal) where your character is (some follow you, some stay where you open them) and inside it the world changes in many creative ways (the idea is the portal leads to another world/dimension and properties of that world are transferred to where you are now, but they are only active inside the "bubble"). The areas of the game often have different kinds of Portals (so with different effects; there are 10 different portal types). In one section it inverts gravity, in another it changes objects which now interact differently, etc. This works really well and I found it quite creative what the level designer(s) makes you do with it. The levels are really well designed around this idea. Note: there are also sections where you don't have the Portal ability, so it's not always available and it felt like there is a lot of variety as a result.It also has a cute little story with two endings (I think) and some optional content that can be quite challenging. Overall I would say the game is not easy, but ofc some platforming pros might see this very differently. I'm personally not that good in platformers. For me the most difficult sections were optional, but if you are not good at platforming, even the main story sections might be difficult.The game orients imo a tiny bit at e.g. Super Mario World (I mean the jumping and how it feels, there is no sprinting though), I think it even has regrabbing (you fall slower when you hold or re-hold the jump button). Overall I found it controls and plays very well and for me it was a lot of fun. There was only one optional section I found a bit frustrating, else I had a blast, I even got 100%. I would say you can beat it 100% in like 10-12 hours, if you are good at platforming (unlike me) probably a bit faster.They did also a good job to keep tough sections optional. I think if you just want to complete the main story, it does not become too difficult. There are some boss fights, which also evolve mostly around platforming and maybe with one exception they never overstay their welcome. Instead of 10 hits it's only 3, which might be a bit too easy for good players, but for me it was the right amount of hits.In my opinion one improvement the developers could think about, would be adding a "Reset Portal" function on e.g. L2/LT. Ofc the toggle is needed for some sections, but every time you need to re-open a portal fast, you have to press L1/LB two times. One input to close it and one to open it again. That is often not a problem, but if you only have a very short amount of time (far less than a second) to do this and you have to repeat this in succession on top of that, it becomes a bit frustrating and exhausting for the hand. I had to rebind it (you can rebind buttons freely) to another button for some optional areas, so I could press it faster (for me double pressing L1 is quite slow). Having the close and open input (so basically a "reset") on one button, would have made it a smoother experience in those optional areas. In addition you also always have to keep track if you closed the portal already or not, which makes it imo a bit more complicated than it needs to be.Another thing that would have been cool (maybe I did not see it), would be an icon on the map where those portal ability on/off gates are. For some puzzles this information is useful.Overall absolute recommendation!
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: It is an enjoyable fun game at parts, but the difficulty spikes are uncalled for. One part of the game is all happy and fluent, you move around swiftly and do a few puzzles. I enjoyed those parts, would have loved the whole game to be like this. Because suddenly with the challenge areas the game becomes I wanna be the Boshy... _childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - Trust Fall, the game.$4 - A steal. $10 - a bargain. $20 - wouldn't have tried it.[+] The tutorial of this game is an absolute masterpiece.[+] The game clearly wants to tell you a story but it doesn't force it.[+] The gimmick of this game is the game. It isn't part of the game. It isn't stapled to the game. It is the game, and it's an absolute treat, and we can all learn a lot from this.This game is an absolute delight. You're going to either love this concept in it's entirety or you're going to find another game. That's about all there is to it. There are clearly situations in this game that you legit just have to trust that the developer put a platform over there, cause the only way it works is if they put a platform over there, and they did put a platform over there because they want you to know that you can trust them. You have to trust them. This is Trust Fall, the game, and I love it.I'm also sad. I played 4 other games before this that all had 10 - 20x the reviews and exposure that this cheeky little game got, and this game takes a multi-dimensional dump on the lot of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastical Journey: Adventures, puzzles, and skills... oh my. 8.5/10The artist in this game did an amazing job. The characters, level design and overall universe is unique and inspiring. Visually, this is such an amazing looking game. The overall game play and level design is well thought out and executed. Progressing through the game, obtaining the base upgrades and unlocking new magic abilities feels rewarding & keeps the game interesting. The game keeps you on your toes and fully immersed throughout the majority of your game play. Each magical skill brings its own skill set and way of approaching puzzles, which often feel engaging. _childDocuments_.review: I have a real soft spot for this game. It's 8 hours of endlessly expanding and innovating platforming action that scratches  a special itch in my brain. The artstyle is pleasant and cute, but can flex those horror muscles when it needs to. The story is good enough to keep me invested without feeling overbearing.The downside comes with the music, which is too simple and repetitive, especially for this kind of game, and the animation, which is honestly pretty bad at times, only passable the rest of the time.  But, I'd say those elements are fairly easy to ignore.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game and i have to say, this is a pretty solid and unique experience! Unlike others, i really wouldn't compare it to Hollow Knight or Ori, not because it's bad, but those games clearly have a bigger scale in terms of freedom and length,  Unbound is really interesting when it comes to gameplay, there isn't explicit combat, any encounter with enemies is dealt with changing the environment with the portal mechanic, and any puzzle also makes use of this mechanic, this is the ultimate charm of this game. The story may not be the most mind-blowing thing, but it's got it's thing going, it's interesting with charming characters and a great background, artstyle is great and the soundtrack is pretty good.All in all, i really liked this game, i do recommend buying it.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Unbound: Worlds Apart's main portal mechanic is a breath of fresh air for a puzzle/platforming metroidvania that allows the player to create pocket dimensions to other worlds, the inner workings of which greatly vary (gravity reversal, augmented strength, time manipulation, etc.). While some dimensions are used only one time and others are frequently encountered, the game allows the player to feel as if they've mastered them all. The game opens up and allows the player to explore at their own pace, leading to them picking up abilities such as double jump and dash. When these abilities are combined with dimensional puzzles, the depth of puzzles increases vastly. The story is relatively short (you can beat the game in about 3 hours if you leg it) and simple. It prioritizes being nonintrusive to the complex gameplay, frequently allowing the player to speak to characters more than once if they wish to know more lore details. Much of this lore is hidden behind the side quest of rescuing lost villagers scattered around the map, making completion and immersion go hand in hand. The game's score is phenomenal and deeply atmospheric. When taking on difficult puzzles of boss fights, these map themes often take on more intense instrumentation, driving atmosphere and immersion above all. Overall, Unbound is a great puzzle/metroidvania experience with a lot of Hollow Knight and Ori and the Blind Forest inspiration and a passionate development team.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: AAAAARGHH!!!! was my thought when trying a certain spot for... 30th time.Okay okay okay okay... Before I start frothing how much I like the game, let's get the poopoo out of the way first.The controls are not tight enough. I feel like precision platformer should and miniscule precision controls so I can make a split nanosecond decision to flip the dimension switch so the fireball coming at me becomes a bubble.The momentum feels weird. If there's any. when you boing boing up and down you get some momentum but it seems to just poot away at some point and that is infuriating.SIDES OF SPIKES SHOULD NOT KILL YOU! The game has abolutely merciless sequences and getting killed by slightly touching the side of a spike is just mean.Otherwise. I really enjoy the game. People compare this to Ori and Hollow knight but I don't buy that. This game gives you a jump and a ability to fart so hard you rip dimensions apart. There, now you may imagine a fart sound every time you finger the dimensional button. The game is beautiful and cute with some WHAT THE HELL IS THAT THING COMING TO KILL ME moments and it makes me tense up like a horrorgame. The platforming is the main thing here, you jump jump jump and jump while farting out dimensions of different flavors. Anyone comparing a PLATFORMER like this to Ori or Hollow knight must have their genres mixed because this is classic platformer on the rocks. You will need your reflexes and second counting brain close to hand or you will fart a dimension half a millisecond late and a fleshy sperm with teeth will make you it's dinner. You will die 50 times on the same spot and see the game looming over on your grave being like ''Ready to give up?'' And your job is to say NO and then wipe the sweat off your palms, to grab an aspirin and try again.This game is beautiful like an almost naked lady wearing jewels for lingerie. And notice that all the surroundings have probably been drawn twice since there is always something different on the background when you pop a dimensional cork. Sometimes it's pretty, sometimes it's like dimension of the butchers leftovers. But there's always something interesting to see.Mechanics. Jump and dimensional flatulence. sometimes your dimension popping pops the gravity upside down, sometimes it just disappears stuff and a appears some more dangerous stuff. Flavor or should I say fragrance of dimension depends on where you are so you don't have to worry about what dimension to fart about. It's not new for certain, anyone wanting to see the proto version can go to newgrounds and play Time ♥♥♥♥. This game is just less depressing and more colorful. Which is nice.Story. Evil is here. Banish it by jumping. It's not exactly epic for the ages but it does it's job. Tidbits here and there by villagers give a meager engagement because everyone has no face or voice to emote with. And since everyone is apparently Orko from He-man and the muscular bastard is nowhere to be seen so it's your magical self's job to fix things. So get to itAll in all I started playing today from... 11 am and it's now 19:00 pm so it's doing something right! So I enjoy the game where for once you aren't violently presenting sharp suppositories to enemies rear ends after rolling past them, which is most melee combat in 2D games. Nor are you going to the very edge of the screen to shoot your enemy  which is most 2D shooters. So here you are armed with jump, dimensional fart and candle at the end of your hood. I swear I wanna see that stupid hood phallus catch flame.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, i enjoyed my time with this game, Exploration, platforming, music, art, its all mostly great. This game doesn't have combat, it is platforming and puzzles. _childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: The art for both the environment and the characters is good, with small effects here and there that catch your eyes. You will admire the background when advancing through the level. The music is also nice, and fits the level design, getting more dynamic in the difficult areas making it feel more rewarding when you clear them.It starts easy but it gets challenging as the game goes on. The portals are an important part of most of the puzzles, yet there are areas where you only have to use your jumping and (later on) dashing. You will die trying to figure some puzzles but the checkpoints are nicely spaced out, so it won't feel punishing. Until you reach the optional side areas where things get very hard, where tight timings and quick combination of jumping, dashing and portal toggling are required. Here the checkpoints for some puzzles are farther apart and it may become frustrating redoing it all over trying to figure out the patterns and timings. There were times while I kept dying in the same spot over and over and wished the devs would step on a lego. But it feels rewarding when, on the n-th try, you do the full sequence perfectly and clear the puzzle. You will also unlock more clues related to the story.Took me 15h to 100% it and I don't consider myself good at platforming. I did not encounter any major bugs just a couple of times where the map was not zooming out, that was fixed by going to the main menu and back in. I personally liked it and I would recommend it to someone looking for a platformer.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome awesome game, had such a great time playing it. The atmosphere is amazing, the art design is beautiful and the soundtrack perfectly matches the world. Had a great time solving the puzzles and losing myself into the world. All in all, great little game with superb atmosphere and super engaging puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: It`s a platformer with puzzles and non-linear design, in which you use a bubble to switch between two worlds. This allows to bypass obstacles and find various solutions. The combinations of movement and ability becomes complicated as you progress, which gives the feeling of challenge.The story is typical, a disaster fell upon your village, and you must find a way to rescue your world or at least, your community, from what I`ve seen until now.I liked the feeling of fairy tale since the first time I saw the project and I was one of the backers on Kickstarter. The levels may feel a little empty in the beginning and is not about fighting, though. It becomes difficult, but not exactly in a Dark Souls Metroidvania style.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best looking puzzle platformer I've seen recently. Even though there's no voice oacting, you can totally understand what's going on with the animated cutscenes. Overall I really enjoyed this game and I am pretty sure you will too. Go and buy it while it's still on sale!
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Cute, Fun, and charming.The Devs are the worst trolls, in a good way, with the jumping puzzles and fiendishly sneaky traps.Unbound: Worlds Apart is a worthy little indie Metroidvania game. The art and the music tips its hat to Ori, and the NPC's to Ori and the Will of the Wisps as well as to Hollow Knight.I was wholly surprised that this game was going for so little money, it is extremely inexpensive for what you are getting. Yes, there is no voice acting in the game, minor grunts and such from the big NPCs whom you interact with, and mostly just silence from other minor ones. This however is not a detractor as the art style and music is full of charm. This I feel should also be taken into consideration whilst playing the game, that will have you pulling your hair out, and then celebrating once you've overcome what feels like an insurmountable obstacle.The puzzles are simple, though they don't feel it the first few times that you die, and doesn't take too much time to solve, if you die 45 times at a certain spider at the start of the game, then I would say that it is much more of a YOU issue than anything wrong with the game, and yes, you do die a lot in the game, but there is no real downside to this as you have infinite lives, and this mechanic is used to help you learn, and to frustrate you whilst the anxiety of slightly missing your goal crushes you under its full weight.Unbound - Worlds Apart has drawn me into the world that they have created, and I so wish that there will be something to add to the lore of the game, as the back story is very enticing.Don't expect this game to be Ori, and don't expect it to be Hollow Knight. It is very much its own little gem of a title. It's not very difficult, yet it can feel challenging. The negative reviews that I have read is mostly just people who expects more of the same, nothing dares to be a little different to those opinionated and self absorbed fools/tools/insert adjectives for annoying people who need to learn how to create their own games so that people can tell them how much of a clone their games are... instead of leaving a negative review, for what is the most stupidest of reasons.Unbound is fun, the music is chill, the puzzles feel good, and the game costs hardly anything. If you like Metroidvanias, consider getting this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: What a great game! If you like jumping puzzles, nice artwork, good level design with an interesting story and sensible checkpointing to return to when you die (so it doesn't get frustrating to get back to that 'one bit' you failed at), then this is the platformer for you. Love the characters in the game too! Defo worth having in your library!
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: A cool Metroidvania Puzzle Platformer with a magical artsyle and nice level design.- The main mechanic, the Portal, is cool and explored well throughout the game, especially in the later levels when it all comes together and all the cool portal effects help you get through the levels.- Level design is tight and smart, comparable to Ori and the Blind Forest- Art is great and the monster design is out there, but interesting- Music is pretty cool and flows relatively well with the game- Even if you get tired and have to take a break, you get the feeling of wanting to see the game through and beat the challenges it gives you. It's engaging, which is nice.- It can be a hard game, the tolerances for the platforming are often very tight and you'll find yourself repeating sections pretty often, even if you're used to these games. Not a negative though.- Bosses can be the most difficult aspect of the game because of having just 1 Life, but most of the longer fights had mid-encounter check points, so you don't lose much progress. It's the nice kind of 'hit your head against the wall until you learn' situation that might not be for everyone, but wasn't a problem for me.- None currently, only had 1 crash otherwise the game runs solid. Will report back if I find any.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the best I have ever played. The game not only look so good it gives AAA devs a run for their money, but the game itself. The levels are designed very well, and I like the ways they spice up the gameplay. From using new powers granted by unknown entities to none at all, the game is pretty varied. I only have a single gripe with this game, and that is the odd hitboxes. The hitboxes arent a problem themselves, but rather they dont cover all things that they should. All in all, get the game. 9/10 (would be 10/10 if the hitboxes where fixed)
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: I believe this to be a great platformer, I had lots of fun solving puzzles and unlocking sections of the map. The sound effects and ambiental music are great, definitely a 10/10.The visuals/ art are also great, I find the game to look better than it looks in the screenshots/ trailers while playing it. I would give the visuals a 9/10.The controls (I'm using a keyboard) are not as smooth as I would've expected, but this doesn't make the puzzles any harder to solve or anything like that. I'd give the controls an 8/10.Now, time for the story. If you're person who only plays games for the story, this game may not be for you. There is a backstory, but that's definitely not the point of the game. Dialogues are hard to follow and it seems like the story was added just to justify the game/ game mechanics. If you are however a person who is looking for a good platformer puzzle/ metroidvania/ precision platformer, then this may be a great choice for you.Overall the game is good, I'm gonna give it a positive review, and maybe update the review after I play it a bit more.

_childDocuments_.review: With its own Art Style it has comparative gameplay to like of Hollow Knight; its very challenging and each boss has a certain pattern of movement in order to progress and remain alive. _childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: 7.5/10 overall for the game. It's polished and well put together, and some very fun level design mechanics that are well utilised. The art is a bit budget but has its charm and is good enough for what it is. Music is nice, perhaps a bit repetitive after a while. The story was fairly intriguing but was more like a childs book. Why can't I recommend this? The difficulty spikes.... I was often having fun but then hit moments where it required micro micro millisecond input to get around a puzzle, the kind of the thing that you die and die and die again just to get that fraction of ms through. I found that more frustrating that fun and actually made me quit the game not wanting to go back. If they were a bit more lenient this would be a great recommended game. However I've got better things to do than punish myself on a 2D platformer for getting one more pickup that doesn't do anything special.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Generally a good game, needs a few more months of polish.Controls can be a little janky, hitboxes tend to be unforgiving, camera tends to follow rather than lead.There's a few pretty bad difficulty spikes where you have a couple minutes of platforming with no checkpoints.Probably worth it on sale if you really like hard platformers and metrodvanias.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Precise platforming and interesting puzzles, and while not uncommonly on a verge of difficult, it is very forgiving game and never felt stressful to play. Unbound has no health system and you die in one hit. However the autosave is set in pretty much every room which means that most of the time you're only  dealing with one obstacle at a time.The platforming and puzzles all felt great and fun to go through. When the game introduces a new mechanic, you get to explore it in depth before moving on which makes you feel like you really mastered all of them by the time you finish the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I don't like it. It just does not feel interesting or rewarding.The biggest point for me is the missed opportunity here. In each area you can open only one kind of portal, which one is predetermined, you have no choice whatsoever. This means, that combinations of portals are not possible, and not even try to overcome certain obstacles with different portals by switching them. Consequently, you figure out quite quickly how to overcome each obstacle (since you can only use one specific portal) and the difficulty stems more from the millisecond you have to hit the right key. I do not find this fun, this feels more like an ongoing QTE. As a result, the game is pretty linear. Yes, you can come back to already visited areas, but why should you? The only reward is to pick up some lost villagers that open up some bogus bonus level. Other than that, there is really no incentive to explore. Boss designs (there are a few) are interesting, but, again, you figure out pretty quickly what to do with the one and only portal available, to it transforms again into a very linear challenge where you have to follow an exact path to victory. Not sure whether I will have the motivation to finish the game. Probably not.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. I kept coming back to it even though I would die countless times. The music is fantastic and levels are fun. When I think I'm going to uninstall this game from rage quitting I come back and beat the part I was on. It makes you think on how to use your limited abilities to get to where you want to be. Very fun game! 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Unbound: Worlds Apart is a fantastic side-scrolling platformer that fondly reminds me of the platformers of the 90s on consoles like the SNES, but graphically updated. I love the dark atmosphere and mysterious tone, and I feel the story is compelling without being too convoluted. The gameplay is fun and often times extremely challenging. Some of the puzzles you'll come up against are substantially difficult, but the game is also forgiving - with an abundance of check points and immediate respawns with unlimited lives.I wholeheartedly recommend checking out Unbound: Worlds Apart to anyone interested in a modern take on the timeless platformer.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: ***TLDR AT THE END***Great game with LOTS of content. Unfortunately most of my time spent playing this game was offline with no internet so I don't actually know how long it took me to 100%. If I had to guess after beating the final boss and scavenging for all the collectibles I'd estimate it took somewhere from 10-13 hours. The game itself feels great to control, feeling very responsive and for the most part never really feeling like it was the game's fault for me dying more it was my own. The exception to this being certain segments of the game are long corridors with no check points that you have to do without getting hit once, and in order for these parts to be challenging the game does throw some obstacles with little to no reaction time available, requiring you to go through these segments multiple times based off of memorization. That being said however these segments were far and few between with a VAST majority of them not being necessary to beat the game, only to gather collectibles. Game play wise Unbound never felt like it got stale. It's a metroidvania-esc platformer that has a "portal" mechanic that lets you open doors to alternate worlds, changing the lay out of the map as well as the function of many monsters and traps. At first I thought this might get old really quick as the game's first type of portal doesn't have very much functionality, but as you progress you unlock more portals that allow you to access more worlds all with their own powers. One world might let you swap gravity, while another lets you freeze time, another letting you move enormous objects that only giants could lift, and more! These mechanics are all intertwined in a way that you're never left with one portal for too long as the game will swap it out with another one, presenting new challenges and puzzles.Combat in this game is... well non-existent. There is no fighting in this game as enemies are more obstacles than anything, requiring careful manuvering and strategy in order to either avoid them, or use the environment to kill them. Utilizing each unique portal grants a different way of dispatching enemies and each environment presents even MORE ways. There's only one time you ever really "fight" in this game but it still feels natural and doesn't break the way the game is played.The game has only one type of collectible that you can gather throughout. Trying to avoid potential spoilers these collectibles basically function as pages that you collect to fill up a book, each page telling more and more of the game's story. Don't fret though as there are PLENTY of these to gather, and while through my first play through I thought I'd managed to gather all if not almost all of them, it turned out that I'd only gathered 70-80%, which as somebody  who explores every nook and cranny imaginable, I was surprised to see how well hidden some of these secrets were. The reward for gathering these collectibles (again avoiding spoilers) is you get to read the full game's story and really understand the characters motives and the world around you. But the best part?If you couldn't care less about any of the story guess what? You don't have to read almost any of it! The game play alone is enough to entertain with 95% of the story being completely optional and only there for those who seek it out. This story, for those who care, gives it that extra nudge to truly make the game feel immersive. That being said, the story itself doesn't go very in depth without gathering the aforementioned collectibles, meaning that if you do want to explore the whole story (and see both endings wink wink) you have to gather A LOT of collectibles which, if you're not interested in or simply don't want to invest time into, will leave the story feeling lack luster.***TLDR/Conclusion***Unbound is a great game with lots of mechanics and puzzles that keep you thinking and ensures that the game never gets too stale. I had a fun time completing this game (played offline so sadly no achievments or much time played :( ) and would absolutely recommend this to anyone looking for a fun metroidvania-esc platformer. 9/10
