_childDocuments_.review: Unbound has only one gimmick--the use of portals that do various, generally-uninteresting things--and that gimmick gets stale pretty quickly. Especially because, rather than trying to flesh out the idea and make it truly interesting, the game just requires more and precise combinations of opening and closing portals while jumping. After a while, Unbound feels more like a rhythm game than anything else.And that wouldn't be bad, necessarily, except that there are frequent micro-stutters that simply don't belong in a game of this size and scope, and those micro-stutters happen when the screen is moving, which generally means you're in one of those movement rhythms. Then you die because of the stutter and have to do it all over again.There was one particular stretch that seemed like endless cycling between open--jump--jump--close--open--jump--jump--close and the stutters caused me so many deaths that I just gave up on the entire game. If the game were interesting and fun, I'd power through the stuttering issue, but it's not. It feels like they built the entire game, put in all the lore, secrets, quests, etc., and then just forgot to put in the gameplay.It should have been a puzzle game, with all types of portals slowly available to use in whatever combination required to solve the puzzle. Instead, each portal has its own section where only that one portal can be used, so there's no mystery at all about what needs to be done.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game because one of the top reviews said "If hollow knight was your favorite game and you liked Ori, you'll like this game", and I'll somewhat agree with that; This games does feel like it has the art style of Ori 1 but significantly cheaper looking, for the most part it looks decent though a lot of the enemies and spikes, really anything with multiple layers looked unfinished or unpolished, a bit too much like everything was in pieces rather then actual objects, also a lot of things were on the top layer when they shouldn't have been (the climbing vines animation/things inside of spawners). (Though the cutscene's are FANTASTIC, I'd say those would make up for the art style but there isn't enough/The games too short) (Also the Character design was pretty cool for the MC and the funny blue cat, and just in general) Other than that, the map looks the exact same as ori 1 but there are no mapstones, it just updates as you go along-There's literally 0 interaction you have with the map after getting it, which I feel like is a weakness for a metroidvania but given how linear the game is (I got more into this below) it wouldn't make any sense for you to get a map midway through an area because you can't really get lost. Also by the end the map looks suuuper unsatisfying because like ori every "room" you have to light up the edges by going near them, but in this game it doesn't show you a grayed out version of it before hand, and it's also literally impossible to reach the edge of all the rooms. (Also you have no reason to explore that much of any room). So by the end your map has a lot of ugly black all over it. Outside of the map and art style, this game isn't anything like Ori besides the fact that it's a metroidvania. (The puzzles might be a bit like Ori 1, if they are I don't remember Ori 1's puzzle's enough, I think the move-able blocks are a similarity I guess)As for feeling like Hollow Knight, the character's movement upgrades are  Though unlike hollow knight, the movement upgrades have no story relevance and feel like you're just handed what you need at the time, rather than finding it. Also there are no collectibles in this game, all the secrets are the same thing, just someone giving you a fragment of the story. There's no upgrades outside movement. Also there's no combat in this game besides boss "fights" which are all just dodge until you can jump on it or make it shoot itself or use a portal near it. I'd say 2 or 3 of the like 5ish bosses were actually pretty neat though still too easy. I don't know if this game would benefit from adding combat or not, feels like it's too small for that, and the way you avoid "enemies" is cooler than just slashing them (even if a little tedious at times)As a metroidvania, the game feels way too linear, there is some back tracking but there's really only 1 general pathway of doing things, this somewhat makes sense because of how annoying it would be to constantly re-traverse some of the platforming puzzles, though the game already has way points you can teleport to at any time so you wouldn't really have to do that. However, the custom mechanic was one of the most unique thing's I've seen in a metroidvania, and though I think the game would have been wayyyy better if each portal variant was a permanent that you could find and you could swap between them making the puzzles way more open ended, rather then locked to an area, I understand why they didn't (mostly because they'd have to "draw" the map like 10 times or something stupid like that). Kind of annoys me that one of them makes the movement feel actually SUPER fluid and fun and then you only get to use it for like 3 minutes and never see it again unlike every other one. Another critique is nothing feels special, like Hollow Knight or Ori, everything feels the same. No areas feel like they have any plot relevance (even the are they tell you is plot relevant just feels like everywhere else). The exception to this is the final zone, but even that felt like it was just a darker version of everything else, which is sort of the point I guess. This game also features After playing the game I read some more reviews I read a lot of people complaining the game was too difficult and that difficulty/gameplay was similar to that of Celeste and meat boy, which though I think this game was a bit easy, I didn't breeze through it though no boss took more then like 3-5 attempts. (Though Not to be cocky, I've an above average player as I tend to do a lot of really hard stuff in platformers, so this game didn't compare). The game is VERY forgiving because you don't really have health in the game, any time you get hit you just respawn before the puzzle/platforming challenge (which are typically really short). The game play is  like either meatboy or celeste, meatboy is a game with slidey/floaty fast paced controllers (the complete opposite of this) and Celeste is all about how you can utilize your dash to move around a room + how you can use throwable objects, neither of which are like this game. The only comparison I can draw to those games are if you get hit you quickly respawn at the beginning. Which is like every platformer ever, and this game isn't super huge on actual platorming, it's like you mashed platforming and puzzles together (which is what a metroidvania should be) but only went halfway with each. Though I'll say some of the most interactive platforming I've played besides Celeste. As for difficulty, not even close to either game since meatboy's gameplay is soooo fast paced and you can take this game super slow, and celeste has difficult cycles and is just wayyy more precise while this game only had 1 thing i thought was even remotely precise.The story of this game is a liiiitle generic and I've seen mixed reviews on it. I personally think the story they told was pretty good, though I felt like it needed more, and the way they told it could have been a bit more immersive (this spawns off the art style feeling like it's not super polished). The super high quality cut scene at the beginning made me think I was in for something better than I was, but there weren't enough cut scenes or dialogue. Though I did really like the world building they did, I felt like they should of had more then 1 reoccurring lore npc and just more story overall. Though I'll say I was satisfied with the story after reading through the collected dialogue at the end. (Imo there should be a place to read the spirit dialogue too, I don't see why there isn't.)Also the only bug I had was I didn't get the last two achievements when I was suppose to so I had to do the final boss another time. Also the game crashed like twice, though I joined the discord, people have reported more bugs that have to do with getting stuck in walls which they said they're gonna fix, I never had that issue.Overall this was a pretty good experience. I'd say it's a very average metroidvania with a super unique mechanic. I got it on sale, but because I 100% completed the game in 10 hours I wouldn't exactly say the $16 I payed for it was super worth it, no way is it worth $20. I think it's worth like $12. The game really just needs more, both story and gameplay, and a more polished art style. My biggest issue with this game is honestly the artstyle. With the custom mechanic it could of been one of the best metroidvania's out there, but just didn't really reach that.

_childDocuments_.review: I see many comparisons in other reviews to Ori and Hollow Knight, but make no mistake: this game's pacing and gameplay fall VERY short of both games.  Hollow Knight incorporates a lot of combat, has a rich modifying layer through the charms you can purchase and apply, and has deep lore that gets more meaningful through the voiceover acting (even though it is a foreign mumbling language).  Unbound: Worlds Apart is nothing like that.  There is no voiceover at all.  NPC's don't have character like they do in Hollow Knight.  Worst of all, there's basically no combat.  In most scenarios, you are forced to use your environment to kill enemies unless you are in an area where your portal ability allows you to deal damage (so far 3 hours in, the only such ability I have come across is a ground-pound ability by turning into stone....).The game is paced like this:  Reach area with portal ability.  Use portal ability to solve a puzzle.  After puzzle, walk through boring wide open areas with basic platforming while jumping over spikes, water, and enemies.  Lather, rinse, repeat, until you reach a boss fight that requires you to kill it without taking any damage due to the ever-present one hit deaths.  Die enough times and you'll get the pattern, but it's not particularly fun or challenging.  None of it is.The art is pretty and I like the style, but it honestly just makes me want to play Hollow Knight instead.  That game is so much more interactive with the combat and varying tactics used by the mobs' AI.  As a whole Hollow Knight is a far more satisfying and polished game while this is an appetizer that leaves you wanting more.**********************************************************************************************************EDIT:  The developer deleted their first comment where they claimed I was being unfair by comparing their game to Ori and Hollow Knight.  My original responses remain.**********************************************************************************************************@Developer Comment:  LOL.  I offer constructive criticism pointing out valid reasons why this game failed to capture my interest and simply wasn't fun to play, and you complain that I compared your game to another game in the same genre that did everything better?  You can't see the forest for the trees.  Bottom line, your game wasn't fun.  The reason I like Hollow Knight better is because it did everything better.  Animations, music, voiceover, worldbuilding, combat, usage of screen real estate, EVERYTHING.  Unbound: Worlds Apart is full of far too many empty boring sections.  There are long drawn out sections with nothing to do but jump over a few platforms with no combat to keep things interesting.  It feels like a walking simulator where most of the screen is empty and I'm slowly walking from one side to the other just to enter a new room filled with a few platforms and nothing to do.Instead of being offended by the fact that I didn't enjoy your game and prefer Hollow Knight, you'd be better served asking yourself the question "Why do they prefer Hollow Knight" (hint:  I tell you exactly why) and either consider incorporating more engaging elements to capture more customers' interest, or discard my feedback if it does not align with your design goals.Regardless, my feedback was entirely fair and reasonable despite the fact that it was critical.

_childDocuments_.review: People slamming Unbound for being a poor metroidvania seem to be missing the point: it's not really primarily a metroidvania, and it shouldn't be judged "merely" as such. At its heart, it's a puzzle platformer sharing more DNA with games like Limbo or Braid, than it does with Metroid or Castlevania. Of course there are shared elements. Yes, there's a map. Yes, you'll unlock traversal abilities. No, that's not enough to squarely place it in the metroidvania camp. The point being, if you expect a "pure" metroidvania, you run the risk of getting disappointed.What's the good stuff, then? The puzzles are good, even if not terribly difficult to solve, and most of the time you'll soon know what to do in any give set piece. Unbound is in my opinion better than average at giving players the clues needed. What's harder is usually the platforming that follows, but even that doesn't feel needlessly sadistic. At least for the main content. Some of the side content offers some seriously challenging platforming, and for some collectibles you'll have to think way outside of the box. All in all, the main content feels mostly fair to the player, but definitely challenging if you're not used to harder platforming titles. Fantastic looking game, too. Don't let the comparisons to the Ori games fool you, though. Unbound doesn't quite offer the same emotional gut punches, and it's not as fluid in its traversal mechanics. But I reckon fans of Ori will also enjoy Unbound. I know I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Having just recently rekindled my love for platformers, was very happy to play Unbound. The storytelling is immersive and the mechanics are very efficient. For the most part, the game has a very ingenious way of mixing puzzles and platforming with a very detailed map layout. The graphics are very polished and the transitions between the worlds are very smooth. I tried the game out with no expectations and was very pleasantly surprised by the level of detail, content and difficulty. I won't say it's an easy games by all means but it's very accomplishable with some effort. The platforming can be very tight in some areas, especially when going for full completion. I don't know that I would recommend this as your entry level to puzzle platformers but it's certainly doable for gamers with relatively limited experience. Overall, very pleasantly surprised by this hidden gem.  PSA. The game can be frustrating at times if you are unfamiliar with puzzle platformers but it's very doable.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked that game, even though it was pretty short. I'm not a very fast player, and got 100% achievements in 21 hours (two of which I was running around, trying to find the last spirit).As for the style of the game, it REALLY reminds of an Ori franchise. Honestly, I would have liked to see more original ideas (like the portals), but I do like Ori, so it was a nice experience.Good points:- graphics. Looks organic and beautiful, congrats to whoever designed the worlds, I love it!- music. Same thing, gorgeous atmosphere, I was completely immersed.- platforming challenges. Sometimes it got less like Ori and more like Celeste (with instant respawn and all). Pretty hard, but not impossible, and the puzzles are quite clever.- metroidvania side. Not very deeply exploded, but with new abilities you have several ways to approach each challenge.- bosses. They're original, and need to be "solved" instead of just punching right through them. Both arenas and chase sequences were very satisfying, and did also remind me of Ori.Bad points:- hitboxes. They don't always fit with the shape of the walls, sometimes with a very big deviation, it's not very good on a platforming game. I understand it's to reduce calculations, but then maybe a slope isn't the right design choice.- glitches. I'm playing on the native Linux version, and I got a few repeating bugs: a double death animation when falling into spikes, the double jump sprite leaving its trail until the next double jump, and one time I didn't respawn at all after dying, had to reboot the game. These are small things, but when they happens dozens of times in a playthrough, they do hinder the experience.- story. I finished 100%, got the whole lore, and still don't understand what the hell happened. Some would say it's supposed to be cryptic, but in the end I didn't really connect to anyone's struggles.- accessibility. I wanted to let my friend play, and she cannot press the buttons that fast, so I was looking for an accessibility feature, like Celeste's slowed down time. Didn't find one, which is a shame for a game that requires really precise movements. It's part of the challenge, but makes it impossible to experience for a lot of people.- linearity. Goes in pair with repeatability. Starting from the midgame, the game becomes very linear, similarly to Ori. I sometimes wanted to "leave a challenge for later" and go do something else, but quite often it was the only route left. It makes for predictable gameplay, but it means I cannot really play the game differently a second time.Keep in mind, indie games have small teams, many of these points are simply a consequence of a lack of time/budget. I got a really good time playing it, and would recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the Ori games.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't ever review on Steam but this game deserves much  much more praise than it's getting. If you're a fan of the Ori series or Hollow Knight, you'll enjoy this title and the beautiful hand drawn graphics. Unbound is a platforming Metroidvania that demands precision at times. I think it's funny that everyone LOVES souls-like (I don't) but most of the reviews about the difficulty of this game are negative. I think the difficulty is to it's credit. If you die, you respawn instantly, right before that challenge, without distant checkpoints to walk back from. This is an awesome game that I can't wait to finish and I can't emphasize this enough, it's a shame the developer hasn't been as successful as those other hand drawn titles because they truly deserve it. Graphics: 10/10, I love hand drawn games.Sound: 8/10, pleasantly moody atmospheric tracks, inclusion of sfx for speech would be good addition in next entry.Controls: 8/10, minor things like character walking inertia are missing but forgivable.Plot: 8/10 So far plot isn't mind bending, but writing much better than average.Strong recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I was captivated by the art style and concept at first, thinking that this will be a game with great story, beautiful art, and creative mechanics.I love the style on this one. However, I find it a bit wasted that we don't have different skins for different worlds after the player progressed through a portal.Not exactly a novel and groundbreaking idea, but I find the concept to switch between world to be quite fresh. Furthermore, it is implemented very well, I didn't experience any bug or glitches using this mechanic.The gameplay is relatively fun. Some puzzles are feel intuitive that you could just finish it with no effort, some would make you pause and think for a while, and some are annoyingly hard. I enjoy trial-and-error puzzles, but puzzles that require impeccable timing with long sequences with no checkpoints in between is not fun at all.Though just playing in for several minutes already made me feel that this game seems to be heavily inspired by "Ori". Can't disagree on that train of though, Ori is a fantastic game. But Ori had very intense and fun boss fight sections, where it gets your heart racing and feels very rewarding at the end. A very nice occasional jump from the passive gameplay that spans throughout the game. I was hoping that Unbound: Worlds Apart actually have something similar to that. This is a point-reduction for my case, cause it felt flat after a while, even on boss fights.I believe that the story is the biggest flaw of Unbound: Worlds Apart. The opening and intro feels too rushed, it felt like it was added after the game had finished. Players haven't had enough time interacting and building an emotional connection with the village, then it's just gone and destroyed by demons. Me as a player definitely doesn't feel anything about them, not a shred of sadness.The plot is also very predictable. I haven't finished the game, but I could see where this is all going.Not a bad game, fun concept that introduces a whole range of creative problem-solving solutions. Good art style that feels cohesive throughout the game. It's just the story that this game lacks the most, and I feel that's one of the most important component in a beautiful platformer game.

_childDocuments_.review: Take this with a grain of salt as I have not played that much yet, but I wanted to share my first impressions.Unbound: Worlds Apart is a high quality puzzle platformer with some metroidvania elements. You play a small wizard and can spawn portals that will modify the world in a certain area (circle around the place where you placed the portal) and exchange it with another realm. In practice, this means in the circular area, new platforms may show up, obstacles may disappear, or enemies and traps may alter their behavior. Even physics may change, in one section, you walk the ceiling instead of floor in one of the worlds like in VVVVVVVV. It's more much a puzzle than an action or fighting game: I'm not in very far, but I cannot attack enemies (other than by using portals to lure them into traps) and I doubt that this will change.Pros:* beautiful presentation, feels very polished in everything* good controls* world is split into tiny separate sections, and if you die, you instantly respawn right before the current puzzle without delay or punishment, and without any wait time or need to press a button. Perfectly done!* good and creative puzzles, and many require some precision, e.g., you may need to switch between worlds very quickly at precise positions to overcome some sections* different portals in different sections of the map, fresh mechanics in each section.* metroidvania-style large map, a good in-game map so you always know where you are, and great quick-travel options at fixed points which are clearly marked on the map* great difficulty. the game is rather hard, but definitely not too hard, I would say its not made for young children, but apart from that, everyone should be able to enjoy it. It's really no way like Hollow Knight or these games. It starts quite easy and slowly gets harder.Cons: none so far, I have to say. I am really impressed. Note: I am not in far enough to tell whether it gets repetitive after a while. So far, there are only 2 buttons to press (apart from moving left/right): jump and the button for portal on/off, and the gameplay is basically coordinating these two while navigating hazards. Sounds simple, but it is a lot of fun, and so far I can in now way complain about the simplicity in controls. Also maybe more mechanics will show up later. I only recently got the double-jump.Overall 9/10 from me so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts off pretty dull, with not much to do except jump - that doesn't really change even later in the game. The mechanic of opening portals is the main thing of the game, but it's effect changes based on location, which makes it very limiting. You get some others "mechanics" later on but these are very basic for 2D platformers, so don't expect much.The difficulty of this game is very questionable, as most of the time the game is pretty easy, but out of nowhere there are huge difficulty spikes, where it took me really a long time to get over the challenge. The game is very harsh on platforming, which forces very precise platforming and timing. As for individual challenges, its not that rough, as the game autosaves pretty much after every challenge/thing.Overall I enjoyed the game, even 100% completed it, and can recommend to people who like games like Ori.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Cute but difficult game. Gameplay is similar to Hollow Knight, although you are not much of a fighter. In this game, you control certain magic that allows you to get across. The game doesnt have much abilities, and its all about agility most of the time as you get through obstacles. Less combat.Its pretty challenging, I would recommend it if you like games similar to Hollow Knight.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: A fun-sized version of Hollow Knight. Everything about it is simpler than HK, and its enjoyable because of it. Unfortunately, when it tries to get a bit more challenging in some of the more tucked away parts of the game, it suffers a bit mechanically as the movement and control over the character is not as tight as others in this genre. I enjoyed it for its puzzle aspects and almost wished there were less "bosses" and more puzzles to solve. It would have been a great addition to be able to use the portal powers you see individually over the course of the game used more in-tandem than one or two times they tie them together. Still worth the price (especially on sale) and time as it was a quick 9 hour jaunt to nearly full clear achievements and all endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun and quite challenging puzzle platformer. It starts of rather slow, but gets more fast paced and harder the more you progress. The game also has very forgiving checkpoints which makes harder sections a lot more enjoyable

_childDocuments_.review: A unique little game full of atmosphere. Definitely recommend for people who enjoy games like the Ori series. _childDocuments_.review: This game is great i love the art style and the creativity its a really cool game were you get a crystal wich can be used to do things. if you use the crystal near a living creature (plant animal ect) it might change into something that can help you or hurt you normally if it normally dos not hurt you it will hurt you if it go's in the crystals range and like a spike might change into a ladder wich you can climb. _childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Its good for the castlevania nerds and challenging for gamers who like Celeste, wouldn't say it sets a new bar for the genre... but it has some creative designs in using portals in its puzzling that shows you what the apocalyptic feature brings and paths and how enemies will grow up is creatively fun. _childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Great game but it's just not entirely for me. The target audience are probably people who prefer platforming over combat, because it's exclusively a platformer. I'd suggest getting it if you don't have a problem with challenging platforming and don't need combat in a game.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: This game shows a good deal of promise. Its graphics and music are excellent, and it has a good feel to it. However, much of the game time is padded by deaths due to the one hit health system. You take a hit, you die and return to the last checkpoint. This isn't too aggravating in the early portion of the game, but later on through the middle and especially the end it becomes an excruciating roadblock. I would still recommend this game but holy hell it is difficult. Fortunately, it's not too difficult to 100%, but beating the game in general is an ordeal in itself. I do feel that this game has wonderful concepts to offer, but it's overshadowed by mild jank and underdeveloped mechanics. I'd love to see some polish added to various aspects of the game. The story in particular lacks the gravitas the game is trying to sell to the player - again, it feels slightly rushed and lacking some extra thought that would really make it shine.For now, it earns a 7.5/10. I would say I'm hopeful for the devs to polish this game up, but seeing as they haven't updated the game in over a year now, I'm not going to lie to myself or others. I can't see myself replaying this, but I don't mind spending a few hours on it. Go ahead and give it a go, but don't expect this to be the next Ori game.

_childDocuments_.review: 9.5/10A lazy review would be “Limbo’s gameplay meets Ori’s art and music”. A unique game, and a VERY challenging puzzle platformer…you’ll die a lot! The art style, mechanics and gameplay are worth it. (Are these Steamdeck issues or game issues?)Highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: so being brutally honest.the game was good, but only at a discounted price for how short it is.word of warning this may seem like a puzzle platformer, but in a few points of the game it is more of a precision puzzle platformer with a few areas that were designed by someone who likes to see others suffer.the difficulty once you get the mechanics down was fairly average save for those few spots mentioned above,the story/plot is more of a backdrop so the game has a reason to be (its not bad, but its not really something that you need to get into to play the game).only encountered one bug during the whole game whos trigger conditions are highly unlikely to occur (but did blue screen me)all the platforming itself was fluid and responsive, the landscape was pleasant to look at.if i had to point out the largest sin of this game its the fact that they introduce you to this adorable cat like creature at the start of the game, and there are no plushies to be found... and you cant pet them in game TT(IMO. they probably could of made more money making the game super cheap and then just marketing plushies for the critter in different poses)

_childDocuments_.review: I personally enjoyed the demo more than the full game. The full game starts too tedious before becoming good when it hits the stride of the demo, then it returns to tediousness. I wish gates were marked on the map, I wish the demon fight didn't even exist (talk about a trial and error memorisation game), I wish there was a way to turn off screenshake, I wish shortcuts stayed open, and I wish my achievments didn't break. It feels like there's a good game underneath (honestly the aesthetic and mechanics are great) but small gripes add up fast. I feel like the devs had more they wanted to do; there's a couple mechanics that show up once, maybe twice, and then disappear again, and it makes me feel like the game is incomplete.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't bad, let me say that right away. That being said it is buggy (there is a bug in the desert level that keeps causing your character to randomly die for no reason when jumping on a moving block even though there is nothing on the block to kill you) inconsistent with its difficulty due to only being able to have 1 portal of 1 type making the difficulty based on the mechanic of the portal (1 type just makes you able to push or pull bigger blocks and is the easiest level because of that) rather than how far into the game you are which is deeply frustrating and the metroidvania aspect is mostly a lie. The only reason to backtrack is to save villagers which offers no in game benefit despite requiring movement power ups to get. The real problem with the game is that, while it isn't a bad game, there are better platformers (if looking for difficulty try Celeste), there are better metroidvanias that actually reward backtracking instead of it being a collectathon, and the lore isn't interesting enough to justify playing this game over something else, especially when it costs 20 dollars at full price when there are better games that are also cheaper.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: It's... fine. The puzzles are reasonably fun, if pretty easy most of the time. None of the characters feel anything other than flat and tacked-on. The final cutscene didn't really mean much of anything in the context of the (very weak) story. The heroic sacrifice at the end feels shoehorned in. The map isn't much to speak of. All the environments kinda blend together as approximately the same, with slight variations.Done with it after 6 hours, probably won't be picking it back up again to finish the optional areas.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Despite all the bad reviews, I gave this game a shot when I saw it was on sale. I'm very glad that I did.Many people have written that this game is too hard and too punishing, and I do agree to some extent. But it has been a REALLY LONG TIME since I've been challenged by a platformer this much. Also, different portals giving different mechanics was a nice design decision in my opinion.It may not be everyones cup of tea but I love hard challenges, especially platforming challenges. The whole game felt like a really long Path of Pain (from Hollow Knight). So even though difficulty was an issue for some people, it was the very thing that made this game fun for me. However, I agree that instant death can be quite punishing, especially if you miss just one action in a sequence of 20 actions. Maybe an easy mode for novice players would allow for more people to enjoy this game.The art style was very vibrant and colourful. Backgrounds and environments were AMAZING. I can't say the same for animations though. The player's animations and some other characters' were fine, but some enemies were very poorly animated using simple rigging. The music was pretty in the beginning, but in some places it got very repetitive and messed with my concentration so I turned it off.I didn't care about the story that much. The quests were also always the same: collect some crystals so the wizard guy can open a door, then collect some more crystals so another wizard guy can open another door. Some variation would've been nice.For those people who said that this game tries to be Hollow Knight or Ori, I would have to agree. Ori in the sense of art style and environments, HK in the sense of platforming and abilities. The dash and wall jump were almost identical to that of HK. But I don't mind games getting "inspired" by other games, I don't necessarily see it as stealing or copying as long as the game also has unique stuff.Overall, I enjoyed it. It was much shorter than I expected but I had a good time. If you think this game is a metroidvania, it's not. It's pretty linear. But I like linear games too. In conclusion, if you like platformers and want to be challenged, you should give it a shot. The challenges were what kept me hooked.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: It's fantastic, I like it's Hollow Knight style features, and it starts slow but gets faster as the game progresses. The portal abilities are fairly unique and some challenging puzzles with it. The story is easy to understand and gets straight to the point. One complaint is the hitbox of spikes being wayyy bigger than they look (or maybe Soli's head is just that big). Either way, 8/10 game.

_childDocuments_.review: one of the best puzzle platformers i´ve played so far.if you liked hollow knights white palace then this is the right game for you.but keep in mind the platforming is not really momentum based like in celeste or super meat boy. if you search for something like that then you can probably skip this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- You basically get two games worth of amazing art, since every time you open a portal, you see a totally different scenery.- Portals offer lots of different platforming mechanics without building up a huge list of moves (like other Metroidvanias). There are always the basic moves (with their upgrades) and one special portal mechanic.- Story and characters don't get in the way of me enjoying the platforming.- The difficulty structure is very consistent with easy-ish sections on the main path and difficult sections for collectibles and towards the end of the game.Neutral:- The game is very lenient with its save points, so it often throws an enemy or trap at you, you die, respawn, and then you have to figure out how to avoid dying again and how to get past the traps. Or you have to blindly jump into a spike pit and maybe find the hidden platform in the portal world.Negatives:- Some audio issues are present, where in some sections the music becomes extremely loud or there are (loud) sound effects from things you can't even see.- There is no button for placing a portal, only for toggling it - i.e., you have to double-tap to deactivate the old portal and activate the new one. This is not only unnecessarily difficult and stressful in some challenges (when you also have to jump, dash, and avoid spike walls), but also uncomfortable (you need to press the button twice as often).

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Unbound Worlds Apart is a very ambitious, beautiful, puzzle platformer w/ some light metroidvania elements.  There is a lot to like here, but unfortunately, it doesn't all come together in the end.  There are better metroidvanias and puzzle platformers out there, but I still think this is a fun game that's worth experiencing if you are a fan of either genre.What's Good:-This game looks awesome visually, and is the main reason most ppl will give this game a try.  The visual style reminds me of a cross between Limbo and Ori and the Blind Forrest.  There are a bunch of different biomes and each one has a unique visual style, introduces new enemies, and offers engaging puzzle/platforming sections.-This is a puzzle platformer w/ an emphasis on quick platforming.  It feels like a hybrid between the two genres, similar to Evergate.  This is by far the most fun and challenging part of the game.  The use of a portal mechanic is the main mechanic, but you will also gain upgrades that make this mechanic and the puzzle/platforming sections more dynamic.-This game has a lot of charm and finds that balance between good and evil or light vs dark.  There are tons of likeable npcs and really unique villains.  You will learn more about the world as you talk to companions and complete increasingly complex sections of the game.-There are a good amount of secrets scattered throughout the game which adds some interesting challenges.  I really enjoyed exploring the world, seeing what else I could find.  It took me about 8 hrs to complete the main game and find about 80% of the secrets.Could Use Some Changes:-This biggest problem w/ Unbound is that it's not that great of a metroidvania or that good of a puzzle platformer.  It's extremely linear, doesn't really bring anything new to either genre, and plays it really safe.  Evergate is a significantly better puzzle platformer that has similar mechanics.  This game barely even qualifies as a metroidvania, which makes it tough to recommend to metroidvania fanatics.-Even though this game is marketed as a puzzle platformer, the platforming sections near the end start to feel similar to challenging precision platformers.  Some of these sections expect you to have pretty good hand eye coordination and make really fast decisions.  I didn't find this game that hard, but less experienced platforming fans may struggle w/ some of these sections.Consensus:-Middle of the Road Game (Tier 4 and makes up 25% of my reviews).  I more or less enjoyed most of the 8 hr campaign, even if I was slightly disappointed w/ the overall experience.  I paid $10 for it, and I think that price point is spot on.  I'm happy to recommend this to platforming fans at 50% discount or better.  It looks amazing visually, has a solid soundtrack, and has charm for days, but unfortunately never quite reaches it's lofty potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished the Unbound: Worlds Apart yet, but I will say I really like it so far!  The platforming is amazing, and the portal puzzles are SO much fun to figure out! It's definitely challenging, don't get me wrong!  I really like the soundtrack, but it's the subtle 'environmental' sounds that are my favorite. Sometimes I gotta pause and turn up the volume to listen to all the details. Some other sounds are sadly a bit loud so I can't leave the volume up. This is where Unbound loses me personally. The story doesn't grasp me, and I'm not sure if it's the way of story telling, the difficult words (I'm not a native English speaker) or if the story just doesn't feel very unique... But it doesn't bother me too much, because the rest is great!Also: If you enjoyed Hollow Knight, Ori, Limbo or Degrees of Separation: this is a game you should check out!
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: A platformer with logical elements.  The visual style is very polished and well animated. The worlds are quite detailed and pretty. Overall it reminded me of an animated movie.  The gameplay consists of platforming with some logical puzzles. Apart from classic abilities like double jump and wall grabbing there are whole sections where it is possible to switch into another parallel reality with different laws of physics, for example the inverted gravity. The controls are fluid and reactive. I have run into several difficulty spikes, but that may have been because I am not particularly adept at quick precision jumping. That is also why I was unable to finish important side-quest and get the good ending.  Overall it was a great looking and fun game, that began to be a bit frustrating and too demanding for me towards the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly good platformer!I've had this game on my wishlist pretty much since the game was launched. I finally decided to buy it and I must say...I'm impressed.Anyone who has played either of the Ori games will immediately notice a resemblance to it. The overall tone of the game and art direction were definitely influenced by those game. Which is fine. Even some of the in game elements are very similiar. Plants and rocks in the foreground, not something original to Ori but I couldn't help but make the comparison. Also, the way the map is set up with the objectives being big circles is uncanny Ori. It's also somewhat a metroidvania with some light backtracking but not on the scale of Ori or Hollow Knight or anything like that. So far, I've only gotten one new ability and I've gotten pretty far in.Anyway, just wanted to get that out of the way. The gameplay is nothing new. It's a sidescroller, platformer with the gimmick of being able to create portals around your character which will reveal an alternate dimension. Doing so will make platforms appear or make monsters disappear. Pretty standard stuff. At first I actually thought about returning the game because it was so overdone already. But then the platforming really started to pick up. There's a puzzle element and timing skill that really needs to be developed to figure out how to get past certain parts. I was surprised how well thought out some of the sections were. Stuff that really makes you think about how to approach each part. But it also starts to feel fluid and second nature. It's hard to describe but the platforming is really good! The difficulty starts to ramp up out of nowhere, though. If you aren't in love with difficult platforming (think Celeste and such) then you probably won't end up finishing this one. It gets freaking tough! Tough platforming is my jam so I'm all for it but I could totally understand why someone would give up on this game.As for story, I have no idea what's going on. There are some animated cutscenes throughout but they didn't immediately grab my attention so I kind of just gave up on it. There is a bunch of dialogue from characters strewn about the game if you're into that kind of thing. I sometimes am but this one didn't do it for me. It doesn't matter, though. Not comprehending the story has not deterred from my enjoyment of the game at all.If you love tough platforming and gimmicky game mechanics done right, then check it out. If you can find it on sale then it is definitely worth the purchase!
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: To my shame this one lay in my steam account for over a year before I even touched it...what a shame.Imho this is one of the best platformers of 20s so far. If you liked Hollow Knight, Ori and its cousins: Buy this. It is not about fighting but platforming, and challenging platforming at that. Luckily, the controls are very well done 9 out of 10 times.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those "in-between" games. If you have difficulty dealing with frustration, maybe skip this one. First off while I consider this a good game it's not really a metroidvania, it's just a mostly linear puzzle-platformer using metroidvania abilities (which is fine depending on your mood). I found the puzzles were just about right for this type of game. The story is pretty irrelevant and you only get a few abilities. The puzzles are largely pretty good, the controls are not largely pretty unfortunately. At times the character will not stop moving even if you stop holding the button and the dash didn't work well (this improved somewhat when I rebound it to the right shoulder button so it could just be my controller). The game has a really weird checkpoint system, at times it will save really close then you'll have a long stretch of nothing. Like towards the end there's a pretty difficult chase sequence and after that you have dash over a fire after sliding down a ledge, I failed that 2 times and had to redo the chase sequence every time, and this type of thing happened a few times. There are also bosses in the game, which I don't like in 1HP games, most of the bosses are pretty easy but the last one was a pain. There are some puzzles that are somewhat inaccessible due to too tight timing of switching the portal on & off but I could manage them for the regular ending, but not the true ending (I'm assuming the cores lead to a separate ending). Overall I liked this game and consider my time with it well spend, but I also considered myself done after just completing it normally without going for what I assume will lead to a true ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun little puzzle platformer, in which you use magic portals to alter the game environment. I could 100% the game in about 8 hours but i think its worth its price.Finishing the main storyline isnt too hard but if you want some challenge you can find the collectibles (villagers) and do the bonus levels they unlock which are quite challenging.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun platformer. Challenging but not too challenging for experienced players. Low stakes - dying starts you at a checkpoint that is very nearby. The art is great. The powers are neat to see and I was surprised just how deep into the game they kept introducing new ones. Story was more or less a throwaway in my opinion but it wasn't designed to be the star of the show anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: An underrated gem. Quite difficult and precise platformer with some unique mechanics, beautiful beautiful artwork, nice atmospheric music and sound design and thought out lore. If you don't mind getting challenged on your platforming skills, then this is an auto grab. Really the creators did such a good job! The final bossfight is super fun.Each mechanic is first shown in simple examples and then utilized and combined with others in many unique and creative ways. The only little drawback I can think of is that the character control is not as good as some other platformers like Ori or Celeste, but those are the absolute top. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, a well designed platformer. It also has a couple bonus areas if you find enough secrets, and while the first one definitely put my skills to the test, the second one, which I thought would have been more difficult, was shorter and easier, so kind of a disappointment there.But despite the high level of polish, it's a very short game.  Steam said time played was 5 hours by the time I beat it, 7 hours by the time I got all achievements.  So I don't think it's worth the full price of $20.  Fortunately, I picked it up on sale for $12, but even then, that's at the very high end of what someone should pay.  All in all, if you like platformers it's worth playing, but wait for a good sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Unbound is a fun puzzle platformer with great visuals and music.I have never played a game that cares about my time this much, there's a checkpoint after every single small puzzle or jump sequence that you make. It's still challenging like similar games but thankfully it doesn't demand that you master every single section and prove it again and again until you do all sequences perfectly. If you did something once you're good and you will start at the next section even if it's half a screen away. I really enjoyed this system, I think most developers think it's too easy or cheapens their game (or makes it shorter), but for me it just made the game smooth and not frustrating.Similarly you can use portals from anywhere, which makes moving around a breeze with no need to backtrack annoying jump sequences over and over. I think the bosses are also very well designed with the right amount of challenge.A few things worth mentioning: it's not really a metroidvania as the paths are fairly linear, there's no real combat (well mostly uhm), the story is just skippable, the goal is always to get to place x, it's a bit shorter than I'd hoped, and it would have been nice if the little optional puzzles would have given something worth trying for. All that said, the game feels smooth and clever all throughout.Definitely recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Unbound: Worlds Apart is a sweet metroidvania. It obviously takes inspiration from Hollow Knight in its movement, and from the first game of Ori with the overall feel of the game. Despite this, it is not to be mistaken as a clone: it brings a lot of uniqueness and charm to the game with the main gimmick, the portals.Things I liked:- Let's talk about the elephant in the room: the portals that Soli can manipulate. There's around a dozen of different ones throughout the entire game, that act as abilities and they all have their own main gimmick. Some will affect gravity, or time, or possible alter the layout of the world within the range. Most also have a secondary feature (with some overlap), such as how they will transform enemies or projectiles. These different powers get granted and taken away by the game constantly, which means you only own them for specific areas. This may sound like a bummer, but I think it's a positive. With the large amount, it would be hard to remember which one does what niche little thing, so it's nice to be limited to only a couple per area and have that built around it instead.- Soli can essentially never defend themselves directly. There are two portals that allow them to attack, and that's about it. Instead, the game tries to use enemies as a part of the environment to navigate. Often, it will push you to use them to press buttons, or jump, and sometimes they will simply hinder you. Regardless, it uses them more creatively than simply being a minor inconvenience you will kill.- The game is very beautiful. This is especially the case with the few cutscenes sprinkled into the game, but it generally is quite nice. My favorite part of it are the backgrounds, but the characters and environments are pleasant too. It also has really cool music. Things I may have disliked:- The movement can be a little clunky at times. I believe this gets fixed as you get more and more permanent movement upgrades, and the issue isn't necessarily there. The way I saw it, it was more that certain rooms may feel awkward because they weren't fully adapted to Soli's current kit, and not necessarily the kit itself. I had very little issues with that personally, but I am pointing it out because it appears to be a common complaint.- While it does have a story, it ends up being quite forgettable and anticlimactic. It obviously had a vision, and you can see it, but I wouldn't buy the game if the narrative is your main focus.- The game is a bit short. It took me around 5 hours to first beat it, and I had every achievement in a bit under 9 hours. I would give Unbound: Worlds Apart a solid 8/10. It was a super enjoyable game, and I had a great time playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: The tone and mood are enjoyable and there is enough difficulty to be interesting, but the game is kinda small. Got all the achievements in a little under 3 hours of play time. I would have liked the game to be a little longer as there was definitely some unexplored space around the core mechanics. In particular, I would have liked to see more puzzle or platforming sections where you are able to switch between portal types.The 'open' world wasn't really all that open. There were very few areas you could access early or via alternative means and usually those 'shortcuts' immediately hit a dead end due to missing some mobility power or another. Several zones are mentioned by NPCs that never actually appear as well. The lore speaks of all these worlds and places that the population is spread out across and you go to a sum total of 3 of them. I also think the progression was a little weak. Your mission largely boils down to 'go here and fetch me some gems so I can open this door so you can fetch some more gems.'I'd put overall difficulty around that of Ori and the Will of the Wisps or maybe the primary campaign of Celeste. Some of the extra puzzles or 'challenge' areas maybe dip a little further than that though.Overall, I'd say this game is worth it, but only just. While there's not a massive amount of content, the core mechanic is interesting and engaging enough to be worth the experience.Pros:- Interesting core mechanic- Sufficient challenge to be engaging- Lovely art style- Music is enjoyableCons:- Not a lot of content.- Main game is largely a collection of (nested) fetch quests.- Open world isn't all that open after all.- No replayability

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - Unbound: Worlds Apart is a fun platformer and well worth a playthrough! Although the playtime:price tag ratio seems a little high.A super adorable looking platformer! Some of the sections are tricky, particularly when aiming for 100%, but it's enjoyable throughout. Respawn points are frequent so you rarely have to redo long sections when you die (and that WILL happen, a lot), and they also autosave the game.The puzzle aspect didn't seem too challenging, which was a good thing - there were very few points where I couldn't work out what to do within a few attempts (the only one that really sticks out to me was in the first trial).Playtime for me was about 7 hours for 100%, probably 5 or so for just the storyline - there's not too much off the beaten path, although revisiting areas is needed for 100%.Story is a little confusing at the start but very quickly becomes clear. There is a bit of lore around but you only get fragments at a time, and you're quite likely to get them out of order so the backstory can be hard to grasp. There is places you can read it in order, however. Overall however, the story isn't terribly important to the gameplay, and you can get most of it in hindsight.I did encounter a couple of bugs/glitches, both tied to respawning - one just insta-killed me one extra time, which is very minor. The other was bigger, in which the game failed to actually load anything aside from the background, and the controls all did nothing. Force quit and restart solved the issue at least.The fun factor of playing this game far outweighs the small negatives (ie the bugs mentioned), and I would definitely recommend this to anyone who likes platformers! It has vibes reminiscent of Hollow Knight and Ori so if you enjoyed those you'd probably like this one too :)(Shoutout to the dev Alex who dropped by my stream to say hi!)
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game. It's incredibly difficult in places, but every level is intricately designed and looks absolutely beautiful. _childDocuments_.review: I think it's really important to go into this with some lowered expectations.  The visuals are absolutely stunning and from watching gameplay, you'd think this would be a pretty great metroidvania.  It isn't that though.  There is no leveling, there are no items, there's no equipment, or even fighting in general.  You only get 3-ish progression skills the whole game.This is basically a puzzle platformer and nothing else.  But it does this well.  Along with the aforementioned visuals and good music, it's a very good experience.  I do fell like certain areas the difficulty spikes incredibly sharp at certain places, but goes back to normal shortly after.  But yeah, if you come in with tempered expectations, I am pretty sure you'll have a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great! A fun metroidvania heavy on platforming with very little combat, interesting mechanics, good level design and beautiful art. The soundtrack by Alexey Nechaev is cinematic and swelling, and really adds to the experience. I didn't find the story super interesting but it's also not very intrusive so you can ignore it if you want, or look for lore, which there is quite a bit of because each villager you save (there are 40+) gives you a bit of the story which you can piece together to get the whole thing. Movement is very Hollow Knight-esque, combined with the mechanics of different portals make this game very fun to play the whole way through. Very nice game, would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: This game was definitely an enjoyable experience.Don't go into it expecting Hollow Knight. I'd say it's closer to Celeste.The gameplay is, for the most part, a series of platforming challenges using a large variety of different portals and mechanics. Some of the platforming is pretty difficult, especially toward the end of the game. The hardest stuff was taking me 15-20 attempts and sometimes even more. If you don't have the patience to keep trying something over and over until you raise your skill enough to succeed, then you probably won't like this game. However, if you're willing to keep trying, the moment you finally do succeed is very satisfying.There are several boss fights in the game, and the first couple times I encountered one it was daunting. However, once I figured out how the fight worked, in terms of the attack patterns and the way to damage the boss, it didn't take long for me to get really good at them. The final boss is one of the hardest challenges in the game, as it should be, but it has several save points throughout the different stages so you don't have to start from the beginning. Just the first stage alone took me a huge number of attempts to beat. Later though, when I went to beat the boss again to get the better ending, I beat the first section in two attempts, since I still remembered how to do it. The noticeable increase in your own skill level just from trying something over and over is the reason I play games like this. It's very rewarding. If you also enjoy challenges like that, I can confirm this game has plenty of them.While the majority of the challenge comes from the platforming, there are a few puzzles in the game as well. None of the most difficult puzzles are required to get the normal ending, or even the best ending, but they are required for learning the full story, and getting all of the achievements. There's a bunch of villagers that you have to find hidden around the map, and my understanding is that you only need half of them to get the best ending, so you could theoretically skip the puzzle based ones. If you like puzzles though, there's a couple that have very clever solutions, requiring outside of the box thinking.The story is pretty simple, but the way it's slowly revealed bit by bit is well done. There are several twists that make it worth paying attention to, and taking the time to learn it all.I played through the whole thing within a couple of weeks of its release, and I encountered several bugs. However, the great majority of the bugs were super minor things that didn't affect gameplay at all. The one time things went wrong for me was when the game suddenly crashed in the middle of the final boss fight. I think I just got super unlucky, since this was after around 10 hours of gameplay with no crashes, so its certainly not a common occurrence. I checked the steam forums for the game, and the developers are actively working on fixing bugs, so if you're concerned just wait a few weeks and they'll probably be gone.The one negative thing I have to say about the game is that the price seems too high. In my opinion, there's not enough content in the game to warrant $20, so you might want to wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: I really had no idea what a delight was in store for me when I downloaded this charming looking MV. I had heard "if you liked Hollow Knight and Ori" but what really hooked me about Unbound was it's nod back to one of my favorite non-MV games, Celeste. The instant respawn and breath holding platform challenges really kept me jolting on the edge of my seat and gasping in victory on success. I was also really impressed with the cleverness of the portal mechanic, juggling between level and enemy states to navigate tough areas, and how they implemented this mostly combat free system into really engaging boss fights, including one of the most exciting and toughest final bosses I've encountered in a while. So yeah, I HIGHLY recommend this game, especially if you've already hit the doldrums of having played all the top tier MCs already out there. But hugs to the creative team, great job!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Unbound: Worlds Apart

_childDocuments_.review: Lets start with this. This game is a platformer with no real combat, more akin to Celeste or Super meat boy than games like Hollow Knight or Ori. Having fully completed the game and all of the side objectives the whole impression about the game I'm left with is mixed. The underlying mechanic of using portals to alter the environment or physics around you is fun to play with. As the game goes on the portals you can use changes, however you can only use one portal at the time, and most of the game sections are built around one portal type. This works well as you are introduced with a new portal power, however, in the long run it makes the game feel blocky and sometimes repetitive. You are intorduced to new power, and easy puzzles at the start to learn the power, and at the end of the section you get a couple more difficult puzzles and thats it unless you want to do side quests. Cue in a new zone and a new power, and the same cycle begins. This type of game progression would be okey if there was a lot of different powers, unfortunatelly the portal powers get reused a couple of types in different sections making those sections feel similar and since you have already learned the power before in turn makes the "new" section either easy or boring. The most annoying thing is that close to the end of the game the game shows its potential as you are actually presented with a section that incorporates multiple portal powers. WHY ONLY ONE SECTION?? In my opinion this was the most fun part of the game and multiple powers should have definately been incorporated into more levels. The game has a story and side charracters but none of that really grabbed me as the game progression overall didin't really feel as it was leading me somewhere due to the blocky nature of the game. Celeste would come to my mind as a comparison as I was playing this game, unfortunately this game did not provide that feeling of accomplishent, tension and continuity you get when you climb the Celeste mountain.Overall, Unbound: Worlds Apart is a game, which in my opinion is neither bad nor is great. If you like 2D platformers with some more interesting mechanics, I would suggest getting it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Unbound Worlds Apart is a fantastic platformer/metroidvania. Clever puzzles that arent too challenging. Some sections of platforming are blood pressure raising. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a treat. You'll find many familiar elements from Ori and Hollow Knight, so if you enjoyed both those games you'll almost certainly enjoy Unbound: Worlds Apart. However, despise some similarities, ultimately this game stands on its own with its brilliant core mechanic. This game is a puzzle platformer with Metroidvania elements, meaning you'll spend your time puzzling your way past enemies rather than fighting them. The exception is the boss fights, which serve as a test of reflexes and mastery over each puzzle mechanic.The game is gorgeous, the puzzles are clever, the world(s) are interesting, the exploration is fun, and the core mechanic is great. Word of warning though, if you want the 100% completion you're in for some brutal (but fair) platforming sections.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been following this game since the Kickstarter campaign and I would highly recommend it, especially to fans of platformers and metroidvanias.The controls are super responsive and are really nice to use. My only complaint about the control and movement is that during some “portal” switches, you gain the portal mechanic before the portal animation is finished. There were a few puzzles that required precise timing and it wasn’t until I understood this concept that I could easily complete the puzzles.The art style is really beautiful. Due to it being hand drawn, the character animations can feel kind of static and blocky. But after you immerse yourself in the world it becomes hardly noticeable.The puzzle difficulty scale is reasonable. There are plenty of “easy” puzzle blocks that build you up to solve the more challenging ones. I haven’t finished the game yet, but there hasn’t been any puzzles that I found too challenging that would have caused me to ragequit. I absolutely LOVE the different portal mechanics. The very first mechanic, and the one that was demo’d during the kickstarter campaign, is kind of basic. As it should be for the first mechanic you are introduced to, but how they were able to build off of that to create 10 unique mechanics is absolutely brilliant.What I think separates this game from a masterpiece such as Hollow Knight or Ori is the writing and the soundtrack. They're not by any means bad, but I would rate them as Average or Good. For me, the gameplay is the most important part, and in Unbound: Worlds Apart, they pass with flying colours!

_childDocuments_.review: After 7 hours I feel confident I can offer my point of view.First and foremost the game is good and fun to play.Basically it is a puzzle platformer with no combat, one hitpoint (but the automatic save is really forgiving) and you can do a bit of backtracking if you want to get all the side quests (save all the villagers and a few more achievements...).Don't be mislead by the many reviews that define this game as a metroidvania like Hollow Knight, there is no combat and even if you can go back pretty much everywhere, it feels quite linear.The comparison is closer to a mix of Ori and Celeste, if you like those you will probably enjoy Unbound.The main mechanic is about portals, which you can open whenever you want and offers a multitude of powers which change based on the area you are playing; it is a fresh idea and it makes this game stand out.The puzzles are fun and engaging, almost always fair even though they are quite hard at times.The game needs more polishing (some visual bugs here and there, a spider blocking my way, but nothing major), but since it was released few days ago I am sure it will improve over time.I'm enjoyed the puzzles, not a lot the lore: I know it seems harsh but it looks to me like the story is an afterthought to justify the game world and the portal mechanic (which again, it is good!). I really like the visual style, but the story has no charm for me.I will edit this review when I will complete the game.EDIT:I've finished the game (100% achievements) and I have to say, it's a bit short but it is worth.The bosses in the final section are bit more fun, still they are not too hard and after a few attempts learning how they behave they are ok.The real fun was looking for all the villagers and spirits, a few of them were really well hidden (still the map always shows pretty much were they could be) or just hard to reach.11 hours of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: At first look it’s easy to see that Unbound: Worlds Apart borrows quite a bit from Ori and the Will of the Wisps. The vibrant, hand-drawn art style, the fairy-tale like story telling, and the challenging platforming are all hallmarks of the Ori series. However, once you dive just a little deeper into Unbound: Worlds Apart, you find a side-scroller that relies more on puzzle solving and pure platforming precision than combat, and keeps a wealth of surprises under the hood.In fact, there really isn’t much combat at all in Unbound, which is in stark contrast to Ori and the Will of the Wisps. Soli, the game’s protagonist, must use his portal generating ability to use the environment to solve puzzles and defeat enemies. His jump isn’t very high, he can only take a single hit, and he has no weapons. This portal ability is what truly separates Unbound Worlds apart from other Metroid-style platformers.Each region you visit gives your portal a distinct property. First off in reverse gravity. Activate your portal and Soli will flip upside down and rise to the ceiling. This allows you to avoid dangers, kill unsuspecting enemies, and also float in the air by quickly activating and deactivating the portal. It very quickly takes the lessons you learned in the fairly simple tutorial and literally flips them on their head. And this was just the first area.Soon after solving the puzzles in that region I found myself in a completely dark underground cave. Here my portal acted as a huge bloom of light, allowing me to see obstacles and enemies previously hidden in the darkness. There was a catch though; the faster I walked and more I jumped the smaller the circle of light emanating around Soli got. It didn’t restore to full strength until I stopped and rested. This meant I had to survey the area and do a lot of the platforming my memory in almost complete darkness. It was a totally different mechanic and pace than the previous region, and was indicative of the large variety of mechanics the game offers. Who knew a single button and ability could be so dynamic?It’s that endless possibility that really struck me about Unbound: Worlds Apart. In a landscape of games that borrow, but rarely come up with unique mechanics, Unbound: Worlds Apart had me excited to see more from the very start. Part of why I like video games, especially indie titles, is their ability to experiment and provide new experiences, and Unbound: Worlds Apart is perfect encapsulation of that.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game.  The platforming was delightful, the dimension mechanic felt fun and unique, and it controlled really well.  The bosses felt creative and interesting to fight because you didn't any offensive abilities, so you had to figure out how to interact with the boss rather than unload on them.  It's not super long outside of plowing through the story there's still more to do and explore.  Worth the $20 for what you get.Game looks beautiful, and the music really sets the atmosphere.  The world and story is set up well.The main thing that I thought was overkill(but won't matter to some, and others may love, it's up to taste) was how much it autosaves.  It autosaves almost every single obstacle so there is almost no punishment for dying to something, and on average you maybe lose a few seconds with just a couple parts putting you back further.  Even some bosses had autosaves in middle of the fight.  The platforming throughout and nearing the end can get a little difficult in a fair and rewarding way, but the autosaving makes it feel like you're playing through it with save states between every jump.  It'd be awesome if they eventually released a higher difficulty mode that toned it down juuuuust a little on the autosaving.Overall though I loved the experience. Would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: ----------------------------------------Unbound: World’s Apart is an old school platformer with modern mechanics and sensibilities. This isn’t a metroidvania although it is obviously inspired it. The graphics are cute and charming with more than a passing resemblance to . However, gameplay-wise, the bulk of Unbound is closer to platform games such as  and  while the timed events and boss fights are indeed, straight out of Ori. The portal mechanic although not new, is utilized intelligently without creating confusion. By the way, there is no combat; there is no attack button, not HP bar, everything (except the bosses) are one shot kills. In this regard, it’s an especially old school platform game a la Super Mario. While not perfect and certainly not original, Unbound as a whole is greater than the sum of it’s parts and for the price, it’s a good game for platform beginners and provides moderate challenge for veterans. Recommended. ---------------------------------------- Each section of the world pass through a gate which will grant you the ability to conjure a portal that changes your immediate environment (think Gateway but without the Gateway Guns). This could be changing gravity, changing your size, changing placement of an obstruction and even change a hostile.  and you won’t get confused by how, where and when to use them. Your power-ups and level design are in fact,  and  this speaks to a clever and considerate game design. . They are tight enough that you can do precision timing and precision platforming. Although I do feel that movement is just slightly heavy but on the whole, movement has an enjoyable flow. . Unbound doesn’t require precision platforming but it does require some precision timing (think Braid). Having said that, it isn’t too difficult nor is it too punishing as provides you with ample respawn areas and teleport points. ----------------------------------------Unbound . From the artwork, to the level design, to the boss fights and the timed events. You could forgive them this since they are a Kickstarter studio with very limited resources which they used to focus on gameplay rather than original graphics. . There is way too much exposition from characters rather than naturally incorporating them in the gameplay. The emotional payoff at the end is also a miss since there wasn’t adequate build-up to give the ending the impact it needed. But again, the money went to make a better gameplay so you can forgive this oversight. ----------------------------------------. Unbound is more akin to an old school platform where you one shot the enemy and the enemy one shots you. There is no attack button and you generally use the environment (some times your powers) to kill hostiles. The boss fights is like Super Mario 1 or 3 where you have to strike the enemy 3 times to kill them and the bosses have elaborate attacks and phases that you have to memorize (think Ori's boss fights). I think there only like 3 or 4 bosses in the game and they are very unique and distinct. On the whole, I think it works and is generally fun, except for the last boss which personally, I find annoying and just long-winded.  though I’m a 30 year gaming veteran and I steamrolled everything. Still, 6 hours is a short game and it may disappoint some people. In Alien Pixel’s defense though, this is their first game and considering the amount of things that they managed to accomplished here as well as the price of the game, I think the short game time is reasonable. Still, buyer beware. ----------------------------------------I really enjoyed this game. For an Indie Kickstarter game, I think Unbound: World’s Apart is a pretty accomplished. If you like platformers, you’ll probably like this. If you’re a beginner, this is a good place to start. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay loop here is most similar to Celeste in that the gameplay focuses on a lot of short, challenging fine-tuned platforming "levels" even though holistically, the art/story/atmosphere/music/exploration/environment/map is much more similar to Ori and the Blind Forest. If you die on any section you restart on that same spot which is pleasant. IMO the game starts getting challenging after about 1-2 hours in then the difficulty stays pretty consistent after that, comparable difficulty to Celeste A side.The vast majority of the game's difficulty comes from the mechanical/platforming side rather than the puzzle side, definitely there are tons of spots where it will not be immediately obvious what to do and you need to use your brain a bit to figure it out, but very few hard puzzles- IMO there are only 2 villagers on par with the Crystal Hearts in Celeste in terms of puzzle challenge (I kind of feel like anyone who has 100%'d it will know exactly which 2 I am talking about lol). I would have liked to see more sections like  to really amp up the puzzle part of the game but that's just my personal preference.Overall the quality of the game is just great in every aspect, would highly recommend if you enjoy moderately challenging platforming. The monster aesthetics are especially unique which was offputting to me at first but I grew fond of them throughout the game.
