_childDocuments_.review: HROT (or Slavic Quake as it's know in retro FPS circles) is an excellent little Quake style shooter. Running on it's on engine (written in Pascal which couldn't have been fun), it nails the atmosphere, visual artefacts and general vibe of the engine John Carmack wrote back in 1996 down to a tee. Unlike retro shooters before HROT that used shaders to make Unity look old, this is the real deal. It's hard to convey just how beautifully old this feels, you just need to play it.The movement in HROT however is a little weak. Walking around is okay but the jumping is pretty clunky and hard to pull off. There's one secret that I just couldn't reach because of the weak jumping which felt a little unfair to me. I also felt that the game was a little too easy on Normal which admittedly can be remedied by picking a higher difficulty but at the moment I feel it could still challenge new players a little more. The enemies are great I feel! Their designs are fantastic and utterly inspired! The humanoid enemies walk around with their Soviet gas masks and trench coats and leave you wondering if they're even alive in there. The enemies telegraph their attacks well and communicate damage well. Nothing to complain about there!My last gripe is the weapons. They feel fine and as long as you ration your ammo, you should be good on that front. But the weapon sounds and introductions are the weakest link in this whole game. They sound far too delicate and weak, some more oomf in their sound would be excellent! As for the introductions, I felt that at the moment I got a new weapon, it wasn't too bad... but later on I'd forget I even had some very powerful weapons and I feel that stronger and more memorable introductions could fix this. However, If this is just me being dumb and everyone else got on hunky dory then I guess I'll just shut up :PHROT is a little short for the price but that will change! Its in early access and has more chapters coming! So I'd 100% recommend you buy this! You won't regret it!

It really captures the speed of the old 90s early 2Ks FPS games along with great weapons and fun shooting. The levels are kinda mazes and that is fine, but sometimes everything looking similar can throw off your sense of direction as you can't tell if you have been there before or not. Trouble finding keys and new areas with the backtracking can slow down the combat a little. Maze like level design is also a note taken from the retro FPS and can be interesting.I really like games like this and wish a lot of success to the developer, and hope to see more from them in the future! Great game!

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wondered what would it be like if DUSK was set in a soviet republic? If the answer is “no”, this is perfectly understandable. To all 3 of you for whom the answer is “yes”, this is an oddly specific request but you are bound to love what comes next! HROT may not belong to New Blood brand of modern boomer-shooters, however it sure as hell looks, feels and plays like it could. This Quake-inspired piece of action is work of a single Prague-based developer by the nickname Spytihněv.Set in a post-apocalyptic depiction of Czechoslovakia, this title blends a smooth, old-school gunplay, references to communism, copious amounts of brown and a peculiar sense of humour to deliver a premiere retro experience.No matter whether it is  or the new wave – if old-school shooters ring true at all, you will soon recognise that HROT comes from a place of deep understanding of what makes such games tick. All of the components you would come to expect from a title like this are in place: a level-based structure divided into episodes, memorable setpieces, a key-based pacing and a secret behind a cracked wall in need of explosives. Thus, not only the game manages to check all of the retro boxes, (even nods to the classics are there) it does all of these things really well.Possibly the best example to highlight that the smooth flow of the game is hardly a coincidence, is how well it handles enemies’ visibility. One of the more distinct facets of HROT is that out of 100 colours used in the game about 90 of them are various shades of brown. With this in mind, it is quite amazing that the opposition never truly blends with the surroundings despite chaos often ensuing on the screen. Through careful application of contrasting pieces of equipment or something as mundane as red eyes of a rat, threats remain easy to follow across well over 40 bestiary entries.Now, it needs to be stated that while HROT definitely dedicates due attention to roots of its chosen genre, it would be a disservice to imply that the game merely follows the footsteps of its predecessors. Beyond a shadow of a doubt, this title has an identity of its own – it is a mix of extreme soviet brutalism, Czech references and dank memes. I would venture the end result may impair your ability to drive.Simply put, the setting of HROT is utterly bizarre and what I can imagine to be one of the game’s most polarizing aspects. On one hand, the player traverses an oppressively bleak world of gas masks, ticking away to the rhythm Geiger’s counter. On the other, an animate bulldozer springs to life to fill the role of a minor Boss and one of the levels has a dance party worked into progression route. If you prefer your dystopia morose with a gravel aftertaste, I can imagine “Dank stuff” tab in the main menu is going to be a letdown.For better or worse, this title doesn’t take itself particularly seriously and to be fair, I find the absurdity to be working in the game’s favour. Taking into account how deeply entrenched in soviet-era Czechoslovakia HROT is, a sardonic spin on the setting goes a long way. Especially in a game which is ultimately about gunning down lots of dudes with extreme prejudice.Speaking of the devil, HROT’s rouges gallery fits well with the game’s peculiar sense of humour. Most prevalent enemy types consist of faceless invading army, suited with full environmental suits – they seem to help little though, as soldiers are often seen throwing up through the filters of their masks. Once bunkers and cityscape give way to castle-themed levels, meat for the grinder follows suit to include hooded maniacs, leaping at the player with axe in hand. Harsh and gritty. However, it wouldn’t be HROT if things were to remain this subdued – an enemy called “Konfident” is a large flying head of Lenin, which shoots vision-impairing bullets. There are also mutated chickens, Nazi Newts and hostile inanimate objects, which prompt concern for protagonist’s mental state.No less interesting level filling is a myriad of curious little details scattered across the game. Random interactable items provide a fun change of pace from action-packed gameplay, rewarding the player for sparing a while to take in their surroundings. Some of them are simple distractions, such as a grinding washing machine or a fully interactive keyboard; while others can be a fully-fledged minigame or have an achievement tied to them. One may be tempted to write-off dedicating attention to seemingly pointless items, nevertheless to me this is a chef’s kiss, making HROT’s world vivid despite its bleak colour palette.Worth a separate mention is the level design itself. For the most part, the game maintains a steady flow, with progression route looping nicely as new areas become available. Crossing certain sections of the level multiple times is often used to provide smart visual clues regarding the way forward. In spite of all that, I did get stuck in HROT on several occasions, as the game at times considers finding the correct path as a sort of environmental puzzle. In few instances, I scolded myself for missing a passage that seemed obvious when I finally found it, in others, extra hoops left an aftertaste of mild frustration.Having reached the nitpicking part, if HROT has a single genuine caveat, it is the uninspired arsenal. Overwhelming majority of guns available you have seen in every shooter, especially a retro one. The few exotic pieces being a lightning gun pulled straight from Quake and my personal favourite - Veltlínske zelené, a bottle of healing wine which doubles as a Molotov. Using tried and tested guns isn’t terrible in itself, they also have distinct quirks making certain weapons more fitting to a given combat scenario. Unfortunately, the player often will be shooting whatever currently has ammo left as HROT seems to be optimized towards giving the player “just enough” ammo to get by, somewhat undermining the nuance of gun performance. With all that in mind, I need to stress this is nitpicking rather than a true issue with the game.Ultimately, HROT’s Steam rating of “Overwhelmingly Positive” seems fully deserved. While I am tempted to call this game niche, with boomer-shooter genre becoming increasingly more popular over the years, I believe it reaches out to a sensibly wide audience. I especially recommend the game to inhabitants of former Warsaw Pact countries, as all the soviet references will hit harder, particularly the mature players who experienced the reality of communism on their own skin. In both content and gameplay, HROT is a proper blast from the past, delivering a true morsel for all fans of retro FPS.

_childDocuments_.review: Played up to E2M5, the last level at the time of reviewing.HROT nails the Slav Quake vibe right on the head, but isn't perfect. Ambiance is spot-on and the gameplay is a slower pace but still fun. Levels are laid out in really fun and interesting ways that play really smoothly, but I feel like resources are a bit tight. Playing through on Hard, it's not uncommon to be struggling for ammo, health, and armor. Ammo/health economy are great ways of creating tension but in HROT it feels more like walking on a tightrope where you have so little room for error and can make some levels a chore to play. Not only are items really rare but on higher difficulties a single hit from some enemies can deal about a fifth of your HP. I think that with some tweaking to damage numbers and being a bit more lenient on the amount of items will iron out any of the gameplay problems I had. Definitely recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: HROT

_childDocuments_.review: It's... Weird but fine. You never, ever get a story, but that's somehow ok, the world is brown and grim, and everyone wants to kill you, that's all I know for sure.The gunplay is solid, and you never really run out of every ammo, so you always have enough to take care of enemies, but, there actually somehow seems to be too many weapons instead of too few. Two of them in particular rarely even come up, and their ammo is basically nonexistant, those being the lighting guns. Two of them just fill holes that don't actually exist, those being the crossbow (which you'd assume would be the sniper, but no, it does less damage than the basic shotgun) and the mines (which are hazardous to use when everyone has melee attacks, quake grenades, and shotguns/the equivalent to assault rifles).The levels themselves are varied and well-built, and though they're all key-hunts, they're less-so hunts and moreso just level progress blockers so you do everything in the right order, which is fine considering the clear setup and timing this dev has. Turn a wheel infront of you that doesn't make immediate sense? You either get attacked by a low-damage enemy to get you to face where the key is, or you passed by a gate earlier. This applies to everything except the cursed 4-switch puzzles with their solutions SUPPOSEDLY in the environment, though I only found the pictureframe one, and brute forced all the others because they don't have their answers as obvious as those picture frames, totally killing the pacing the 4 or 5 times they come up.That being said, there's only one level that kinda sags in quality, and it's the penultimate one, where you get 3 arenas that last as long as the ones in Boltgun, and it... Sucks very slightly.Other than that, there's random teleports, tons of small interactible fun things, wacky bosses that make no sense, and it all just leaves me... Confused. Clearly there's something going on, clearly a story just progressed, but you're gonna leave feeling uncertain about what you just experienced. 9/10, cause it's still a very solid and well-made shooter and clearly doesn't necessarily need coherency or a told story to succeed and be good. If anything, the questions and mysteries just make it that much better, since it doesn't really go over the brink aside from the first level of the third chapter, and even that gets explained away without words.

_childDocuments_.review: HROT is an old-school, fast-paced first-person shooter.It is heavily influenced by the designs of Doom, Quake, or any other similar games. There are also references to other games like Project Warlock, Half-life, etc.There is nothing new as far as gameplay is concerned. It plays like a standard shooter.It is divided into three episodes, each having eight levels (plus a couple of secret levels). The majority of the levels also contain secrets to be found.I liked episodes 1 and 2 more than the third episode. I think they have run out of ideas for the later part of the game (especially episode three).The level design is serviceable. The music and sound are quite good. Some of the soundtracks gave me an eerie feeling.There are five difficulty settings. Very easy, easy, normal, hard, and very hard.Gameplay-wise, there is a theme here. Find a key. Do backtracking. Kill the enemies that spawn at previous locations while backtracking to the door. End the level with some sort of boss fight. There is a major boss fight at the end of each episode. Rinse and repeat. This may sound monotonous. And it is, to some extent. But if you are a fan of such gameplay, then you will have a blast for sure.You will start each episode with a basic weapon (the weapons do not carry forward from the last completed episode) and will get more weapons as you progress. After completing an episode, you have to start a new episode from the select menu. You can also play a specific level from a specific episode from the selection menu.There is enough variety in weapons. But some of the weapons sounds may lack punch. The enemy designs are amazing, bizarre, and funny. I was surprised to see some of the enemies. The enemies' shooting is projectile-based rather than hit-scan, which is a good thing. There are some minigames throughout the campaign. Those were cool additions.Story-wise, there isn't enough explanation, and it is up for interpretation. There is so much written material scattered throughout the levels. These are written in the Czech language. You need to press the "E'  or 'use' button to read them in English. There are no voice-over dialogues. Voice-over is there to make various sounds of enemies. I didn't like some of the messages that were conveyed through the scripts. It could have been better if they had hired some story writers and voiceover artists to streamline the experience. I faced some visual stuttering (or low frame-rate on some occasions); this may be due to some optimisation issues.Each level may take around 15 to 20 minutes to be completed if you are playing for the first time. Some may take less time than that. There are two secret levels that I missed on my first playthrough.I have completed the campaign on normal difficulty (without going out of my way to hunt for the achievements and secrets) in around 7 to 7.5 hours. There is an endless mode. Which contains four maps from the main campaign. This is standard wave-based gameplay. Nothing new. Just try it out if you want to have fun for a bit.Overall. I have played this game in 3–4 sessions. And I've enjoyed my time.But if you decide to play in one sitting, this will become repetitive.I read somewhere that only one person has developed the game. Kudos to the developer (you have done a remarkable job).I'll play this game again to get the remaining achievements and also try out the higher difficulty setting. I'll add more to this review if needed.I'll recommend getting this game when it's available at a light discount or in any bundle if available.My verdict: 7/10
