_childDocuments_.review: This game is terrible. Sorry to all of the RTS fans out there, this isn't the game you're looking for. The set up for the game is great. Interwar technology with mechs set in eastern Europe. The problem is, first off, the story will make you cringe really hard. I don't know why, maybe it's the voice acting or the dialogue itself, but the story is really hard to listen to and not roll your eyes at how dumb it is. This obviously isn't the most important part of an RTS though, that's the gameplay. Unfortunately, that's terrible. For whatever reason, I always felt that the units weren't interacting in ways they were meant to. Anti-tank soldiers are useless and can't perform anti-tank duties because they have no range. Flamethrowers have the same problem but for infantry. But the biggest problem I have is just that it gives me a headache to play the game. The combat seems to be very stiff and units won't take cover when ordered. Units will die because instead of shooting the enemy they will attempt to walk around the enemy's fortified position and attack from the rear despite being in range. Things like that which make you wish you'd just finish a third playthrough of Company of Heroes instead. I never once had fun playing the game, and that's the biggest problem. I can't recommend it to anyone. Especially anyone who has a very low tolerance for poor mission design and bad dialogue.

_childDocuments_.review: There are parts of this game that shine. The aesthetics, the theme, and the concept are without a doubt a much welcomed update to a dying genre. It most notably takes inspiration from Company of Heroes, though there are characters similar to Rise of Nations/Legends. It will scratch that old RTS itch if you have one, but the game is in desperate need of gameplay adjustment/evolution. This game is much more king of the hill, focusing heavier on the combat, than base building or anything of the like. It has no Supreme Commander level of defense opportunity, and the heroes cannot be customized to fit certain play-styles beyond what they offer from the get go (a la Total War Shogun 2 multiplayer). Defenses in general feel extremely undermining, whereby you are much better off spending your resources and yes, unit pop, on an actual unit. As a result, engineers play more as a scout/rat class to find resource boxes or to run far beyond enemy lines to capture an unprotected resource node. That's at least how the AI plays them. Upgrades to the resource nodes themselves are expensive, and the ROI is only worth it in the long haul. What I'm getting at, is that the game ultimately comes down to a somewhat predictable and usual tug of war. First to build mechs and push can slaughter and get an early advantage, less you go full guerrilla warfare to win. I'm no pro at this game, so maybe this sentiment is wrong. However, I've seen much more variability in many other RTS games over the years than this one in terms of how you can approach positioning, rushing, capturing, etc. Something like zerg rushing or protoss cannon spam just isn't even an idea in this game because the baseline mechanics are all very simple. In someways, this is great. It keeps the overall pace very fast and gung ho. Big units hit hard, move slow, can stop most bad guys. That's the core of this game boiled down. No unit cannon, no nukes, no nothing that would allow for more turtle/tall approaches to gameplay.It's fun. I really like the idea of this game, and it's refreshing to see new RTS games come out with innovative designs for units that aren't aliens or goo monsters. The factions are each unique enough to be played separately with different approaches, yet they all ultimately march towards the same gameplay loop which rail-roads the difficulty to pop order, rather than conquering. Hammering this down with the AI's rat approaches, which is somehow supported by the ease of retreat despite being fully surrounded by units, and this game can quickly turn obnoxious if you break from the norm.

_childDocuments_.review: I am changing my review from negative to positive.I wanna say the devs though originally they were kind of shrugging off complaints and not listening to us, or it appeared that way... Where actually taking it all in and planning on what to fix etc.The game since multiple patches now, is in a fun playable state. I will say it's more linear than COH2 and that makes it easier to play.When teching you start with some infantry but HAVE TO get mechs by late game, the war's become mech vs mech and infantry besides to capture a point become useless, and most defences you can build via engineers become useless at this point. This makes the game easier because a unit living from the start to end isn't needed, they just need to live long enough to become useless before they die.I am hopeful that the new dlc and air units being added will maybe change this up, I wouldn't mind seeing a soft rock<paper<scissors type thing, where infantry are better vs air, air is better vs mechs and mechs are still better vs infantry, this way building the right units at the right time and positioning them right will add more depth to the fighting in the game.The game hasn't in my opinion lived up to it's full potential yet, but the devs are working toward it and every patch gets us closer to it, this is a diamond in the rough when it comes to tactics but they are improving more and more, and content wise, level design, stability of the game to not crash.ALL IMPROVED!!!So I am going from a thumbs down and AVOID at all cost, to a thumbs up and buy this if you are a fan of the Lore or a fan or COH type RTS games.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of strategy games. This game is definitely one of them that I enjoy playing. Been playing it the past few weeks and it's been nothing but fun and entertaining. The soundtrack is so inspiring that you would want to add it to a playlist to replay it on the other missions. Some of the missions are difficult like the stealth ones, but that's what makes the game even more interesting. I've never seen a strategy game have stealth missions like these that are also very interactive, like managing your troops against enemies that are stronger if you have the wrong troops facing them.I like the units, especially the mechanized ones. Their voice lines sound amazing, their movements are fluid, and reloads are  cool. Like the PZM-7 "Smialy" in the Polanian campaign, its reload has to be the coolest in the game in my opinion. It's also got multiplayer sessions where you can face your friends. Some of the maps you can use in those sessions are huge and open where you can have large defensive frontline battles. Overall, its a fantastic game to play and would highly recommend playing it.

It's just bad.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good BUT <insert long list of caveats here>. It's so long actually that i don't think i could do it justice. The game has so many little issues - starting from little nitpicks like a missing texture or a part of a model hovering in thin air. Then there are mildly annoying things like having great character models standnig on muddy ground textures and mech textures that seem like they should be sharper. Finally there are grievances i got with the game like mediocre path finding and ai as well as underdeveloped multiplayer. But what it offers is a very unique scenario in an undersaturated genre with decent gameplay and an overall pretty good and ambitous campagne. And that would be my reccomendation: If the setting speaks to you and you like single player campagnes then it might be worth a look. The campagne tells the personal stories of multiple characters while also exploring their representative factions role in the conflict. It's very ambitious and it suffers from that. Often i had the feeling the game just doesn't manage to reach the narrative and dramatic heights its writers had in mind. Gamepaly wise i'd say it's decent. If you liked Company of Heroes 1 you might be dissapointed to hear that Iron Harvest is closer to a streamlined version of Company of Heroes 2. Cover determines wheter a unit dies within seconds or can hold its position for quite a while - unless it gets hardcountered or flanked. Speaking of hardcounters, IH is very rock-paper-scissory with its damage types. There are unarmored, light, medium and heavy. Both in terms of defense and offense. If you deal 'heavy' damage against a 'heavy' target you'll do the most damage. Otherwise, the incoming damage is reduced. Which leads to the awkward situation with robots firing against each other for minutes without either one being able to kill the other because they have the wrong damage types. Which was fine in COH 1 because it felt organic - a small shell bouncing off from the front armor of a tank made sense looking at it. In IH, the damage looks the same independently from its actual effectiveness. So a shot that looks like it should pierce straight trough the enemy doesn't deal any damage. IH has a simple "backstab" damage system - some armored units take more damage from behind. However, if you are the type of player that loves to scout and play counters this might be your game. Every unit can be countered and flanking with the proper unit can turn a battle around in an instant. However, Multiplayer at the moment has only six maps and is hampered by a janky progression system. Anyway, just to make up on the negatives i listed: In terms of campagne it's probably one of the best RTS campagnes you can get at the time of writing. Overambitious or not, you can see the work put into it in the mission design and cutscenes.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard one to review.  On the one hand, this is one of the most professionally done games I have played.  I say this to some large degree based on the "maturity" factor of a game.  This is to say, there is a great deal of complimentary material such as game play videos and voice acting etc., and general overall production quality, that goes along with a mature and well done game and Iron Harvest have has this is spades.  I am very much enjoying the story and the story telling.But... (there is always a but)... I have so far not been impressed with the actual tactical game play elements.  For the most part this game plays much like the early RTS we knew in the 90s and 2000s.  So far, the actual battle components are mostly making sure you have a larger and better equipped force than the enemy and then just rushing your troops in to attack.  Aside from the potential to take cover behind a fence or rock, there is not much in the way of actual attack strategy to employ.  This is not for example a game like Star Craft where a great deal of strategy can be employed by a player of finesse.  I admit that only having 5 hours of play time under my belt does indeed limit my exposure of the game, but surely I should have seen these aspects of the game by now and I have not.But then again, I have to go back to what I call the maturity factor in this game.  I get the real feel of a large world at war with this game, something that most other games of this genre cannot deliver.  I attribute this of course to what I noted which is the super high production quality that has clearly gone into Iron Harvest.  For this the game is worth playing, especially if you can get it on one of the sales.I do recommend it, but mostly for the story telling, and not so much for the actual battle play.  Maybe the multiplayer will offer more in this regard.

_childDocuments_.review: A thin recommendation. Just finished damn near marathoning it over a weekend and did all of the campaigns. The setting and premise are great - very dieselpunk, the factions are fairly interesting, and the campaign story is a 7/10 that shines through having some characters you love to hate.Gameplay-wise, the campaign is probably a 6/10 at its low points and a 8/10 at its high points. Several missions, especially plenty in the Saxony, Ursonia, and Rusviet Revolution campaigns, are absolute slogs that take way longer than they should. Mechanically, it's a Company of Heroes-type, where you have a 'base' with three buildings and have to capture and hold resource generating sites elsewhere in the map. Many of the campaign missions give you hero units, and they're generally overpowered, but it's fun to use them as force multipliers. Something else to mention is how damned slow every unit is - even aircraft - and I ran into pathing issues every so often given how large some of the mechs can get.Certainly worth about $40 if you get the all inclusive release. Hope they do a sequel!

_childDocuments_.review: I tried really hard to like a game that is basically Company of Heroes but with Dieselpunk Mecha.The game is somewhat clunky, lacks many campaign mechanics, has little cover where you want it - and no concealment cover -> all those trees and bushes that would make great "soft" cover for ambushes or flanking infantry? Useless decorations. Building corners and trees? Garrison them with a single unit or fight around them rather than use them.The game also has sadly low FPS prerendered cutscenes, no pause in single player (makes it tough to read any tutorials while you're actively being shot) and an escape menu that takes a few seconds and always buffers the second time I press it and then just closes itself leads to many frustrating components. The game tries to take on the same space as Company of Heroes and Dawn of War 2 - a void that has been unfilled and adds WWI but with stompy Mecha instead of tanks. This falls flat and is clunky with weak controls - it has all the same problems DoW2 got mostly right by the time of Retribution and CoH got better at in CoH2; that is units running through the open, clumping up around cover rather than behind it, and an inability to use half the "terrain" in the game. Abilities and positioning becomes a micro game which pales compared to well iterated RTS like Starcraft or even the first DoW. This game needed either more dev time or devs who played a lot more of the predecessors it is inheriting mechanics from. Also, small note, but my inability to win a snowball fight via superior cover (the tutorial) and then hunt a deer using a useless stealth mechanic which will not be re-used for the rest of the game SHOULD have been a heartfelt and clever way to introduce me to the main character and the specifics of the game - but instead proved to be a disappointing experience like the rest of my first couple of hours. The game has a good story and world to show - but you'll have to work hard rather than play well to get to see it.

_childDocuments_.review: While it does not quite stack up to the complexity and balance that Company of Heroes 2 offers, its fun nonetheless.  The RTS base building it there, a rudimentary cover system is in place, and there are different factions.  However, its hard not to compare this game to COH because its obvious a lot of systems (cover, queue, destructible terrain) are from the former game.  The problem is those systems are not quite as impactful  and well implemented as u think.  For instance, the cover system works like in COH but only certain areas work.  You cannot destroy a wall and then expect to use the crumbled building as cover which is disappointing.  Another problem is that the pathfinding of the AI is not very good.  A lot of micromanaging will be required since units have this tendency to clump together which = deaths in big battles.  The machines also have love to expose their back when u tell them to retreat.  Why not have them run backwords when double clicking terrain?  Anyways, this game has potential.  And thats why I am recommending buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey there, I would like to share a few words about IH. First and foremost, I believe that the game strikes a great sci-fi setting, with a great IDEA behind the whole game. The mechanized scenario of the WW1 is pretty neat and deserves atleast a try. However, in its current state, it might be a bit underwhelming. I myself didnt expect much from the game at launch. It has a decent campaign (although the humongous lenght of some missions can be a tid irritating at times), and the mechanics are not too bad as well (and getting better as time goes).Where the game lacks IMO is the multiplayer aspect. Yes, the game offers a various choice of mechs for each factions, but most matches tend to end before you can even get them out. The low variation in the first 'infantry' phase of matches is pretty abysmal. Same infatry units for every faction just dont cut it for me I am afraid. Also the absence of a proper tutorial can leave some players confused and scrambling for what to do precisely. With all this said, I will still keep a close eye on the game and keep playing the SEASON trees which are a great feature IMO. Rewards in terms of skins and portraits and such keep an collector like me up and excited for the game. But this might not be the case for everyone.Peace and love, Dokiwan.

The mech combat is wild and I cannot get enough of those artillery units. (All 3 factions have unique artillery)This is one of the best rts games in recent memory. I LOVE that any squad can take gear of another squad and change their specialty. The ONLY bad thing I have to say about this game is the selection of maps for skirmish/online play leaves a lot to be desired. Please add more maps asap!

_childDocuments_.review: Iron Harvest is a fun and uniquely atmospheric game with creative world building and design choicesPlay through any of three engaging campaigns in a steampunk alternate early 20th century. The voice acting is a tad over the top but...........eh it is what it is, each campaign is still an immersive experience you won't find anywhere else. The missions are all interconnected but unique with different settings and objectives. as well as differing degrees of available resources and strategies. However the actual game play is at times clunky and the AI isn't great. It's still playable but if you were expecting Men of War with Mechs, this isn't that. That being said, even by the developers own admission this game is still in Beta. What bugs it has now are being put up against a wall and shot daily with every new update. Diversity in factions and units are impressive, you have the basic cannon fodder grunts, engineers, machine gunners, artillery, and of course mechs. And these mechs aren't just skinned differently from faction to faction but mechanically different as well while still being similarly balanced. (the cheapest scouting mech for Polania holds a comedically large bolt action anti tank rifle and shoots it like a large metal man..... the cheapest scouting mech for the Rusviets flings Grenades)Multiplayer is fun and more to the point. You have  a base, they have a base................ you know how this goes. Overall while still undeniably in beta there's no where to go but up7/10

_childDocuments_.review: For disclosure: I played this game during a free weekend.Phew, where to start...The looks are cool. The Mechs, for the most part, have the right look to them. I admit that some of the walkers feel... excessive. The SKS 156 "Wotan" is a good example, it just doesn't look practical. But that's personal taste.The handling, however, isn't just a matter of taste, it is a key element of the game that is flawed. Especially the melee mechs feel awful. Lech and the "Serp" LOOK badass but struggle against simple infantry units because of their low attack speed and basically NO area effect. Couple that with their clunky moving animation and bad pathfinding capabilities and you have a box of steel easely outmanouvered by a single infantry squad.This nugdes another fundamental flaw of the game: LONG reaction times. The infantry units take about 1 to 2 seconds to process your order until they start moving.Speaking of infantry movement: No firing while moving.The blank line symbolises the heavy frustrated sigh leaving my body.The basic infantry units for the Germans and Russians (let's leave the cringy pseudonyms behind) use either MPs or shotguns - meaning they need to advance closer to the enemy to use their weapons effectively. But during their advance, they don't use said weapons, though they could counter their reduced accuracy by the high fire rate or pellet spread. This is not rocket science (or science at all), CoH did it in 2006! Oh, and this oldtimer also had a working attack move.Infantry squads don't feel like squads, too. They scramble all over the place.Also, the barracks are expensive as heck and make the only unit you can train at the start the pioneer unit. Which is basically useless as most of the bulding and repairing can only be done by one unit, which artificially stretches the game duration.So you skip the infantry and go straight to the mechs. Do they fare better? Well...There is a mech that does moving fire, which is nice. Unfortunatly, it's attack move will act like a normal movement command. Stopping to kill the infantry on its way? No, it will walk away, out of range, so the enemy can mind their business again.The main complaint I have with the mechs is that they don't feel mighty. This starts with their Idle animation which leaves them shivering like from a cold.And the rest of the behavior and movement is just clunky. No fluid transition between moving, aiming and firing.I could go on about the misplaced tag "Base building" (three buildings, oh my!), the lack of base defence (which I think is the main reason for the expensive barracks and long building times) and the overall feeling of a turn-based RPG core pressed into a RTS frame.All of this comes with a price tag of 50 bucks for 12 maps .Really?I played this one for free during the weekend. And it left me disapointed.I'd be livid if i spent 50 bucks on this.

_childDocuments_.review: Not entirely certain if many of the complaints are justified. I played COH2 before I ever played this game and a'lot of the complaints about slow moving and stupid AI is just as prevalent in COH2 and MOW as it is here, and you cant tell me it isn't, because I was just playin it on saturday and had a blast despite watching troops rush MGs and stand around shooting at eachother not taking cover.  I think people just thought maybe this game was going to change everything they ever knew about RTS and were disappointed that it didn't. When I first saw this game on Sunday (two days before its release), I thought it looked absolutely stupid, but I signed up for the last two hours of the beta. Tried it. Loved it. Bought it. Don't regret it. Having a blast with the cool mechs and graphics. I especially enjoy that there is a challenge and reward system built into the game. Remember the days when you could earn cool unit skins without having to pay for them with microtransactions? Welcome back! I've never had an RTS that interested me beyond skirmish mode, but this game has me all over the place trying everything out. Even the campaign is fun and I have always HATED RTS campaigns. I thought mechs and ww1 made a dumb mix, but man its grown on me. The cover system is cool, and the rock paper scissors unit setup is also fun. I could see how some of the strategy may seem limited though compared to most RTS. But I like having less micromanaging to think about and more time to enjoy the cinematic experience of watching WW1 mechs shell eachother. This is a great game if you prefer looking at units rather than icons.Buy the game and add me if you need a total noob to practice with.

_childDocuments_.review: Comp stomp is my favourite way to play RTS with my friends and I think that's the case for a lot of people, that being so - why is the AI so bad? Easy and medium might as well not exist, hard is brain dead. I'm not interested in the campaign, or any singleplayer or PVP content for that matter.They added a new faction since I played the beta and they don't really seem that viable? This game already had two underwhelming factions, it didn't need a third.Infantry combat is a joke. Severe lack of quality and quantity in this regard. Their implementation is inconsistently bullet spongy, often so slow it's frustrating with no half tracks or similarly useful troop transports. Upgrades aren't as satisfying as  either, in CoH equipping a rifle squad with a BAR for example is cool as hell, and they do veterancy stuff on top of that. MG gameplay is boring and tedious and mortars need a second look too. I think it's fair to say every aspect of infantry combat in this game is flawed in some respect. IH feels like they took all the worst parts of vanilla CoH, tried to simplify them and said "that'll do" at some point way before it was actually finished. Armor isn't even that great beyond the spectacle of moving the big stuff around the map. Using armor is tedious at best. Again, lack of quality and quantity. This game is the epitome of cool concept, terrible execution. Asking for 35 hard earned dollarydoos ON SALE is atrocious. In comparison to Company of Heroes, Iron Harvest plays like crap. In comparison to Company of Heroes: Blitzkrieg, Iron Harvest plays like 15 year old crap covered in mold.An example of an experience that can actually be fun to play with your friends is . It's free if you own Company of Heroes.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had my eye on this for a while but could never get myself to pull the trigger on it, I've been glad I did this time around on sale. 25 hours in and only about 60% the way through the numerous campaigns(with dlc at least can't speak to base game) It feels like a real mash up between some early 2000's RTS power houses. The Hero units have an almost Warcraft 3 or Dawn of War feel to them in terms of combat effectiveness and being able to turn the tide on an overwhelmed front. The scale of battle and cover mechanics are right out of Company of Hero's or Dawn of War if not slightly toned down. If I have 1 gripe so far it's been how ineffective infantry units are but against what are basically titans on some maps it's kinda makes sense thematically. some of the unit mechanics are ripped right out of other games too. I hopped into a skirmish mode to check out some more of the game modes and units and low and behold the USA themed faction as StarCraft-esk carriers and the Germans a Reaver like unit as well as a towering end game unit that feels akin to a colossi yet over all manage to play like the Imperial guard in DoW 1 and 2 with Death Guard mortars and a giant Steampunk AT-AT as their heavy hero unit... The Russians feel damn near like 40k Orks with heavy jump pack melee units, flame spewing mechs and massive indirect rocket barrages. Like I said this game feels like it took bits and pieces from some of the best RTS games ever made and tried to roll it up into something new that's really been fun so far! The lack of Workshop support is concerning as some of the maps feel like complete reskins of maps I've played for decades in the DoW series and I'd love so see more battle scaling something akin to the Apoc mods for DoW as well as more control over AI setup in skirmish games. There is a lot of inbuilt retooling for missions it looked like. You can change factions and all sorts of stuff in the in the pregame so for the creative there is plenty of replay-ability built into the single player experience. _childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: They sold out by adding DLCs when the base game still has an abundance of issues and QOL concerns. Game is repetitive and lacking in almost every way. I'm done sticking up for the devs. This game is ♥♥♥♥.ORIGINAL: *I was very skeptical about buying this as I saw how the devs released the game with some missing features and content, but I decided to try it out and let the game speak for itself. I like what the game has to say.*I think it's pretty good. It's not perfect by any means, but you know what, that's okay.I have experienced NO BUGS and NO CRASHES. It runs VERY smooth at 50-60 FPS steady on high graphics for me.I played the tutorial campaign mission, the first mission for Polania, and 3 skirmishes so far (1 as each faction).The sounds in the game are really good and crisp, the graphics are absolutely beautiful, the gameplay is a hell of a lot of fun. _childDocuments_.review: First off I need to preface my review by stating that I entered into this game with low expectations, and i was pleasantly surprised. So lets break this down a bit:The GoodThe graphics are quite stunning, first of all. You really feel like you are in this desolate wasteland like battle during the World War I period of the 20's. The story is well done, involved, and really grips you into the throws of the situation and can even tug on heart strings at times. The sounds are also atmospheric and directional, meaning you get the sense of proximity and distance. Gameplay is smooth, and quite intuitive if you are comfortable within the RTS platforms of other games. Overall this game is well designed, thought out, and generally speaking a great play. Except the thing that makes it bad for me.The BadYou come to this game seeing the steampunk mechs and the battles, so you expect this new "world" in this space. Except, its wildly undelivered. Per culture, you have 2 mechs and maybe a special if you select it. The variation of the troops is also limited, which means you have a very small toolbox to reach into for options. So while you are enthralled by the game story and other, once you venture into skirmishes or other, strategy is pretty repeated and consistent with little variance based on troop choices (because there is little troop choices period). It makes the game very mundane, really fast, to not have such a depth of choices to build and utilize, ESPECIALLY in the mech space.Comparing this to Starcraft or Warcraft (before MMORPG status) is almost unfair, but you kind of have to. This game has all the markings of a challenger to those franchises, except its only got 1/3 of the unit choices to play with. That creates a short lifespan on a game like this, which is sad.Bottom lineI paid their full price for this game, and my rule is $1 per 1 hour of play potential. This game really does not have it for me to rationalize the price. It is good, but it definitely is not repeatable due to unit selection. This game may age with content over time, and become worth it. Right now, it isnt really there for a long running title. It misses the mark because of the lack of choice.

_childDocuments_.review: -------------------Are you a fan of old RTS games?  How about old-school Warhammer?-Do you enjoy when an RTS provides elements, such as fortified positions, defensive positions, and the feeling of establishing kill boxes?Do you enjoy big clunky war-bots, that can pulverize buildings and turn fleshie things into paste?-Well, you're likely going to enjoy this game~-------------------------The General==================================Let's get something out of the way early on; this review comes from someone who has been enjoying the campaign side of things.  For comparison, this game feels a little similar to starcraft, and Warhammer had a kid.The Warhammer side of things is that units can take a bit of a beating before going down.  (Depending what you pair them up against.  Don't expect normal footie-units to stand much chance against war machines.  Well, unless you enjoy the sight of viscera. This game provides base building, but it also has it's own built-in class system.  Foot soldiers can modify their class on the fly, depending on what weapons they find on the field.  So, want to turn an engineer into a regular infantry?  Find a standard gun.  There are other such options, like machine guns, cannons, etc.Though I really enjoyed the way of being able to modify your units on the fly, it really allows you to evolve through combat.---------------The only thing I would recommend is to avoid diving straight into multiplayer right away.  Unless you really like utter chaos.This isn't starcraft, so you don't have hundreds of units rushing down your gates.  However, there is still a solid sense of ground control and micromanaging that is at work here.  You've got your resource zones, which you'll need to upkeep (like oil and iron mines.)  However, some of your bigger units are naturally pretty slow.  (Especially when your poor units are hauling artillery along the course of the map.)----------One thing I really enjoyed so far with the campaign is the lack of a real timer.  A lot of RTS style games encourage you to blitz through maps exceptionally quickly.This always gave me the sense that my troops were disposable, which I always felt a little reluctant about.This game rewards proper planning and care given to creating fortified positions and strategies.You'll sometimes know a little ahead of time where the enemies may be approaching; this allows you to set down sandbags and razor wire.  This gives me far more of a sense of appreciation to the developers because it provides weight to your units.  I've actively tried to ensure that none of my squads ever fully die during missions.  (Gotta bring the boys home after all.)This is an RTS game I've waited for for a very long time.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: This game is like Company of Heroes, but not as good. I bought it on 50% sale and I do not think it is worth the full price because of my criticisms. If you don't agree with my story/campaign criticisms then it might be worth it for you. DLC campaign is reasonably priced though. Absolutely trash in terms of multiplayer and not worth it at all for multiplayer games.Pros:1) Mechs instead of tanks (if you like that)2) Mechanics are straight forward and user friendly (mostly).2.1) Mechanics are very similar to Company of Heroes and easy to learn if you have played CoH or similar games. There are some changes, but I did not find any instances of them pointlessly making stupid changes just to be "different".3) Native languages. Very cool option. Absolutely love it for immersion. Great voice acting.4) Great voice acting deserves its own point. Regardless of language.5) Campaign mechanics are solid and fun. Majority of levels are fun and well-designed. (However, the maps and mission preparation are not on the same level as CoH but I won't list this in my cons list. CoH was pretty superb and I would say Iron Harvest just looks bad in comparison but still did this aspect at a good level.)6) I have campaign story criticisms which I discussed a bit below, but I will say that the overall design of each faction is solid and the general feel of the factions was done very well. It's only getting into the nuance that I start to become displeased.7) Interesting/kind of fun hero design/implementation.8) Co-op functionality on campaign. I haven't had the opportunity to try this out, but more games need to include co-op and if any of my friends end up buying this, I will be keen to try this out with them in co-op mode.9) Skirmish missions are solid and fun. (Essentially additional campaign missions that don't fit anywhere specifically into the campaign.)Cons:1) Mechs instead of tanks (if you think that's stupid)2) Stupid story for the campaign. Skip all of my part 2 criticisms if you don't want spoilers. In brief, my issues with the story are essentially as follows.2.1) Campaign story does nothing interesting with fictional setting. No meaningful or thought provoking ideas are explored. Starship Troopers this is not. Even worse, the fictional story is basically Illuminati ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ which has no relevant bearing on reality, no meaningful moral or fables, and not merely fictional in the sense that it is not historical, but fictional in the sense that there is no connection with real human beings and how they think or behave. The overall message is, "Fighting is bad! we should unite and only fight evil people that want to make chaos!" A pretty nonsensical when your examination of human behaviour is completely unrealistic and stupid. There is no shadow organisation that is behind all of the wars and evil stuff in the world. Trying to do good in the world requires knowledge and wisdom. Learning moronic nonsense will actively prevent you from doing any good. You can't unite peacefully with people when you are delusional about reality and delusional about what motivates human beings.2.2) Campaign story is wholegrain mainstream nonsense. All the villains are masculine men. And 3 out of 5 of the main heroes of the story are strong independent women with terrible development. Not the most offensive woke nonsense, but still annoying if what you are looking for is a more realistic and gritty sort of war game, and just generally sick of modern politics being injected into video games.2.3) Anna (Polish female hero) is simply constantly referred to as the Polish Joan of Arc. Clearly, the writers have no idea what make Joan of Arc the incredible hero to France that she was since the two characters have no meaningful overlap. Joan of Arc was a pious, self-sacrificing woman who revitalized the morale of her demoralized countrymen, and effected critical strategic and tactical theatres politically and militarily. She suffered greatly for her people and her beliefs, and ultimately died burned at the stake by the British and refusing to renounce her beliefs under disgusting mock trial and torture. (A gross oversimplification of a great woman, but I digress.) On the other hand, Anna almost never understands what is happening around her and just plunders around to victory based on her ability to shoot better than anyone else and be friends with an immortal bear demon. She also does not demonstrate piety, self-sacrifice, or much of any overlapping quality with Joan of Arc. For someone who is supposed to be a 'Joan of Arc' type, I found her to be incredibly underwhelming and essentially the game qualifies her as such based on being a hero unit and a female. Game dialogue also constantly reminds you that, gasp, she is a girl! Massively disappointed because an actually good "Polish Joan of Arc" could have been great.2.4) Olga (Russian female hero), a lot better than Anna, but kind of similar problem. We are just told she is a spy, but really she can inexplicably turn invisible and is again just an incredibly powerful fighter. Espionage and counterintelligence has so much interesting potential for both story and gameplay, and I think that this was a massively squandered opportunity.2.5) Frieda Ruete (German support hero), has almost no development whatsoever. Considering the poor development of the other characters, just an unnecessary waste of time/resources.2.6) Going to stop breaking down characters now as I am running out of steam (though most of them are pretty stupid too) and just get onto my gripes with multiplayer/skrimishes.3) IMHO, the reserves/hero units design is a lot less dynamic and fun than choosing a commander type and building your talent tree. I think heroes would have been better implemented if they actually connected to a commander talent tree as well, similar to CoH design. Instead, you choose a hero for your skirmishes which will just be a strong unit that you can buy and revive if they die. Not terrible, but I found it kind of disappointing playing skirmish. I found it got old pretty fast and that's before even getting into my next criticism.4) Stupid multiplayer interface design decisions that make the interface hostile. Example: they remove the ability to quit and instead have a call for surrender option. The only way to quit becomes to Alt-F4 and terminate the program. Compounding problem is that the main reason to leave a game (at least for me) is that 1 or more allies have left the game therefore making vote to surrender impossible. Just a stupid user hostile design. If I want to leave a game, I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ will. Punishing me for my choice is stupid. Want me to stay? Make the game fun. Or at least make the AI auto-accept votes. But no, just a hostile design.5) Very few multiplayer maps. It's like 3 maps for each game type of 1v1, 2v2, and 3v3 so only 9 maps in total. For a game with such simplistic gameplay, it's frustrating that there is so little variation in terrain. Another reason why it gets old fast.6) Squads regularly get lost/separated which massively and infuriatingly results in inability to actually control your units properly.7) Factions are extremely imbalanced. Overall, multiplayer skirmishes are trash.8) No custom games lobby. Unbelievably stupid design for custom games. You QUEUE for custom games instead of just perusing a custom game lobby where you can see the details of the custom game details, you can at best "queue for custom games" where you will randomly join custom games held by people. I have never found a game this way and it's no wonder why. It's incredibly stupid and user-hostile design.The hugest flaws about this game, in my opinion, are about its super ♥♥♥♥ interface and designs when it comes to multiplayer. Really makes the game frustrating for no good reason when you want to do something that should be extremely simple like playing a custom game.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Engaging Alternate History: The game's alternate history setting, with its diesel-punk mechs and a post-World War I backdrop, offers a fresh and intriguing premise that sets it apart from other RTS games. The world-building and storytelling are well-crafted, with an immersive campaign that explores various factions' perspectives.-Beautiful Art and Graphics: "Iron Harvest" boasts impressive visuals, featuring detailed environments, well-designed mechs, and visually distinct factions. The game's art direction successfully captures the essence of its alternate history.-Variety of Factions: The game offers a diverse roster of factions, each with its unique units and playstyle. This adds depth and replayability to the multiplayer aspect of the game.-Tactical Gameplay: "Iron Harvest" emphasizes tactical gameplay, with cover mechanics and terrain playing a significant role in battles. This adds depth and strategy to engagements, encouraging players to plan their moves carefully.-Single-Player Campaign: The single-player campaign is engaging and well-paced, offering a compelling storyline and challenging missions that help players become familiar with the game's mechanics.Cons:-Pathfinding Issues: Like many RTS games, "Iron Harvest" can suffer from occasional pathfinding problems, with units sometimes taking inefficient routes or getting stuck in terrain.-Balancing Challenges: Balancing issues in multiplayer can be a concern. Some factions or units may feel overpowered, leading to potential frustration in competitive play.-Learning Curve: The game's mechanics and unit management can be complex, which might pose a barrier for newcomers to the genre. A more comprehensive tutorial or beginner-friendly mode could be beneficial.-Limited Map Variety: Some players may find that the game's map variety is somewhat limited, potentially impacting replayability over time.Overall, "Iron Harvest" is a visually stunning and engaging RTS game with a unique alternate history setting. Its story-driven campaign, diverse factions, and tactical gameplay make it a compelling choice for fans of the genre. However, it does have some technical and balancing issues that could be improved, and the learning curve may be steep for newcomers to the RTS genre. If you enjoy alternate history and mechs, "Iron Harvest" is worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: As a Company of Heroes, C&C, AOE2, and Starcraft 2 player I just could not enjoy playing this game. I would describe Iron Harvest as a failed steampunk copy of the Company of Heroes franchise. It has infantry squads, infantry cover mechanics, unit retreating, armor facing, and capturing resource territories. All of the listed can already be found in the 2007 Company of Heroes and believe it or not, all these mechanics work better in that game which was released 14 years ago! I'm going to list just a few problems and my PERSONAL observations below. Remember this review is based on MY EXPERIENCE. If you enjoyed the game I'm happy for you.Firstly, I do must say that the game has good graphics and the overall art style is amazing. The unit design looks unique and every faction has its aesthetic. There are three nations with their campaign and unit roster. Saxony is a german nation with, with emphasis on technological supremacy and superior firepower. Rusviet units are robust and rely on brute force to win. Polania favors mobility and long-range fighting. The newly added Usonia relies on air supremacy to win the day. In any case, every faction feels unique and plays a little bit differently.  The story however is dull.  Back to the gameplay: Unit control feels so unresponsive and the pathfinding is terrible, units turn and move too slow, they have a problem navigating tight corners and narrow paths. These problems are most visible on a skirmish map called "Dark Forest" (overall a terrible map IMO, because it just consists of linear paths). On the topic of movement: Why is retreating soo slow? It feels like they are walking back to base. Some units like the Field Gun retreat so slow that it is not even worth it. Next up: Cover! Only green cover exists and even that is on certain maps scarce. Destroyed buildings and mechs can't be used as cover. Again, something that a certain 14-year-old game had.Base Building: This game is tagged on Steam as "Base Building RTS". Comparing this game's "bAsE bUiLdInG" to games like Age of Empires 2, Starcraft, Command and Conquer, Supreme Commander, Act of Aggression, and Rise of Nations is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ joke. In Iron Harvest, you can only build TWO BASE STRUCTURES (no, the fortifications don't count), and even those two, like in COH, can only be built around preplaced Headquarters. There is also no technology to research (upgrading 2 base structures in my book isn't research). Please remove the tag on steam because you don't deserve it.Overall I can't recommend this game at the moment. The developers are working hard to add new content and fix the existing issues, but this game is a sinking ship. It doesn't bring anything new to the RTS genre other than the setting and there are way better strategy games on the market than this. If there are any plans for a sequel I hope the developers at least learned some valuable lessons from the community and will make a kickass RTS in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this game on Kickstarter and have watched it evolve from the early stages of the Alpha for over 2 years.I loved the premise, but was a little worried once I tried out the Alpha. The maps were bland, there were barely any units, and the 2 factions had a boring dynamic. However, it was just an alpha and I can say that, now that there's 3 factions, heroes, and a lot more units, and that this game is certainly worth playing if you're a fan of this style of RTS. I've logged far too many hours into every installment of Company of Heroes since 2006, including all of the expansions.  I have an intimate familiarity with this style of game, of which Iron Harvest has taken a deep inspiration from. At face value, COH has further depth than Iron Harvest which is objectively apparent. In COH, each faction has 95% unique units, with the exception of a few "borrowed" units which reflect historic details (Lend Lease Act). Cover is dynamic, there's a plethora of devastatingly fun off-map support mechanics, the nuanced Commander system, dynamic vehicle damage, and a very strong emphasis on micro management. In COH, if you're skilled enough, you can win with only a handful of well managed units. COH is a highly detailed game with high replay value... With that in mind, and I can't stress this enough, COH was also priced at 60$ when it released. COH 1 was 60, and the expansion passes, Tales of Valor and Opposing Fronts were roughly 30-40$, which brought in 2 more factions for a total of 4 factions in COH1. COH2 also released at 60$ and only came with 2 factions on launch. 3 more factions were eventually released, but each was 10-20$ depending on when you grabbed them. So each COH would cost you 70$+ just to have more than 2 factions to play with. And even with that, COH still only offers 2 campaigns out of the 5 factions, USSR and US. There is no Axis campaign. I bring this up because the biggest complaint I see about Iron Harvest is that it's "overpriced" for what it offers.It is here where I will recognize that Iron Harvest is lacking in the multiplayer map count category. Now that we’re post release, the same 6 maps we’ve had since the Alpha represent the ONLY maps to play in multiplayer. COH on the flip side has dozens of official maps, and an endless supply of community maps. Despite that, Iron harvest is still of worthwhile value for the dollar. There might not be much map variety (at this current time) but instead there are 3 very different factions with 3 full campaigns, and this is where the game shines. As for the gameplay, I will have to revisit because I expect it to evolve further.In general though, each faction feels distinct enough that there's an enjoyable sense of variety when picking who to play as. Polania is all about hit and run tactics, focusing on mobility and range.Saxony is pure brute strength, but is expensive and slow.and Rusviet brandish odd units that keep your foe unbalanced with their use of rush and CQC tactics. Some have criticized that the infantry don't vary enough since each faction shares the same 4-5 core infantry types. I'd argue that their ability to swap gear on the fly adds a level of depth that COH only hinted at. In COH, sometimes and not always, will a squad drop its heavy weapon upon death. Then when your squad picks up the heavy weapon, you only are giving this to one soldier in a squad of 5-6. In IH, the entire squad becomes an LMG or Anti-Tank squad. While COH's approach is more grounded and still dynamically meaningful, IH's take on this serves its purpose to give the player a constant means to adapt.  This is most apparent in the campaign missions where you're given a finite number of troops and have to adapt to each situation. When you realize any squad can just become engineers out on the front line to keep your mechs up and running, you'll appreciate this design choice quickly.But the game isn't perfect, of course.-Mech combat could be slightly more dynamic. There's no "critical damage" of components like in COH, such as a broken engine or destroyed cannon. It's simplified to just "rear armor" crits that deal more damage to a flat HP bar. Each mech does get a "special" move though once it’s ranked up at least once, which are fun to execute. -Weapons you wouldn't expect to damage mechs still do chip damage, like small arms. In COH, a tank is a tank; a .306 cal rifle isn't going to scratch it. Here in Iron Harvest, a light or medium mech, if left unchecked can get chipped away by a crew machine gun. -Infantry are tanky in an off-putting way that sort of takes you out of the moment sometimes. -There's an overall sense of "clunkiness" to the map design and unit pathfinding. While mechs can plow through entire buildings, they can't topple trees or climb elevated terrain (even though they literally have legs, the one benefit over tank-tracks). Also, smaller mechs are stopped by barbed wire, even if they tower over it which is…odd. Overall though, I find Iron Harvest to be worth the value it's asking for, especially when you look back and compare it to its main source of inspiration. If there’s anything I’d be weary of for the purchase, just know that there’s only 6 maps for skirmish/multiplayer. That’s a big weak point right now if you’re thinking to buy for the multiplayer component. Hopefully they’ll release the new maps they promised soon. _childDocuments_.review: Is it good? Yes. Do I recommend it? No, well not at release.Full disclosure: I'm a backer and thus alpha and beta tester.There's certainly too few RTS games on the market which get right down to buissness and skip the economy build up. Iron Harvest certainly fills that niche. Ressourcepoint are captured by infantry, Iron is the ressource of immediate conceirn, however lategame units will cost Oil and the balance between the two works really well. Units aren't too many and quite fun, you can understand them quite quickly. There's a heavy focus on positioning, mechs take time to turn and so on. So in terms of the core gameplay this game is top.But the core gameplay doesn't exist in a vaccum.Do you come for the campaign? Well, it's there, it has some interesting ideas, but most of it was withheld from the testers and what we saw in the testing was quite buggy. However most money resources seems to have been spent there and it consequently steps into the same trap Grey Goo did.Do you come for skirmish? Well there's only 6 Skirmish Maps and no way to add more. The AI is braindead, even on the highest difficulty. And even cheating doesn't help it, when the plan is to reenact D-Day from the American's side, but sending in units one at a time. Even the openRA AI, who literally just builds stuff at random is better. You can't even choose a random faction. You always have to specify stuff. And a "reinforcment" system was shoehorned in last minute do give the appearance of more depth, but really does the exact opposite and makes setting up a game more a hazzle than it needs to be.Do you come for multiplayer? Well, from what we tested, the lobby system didn't work properly and was clunky. Dunno if this is fixed and besides that all skirmish drawbacks apply as well.This games has been released, not because it was ready, but because the devs wanted the release money. Don't buy at release, wait for sale and patches, but keep an eye on it, because the core gameplay is pretty good.(Note on being a backer: So I'm a skirmish/multiplayer player and I don't care much about a story campaign. What I wanted is barely existing, so for me it's money not well spent.)

_childDocuments_.review: When Iron Harvest blipped onto my radar, I was eager to dip my toes back into the RTS genre. It had been AGES since I last played one, and this weird alternate history take on the 1920s seemed like a perfect reentry point.  In some ways, Iron Harvest succeeded in filling the RTS-shaped hole in my heart. However, it also revealed that I had rose-tinted glasses when looking at that hole. Um that was a weird metaphor... Let's move on. I spent most of my playtime with the single player campaign. Similar to some older RTS games, the campaign is split into multiple acts with each act following one of the three playable factions: Polania, Rusviet, and Saxony. The plot itself is riddled with tropes and frequently cheesy (a flavor not everyone enjoys). On the flip side, I found the core cast of characters to be an endearing bunch. Despite the weak overarching story, these characters do an excellent job grounding the emotional and narrative stakes for each mission. Also, several of the hero characters have an animal companion. I'm not sure why the devs did this, but I'm a fan of this decision. I'm also a fan of Iron Harvest's individual mission designs. Missions tend to change and evolve as you play through them. You may initially be asked to destroy an enemy base, only to shift to defending that same base from waves of enemies. Or a mission may start with a focus on stealth and ultimately become an escort mission. This is nothing groundbreaking of course, but Iron Harvest used a wide variety of mission components to keep me on my toes and engaged throughout. I was raised on games like Starcraft and Age of Mythology, so I was expecting the core gameplay of Iron Harvest to feel pretty similar. However, instead of letting me relive my childhood gaming memories, this game shattered my nostalgia by revealing that… I actually sort of suck at RTS games. The minute-to-minute gameplay was the same: moving units around a map and ordering them to shoot at things. But it turns out that I had developed some very bad habits as a younger gamer, and Iron Harvest is not very forgiving. I was surprised to find myself struggling to get through some of the early missions. Before calling it quits, I decided to take some time to practice and internalize Iron Harvest's mechanics. And from there, the game really opened up to me. Engagements began to feel more tactical and less like a meat grinder. It shouldn't have come as a surprise that I needed to use strategy in a strategy game, but I wanted to bring this up just in case others encounter similar difficulties. You can definitely brute force your way through the campaign like I initially did, but I can't see anyone truly having a fun time playing that way. One difference from other RTS games worth noting is that… Iron Harvest is SLOW. Most of the mechs are lumbering with glacial movement and attack speeds. This is thematically appropriate, but I can see it frustrating some players. On the one hand, as a person with very low APM (actions per minute) having more time to direct my troops is a godsend. On the other hand, waiting 9 seconds between a heavy mech's attacks feels like an eternity. This design decision seems very deliberate, and I personally don't hate it. However, some will likely be turned off by how unresponsive the units are. This last point doesn't have any gameplay significance, but I'd be remiss if I didn't give a shoutout to the best part of Iron Harvest's world: it's got WAY better mechs than the real 1920s. In setting, these monstrous war machines are absolute terrors that revolutionized the face of warfare forever. From the outside looking in… they are wonderfully silly chonkers, and I love them to bits. There's just something about the obvious inefficiency of the mech designs that I can't help but find incredibly charming. But I'm strange, so your milage may vary. Overall, I enjoyed Iron Harvest quite a bit. It's a little rough around the edges, and demanded more from me than other games in the genre. However, I found it surprisingly refreshing that the game forced me to become a better player to get through its campaign. I'm not one for multiplayer, but if more campaign DLC is released, I would definitely pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: I had my eyes on this game for a while now, but held off until a sale because of the mixed reviews I would see. I got the deluxe version for $10, but should have just purchased the base game for less. I played for about 13hrs and I'm not sure if I got my $/hr enjoyment ratio. The world building and mechs were a nice break from more futuristic designs, but it felt like the tech was from truly from the 1920's at times. I only played through the first two of three campaign factions (Polania and Rusviet) before I decided to uninstall and move on. Issues:-Pathfinding was an issue from time to time-Line of fire could be very frustrating (there would be enemies right in front of my troops or mechs that just couldn't be hit until I moved them around to the side). -Your units will just stand there taking fire and not attack unless you actually move them in range. -Just about all of the mechs were painfully slow - the larger ones could take 5 or more minutes to get to their destination. -Base building consists of three buildings. -Resources are just claim spots which seem off balance (you have more of one resource than the other) and it seems random if the AI will try to reclaim them or not. Most of the time you could just claim rush them and forget about it for the rest of the mission. Some of the other things could be forgiven a little bit, but the speed was the deal breaker for me. This made it impossible to react to enemy attacks in any meaningful way. They would break through one of your defense points and then you'd have to fight them at your base, because you don't have the speed to cut them off anywhere beforehand. Unresponsive units just added on top of this. I will say that I didn't mind the first campaign faction (Polania) and did have some fun, but the second (Rusviet) just increasingly became a slog. This is a game where the creators were so close, but just couldn't make it over the hill. If they make a second one and solve these issues it would be a real gem.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on December 2020 during the winter sale. I'll summarize it here very easily, after nearly 300 hours of play.I have been looking to replace CoH 1/2 from my library and was looking for something 'fresh'. This is it. - , simple. It plays similarly to CoH, but is different enough not to make it a 'copy'. Don't expect what you know in CoH can as easily transfer here, though it does help.-  is great and teaches you the basics, strengths, and weaknesses of each faction.- . There's a lore section for those invested. - . The official IH discord is where you will find most of us. We run in-house matches and tournaments, as well as training new players and give them tips on how to play their favorite faction. Tournaments are also sponsored by the devs, so there's prizes (like the limited edition Eisenhans statue). Probably the  online community I've met to date.- , twice a month regularly. Although at the time I'm writing this, the devs are focused on releasing the new faction before moving to further balance adjustment and adding new mechanics/abilities. -  is atrocious. Even on 'insane', they're still quite easy to beat. -  is slow, though this . Weekends is usually the best time to find one. Though if it's taking too long, there's always the community in discord to find someone to play with. - , a bit wonky. Though this just takes getting used to. It's not outright imbalanced to the point it's broken. Some units counter one unit or another and each faction has something that counters another. As they say, you can adjust numbers, but you can't adjust experience and skill. - , moderately high. Though the game is easy to pickup, it can be quite difficult to master. IH is a game where the 3As  (Assessment, Assembly, Action) happen in split-second. Throwing units to the wall only lead to miserable consequences and smell of inexperience. When things fail, improvise. Should you get it? Definitely. You may want to hold on for just a bit after Usonia is released and the coming balance patches comes out. Do grab it when it's on sale and come find us in the discord. See you on the battlefield.

_childDocuments_.review: Early in my childhood my days were often grim and lonely. Feeling the cold isolation from my family I sunk into a dark, deep depression that dictated the course of my young adult life. Even today I regress into the deep shadows of my mind, lost in a chaos of emotions and regret. Then on the morning of September 1st 2020, a crack of light shown through my heart and into my soul as KING Art released the masterpiece title Iron Harvest 1920. _childDocuments_.review: From what I've played so far, Iron Harvest has the potential to be a fantastic RTS.From environment destruction to unit variety and factions, everything looks and feels polished. However, the game in its current state seems to be missing much of what was promised in the Kickstarter campaign, and thus the game in its current state feels like a promising exclusive backer demo or early access.For £46.99 at time of writing I cannot justify recommending this game to my friends in its current state. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I love this game. I've always been an RTS nerd since Warcraft 3, Star Wars Galactic Battlegrounds and Age of Mythology, and I felt like this captured the modern ideals of those games. The campaign is fantastic (just brutally difficult on the normal difficulty), bringing out mission that resemble WC3 missions. The multiplayer is great too, there is just one problem I find with it. Ultimately, I like the problem, but I can see others not liking this. Multiplayer feels like a race to get the biggest baddest mechs. If you get the Tur before your opponent, and they are not prepared, it is essentially game over. With that said, there are ways to deal with the mechs. Anti armor gunners are your friends. Not like they can really stand a chance against a Tur, but... There are two huge spikes in power that, if you're new, you can't really anticipate. King Art seemingly has tried to smooth these lines, but there is only so much that can be done. My favorite part about this game is the strategy (obviously). It feels more strategic than any of the other RTS games I've played. I truly feel like a commander overseeing the battlefield. There are campaign missions that feel like trench warfare. You have a giant line of soldiers and mechs that cant move forward or back, and you have to turn small victories into extra ground eventually overwhelming the enemy. This can take a long time, but damn is it fun. If you like RTS games, especially the strategy rather than the city building, as well as WW1 feels with mechs (dieselpunk is awesome), then get this game. I bought it full price and I haven't looked back. Its worth. The hours I spent in the campaign alone made up for the hefty 50$.If you don't like the idea of having to rush big mechs in multiplayer and the big spikes in power or want to city build then don't get it.
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Harvest

_childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty janky but it's at least fun jank. Or at least it was until the most recent update that completely broke the AI and not only made it way WAY more aggressive, but also gave it cheats so one AI of a given difficulty basically produces as much as two AIs of the next highest difficulty in the previous patch, which means that they have to be getting an increase in how many resources they get/discounts on everything they build and decreased build times. To top it off, all the AI's units are noticeably more durable and put out more damage than yours. Even if you don't use the already in-game difficulty adjuster that let you reduce your units HP by up to half to make skirmish games harder. Currently I legitimately don't think that being able to get a platinum medal on a skirmish map is even possible without external cheats, which is unfortunate since one of this season tree's goals is to do just that and if you didn't do that already you're kinda SOL.To add to this, if you backed the game's "Deluxe" edition on kickstarter, you DON'T get the new DLC for free, despite the people who bought the "Deluxe" edition on steam getting it. So if you're like me and decided to back the game on Kickstarter, you have to buy the DLC still. I really do enjoy this game, for all it's flaws and jank, but as of right now the developers kinda decided to put themselves into a bad spot and it's unclear if they're willing to listen to the players. If they fix the AI and/or resolve the kickstarter edition in a satisfactory way, then I'll go back and edit this review, but right now the game's future looks questionable.

_childDocuments_.review: A breath of fresh air to the dying RTS genre.Really fun units diesel punk aesthetic is really enjoyable and new to many.Combat feels impactful and the story was not tossed to the side for the sake of skirmish or multiplayer its actually really good and enjoyable.The 3 factions so far feel very different from eachother and play differently but neither feels to be stronger than the other balancing seems to be done well at the moment. (who knows if a patch will mess that up)Now for the cons:The AI is REALLY dumb.You will be playing it on easy at first to try it out in skirmish and then find yourself going all the way up to hard and only feel very slight increases in tactics and ability, and then you'll try insane thinking its going to be very difficult but if you just have a baseline idea how to play your faction you are going to steamroll them as well, which then brings us to the things that are supposed to make the AI more difficult or challenging the modifiers.There are 3 modifiers for an increase in challenge.1. Time limit on completion of the skirmish2. Unit loss cap3. Unit max health decreaseThese are great to have and feel really nice when doing them, but they shouldn't be the thing that makes the game worth playing against AI because not everyone wants to play against other players. The AI is not very advanced at all and needs a serious rework in order to be reasonable. There is no reason that I should be able to ROFLSTOMP the insane AI after just playing the game for 30 min. (I am not a good RTS players just an avid RTS player I could only get to silver in Star Craft 2)Other than that I can definitely recommend the game as a buy for sure. It may feel weird paying 50 dollars for a game nowadays but I personally feel its worth supporting the devs for helping carry the torch of RTS games forward.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, the greater concept of this game is 10/10 - an alternate history in the WW1 era with steampunk mechs, but it wasn't quite what I was expecting. It's a slow game: the mechs are slow and the story is slow and the gameplay is very siege oriented on top of that. If you're a history nerd you'll get some extra kicks out of it but some people might find the campaign a slog. The RTS half of it is a bit shallow compared to other titles (base building/upgrades/tech trees), although the 4 factions were pretty interesting and some of the mechs were especially fun to use. There's some great elements (destructible buildings, flame throwers, awesome mechs, fun maps, epic 2d art), some interesting elements (those minor squad mechanics and random animal helpers), and some not so great elements. Overall, I had fun, 6.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: OverviewIron Harvest is a real time strategy game where you play as 4 factions in a dieselpunk alternate reality setting. The game takes heavy inspiration from Relic games such as Company of Heroes and Warhammer: Dawn of War. The game comes with a campaign for all factions and an extra story. The story can also be played in co-op. The story I wouldn't say is anything mind blowing, at times I would say crosses almost CnC Red Alert levels ludicrously but still tries to be mature as possible.GraphicsThe game is visually stunning and very beautifully designed down to characters, vehicles and environment with a lot of effect such as fog and craters in areas where battles take place. Units are really unique since they take heavy inspiration of a ww1 era but with mechs instead of conventional weapons.GameplayIf to compare it with company of heroes 2 then the gameplay is faster in Iron Harvest. With units being a lot more snappier on command and having some quality control. It's also not too heavy on the micro managing allowing the player plenty of time to focus elsewhere.MultiplayerUnfortunately the multiplayer is very much dead. Tried many times to join a ranked, quick or creating a custom match yet there have been no such luck. if there are players then it's most likely diehard players or needing to find a group forum.Skirmishthe game comes with a skirmish mode against AI, some challenge maps and a conquest mode where where you capture regions and duke it out with AI in real time. Speaking of AI, it behaves rather strangely. While keeping the player on their toes but only for a brief time as the longer the game goes on the AI sort of "gives up" half way through. From sending units consistently to just sending like one or two at a time. not sure if this was intentional or a bug. If we were to compare with Relics games the AI will always be on the move and even if there are pauses the AI will be massing an army to attack, in this game, not so much. It functions rather bluntly and straight forward.Custom ContentThere is none... Which I think is the biggest flaw in this game as the maps are very limited and game modes pretty standard to most RTS games. one of the things that makes Relic games stand out is their modding and custom content support, making their games replayable and having a talented fanbase that pumps out new stuff 24/7. The current existing maps are not bad but playing the same level over and over can get you as far.Is the game good?the game is definitely enjoyable and plays really well even on my ancient computer. If you have friends to play then you will most certainly have a good time. however don't expect multiplayer as that will not be active unless by some revival miracle. But other then that it is not a bad game there was definitely a lot of love and care put into it and the devs had a lot of fun making it.

_childDocuments_.review: Totally recommend this game!I backed this game on Kickstarter (so really, I was lucky and got this game on a discount already) and played a little bit of the closed beta- there has been a ton of refinement in just the past 3-4 months, and though there are a couple items not in the release as of this writing, devs have a roadmap detailing that all features from the store page will be up and running in the next 4 weeks. There is no fraud here.That said, what is in the game already is very worth. The campaign is well written, music is good, great graphics and art- if you like the Scythe-Boardgame world this is based in, it is a must-play.It is very similar to COH2, however it is also different- many of the 'same' mechanics (cover, destructible terrain) are here but they are also slightly different. To say one is better or the other is better, I think it is just better to look at it that this is a different game, period. You can de-crew weapons in this game, something you can't do in COH2. The cover system is a little weird (compared to COH2) but it works, just takes getting used to. And most actions you set your troops to doing will have an interruptible time-counter (sorta like 'channeling' a spell in some games) which is a mechanic you have to get used to- different than COH2. Armies/"army cards" and pop-cap have different rules, so your army is limited in size by a couple adjustable constraints. Retreating is also different- you don't have added resistance to damage and run-away at light speed when you're in retreat mode so if you have poor timing or a bad retreat path you will have your squad get wiped! There are other differences, so playing through the campaign you do learn what they are and how they work (or just trial-& error some skirmish matches and you will get most of it).If you like Starcraft/Warcraft, C&C games, COH and the Dawn of War RTS games, and like that they are all different in their different ways and yet you like them for how they are... you're really going to like this game, because again it is like those games, but different in sufficient ways to be unique. When you smash through some buildings with your biggest 'mech like Godzilla and blow up some stuff, it is just a little bit easy to really like this game.Other nice comforts about it are that there is a good achievements system set-up in the game with like a goals-map to unlock cosmetics, which I think is pretty well done (almost have to have stuff like that nowadays, and this game has a good one).  Full campaign for each faction (there's three), and I already saw some hints in the campaign that possibly some of the other factions from the boardgame might someday be added? Who knows.So if you are an RTS fan (campaigns & light multiplayer) or a Scythe fan, I am sure you would really like this game. If you want to play an extremely-well made new RTS game, I am sure you would enjoy playing this game. There's nothing else like it right now, I doubt there will be another game like it really. Get it!
_childDocuments_.name: Iron Harvest

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great RTS title, if a little expensive.The easiest comparison to make is to the Company of Heroes series. If you'd played that, you've effectively played Iron Harvest. But where CoH was constrained by history, IH is allowed to go hog wild with their unit designs. Bipedal mechs with missles and flamethrowers and machine guns are the norm here for a game set to take place during and before World War I. One hero is a guy on a horse, and the very next hero in his own faction is a gigantic gorilla mech. It's ridiculous and awesome.The only problem I have is the game's rather pricey for what you get. And don't get me wrong, multiple faction campaigns and some skirmish maps ain't nothin'. But when it comes to playing with other people the map selection is pretty small. And if you're into RTS games for the comp stomping, the AI difficulty takes a pretty stark climb from medium difficulty, which is very manageable, to hard, which I'm pretty sure is cheating its ass off since it can double the size of your army in short order with access to the same or less resources.Still, this is a game worth supporting and I can only hope the content (and hopefully sequels) will keep coming. Get this on a sale and you'll be happy, I'm sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Tbh this is the sort of game that grows on me. The campaign started out annoying, with the attacks on all fronts making it feel like warcrime wackamole rather than an engaging battle but the story hooked me in through generally fun characters and genuinely awesome moments. On the multiplayer side things are a lot better but the factions feel a lil samey, at least on the infantry side (any unit can turn into any other unit if they pick up the right weapon, is alright but encourages engineer spam and if someone starts winning they'll end up with an unstoppable army using all of your equipment) but the mech combat is really fun and the heroes manage to add something without feeling too game changing. overall I think this is a really good game, although I wasn't following the development too closely so I probs didn't have my expectations bloated

_childDocuments_.review: On the outside this game looks cool as hell but when you play it just isnt. The mechs are cool but once you can build them thats that. The story is terrible and very forced, the accents are really bad, the game is laggy in menus but all these things you can look past if the game play was good but with how bad the pathing is it just becomes unplayable for me.You can try and skirt around the enemy to flank but for what ever reason you guys always want to take the weirdest and widest rout available and will pull the enemies before you are ready so you need to micro manage the hell out of every unit and when you have 15 or 20 to do that with it becomes a chore and not fun at all, personally never had this problem with other RTS games I have played and this is a really really big issue for a game like this.The balance seems wacky too, unless there is a mechanic in the game I dont understand or am missing, sometimes a unit destroys a certain unit quickly so you think it can take on the same kind of unit again so you let them attack and move to micro some other unit only for the unit to just die to the same unit type it just dominated.The game also looks like its from the 2010s but that is not really an issue.It has its good points, the units are really interesting and open up a few play styles and the mechs are fun but with the pathing issues even they suffer.Ultimately if it ever goes on sale for £5 ill get it or if they fix the pathing issue but I doubt they will seems DLC is already here.
