_childDocuments_.review: The fact that I have sunk nearly a hundred hours (not counting a chunk more in offline mode) into this game without ever coming close to beating it should tell you everything you need to know.If not, allow me to illuminate. This game has the uncanny ability to not only kill runs as soon as they drag on into mid-game, but also the player's will to live. Normally that would be a great thing. That usually indicates challenging gameplay, which is rather important to a strategy game.Phoenix Point is not challenging. Not in any desirable way. It's main approach to difficulty are increasingly bigger numbers. Sure, it sometimes throws a curveball your way by introducing somthing new, but 90% of all enemies are simply reused, more tanky versions of prior ones that deal more damage/Have a scarier weapon/one gimmick added that three other types of enemies already reused. However, despite the inflated number of enemy types, the optimal approach basically never changes. It usually boils down to a certain body part being implicitly marked as "Shoot here to win". There's little actual strategy involved. Now, by itself, all that is tolarable. The real issue starts arising once this is combined with Pheonix Point's addiction to speed. I usually prefer to speak for myself, but I know for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fact that many enjoyers of turn based strategy games do not appreciate being rushed. Phoenix Point is a game all about rushing everything you do. Everything is on a strict timer. Enemies evolve rapidy, mist spreads constantly, Havens are being attacked over and over and over again, every time only providing a very limited window to assist them. Meanwhile the player is tasked with also juggling expansion, resource procurement, exploration, upgrading, faction relations, Story missions, research, troop management, troop logistics and so on and so forth. None of that would be half as bad if it wasn't asked of the player constantly, all the time, at the same time. Working the Geoscape is absolutely tedious and involves a lot of micromanaging.However, it gets worse. This tendeny extends into the tactical game as well. Most missions involve getting somewhere or killing something as an inexhaustible amount of enemies pours onto the map from all sides. Whoever decided implementing this type of mission into a turn based strategy game with limited ammo reserves is a good, fun idea might want to think about switching professions.I assume it's meant to add a bit of pressure and tension, but in essence just turns into a tiring exercise of getting from point A to point B as quickly as possible before too many bullet sponges spawn... Which can fairly easily be accomplished thanks to the many exploitable abilites, units and mechanics.I guess this is as good a time as any to mention how utterly broken this game's balancing is. There are so many fairly obvious ways to completely trivialize aspects of this game that even my dumb ass found most of them organically. Some of them are so blindingly apparent that I seriously wonder if they were intended, otherwise I have no idea how they didn't come up in playtesting. For instance, bringing a vehicle to any type of scavenging mission basically removes all danger from it as you can literally drive-by crates and even enemies by briefly popping out with the units inside, effectively never exposing your designated supply hauling soldier to enemy gunfire. The fact that by virtue of having a vehicle, the player can drive around the map, taking pot shots at the enemies they are kiting with relative impunity is just silly.Even without vehicles, it's fairly easy to just have a soldier literally cross the entire map in a single turn, attack a ridicilous number of times, get immunities to use an OP ability without any of it's downsides and snipe many objectives in very short order without much risk or resistence.This game isn't difficult or challenging. It's just tedious. There's no other way of putting it. I've caught myself actively avoiding missions not because I lacked proper equipment or my soldiers needed rest but because the tactical game feels lika a chore. A formality. I've literally restarted maps to have the objective spawn in a better spot so I could be done two rounds earlier.To compound this issue, despite it's affinity for speed, the game feels so DREADFULLY slow. Due to the relentless unit spam and the game's need to play animations for eyerything, enemy turns take ages to complete. Entire EMPIRES have risen and fallen in the time it takes Fireworm #23 to slowly crawl it's suicidal behind slightly closer to the frontline. There is a noticable delay to everything. A delay that becomes more noticable with every passing hour of play.The worst thing about all of these issues and annoyances, the reason I even bothered writing this overly long review.. Is that this game has a very solid core design. If it weren't for what seems like avoidable mistakes, this game could have been a worthy successor to games like Xcom. Some It's innovations over it's predecessors are downright genius. The dynamic action point budget system is a great idea, allowing for much more flexibility when moving units. Manual Aim and the weakpoint system are something straight out of fallout and it's a novel concept worth exploring in this type of game (as long as it's not an instant win button, of course. Looking at you, Arthrons.) The game's story, art direction and faction designs are also incredibly well done. Each faction feels distinct, has it's own goals, interacts organically with others and the player faction and makes sense in the setting. That's the issue. There is something here. That's what makes me so UTTERLY LIVID. This game had all the potential. All the chance to swoop in and step into Xcom's footsteps as it's unique, own franchise while it's designers were off on their coke binge, designing their own ill conceived, bastard heir to the series.No, I'm not a fan of that game. How could you tell? Aliens are for shooting. They're not something to ally or coexist with. Not in the xcomverse, at least.So in summary: "You were the chosen one, Phoenix point! You were meant to fill the void Firaxis has left, not add to it!"Holy hell, this turned into an essay. If you actually read all this directionless, mad rambling and ranting, absolutely do play Phoenix Point! Because by god do you ever have the patience and disposable free time to do it.

_childDocuments_.review: I am an early backer for phoenix point from the beginning when they first announced its creation. I received the year one version on steam for free because of this. I have played this game for hundreds of hours on the epic platform. It has vastly improved since then. I thoroughly enjoyed this game. -The ballistic features make the tactics portion of the game challenging and enjoyable. -The story is compelling, there is a definite sense of urgency to save the planet and stop the extinction of humankind. -The factions are fun to side with and all have very different ideas on how humanity can move forward, non of them are alike, but all are useful in their own right. -The enemy is also interesting and hateful, you can understand why the population fear them.-There is real strategy needed in fights and using various types of soldiers is necessary, there is no one shot kills all. This makes each battle very dynamic with its own challenges.  I do have some gripes with this game, its been worked on for so long, yet it continues to lack certain physical elements to it. -Doors don't open, they disappear. -When heavy's use their jets, their guns disappear from their hands and hang from their butts. -They made the dash ability use an action point in addition to will, this diminishes its usefulness quite a bit (granted this was changed long long ago, I'm still bitter about that though) -augmentations are limited to two parts of the body instead of three. This is one of the most frustrating aspects for me. There is no reason for this. most of the time when augmenting , you get this awkward looking soldier that has a huge head and body, and these tiny stick legs. Snapshot seems to refuse to change this. -the music is boring and depressing when it could have been an action theme like x-com-there is a lack of life in your bases and characters (admittedly they added a couple of characters in the beginning, but they don't seem to play a role in the rest of the game)all in all, if you like tactics, this game is definitely very focused on tactics, that's what makes it fun.after finishing all the achievements. This game was challenging and fun, however I wouldn't recommend doing all the achievements. By the time you reach the end of the game for the 5th time you really get board with the repetativeness of the game. Its great to play through a few times, and then stop. Great game and great mechanics. Hoping for another one with better music and less depressing setting.

_childDocuments_.review: The overwatch mechanics is really stupid with AI just cheating and going around our overwatch if they have movement exactly knowing how we established it. The close quarter overwatch should be 180degree and not 15-30degree cone.Then we have the cover mechanics which is useless for melee, and considering that shooting enemy somehow always hit, the half cover guarantees a headshot to your operative.The movement of enemy is also far higher than your own units. Enemy can run half of the map and hit you twice when you can only move and shoot once. The melee recruits are completely useless with their melee because melee costs 2 action points to use. This also happens when you are behind a corner and there is no possibility to do a peek, while in overwatch the character will peek around the corner. _childDocuments_.review: As a long time player of Gollop games, going back as far as Chaos and Rebelstar, and of course X-Com and it's descendants, I was warily excited about Phoenix Point. I put off buying it until DLC4, to give the game time to polish out some of the bugs and build on the content base.I'm giving this game a qualified recommendation. If you're a particular fan of the genre, you might well be interested in giving Phoenix Point a burl to see what it does differently. If you are a fan of XCOM (2012) specifically, you might find that PP suffers somewhat in comparison with a certain lack of polish and accessibility. If you don't like the genre, this game is probably not going to change your mind.While it perhaps wasn't the amazing new reinvention of the genre that XCOM (2012) proved, I found Phoenix Point still generally enjoyable. The 'direct aiming' model worked better than I was expecting, and I generally found the geoscape and metagame detailed enough, even if some features seem redundant due to balancing. The inclusion of multiple different victory paths is a nice touch, and I found gives some replayability.I enjoyed the range of missions, ability to interact with multiple, very distinct factions, and some of the tactical features such as requiring ammo. I also found the general scavenge/fight/research/expand gameplay loop generally engaging, with lots of choices and options available at any time on the strategic screen. I mostly enjoyed the geoscape, but definitely felt that it could integrate far more with the tactical component of the game. Aerial combat - added by the Festering Skies DLC - definitely feels excessively basic and extraneous, but in that sense it isn't much worse than classic X-Com or XCOM2012.The game does suffer from very repetitive, small maps, a number of bugs (some of them game-breaking; I did have a corrupted savegame at one point requiring a restart) and some mechanics being very unbalanced in relation to others, leading to 'no brainer' choices and exploits. The gameplay does allow a number of different playstyles, but due to being unbalanced, several of them are pretty counterproductive. Explanation of some mechanics can be vague at times, and occasionally some useful information can be difficult to find in-game. The UI isn't the worst I've seen, but it is far from the best. I found dealing with inventory particularly irksome.Time pressure is quite intense in Phoenix Point, even more so than XCOM2. It is relatively easy to end up in a soft defeat - to find yourself in a position where it's virtually impossible to win. This isn't a deal-breaker for me, and as a rule I haven't found PP too much harder than vanilla XCOM. The game DOES feel much longer than a standard game of vanilla XCOM, and you will likely do many more missions in a full game of PP.I've only played with DLC switched on, so I cannot comment on how the game plays without DLC. Like the game itself, DLC is a mixed bag, with the aerial combat of Festering Skies being pretty basic and unimmersive. Corrupted Horizons has some interesting ideas, but again the balance is messy, which is part of the problem of having central game mechanics included in small DLCs - it becomes quite difficult to balance both the vanilla and different combinations of DLCs. Hopefully, this model will be reconsidered in any future games.

_childDocuments_.review: For players of the Xcoms (like me, who played them all from day one, including ironman):  PP is suppier to X when it comes to combat.  Aimed shots at different body parts can really be interesting and strategic; there is also stealth; armor and shredding; poison, virus, paralyzing, stunning, mind, control, vehicles and more.  Recourse management and soldier equipping (weapons;consumables;armor;bionics; mutations; multiclassing and tweaks galore) also make this part of the game better than the Xs for me.    You will also meet 3 other factions, who have pretty decent personalities and diverse goals and technologies.  Depending on how you handle your diplomacy,  1, 2, or all of them can give your some pretty amazing help and tech.  Although, their fighting among themselves can get kind'a annoying.Sadly, unlike the 3 NPCs, you and your bases are just, well, "there".  Barely.  Bases are pretty much just paper-doll cut-outs, where you place generic "pictures" of what you construct.  And you will have to build more than one around to world in order to help you in your goals in the game.    I felt almost no emotional attachment to my bases, or to a lesser extent, my soldiers, except they are very interesting icons and strategic tools to use in the game.The game balance is what almost had me giving thumbs down.  I got slaughtered on my first playthrough on Normal difficulty (I should have started on Rookie, like others suggested).  Only made it half way through the game on my second try, and am currently barley holding on by my fingernails on my 3rd attempt.  The game can be downright brutal, and even if you have played Ironman Xcoms (like me), get ready for some hair pulling moments.  It can be a frustrating game, and unless I am mistaken, it almost seemed the AI got better units and abilities the better I got (which would remove any sense of progression you achieve). Ironman has always been my 3rd playthrough setting on every Xcom (Normal, then Hard, then Ironman Normal),  but to finish my review with a warning, I will NEVER play PP on Ironman.  Only the ability to reload my saved games kept me from quitting this game and giving thumbs down.  But I can see how some hard core fans would totally love this aspect of the game.  Still, it gets a thumbs up from me due to all the great new innovations and additions to the genre, and a definite buy if you can get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Played on release on Epic and overall I can recommend this game to any XCOM fans. It has (or had) some flaws but I've read that they've greatly improved almost every aspect that I didn't like. The biggest offender being dynamic difficulty which punished you for doing well but I think that has been (mostly?) removed. They've also improved the pace of the game along with a lot of minor things.I feel like it has enough "new" things to not call it XCOM clone with my favorite being the free aim and shooting at different body parts actually having strategic value. You'll learn to abuse it eventually against certain enemies. Another great thing is flying with multiple squads on different parts of the map later on.I also like the action point (AP) system that lets you freely do actions however you want as long as you have the AP for it. Shoot two times in a row? Sure. Move one square, shoot and move again? No problem. Want to move far but afraid of running into a bunch of new enemies? Not an issue as the unit will automatically stop when sighting new enemies. You can also move just one square at a time if you want without wasting any AP moving like that.Update 2021-05-05: Finally finished my first Legend playthrough. I can still recommend the game but helping havens and clearing out Pandoran nests/lairs/citadels becomes a chore after doing them so many times already so that's definitely a negative. At one point I probably spent 10 hours not progressing the story missions at all but instead just making sure the planet stays alive long enough (and getting the resources I needed by saving the havens).Legend was hard but not too impossible after already learning how to abuse some mechanics (full stealth Sniper/Infiltrator was my favorite so I had like 3 in each squad) but I did have to "save scum" a little bit in some missions when some important soldier gets oneshot from miles away while in full cover. In general it felt a bit too easy for enemies to oneshot soldiers but I guess that's kind of my fault for going with lower armor gear to have other stats higher.Free aim and AP system is still what makes this game overall really good. It felt so good to move a heavy soldier a few squares over so he can shoot a hole in the wall and then be able to go back to cover and use other soldiers to kill the enemies through the hole I just made by free aim shooting.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good: The free-aim system this game implements is unique and interesting. It requires you to think about a tactical situation very differently from XCOM EU and XCOM 2, where each individual must be placed carefully so they don't get caught in the cross-fire as opposed to bullets magically passing through. Its also important to consider cover and line of sight with the free aim which impacts the success of your shot. There is also the added benefit that even if you miss you still can score some damage on your opponent. I also like the fact that the soldiers have accented English in accordance to nationality, something XCOM has not really done except for very specific characters. Plus the story has a cool premise that is not boxed in by the precedent set by XCOM UFO Defense.The Bad: Unfortunately, it seems this game has put all its bets on the free-aim system and it has definitely not paid off. The strategic layer has nothing more to offer than XCOM 2. Base building is boring, and resource management even more so since your involvement with either component is pretty surface-level. The various factions aren't that interesting because acting on behalf of one makes the others unhappy. Not that this makes a difference in the overall game as the negative impact is negligible. The game looks and feels like a bad XCOM 2 mod. The character models and customization is bad. The collision physics are bad since the environments feel like its all made of cardboard when it is destroyed. The controller support feels like something the developer slapped on last minute. The mouse pointer is always in the middle of the screen even during dialog and cutscenes. The cutscenes seem to be entirely comprised of concept art and textboxes. I have not finished a full campaign as of this review because the thought of going back to this game makes me consider what I would rather be doing. The game has committed the worst sin imaginable; it's boring and the developer wants you to pay $60 for a game that's realistically worth $20-15. It's highway robbery.The Ugly: The mutants are, of course, pretty ugly. So is the EULA, which admittedly I did not read very carefully.Conclusion: The free-aim system is a cool and interesting spin on the classic XCOM dice roll as was advertised. I was waiting for this game to be available on Steam for a year and was happy about it being on 50% sale.  However, it seems that the year was not spent wisely on this game. Its pretty buggy, the gameplay is boring, its badly optimized, and its a far more expensive as a game than what is called for. Plus, its like all of the things I did not like about XCOM EU ended up here. I wanted to like this game but sadly I cannot recommend this game and I have a feeling the situation will not improve with time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves better reviews in my opinion. I have played it on Epic for over a year now, trying it here and there after each update, and now with the year one release I think it's in a really good place and I am excited to see how it develops going forwards.Most of the negative reviews here will compare this to XCom 2 or complain about Epic Games or some random tech issue. I understand that the epic games deal, and if you have tech issues starting the game, that you might be frustrated and leave a negative review. That said, the vast majority of players reading these reviews likely are curious about the game itself. Let me tell you that, as a fan of the original UFO Defense, this is a huge step forwards from XCOM 2.Why do I prefer it over the latest entry in the XCOM series? Mainly for three reasons.1- No more bullcrap pod system for enemies.2- A real action point system3- A combat system that isn't just a dice roll.1- The pod system in the modern XCOMs completely changes the way you play once you get used to the game. You inch forward with your first soldier to draw out a pod of enemies then proceed to fight with the rest of your soldier. If you move forwards to far with your last character, you are screwed on your next turn. This is unrealistic and boring.In phoenix point, the aliens are not acting in pods waiting to be "woken up" but they actually explore and move on their turns and also will move on their own. Xcom 2 tried to address this but failed in my opinion. 2- Action points are back! Instead of having two big actions like in the modern XCOM games they went back to the original where you have full control over your characters. If you have enough AP you can move, shoot, and then fall back. You can loot off the ground, shoot, and then hide... You have options and moving one square to far into your "2nd action" doesn't completely end your turn for that character. It gives you freedom to make tactical decisions just like in the original xcom.3- The combat system is honestly the best I've seen in any game like this. It's a big meme that LOL YOU MISSED A 95% SHOT in the new XCOM but it's a meme because it feels like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Why? Because it is. Your trained soldiers should not miss a point blank shot. It is unrealistic. In this game you have a cone of where your bullets can spread and your shots fall within those cones predictably. This means cover doesn't just effect the dice roll, but it actually acts as cover. If you have a light pole between you and an alien, you might hit that light pole! Even if they aren't ducking right behind it. It's completely realistic and so refreshing compared to the RNG of the modern XCOM games.This game isn't perfect. In fact, I think XCOM2 has much better mission variety and production values. That said, even with those things I just don't want to play it anymore because I feel like I've figured out the puzzle. I know to creep forward and then wake a pod up and shoot. I know when to take cover and how to bait enemies out to improve my dice rolls. The tactical game in Phoenix Point is much more interesting and dynamic.This game is like Xenonauts with a better budget. Julian Gollop really recognized what made his original game special over the modern franchise. I am thankful for it. I hope that Snapshot continues to work on it though because, while it's wonderful to play, it sure could use some more personality, something UFO Defense and the new xcom games are dripping with.Pros:-Combat system is more fair and more exciting than any other tactical game IMO.-Action points give you more freedom than in the modern XCOM games.-No pod system! Enemies move and behave in more realistic ways.-Geoscape is easy to understand and there are some neat mechanics with factions.-Enemies evolve! They'll try to counter your tactics by changing as the game goes on.-I'm a sucker for the aquatic theme of the monsters. Makes me want to go play terror from the deep again!Cons:-Lacking mission variety compared to XCOM2.-Lacking personality. This is probably my biggest gripe. The voice acting, customization, and even environments are pretty dull. You'll want to play this game for the gameplay, not for the personality or graphics. Hopefully that changes one day. Especially with the underwater theme of the creatures... It could have been so much more interesting looking.EDIT:I'll add one more con to the game. The ending mission is weak and requires a ton of AOE. Almost out of character from the rest of the game. I love the lovecraftian boss but it's a slog to get there and more of a chore than a fun mission. I can see it ruining an ironman run quickly and I hope it's addressed later.That said, still the best xcomish game out there and I'm replaying it now after 120 hours. I spent my 120 hours split between two runs, one which I gave up on. I used all the DLC and enjoyed all the lore and missions. Some complain about the frequency of the missions. I agree some of them aren't worth much but honestly, I like having tactical puzzles to just run my guys through. I play it for fun not to rush the ending.Love the game. Cybernetics and mutations seem tacked on but that's a small complaint. This game deserves more love, full stop.

_childDocuments_.review: I am 32 years old.My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is needlessly complex and, to me, uninteresting. Are we dealing with aliens, a genetic experiment gone wrong, or is this some eco-disaster? Who are these Phoenix people that have implausibly built a base on the moon? Why are there so many factions who can't get along when the Earth is crumbling around them? So many questions and none of them introduced in a way that drew me in. With X-Com 2, you knew you were dealing with aliens, and despite some disagreements with methods, the Earth had a common goal.So, if you ignore the story, then what do you have? A convoluted tactical game. There are so many units and so many different monsters and weapons, and none of them seemed to be distinguished from each other. When I got to my fourth different type of assault rifle, with statistics not very different from the other three, I kept asking myself, "should I be taking multiple weapons into combat to test them?" So, I did. It turns out I couldn't really see a major difference between them, except for ammunition types, which is super annoying.Here's another thing that's simply not well thought out: you have assault characters who are proficient in assault rifles and shotguns, but you don't get shotguns to start. You can't make them, nor did I find any several hours into the game. How are these units proficient in something that doesn't exist? Why are shotguns so special that they have to be found buried in research or in some latter game discovery? All weapon types and classes seem to suffer from this lack of logic. There's also no map in the zones, which makes it often a guess as to where you started and where you are now.This is one of those games that has a lot of meh, but also tends to frustrate, too, so that even when you are having any kind of fun, it's short-lived.For a game that borrowed HEAVILY from X-Com, you'd think they could have gotten the balance and fun parts right, too.

_childDocuments_.review: Best way I can think of to describe this game is a blend of classic and new X-Com with some interesting elements of its own to help it stand out from the crowd. I say it's a blend of the previous games because the interface is fairly similar to the newer games and it features a half cover/full cover mechanic. That said though, the actual combat is more akin to classic X-Com. Rather than having two action points and every action you take consuming either one or all of your action points, you have four turn units. The distance your units move determines how many TU they consume rather than just having a simple move or sprint that consumes either one or all of your AP and different equipment, skills, and weapons consume different amounts of TU as well. Shooting is also based on line of sight and projectile trajectory as well rather than being based on an RNG system where your shots either hit or miss. I mentioned it has X-Com's cover system but it functions quite differently here. Rather than just being a factor in the RNG system it actually determines how much of your unit is exposed and their stance. Units in full cover post up against some tall cover like a wall or tall stack of boxes which allows them to shoot around corners and as long as the enemy doesn't have a clear LoS on them, said cover is going to actually protect them. Units in half cover are in waist high cover   and crouch behind them which allows units behind them to (somewhat) safely fire over their heads without the risk of blowing their heads off (yes there is indeed friendly fire here).The game also does a few of its own things as well. It uses a locational damage system where  each body part has its own separate amount of HP. In addition to dealing damaging to the unit's overall health, you can also disable that body part which affects them in different ways while also inflicting bleeding to organic units which deals damage over time to the unit at the beginning of their side's turn (also it stacks which can lead to some pretty satisfying moments where you disable multiple parts on a enemy to the point where they're taking 40 damage per turn and just drop dead in one or two turns). In addition to that, there's also a free aim mechanic where you go into a first person view of your units and manually aim their weapon which opens up a window for a lot of strategic opportunities. You can line up a shot to destroy a specific body part, use a burst weapon that fires in bursts, aiming it so it'll inflict damage to multiple parts, or even line up a burst that'll hit multiple enemies. Personally, of all the X-Com style games I've played, this is probably my favorite system. To me, it just feels more natural rather than being based on hit percentages. The only real complaints I've had about the game so far is that haven defense missions (basically the game's equivalent of terror missions) can sometimes feel pretty cheap at times. I've had a few haven defense missions where enemies started off right next to the objects you have to protect for said missions while my units started clear on the other side of the map. When it comes to the geoscape, I'm not particularly fond of how establishing new bases works either. Rather than just building new bases, you have to find and reactivate bases so actually establishing (or even finding) a base in a key location literally just boils down to pure luck. There's also the weapons as well. Don't get me wrong, they're generally satisfying, but as others have pointed out, a lot of the weapons just feel like sidegrades. A big contributor to what made X-Com such an intense game was the constant need to stay ahead of the curve in terms of technology. Bigger and badder aliens were constantly being introduced and they didn't stop being introduced just because you were putzing around shooting down the occasional UFOs. You were in a constant arms race with the enemy and that went a long way in creating tension. Without the need to research and pump out superior equipment as quickly as possible just to keep up with the enemies a lot of that tension ends up being lost. Aside from those issues though, I've been thoroughly enjoying the game. The main thing to keep in mind before you buy it though is that this is indeed an X-Com style game so you're in for a rollercoaster ride of victories and defeats. When your soldiers die, they die for good. You will lose soldiers and you'll probably even lose some of your best soldiers at times. There's going to be times when most of your guys don't make it home from a mission or maybe even worse, they all get wiped out. There's also going to be extremely satisfying times when you pull off flawless victories that are insanely satisfying (and let me tell you, there's few more satisfying than steamrolling sanity destroying eldritch horrors so badly that they actually try to flee the battlefield entirely as their buddies bleed out and try to limp away on mangled legs in sheer terror). As long as you can stomach the deep lows you'll face enough to enjoy the satisfying highlights you'll experience, I'd strongly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a difficult recommend. The graphics are decent and the tactical combat has some surprising depth.The reason you might not want to pick up this game can be described in a word, JANK! There are all these paper cut issues that remove some of the enjoyment. There are huge pauses all over the place, so turns take much longer than should be necessary. The interface often feels laggy. The world map is clunky, requiring all these unnecessary clicks to activate locations. Line of sight can be deceptive and a hundred other minor annoyances. _childDocuments_.review: - By far the single best thing in this game, for me, is the ability to have multiple squads all carrying out missions around the planet simultaneously. Being able to fill up several ships, zip them around, and explore, defend, fight, and rest all at once is fantastic. - The lore of the world is pretty darn cool to me. The Pandorans, the virus that makes them, the lore before all that, the factions, Phoenix Point itself. All of it is pretty cool to read and listen to.- The variety in architecture and the levels themselves. There are definitely some lackluster tile sets in terms of playability, but aesthetically they're all super cool.- The voice acting can be really solid. Not the soldiers you're playing with. Those are pretty mediocre. Especially the weird sound clips of the actors pretending to be doing slow-mo instead of slowing down the audio tracks themselves. At least, that's what it sounds like. No, I mean the faction members talking to you in the geoscape. Whole paragraphs of text that they read out convincingly and entertainingly. Good job on that. - The inability to pause the game or open up a menu while the enemies are doing their turn. Once their turn starts, you're locked in and considering that there can be like 2-3 dozen enemies swarming around one at a time, it takes forever. Forever being like 5-10 minutes per turn. It's absurd that we can't pause mid-enemy turn.- Maybe I just never unlocked a way to do this through the myriad of potential research options cluttering up the awful research UI, but there are no base defense options. You can leave soldiers in a location but that's it! No turrets, no traps, no robots. So things are constantly being attacked and ya know what, 30 hours into my playthrough I'm just sick and tired of dealing with enemy invasions.- In XCOM, you have what we call pods. That's the general term for a group of enemies in any given mission. Each mission usually has several of these pods. When you enter the mission and explore, you find and alert these pods. This results in several small encounters of your squad vs 1 or 2 enemy squads at a time. Phoenix Point doesn't do that. Do you like being swarmed by 1-3 dozen enemies all at once from all angles? I sure as hell don't. Especially when paired with the inability to pause/reload mid-enemy turn. It's tedious.- The gear progression blows chunks. 90% of the gear is horizontal in quality. It's not better than your starting gear, it's just slightly different. Ooh, this gun has 10% more of this and 10% less of that. Lame as hell. Horizontal is fun for variety in a given portion of a game, but vertical progression is fun longterm.- My soldiers never felt stronger. They could move further, they could use more boring abilities, but they never felt better at doing what they need to do. They don't improve in damage, they don't improve in accuracy. They're the same from the beginning but now they can run 10 squares instead of 4. - The hitboxes are complete trash. Full reticle in aim mode within an enemy's model? MISS. For a game that prides itself on the physical simulation of the bullets meaning chance isn't a thing, or shouldn't be, it sure FAILS at that. The amount of times I save scummed because 100% of my reticle was within an enemy and then, oopsie daisy, it's a miss! The hitboxes are so poorly made that this happens constantly. Another reason I save scummed frequently. - The cover system in the game is worthless. Again, bullets are supposed to actually collide with cover so you'd think cover would be valuable. You're wrong. Your soldier will stand like 2-3 feet off of some cover options, meaning that full cover does absolutely nothing for you.- Overwatch setup is also worthless half the time. Lets say you position your soldier on a corner wall. You want to setup overwatch around that corner so that when an enemy approached, your soldier will step out and take a shot. Nope! Overwatch from the in-cover position resulting in nothing happening OR the system glitching and your soldier just shooting the wall instead.- There is no hunker option at all. No way to make yourself smaller and take defense in a moment where you might need it. This is especially frustrating in missions where you have a person you're trying to protect. Actually lazy design.- The classes are BORING. On paper they're pretty much the same as in XCOM. They seem like they'll be cool until you read through their class abilities and realize that you're just shooting. No special tricks that make things fun or interesting. No rapid melee rampage, or multi-enemy quick taps. Just shooting a lot with your boring, inaccurate guns you've been using since the beginning of the game.- So it's late game. You've earned some extra vehicles you don't need anymore. Can you salvage them like with gear? Ha. Nope! They just clutter up the geoscape and your menus. - Infinite spawning enemies. I get it. They're a horde-like rampaging enemy with many millions or billions of troops. Lore-wise, it makes sense. But again, it's just not FUN. Slogging through 1 mission for an hour straight because they're pumping out infinite enemy spawns until you finally cut through and take out the enemies that can summon reinforcements isn't fun. This should have either been a deliberate cap for the mission or there needs to have been cooldowns. Instead, some enemies will summon more help every single turn, and some enemies will literally birth out more and more worms every. single. turn. - Relying on random chance spawns in order to progress the story is a stupid f'n decision. I need a Pandoran Citadel to spawn. I have the world covered in scanners. It's April (late game) and none are spawning. I have lairs just sitting there being annoying but they're not growing. It's been some 10ish hours of waiting now on a damn citadel to spawn. So, I haven't actually finished the game even once yet. I have about 50 hours logged right now with about 38/39 of those in this playthrough. As mentioned in the last point above, I've been waiting a long time for something to spawn for me to progress the story. Maybe it's a glitch. Maybe it's just chance. Regardless, I'm bored of this amateurish, broken, poorly balanced mess of a game. I really wanted to like this game. I've owned it for years and have been looking forward to it. Now that I finally had a chance to play it, I can't stand it. I don't typically review games before I'm done with them but I needed to review while it's fresh in my mind. They clearly had some solid inspiration here but the execution is just so darn awful that I can't recommend this game. There are so many better tactics games out there. In the end, I give Phoenix Point an . It's so rare for me to give a rating this low but this game was such a bad experience, I refuse to go any higher. They could have fixed this and they chose not to. Shame on Julian Gollop for slapping his name on this like it's a work of pride. It's pure disappointment and nothing more. I'm going to continue slogging away until I either get a citadel to spawn or I end up losing. I don't want to have this game looming over me for an incomplete playthrough. But I don't recommend it at all. Get something else.When I rate games, I use an M/S/A/B/C/D/F scale with general thoughts for each below.M: Masterwork games. Near perfect games with no real complaints.S: Great games with maybe a few preferential complaints or desires.A: Good games with a few issues but nothing that hampers the experience.B: Solid games that do a lot right but could use something more.C: Average games Nothing special. Not great, but not bad. Worth playing still.D: Mediocre games. Maybe they have some good systems but the cons outweigh the pros.F: Failed games. Something just ruined the game as a whole for me. I rarely go this low.

_childDocuments_.review: Not often I review a game, but here I am. Reviews at release kept me away, cause of bugs and other grips I saw. I can say that all that seems to be a footnote in the history of the game. I've been an X-Com fan since the 90's. UFO EU, Terror from the Deep, the games I was raised on; would have them as a combined entry in the top 10 games of all time. Appreciated the remakes, they were a fine addition to the universe.Phoenix Point has done great job in capturing the Geoscope/Tactical/Resource Management feel. I'm sure I'll restart soon, now I got the feel of it. Yes, the difficulty can swing, and sure the resource management can be a pain at times, but there is no perfect balance. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, hell I didn't even really mind that it was locked on Epic Games for a year, but after all this wait, I gotta say I am thoroughly disappointed. I only got six hours in before biting the bullet and requesting a refund.The Pros----------~ Removing RNG in favour of Bullet Spread is a fantastic idea~ The Vats Like "Pick Your Shot" system is very cool!~ You can shoot your own men if they are in your line of fire, making for importance of spacing~ Crippling Specific Body Parts and Bleedout is fun to play with~ The factions all seem pretty cool from where I was at.~ The maps look cool~ You can shoot then move~ It's different enough from XCOM to be its own thing while also retaining core ideas you understandThe Cons----------~ The game is honestly just insanely easy. The fights are always super manageable and rarely did I ever have any of those "oh ♥♥♥♥" moments XCOM gave me.~ Their introduction of new content is poorly designed and leads to unfair moments. In XCOM when a new enemy is introduced you are at least told it is new or it has a distinct enough style for the viewer to understand "I am about to fight something with different abilities" in Phoenix Point it just catches you off guard. Surprise! These enemies fire back when you shoot them! Surprise! These guys can shoot 4 times in a row despite looking similar to another enemy that can only fire twice. ~ Research is very vague. While it does sometimes tell you the benefits you get, I ended up missing out on super integral research because I wasn't told its value until a bit too late~ The sight lines of where you can shoot and where you can't feel very wonky. I can't shoot down at someone directly below me, but if I move one tile to the left I can! Even with the site indicators I sometimes move a soldier to set them up in good sightlines only to discover it wasn't a good area~ The vehicles just sometimes break. This is what caused me to quit. I did another pastey mission but was gonna get a vehicle out of it. Eventually for no reason the damn thing locked up and I had to restart~ The maps are way too big for the number of enemies. It's like double the size of XCOM maps with a 1/4 of the enemy~ The abilities the soldiers get feel very weak or impractical. They get a lot of options but very few feel that strong or are worth using when you could just...shoot the enemy.~ The customization for soldiers is bad. Like even worse than Enemy Unknown and that's saying something.Honestly after all this I only have one thing to say. You absolutely should buy XCOM Chimera Squad. While not a full XCOM game it toys around with some new mechanics while retaining the XCOM goodness. It's short cheap and better than this. I'm probably gonna go back to Enemy Within or another round of Chimera Squad, because while I wanted something to fill that itch. Phoenix Point definitely is not the answer. After a long wait and a year trapped in Epic Exclusivity I sadly cannot recommend this game and I really hope that Steam will accept my refund.EDIT: Refund got declined. Guess I might as well play through the rest cause I own it now.

_childDocuments_.review: Not an easy game but very good. Some people say it's too difficult or not well balanced. It wasn't well balanced at first, but many updates have fixed that and added many options to win the game and lore that's actually motivating to continue playing.It's a complex one, I'll give you that. It's not only about field tactics, you need to play the strategy game too, take care of the economy, choose well your alliances and get to know them so that when they ask you know how to respond. Research is very important: you need to choose well what to research both for advancing the game and for your play style.Most importantly you need to understand you MUST NOT research it all. The strategy layer is mostly a war against time, so poor choices on what to research, build, or not caring enough about your alliances will kill you later on.The good news is that the game is very replayable, all locations are randomized at the beginning of the game. So you can take as many runs as you want to learn the deep mechanics and not get bored.The battles are difficult too. Cover and positioning is key, and making the right decision on when to rush or when to stay back until the enemy makes a mistake will save your day. My advice, don't save every move and load when you fail. Play each battle till the end. If you reach the point where you know it's lost, then restart it and try a different approach. You'll learn faster on what works for each situation. Restarting a battle randomizes enemies and their positions which will be a real test for your tactics. If you pass you are ready for the next level. Loading saved games in this game is like cheating on exams, you'll pass now, but sooner or later the reality catches with you and you won't be able progress no matter how much you reload.It has a long learning curve but it's fantastic if you enjoy both strategy and tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a hesitant yes from me. This is one of these good news bad news games.Good news:The free aiming system adds a lot. At first I thought it was going to be a gimmick, but once you learn to read how the system displays information and learn the value in targeting different body parts you wind up making a lot of meaningful choices and getting a lot of gameplay out of it.The class combination idea is excellent. The game doesn't have that many classes, but every character gets two. In addition they get three unique masteries which can include the ability to grab proficiencies form other classes. Want someone who uses the heavies jetpack to fly on top of a building where they can deploy an engineers turret while taking shots with a sniper rifle? You got it. There's a lot of uniqueness to the performance of different soldiers.The geoscape level gives you good reason to run several squads. They need recovery time between missions, even if just to rest when they're not injured. The aircraft are only so fast and missions can pop up worldwide, there's no guarantee of them being in range of any one squad. Juggling a bunch of different squads keeps the gameplay fresher than having one A-team that does everything.The mission variety feels decent. While every mission boils down to one of essentially three things (Go there, grab that, kill that) there's enough difference between mission types that they feel like they reward different approaches. Some feature infinite reinforcements and are best served by a fast squad that does the job and gets out. Others require you to clear the map and benefit more from something slow and careful. They also offer decent trade offs between grabbing extra loot and winning that can make you question if it's reaaaally worth going for that last box or if you should retreat with what you have.A lot of thought has gone into giving the aliens unique powers that go beyond "Have more hitpoints, do more damage". There's already a lot of this in existing titles with psionic and melee enemies doing special stuff, but this at least doubles the sorts of weird attack you could be subjected to compared to other games in its genre. I'd rather not spoil them but it's nice to see.The willpower mechanic works pretty well. All special abilities use willpower. Seeing allies die uses willpower. Some attacks drain willpower. Having a body part take severe damage drains willpower (especially the head). If you hit 0 then you miss a turn fleeing and taking cover. Also all psionics are based on "Is my willpower higher than my targets" rather than a percentage chance which makes critical moments like mind control feel less RNG. Conversely you can skip a turn to regain willpower and some abilities offer other ways to restore it.Bad news:There is a lot of not fun micromanagement to get to the good bits. At the end of a mission you get a button to buy back all of the ammo you fired during the level, but if you don't have the resources there and then you'll have to do it manually weapon by weapon once you do. Doing things requires the right balance of tech, materials, and food - trading one for the other means flying to an outpost and trading things they don't have for things they do - but each outpost has limited supplies and replenishes every so often so you'll need to do a circuit of them every now and again to do basic building and supply.The documentation in the game is so-so. Some abilities, equipment and modifications won't work exactly as advertised. Some critical features of them aren't mentioned and you discover them by trial and (mostly) error.The game doesn't autosave each turn, which is for the best since it'd be tempting to save scum every death given how tedious hiring and equipping a new recuit is (trade resources for the right types, queue up their leg armour, body armour, head armour, weapon, and equipment to be built seperately) and it seems like the odd misfortune is part of the game rather than intended to be avoided. The thing is: Sometimes the game crashes, or gets stuck on an infinite enemy turn. It's not a lot, you'll only see it once every ten hours of play or so, but if it happens near the end of a long level it's frustrating.The interface lets itself down in places and there are a few times that the game seems to trip over its own feet. The first of these you'll probably encounter is that its realistic bullet physics are based on where the character holds the gun, so the heavy weapons users who start with jetpacks are also the ones who can't take advantage of high ground because holding their gun at waist height makes them most likely to shoot their own cover if they're angling downwards. Also just little things like the game automatically switching off a character every time they run out of action points, even if they can overwatch for 0 cost or the last thing you did was activate an ability that reduced the cost of their next shot to 0.Overall:There's more pros than cons and it's taken some risks doing a lot of worthwhile and interesting things. It's a shame that they've failed to nail some of the core stuff, but the bells and whistles? Very ringy, very whistley.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like XCom style tactical combat games, you will enjoy Phoenix Point. Probably. The good*Fantastic map, weapon, and enemy design*Great lore, from the main plots and factions through to the incidental details/encounters in the world*Lots of improvements on the XCom model - equipment, actions, etc.  Vehicles are cool, but almost never better than just having more soldiers.*Real depth and breadth.The bad*A lot of things are nonintuitive. Understanding how to play the Geoscape is really opaque - be prepared to watch lots of YT videos to learn it.*It's hard. Very, very hard.  You will lose a *lot*.   I don't mind a challenge, of course, but I am a pretty seasoned gamer, felt I was pretty good at XCom/EU/2 and this is a step beyond. I restarted on Rookie mode (lowest difficulty) and even that is hard as hell.  Just be prepared for that - if you want chill casual gaming, if you like winning, this is not that.   I find myself playing a bit, making some progress, getting frustrated and giving up, then going back to it later.*I'm not sure the Festering Skies DLC is actually fun.  Aerial combat feels rushed/tacked on, but is also hard as hell and so feels a brutal drain rather than adding fun.  I'm mostly rushing trying to kill the Behemoth at the moment just so I don't have to deal with it any more.

_childDocuments_.review: XCOM 2 is currently my all-time favorite game, but Phoenix Point is growing on me. Things I like: - Free Aim: Being able to target specific areas and shoot around shields and obstacles is a great enhancement to this gameplay genre. - Realistic ballistics instead of dice roll shot chances. One of my biggest complaints about XCOM is missing shots at close range that have a 95%+ chance to hit. Things I don't like: - Maps are very static. One of the joys of XCOM 2 is the dynamic map building. - Limited enemy types. So far the aliens are two primary types that just morph to have additional abilities. Similar to having more enemy types, but not the same. - Lack of (so far) variety of character types. This may change some as I get deeper into the game. Things that are different that I am adjusting to that I haven't yet decided are better or worse: - Less linear story line. On one hand, I think it will create some interesting possibilities for encouraging going through the game more than once. One the other, it can be very confusing and unclear what you should be doing. Perhaps more playing time will reduce some of that confusion. - Much more detailed approach to weapons. Again there are pluses and minuses. Soldiers can carry more, but the management of "stuff" is for time consuming in the game.All-in-all, my initial reaction to the game was a little negative because of the added complexity, but the more I play, there are aspects of the game that I like and will miss the next time I play through a game of XCOM 2.

_childDocuments_.review: The X-com we deserve. ©Yeah, we don't deserve much, it seems. And I really, really want to recommend this game, but it's just... underwhelming. Sadly, Steam does not allow me to post a neutral review.- Lore. Lore is freaking awesome, especially if you read the short stories on the game's website. Lovecraftian eldritch horrors that come from the sea.- Damage model: you totally can (and should) snipe the pincers off enemies, rendering them harmless- SIMULATED ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ BULLETS. Hell, this would make this game the best in its genre, but...- It plays almost like the Firaxis' X-COM: base management, soldier classes, with its own twist like vehicles (they take 3 slots in the transport, so almost useless), willpoints/panic, and - It's plagued by minor UI issues, like scrollwheel not properly scrolling the list, etc- Its bullet simulation fails to work sometimes, and bullets pass through enemies or you. I can live with that, frankly- UI is lacking. Not that it's missing something, it's just not that good IMO- This may be a matter of taste, but the voice acting is meh: the soldiers sound lifeless, and sounds for enemies, frankly, is weird: almost all the enemies sound almost the same (not human-like), except for the , that sounds almost human. Dunno, maybe it should be a part of the "horror", but it's very meh- The game is shallow: there's research, sure, but you're not really progressing. The new guns are mostly situational, apart from some notable exceptions. Nothing game-changing, almost nothing . You want to equip some new and cool armor? Nope, you only can cosplay another faction, whose armor is generally the same, with some stats shifted around.- There are about 15 maps total, or so it seems. It gets old pretty quick.- At some point you're sent to Antarctica, which is a... tropical rainforest, the environment is a copy of another mission that took place on the equator. -_-- The game was originally kickstartered, reaching some additional goals, then the management sold its soul to Epic for additional cash, throwing a part of its backers under the bus, yet still failed to deliver the "evolution" mechanic: currently the progression is tied to some obscure checkpoints, with enemy variants appearing in a sequence, instead of the promised "evolution", when the AI would adapt and evolve its minions to adapt to your playstyle- The game is lacking some features that should be in the game, yet present in, you guessed it!, DLCs. You want to actually distinguish between different ground vehicles? Pay up!All in all, the game is kinda cool, something to pass time until Xenonauts 2 comes out of the EA. I'd say it's worth buying only heavily discounted, and don't bother with DLCs, they don't add much substance, only clutter.

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenix Point is an X-COM variant made by someone who really wants his old X-COMs back, a sentiment I feel very neutral about because I never played the old X-COMs. Phoenix Point is a game I want to love, but manages to bump itself down to a like. Interestingly enough, it isn't the difficulty spikes that make me feel iffy about it, though some of them did feel annoying. I am quite a fan of the bullet projection model, or whatever it was called. It got rid of one of my biggest issues with the X-COM games by making it so a machine gun having a 50% chance to hit actually means something different from a pistol having a 50% chance to hit. Instead of wondering how your people managed to miss all five shots in the span of one attack, some nuance is added where two or three of the bullets might actually hit, making it so that riskier shots may actually prove to be worth it. I also like the base management and troop transportation, as it allows you to react to multiple havens being attacked back to back, even if the havens are on the other side of the world, by letting you use multiple squads, and you can  set up multiple bases with infirmaries and stuff.But that havens bit brings me to my biggest issue, the factions. There are three factions, and the game uses the standard conflicting factions model. Fascists vs Nutters with an optional other faction, in this case tech hippies. The factions themselves aren't what I take issue with though, it's their extra quests they give for raising their support of you. Every single quest involves attacking one of the other factions, which makes no sense to me considering the whole WORLD WIDE INVASION. Are you guys seriously asking the one neutral group in this world to be less neutral to progress your ideology? You don't have any soldiers you need rescued? Havens to recapture from the Pandorans? No army of Pandorans marching towards one of your cities that you want stopped BEFORE the haven is attacked? The Phoenix Project was made specifically to protect humankind, and it's a little weird that none of you are interested in capitalizing on the army of Pandoran slayers that keeps destroying nests and protecting havens without asking for payment. The most annoying part about the lack of neutral quests from the factions is that a lot of research is locked behind the factions, so you need to pick some extreme if you want to access them, usually without much input on your part due how much they hate you protecting the havens of their enemies from Pandorans. Protecting people is my job, though you people do keep giving me good reasons to retire.In conclusion, I recommend the game because it has some interesting concepts that can be fun to play with, despite my rather lengthy rant about how annoying fascists, nutters, and tech hippies are when they are in the same room.

_childDocuments_.review: WALL OF TEXT: After the equivalent of one workweek playing Phoenix Point I've hit a wall. On one hand the game is a great tactical turn based sim -- but on the other hand it's a busy mess that punishes more than it praises. Victories bring little reward while failures are crushing and brutal. One mechanic in most of Xcom's iterations (and spiritual successors like Phoenix Point) have in common is a research tree that allows you to take your victories and shift the balance of power back in your favor. Enemies have deadly weapons? Kill them and reverse engineer them. Powerful new aliens arrive? Research powerful new weapons. In Phoenix point it seems like this would be the case too -- but the better guns never arrive. You start out against a foe more than fairly matched with the initial evolutions of your foe being easy to knock over, but they rapidly get every advantage you do, plus a whole lot more and they just get harder and harder without the player (despite a complex research tree and factions to share research) giving you anything that really helps you overcome your enemy much less turn the tide. The closest to a weapons breakthrough I was given was a powerful but woefully inaccurate cannon weapon but even that got outstripped by the endless march of the armor and size of the opponents you face. The game gave me resources I didn't even know how to use or have an avenue to utilize, and had numerous "artifact" resources I only learned how to find by the time it was too late. You can never have enough men to cover all your bases, and unprotected bases if raided are totally destroyed making it economically unfeasable to restore them to functioning. There are lots of different craft to choose from to move your squads, but the ones that allow you to move big squads are too slow, and the fast ones don't move enough troops into an engagement to win. You'll only be able to maintain about 1.5-2.5 good squads of troops, and losing anyone will be devastating forcing you to save scum (though I consider this standard in the genre) ... what is NOT standard is how 1-2 squads simply cannot get done what is called for to be done and that's all you get. When I hit the "Wall" I had as stated only two squads/vehicles, and the map was COVERED in plot advancing quests on the other side of the earth Where it took forever to get to and back from, with multiple havens getting raided at the same time. You inexplicably don't pick up most of the guns off the people you kill forcing you to spend/waste resources restocking after every mission and frankly it's a losing battle even keeping your troops supplied. A good metaphor for this game is a 4-star meal served to you with fine presentation only to learn your silverware is the size of toothpicks and the bites of the food are huge and you're incapable of cutting them into manageable pieces until the waiter starts grinding your face into your meal by stomping on the back of your head with a combat boot and as you slowly lose consciousness things start to get REALLY mean. Seriously -- I felt like I had access to scores of weapons in my playthrough -- but none of them were effective against the aliens. Shotguns that promised to do deadly damage at close range PINGED off of mid-late game enemies armor. Only sniper weapons and unwieldy cannons seemed to harm foes AT ALL, with opponents cleaning your friggin' clock with comparatively similar weapons... because your armor isn't nearly as broken as the aliens.The faction dynamic in this game is really flavorful and dare I say cool on the surface, but it boils down to a ridiculous game of "three-stooges" with all of humanity on the brink of extinction and each faction being more absorbed with hurting each other over conflicting ideals than fighting the monsters that are LITERALLY EATING THEM. It's like a synedrion scientist would be getting devoured from the waist down by an alien while he is ordering you to sabotage a New Jericho factory for reasons that are completely unexplainable. Humanity is in the same boat, but everyone is bailing water into each others parts of the rowboat, with predictable results. It looked like there was plenty of game left when I stopped playing because like I said, it just kept getting more and more brutal. It ended for me when I finally faced an alien that was as big and armored as several vehicles with a health meter to boot, that pooped aliens that mind controlled your characters and if you even grazed it would put up a smoke screen to hide it -- and there I was looking at the same damn toothpicks and inaccurate cannons to take it on. I gave up, unwilling to waste another 40 hours to hit the wall again because even with everything I learned in that long of playing a campaign I didn't see hope in trying again with knowledge and optimization. If I were you, I'd move on, and give up in advance. If you want a good Xcom game play the actual Xcoms or try PHANTOM DOCTRINE which is a refreshing departure from the genre, instead. This game is just a pretty Xcom clone that turns you and your danglies into a punching bag.edit: gave the game a second chance on the easiest difficulty. This just made the tactical combat boring, but did nothing to resolve the greater issues, just takes longer to for things to become unplayable. Game is a mess. Discovered Cybernetics and Building Mutants but didn't even bother because you needed to build facilities and have your troops occupy them when instead you have to run around. Found three new resources, only two of which made any sense. Artifact resource is not explained how it's acquired, and how you think you get artifact resource you get unrefined mutagen (with no obvious way of refining it.)This game stole two work weeks of my free time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my 2nd go at Phoenix Point.  I was an original backer and I love games just like these.  That being said this game still suffers from a few things.Monsters are basically humanoids with weapons.  Sure at first they are interesting and mysterious but as soon as they are able to "mutate" and hold the same weapons as you do they become very one dimensional and boring.  For example: Aliens at first can only melee and paralyze you with tentacles. Later on, they will get sniper rifles and machine guns who are able to shoot you as well.  To the devs: I really want to play a game against interesting enemies who do cool crazy things, not pick up guns and shoot...Different factions.  These guys are hopelessly useless yet vital to your game.  Every faction have somewhat different classes but of course once you learn them all, they are exactly the same as your guys which in turn the aliens will get the same thing soon thereafter.  Factions will outclass your armor and weapons and technology when you first meet them. I'm not sure why we are playing the game because it's just disgusting how far advanced they are.  My question is this: if they are so strong, why do I have to go around saving their havens?? Or even Earth for that matter??AI are the biggest DUMBASSES I've ever seen in my life.  They will move into stupid crazy positions and get killed.  The AI on the monsters aren't always that bright either but at least they display some strategy.  Even then, they monsters will take low percentage shots while sometimes utilizing cover.  Sure I can control the AI if they are on my side but now I have control over a guy who somehow possess less or the same technology that I do despite them outclassing you (outside of the map)Speaking of battles, the line of sight on this game still needs major reworking.  Free aim is probably the best thing about this game. However, if your guy isn't a sniper, good luck firing from the 2nd or 3rd floor down to the first floor... YOU CAN'T!!  I'm glad to see that this has been fixed from the first time I played this game. Free aim was not very good since you could not be behind cover to fire at anything.  Being able to multiclass sounds good on paper but in the end, you can tell that it is a must to mix a few classes.  The nice thing is that there will be some characters that can do more than just one other class and can be multiple. However they better be an assault first or they're not gonna get much exp.  In my opinion the classes really need to be rebalanced.  Heavies and Snipers require 3 action points to fire instead of 2.  This makes them hard to move into a good position and fire.  This consequently makes them waste 2 or 3 turns getting them in a good spot.  Unfortunately since the Assault classes are so good in this game, they will have already done all of the work and neither my sniper or my Heavy has done anything useful in the game.  Did I mention that all you'll ever need are the assault classes?  Who needs anything else?  I don't know.  The overworld map is very confusing. I've touched upon this already but the AI factions have way better technology and access to vehicles and weapons and everything else, yet you are the one running ragged around the Earth trying to save everybody while they are somehow dying.  Faction havens are ALL OVER the map.  While I am dying for materials and food, this game really wants me to trade.  I've got nothing to trade because all I do is find havens all over the map!!  If I do get into a fight, almost all of my materials go back into purchase a FULL round for my guns even if I only fired one shot!  Resources are so scarce that even if I prioritize research first, it doesn't matter because I can't create enough things for my 6 or so guys that I have!  Then by the time I actually do produce them, it's already obsolete!!!  WTF!!!  FRUSTRATING AHHHHHHHH!!!!The expansions aren't even that great as all they do is add more to the difficulty.  It's actually advisable from many veterans of this game to not even get those for first time players or to turn them off completely. Storywise, the factions do make a lot of sense and leads to some different story options and missions.  In the end, frustrating gameplay mixed with horrible execution with uninteresting baddies make for a bad time overall.  Once again, I've made it to a point within this game where I am fighting baddies after researching just about everything and having barely enough supplies and my guns are barely making a dent on the armor of the baddies.

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenix Point is a turn-based strategy game developed by Snapshot Games and released in December 2019. As a fan of XCOM and other similar games, I was excited to dive into this one and see what it had to offer.First off, the graphics are impressive. The environments are richly detailed and the character models look great. The game takes place in a post-apocalyptic world where humanity has been devastated by a virus that mutates the creatures around them. The design of these mutated monsters is really cool and they make for formidable enemies.The gameplay is solid as well. The turn-based combat is engaging and requires strategic planning and good decision-making. The game offers a good variety of weapons and abilities for your soldiers, allowing you to customize your squad to fit your playstyle.One aspect of the game that sets it apart from similar titles is the ability to target specific body parts on enemies. This adds an extra layer of strategy and can be really satisfying when you manage to take down a particularly tough enemy by targeting its weak spot.There is also a base-building element to the game where you manage resources and research new technologies. This adds some depth to the overall experience and gives you something to work towards outside of the combat.One downside to the game is that it can be quite difficult at times. The enemies can be tough and the permadeath feature means that losing a soldier can be a devastating blow. However, this also makes the victories all the more satisfying.Overall, Phoenix Point is a solid turn-based strategy game that offers a lot of depth and challenge. The graphics are great, the gameplay is engaging, and the ability to target specific body parts adds a unique twist. If you're a fan of the genre, I would definitely recommend giving this one a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m a long time squad game strategy fan… from Sabre Team on the amiga through to X-Com 2… and I have to say this game pushes my buttons in all the right places.I’ve avoided it until recently because of the criticisms stating it’s buggy and repetitive. Apart from an odd animation glitch that occurs here and there I’ve encountered no bugs and no crashes. In regard to repetitive, if you found X-Com 1 mission repetitive then you will find that here.I’ve read a lot of comments of comparing this game to Firaxis X-Com (a franchise I also love)… and I’d say that’s a tad unfair. PP makes X-Com look like a Saturday morning cartoon in gameplay and tone, which is not a bad thing. With X-Com you except quick gameplay, bombastic explosions and powers… PP is much more subdued matching it’s nihilistic world.A huge plus point for this game is how accuracy is handled with visual circles rather than percentages. That and how the bullets are “physically” in the world leaving you with this tangible feeling of ballistic combat (rather than an animation playing saying you hit or miss).My one criticism would be the music during combat encounters. It doesn’t match the tone of gameplay and the track keeps changing (not in a dynamic way) from turn to turn leaving it feeling a bit disjointed.If you are an old school x-com fan this is a must have game.

For example: One faction you can help them claim a ritual site from another faction and the options make you think its a yes or no answer. One would think you have to say yes or else you will lose favor with you faction, but instead if you say no you reveal a schism within the faction and can still incur favor with the faction anyway. Managing multiple transport ships is a mess. I forgave a lot of the bugs in this game because I rally wanted to like it, but what broke me was after 45hrs of playing I was on a long 2hr mission to destroy a spawner and only at the very last objective found out that my vehicle could not be extracted because of how the map was set up and I could not complete the level.
