_childDocuments_.review: I can't say I've really ever got to deep dive into the tabletop games such as Mansions of Madness, Arkham, or other Cthulu Mythos tabletop experiences, but I do enjoy me some Lovecraftian lore. Arkham Horror Mother's Embrace is an exploration adventure game with turned based combat sprinkled throughout. The lore and environment is built very well. Like most lovecraftian content the course of the experience starts out normal enough and eventually explodes near the end. There are seven different investigators to choose from at the start and each stage you can choose to take whichever unlocked investigators you'd like during each scenario. There are 9 scenarios to complete and they each feel pretty diverse. New enemies are introduced through out the game with new abilities and there is a decent enough variety on weapons. Although the animations are serviceable, the voice acting is acceptable enough for a game of this caliber. The music is fitting to the world. So I have quite a number of gripes about this game, however they are all pretty small. The animations, movement, interactions, and camera can be a bit clunky. The hold a button to accelerate at all times gets a bit annoying. I ran into a few bugs when it came to inventory movement. The game is a self contained story that you may not end up replaying too many times. There are times the dialogue and reactions really doesn't make sense such as a character saying it must have been something they ate when they are affected by blind status or trying to stretch when searching through a table. There is a character who is a narrator in the game, but this just seems to provide unnecessary exposition on actions and moments. I think my largest gripes was just how simple and repetitive the combat and consequences is. Characters have strong suits such as range, magic, or melee; but you can just hand everyone a gun and they can handle pretty much every combat situation. In games like this you normally need to keep a heavy gaze on your sanity meters. This game has them and there are consequences for them going down, but they never really seemed to be all that bad or to make the game much harder. A dice roll to see the consequences of your actions would make a nice addition. It's probably to avoid save scumming since all actions provide the same consequences (aside from sanity rolls) but you have no save slots, but one save that auto saves at various points. The last gripe I had may have just been something I was running into, but the game refused to accept my graphics settings between sessions. It always defaulted back to medium. This isn't a grand lovecraftian game to look into with it's simple combat and lack of depth systems, but it is an enjoyable title to hop into. Asmodee Digital isn't a huge AAA company so I didn't expect a title in that scope. I enjoyed the seven hours it took me to clear the title and I intend to one day go back and try to get the rest of the achievements. The exploration and interaction was pretty immersive and I never felt like I was playing for very long until I closed the game. Those kind of experience be they big, small, buggy, or perfect I will always enjoy. I would say grab this one during a decent sale if you enjoy lovecraftian content and can look past smaller studio issues and commodities. 𝕀𝕗 𝕐𝕠𝕦 𝔼𝕟𝕛𝕠𝕪 𝕋𝕙𝕚𝕤 𝕋𝕣𝕪

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions from only 30 minutes or so of play time: The voice acting and controls in the game are just awful. It feels like this was originally developed as a mobile game and then someone did the bare minimum amount of work required to add keyboard and mouse support. Camera is so tight to the character that you cannot see the environment and the only camera controls that exist let you pan around the character - there is no option to zoom out or change the angle. Animations are poor and there is zero lip syncing. Mouths just flap when it's a character's turn to talk, continuously waggling around even when there are no words coming out and the game is waiting for you to press a key to hear the next line of poorly voice dialogue. Calling it voice acting is being extremely generous - the voice work is atrocious. The choice of actions are idiotic - like "examine" vs "look through". One makes the Mythos clock advance while the other doesn't, but which one triggers it feels like they were assigned randomly. If you stand idle for a few seconds, little word balloons start popping up over the character's head with stupid quotes which feels extremely out of place given that everything else is voiced. This game just feels like an unfinished mess. Requested a refund on this disaster.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't get me wrong, I am a HUGE Arkham Horror universe and Lovecraft Mythos fan. I have played "Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace" multiple times on both Xbox and Steam. I got all the achievements on both systems, except for the one achievement that refuses to unlock for anyone in the Xbox version. But, to be honest, AH: ME is a VERY rudimentary game. It reminds me fondly of the old "point and click" adventures for the PC in the 90s. The game, other than the Investigators used, is not much like Arkham Horror at all. If I had to pick one board game it is like, that would be Mansions of Madness. Even the "Lovecraftian" elements in the game are not very...Lovecrafty. Also, moving the action to New Orleans from Arkham makes little sense. There are cultists aplenty and an evil scheme to summon an evil god and all that good stuff. But most of the monsters are evil human cultists or exploding snot globs.The voice acting is decent, if a bit hammy in some cases. And you'll hear a LOT of dialogue in the  course of the game. I have not played all the available main heroes. I understand some of them are better to listen to than others.There is turn-based combat that comes up pretty regularly. It's not bad. Nor is it really difficult, if you figure a few things out. For example, it's always better to shoot than to use melee weapons (especially with the exploding snot globs). There are four different kinds of guns--and all of them degrade rapidly when fired. Magic is also a good ranged attack, but there's only really one offensive spell. The rest are either buffs or stuns or defense. You can probably get through this game once and see or experience nearly everything in 8-10 hours. The price tag for the game is a bit high for not a lot of content. The computer autosaves the game at random intervals or before big events. There is no "save" button for the player. You can't go back to levels you've already played (to get special items or unlock achievements) unless you start the game over from scratch. You have multiple unique heroic Investigators to choose at the beginning, and the ones you don't choose are never involved in the game. You'll encounter the same five supporting characters/Investigators over and over again, however. Though you can miss some of the supporting Investigators or get them killed off if you don't rescue them from peril. I recommend either Jim Culver or Kate Winthrop for your starting hero if you intend to try to get all the achievements in one or two playthroughs. I have played about 40-45 hours of Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace. It was a mix of fun and frustration for me. And I'm happy that I'm done with it. Though I would likely play any DLC, if they bother to produce any. I originally bought AH: ME on Steam and then had to get it on Xbox because the keyboard/mouse combo movement irritated me. I literally bought an Xbox controller for my PC in order to play this game on Steam. I would NOT recommend this game unless you are a huge Lovecraft/Arkham Horror fan or have a serious love for "point and click" style adventure games. Caveat emptor!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one. I'm split down the middle on this game. I love the setting and I've played all the board games it was adapted from. I'll keep it simple.+ Nice dive into Lovecraft Lore.+ Good atmospheric presentation through sound, sprites, and lighting.() Decent story() Ok voice acting- Horrible Camera and controls- Story on rails, No actual player choices or branches in the plot line.- Little depth to puzzles, and no real punishments for spiking mythos level.- Bad character animations and interactions (no sync to voice and often not even facing the other characters they are speaking to.)- Very basic and easy turn-based combat. I had the big bad down and only one member of the team took 2 damage.- Really bad character reactions to status effects.  (Blind: "I don't feel so good.")- Magic system was worthless, Just kit everyone with guns and possibly one melee. Spam shots and overwatch.If you like Lovecraft lore, you'll like the game. If you enjoyed the board games for their innovative mechanics, random encounters, and endless replay-ability... skip this game and launch the Mansions of Madness App.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game might be interesting, but it has some downsides that make it really hard to play.1) Everything is clunky. Movement, inventory, item use, combat actions. *Everything*2) Having mentioned the inventory, it is bloody tiny. Any investigator can carry up to 4 items, consumables stack up to 5 (which isn't much concidering how much use some of them see). Ammunition is tracked separately and does not require inventory space, fortunately.3) Use the wrong interaction on an item (say, you read a piece of paper instead of examining it) you get a Mythos Clock tick. Every few of those something bad happens and investigators might lose sanity as well. This clock is like appendix-cancer: A greatly detrimental condition on a system that is not necessary to begin with.4) Speaking of sanity, it gets lost WAY too often. Read the wrong book? SANITY LOSS! Enter combat with some thugs? SANITY LOSS! Examine a corpse for clues? SANITY LOSS! Mythos Clock rings 12? SANITY LOSS! To put it in terms for people who understand the Call of Cthulhu mechanics: Entering combat requires you to check sanity (which, by the way, most investigators suck at, being stuck at a POW of ~50) and then take the equivalent to 1d6 sanity damage. For entering combat. No joke, unfortunately. This is because this game tracks sanity in single points, and just for comparison's sake, an average investigator has 7 sanity points, a 50% chance of saving or failing their sanity checks and roundabout 20 opportunities per chapter to check sanity. If this sounds insane, that's because it is. A one-shot adventure can drive a party insane, but a single-scene visit to the university should not be enough to do that already.4.1) Heck, some weapons you can use require sanity checks, meaning a good weapon can make your investigator go nuts even faster. Because yes, defending one's own life effectively does take a toll on one's mind, whereas doing the same thing with a less effective weapon is harmless, but might lead to one's demise. Who came up with that?

_childDocuments_.review: It's really bad, worse than you thought it would be even though you were going to give it a lot of leeway due to it being FF Arkham License.Let's forget that it isn't multiplayer or co-op like the board games, let's forget the graphics are poor, its worse than than that. How about an avatar that moves super slow, and a space-bar run button that makes you move only very slightly faster? Bad animations and voice acting like its 2008 or something? Out of combat gameplay: click objects of interest to advance the story, a chapter will consist of a few rooms and maybe 10 objects of interest. The door is locked, find the key. Yawn.In combat: The most basic turn-based combat you can think of, not even dice-based like the board games it's just basic and dull. Each investigator has a rating for magic/raged/melee combat of low/average/skilled. That's it.Your inventory per investigator is 4 slots yet they still made inventory management clunky and take more effort than it should.And then there's the bugs, a game so small with so few things going on shouldn't have a bunch of bugs. Oh you killed an enemy, well the way it fell was weird so now you're clipping on it and you cant move where you want to kill the next guy. Oh you tried to look behind a desk and now you're stuck, restart checkpoint.I was expecting a pretty average game that I'd tolerate because I like the FF license but this is dire.

_childDocuments_.review: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace is a good example of a game that could do with an option to give a neutral Steam review as the game has enough good things in it to be worth a playthrough while also having enough much of negative aspects that drag down the entire experience. Ultimately whether the game is for you comes down to your interest in the setting and how high your tolerance to jank is.What the game does well are its narrative, which is fun even if predictable, the variety of characters and especially voice acting. Also the core gameplay loop is entertaining despite not being used to its full potential.So what about the negative aspects then? I think it is pretty clear that the game could have used some more development time as it lacks polish and it is noticeable in almost every aspect of the game: - A lot of QoL issues such as default movement speed being way too slow and faster movement requires you to constantly hold spacebar + movement keys which is an awful combination. But since the game does not support rebinding keys or toggling faster movement, that is your only option.- UI feels clunky on kb/m- Sound mixing has some inconsistencies and there are some occasions where the voice lines cut off abruptly- Bugs bugs bugs... From smaller things like graphics settings resetting every time you restart the game, a very high preset that sets everything to low quality, multiple objects with missing descriptions, visual bugs like almost every ranged attack shooting at a trajectory that visually misses the enemy but lands the hit (as the game has no miss chance) to more severe annoyances such as UI locking up mid combat and forcing you to restart from the previous checkpoint.- Some sanity checks simply don't make sense in their context- Combat starts off easy and relatively basic but never really gets any more complicated which is a huge missed opportunityThat being said, it took me roughly 7 hours to beat the game and I had enough fun with the narrative to want to see how it all wraps up. If you are interested in the setting, have huge tolerance for bugs along with jank and don't mind the fact that the turn based combat never really goes beyond very basic - I'd say the game is worth playing. For everyone else though, I would recommend waiting and seeing which issues get patched.

_childDocuments_.review: As others have written, this game is no huge shakes. Nor is it a patch on the brilliance of the board game, though it does capture  of the appeal (as well as that of Mansions of Madness, a spin-off board game this honestly bears a closer resemblance to).   After choosing your main investigator from a handful of options - I chose Jim Culver, as he seems to aid group Sanity, and Sanity's always a big issue in these games! - you're thrown into fairly familiar "adventure game" mode, walking around trying to solve puzzles using items and whatnot. You know you're in slightly...unconventional territory, though, when your solution to entering a locked mansion is to find some ...which you then proceed to TOSS THROUGH A WINDOW in order to SMASH it. Ooooookay, then...   Not long after that, having broken-and-entered my way into the mansion where I was asked to play some music for a kindly old female professor, I need to find the key to her office. Trying various other doors tells me that "this door doesn't lead to where Professor Tillinghast is", yet moments later the game permits me to enter a totally random bathroom...despite the fact of that  not leading me to where the professor is, or even providing me with any means with which to enter her office. Hmmmm...   A lot of the "investigation" truly seems to come down to trial-and-error, and your punishment for making the wrong decision is the wasting of valuable TIME. But really: it's a crapshoot half the time (as opposed to "doh, stupid me, I should've known that was the solution")!  So if it's a genuinely clever "puzzle game" you're in the market for, you may wanna keep looking (I eventually found the key to the professor's office in a "mobile" hanging above a child's crib - don't worry, not much of a spoiler! - so again, expect the obscure).   The turn-based combat is perfectly okay but not terribly strategic, the voice-acting is competent but less than inspired, the graphics are passable but far from jaw-dropping, the sound design is perfectly adequate but...I'm sure you're getting the picture by now. Enter with low-ish expectations, and this game is "fine". Expect the video game equivalent of the exceptional board game it's allegedly based on...and you'll find it more than a mite wanting.   Even rabid fans of the original game should probably wait for a sale. As someone who cites said product as my favourite board game of all time, I have to say...I gave up on this adaptation pretty early on. I  return, but for now I can honestly say I wasn't the slightest bit inspired to continue (and I wasn't even silly enough to get my hopes up in the first place)!   Verdict: 6.5/10.(PS If you enjoyed this review, feel free to check out my two Curator pages: Cheers!)

_childDocuments_.review: It's so incredibly scuffed, but it has some interesting ideas. You might click with it if you have a high tolerance for jank.Mother's Embrace is a feature length campaign for an adapted version of the board game Mansions Of Madness. This is already a few weird jumps away from stable design, and I do not envy the team that worked on this for juggling faithfulness to the brand with attempts to make mechanics that function in a more conventional crpg environment. As is, they don't really succeed, but the game also feels like it was made for touchscreen and that's another mechanics design gate and honestly it's a miracle that this thing plays at all.So how does it play? You wander very very very very very very very very very very very very very very very very slowly around cramped environments, interacting with flagged objects and losing sanity and/or getting random drops as you do. Sometimes the game tests you on your reading comprehension with a puzzle, so you can't just click through all of the filler text, but there's a lot of filler text and the writing is okay but not compelling enough to justify the stagnant waddle that is your walking speed.You do have a run button, but it only upgrades your stagnant waddle to a dead mosey.Fortunately, there's combat. In combat, all attacks hit, but weapons have a set number of uses (that the game doesn't tell you, only gives you vague clues about.) Ranged weapons use ammo, and spell tomes can miscast and do trivial and irrelevant things to other characters in your squad. This means that you kind of have to hoard weapons or fall back on your 2 damage punch. And this is difficult considering how limited your inventory space is. So combat is basically a resources check, with the occasional crit to KO one of your characters at random.Fortunately, combat is one of the safest places for you to be. If you get a mythos clock rotation in combat, the fight just gets a little harder. Out of combat, you might get the "fail all sanity checks for the rest of the scenario" result, which means you'll pick up 2+ madnesses on each squad member if you got it early enough.The mythos clock theoretically exists to keep some pressure on you, but all it does is arbitrarily punish you for wiggling cabinets instead of lifting them over your head and emptying them out. When you interact with objects, sometimes the game will ask you to choose how you proceed, and the choices are arbitrary. If you have the right skill, you might get a clue as to which choice is correct, but the clues are like "If you wiggle and juggle this cabinet, the jello man will arrive" and then the choices are Wiggle / Jiggle / Wait For The Jello Man To Arrive.Also, in amongst this mess, your companions have collision turned on. They will trap you in rooms. And you'd better hope you don't wedge yourself behind a potted fern or something, because this game is an autosaver with very hard boundaries and very few protective measures against you getting permastuck.So why do I recommend Mother's Embrace, when 90% of players stop halfway through the game at 3 hours in?Well, I think it's on to something. Stygian does everything in Mother's Embrace better, and you should absolutely check out Stygian if you're reading this review, but Mother's Embrace has the rudiments of a good game in it. I wouldn't mind seeing this team make another title in the series, tighten a few bolts, make combat less vanilla. Call Of Cthulhu is a fun roleplaying setting, and it really hasn't had the crpg it deserves. If you're going to get Mother's Embrace, definitely get it on deep sale, but if you like jank and you like games that almost succeed with all the odds against them, you might enjoy this.Edit: Holy nebulous objective flagging, Batman. "You need to hold out for as long as possible" actually means "you need to dps rush this boss." "You should knock down all these ritual altars to disrupt the cult" actually means "if you knock down too many of them, you'll get the bad end." Not really sure what they were going for with this, but the madnesses equals bad ends system is let down by sanity checks being pure 60% RNG (unless you get the mythos event that makes them worse.) So you can do everything right and still get the bad end---which is basically what you do in the tabletop game, but in that you're at least not stuck in a box canyon walking two miles per hour.2nd Edit: Had to rotate my camera to find the interact point inside of a door. The door was essential to progress and the interact point was in the black void on the other side and the only way to see it was by slowwwwwwly rotating the camera into the black void on the other side. If the most recent cutscene hadn't made such a big deal about the door supposedly being open, I wouldn't have thought to try this. Certainly not the biggest problem with the game, but it makes me wonder how many items I've missed because they required me to rotate my camera inside the level geometry to see them.3rd Edit: I didn't bring it up before now because I was trying to give the game a fairer chance, but the majority of items suck and there's no way to know this going in. Guns are the good weapon. Character has weak ranged? They're trash. Character has strong magic? They're double trash. Exactly two spellbooks are viable, damage and heal, and the damage tome is just a suckier gun. Heal is a suckier bandage. Theoretically you can use these spellbooks to sub occasionally for your better equipment, but by later game you have a decent supply of bullets and there's no reason not to only use guns. Also! There's one passive item, the one that buffs firearm damage, that's any good. The rest are a wasted inventory slot. And of the consumables, the one that removes conditions is maybe the worst item in the game. If it had no AP cost it would still suck. Also the melee weapon that SAN checks you every time you use it in exchange for just regular mid damage output is bad. This is a lot of small things, but they each play their little part in making the game not better.4th Edit: So, the thing I don't enjoy in CoC tabletop is the way the gameloop fights itself. You need to explore to engage with the mystery, but each time you explore you get hit with a SAN check. The game punishes you for doing the thing it wants you to do. And this is ultimately fine. Most people play CoC as play-to-lose. But in a tabletop game you can kind of lean into that, enjoy acting, see what kinds of dramatic messes you'll get into. In a crpg, it's not really satisfying to play-to-lose, and this is why Stygian and World Of Horror and other lovecraft-derived roleplaying video games tend to modify the SAN system a bit so that the player can interact with it as a game element. In Mother's Embrace, aside from the very rare cigarette you can smoke, the sanity system just happens to you. It's an RNG that determines whether you get a good ending. And like. I dunno if I can recommend a game that makes you put up with all this nonsense and then coin flips you for the ending. Thumbs down. Although you still might enjoy it if you have a high tolerance for clunky games.5th Edit: Final boss is an absolute chump. You'll three-round him without trying. And I don't know how you're supposed to get the madness ending on that level without intentionally bringing a squad of three pre-maddened investigators. There's like one sanity check, and it's upon entering combat. Oh, and there's no ending other than a paragraph of text which maybe only changes if you somehow got the madness ending for the last chapter. Your choices most assuredly don't matter. Also the game permanently blackscreened when I skipped the end credits. The overall storytelling is fine---if you paired this plot with better mechanics and gave it room to breathe I think this'd be a sleeper hit. But the plot's not anywhere near good enough to carry the game, and the game doesn't provide any substance to the plot.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Lovecraftian & cosmic horror in general, and a huge fan of the Arkham and Eldritch Horror tabletop games, I was nervous but excited to play this game. Needless to say while not a perfect translation of the board game to a video game, it had a lot of charm and I did enjoy seeing some of the characters from the games make their way here. Certain characters were obviously miles better than others, and some I never even used. Melee is very powerful in this game, spells can hit or miss and most not worth running, and while guns can often save rounds of combat, the action economy of the game sharply turns up as you progress passed a certain point, where enemies will do their best to make sure you're hurting or trying to make a call that does the least amount of damage to your team. I enjoy the game and will probably look to start speed running it. While it isn't perfect, it breaks the seal and opens the opportunity for future improvements I look forward to. A bit of dialogue outside of scripted conversations would be nice, especially between investigators who are on your mission to help build that camaraderie that pushes the game forward in a way where you care more about them for just their stats. Aside from that I enjoyed the turned based aspect, being able to visualize a move before committing to it is fantastic. While I wish there were a bit more variety for the basic enemy types, I really liked the boss battles. Here's hoping to see future installments because I'll certainly support and pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace is a pretty decent adventure RPG. It has a decent story and I enjoyed the thematic puzzles and constructing well-rounded parties. However, the game struggled with smooth controls, weapon balance, and replayability. Potential players should also note that while the game is themed after the Arkham Horror board game, the mechanics are very different. I recommend Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace as a decent adventure RPG for players more interested in the theming and investigation than strategy or replayability.Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace is an adventure role-playing game with turn-based combat. Players choose from one of seven starting characters and then begin a journey to uncover the truth behind the occult murder of an elderly professor of Arkham University. The professor provides narration throughout the adventure, primarily with information the player already knows, but occasionally with foreshadowing. As players advance the story, they uncover increasingly unnatural phenomena and a greater evil threatening humanity. The game can (mostly) be played with a keyboard or keyboard+mouse, but some actions require explicitly one or the other meaning the mouse hand has to switch fairly often. The controls can also be frustrating in terms of responsiveness. It can be hard to maneuver characters into position to interact with an object and finishing an interaction often leaves a pause before characters can start moving again.In each chapter, players bring a party of 2-3 characters (most unlocked through the story) to investigate, interact with objects, and gather items and equipment. Based on the investigation knowledge of each character, they'll provide advice in relevant areas to help the player get items and avoid pitfalls. If no advice is available, players and still interact with items and try to deduce the best option from the description. Failure advances the mythos clock, eventually triggering random bad effects and sanity checks, but players can still try again. Certain rooms or areas are marked with red fog and entering them reveals enemies are triggers turn-based combat. Each character has proficiency with different weapons allowing them to use fewer action points to attack with weapons they're proficient in, but they can still use any weapons. Weapons, ammo, consumable items, and equipment are readily found throughout each chapter so inventory management is usually more of an issue than finding enough gear.While Arkham Horror: Mother's Embrace offers seven starting characters, multiple combinations of characters in each chapter, and fully voiced conversations no matter which characters are chosen, I found the game to have some major replayability barriers. First are the puzzles, there are a number of puzzles within the game for players to interact with and solve. Clues are found within the chapter and are automatically recorded in the logbook. These are set so there's nothing new to discover if a player replays the game. Second, while there are some minor side story options in some of the later chapters, they don't seem to have a strong effect on the game and it seems fairly obvious what happens if players take the other option. The game and story are quite linear, meaning there's not a lot to discover here by playing again. Third, maps, interactions, and items are fixed. This gives some appeal to replaying the game for a speedrun attempt, but that's about it. Lastly, character's backstories and personalities seem to have only a minor impact on dialog, so despite all the colorful characters players can start with, everyone is quickly reduced to their combat proficiencies and investigation knowledge.Speaking of combat proficiencies, I found guns to be vastly superior to every other weapon in the game. To the point that I started using them even on characters with the lowest level of proficiency with them. Ammo is pretty easy to come by after the first few chapters and reloading isn't much of a hindrance for everything other than shotguns. Guns also have a huge range and can go on overwatch for a reduced cost to taking a shot. I routinely found that the story character players are immediately given, with max proficiency in firearms, would do three times the damage of any melee or magic-user while staying at a safe range and never having to move. While magic is ranged, there's no character with max proficiency in it and magic can't go on overwatch. Melee also has to spend action points to move in range to attack and while it can overwatch, the range is tiny. The only thing that stopped me from giving all my characters overpowered pistols was the fact that weapons have durability and randomly break over time. Frustratingly there's no way to track this, players are just told a weapon is normal, ruined soon, or ruined. However, these labels are very unreliable. I've had a "ruined soon" weapon become ruined and break all in the same attack while other "ruined" weapons lasted several fights.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the Arkham Horror franchise and was excited to try this out despite the bad reviews. The theme, the turn-based gameplay - it all sounded promising at first.The 3d environments and 3d assets are actually kind of decent looking although the lighting and textures could be better. Especially the lighting makes everything look extremely bland and dull. However, the haircuts and clothes of some characters were really remniscnet of the times the Arkham Horror franchise plays in.Now to the bad parts: The gameplay is extremely boring. It is a very linear adventure game and the puzzles are... not really puzzles nor are they fun. There is no meaningful choice in the game and no meaningful challenge. During fights, the game presents itself as a simple cookie-cutter turn-based combat game. Also some things just appear odd with the battles: After the third encounter against three bare-foot cultists (who apparently walk around like this in daylight in public on a work day in a fully staffed and attended university) I got kind of bored of this immersion killing, tone-deaf atmosphere. I mena do these cultist have zero self awareness or shame? It just seem silly to me, like something from a teenage cartoon flick, not at all like i envisioned Arkham Horror. Imo, game devs should have focused more on making every room and the overall locations more mysterious and instead should have not done all those boring clichee dialogs that really no one needs and weren't part of Arkham Horror anyway. I rather would hear some dark noir style monologues or just read atmospheric descriptions. Ah yes, the descriptions in tis game: So the descriptions of clues were often extremely off-putting and killing the theme and vibe for me, almost like someone just wrote whatever they found funny at the moment and no one proof-read it. It just feels like no one truly gave a ♥♥♥♥ about this game and no one cared to create a Lovecraftian atmosphere, everything therefore came out cheap and dull and the gameplay is so unpolished it could be taken from a marketplace asset. At no point did I feel thrilled or excited, i was just clicking through clues (without real puzzles presented)  and sometimes they would hit me with a punishment, which seemed just random (wow, so rewarding, so engaging, so fun) and i would then have to beat up and stab more cultists to death (who, I have to say it again, just walk around in bright daylight in a crowded place, barefoot, in very specific cultist clothes, looking to stab professors and FBI agents with their knives- ooookay?).Where is the resource management? The atmosphere? The lovecraftian subtlety? meaningful choices? Fire? Barricades? Randomized events and enemies? Randomized challenges to resolve? This game could have been really great as a PC game, it has a huge amount of possibilities to create an emergent narrative based on randomized events, items, encounters but instead it is made as a linear boring trite tone-deaf cookie-cutter adventure game with TB combat and bad jokes and dialoges. This game , in the form it was done, gives me absolutely nothing in no regard, that makes me want to look at it again.As a big Arkham horror fan and game dev I would have wished to have had the possibility to work on such a game and had some say on it, because I swear to you it would have turned very different and much more in the vein of an Arkham Horror game (2nd or 3rd Ed, LCG or MoM)

_childDocuments_.review: So what can I say about this "Mansions of Madness" board game conversion? The GFX are average. "Investigation" boils down to point and click (not to mention every second thing you click on drives you insane). The "tactical" combat is kind of repetitive and deficient in the "tactics" department. With all done and said, what kept me playing for 13 hrs (including repeating a level which glitched out)??It's that dark, forboding atmosphere as you creep through a decrepit mansion. It's the hollow echoes and distant screams as you explore a fetid asylum. It's the horror you feel when you encounter a new monster (then slightly less horror after you encounter it for the 4th time!). It's the thrill of picking up a new weapon and organizing your investigation team. It's the pleasant surprise you feel as you travel from musty mansions to lush swamps or the bustling streets of New Orleans. It's the dread you feel as you creep inevitably closer to an encounter with the Dark Powers...There's no question the game is flawed; but if you're a fan of Cthulu and Lovecraftian story lines, then this game Will grip you... 6.5/10 from me :)Tip: Jim Culver + Roland Banks + 2x Colt .45s + stacks of bullets = awesome!

_childDocuments_.review: First off, if you're not a Lovecraft fan, stop here and go read a book.  This game probably won't do much for you if you aren't already familiar with the Cthulhu Mythos.  If you are a fan, you probably already know the long and storied history of failures to adapt the stories to any other media and are already braced for impact.  So, what do we have here?  Basically the video game equivalent of a very lovingly made student film based a Lovecraft story.Coming in, I was expecting something like Sinking City without the combat, but I was way off and it took me almost an hour to grapple with the fact that the game has very little to do with solving mysteries and is more a tactical rpg with surprisingly robust combat mechanics and very easy to use system.   Where the controls for walking around and investigating feel like they're from a point and click game which was poorly adapted to a ps2 or something, the controls during battle are really cool and have a great deal of qol improvements over similar titles like Wasteland and Shadowrun.  However, you definitely want to play this with a controller.  The keyboard and mouse set-up literally made me feel like I was playing Shadow of the Comet.TLDNR; if you're a norm, run away fast; you will hate this.  If you already have a Cthulhu statue in your house, you will be kicking yourself for missing this one.

Overall, this game isn't worth playing at any price. It's simply a waste of time.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of this review, I have played Arkham Horror: Mother’s Embrace for about 7 hours.  That’s one complete playthrough, and it’s my biggest criticism of the game.  I still very much recommend it and encourage you to look beyond some of the nit-picking in many other reviews.First, understand what this game is.  It is a dramatic video game rendition board game (Arkham Horror), which is itself a simplified take on a tabletop roleplaying game (Call of Cthulhu).  That’s not to say it attempts to recreate a board game, merely tell a story the likes of which you might find in the board game.Second, this is not some AAA title, nor should it be.  Animations are serviceable, but not impressive – exactly what you should expect from something emulating a board game.  Surprisingly, it has voice acting.  The voices and lines are actually decent, and there are different lines depending on the characters you use in each scenario, but there is very little animation matching up with the voices.  Actually, the decision to include voice acting is probably my biggest concern with the design decisions made by the devs of Mother’s Embrace.  While it definitely provides a good feel in terms of the story, it also opens the game up to criticism about the voice animations.  More importantly, I wonder if the inclusion of voice acting might be a limiting factor in adding to the game in the future.Back to the issue of length.  I made a point of exploring as much as possible and was done in 7 hours; you could finish it quicker.  By itself, having the story only take 7 hours isn’t actually a negative.  I think they did a good job of telling a story without padding it, making it more convoluted, or putting a lot of extraneous gameplay activities to artificially extend the length.  The length of the story is where it should be.  But that story is all there is – there’s basically no replayability here.  You could start again with a different character, but you’ll be experiencing the same thing with slightly different lines at times.As for the actual gameplay, it does a good job of emulating an investigation in the traditions of Arkham Horror and Call of Cthulhu.  You’re exploring, looking for clues, finding stuff to help you, finding stuff which disturbs you, and occasionally getting into combat.  The combat is decent and balanced – kind of a stripped-down X-Com turn-based affair.  It’s not difficult, but you do have to make decisions about positions, when to use what, etc.  It’s not the focus of the game, but it is a key part of every scenario.  It’s what it should be.  As far as the exploration goes, it’s done well.  Points of interest are highlighted without overdoing it, and it’s easy to see if a POI is something you’ve already looked at or not.  There are also helpful icons added after you’ve already checked something out so you can easily tell if you left an item there because you didn’t have room in your inventory.  You don’t have much space to carry stuff, which again forces some decisions.  You also frequently find things that affect your sanity.  At times, it can seem like you’re getting hit with sanity checks a LOT.  But that’s actually appropriate for the genre, and the effects of losing sanity are not crippling.  Drop to zero and you get a trauma that impacts your gameplay in an inconvenient but not abusive way.As for bugs, I didn’t encounter any personally.  The biggest bug issue with this game has been well-documented and involved the inventory system not kicking in correctly.  If it’s working, you’re good to go.  If it’s not, you basically cannot play.  I also found play to be much smoother and simpler playing with a connected controller, as opposed to mouse & keyboard.In addition to correcting this inventory bug (quickly), my biggest suggestion for the devs is to expand on this game!  The bones are good, and it could easily benefit from expansions that add new stories.  I think the biggest challenge would be offering such expansions at an appropriate price point (I’d say $10 for a similarly length story) while still including voice acting and the like.Alternatively, if they really wanted to open things up, they could look at ways to make the game more replayable.  Adding some sort of New Game+ with added secrets or some sort of procedurally generated content would be cool but would likely require a fair amount of development.If they really wanted to turn this into something that could generate some cash, they should actually make it a platform for others to tell their mythos stories.  Create an editor that lets us develop our own scenarios and share them, then the devs could sell asset packs for use with the editor.  Lots of details to figure out how to make it work for everyone, but there is a market there that isn’t being tapped.Anyway, lack of replayability aside this is a solid game if you’re interested in the genre.  I’m hoping to see more of it in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long-time fan of Arkham Horror, I felt the the game was missing it's core essence. The entire time I felt railroaded along with no real actual choices, and no chance to really take meaningful risks. Choices are distilled down to: do I look at the scary thing and risk taking a horror and getting an item/flavor text/or story checkpoint, or do I not? Do I bother with who to take on my scenario? None of the investigators really felt particularly unique other than voice acting (pretty flat to begin with), and combats are monotonous. Ammunition, weapons, and healing items are plentiful, so there's never really that Arkham sense of desperation I was craving. Fiddling around with things your particular characters don't intuitively understand can accelerate sanity loss, but that was the only sense of urgency.The story was fine for what it was, and touches on some classic Arkham tropes, but I can't help but wonder if a Telltale style interactive game mechanic would've the flavor of this game better. Bland exploration mechanics neutered the mystery and dread: every interactive object is flagged, and combats usually have an obvious visual cue. Why give the player an obvious warning a combat is coming? This is a horror game! Spring it on the player and increase the desperation!20 bucks for a game I finished in 6 hours is not worth the price of admission. Unless you're a diehard fan of the Arkham Horror world, I'd suggest skipping this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Played for a couple of hours and am inspired to express my disappointment. I have read every HPL story I could get my hands on, played CoC tabletop for years and have spent many, many hours playing these characters in FF's games.  I understand that the direction of the project changed and that -- instead of a Mansions of Madness video game scenario -- what's being offered is a completely different game set in FF's Arkhamverse.  Despite that, I've really been looking forward to it. So, if they're going to go their own direction with it -- then it should at least be a good game.  The setting alone isn't enough.  I'm not trashing this because it's not Mansions of Madness, I'm weighing it on its own merits.At the end of the day, I really only care about two things: 1.  Does it capture the mood of Lovecraft?2.  Is it fun to play?-----------------------------Good Stuff:The story seems engaging so far.The ambient music and sounds are good.The voice acting is not bad performance-wise.-----------------------------Bad stuff:  The controls:  Keys can't be remapped.  Do they not know that some people are left handed -- or disabled?  In my opinion, this is the most egregious, lazy and thoughtless design choice a developer can make. The controls: What's with the camera perpetually pointed toward the ground?  It's a constant frustration that the pitch of the camera can't be changed to look across a room or down a hallway.  It completely ruins immersion to not be able to look around like most people (those with working necks and eyes) can do.  No need to re-invent the wheel here.  Just some standard camera control would be nice.The controls:  The walking character can get stuck behind objects or the other characters as they follow and close in behind him/her.The controls:  Inventory management is an exercise in how to turn a one-step process into a three-step process.  Clunnnnky.The voice-acting:  While it's adequately performed, it's ill-conceived.  Everybody so far sounds like a Disney character -- not suitable for Lovecraft.  The cook is an inanely offensive religious stereotype ("Sinners!").  These may look like the iconic FF characters, but (of the ones I've experienced so far) most are poor interpretations.The choices:  This game plays like Russian Roulette.  Do you want to "look at it", "examine it" or "look at it"?  Do you want to "slightly disturb it" or "gently move it"?  Do you want to "open it" or "look inside it"?  "Force it open" or "break it open"? One of these choices is good and the others are *bad* -- you will be punished!The motivations for actions make no sense:  Why would you break that window?  Why would you break into a friendly character's locker instead of just asking them to open it?  Why do you need to put a vase back together -- without glue -- to determine it was on the knocked-over table right next to it so you can -- walk through a door?Unreasonable punishment:  Every time I hear the same unfortunate detail -- *sanity loss*!  Every time I see the same dead body of a person who I killed in self-defense -- *sanity loss*!  If I find a scrap of paper with the word "boo" written on it -- *sanity loss*!  I get that it should be a meaningful mechanic -- at least try to make its triggers less ridiculous.A bug:  When I examine a door in Miskatonic, it tells me it's the door back to administration.  Fine.  When I examine a bookcase at the end of the hallway, it tells me it's ....  the door back to administration.  Bugs happen, but how does this -- in the first 20 minutes of the game -- make it past *any* playtester?  If something so simple and obvious didn't get immediately noticed the first time somebody played the game then what do we have to look forward to?  Did the game get playtested at all?-----------------------In conclusion:1.  Does it capture the mood of Lovecraft?  Largely not.  If the story is actually good, it might save it.2.  Is it fun to play?  Not yet.  Bad controls and stupid choices indicate poor game design. If these things don't get better (I don't know why they would), then they will be too much of a distraction.  I'm really on the fence as to whether or not to get a refund.  If I do, it will the first game I've ever done this with.

_childDocuments_.review: Arkham Horror: Mother's EmbraceI played the Arkham Horror boardgame and was hoping for a more similar feel when I saw this game (honestly, a ported boardgame would've worked for me just fine). I didn't get that, but I don't entirely mind. What we have here is an adventure of almost point-and-click style that is also part RPG with turn-based combat. I'll split my review in three sections: the bad, the good and the tips. The Bad Gameplay. It's customized for console play, which entirely goes against the grain of an ardent PC gamer. Yes you can use the mouse but that clearly wasn't the idea. My biggest peeve was the fact you need to hold down the right mouse button to rotate the characters and camera, but it's also the cancel button. So when moving my character and changing direction during a combat turn, I kept cancelling the action. Quite annoying. (The way to deal with this is to only drag and never click with the RMB while doing it, but it's harder to get used to than it sounds.) For some reason you can't look up or down. As the camera is tilted some 30° down, this means that in a long room or a corridor you need to walk up to the other side to see what's there. To add insult to injury, the controls are locked. Another peeve of mine was that you have to hold down the space button to make your characters move faster - not shift or leave the caps lock on as is normal. And by faster I mean not-quite-as-slow; they drag they feet so much, it's lucky the maps aren't very large. Then the four-item-per-character inventory. Needlessly compressed; before every mission I had to think hard what I want to bring along and what I'll leave in the office stash, lest I brought something I'd be forced to leave behind for something more useful. The game is sort of an RPG, but without character advancement. The number of item types is low - for example, only two types of a pistol and one of shotguns and rifles? Hell, the boardgame had more (I distinctly remember a tommy gun). The buff items are the only way to improve your character, but see "inventory". Anyway there aren't many types of those, either. Spells are weak and you only get a character that's any good with them around midgame. I'm not quite done here, but I'll get back to it. Let's say a couple of things about The Good The story is interesting and upon finishing a level I was compelled to start the next one. This alone makes for a positive review. The voice acting is quite good with many lines recorded, often the same ones for different characters (depending on which ones you choose to take on a mission). The combat system is simple but effective, other than character movement I had no complaints. More bad There is no difficulty setting, and the game is sort of easy. This is particularly important for something that's supposed to be a horror game; the confidence that you can get your party through any situation is fairly detrimental to the fear factor. And now for my biggest complaint... It's short! You can finish it in some 10 hours of leisurely gameplay. For this reason I'm glad I bought it at a discount... but it also means it was fun while it lasted. So there you have it. A good way to kill some two afternoons. If you're into these type of games, at least put it on your wishlist. TIPS 1. Ranged > melee > spells 2. Mental stability > health. You can keep your characters standing fairly easily, keeping them untraumatized is harder. For this reason I suggest taking the Musician (strong ranged, highly stable, added mental stability for all) for you first character. You'll be collecting one per level for the next couple of levels. Other characters to bring along are the Fed (best ranged), the Parapsychologist (increased initiative for all, two aptitudes) and the Journalist (melee, random aptitude assist). Until late game, you can only bring two. 3. There's plenty of bandages around at all levels. Never use the filthy ones, not worth the stability check. Don't bother with the medical book (healing-enhancer), save the spot in inventory for something more useful. Ditto the spell. Don't bother with epinephrine, characters very rarely go down. 4. There aren't very many cigarettes (stability boost at a small price in health). Be careful. 5. Always use the pocket watch when your mythos clock hits four. There is no other way to reduce it and it doesn't get reset at the end of a mission. 6. Keep track of the state of your weapons. You don't want to go from a Colt Government to fists in the middle of a difficult fight. Plan ahead. When able, use the less valuable/scarce weapons. 7. Mythos effects usually aren't that bad but can be quite annoying. The item-destroying ones are the worst I've encountered; they can and do take out unique items. 8. My preferred composition was the Fed, the Parapsychologist and the Journalist (alas, I hadn't picked the Musician at the start). Enemies with ranged weapons tended to go for the Detective. Putting a vest on him was a good idea. 9. Give ranged weapons to everyone (this helps keep your character's HP up and shortens combat). Keep spares if needed. Not everyone needs a melee weapon. 10. If a character catches a trauma, consider whether it impacts their usefulness in any meaningful way. If not, don't hesitate to keep bringing them along. Characters heal only one trauma per mission they sit out. That's about it for now, may update as needed.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, the  is: it's not good. Take it from from a fan of the Arkham Horror card game who went in to this wanting to like it. Whether you're here for the Lovecraftian narrative, the turn-based combat, or the mystery-solving gameplay, it's all just mediocre at best, and even saying that may be giving it more credit than it's due. I tend to give a lot of leeway to mediocre games if I like at least a few aspects of it, and considering that I bought this almost entirely off of brand recognition, you'd assume that if there was a person to endorse this game then it'd be me. It's kind of impressive how disappointing I found this game considering my expectations weren't exactly high. I could guess from the trailers that it wasn't going to be mind-blowing but I thought I'd at least have enough fun to justify $15 (sale price at time of purchase). I did not. Is this review scathing enough yet?    The gameplay feels more like what I'd expect from a Scooby Doo game from 2006 then what I would expect from Arkham Horror. The core loop consists of your character walking around a confined, mostly linear environment and clicking various highlighted elements that reveal paragraph long blurbs that more often then not add nothing to your progress while also adding little to the atmosphere. These are things like paintings, bookshelves, and whatnot. Occasionally you're prompted to make a choice into how your character will further inquire into the thing that they're looking at. One of the first examples of this in the tutorial is a broken vase. You click on it and are told to choose to either "Manipulate" or "Put together". Aren't these almost synonymous? I suppose it depends on what they mean by "manipulate"? Choosing the wrong option penalizes you with a progress point on the "mythos clock" which if given enough points will randomly roll for some bad effect to take place ranging from a debuff that effects you throughout the rest of the level to a sanity check. I don't have any particular gripes with the concept of the mythos clock but I do take issue with how disconnected it feels from the narrative. When the mythos effect goes off it gives a brief sentence description telling you what occurs, something like "you swear you hear voices", but the way it's just not acknowledged by the characters in any tangible way... feels off. Anyway, that's more of a small nitpick in comparison to the rest of the game. So back to these environment interactions, they're very weird. After picking what was deemed to be the correct option for the mystery of the broken vase next to the nightstand, you're given a description of what you've concluded. It's something along the lines of "It looks as if the vase fell from a small table nearby". With findings like that, these cultists are done for. Almost all of the interactions prompt you to choose from 2-4 options that usually sound very similar to each other. Do you "examine" or "look through" the leather bag? What the hell is the difference?  And there's a chance that if I get this wrong that the mythos clock advances and I start hearing voices again? Oh I glanced at the purse instead of prodding at it, now I'm hearing the voice of Hastur telling me to find the gateway to Carcosa by drowning myself in the ocean. It just feels arbitrary. These environmental interactions is one of the ways in which your character choice is factored in so let's get into that.     When the game starts you get to choose from about 10(?) different characters, all with different health and sanity values, combat strengths, investigative skills, and abilities. Progressing through the game also unlocks even more characters and you can swap out which ones you want on your team (max three characters on a team) between levels. sounds fun so far, but how much variance between the characters is there really? Well, not much unfortunately. If you're a fan of the card game, Mansions of Madness, etc. you'll be familiar with these characters, and you'll be as disappointed as I was when you scroll over to Sefina and find that her ability makes her slightly better at healing for some reason. That's what all the abilities are, just uninspired, dull passives that don't significantly change your strategy in any way that matters.  Do you want higher sanity resistance or higher resistance to stuns? who cares because you're already in a coma from the boredom. It always bewilders me when game devs decide to add distinct, unique characters and then they choose to make the main gimmick that separates them basically amount to a small percent increase to a stat. Anyway. So the combat skills amount to how many action points you spend using a certain weapon type and then the investigative skills will basically just have your character tell you which option to choose whenever you are interacting with a certain type of thing. This character is a parapsychologist so her multiple degrees help her to know that it's better to *pat down* the corpses of the cultists we just killed instead of *examining* them. Whatever the difference is.    Oh my god can we talk about the voice acting? Hilariously awful. Maybe I'm biased because I've known these characters from playing the card game for years, so hearing them brought to life was always going to conflict with what I imagined for them. But man, I did not expect Sefina the art forger from Tahiti to sound like a college kid with a monotone. What part of Tahiti is she from? Ohio? I hate to sound like I'm making fun of the voice actress. You never know what notes the voice director did or didn't give to each of them. It's not just the quality of the voice acting but the quantity too. There is so much unnecessary talking in this game. After almost every interaction that made you make a choice, the gameplay is interrupted with a cut scene that basically just vocally explains exactly what you just read. It got to the point where I just wouldn't read any of the descriptions as I became accustomed to having it explained to me in voice. Why would you do this in your spooky mystery investigation game? And speaking of which, let's discuss the tone.    I have no idea what kind of tone they're trying to go for with this game. I mean it's based on Lovecraft right? So you expect that you'll be steeped in a dark mystery, constantly questioning whether you really understand your surroundings. And yet, you're constantly being barraged with these useless quips from female Deckard Cain. The story is sparked by the death of the woman you're visiting and she also plays the role of the narrator. And it's like... why? She talks constantly and she adds nothing of value  (That's right, i'm invoking bold text to emphasis this point that's how you know I mean business).  I think she speaks after literally every other line of dialogue in the first level and it doesn't improve much from there. And I mean she's really just not saying  They're like... kind of jokes? It feels like watching a movie with the most annoying audience member ever sitting next to you. Any loss of sanity induced from this game wasn't from any horrifying, lovecraftian undertones in the narrative, it was from listening to this narrator. Maybe her contribution as an out-of-body voice-over culminates in something later down the line, but that still doesn't justify forcing me to listen to her every intrusive thought for however long this game is. I give her a -2 out of 10. I hate to harp on her so much but her sole contribution really throws the tone off so much. At one point I started skipping all her lines and the game got better because there was finally some tonal consistency.    Now to the combat. I'll keep this short: it's about what you'd expect from a turn-based game except with clunky controls and a janky ui. It succeeds in being mostly average. Anyway, I've written more about this game then anyone ever should. Just get Gloomhaven.

_childDocuments_.review: A quick first impressions look for the curious since it seems like nobody had a preview copy and that naturally makes anyone wary.  Note that the below is all based on the first half-hour of play through the introductory scenario and does not reflect final thoughts on the game itself.  I mostly put in this time just to see if I liked it enough to keep it.  Short answer - I will keep this 'cause it seems cool.Fans of the boardgame should note that this is an adventure game inspired by it, but by no means does it play like it at all, no matter what edition is your fave.  This is more like the LCG than anything else.  That said, there are very familiar elements here that will please fans should they take the dive.  You will choose from a set of initial investigators that will be familiar to you if you've played the tabletop game or any of its spin-offs and while your favorites might not be there at first, it's very possible they will show up later as NPCs such as (minor spoiler) Roland showing up in the first scenario despite not being a choice for yourself.  It seems like the game is broken up into connected scenarios whereby you search a location for clues (yes, you even use a magnifying glass), encounter enemies and complete your overall objective.  Encountering horrific things cause your sanity to be checked, though at present, it's obfuscated on how these checks work - all I know is that you may or may not lose a sanity point.Losing all of your sanity, unlike the boardgame, will not kill you, but rather introduce trauma.  When selecting a character, you will see that they have three potential traumas they can suffer, though there is no explanation on what these traumas are other than unhelpful names (at least I could not find an explanation at the outset).  Also unlike the boardgame, there is a Mythos Clock that is ever-present and it ticks up when you choose wrong (or when an enemy purposely invokes it) during "complex interactions" which are basically 50/50 choices to make when interacting with hotspots.The game itself, then appears to have been developed with controllers in mind so it is a little wonky with kb+m controls that you  rebind.  Maybe you can through config files, but not in-game.  Helpful tip - if you have a controller plugged in and don't want to use it, you will want to choose it as your control method in order to disable vibration and then switch it back.  You control a single investigator, though you may pick up party members as you proceed, wandering around locations and interacting with highlighted hotspots.  At various points, you will enter turn-based combat which operates on an action-point system.  Movement is not grid-based, but rather focused on free positioning and range indicators around characters.  Otherwise, actions cost points and it's pretty straightforward.  Damage is not set and again, there's probably stuff going on under the hood but it's never really made apparent on what is actually being rolled/checked.  Not a big deal - just swing for the fences.In the short time I spent with the game, I only encountered minor issues.  As an example during combat I tried to move someone into melee range, but could not 'confirm' my placement.  I simply backed out of the action and tried again and no problem.  The option menu is pretty limited as well, giving you the standard low-to-high configs, but not much beyond that.  However, special note for some PC freaks is that you can set the framerate to unlimited, so you won't see complaints on that front.  Like I said above, some stuff like having to enable the controller to disable vibration is counter-intuitive.  If anything, I'd say the negative points (thus far) are more clunky than broken.The art here is simplified (reminds me of Evil Genius for some reason) and textures are pixelated, though that could be a stylistic choice.  It seems that this game is really targeted for multi-platform so don't expect it to put your PC through its paces.  That said, it ran very smoothly and I didn't get any hiccups or weird artifacts while playing, but again, I admittedly haven't put in the time.Narratively, it feels right for an Arkham Horror game.  Some Miskatonic Uni prof is dead and no matter who you are, you'll band up with an unlikely cast of characters (though boardgame fans will know all of them already) to figure out what's going on.  There's no reason for a Fed to take a civilian along, but you know, why would a jazz musician, a librarian and a reformed cultist get together, either?  That's kind of how it always plays out on the table.  In short, this is going to feel more like the Arkham Horror card game than the board game, but the overall atmosphere is correct and that's a big bonus for a fan like myself.In short, I'm willing to put more time into it and explore its depths.  The narrative is typical Arkham fare so it's not like it's going to knock your socks off.  The goal here is to stave off an Old One, I'm sure, but it's not clear which one it is yet so that's enough for me as a fan.  As a casual passerby who knows nothing of the franchise or the Call of Cthulhu RPG, you might find this a middle-of-the-road game as is the general consensus on most Artefact Studio games, but as far as I can tell, it's a capable port and doesn't give me any indication of rough seas ahead; it should be smooth sailing.I will probably throw this out and rewrite it should I make it to the end of this adventure, but hopefully you have a better idea of what's in store for you given that there hasn't been much else said in the past couple of years.

_childDocuments_.review: Arkham Horror: Mother’s Embrace is done and dusted. It’s advertised as being inspired by the Arkham Horror boardgames, and I can see that. A lot of the automatic sanity damage in certain battles and the random seeming choices during investigations (despite it not being random) have a definite boardgame feel to them. It also definitely pulls from actual Lovecraftian lore, which is always nice.From a feel standpoint, this game definitely captures the dark and often visceral horror aspects of Lovecraftian writing and imagery. Sanity factors in heavily, both from a gameplay and story aspect. Sanity is handled in a way similar to Darkest Dungeon inasmuch as it triggers negative personality aspects. Because it’s written into some encounters and in others it’s based on your decisions, it can feel a little unfair at times. However, it never actually gets in the way of the game, and so it still works. And, much like DD, characters can rest for a mission or two to reverse an insanity penalty.The gameplay is a mix of turn based combat without cover or environmental factors; and RPG style inventory management where each character is given four inventory slots. As a result, inventory juggling is a very real thing. In between missions, all items you had on your inventories at the end of a mission go into a chest which is shared by all characters, and as you start a mission, you can assign up to four of them per character to take with them. Weapons and spells degrade with use and can’t be repaired. Everything has a destroy option, but the only things with any benefit to doing this are guns, during missions, as that allows you to put that guns ammo back into the ammo reserve for reloads. There are of course some single use items as well.I thought the graphics looked cool and were quite faithful to a pure Lovecraftian experience with solid design and nice looking still frame cutscenes. The voice acting was also done well and captured that Victorian era feel well, with accents appropriate to the setting as well. The characters were likewise well written and appropriate to the setting. You will add four story characters to your group in addition to your starting character, of which you have a few distinct options.There is a fair amount of reading, so I imagine you could skip through stuff to enjoy in a later playthrough. You do also become pretty OP by the end, so that’s worth mentioning.It took right at eight hours to complete the nine game missions and all sub quests within the levels. I don’t really feel like there is much in the way of replay value unless you just really want to try the different starting characters or rushed through the game and missed a lot of the lore. It is, in my estimation, quite worth a playthrough if you enjoy Lovecraftian game. This is a pretty honest addition to the genre. Perfectly Steam Deck compatible as well.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty fun overall. Gameplay is more similar to something like Phantom Doctrine than XCOM; you move freely out of combat and your party follows, and you spend that time finding clues and investigating locations. There are primary and secondary objectives to accomplish, as well as items to gather and stockpile, though exploration isn't encouraged or rewarded as much as I'd like. Combat is pretty standard turn-based combat. As for the controls, I don't really understand the complaints about the M&K controls, and the comparison to mobile games seems absurd to me. The game controls fine, if a little clunky at times, but it's nothing that has actively gotten in my way.As for everything else: art style is simple without overdoing it, and the environments are really well designed. The OST is nothing exciting but that's to be expected of Lovecraftian games--it's mostly ambient music with the exception of boss fights. The story itself is well written although some of the dialogue seems stiff, with characters sometimes repeating things that another character just said (this admittedly only happened a couple of times in my first playthrough). The voice acting is hit or miss but you can always turn voices all the way down if it's bothersome.If you're a fan of the AH board game or LCG, don't go into this expecting the same experience. This isn't a tabletop-to-digital conversion, it's a turn-based game based in the Arkham Files universe, so tempered expectations are good to have going in. But honestly? It's a fun game, and I don't regret my time playing it at all. There isn't much incentive to replay the story unless you wanna choose a different starting investigator, or just make some different choices, but I'm hoping they'll release expansions or something to spice things up.

_childDocuments_.review: Light spoiler - this game sucks.  To begin:  It's 1920 & I've been invited to play some jazz at a professors house.  No answer at the door, so I look around for another way in.  I don't feel comfortable going through the cellar door as "There is nothing for me down there".  So I find a pair of pliers in a wheelbarrow and immediately think - "these will let me smash open a window", why I didn't just use a stone from the garden I don't know, or just go home.... but me smashing my way into peoples houses is probably why I don't get invited back to play jazz all that often.  After murdering a person in a bathrobe - lets call them a cultist if the police ask (they won't) - I find the dead body of the prof!  Add this to the pile of carcasses I'm leaving in the entrance hall, and landing, and bathroom, all dressed in comfortable bath robes like they live here and were just getting changed for dinner and a jazz recital, & I should be worrying less about Cthulhu and more about the cops pinning all these murders on me - a black guy in 1920's America (OK I did murdered them, but not the old lady soooo I'm the good guy right?). OK, this is just the intro level to get the game going so lets give it a pass....The next level should be more thoughtful right?  Nope, its about a school shooting, tasteful.  Also if you are a student coming out of the shower in a bathrobe look out that's all the reason I need to blow a hole in you ... wait I'm the good guy right?OK so a misstep there...  The next level is in an asylum, lots of room to explore the subtle distinction of insanity and knowledge no human is meant to possess.  What IS reality and what a construct of the mind after all? ... Naaaa cue crazy nutjobs with knives coming at you.  The psychologist says things like "We should really work this out in therapy" which made me laugh.That's as far as I have got...A lot of reviewers don't get why some of us really don't like this game.  Here is why. Fantasy Flight make very well designed and well written board games under the Arkham Horror mantle, using the characters depicted in this game.  They are fun and interesting, and sure you kill a lot of people in bathrobes who may have just got out of the shower, and sure their depiction of mental illness is, frankly, disgusting, but the games have meaningful choices that effect the out come of the whole campaign.  There is no choice in this game.  The choice between hitting someone with a knife or hitting someone with a pipe is NOT a choice.  In the board game you are piecing together clues and puzzles that if you manage to solve will put you in an advantageous position for the boss battle.  If you take too long then the baddies have finished their ritual and your game is a lot harder.  In this computer game you just walk along on rails vacuuming up the 'clues' until you get to a final battle.If you wanna play a scary Cthulhu PC game play Song of Horror; if you want to play a shoot'em up play Resident Evil; if you wanna play Arkham Horror go play Arkham Horror the card/board game.'People' make a big deal about HP Lovecrafts prejudiced depiction of races.  His excuse is it was the 1920's.  I have a feeling future us's are going to look back on our depictions of mental health in the same way.  Whats our excuse in the 2020's?  Don't buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't managed to get too deep into the game yet, and that's partially because I got stuck between a telescope and a desk at the Miskatonic University. It must have been one of those odd angles that H.P.L. was always on about.So far, the writing isn't compelling, there's no Lovecraftianness to it and it's poorly edited. There's a disembodied narrator that breaks any semblance of immersion and most of the interactions you have with objects seem completely arbitrary. There's a broken vase on the floor--do you put it back together or "manipulate" it? "Well, I don't have any glue and I'm on a time crunch so...manipulate?" The Mythos clock moves ahead!I realize this is basically a board game, but I fail to see how "manipulating" a broken potsherd attracts the attention of Yog-Sothoth.The combat is a very wordy version of what you get in the Divinity: Original Sin series or Baldur's Gate III, with a lot of obscuring dialog and double confirmation. The very first combat I ran into was a barefoot, raggedy-looking cultist that exclaimed "Wha!" before throwing a punch at me. I opted to beat him up rather than shoot and stab the guy to death, because maybe I'll get some information out of the guy if he survives! Nah, the body just vanishes and you're cleared to unload hot lead into more barefoot, robed assailants.I'll probably play through the game, but it isn't worth the price.
