_childDocuments_.review: Honey I joined a cult is a quirky colony builder where you manage your own cult. The theming is great, the mechanisms entertaining and funny... To start with.The problems with "Honey, I joined a cult" is its progression. It's all a long grind of "research" which empowers you and your minions so you can eventually grind out the next influence, faith, fame or divine intervention score, giving better minions and still more power. Sadly, even making modest progress on them makes you overpowered. And the longer you go, the flatter the game becomes. There's no new complexity triggering to raise the challenge as you advance, instead you get more and more tools, turning the cult into less and less of a challenge and more of a dollhouse.Sadly the roadmap seems to be yet more content and items, rather than interesting mechanics to raise the challenge, and make the game worth to keep playing. I'll still leave a positive review for now as it's still early, but I hope the developer reads this (and other reviews, many talk about the same thing) and plans out what complexity and conflict will keep the game worth playing after a few hours. The game does not need another theme/divine inspiration, nor a ton of items. It needs more interesting conflicts to keep me from fast forwarding the game over night. Ideally ones that are NOT visualized as a bar, that needs to be keep away from a certain value.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know why I keep buying stuff from Team 17 as they only seem to release games that have a bare minimum level of quality. The premise of Honey, I Joined a Cult is great but even only about an hour in it is clear how bare-bones this game is. For starters, this game does not have a workshop of any kind so you are limited to the few options of customizing your cult that the game gives you. There is also the fact the theme is not really taken far enough. Like yes, I am running a cult but what about taking over the surrounding town or fighting the government? You know cult things. These mechanics seem superficial at best. This next one may be a personal gripe but the fact construction is instant really rubs me the wrong way. Like I have all these followers shouldn't they be building my stuff for me? Prison Architect is a good example of a similar game that does all of these things better and actually feels like its the environment it says it is rather than just slapping a basic theme on a tycoon game and calling it a simulator. While other reviews have complained about balance issues and other things I will leave those out of this review as I have not played long enough to encounter them. Refunding but may buy it again later if they decide to add workshop.

_childDocuments_.review: I have very mixed opinions on this game. The game is very similar to Prison Architect but is far less buggy. Like prison Architect you need to research, build rooms, manage needs, decorate and make things look pretty :), whilst considering efficiency and timetables. However at a certain point through each part of the gameplay loop you end up just waiting for things to be done. You cannot expand your compound, you reach the limit of members in your cult at a relatively low number and tbh it feels as though your cult is relatively self managing at points just needing mini-game inputs and managing missions and in-game events etc. One thing I really did enjoy was the traits and quirks mechanic and how much it could affect gameplay and create a challenge. The price on sale is very fair and I hope they do continue to update the game and add to the replay-ability.

_childDocuments_.review: is a misleading title.  It's more like "Honey, I  a Cult and Built Its Compound." You're really playing as a cult leader here.If the sight of the idol being worshiped in the game trailer hinting that you might be able to play as a cult that is (merely playing at being) one of horror's most famous fictional cults does NOT have you thinking "TAKE MY MONEY NOW!!!" ... then this game is not for you.And you should probably turn in your nerd card.Kidding!There's ten preset cults (with more on the way!) here, offering something for everyone.  You can also sort of play as the bomb cult from .  If you wish something closer to real-world religions, there's Anubis or the Ark of the Covenant as well as Halloween and Christmas cults.  Or play as something that looks like a combination of 50s cool and a motorcycle club, if without the cycles.Beyond the presets, the game offers a TON of customization.  You can choose the look of your leader avatar and name them.  You can give your cultists and leader uniforms, complete with a selection of colors the devs feel would be appropriate.  You can also rename the titles you give your leader and cultists, including singular and plurals.  Sadly, there's no Sister/Brother gendered option, as your cultists do not have gender flags, but their looks are gender-coded.Don't like what you started the game with?  Happily, the game lets you switch customizations even after you are in the game.  You'll find there's a gameplay reason for this.When you start a game, you have the option of viewing a cute opening cutscene.  A lengthy tutorial that walks you through the starting basics is also skipable.Building your cult compound is a breeze once you learn the system.  You are given a sizable amount of money, but much of it will be plowed into building your starter compound.  You will need a dorm with beds, dining, showers, and toilets.  Later you will unlock a rec room to keep your cultists' morale up.  You'll also need a Holy Room (think chapel or temple) to hold daily sermons.And, you'll need to receive Followers.  Much of your work is centered on them.  Followers are your source for money and Influence, two of the resources in the game.  They are also where you find new cultists.Followers enter your compound, speak to someone at the reception desk in the Lobby, and then go find "therapy."  These range from simple meditation to seances to weirder options.  They pay you for this privilege and the leader earns Influence points.As Followers spend time in the compound, they earn Recruitment XP.  Fill the bar, and they are pretty easy to recruit.  However, Followers will eventually lose interest in the therapies you have on hand and stop coming.  Fortunately, there are plenty more citizens passing by.There are five total resources to juggle in the game.  Money is almost always spent on building and placing stuff in your compound, and is earned from Followers.  Influence is also mostly earned from Followers and spent on certain Leader activities, including advanced sermons or sending cultists on missions.PR is, of course, the good kind of attention and helps attract Followers and better quality ones.Heat is the bad sort of attention and is generated by your various activities.  Too much Heat brings protesters which quickly lower PR, or, worse, a Police raid that arrests random cultists and confiscate a few items.  (To be fair, some items will have been stolen on missions.)Most of the usual colony sim systems are here.  Your Cultists have levels, skills, Traits, and Quirks, as well as a Mood to keep up and needs to meet.Performing tasks around the compound earns XP for your cultists, which turn into levels that earn skill points.  However, a cultist's quality limits their max level and the max you can put into an individual skill.The game has about a dozen skills, but sorts them in three categories:  People for mostly interactions with Followers, Practical for doing some tasks, and Logical for thinking skills.  Each skill factors into a couple categories around the compound and each skill point adds a bonus to a cultist's performance in that task.  Naturally, a job priority system is there to help you put the best available cultist in each job.Skills also factor heavily into Missions, which must be completed in order to progress and survive to the end.  Missions are mainly to find/steal objects, increase PR or reduce Heat.Each mission takes a certain total score in three skills to be absolutely certain of success.  Failure means the cultists on the mission might suffer injury and you might earn other penalties. Later, some Missions will be of so high a level that they require the use of a Covert Ops room, where someone will plan out the mission to give your cultists a better chance of success.Once in awhile, a Mission will come with an encounter that require you to make a few choices and a chance to win some award.  Encounter choices are never random and encounters for certain types of missions repeat often enough to figure out the best path on the decision tree.  Some choices require the group to have a certain native score in one of the skill categories.  This is something mission prep in Covert Ops can't help.Traits are other stats that factor into gameplay calculations.  One Trait is always a quality rating.  Others might give penalties or bonuses to skills or movement.  Quirks are cultist preferences that affect mood.Mood is affected primarily by satisfying various needs, including hunger, toilet, hygiene, and energy.  When mood falls too low, a cultist might have a bit of a breakdown or temper tantrum that the game calls a Mood Break.  Such breaks might just be the cultist hitting an object in anger or them finally storming off in anger, never to be seen again.You have two tech trees to research.  One is explored in a standard Research Office and unlocks new rooms and many upgrades.  The other can only be researched by your dear leader in a Leader's Sanctum.The Leader's research centers on a Theme given to your cult.  This includes new uniforms for your cult (a reason why you can change customizations after starting) as well as generating missions to retrieve items for an endgame room.  Assemble everything together, and you get to trigger an ending scene.The leader also gets to research and instantly recruit a couple powerful cultists.  These have their own unique look and will not wear cult uniforms.  They become very useful in the late stages because they can be loaded up with many skill points.A complaint I have about recruiting normal cultists is that it is difficult to keep PR up because Heat rises too fast and you are spending much mission time on managing Heat instead of raising PR.  This makes recruiting anyone above average nearly impossible.  The leader's recruits, however, make up for this somewhat.Once in awhile, a newspaper blurb announces a random event that lasts for two game days.  These run a wide range including flowers spawning on grassy areas or a special limited-time mission.The art style is simple, with my biggest complaint being that there's little room to show uniform details.  The music, on the other hand, is an appropriately trippy 70s retro sound.My one other annoyance is that you'll need to keep buying food and cook it in the kitchen to make yummier meals, but there's no auto-purchase for food.The devs managed to pack in a lot of nerdy references in Follower/Cultist surnames, the names of the cultists the leader gets to recruit, and mission text.For an Early Access game the devs consider to be v0.4 at the time I played and wrote this review, it is very playable with no gamebreaking bugs.  More content and tweaks are promised in future updates to what is already a fun and funny game.

_childDocuments_.review: Yep, in this game you create a cult to gain money from your trust followers in order to expand your cult. By create a facility building for serving your customers (low rank followers) activities such as meditation, yoga, etc. And manage your staff (high rank members) by satisfy their need like food, sleep, shower, etc. so they can serve you customer better.If you start to feel like this is a management game, yes, it is. The cult is just a theme, because it is a business after all, and money make your cult go around. There are missions where you can send your staff with the right skills around to get reward, and there is a research tree too, like in many other games in this genre.One thing to mention is that there is no construction animation or process here in this game. You just click, and it done. And there is no water system or electric wire to handle, so, it's quiet easy to expand or renovating things later, you can relax and enjoy building thing anyway you like early without worry. However, it feel a little bit chunky sometimes for the User Interface because the button is so big and the catalog will show you only a few items at a time, so there will be a lot to scroll, and filtering to find what you want to build. But the overall graphic and animation is nice.It's still an early access after all, so I'm sure that will be a lot of improvement later. So far, the game is fine and fun in a relaxing way.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun for some time, but right now it has very few content, only one "path" to choose, same missions everytime, low maximum prestige (that kills one of the three missions), rooms are basically all the same but with different items, when you upgrade a room you get the same items but better, and too soon you get to a point where you spend a lot of time waiting for time to pass accumulating infinite money. The micromanaging part where you assign your workers to their chores needs a rework, you have to spend boring time going from square to square checking every skill level on every worker.When you click on a room, you should be able to see and click whoever is working on that room, you don't know how many times have i had to pause the game, go to the workers list and go to the chores tab to look for the guy that was working on maintenance at that time when an object was broken, because the maintenance guy AI just wanders around room to room cleaning and the time goes so fast and he loses so much time that he just can't check the whole building in his working time, that leads to broken things accumulating and everyone pooping their pants and going to run to the street.Maintenance needs to go to the broken items that the player can see, because wandering around makes sense from a realistic point of view, but what the player sees is a guy wasting time while five circles beep on your screen. The game needs a lot of polishing apart from content, i will finish it and play it again in some years.The 20€ price is definetly way too high for the moment, taking in mind it's basically the same as Prison Architect with 10 times less content and 10 times the price.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is AMAZING, especially when you consider it’s early access with a whole roadmap of content still coming.  I’m soooo happy I found this game; it’s great fun and I find that this game calls to me to constantly play it, rather than me being bored trying to talk myself into which game to play.  It’s very easy to jump into and there is no lack of content whatsoever.  You decide on which cult theme you’d like to choose (out of 30 choices I think it is), you get to customize everything about it, the leader, what the cultists will be referred to, as well as your followers.  You choose names, appearance, colors, icons to represent your cult, what you worship, clothing, etc.  You hold daily sermons and invest in various therapy rooms with the money you rake in from new followers.  Your cultists live at the compound, which you design.  The is a massive research tree, you also go on missions and skill up your cultists to make them most effective for various tasks (therapy rooms, missions, covert ops, kitchen cook, maintenance, recruitment, research, preaching, etc).  Different things that happen can raise the heat (negative attention) and can result in protests by activists and police raids.  Missions can grant special objects (dark themed) or prestige items to use to decorate the compounds many rooms.  They also grant PR, which is VERY important as it will effect the quality of the followers you attract.  You can also ask followers to join your group as a cultist (employee).  All followers have traits and a quality level.  They can have special bonuses that result in extra stat points or a bad trait that gives you stats in the negatives.  They all usually possess other traits that don’t necessarily effect stats such as make them need the restroom more often or just have a sunny disposition, for example.  Both your cultists and your followers can become seriously unhappy if they start to lose faith rapidly or become too mired in negativity or bored with the high multitude of attractions at the compound, resulting in a mood break where they just sort of go crazy and perform random chaos - it could be something as simple as walking off a job shift or something more serious like breaking things or assaulting someone.  You manage the jobs schedule and decide who will work in which position, what their work hours and breaks will be, as well as their sleep time. You can set priorities for each person for each job to high priority, low priority or not allowed at all in that job.  You can set multiples so each day they choose from several job choices or you could ironclad assign them one job to do and that’s it.  The game is also very humorous in the various themes, therapy room functions, work attire.  Although it’s early access, I’ve personally experienced NO bugs whatsoever and reading through the forums, you rarely hear of others mention them.  This game is a BLAST, I look forward to playing it daily and can’t wait to see new content as it’s added in the future.  Highly, highly recommend!!

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but I just can't get into it.It's basically a Prison Architect clone, with even less flavour.  The different rooms and modules have basically no meaning except as automatic money & influence generators.  The pace is very slow and everything just feels very bland and uninteresting.  In fact it's even easier than PA because there is no build mechanic or need for resources.  There's only money, and everything is built instantly.  If you run out of money you just wait for your $ generators to make enough to build more things.If this were a $10 DLC for Prison Architect it would be worth it I guess, but as a standalone game it just does not hold up, in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. It's 1000% the type of game I play and will sink hours into. I kept waiting for it to get fun....but it never did. The graphics are cute enough, but the game play mechanics are just not engaging. The interface isn't really comfortable? It felt just a little awkward to use. I'll come back to it again in a few months before I decide fully, and hopefully revise this review. But for now... Huge nope.

_childDocuments_.review: A cult management game/simulator. Unfortunately it's another one of these games where there's not much to do but fast forward. Once you've built your initial facility you're just unlocking new tech to replace the furniture you have with better furniture, increase how many cult members you can have, that sort of thing, but there's not really many interesting things that are happening or decisions you have to make.
_childDocuments_.name: Honey, I Joined a Cult

_childDocuments_.review: Have you played Rimworld and/or Prison Architect and have you ever wondered how it would be to lead a cult? But without the deepth and difficulty of these games? Then this is the game for you.I played a round in 2 real days over the weekend and I enjoyed it. There is a certain charme and humor to it and the game loop is good. For the price is it very good. As a bigger game like RimWorld or PrisonArchitect it lacks of deepth, complexity and alternatives. It is a bit grindy and there are times when you have to wait but can't do anything really.Also there are some Quality of Life features missing - the management of your cultists are a bit tedious, they will ignore your work requests if they are assigned to a room with the same priority, but being "more on the left". They will ignore going to the toilet when they are assigned to working - this isn't a warehouse. At the end you have tousands of objects you can buy, but the filter are to weak to quickly find new ones or the most useful.Finally: It is a good game missing a bit of polish. I would like to see more of it with some QoL patches before running a new cult.

_childDocuments_.review: very nice and well done thematic, but as for the game management aspect, damn it, it becomes quickly laborious. just one example, to assign the priorities of the activities to the cultists, you have to navigate between several menus, or even take notes because you can't have the list of the cultists, their skill levels and the activities to prioritize on the same screen. in the end the game imposes quickly too much micro-managementit's really hard to ignore it after playing Oxygen not Included or Rimworld (well, especially its Mods) and it's unfortunately the weak point of many management games lately

_childDocuments_.review: This game broke my heart. It seemed like it was going to be a game to eat up hundreds of hours of my time like Oxygen not Included or Rimworld. However it is just an empty shell. This game feels closer to a bare bones tycoon game than a colony style simulator. The cult customization is purely cosmetic and you don't get the same feel as rimworld ideologies. The base building isn't complex enough to warrant the complete lack of general activities to perform. I regularly spend my time staring at my screen waiting for $ to hit a certain amount so I can build a new thing that generates a form of currency.I like the art style. I like the theme. However it just has very little in creativity in regards to the systems in place in the game. If you enjoy choices in these games or any since of complexity I recommend you stay away. This is unfortunate because Rimworld Ideologies shows how much depth there is in this subject. Imagine how bogus you could actually get with this concept outside of cosmetic that feel lazy.TLDR: It feels more like running a club that charges customers by the minute than it does being a leader of a cult.

_childDocuments_.review: I really don't want to give this game a bad review, but here it is.AS THE GAME IS NOW I cannot recommend it. Some of the most major complaints I have:- The skill tree is arranged as a web that doesn't make much sense and forces you to play as a generalist and disallows specialization. If you want to focus on missions, you first have to unlock hamburgers for some reason. To increase your max number of workers, you have to research maggot rejuvenation therapy. To get a better recreation room with more games, you first have to unlock a silver idol. This severely limits your ability to build your cult in your own unique way. You basically have to unlock all the same techs in roughly the same order in every cult you manage.- The AI seems to have trouble taking care of itself. Even a cultist given a full day off will starve and ♥♥♥♥ themselves because they choose to wander around instead of get food or go to the bathroom. This can lead to a cult collapsing as followers give a debuff to other followers when they leave.- Room grades are seriously flawed. You can unlock upgrades and spend literally thousands decorating a room and it still gives followers a debuff as the game considers it poorly decorated. - Speaking of decor, there's very limited aesthetic options. Cult themes are as follows: dinosaurs, cthulu/fish, Egyptian, and the moon. Cultists can't wear black for some reason - the darkest color you can pick is brown, even when you unlock the "cult of darkness" outfits. There's a very short list of decor, most items can only be placed in their specific rooms (so no using functional objects like a desk decoratively, it can only be placed one time in its designated room), and no ability to place indoor colored tiles or change wall colors. Indoor tiles are determined by the type of room and cannot be changed. Doesn't matter if you're a cult of darkness, your lobby is going to have a bright sky-blue floor. Wall options are wood, brick, gray, gray, and gray.All of these things are repairable. If these issues are addressed, the game has some great bones that set it apart from most other top-down management games. I really appreciate the degree of micromanagement. You're able to set individual schedules for each cultist and tell them exactly what they should be doing (though they may ignore you). The mechanics behind growing faith and influence are potentially interesting. There's some great humor and subtle references that I enjoyed. And while the opening cut is as slow as frozen molasses, the tutorial itself is actually well rounded and does a great job teaching the basics and keeping you engaged. It's easy to grasp. Just temper your expectations for now. I hope to change this review in the future. I want to like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is nothing new to the genre- of course it will be similar to games like Rimworld and Prison Architect. This was just released into Early Access so there will not be the maximum amount of content but the game so far is really fun. Anyone who buys an Early Access game should have the patience to wait for bug fixes and content updates. Pros:Fun AestheticEasy UI (at least for me)Clear and Easy Tutorial Good humourFun Soundtrack (nothing revolutionary but its funky)Lots of fun rooms and items to play withYou can see all of the people's stats and what they are doingLots of cosemtic customisation for your cult (naming, clothes, symbols, idols, etc)I personally haven't run into any HUGE cons yet but that is just my experience. I have spent 140 hours playing Rimworld and about 20 playing Prison Architect which are both games people tend to compare this one to. I am not an expert at either of those games but this game just stands out to me as more fun and simple. I am a more casual player so this game suits my play style more than those who prefer a Rimworld hard core experience. Also I was able to make a cult based on Lord Farquaad :)TL:DR: Fun and simple game with an interesting plot and good humour. It's worth a shot if you are interested in a more simple, fun, and easy city builder/colony sim management experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being out for a while, it's very bare-bones, and what makes the cult theme usually so interesting just isn't really present here. I was hoping for cutesy morbid humour but it really just felt like a retail waiting game where the workers just stay at the location. The UI is especially clunky, with a very weird inventory/buying system, a weirdly tiny x button when every other button is huge, confusing scheduling system where you cant actually see the persons skills in the mass priority section but then can't see if someone's already been assigned to it in the personal priority section and you can't just memorise them because the uniform either covers all their features or just makes them all look the same(The fix is just to label them with only numbers as a comedic way to show that they are just mindless followers), when you go to try mass removing followers you must click on every single one of them and go through two menu's each with some of them flipping to the recruit tab so you may accidentally recruit the worst ones when all the others were automatically on the other tab where the remove button is.Not to say I didn't have some fun, the missions sometimes being glorified pop quizzes were kinda fun, and then they repeat. The maze one was quite frustrating as well, as most parts of the riddle have no actual indicator of either going left or right when you're told to avoid them, and the rival part usually makes you think that the man statue is the rival until you read a little further in and it Tells. You. the exact way to walk.So essentially, it is a slightly strange spa simulator.

_childDocuments_.review: After having such high expectations and a waiting period for full release, unfortunately "Honey I joined a cult" remains the same.Lacking in classic cult references (minus a tentacle or two), simulated potential and humour this game went from the expectancy of a funny, satanic panic era simulator to nothing more than an idle clicker game.The game is playable and has a cute art style, however, by playable, I mean it runs... To the point you can have almost zero interaction and just allow the game to play out on 100% speed as money comes in, buy all research and items, and then just resume idling again.Sure, you have to pick your research paths and withstand a few "emotive breaks" from your followers, but, in my experience, it has no consequences.. You might lose a follower if you're lucky.Don't get me wrong, you can see that the developers have made an attempts but i personally cannot move past the fact that this game, which has so much fun potential, is nothing more than one of those mobile idle simulator games.So disappointed in what could have been with this, and with what was achieved.Save your money on this, and buy Cult Of The Lamb.

_childDocuments_.review: Honey, I Joined a Cult is an interesting little sim game where you get to play the leader of a cult, drawing in followers, recruiting cultists, and building up to a world-changing finale. While it has some interesting mechanics and a decent sense of humor, it's a bit shallow, so multiple playthroughs will mostly be the same.In Honey, I Joined a Cult, you're ultimately building a mall with residential facilities for your workers. There are rooms to house and feed your cultists; rooms to occupy your followers (your primary source of income); and rooms for some of your more devious plans. There are three types of cults you can create, each with a small selection of special rooms: peace and love, darkness, and futurism. Each of the three types has two "finale" options to build towards. There's plenty of customization provided in how your cult looks, including what your cultists are called and the name of your deity. These terms are used in various places in the game.There are a handful of bugs that aren't game-breaking but are annoying nonetheless. Sometimes one of your custom cult words won't be used properly. There's a perk that will be generated on new followers that isn't functional in the game (cut content). Aside from minor bugs, there are some parts of the interface that are a little annoying to work with, but nothing major.It's not a bad game by any measure, and it's good for a few hours of entertainment. If you're chasing the achievements, you'll end up doing the same thing multiple times (save before choosing your path to save some time on multiple playthroughs), which is really my biggest complaint. The game feels too shallow for the current price of $22; half that may be more appropriate; I received the game as part of a monthly Humble Choice bundle but likely wouldn't have purchased otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game for a couple hours, but as of now there isn't really enough content to warrant the current cost of the game. _childDocuments_.review: For the most part, I've enjoyed the game thus far. My main issue is that the generation and management of the faith resource is incredibly difficult, and the research tree takes FAR too long to get through. I was bottoming out my faith every day until I upgraded my pews and got better food, and then I was suddenly hitting the faith cap after every sermon! After recruiting a few higher quality cultists, I'm now bottoming out faith again, and the new pew upgrade is many, many days away. I understand it's a balance, but the balance needs more tweaking. I don't know what the expectation is, but I'm at day 76 and I'm not even halfway through the research tree, while having someone assigned as much as possible. Seems a bit much. Oh, and can we please sell objects instead of just deleting them? That would be helpful early on.

_childDocuments_.review: My Early Access ReviewPROS- Good humor- *Most* things feel pretty balanced- Customizing your cult- Multiple Cult Themes allows different things to happen with your cult- Creative therapy rooms & decorations- Signing soul contracts & sacrificing followers is fun (but maybe too costly)CONS- The Peace & Love theme is impossible to beat currently due to a bug  (I had to start a new game about half-way through)- The Darkness theme has one compound task that was impossible to beat but I was still able to beat the game without it- Compound requirements giving negative effects are really annoying near end game- Recruiting high quality followers is probably impossible (besides the ones you research) even with MAX PR rating- Heat needs balanced or provide more ways to decrease it- Positive Faith stat basically does nothing. When negative your followers are unhappy but that's about it.  Having maxed 3000 Faith means basically nothing.- Faith sermons are useless and cost to much.- I maxed my compound & all stats (plus no Heat and max PR) and still never had a 5 star sermon.- Need more ways to customize your Cult Leader (he basically just floats around and does his own thing)- The ending of the game is just a picture and a "Congrats" :( I hope they fix this for final release.- The compound tasks force you to have one of every room. I didn't like that because I wanted only certain types of therapy rooms and it kept telling me to build all of them.- Infirmary is useless and I didn't use it once.- More variety of missions would be niceOverall, it's a decent game and a bit grindy (normal given it's a management sim). I do like it but it has very little reply value since play style is not flexible. If they make the compound requirements more flexible it wouldn't lock you into one play style (i.e. build one of everything, upgrade everything multiple times, then push for end game).  Also, certain rooms like Research, Covert Ops, Propaganda,  etc. you can only have ONE. Why not allow multiple rooms and allow the effects to be compounded???I feel like the devs are working on hard on the game so I am going to recommend it. I think it's pretty good in the current state, but I hope they listen to the players and fix some of the things holding it back. It's a solid 7/10 currently

_childDocuments_.review: From an achievement hunter point of view: I could not wait to uninstall this game.  The mid- and late-gameplay was an absolute slog of waiting on poorly optimized NPC AI and over-extended goalposts.  About half of the achievements were accessible in the early-game, but the rest require resorting to prior saves for branching choices and save-scumming for artificial fulfillment of total recorded values.  And worst of all; you can't just let the game run on its own while you go do something else more engaging.  Every in-game 24 hours, the game pauses to show you a status screen, and will not continue past it until you manually exit it.  Gameplay-wise, I was hoping for an experience along the lines of Prison Architect.  What I got was terrible path-finding, limited controls, and skin-deep mechanics for customization.  The game isn't even finished yet; as the developers currently maintain empty promises/threats of releasing additional ending options that would oblige the agony of enduring whole new play-throughs (or loading saves right before the lock-in point, which is unfortunately at mid-game).Overall: an interesting concept for the management genre that fell flat on its face and dragged the adjacent pedestrian down along with it.Edit: at time of writing, it has been over a year since devs contributed any updates or even any commentary on the state of the game on its Steam discussion forum.  It seems that they were active with the game development during the month of its release, and then dropped it.  This instance adds to the growing trend of Team17 games coming to Steam dead on arrival.

THIS GAME IS AN INSULT TO YOUR INTELLIGENCE!I have like 10k+ hours in grand strategy and simulation games, Paradox games, Rimworld, etc... if that means anything to you please trust me and save your money.Game is entirely gated by time, you are maxed at 1 researcher and have to wait on him for everything. You can level intelligence but researcher seemed to make the least xp, i meta leveled 3 cultists to max and they still took days to complete reasearch with 3 people working the reasearch table around the clock at. Your first goal is to build a leader sanctuary where you can then get "divine inspiration" for your cult. Guess what, its another research bar, with more useless tech than the last one. This game feels like it was designed entirely around getting you past the 2 hour mark so you cant refund it. I promise you theres no game here. all in all you can unlock around 10 rooms that make different percentages of 2 resources you need. you can get 17 people which is not enough for all the things you get but dont worry you wont care which one of the rooms you use because theres 2 resources. the only "progress"you feel is upgrading your peoples rooms from things like bucket toilets to regular ones, but that from the start was just dangled in front of you to make you play the 2 hours so you cant get a refund. I have no enthusiasm to say more if you read this far just trust me. Worst part is, this game was recommended to me through Rimworld. This game was also in early access, I can't even imagine how little might have been in the first version they let people pay for.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though the game’s premise seems interesting, it does not deliver the expected. Sadly, the game is pretty boring after mid game and it feels like an abandoned game. Most of the time you have to wait for something to gather but you cannot do something else in the meantime, since the game pauses at the end of each day. Also, for some reason, some of the missions have some kind of adventure mode which is not numerous and also another thing that pauses the advancement (just missions). As you can understand, there is a certain need for micromanagement which I hate. Another annoying thing is the special characters; unfortunately, you can lose them and that means you won’t be able to bring them back in any way. Other than that, there are 3 different themes that offers endings and they are not worth the wait, since it only shows an image at the end of the game. _childDocuments_.review: Let me begin with people who negatively review this game forget it's currently early access and only released 2 months ago (at the time of this review)Honestly I usually find these games kind of boring, but the simple and absurd nature presented just appealed to me. It's still quite clearly an unfinished product, with ultimately somewhat limited things to do other then base building and minor management elements. Ive also crashed a few times and when you get to a large base with lots of rooms and maxed out cultists, some get stuck in place during breakfast time, making their moods drop purely because of imperfect coding.Although the initial cult customisation is cool with a surprising amount of options, it's all ultimately meaningless. I wanted to make a cookie themed cult (obviously) but in the end was forced to  It's a little underwhelming that there is an end goal that changes nothing once you complete it, and to even do so is just more of what you've been doing the whole time. Researching stuff, sending people on missions and buying stuff. However it seems the "Darkness" route is one of 4, with the other 3 not being released yet and presented as locked, so there's potential.Customising cultists themselves comes down to purely RNG when it comes to traits. What profession you want them to do and how you level up their skills are mostly also dictated by said traits. Assigning them to specific tasks is also interestingly presented and although its intuitive to let members work where they are needed, having to manually set where I want people to work while I cross reference it with their mismatched traits is annoying at best. Id rather when the game spawns a cultist they have a recommended place of work (Reception, Therapy Rooms, Module Rooms, Etc), and their traits that boost skills revolve around whats useful there, rather then having a mixture of traits boosting skills that don't compliment eachother due to only 2 specific skills ever mattering for each job.Or you know, each skill could have more depth in side bonuses so I don't feel forced to max out specifically 2 skills for specifically one job, or have jack of all trades type cultists who arent excelling at any job since skill investment is limited. Its not like missions make it worthwhile to have mixed skills either maxing out a single skill is more helpful because like I said, theres only limited skill investment.This is a late game nitpic however, as early on you really just take who you can get.The gameplay loop itself addictive as all hell too, but all that stops the moment you beat the game as there is little to no replay value currently. I don't get anything special for completing the finale, and there is only so much I can build up my base until I run out of room. The potential for depth is there however, and my issues with the game come from it purely being an unfinished product, rather then it being a not thought out product. There's room to grow is what I'm saying.The only thing I don't like right now is the pricepoint at $29.95 in my local currency, which seems a little high for whats on offer here currently. Quoting the developers:  This implies that the full release will go up in price, and I'm not sure if that is justified. I personally think if the content I'm expecting to see comes to fruition, then sure, full price at $30 is fine and inline with other similar games published by Team 17. But $40+ seems a little ambitious for the type of content being provided. I don't mean to discredit the hard work and clear love put into this game, but besides games made by well known developers I cant really think of any games in this genre that push into low priced Triple A game territory.Due to its early access nature I can't give it a fair score out of 10 (if this was a full release it would be a 4-5 tbh) but I can definitely recommend a purchase as it is quite  enjoyable to see people worshipping "The Cookie Godess" or whoever you decide.Overall for a newly released early access game, it's actually quite impressive what it already has to offer. It truly does feel like early access rather then an unfinished product. But the fact it's open access is why I can easily recommend this game as although its limited, buying into early access is basically paying to play an unfinished product, isn't it?I don't see this game ending up in Early Access hell either, with Team 17 funding it, you will get your moneys worth one day.Just have a little faith :)

_childDocuments_.review: I'm actually really pleased with this gem of a game. At first, I thought HIJaC would just be a goofy little colony simulator that would die a slow death in Steam's mass grave of unfinished pre-alpha cash grabs, but the amount of fun I ended up having surpassed my unreasonably high expectations. The colony management is satisfying, the engine is robust, and the customisation is unusually vast. The jokes are dry but land well in context. Me being a mindless psychopath, I created The Order from the Silent Hill games. My cultists worship Alessa with fear and pride, and we have daily conversions in the Church of The Rebirth. Sadly there is no flesh peeling from the walls at dusk, no fire sirens, and I cannot flay followers who leave in anger and throw the bloody refuse at the church doors. I hope Konami doesn't read this review. They'll flag it for IP infringement. Going forward, I have two ideas. First of all, I'd love to see some mod workshop integration. Community contributions would compliment the style of HIJaC well, and I believe modding is the last step into really involving the community (that doesn't really exist yet) in the final stages of development. Second, what cult is complete without some innocent murder? Give us the framework to harbour dark secrets and the high stakes risk/reward elements of HIJaC will be much more satisfying. Thank you for your time,Ynsin.

_childDocuments_.review: After a few starts, ups, downs, and a multitude of craziness. A finale has been reached.  This game runs with the same feel of management builders on a grid base. This will most likely change as other directions are in the works which will allow for more options in the end.Overall if you are a fan of games like Prison Architect, Academia, and other management builders on a grid map, you will have a place in this cult.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game being a bit of a cult nerd; I know a lot about them and at one point, an ex and I had talked about making a cult simulator game because of my weird passion. So, I was STOKED to see there was a game coming out similar to what I'd envisioned and it's okay. Like, it has room to grow. A lot of room. But it's a good foundation.Some feedback:Cult lore: Often power and control are major themes behind the origins of cults, and that's something that isn't really explored in the game. It's more so a financial theme. What if I want my cult of Herbologists to be off the grid farmers who recruit people by selling their vegetables in a mini market that can be upgraded over time? Rules: Many cult leaders run a tight ship to control their flock and have many asinine rules for their followers to adhere to. We should be able to create our own asinine rules/10 Commandments for our followers to follow. That way I know who's following the rules, who gets a good bed and who's sleeping on a dirty mattress.Hierarchy: There's usually some sort of hierarchy in place that lets the followers know who's who, and who you have to get through to become someone worthy. Let's get an inner sanctum going, y'know, or let us segregate cleaning/menial tasks to our newbies, and work their way up to doing cooler stuff. Maybe grouping of jobs/roles within a pyramid (hehe) on the Cult members job page.Better quests: Not sure if you've seen what stuff cults get up to, but it's rarely talking to the media. I've noticed you can unlock other quests after a while, and they seem like the type of quests that are better for the beginning of the game (especially because there isn't a campaign, storyline or active quests within the cult or quotas to unlock levels that provide you with more content). It would also be cool if my cult members, who have their own info/job history/needs had their own side quests.Overall, the game has potential but it doesn't play like an actual cult game. Which is sad, as it's the only game of its type on the market. I'll continue to play for a few hours here and there, and look forward to more content coming out in the future. If you're looking for a game that has room to grow, I'd recommend it. If you're looking for a game about cults, I wouldn't really recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I agree with almost everything Nayu says in their review . With regards to the protests, I think that they missed a mechanic (which, to be fair, is never spelt out and you might miss it) where if you mouse over the protester that's banging on your fence, the relevant skill will highlight over all your cultists at once making it pretty easy to pick out the relevant cultists. Other than that, I agree with pretty much everything.Additionally, the endgame SUCKS... With regards to the cult-specific ending, all of that research can be done ***only*** by the head of your cult (this is the Divine Inspiration tree). Even with maxxed out items (that you get from the regular research tree), this research takes a significantly long time. At this point in the game, I have completed the regular research tree, maxxed out every building, and had every single follower at 'good' or better. There's a couple of very short research spots, but they are to place a cult-specific mission on the mission map, which are thirty (30) hours in f'ing duration. While these missions are underway, the head of your cult cannot do any Divine Inspiration research. For no good reason, at all.In addition to this there are 4 buildings that can be operated *only* by the head of your cult, 2 of which affect followers (non-cultists) and 2 affect cultists. Followers, of course, only appear during the day which overlaps with the default schedule of your leader, which means that if you want to use those buildings you have to stop doing the Divine Inspiration research. (the other two rooms can be used during 'rest' time)So my last several hours of gameplay were just... waiting out the clock on either research or missions, and then spending hundreds of thousands of $$$ to build the Finale Room. And. The game ends. With a big picture. Just an image.Extremely anti-climactic.While there are multiple endings (3 cult specialities and, I assume, 2 endings for each), why the f*ck would I sit through ALL of that again for, essentially, a low-effort 'congratulations' screen?For the most part, I found the game to be astonishingly easy (and I am NOT good at colony sims), just unnecessarily long.If you want to kill 3-4 hours? Sure, this is a good buy on a deal. Playing it all the way through was a complete waste of my time, and I regret doing so.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: It's fine. It's not going to blow your socks off, but it's an fun time-waster that's difficult to lose.It's a base builder about running your own cult in the 70's!  The music and theming all add to the 70's vibe in a funky way, but once the novelty wears off, it feels more like running an amusement park than a cult. It's easy to pick up if you've never played a base builder before. Even on challenging difficulty, I had no problems managing my resources and typically read a book while the game ran on full speed. The biggest downside to the game is that it's just... boring. There's a lot of waiting for things to happen, either building resources, waiting for research or waiting for missions to complete. Bad events are either entirely avoidable (if you don't forget to click something), or unavoidable and relatively harmless. They don't add any challenge or pressure to the game, and for the most part I was annoyed clicking the "accept" button three times a day because my cultists forgot to wash their hands and now their tummy hurt. The variety of decorations and rooms add some spice to the gameplay, and I'll admit that part of why I played as long as I did was to make a couple of pretty, themed compounds. Towards the endgame, you tend to have more money than anything else, and I enjoyed spending all of it to make extravagant bathrooms. The system for improving decor is more complex than just adding a bunch of rugs and pictures, and I personally enjoyed trying to max out scores while keeping with my theme. The writing is light and witty, and there are numerous events that quiz you on your everyday knowledge. Being able to successfully jump a car, for example, can give one of your cultists a permanent +6 to their skills. Sometimes, it feels out of place, especially when running an evil cult. I'm liquidizing followers for their purple goo, but the music is cheerful and cultists are joking about The Minkler. It never really felt like I was running a cult trying to take over the world, but rather a fun, afternoon retreat for everyone I hadn't eaten yet.Overall, it's a fine game. It doesn't have the addictive quality I usually find in base builders, but it's easy gameplay and groovy vibe might appeal to those new to the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Honey, I Joined a Cult

_childDocuments_.review: While I don't have that many hours in the game I was hoping on at least a little bit realistic version of a cult game. In this game you run a religion where your members reach out into the community and prosthelytize to people as well as share your religious propaganda and occasionally commit robbery and such to steal artifacts (kind of like in evil genius). You need to keep your followers happy and satisfied with food, bathrooms, cleanliness and entertainment.While there is cult-ish elements in the game, it takes an approach of tricking people out of their money rather than the real issue of lust of control over others at any expense.In short, this game feels like rimworld meets evil genius rather than anything really cult-like. The lack of the devs ever (last i checked what they said on the matter) having a plan to add mods also makes the game pretty stale with little point in re-playing the game. (and I will explain why)The cult designer (at the start of the game) has no relevance to gameplay in any way shape or form. The design of the cult is ONLY art style and has no impact of what your 'cult' does or how others react to it. There also is no real way to have your people outreach to people or force them into the 'cult'. Rather, you have a few rooms that have the ability to let people come in off the street and talk to your people (without prompting, pamphlets or anything else other than them just walking by). If you are expecting to customize your cult to be like Aum Shinrikyo and appeal to the anime crowd, Peoples Temple Agricultural Project (jonestown) and appeal to christianity x communism x Socialism or Heavens Gate and appeal to christianity x UFO's, then you can save your time and wait for another game. Every playthrough in this game will have the same flavor as there just isn't another way to build the 'cult' other than the generic way they have you play through the game.Other than all of that, the game is just ok. The one part that does truely shine in this game is the people you can recruit to be your 'workers' as you can recruit 5 different ranks (as far as i can tell) and each come with traits that are a bonus and a curse. They gain xp and level up as they work and go on missions. They have the standard way of keeping your people happy with nothing really new other than the rooms can become crowded and you get a debuff on the room where they are too full of objects or have a broken object in the room.On broken objects and logistics, you can assign a worker to a repair room, however, they randomly wander through your buildings and look in them to clean and fix items. The issue is that they occasionally miss entire rooms of broken objects that can leave you with a room that is non-functional for days at a time unless you manually direct them to fix the object. The food in the game is basically 4 tiers of food with 'snack machine' being the least and 'meat and vegetables' being the best. While this is ok to start with they do not have a way of auto-ordering new ingredients for your people to cook with for the 3 higher tiers of food. This means if you forget to top the food off by purchasing more for 2-3 days then your people will revert to eating vending machine food and suffering large debuffs to their moods. I would expect the devs to change this in the future as it makes for a annoying and frustrating way of playing the game.workers will randomly man rooms as they feel like they want or do not want to. I don't know if this is intended or not but it becomes increasingly frustrating to get your workers to work at rooms as your amount of workers grow from the researches you do to increase them. There is a way to forbid them performing other jobs and this is what you end of having to do for every single worker for them to even work and man the open rooms as they tend to just wander around the starting area and sometimes get stuck. (them getting stuck i would lay at the feet of a game bug and not intentional design)In summery, I personally would call the game ok. It has a few interesting elements and only really 1 new idea to bring to the table. Without mod support the game will very likely fade into obscurity unless there are some pretty drastic improvements to make the game more interesting and replayable.

_childDocuments_.review: My review is neutral, but more on the no than yes side for now. For clarification, my example game I use as the base line when evaluating management style games is Oxygen Not Included.The reason why I've decided to not recommend the game is the following:- The UI is not intuitive- The management side is made hard by not having clean overviews. I want to have an overview that is easy to use + provides at a quick glance what you need to invest in to make your cult + cultists thrive.- The misson tab is overwhelming with whats on the screen, but its very unclear what certain missions provide- The mission tab, when assigning a cultists does not show what impact certain cultists have over others. Only the success % changes when I click around on a few of them.- The skills are confusing and it's unclear what to focus on (prioritize)- It's not easy to assign cultists to certain roles because again, the interface + skills are not intuitive- The way the research tree has been set up is not logical to me. Stuff like better toilets + bedrooms should be moved to earlier in the tree, to ensure cultists stay happy/healthy (no heat early on). Perhaps adding another branch to the tree which solely focusses on the cultists needs might help?- There is a lot of text, but all this text does not make things any clearer- Cultist management tab is not helpful at all. I'm resorted to having to click on each cultists separately, which is not great- Cannot save your custimized cult settings (appearance). So I have to keep recreating it when I want to restart . Would be great to save a custom template.- When you demolish/delete something, you do not get your money back- There is no undo button- The toilet mechanic makes no sense to me. It feels like you have to build a toilet next to every room to ensure your cultists don't pee their pants

_childDocuments_.review: It's lacking a lot of qol that would make it fun. Premise? fun. Style? fun. Story elements? mostly fun.Research balance is very wack; there are major qol features that simply aren't in the game; there's only really one way of building your cult due to the debuffs you receive late game. There's no storage for items you collect, you simply have to sell them and repurchase them (I say repurchase because when you unlock new items in missions where you're told "you found this item :)" you still have to purchase the item. You find 1 copy of that item which you can then buy. It's ♥♥♥♥. lol.) if you don't want to individually take items from one side of your cult to the other; there's no way to get rid of the AWFUL and horrendously un-fun debuffs you get at the end of the game that require you to do certain things to provide for your followers... including some that are contradictory (like needing multiple bathrooms AND requiring that all rooms be above a certain prestige level)... and the debuffs are the same every run. Quirks are only negative - who thought of that ♥♥♥♥ idea? why not instead of "acolyte gets a bad mood if near X" you could get a quirk that was "acolyte gets good mood if not near X"? That would be effectively the same mechanic, but it wouldn't feel like the game was punishing me for literally everything that I do. Which, now that I'm phrasing it that way, is pretty much what the entire game feels like it's doing. There is very, very few things that feel like bonus that are just nice to have - all of the things that are supposed to be bonuses feel like they're a requirement for not having to struggle 70% of the game, or they just feel like ♥♥♥♥. If you're reading this and decide that it still sounds like you might have fun: A - lol and good luck, but more importantly B - just play on the easier settings. I've done 3 play throughs for the 3 different finale achievements, and the harder difficulties are actually harder, sure, but because they game forces you to play the same way regardless, I'd say the difference is mostly equivalent to a boss fight where the only change between easy and hard is that the boss has 3x the health. Don't play it. If the devs make a miraculous return, rebalance much of the game, remove the debuffs and/or otherwise fix them, fix a LOT of qol moments, and allow more options in gameplay (as it is, there's exactly one way you can play this game, with 3 different flavours and technically "6" endings (2 per flavour).)Also the achievement for earning 100k influence is bugged. idk what it's measuring, but it's telling me I've only earned 51k, when I have, in fact beaten the game 3 times, and earned several hundred thousand influence at this point. When I was first looking at the achievements on my first play through and comparing them, I have something like 60K influence 70% of the way through that run.  I'm counting this as 100%'d. I'm uninstalling it and then going to pretend I've never heard of this game before.Also it's late, sorry about the walls of text. This game isn't even worth me trying to make it more readable.TD;DR: don't. If you do, play on "easy" (see explanation in the wall somewhere). But more seriously, don't do this to yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun resource management game that sucks you in and will have you playing for hours without feeling like time has passed. The game became more difficult as it went on in terms of gaining influence and maintaining it. I started playing right as this game was released in early access so it's still rough around the edges and has room to improve but it was a good first impression that had me obsessively playing away for days! Hope this becomes a cult favorite, pun intended! If you like resource management games, you'll probably like this one. It takes a dark subject and takes a wacky spin on it that still depicts the dark aspects of an unfortunate reality.Pros:- fun resource management- wacky style and music- light-hearted satire- fast start - easy to make money in gameCons:- research and maintaining influence in later game becomes grueling- missing 1 or 2 sermons in game can cause you to fall into negative faith and makes it difficult to recover from- not enough negative consequences for your actions, even police raids feel more like a minor nuisance than an actual threat to your livelihood- follower cap feels nonsensical to me, why would a cult based on making more money restrict its number of followers? If the goal is to make more money, shouldn't they want as many followers as they can get?- Cult leader feels practically useless outside of sermons and divine inspirations. As for the cult aspects of the game, I like that the game overall portrays the cult you run as a money making scam. True real life cults are best categorized using the BITE model (behavioral control, information control, thought control, and emotion control), and I would like more controlling aspects of this to appear in the game in the future. The game approaches the darker aspects with a wacky pizzazz - you're taking financial advantage of your followers, your recruits are isolated and alienated from their families, you recruit and discard your cultists as assets instead of as people, your followers will steal and vandalize in their missions for the good of the cult, you can even sacrifice your followers later in the game. Those are real things that can happen in cults, yes, but I would like to see More cult aspects in the future involving the followers. Things that I would like to see in the future with this game to make the cult more cult-like (these aren't requirements for me to enjoy the game, these are just suggestions to give more cult aspects that reflect the real life counterparts): -Having a reward and punishment system for recruits and followers to maintain control would make sense, as well as the possible ability for recruits to start families while within the cult and have a cult-ran school to have children grow up indoctrinated by the cult. -Have the option to ban or encourage specific kinds of clothing and entertainment for your followers and recruits. -Add missions involving slandering ex-followers, as well as add more consequences for dismissing longtime recruits and followers. -Add undercover agents that infiltrate the cult to try and destabilize it and rescue people from the cult. -Add missions involving cultists committing violent acts for the leader. -Add the ability to give titles and hierarchical roles to the recruits so that they can be managed better. -Add one or more initiation ceremonies such as baptisms or confirmations. -Add the option to re-invite ex-members back into the cult if they still hold faith aka allow some ex-members to still be brainwashed and want back in. -Add missions to spread cult propaganda or establish auxiliary churches in other locations that follow your cult. Basically add missions involving door-knocking and evangelism.Hope to see this game improve and expand as the developers update it! Hope this review is helpful!

_childDocuments_.review: Mindnumbing. The cult theme is just a half-baked skin on top of this simple Prison Architect clone. There's very little here that even feels cult-y besides being able to dress your people and customize the name of your cult/idol/deity. That's something that happens in the start screen, and after that, the theme mostly drops in place of a very basic retail management game. Progress is slowly doled out exclusively through adherence to the tired "research" trope, and research is essentially the only currency in the game that matters. The game is so poorly paced that every night consists of 12 in-game hours of watching your characters sleep or maybe you'll get to send them on off-screen missions like it's a Facebook game from 2008. Because such missions are nearly worthless in favor of research, up to the mid-game where you need them to 'reduce heat', you'll spend half of every in-game day just staring at the screen waiting for night to end.The game markets itself on being scandalous in theme, but nothing provocative happens in the game besides the appearance of a facility designed to mock spiritualism. The tutorial opens and closes with a 'hilarious' squid costume cult getting arrested for 'being brainwashed.' Compare that to the jaw-dropping opening of Prison Architect's double-homicide scene, and you realize this game is a cheap cash-in appealing to Streamers and Youtubers. 'Huhu, I made a cult and named it after myself. My community is a cult! It's a joke I came up with!'The one thing going for this game is it's pretty chill. If you just want to watch numbers tick up on three-speed for the illusion of progress, this is great. Otherwise, it's certainly not worth the retail or even the sale price. If my child made this I'd be very impressed, but a team of grown adults should be able to do something better than carbon copying an already popular formula and then dumbing-it-down close to oblivion.

_childDocuments_.review: So coming to this after playing very briefly immediately after its early access launch and being burnt out on early access games in general I was excited to see the full 1.0 product release. A cult-themed "colony builder" like Rimworld/Dwarf Fortress/etc. sounded fantastic and I was hopeful to play a great one of those with some direction to the gameplay. Unfortunately, what I played was a boring plate spinner management game without much substance that drags itself out.The first and primary issue is largely my fault, I came into this anticipating it to be a sort of colony game like Rimworld or similar, and this game is actually only like that on the surface. Instead, it's more akin to a management builder like Rollercoaster Tycoon or any of those where the building is in service to and very limited by the actual overall progression of the game. To that end, most of the cultists and followers you get are disposable by design and that's fine, that's actually in the spirit of a cult. But it lends itself to making a substantial part of the game just checking boxes and raising numbers on someone you actually don't care about and undermines the personal aspect of the title.Beyond that, the management itself is dull, shallow, and also drawn out to a massive degree. The numbers go up slowly, the requirements to unlock things keep needing larger numbers which take forever to achieve, and there's little to actually worry about. There's the notion of running out of any of the resources you need or possibly accruing too much negative attention in the form of 'heat,' but I never actually had any of these matter in the course of the game. Instead, even playing on the fastest speed for the overwhelming majority of the game it still claimed twelve to thirteen hours of my time and I would have left satisfied and happy if it was half of that.The cult aspect is also pretty undeveloped. The brief tutorial intro shows a neat compound and shows followers and cultists and also hints at possible different types or evolutions by joking about one of them mid-transformation into a fish person. However, it ends up that there's very little to the actual cult beyond what you see at first glance with nothing beneath. There are some silly rooms and you can dress your cult up in various different ways but beyond the thematic aspect of running a cult there's almost nothing to it.Honey, I Joined a Cult is, on the surface, a fantastic concept and a great themed game. But in execution it comes up woefully short and lacking, leaving you spinning plates you've already mastered for several hours after you've seen and experienced all there is to it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing the game for the last few days, and put in about 10ish hours or so. If you're looking for a full game, I'd recommend against buying right now. But there's not only great potential here, but the developers (a two man team, it sounds like) have done a good job at adding whimsy and humor to the game. The mechanics have been thought out pretty well, and as content gets added, I'd wager that this will be a pretty great game. I ran into a few minor bugs. When I was trying to put the foundation down for a new building, I'd extended it out and was about to let it build when the "worship" window popped up from the nightly worship thing. When I closed the window out, the foundation wasn't there, but the money it would have cost was gone. That's a hard bug to catch, so I wouldn't be surprised if that got through a QA shop for a larger team. Also, the maintenance system seems wonky on occasion. Sometimes a member won't automatically go fix a thing, ever, and you have to manually have someone do it. It can become a pain to manually direct that over and over again. I very much look forward to more content as this goes along, and would encourage folks out there to consider buying it to support the developer. And if it's not in the roadmap already, I'd encourage the developers to add a mod system so that we can add content on our own volition as well. Great job to the dev team, and keep up the good work.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting building and management game.In short, it's something similar to Prison Architect, however you manage a cult in the 1970s rather than a prison in the 1980s. You have a lot of customization options and a decently large area for your compound. You make money from your followers via therapy rooms, and your cultists act as staff members. You need to keep track of your cultists' needs, as if they get too low their mood goes down. If hunger gets too low they can even start taking damage. If a cultist's mood gets too low they can suffer a Mood Break, which basically means they go a bit looney and have to vent in the middle of the road for a few in-game hours. They can even leave entirely.There are also things to research and missions to go on. You do have to be mindful with the missions though: cultists can be arrested if things go poorly. The game does tell you the chance of success when you select someone to send though so you can easily avoid mission failure. Doing most missions generates heat however, with the only exception being the missions that remove heat. Heat does go down over time, too. Heat generally represents the amount of negative attention your cult is getting. If it gets too high, people will start protesting and you'll get police investigations. It has a cap of 1000 though, so I'm pretty sure you can afford to be a little risky.Also, construction. One of the main bits of the game. The mechanics are pretty much what you'd expect: you can build walls, foundations, doors, assign rooms, and put objects down. Things are built immediately too, no need to wait. One tip though: don't mess up. Removing objects doesn't give you a refund and demolishing walls and foundations costs money. It kinda makes sense realistically but its not what you'd expect in a video game. Also, there's no planning tool.Overall though, I would very much recommend this game if you're a fan of games like the previously mentioned Prison Architect. Even if it does somethings differently.Also, for my fellow Linux users: this game works great under Proton!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for June 2023, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before July 4th, 2023, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.All hail the great Chet GeePeeTee.Honey I Joined a cult is pretty funny.  It starts with a disgraced cult leader escaping getting plastic surgery, and thus forming a new cult, which you run.  You have the cultists that you can order around and followers who you bilk for money. You can order people around but the main part of the game is similar to Simcity, or Cities Skylines, build it and just wait for it to work out.  The game also has a tight tutorial but after that the game just lets players experience what feels most like a sandbox.Pick this up if you like Tycoon games. _childDocuments_.review: At it's core, Honey, I Joined a Cult seems to be a business management sim.  Collect employees, level them up, and put them in places where their talents will be most useful.  I appreciated that it's going for some more complexity here, and it seems to want to focus on a more manageable group of individuals but ... well, the whole cult thing is pretty much just the framing device.  Yeah, you are running a cult.  Whether or not the game is going to hold your attention I think depends on whether or not that joke is enough to carry it for you.  It reminded me more of Academia: School Simulator than Prison Architect, ie: more emphasis on a business simulation than intertwined systems interacting.My play time here was pretty short and it is in early access, but I don't know that I can blame all my concerns on it simply being unfinished.  I think they have their core loop pretty well finished: build rooms, research new ones. That's the problem: the reason I can't recommend is because a game about building a cult doesn't make me want to build a cult.  Your involvement outside of research and new buildings felt pretty minimal, and I guess I just didn't see what the payoff was expected to be.  I appreciated that it seemed to have an actual progression curve (many games seem to skip this), but disliked the slow pace, hands-off building, and arbitrary feeling it has.  Make rooms you need, wait for money to come in.Again, the joke is in the title.  I assume they'll tighten things up during early access but there is no guarantee that is the case, in which case I have to judge it on what it is and right now I think it's problems are deeper than missing content. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love the concept and design of this game, but the build mechanics and UI are insanely frustrating. (The only other delete function demolishes everything) You drag and drop to create a room, but if you try to add to an existing build with this method, it deletes all prior walls in the selected build area. Each room has a required size, but there is no easy way to locate this information while building. The size requirements also change over time as you unlock more features. Necessary features are locked behind achievements, creating a false sense of difficulty that leads to frustrating gameplay. There is no real "win" or goal scenario, only increased difficulty without much payout. All in all, I had high hopes for this game, and still have the occasional urge to play it again, but quickly quit as my frustration trying to simply play the game builds. _childDocuments_.review: This is a decent if flawed management game. It certainly gets some things right. The customisation of the cult is fun. There are an array of traits and quirks to help your cultists stand out. Information is readily accessible, and though the tables can get a bit busy, the tooltips help to clarify details. What really holds it back is a lack of polish and balance. As to the former, typos are rife and I experienced the occasional crash. The latter is more fundamental. It's strangely easy once you get your cult going. I had a single mood break, zero deaths, zero cultists choosing to leave and a handful of protests in my 18-hour game. However, there is a long mid-game grind as your leader slowly tries to gather points to unlock the finale. With my resources at max and no other real issues to deal with, I wound up spending hours with the game mostly running in the background.  The game does try to impart some artificial difficulty by adding random debuffs every once in a while. These were largely ignorable, but could be frustrating when a couple of them combined to be unavoidable - case in point penalties to mood both if a toilet was not private and if a room was of low prestige, the only solution to which is to build a bunch of lavish rooms consisting of a single toilet and a lot of decorative items, or cop a regular penalty.It is good enough for a ten or so hour run, but overstays its welcome through the grind. Worth joining for a while, but not worth drinking the Kool-Aid for.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw some of the reviews that complained about it being boring, but I assumed they just didn't like games in this genre.I never got to the point of figuring out if they were correct, because right when I started to reach a point where it could get interesting, I was hit with an "event" called Shifting Realities. Here's what it does: it rolls a die randomly and injures one of your cultists, and it keeps doing this for something like 72 hours. By the time I was a third of the way through the event, about 75% of my cult was sidelined--some with multiple injuries. I was STILL in the tutorial phase of the game when this crap hit me.There's no counter play, the event is exceptionally long, it's unpredictable, and it does tremendous damage to your progress because the injuries last SO long.So I can't even tell you if the game gets repetitive/boring, because this kind of game design meets a level of disrespect I don't think players should have to deal with. That's not fun--not even the sort of !!!FUN!!! you experience in games like Dwarf Fortress.Take a pass on this game. It will only frustrate you. I was so pissed I went and put the entire developer and publisher on ignore.
