_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so I originally reviewed Below Zero around Early Access 9, when I had 150 hours in the game. Now I have an extra 40, apparently. The Subnautica series is by far one of the most-played games I have in my library. So in the context of  here's my professional opinion:- The gameplay is the same with several differences, it will feel familiar but different which is good and you will experience a different order of progression -- although I wouldn't blame you if you thought it was too swift.- Story is really cool at parts, mediocre at others. Throughout early access it was clear that the story was a tough thing to undertake at UW but the end product is definitely solid. Uncover the spoiler tag for just a summary of how the story is laid out, it doesn't spoil the content but it will tell you how you will be experiencing it: - You will easily notice how this game doesn't have nearly as much content as the original, which is understandable as it originated as an expansion and still kind of is. There's a not-insignificant lack of creature variety and most of them don't hit as hard as they did in the original. You will not feel as alone or even as scared (if that's your thing; I'm definitely not a thalassophobe) as you would in the original. There will never be a murky body of water with distance roars in the distance; you will be able to see and hear everything that is happening around you at any time, and that is a bit disappointing.The world design is easily this game's biggest fault. The playable area in Below Zero is significantly smaller than the original (and they compensate for it by nerfing your seaglide, which is an absolute , and giving you inferior transport methods). The biomes are all cool and this game wields some of my favorites out of both games. But it will always stick out to you how much smaller this game is than the original. You will never have a moment where there is a big dark crevice a hundred meters below you which has you debating on whether it is worth it or not to go into it with your nerves wracked at the thought of getting jumped by some weird thing in the dark; as you look up and see that the sun is out despite the fact that  Never. I guess you could say that exploring is more straightforward in Below Zero. There are distractions at every corner in the original, but not here. I mean honestly, I can say there is SO MUCH of the original game's map I haven't seen yet, but I can definitely say I've seen everything in Below Zero. Credit where it's due, there's a much larger use of props to shape the world in Below Zero, which makes what  there a lot more pretty to look at. I just wish I could go one playthrough without some resources I want spawning in side of them...whatever, can't catch every little mistake.If going 1700 meters below sea level through a network of like three different perilous cave systems was one of the coolest parts of Subnautica for you, don't get too excited. You're hardly even going to hit 1000 meters here. And again, the biomes are cool, but you will 100% feel how much smaller the game is. This is still one of my biggest letdowns. It overall feels like they completely missed what made the world of Subnautica so interesting and cool.Still, it's not as bad as the land sections. Subnautica's motor system wasn't well-optimized for land, and it shows. Something just constantly feels off about it. The land areas are cramped and it feels like the devs really tried to make them feel open and interesting, but they just aren't fun to play in. Beyond story stuff and a few things you'll want to take care of, once you're done with them, you'll never need to or want to go back on land. I think the biggest reason for this is the very poor transition between land and sea gameplay. There's two main routes onto the main land area in the entire world, and one of them I straight up forgot even existed because they never tell you about it or give you any reason to even accidentally find it -- even though it's been there since like EA6 AT LEAST. Getting on land means leaving all of your stuff back on your sub or in a base somewhere before navigating into the area of land you actually care about. It isn't fluid at all and you will be holding out until you get to jump back in the water and start having fun again.Alright, that was a long point, but back to the list...- Tons of QoL additions and little new features, some of which have been backported to the original. Being able to blast Ram Ranch throughout your entire base on a jukebox is definitely a valid reason to play Below Zero.- On a vaguely related note, my absolute favorite part of Below Zero was definitely the music. Ben Prunty did an insane job and I highly recommend giving the soundtrack a listen even if you don't end up playing this.So after saying all that, you're probably expecting me to say I didn't like it, right? Well, not quite, honestly. Despite all of this, it's still Subnautica, and you can tell the devs really tried to make a worthy successor. They just...well they didn't do a great job of it, quite frankly. Undeniably, there's a ton of room for improvement here. But as a day-one early access player, I can tell you a lot of care went into the game and it shows. It may not stand up to the original, but it's a worthy successor, I'd say. Here's what I'll say. If you were a BIG FAN of the original, definitely play this one. It'll cure your fiending for more Subnautica for sure, add onto the lore dear to your heart, and I think you'll find it to be an overall fun experience which was worth the money. But if you were just like "yeah I liked it," I don't think you'll find Below Zero worthwhile. It doesn't have the same charm the original had that could've brought you in for good if you weren't already sold. But the Subnautica experience is solid, and this is no exception.Anyway thank you for reading my TED Talk.

_childDocuments_.review: Negative review for this because Steam has no ‘Nyeeehh’ option and most people won’t read any more positive ones. I get the feeling that Below Zero is meant to be more of a ‘spin-off’ or ‘expanded DLC’ rather than a direct sequel, but I will be making a lot of comparisons to the original as I feel it is similar enough to use as a fair frame-of-reference. I LOVE the original Subnautica and I want to support the developer so they continue to make nice things, but Below Zero has a LOT of flaws, bugs and questionable design choices that just pushed it over the edge, for me.The game looks and sounds great. Every underwater biome has its’ own look, feel and colour scheme that really help you tell every area apart. The arctic setting is utilized very effectively to create some beautiful setpieces as well as many of the perils an explorer would encounter within that environment. The first hour of gameplay was great. Swimming around discovering survival tech, scanning new creatures and daring myself to go deeper was the core of what made the original Subnautica great. However -Due to the well-deserved success of Subnautica 1, it seems like the devs wanted to expand on what made the original good. There’s a TON more voice-actors, characters and extra lore which, while impressive, I feel is detrimental to the overall experience. Subnautica 1 has a sense of disquieting isolation to it. By contrast, Below Zero is more character driven. You are constantly being spoken to in the forms of audiologs, other characters can just ‘call you up on the phone’ whenever something relevant happens, plus the main protagonist (Robin) just starts talking to herself sometimes. This is fine in-and-of itself, but for me, it eroded a lot of agency I had to the character. You aren’t alone in the original, but the experience is just lonely enough that when the Sea Empress reaches out and starts talking to you telepathically, it’s a genuinely terrifying moment that makes the player want to explore deeper.Instead of being listed in chronological timeline, every data/audio log is listed in your databank alphabetically by some arbitrary title. As such, if you lose track of what you were reading/listening because a bruteshark started munching on your leg, or another story-related voice clip started playing over the one you were listening to, it’s very easy to completely lose track of the story. It’s like reading a book where the chapters are in alphabetical title order, rather than by order in the narrative. I completely lost what I was supposed to be doing and had to refer to the wiki to work out what the game wanted me to do next.The story is delivered to the player in huge chunks, followed by vast spans of total silence when they aren’t finding anything. In my experience, the purpose of audio logs is to offer an alternative to big blocks of text. Audio logs allow the player to continue playing the game whilst absorbing the story. But when audio logs start playing over the top of one another, this completely defeats their purpose. As if there wasn’t enough water to drown in, now the game is trying to drown me in exposition! This is made doubley-frustrating when 90% of the audio logs you find are just pointless character fluff. However, I knew I’d discovered something important or relevant, because of all the overlapping dialogue being spoken! (Keep this in mind because I’ll come back to it later) There are two maps in-game. Both are difficult to follow and one looks like it was drawn on the back of a napkin with crayons. In Below Zero, it looks like the events are happening a few years after the first game, when Alt-Terra is beginning to expand its colony-building efforts. The game doesn’t have the excuse the original has, where you are a lone survivor stuck on a distant alien planet and the map-making and beacon setting is entirely up to you. Alt-Terra not-having mapped out at least SOME of the terrain above or below sea level for their multi-billion dollar off-world mining/colonialization expedition feels a bit unbelievable.The dry land exploration in this game is AWFUL. It feels like there’s a blizzard every 10 seconds and when this happens, you can’t see anything. Whilst this is realistic, it sucks in a game about exploring and finding things. This gets even worse at night when the world is dark but the snow fx are full-bright white. My entire screen looked like TV static and it made an otherwise gorgeous environment look absolutely terrible. It feels like the environment and the VFX teams had a massive fight during development and both were trying to sabotage each other’s work!When I first encountered the glacier where Robin’s sister works, there’s a large broken bridge that needs repairing at the entrance. What the game WANTED me to do was go over to the Phi robotics center, then notice the entrance to the Glacial Basin and start exploring there. And I would have done that, but 1, it was night, 2, there was a blizzard, 3, it wasn’t artificially lit up to indicate that there might be something of importance over there and 4, none of the voice-acting was indicating that area was important after I had explored the base. However, there was lots of dialogue about the bridge that needed repairing and my other companion character said something important was across the bridge. So that MUST be where the game wants me to go, right?Remember when I said the game indicates when you’re making progress with a barrage of voice-acting? I spent a good hour just bimbling around on the other side of the bridge after I had repaired it. Eventually I just got so frustrated with not being able to see or find anything that I up-ended my sea-truck on the lip of the glacier and did the Arctic Spires location in the Prawn Suit. None of the animals or leviathans pose ANY threat to you as they are only geared up to attack when you’re on the Snowfox, or on foot. In the prawn suit, you can just stomp right past them. Felt like I was ‘Seeing the puppet strings’ a little, at that point.This may be a very subjective opinion, but I didn’t think much of the creature designs for this game. I can’t quite put my finger on it, but I think it’s because all of the dangerous creatures have a similar ‘threat level’ to how they sound. That, and Leviathans will no-longer gobble you up in a single hit. This may have been frustrating to some players in the original, but I found to be a natural incentive to not swim over and hug one, when encountering it. Or get out of your vehicle and chasing it with a scanner. Once I realised most leviathans weren’t deadly in the slightest, all of my fear evaporated and they became more of an annoyance than a threat.I streamed a bit of the game and spent some time examining one of the hoop-fish. One of my friends commented “It’s amazing how many thousands of lightyears you are away from Earth and you’re still finding alien fish that have the faces of conventional Earth-fish.” This comment stuck with me as I feel there’s some truth to it. This is an alien world, I’d expect the way the creatures look, behave and hunt to be almost completely unrecognizable to anything that happens on Earth. I think it would be unfair to say that all the new creatures in this game are uncreative, but their designs might be a little ‘shallow’, it you’ll pardon the pun.I found Below Zero unintuitive and a far lesser experience to the first game, even with all the additional content. I can’t say if I recommend this one or not. Maybe play it if you’re burnt out on the first one and want more underwater survival horror in a different flavour? But don’t bother if you’re a fan of the same isolating tension and mute, contemplative narrative. This is where a hack reviewer would say something like “the amount of tension in this game is BELOW ZERO LOLOLOLOLOLO” but I ain’t doing that. Just play the original.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore the atmosphere of this game and the first one. Subnautica does the best job of any game I've played at creating a sense of deep mystery and wonder. I also love chill synth-y music, so I am also in love with the soundtrack of these games. If you are into sci-fi mystery stuff like The Expanse, these games are pretty much required playing for you. I would really love to see the creep-factor of these games amped up, though. I know many people already find these games scary, but I think the creatures are a bit too cartoon-y to get me there. I'd really love slightly more realistic graphics, and for dark places in the game to be REALLY dark, and for there to be some legitimate jump scares here and there. Still, fantastic game, and I can't wait for subnautica 3!

_childDocuments_.review: You should go buy this game right now and enjoy it. However, I'm giving it a negative review because there are some aspects of it that are super frustrating and if they aren't fixed, Sub 3 will be my last Subnautica.Now you could make the argument that everything except item 1 can be fixed by going to the internet and looking up the answers. But I would rather not play the game like that:1) Again, no amount of YouTube fixes this - The collision detection on land is horrible, borderline unusable. I have never spent more time in a game trying to get up, wait for it - stairs. Something as simple as a six inch step or tiny rock becomes an impenetrable barrier in this game. Underwater, this engine is fine, no complainants, but DEVS if you want to make more of the game above ground as you have here, you must fix this game engine or use a different one.2) There is no real map. Again I don't want to install a mod because I can't play the game without a mod. There are however terrible maps that you find in game but they are just rough simplifications of an area and really no use in the endless array of tunnels.To this point, commonalities on the internet for others (and I agree) seem to be:- The arctic basin. This is enormous and the provided map is a joke.- Inside the Mercury. Again, there's 15 ways into and out of every room and you're fighting a battle w/ oxygen. - The tunnel system near the pilot last known location. You can get lost here for hours and I don't mean in a good way, I mean in a frustrating way. And this is where a lot of the beef of the game takes place.And before you say = "just explore!" you'll find everywhere you NEED to explore is inhabited with giant fish that are constantly trying to eat your face off.  Figuring out - "Have I been to that tunnel that looks exactly like these other 19 tunnels before?" with a leviathan tethered to your head isn't really good game play.3) Story - I can't think of how to say any of this without going into spoilers but there are some really weak - "once you know piece of information A, you'll know to go to area B and do C.". It's a GOOD story line, but the gameplay aspects of it suck. At one part of the story, I indeed found out piece of information A, but figuring out where B was and what C to do was an enormous stretch. The first Subnautica I thought was excellent at "ok, now I have this thing so I can visit this area and do this thing that I couldn't before.". You will stand around scratching your head a lot in this game - "Now I have this thing and "..... nothing. At one point I literally had to go back and explore every area of the entire world map I was aware of before Alan gave me a new clue. This was not fun. Even a nudge in the right direction would have made it bearable.4) I'll be really vague here but it's technically a spoiler so skip this item if you don't want to know - Something really important you worked quite a lot for just freaking vanishes at one point in the game. This really pissed me off and I wasted a lot of time replacing it. (Other reviews will go into this if you want to know ahead of time)To sum up - I cannot stress how easy it is to get lost or go in circles in this game. Again, a quick visit to YouTube and you can lookup a map or watch some tutorial to can get anywhere quickly but again, I don't want to play the game like that.I sincerely hope Subnautica 3 (which I fully intend to buy) either gets JUST A BIT more linear or gives you a genuine map or just chills out on the endless tunnels that just circle back on themselves.Again, I never felt this lost in the original. Not sure what happened to the level design.Now All that said, it's still a great Subnautica game and you'll be glad you played it.

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the first game it pains me to not really recommend Below Zero. Whilst most of the core gameplay is preserved, the game does itself a major disservice with both the plot and the land sections.Your original motivation for the story is quite literally sidelined for another, creating a fairly jarring experience in knowing what you are trying to achieve and where to explore. Subnautica's original plot worked because the player had the primary goal of escaping the planet, and an understanding of what they needed to do - everything else is world building and set dressing. In this we're told to care about one thing, and then another, complete with sections where you circle the room waiting for a character to stop talking.The land sections sway between disorientating and dull, with exploration throwing you more resources than you can really carry, and leviathan encounters which are mostly just annoying to deal with when on the hoverbike. Subnautica's first title breaks up the excellent sea-based play with the odd island sections, whilst Below Zero demands you dedicate your time for one section. I think the developers were far too wed to their original vision of these areas.On top of other faults like exploration just not quite being as intricate and interesting, and less polish than I'd expect for the same engine and general gameplay, I just can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: The Emoji Movie is a 2017 American computer-animated science fiction comedy film directed by Tony Leondis, who wrote the script with Eric Siegel and Mike White. It stars the voices of T.J. Miller, James Corden, Anna Faris, Maya Rudolph, Steven Wright, Jennifer Coolidge, Christina Aguilera, Sofía Vergara, Sean Hayes, and Patrick Stewart. Based on emojis, the film centers on a multi-expressional Gene (Miller), who lives in a teenager's (Jake T. Austin) smartphone, having a journey to become a normal meh form like his parents (Wright and Coolidge).The Emoji Movie premiered on July 23, 2017 at the Regency Village Theatre and was theatrically released in the United States five days later. The movie was a commercial success after grossing $217 million worldwide, but was universally lambasted from critics, who criticized its script, humor, use of product placement, tone, voice performances, lack of originality, and plot, with negative comparisons and similarities to other animated films, especially Wreck-It Ralph (2012), The Lego Movie (2014) and Inside Out (2015). The Emoji Movie gained four awards at the 38th Golden Raspberry Awards for Worst Picture and three technical categories, being the first ever animated film to do so.

_childDocuments_.review: I would still absolutely recommend giving this a go if you're a Subnautica fan, but with a couple of [fairly large] caveats.1. The wide open ocean feeling of Subnautica is completely missing. At first, I looked around the snowy environments in  and thought they were pretty cool, and honestly, the game is absolutely a huge jump forward in environment and world design from Subnautica. The underwater environments and vegetation and all the new fish and animals are absolutely stunning in comparison to the prior installment.2. There's far too much time spent on terra firma.The overworld and landmasses are a huge part of the game in , which I feel completely disrupts the tone and central premise of Subnautica. In my just under 10 hours of gameplay, I'd say I easily spend 4 of those on land, in caves, running around. With my feet. In contrast, the  from Subnautica felt so interesting because it was the  piece of land in the game. It went wit the ''less is more'' approach, and it worked amazingly.  tries to spend far too much time on land and not enough underwater. It's a pity they didn't take the on-land sections and put them in underwater bases instead, because it would have fixed the biggest problem with this game, imo.As a final smaller point, I felt the balance for vehicle building was off. I spent what felt like the better part of an hour sourcing materials for the Seatruck's ''storage'' module, and ended up with less space than what I was already storing in the escape pod. It felt like I'd have to make two or maybe even three of them to have a viable moving base. It nearly felt like I was building the Cyclops for the cost of one module for the Seatruck, and the storage available was really slim.Full disclosure, I didn't finish the game. I would like to, but the game didn't grip me with the same drive to keep pushing forward that Subnautica did and I've since just trailed off and not gone back to it yet. Maybe when Subnautica 2 is properly announced I'll finish this off in the mean time.Having said all that, I think you'll probably still enjoy this if you're a Subnautica fan. Once you go in knowing that it was initially supposed to be a DLC, that it's far more narrative-driven and the map isn't nearly as vast as the ocean of Subnautica, you'll have appropriate expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: To preface this, Below Zero is good game, I feel, but it's not *as good* as the original Subnautica.My play time is a bit fragmented, I got really close to finishing it, but got stuck for whatever reason and quit without finishing it.  After getting back into the original game, I tried to give this another shot.There's a bunch of design decisions that are different from the original game, mostly because BZ is a standalone expansion rather than a full fledged sequel.  Some of these decisions were great, others I think stemmed from a misrepresentation of what players liked.Let's start with the good.  The developers are masters of creating underwater alien landscapes.  Glowing purple rocks that regularly "pop" into flame jets.  Lily pads that are attached to chunks of rock at their base.  Massive icebergs with caverns inside.  Deep underwater mushrooms that spit out spores that float in the water.  All of it feels alien and you'll always be amazed at the environment.The progression system does two things: it allows you to slowly acclimate to the environments around you while letting you grind out some resources for your next project, and there's always at least one or two resources that will force you to go out of your comfort zone to search for new materials.  For example, to make a certain material, you need mushrooms from a deep cave.  Your vehicle likely won't be able to reach all the way, so you'll be forced to do at least 100 meters or so outside the safety of your seateuck.  You'll also rarely feel like you need to grind.  The system from the OG Subnautica was changed so that each outcropping now has 1 special resource, or titanium (a general crafting resource for most things and base building) instead of having nodes carry 1 of 3 different resources that was completely random.As for the bad, the story just isn't as intriguing.  S1 had a story of a mysterious crash landing, and you slowly put the pieces together of what happened, and how you'll escape the alien planet.  You're also a silent protagonist, so you're alone with your thoughts and the occasional informational and sometimes snarky PDA.  SZ has a voice protagonist and eventually an alien in your head.  I don't hate this, but it creates a very different vibe than the original.  The game also gives you your objectives almost straight away (find 3 specific blueprints, craft them, then bring them to a certain place, and also find out what happened to your sister).  S1 didn't, you just survived and slowly got introduced to the gravity of the situation you were in.  The character animations for people are also just... Weird, like they couldn't do stop motion so they all feel like cheap canned animations from the early GameCube era.Land areas are too much and Subnauticas engine leaves a lot to be desired.  There are a few neat moments, but for the most part they just feel like a slog.Lastly, I don't like the Seateuck and it's modular design.  I get why the Cyclops from S1 wasn't included, because of the map size, but there's no point to getting all the Seateuck mods.  Half of them are useless (sleeping quarters and aquarium), and the more modules you add, the slower you get.  The Seamoth was a perfect early exploration vessel and there was no need to remove it from BZ.  The Prawn suit is back because I'm sure the fan base would've rioted if they scrapped it.Overall I think it's still a fine game and if you liked the exploraion of S1, you'll find something you liked in SBZ.

_childDocuments_.review: More of the same which is great if you like the original. _childDocuments_.name: Subnautica: Below Zero

_childDocuments_.review: Subnautica: Below Zero definitely has the Portal to Portal 2 treatment. It's a damn good game, yes, but it'll never be able to top the perfection of the first game. By all means, I'm not saying I hated the game, god, quite the opposite. I absolutely adored this game. It's a damn good follow up to a really great game, but of course, there are a few things I personally didn't enjoy about it. Subnautica always had me on edge, even when I knew what was coming, I still was on the edge of my seat. I still very vividly remember my first encounter with a Reaper. Though, honestly none of the various leviathans in Below Zero have left that big of an impact on me as the ones in the first. Certain leviathans you feel like you should worry about, just don't pack the punch to back their staggering size. I know Subnautica isn't a horror game. It simply simulates fear in your brain for two very common fears: fear of the ocean, as well as fear of the unknown. Both of these go hand-in-hand while exploring in either game. Is there a leviathan around the corner? Is there a story element over there? Can I find this material in the gorge? In the end of the day, you push forwards because of nature curiosity, which this game does not lack on. You're always wanting to push forwards, which could back up a comment I made earlier about the beauty of this game, for me, I was just constantly in awe. From swimming to new depths to walking the icy wastes of the surface, this game never fails to put you in awe, and often times I always found curiosity getting the better of me. The sheer size of the different set pieces in the various biomes just pull your attention so easily. I often felt like a spastic puppy, jumping from one toy to another. This game is packed full of little details that never fail to impress you. The size of the creatures felt gigantic, especially for being smaller than most in the original game. For me, appreciating these different aspects just took the edge off of situations, until some creature charges me to attempt to kill me. Speaking of killing me, the damage that the leviathans would output onto your subs I found were just pitiful. Now, the leviathans in this game aren't exactly the biggest (the smallest leviathan in this game is 15 meters smaller than the smallest in the first game), but I personally feel like they should probably do more than 10 to 30 damage to your sub. Personally, I'm not entirely complaining for the lack of blown-up subs, but I feel like the leviathans would be more threatening if they just packed more punch. Both Subnautica games could definitely be described as an art, story-driven game. I made story-telling connections between these games and another called Outer Wilds. You're free to do literally whatever you want. You don't need to do the story. If you want to just build a cool sea base, nothing is stopping you. It's that level of freedom the game gives you that I enjoy so much more over other story-driven games.
_childDocuments_.name: Subnautica: Below Zero

_childDocuments_.review: Subnautica Below Zero is a very different experience to the Original Subnautica. Truly I find subnautica to be more memorable then Below Zero, but this game is definitely much better in many aspects. As it has much better guidance to objectives, better building, and many quality of life changes I would love to see in subnautica. With the game also carrying a much better looking environment then Subnautica as well. With new creatures and beasts that I find amazing and terrifying. The main flaw I see is the lack of ways to play through the game. As I find less of good base locations compared to the vast ones of Subnautica. Making playing the game be a little repedative and less open then the vast map of Subnautica. Yet this does allow the travel time to be much more bearable. Though that can easily be fixed by a simple Cruise function for some vehicles. Truly I recommend this game, but I fully suggest playing the two as both are a wonderful and terrifying experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game, although I will admit it doesn't have the same feel as the original. If you liked the original, you'll still probably like this one, but it doesn't have that same feeling of being lost in an endless ocean. On the flip side, this one feels like it has a lot more story and characterization. The main new element being that there are more land-based areas for you to explore, with the addition of body temperature that you need to monitor to prevent your character from freezing. The Chelicerate doesn't quite have the same visceral fear factor that the Reaper leviathan had from the original, but the Ice Worm is a nice addition to the game. A bit expensive, I would pick this up on sale if you're interested.

_childDocuments_.review: Just as the original subnautica when it was in early acces, this game is waaaaay to green, exploring the sea monkey biome under the lilypads was so much fun, i think the game needs more areas like that, that really makes you feel like you are exploring a brand new world, besides that i felt that other areas where just empty part of the map, in the original game there was the other "survivors" distress calls that made you look for more places to go, i feel that maybe this needs something similar, also the place where there is a giant octopus thing was just astonishing... until i reached the literally empty part, im really waiting for another update, and of course, the end of the story involving marguerit.

_childDocuments_.review: Below Zero is a different flavor of subnautica than the original, but it is just as engaging in its own way. The survival crafting pipeline has changed somewhat in the particulars of how you advance and what's available, with some new tools to aid you. _childDocuments_.name: Subnautica: Below Zero

_childDocuments_.review: Although not as impactful as the original, Subnautica Below Zero has its good moments. If you were to separate this game from the original, it would probably be an absolute banger, but due to the high standards set for it, falls a little flat. The storyline was questionable at times, with essentially three going on at the same time, one of which, being the storyline you create yourself. There are some cool moments with the protagonist, but almost make it feel as though you're a spectator as opposed to the main character within the game. Area design wasn't my favourite, with most environments feeling repetitive & uninteresting, with another negative being the seemingly tiny map. The game overall wasn't remotely as terrifying as the original until you reach the final area of the game, with the rest of the upper areas all feeling like the 'safe shallows'.In all honestly this games saving grace was both its graphics & soundtrack, with both creating unique atmospheres. In conclusion, not the best game out there, but also not the worst. If by any chance you manage to grab the game when its on sale, go ahead. It allows for an enjoyable couple first hours, with the experience being tailored to newbies to the franchise, which allows you to progress onto exploration at a faster rate. Overall, 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: The first one is much better. This one feels incomplete. There's less to explore, the history is shorter and not able to adapt if you do things in an order not expected by the game designers. There are bugs, one of which made me have to kill myself in order to keep playing. All in all, it's an average game, which is a huge downgrade from the first game, which is simply fantastic.I also prefered the way the first game was designed where the character had no voice nor appearance, so anyone could feel that they were the person there, living that experience. This game chose the mainstream design of making up one character and sticking the player to it. It's not a bad experience, but, again, a far cry from the first installment.In conclusion, I would only recommend this game to people that loved the first game so much that even a lukewarm sequel would be fun enough. Which was my case. I enjoyed it, if only because it reminded me of the original game. Otherwise, go play the original Subnautica. It's way better!

_childDocuments_.review: Played both the original, and then Below Zero in experimental mode and now the full release. I absolutely love these games. Below Zero is a creative continuation of the first game that always keeps the player on their toes. Unlike the first game, Below Zero has much more character development, a welcome addition! Furthermore, get ready for more story, fun creatures, and exploration of new world elements... and also a cat named Potato. If you loved the original Subnautica, you'll likely appreciate the new mechanics, like the added temperature gauge, the ability to pin recipes, the jukebox, and many more creatures to interact with (baby Stalkers are my personal favorite). Overall, highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: ***UPDATE***Decided to go back and change my review to recommended after the full release.  Game still has the below flaws in my original review, but it has enough QoL improvements over the original game to nudge it up.  I still think the story is "meh" at best, but the gameplay is great and I find myself wanting to go back just for that reason alone.*****************This was a tough one to rate because the gameplay itself is very solid.  If you played Subnautica 1  you already know what to expect because this one is very similar.  Where it falls short is in the story itself.  With Subnautica 1 you crash landed on a mysterious planet, under mysterious circumstances.  There was exploration, survival, and danger in the deep.  With this one there is no mystery left, Alterra has already explored and cataloged the planet.  The voice acting isn't great, and the times that you find PDAs with recordings I often ask myself "Why am I even listening to this?".  They are random, like people sitting at a table playing a board game having a casual co-worker conversation.  Another one was a boss telling a trucker about stops he shouldn't be making while on company time.  Am I supposed to care about them...?  They have somehow turned what should be an exciting adventure on an alien planet into a boring/lifeless portrayal of what working at Alterra is like.  They were trying to make a fun video game right?

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Below Zero, but with a few moans and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. 7.5/10For myself, the original Subnautica set the bar extremely high! Mostly because it was a fresh new twist on survival and crafting, but also because of its more focused story and exploration... and, , the underwater setting.Subnautica is easily among my top 3 favourite games of all time, next to titles like SOMA and Jagged Alliance 2. Yes, I'm "old"! I've been playing PC games since the mid 90's. The fact Subnautica ends up so high in my favourite all-time games, next to incredible titles like Baldur's Gate, Fallout, X-Com, Half-Life, Myst, etc... says a whole lot about how Subnautica mesmerized me.75% of it, is mainly due to the underwater & horror themes. It plays with my natural, but not too extreme, thalassophobia. This game is among the first games that played with one of my natural fears. It kept the crafting aspect relatively basic and simple. I liked this, because I can't say I care too much about crafting games.Now, back to Below Zero. I enjoyed it, because it's a little more of Subnautica. Unfortunately, I found some of it little weaker. Discovery fell a little flat this time. That was mainly due to re-using many assets. I did not feel on a different planet or place. It felt like I was simply starting over in a much smaller and less intense Subnautica.My favourite aspect of Subnautica, felt slightly diluted by the amount of land you explore. Don't get me wrong,  everything is high quality, just like original Subnautica. But, the underwater world felt much smaller. They packed a good amount of content in it though. But, somehow, I felt less anticipation, or stress, as I was exploring. Sometimes size and scale plays an important role in the immersive aspect. Horror, especially with thalassophobia, can be impacted way more with size and scale.This, plus the very regular audio logs and way stronger story, meant I didn't feel as "alone" or lost in an alien world. I miss that feeling, because part of the fear of always going deeper, and exploring that dark crevice, also comes from a certain amount of loneliness and feeling alone.I thought the modular Seatruck was a move in the right direction, considering the map was smaller. But, the snowfox, I did not care for it very much. Maybe if all land was connected, I would have enjoyed it more?Voice actors all played their roles perfectly. The main voice actress, Kimberly Brooks, and Matthew Marsh (for AL-AN), were spot on! Very enjoyable when they had lines.I did enjoy the extra focus on the architects (especially the end of the game).As much as I enjoyed my time in Below Zero, I felt a longing to play original Subnautica instead. Below Zero felt more like Subnautica 1.5. That's okay though, Subnautica 2 was recently teased. All is good!Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm honestly sad I have to write this review, but here we go:This is simply not as good as Subnautica - not even close - and it all centers around the story.Without adding spoilers here, the story was either 1 of 3 things: Changed half-way through, not well thought out, or rushed to completion. _childDocuments_.review: The first game, one of the best games I've ever played. Takes place when you crash land on this planet and have to explore it to the depths of the planet to find a way off. All while not making contact and just having that feeling of being stranded. But at the same time of being scared, you cannot help but be fascinated by the planets environments, and as time goes on you develop a since of home and safety on the planet, making you never want to leave. Although despite not wanting to leave you always know, that you are utterly alone on the planet. That was the first game.This game starts off with you, a researcher going onto the planet (same as the first game) and looking to study and find out how your (sister I think) died. Once you land you are hit with the harshness of the planet which is completely different than the first game, which adds a new feeling to it. Its not completely new, you recognize some of the plants and animals in the evolved form. Despite it looking new, it doesn't feel new.The game has many of the same aspects as the first game, which its nice but not nice. especially when it comes to blueprints and building. It is the exact same, so you have to repeat what you did in the first game, it feeling more like a DLC than a Sequel in that aspect. I wish there would have been a new way of doing this, making it a new experience.Now, this is the thing that really pushed me away, is that you are not alone, and because of that you never feel scared like you did in the first game, you know there are other people who are there. Later in the game where you get a voice in your head, other than the PDA.Another thing is that there is no real drive to do the story, in the first game its like yea I want to get off this planet but I gotta do all this stuff so I can. This game has it so it force feeds you the story and you have to digest it even though you don't want it. Which makes it so eating more of the story is hard and doesn't feel like you have too do it. Although this game did get one thing right that I hope they build up upon deeply, and that is the jukebox. In this game, you can add a jukebox to your base which plays music you put into a folder on your computer, and it is amazing. Not just that you can listen to your music in game, but also that when you go outside of your base, you can hear the music outside and it being muffled by the water. This attention to detail makes the game so worth the money, and shows the creators care very much about this game and are just trying to create an apeal to a different type of people and making a different game. If they expand on the music system and make a way to have a full on stereo and sound system I would sink 100+ hours into it just for the satisfaction of hearing your music boom from outside of your base.Despite having its downfalls I would recommend this game, the developers are just trying to make a different game, just keep in mind that this game is not going to be like the first one where the bar was set so high. Also because of the jukebox.

_childDocuments_.review: A good game, but a bad sequel/spin-off.I spent 16 hours on my full playthrough of the game, and that's with me taking my time. I feel like I saw everything the game has to offer, which for an open-world survival game feels like a criminally short playtime.The biomes are very hit-or-miss, with the starter zones (Kelp caves and Twisty Bridges) the obviously more fleshed out areas, and every other biome feeling sparse or uninspired. This is very apparent with the Thermal Vents and Purple Vent biomes, which are right next to each other and one is very pretty to look at while the other feels unfinished and barren. The world map is very small yet much denser in terms of layout. I found myself getting lost on multiple occasions which is a good thing for this kind of game, though it was more due to everything looking so similar (or above-ground everything being hidden behind fog 24/7) rather than any gameplay challenges. However, the map feels TOO small. Biomes can be traversed entirely in less than 30 seconds and it barely takes three minutes to go from one side of the map to the other.Gameplay is very much the same as the original Subnautica, except with a new hot/cold mechanic that...is useless. The entire premise of the game is only used above-ground and is negated extremely easily. Not once did I suffer from the cold, I felt no need to invest in making a cold suit, a thermos, or any heat-related mechanics mainly because:The PRAWN suit removes any and all challenge this game could possibly offer. Can it reach the bottom of the map? Yes. Can it operate on land? Yes. Does it protect you from the cold? Yes. Can it deal damage to creatures and kill them? Yes. Is it more like an underwater tank with legs? Yes. Free oxygen supply wherever you are? Yes. And can it be made in the beginning of the game? Yes. This vehicle negates everything the game can possibly offer, and it's potentially faster than the Sea Truck due to what I presume is a bug. If you hold forward and either left or right you start to move diagonally at supersonic speeds, outrunning any creature chasing you and letting you traverse the whole map with ease. The inclusion of the PRAWN suit is game-breaking and feels more like a cheat than a fully implemented mechanic.I remember early in development when the devs said they weren't adding the Cyclops because it wouldn't fit in the environment they were making. They seemed to not realise that cramped environments allow the PRAWN suit to thrive. It was relegated to deep-sea and ocean-floor exploration in the base game because it couldn't propel itself through the water very well, meaning for open ocean travel you had other options. In Below Zero you don't need any options. I used the Sea Truck for an hour at most and then spent my whole game zipping around in the PRAWN. It objectively breaks the game flow, and speaking of flow-The story is just terrible. The nature of an open world game means that you can stumble upon story segments out of order, and this game is rampant with it. Crucial information to help you understand the story is hidden behind PDAs that you can easily overlook, while the blandest dialogue is given center-stage. Numerous times I'd arrive at a location yet miss a trigger for dialogue because I arrived from the "wrong" direction, only activating it once I left. The narrative follows two mysteries, yet one is just...ignored. You literally abandon that mission unresolved (the mission you start with: finding out what happened to your sister), no dialogue or revelation at the end, it's just ended in a PDA recording and then it's off to do the other thing. For all I know I could have missed the "proper" conclusion to that story path but again, an open world game means you can miss crucial pieces. I am aware this story had a MASSIVE rewrite mid-production and the result is just embarrassing.Despite these glaring flaws Below Zero is a fun game that I would recommend. It feels like a bitesized version of Subnautica that was never finished, and I can appreciate them trying a different storytelling approach. A lot of love and talent was poured into this and while the end result still feels like it's in Early Access there is fun to be had here. The base-building especially is the best part; expanding on what Subnautica did with the mechanic and making it feel truly unique. Honestly they should strongly consider retroactively adding the improvements made here to the original Subnautica. But then that's not a very good endorsement for a game if your biggest praise is "they should add this bit to another game instead".

_childDocuments_.review: SOLID DLC TO ONE OF THE GREATEST GAMES OF ALL TIMEIf you haven't played the original Subnautica, definitely play that first. It's not necessary story-wise, but this started life as DLC and it shows. It's great as a stand-alone DLC. It pales in comparison to the original in terms of size, impact, and sheer sense of exploration. The underwater sections are solid, if a little shallow (literally and figuratively) compared to the original. I did not enjoy the above-ground arctic maze at all. I also did not enjoy the Seatruck system as opposed to the more maneuverable Seamoth from the original and the customizable Cyclops full-sized submarine. It can be argued the Cyclops was OP, and it's certainly true that this DLC simply isn't big enough or deep enough to work with a mobile base.While I didn't feel the need to build as many bases as in the original, the base-building is one area this DLC really improves on. Less glitches and a lot more options to build and customize your base. I love my main base that I built. I just wish I had a reason to build out some more like I did in the original, since I love the base-building in this game. Still, huge thumbs up here on base-building improvements.One frustration that carries over from the original is the lack of a mapping function, although there is no in-game logic - quite the opposite - that the tech your character has access to couldn't provide you with a simple map of areas you've already discovered. Subnautica is one of my favorite games of all time. This stand-alone DLC doesn't quite measure up, but that still makes it well worth playing if you enjoyed the original. I just don't anticipate myself replaying it, as I feel like I've thoroughly explored what Below Zero has to offer. Still well worth the price of admission.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the perfect sequel to Subnautica! If you liked Subnautica then you WILL like this game.However, Below Zero has more of an emphasis on challenging land sections; while this is fun in concept (I LOVED some of the spoiler related things on the one land section), the mechanic of temperature really makes islands more of a chore than an adventure.It also feels like there's a lot less to do in this one than the first game. I can't tell if it's because I played the first one, or if it's just shorter, but either way I found myself completing this game a lot faster than the first game. It also feels like there's a lot less predators or even creatures in general, and some feel a little uninspired to be honest. Though, the ones that stand out in this game REALLY stand out, some of these creatures are so incredible in a terrifying way! It just feels like there aren't a lot of them.The story is marginally better, and there are some pretty cool story moments that I don't wanna spoil. I think the inclusion of a non-mute MC really helps it as well. Also, the biomes are incredibly unique and beautiful to look at, even if there are (once again) noticeably fewer biomes compared to Subnautica.TL;DR This is the perfect sequel to Subnautica, though it does feel more like DLC than an actual standalone game. Getting the chance to play more Subnautica is always a treat, and I can't wait to see what they do with a potential 3rd game in the series

_childDocuments_.review: This game is 'ok'. However, since this game is both a sequel to and retains "Subnautica" in it's name, it needs to meet or exceed what was done in the prior title. Due to the failure of this game to actually do so, I'm rating it negatively because there were too many bad changes made compared to the first Subnautica. I would not recommend this over the original. Below Zero set out to address some things that could've been a bit better in Subnautica, and the impressive part about this game is just how far off the mark it is. There are some minor improvements (fabricator doesn't require table coral to build, there's a way to deconstruct items), but the biggest changes, once of which was replacing the Seamoth and Cyclops with the Seatruck, ultimately feel dissatisfying. The Cyclops was a true mobile base. This is ultimately the most important thing that causes the change from Cyclops to the Seatruck to be a disappointment, but is FAR from the only issue with it. Here's a condensed version of why the Seatruck is bad: 1. High crafting cost2. Modules cannot be customized3. Modules slow down the speed of the seatruck. 4. No Playstyles or choicesHere's some more regarding #4: Out of the box, the cyclops has three engine speeds; slow, normal, fast, combined with a silent rigging mode, which greatly quietens the sound of the engine for an energy cost increase. What options do you have as the captain? well, you can try to sneak around some dangerous enemies, and you can try to speed past them, at the risk of potentially igniting a fire in the engines section of the sub. Oh, and, you also have the ability to shoot a torpedo, provided you loaded one, since it is included in the Cyclops from the start. The Seatruck can go one speed, and do none of the above. Upgrades make the difference more distinct, rather than closing the gap.  The Seatruck gains the electric blast, a temporary speed boost which is for a set duration and won't let you stop going forward until that duration is over there's also a 'horsepower upgrade'. Like the prior title, you effectively have 3 upgrade slots, because one of those slots needs the depth module so it doesn't break apart at lower depths. That's it. Those are all your options. The cyclops has multiple different options to pick from, beyond what can be slotted at once, allowing different playstyles and fun options. You can upgrade the decoy tube capacity (yes, it comes with the ability to launch torpedos out of the box, without any additonal modules, unlike a seatruck which completely lacks the capability at all), you can get a docking bay upgrade that repairs the vehicle in it, an engine efficiency module (power cost reduction), fire suppression system, shield, sonar, and a reactor upgrade that lets it charge from being in hot areas. The Cyclops default space fits everything that every Seatruck module has (except the teleporter module, which doesn't exist in the first Subnautica).The Cyclops may be slower and it may be bulkier, but the Seatruck is boring, limited, and uninspired. Honestly, there were so many things that could've been done to make the Seatruck a good and viable alternative, but my impression is that there was a shift to "we want the players to play this way", which is a failure in my eyes. There was a backup camera in Early Access, which was a good addition since it helped you in attaching the modules to the Seatruck, it got removed though. Another issue I found is that there was a shift to putting some sought after resources above the water level, on the surface. The issue with this is that the main draw of this game is that it takes place underwater. Below Zero adds a significant allocation of time to playing on land. This is bad. The end result feels like two parts of games smooshed together and linked with a plot. The above ground gameplay is not fun. It's tedious. There's a lot more I can say about this, but the most important part is that the game still has the main title "Subnautica" and does not stick to it.

In the first game, if you were stealthy enough, you could avoid confrontations with the leviathans.  In this game, a late game biome is so cramped you are guaranteed to be attacked multiple times as you attempt to explore it.The other main issue I had with the game is that key resources and blue prints proved way too difficult to find.  I eventually had to resort to guides to find these items, and the difficulty in accessing them was such that not even a written guide proved sufficient.  I had to watch YouTube videos showing exactly, step-by-step how to find these spots/resources.  The first game did a much better job of creating a flow in which you naturally came across locations, blueprints and resources organically.The story was fine, but I appreciated that the first game had a silent protagonist and more focused story as it let you feel you were in their shoes and were discovering things on your own vs. being pushed along by external forces.Graphics, voice acting, and moment-to-moment game play are all good and similar to the first game.I think Subnautica is one of the best games ever made, and I don't regret supporting the developer by purchasing this game.  I hope in their next game they gravitate back more to what made the first one great.

_childDocuments_.review: So, would I recommend Subnautica: Below Zero? The short answer? Yes. But would I say to go into the game fully expecting the same experience as the first game? That's a little more complicated. First, let's talk about what I did like. Nostalgia is the first thing that comes to mind when playing Below Zero. Throughout the game, it really did capture the environment and feel of the first game. The music and sound was just as engaging to me this time around. When I play any underwater game few come close to Subnautica's unique way of capturing atmosphere and immersing you into the game. Despite the map feeling noticeably smaller compared to the first game, it still left you with a lot of unique biomes to explore and reasons to dive deeper.But let's talk about that. Interestingly enough, I had a completely opposite outlook about the way this game does their biomes than my sister, who also played through the game before me. Which gives me an objective sense in which to view this. To me, Below Zero's biomes all seemed to feel more or less too similar looking to each other. Maybe it was the small map, but it seriously felt like I spent one second zipping through one and then I was suddenly in another. Kind of hard to be curious about what's around the corner when all it takes is a little peak and there it is.My sister loved the blended way the biomes made the ocean floor seem a bit more realistic to the real world. She argued that the vastly different biomes from the first game sort of took her out of the seamless experience. I disagree. And hey, to each their own.Next, the story. There are three-ish story lines in this game, all of which can be done at any time and in any order. Which can get... confusing. I ended up finishing one story line completely by accident, receiving a heartfelt emotional dialogue about closure before gathering crucial PDA's that would have given my play through a cohesive beginning, middle, and end to the protagonist's personal quest. The same happened to my sister. Luckily, the story itself was common sense (i.e shallow) enough that I could pretty much tell exactly where they were going with it from the beginning. So uh, take that as you will. The other story lines? Great. Loved them. Possibly the number one reason why I would play this game again and recommend it to anybody who loved the first game but is still on the fence about Below Zero.My final thoughts. If you liked the first game, give this a go. It was entertaining and met my expectations for any sequel title. The creatures in the game weren't as exciting, there weren't as many, I hardly felt scared to go deeper. If you want a more or less peaceful game with low risk, great. I prefer to play a little on the edge of my seat. Some of the story was a hit, some was a miss. I built a pretty awesome base and killed a few leviathans. All in all, I felt like this game could have been a DLC but understand why it was not. Go play it and experience it for yourself. I had no regrets.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you love Subnautica? If yes, then you'll probably like this game for the experience of it if nothing else. Still, for your own sake, go in with low expectations.  The last game was story-lite and world-heavy and it was a great combo. This game tries to go for more story but doesn't quite hit the mark. Perhaps because 'PDA recordings' was an alright method when it was incidental background stuff but just comes off as unsatisfying/lazy when you're on a world that *should* be populated - and isn't. There is no sense of urgency for any of your actions. There is little reason to build anything. The protagonist has a tendency to muse on the nature of humanity in a sort of 'first year university student' way and words cannot express how little I care about her thoughts on this topic.. There are a couple of good moments and a couple of potentially interesting characters but frankly, the game would have been better set from the perspective of the other sister - or the 'original Robin'. Sadly, the re-write really gives you a feeling that someone made the decision to just string a bunch of level designs together, sprinkle some PDAs over it and call it a day. Less than intended.Sequels always run the risk of being disappointing more because of your own expectations than anything else - but in this case, I can't recommenced the game overall as a stand-alone experience.

_childDocuments_.review: So, look. I put off buying this game for ages because so many reviews said it was too short, and not as immersive as the first game. After finishing the main story and now bumming around making my base pretty and finding all the fragments I want to find; I have to disagree. Here's why:1) A common complaint is that it is too short, and the world itself it too small. I think the smallness of the area actually makes for tighter game design in that the areas flow better into one another and there is more emphasis on cave diving rather than trawling the surface. I did not even realise for the first ten hours that you could actually access the giant ship and thought it was just a piece of environmental storytelling. Finding that first crack in the hull that was accessible made a light-bulb go off in my brain.2) As for the story being too short (as in you can finish it within 30 hours, if like me, you stubbornly refuse to look up guides and just kind of fart about looking at things and for things for ages before picking up the thread of the story again, possibly by chance.) the story did not *feel* short. It felt as enthralling and as exciting as when I first played the first game. I felt that same sense of all encompassing fear of the depths below my feet and I felt as much if not *more* intrigue because of the main stories. (MM, the woman that you are...)3) At the time of this review I have not found a cure, but I have completed the main story missions. I felt it was genuinely a really good story—so much so that for the entire ending I was smiling super wide (even while expecting [redacted] to suddenly turn out to be evil). The fact that the devs and writers managed to tell this story in such a length of time—without drops in quality and without so much endless back and forth (I think) shows how much they have improved from the first game. Squeezing as much story (and multiple through-lines through the characters) into the environment, and making it so interesting that you want to keep playing, shows skill and talent. Sometimes less is more.4) The maps made navigation fun! I really appreciated that inclusion. I will forever be kicking myself that I missed a certain suit super early on and didn't find it till I had already suffered through the Arctic Spires (my own fault)5) The voiced character (and having all of the character logs scripted) made the story feel very real. I saw a few reviews claiming that the voiced character was annoying and a mute one is better, something something 'forced diversity' or some other b.s. I have to vehemently disagree.I felt connection to the character and the loss of her sister. I felt the drive to discover what happened and the subsequent anger and joy that the 'faceless' characters of the transgov corp were made real and had their own intrinsic motivations. I could feel the frustration of the employees towards their bosses and the covert threats by the bosses when employees did not adhere to stringent policies. I think that is awesome world-building, and more fleshed out than the first game. I loved [redacted] and especially the design towards the end, you will know what I mean when you see it. I really enjoyed reading all of the notes from the PDA — which I do not normally do — but because I could tell that each fish and each machine were developed with purpose and care I devoured the information.6) Sea monkeys. Annoyingest little buggers out there. Then, something changes and suddenly they're one of the most useful creatures. This dynamic change is absolutely awesome, shows real attention to detail and allows the MC to feel like they have an impact on the environment besides killing things and being the big hero (which thematically... you could argue actually Robin doesn't want to do anything besides avenge her sister/find out what happened, get [redacted] out of her [redacted], which is pretty human. She's not there to save anyone, she's kind of painted as a bit selfish. Which is an interesting character trait.) I think the ambiguity of the ending is necessary, though to our narratively inclined monkey brains probably a bit frustrating.7) So many more base design options, and earlier access to recipes than in the first game. The devs kind of just chuck everything at you at once (for the most part) pretty early on so you can set to customising your base much faster.8) There are so many throwbacks to Subnautica that it's almost a nostalgia trip.9) Jukebox. Build it. Vibe with the music, most of the songs are actually really cool!Now for some of the negatives:1) Navigation in the overland portions was a nightmare. I got lost and died many times. I wish more emphasis had been placed on using the snowfox as a travel mechanism because once you can build it, overland travel becomes marginally easier.2) Spy Pengling control is a bit janky, which I can guess is on purpose but it made contorting my fingers to drive properly a bit of a problem.3)I 'lost' the main story a lot. Like, A LOT. Having to trawl through 50 days worth of voice lines in order to find one sentence that helps you pinpoint what to do was a little bit frustrating. But that is the price of exploration games, I suppose!4) Sea truck docking had collision issues with the entrance. Not a big one, but mildly annoying.Hey, if you read this all the way through. Thanks. If you liked Subnautica, you'll like this one too. It feels tighter, more cohesive, and has as much variety in animals and plant life as the first game. 8/10 I enjoyed this game.

_childDocuments_.review: "Subnautica: Below Zero" might have been better left as a frostbitten fantasy, lurking in the shadows of its brilliant predecessor. Far from being the chilling sequel we hoped for, it turned out to be chilling in all the wrong ways, leaving much to be desired in terms of both scope and thrill.First off, the decision to make the protagonist speak was an unexpected—and unwelcome—change. This move stripped away much of the eerie, silent horror of the original, replacing it with unnecessary chatter that felt more intrusive than immersive. The beauty of the first game was the isolation, the haunting solitude that amplified every sound and shadow. "Below Zero" lost that, opting instead for a narrative that feels less like a survival horror and more like a chatty walk in the park.And speaking of parks, let's talk about the map. Calling it 'compact' would be generous. It felt more restrictive than explorative, with boundaries that seemed to close in rather than expand horizons. The thrill of discovering vast, unknown depths was replaced by the monotony of seeing the same icy walls, over and over.Then, there's the building—a feature that should add depth but instead adds drudgery. "Below Zero" seems to believe that more building equals more fun, but this is a misstep. It felt less like an enhancement and more like busywork padded out to mask the game's thinner content and smaller scale.The creatures, few of which truly stand out, swing wildly between being deadly menaces and mere nuisances, lacking the memorable terror instilled by their counterparts in the first game. They seem to be thrown in as an afterthought, a way to justify the 'survival' part of this survival game without truly integrating into the core experience. In conclusion, "Subnautica: Below Zero" feels like a missed opportunity, a sequel that could have built on the eerie, captivating foundation of the original but chose instead to tread water in safer, shallower waters. It's a game that, while it may offer brief moments of entertainment, ultimately leaves you cold—yearning for the depth, mystery, and genuine thrill that made the first game a standout. In this icy sequel, there's no need to dive deep, both literally and figuratively, because frankly, there's not much worth discovering beneath the surface. Wait, it has more building??!!

_childDocuments_.review: A daring allegory to international migration crisis. Uninvited and unwanted, our strong black female protagonist intrudes on a foreign planet in search of her missing sister. Immediately upon arrival her path of destruction begins. Completely insatiable, strong black female character will consume uncountable number of living beings, murder quite a few polar bears(a metaphor for rising carbon footprint of black migrants seeking better consumer life) and abuse modern technology to completely deplete her immediate area of all natural resources. In this she is aided by fully automated systems created by people more capable than her, severing her ties to the nature and making the state of consuming effortless and enjoyable. It's beautiful how well this brings to attention the rising problem of obesity and food insecurity in black communities. But not everything is so easy for our strong female black character. At some point of the story her mind is infected by alien voice, telling her what to do and putting intrusive map markers on her pure dark eyes. What is it if not a metaphor for destructive brainwashing of globalist mass media causing black migrants to stray from the righteous path of their religion and culture? And what about her sister you ask? We learn that she was a terrorist and brought death to working people, destruction of private property and even prevented humanity from advancing. Do I really need to clarify what this alludes to? My heart goes out to the victims and their families. Ending drives the point further by transporting our strong black protagonist into even more foreign and unsuitable for her environment of advanced technological beings. How much evil and destruction will she bring? How much handouts will she be able to receive? This and more in Subnautica: Beyond  Replacement. Honestly, I am scared for dev team future. Slinging raw truths like this, it requires courage and artistic integrity. Next thing you know the entire team is fired and replaced by objectively worse workers whose only qualification is sanitized conformist twitter profile. And no one wants something like that to happen.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Subnautica, so I have been eagerly awaiting the second installment and the devs did not disappoint... mostly.Much of ♥♥♥♥ I loved about the original game is back, as well as much of what annoyed me. The story is a light presence in the game, coming mostly in a series of audio logs that you can listen to intently, passively, or in many cases not at all. Some would argue that it's best to either require listening to the audio logs to move the plot or leave them out entirely, but that's like serving you a basket of wings either with no hot sauce at all or just making you drink the hot sauce straight before you can eat the wings. Neither of these options is appealing.The crafting mechanics and the way each new set of blueprints opens up your travel range so you can gradually explore further and further is as fun as ever and the base building is fantastic. In the first game I never found a use for grow beds, but with many of the crafting recipes changed to require rarer and more exotic flora components, as well as new food crafting options the benefits of growing plants indoors and outdoors are huge.Alas, the bugginess is back as well. Texture and object pop-in is as prevalent as ever. This is no deal breaker, but does spoil the immersion just a bit. Clipping is still a problem, though more of a funny problem than an annoying one. It's still hilarious to walk around your base and suddenly see a fish just swimming around in mid-air. And vehicles can be a bit buggy, especially when entering or exiting. The Seatruck, and in particular when it has attached modules, seems to have no consistency. Sometimes I'll enter through the rear compartment of an attached module and find myself instantly in the driver's seat. Sometimes I'll press exit while driving and will just stand up but will still be inside the Seatruck. Other times I exit immediately. All-in-all, though, these are minor problems I can live with.The Good:-Crafting and base building mechanics are top notch-Visually stunning world with more varied environments than the 1st game-Tweaks to food crafting now reward cultivating a variety of food sources, making for more varied play-Engaging story that doesn't beat you over the head with expositionThe Bad:-Bugs!Verdict: This game could have afforded to address some of the bugs of the old game, but nevertheless it is as fun and engaging as the first and there was not one step backward. Everything about Below Zero was an improvement over Subnautica or is at least just as good.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: I like the game, it still has a lot of the charm of the original, but it feels like a DLC that was forced* to be a full game. A lot of the game is empty and there are a lot of problems, just like the original in the early days. The surface segments are probably the most egregious offenders, boring trudges through uninteresting landscapes populated with annoying hostiles. Due to the lacking AI, you can circle around most enemies to kill them without taking a point of damage. With better enemy AI and some trimming in the recycled assets department, I think even the surface could be a really fun zone. I think the closest this game came to the original in terms of the zones having a unique and really "subnautica" feel was with the lillypads and connecting areas, specifically the crystals and the red cotton plant zone under the floating island. The vents were really disappointing imo, and the purple vents just felt weird and out of place, a visual gimmick more than a cool function that you could interact with meaningfully. I think it was a really good decision in the first game to make zones based around special, late-game materials (getting benzene from the blood kelp, lithium from mushroom forest) and giving them some unique flora and fauna.*I say "forced" because this game kinda feels like someone had a cool idea for an extra area in the original game, just worldbuilding for 4546B, which spawned the idea for dlc, but there just wasn't enough content to stretch it out to a full game. This is just speculation though based solely on how the game looks and feels at this point in time. I have faith in the dev team to take user crits and adjust.Recommendation: Buy the game, there is enough in it thats worthwhile, and if you just want to feel a bit more of the first game, you could just skip the surface section, you dont need to go through it to get to see any of the underwater zones, plus they have a lot of unused space and weird empty sections (looking at you eye jelly zone) so there is def more to come.

_childDocuments_.review: Subnautica: Below Zero is a spin-off of the Subnautica franchise.  It's the second installment in the series but not the one labeled "2."  Subnautica itself is an open world survival crafting game.  There is a lengthy story but perhaps the primary draw is the beautiful environments -- many flora and fauna grow bright from most every corner of the game.  It's a visual experience.Overall though, its hard to find good things about this specific installment.  In many ways, its predecessor does everything better.  There are more overland activities which have their own charm but for a game about being underwater, the overland activities do not bring much you haven't seen elsewhere.I think the most disappointing aspect about this is that they messed up the themes.  In the original installment, the main character frequently finds audio tapes of former crew members.  At first they seem reminiscient of what might be called "home."  It contrasts with the deadly aspects of the early game.  These elements and others bring forth this idea of life and living.  The physical environment beautiful but deadly --  home: safe but far away.  Over time you collect more audio tapes revealing your former crew mates are vapid and self-absorbed.  It many ways it paints "home" as a dystopia.  Meanwhile the deadly environment becomes less so as you get more gear and learn how to survive.  You even start to find other's former homes where they seemed to have made a life and home there.  It switches this idea of what living is -- not unlike the desire of many urbanites to just go and live alone in the forest, it's almost like it would be better to stay in that aquatic world than it is to go home.  It's really quite beautiful.  However, this installment portrays the main character as basically one of those vapid, self-absorbed folk.  She seems entirely unimpressed by the setting and is just generally *really* unlikable.  It's such an odd failure by the developers that it almost makes one wonder if they even understood what made their first game good.It's hard to think this one worth your time for any reason.  Perhaps if the first installment didn't scratch the itch but Subnautica 2 is coming out in 2025.  Who knows, maybe that will be a return to form.
